Chaukhamba Sanskrit Pratishthan, 1985. Section on Technical Designations (Saṃjñāprakaraṇam) 1: Having paid homage to the Three Sages and having reflected upon their teachings, [I compose this work].
This Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudī is being composed.

Thus, these Māheśvara-sūtras serve the purpose of designating the phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *la*. The vowel *a* is present in this [final] *la* sūtra as well; in the case of the consonants beginning with *ha*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation.
SK 1: *hal antyam* (A 1.3.3). In the rule beginning with *hal*, the term "final" (*antya*) should be supplied.
SK 2: *ādir antyena* (A 1.1.71).

"The first [consonant], joined with the final one, shall be the designation (saṃjñā) for itself and for those situated in between. Thus, regarding the designation *hal*: "The final *hal* in an original enunciation (*upadeśa*) shall be designated as *it*. An original enunciation is the initial pronunciation. Thereafter, the designations such as *aṇ*, *añ*, and so forth, are established.

SK 3: *upadeśe ’j anunāsika it* (A 1.3.2). In the original instruction (*upadeśa*), a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) that is not a consonant (*aj*) shall be designated by the technical term *it*. The followers of Pāṇini acknowledge the nasalization [of certain vowels] as a formal convention (*pratijñā*). The letter *r*, when pronounced together with the vowel *a* found in the *laṇ* sūtra, is the designation for both *r* and *l*. In the *pratyāhāra*s, those [vowels] marked with the *it* designation are not included, because of the indicative mention (*nirdeśa*) in rules such as *anunāsika*. For in this case, no operation pertaining to a vowel (*ackārya*) is observed when followed by the letter *k*. Those designations formed by the rule *ādir antyena* (A 1.1.71) are designated by the term *pratyāhāra*.
Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.27: *ūkālo ’jjhrasvadīrghaplutaḥ*.

The sounds *u*, *ū*, and *ū3* are denoted by the term *vaḥ*. That vowel (*ac*) whose duration is like the duration of these [sounds] shall, respectively, receive the technical names *hrasva* (short), *dīrgha* (long), and *pluta* (protracted). Each of these is further divided into three types according to the distinctions of *udātta* (high-pitched) and so forth.
SK 5: *uccair udāttaḥ* (A 1.2.29).
Among the places of articulation such as the palate, which consist of parts, that which is produced in the upper part shall be designated as *udātta* (high-pitched). For example: *ā ye*.
SK 6: *nīcair anudāttaḥ* (A 1.2.30) is clear. [Example: *arvāṅ*.
SK 7: *samāhāraḥ svaritaḥ* (A 1.2.31).
That vowel (*ac*) in which both the properties of being acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) are combined shall be designated as *svarita*.
SK 8: *tasyādita udāttam ardhahrasvam* (A 1.2.32). Of that [svarita], the first half-mora (*ardhahrasva*) is acute.

The mention of "short" (*hrasva*) is not restrictive. It should be understood that the first half of a *svarita* vowel is acute (*udātta*), while the latter half is, by default, grave (*anudātta*). When this [acute half] is followed by an acute or a *svarita*, its [acute] pronunciation is clearly heard; otherwise, however, the perception of an acute tone is well-known in the *Prātiśākhyas*. For example, in cases such as *kva vo 'śvāḥ*, *rathānāṃ na ye rāḥ*, and *śatacakraṃ yo hyaḥ*, there is an acute accent. In *agnim īḷe* and similar instances, there is the perception of an acute tone.
Although it is thus ninefold, each of these is further divided into two types based on whether it is nasalized (*anunāsika*) or non-nasalized (*ananunāsika*).

SK 9: *mukhanāsikāvacano 'nunāsikaḥ* (A 1.1.8). A phoneme (*varṇa*) articulated through both the mouth and the nose shall bear the technical designation *anunāsika* (nasalized). Thus it is: for each of the phonemes *a*, *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*, there are eighteen varieties; for the phoneme *ḷ*, there are twelve, because it lacks long forms; and for the *ec* vowels (*e*, *o*, *ai*, *au*), there are also twelve, because they lack short forms.

SK 10: *Tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ sarvaṇam* (A 1.1.9). That which has the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) and internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) as another shall be designated as *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to one another. The throat (*kaṇṭha*) is the [place] for *a*, *kuh*-class consonants (*k, kh, g, gh, ṅ*), and the *visarjanīya*. The palate (*tālu*) is for *i*, *cu*-class consonants (*c, ch, j, jh, ñ*), and *ś*. The head (*mūrdhan*) is for *ṛ*, *ṭu*-class consonants (*ṭ, ṭh, ḍ, ḍh, ṇ*), and *ṣ*. The teeth (*danta*) are for *ḷ*, *tu*-class consonants (*t, th, d, dh, n*), and *s*. The lips (*oṣṭha*) are for *u*, *pu*-class consonants (*p, ph, b, bh, m*), and the *upadhmānīya*. The nose (*nāsikā*) is also [the place] for *j*, *maṅ*-class consonants (*m, y, r, l, v*), and *ṅ*. For *e* and *ai*, it is the throat and palate (*kaṇṭhatālu*). For *o* and *au*, it is the throat and lips (*kaṇṭhoṣṭha*). For the letter *v*, it is the teeth and lips (*dantoṣṭha*). For the *jihvāmūlīya*, it is the root of the tongue (*jihvāmūla*).

The nose is the place of articulation for the *anusvāra*. Thus are the places of articulation (*sthāna*). Effort (*yatna*) is twofold: internal and external. The former is fourfold, distinguished as *spṛṣṭa* (contact), *īṣatspṛṣṭa* (slight contact), *vivṛta* (open), and *saṃvṛta* (contracted). Among these, the effort of contact (*spṛṣṭa*) belongs to the *sparśa* (stop) consonants; slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*) belongs to the semivowels (*antasthā*); openness (*vivṛta*) belongs to the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels (*svara*); and contraction (*saṃvṛta*) occurs in the practical usage of short *a*-sounds. However, in the state of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), it is indeed open (*vivṛta*). And this has been indicated by the author of the Sūtras; for instance: [The following verse: "By the very fact that [the sūtra] prescribes the term 'open' (*vivṛta*) with respect to vowels, it is understood that the short *a* is contracted (*saṃvṛta*). Thus it is established.

Having restated what was explained by the rule *SK 11 a a* (*A 8.4.68*), the present [rule] prescribes the closed (*saṃvṛta*) vowel. And because this [closed vowel] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the entire *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, it indeed possesses the state of being open (*vivṛtatva*) from the perspective of the grammatical system. Thus, the Sūtra states:

SK 12: *pūrvatrāsiddham* (A 8.2.1). This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*). By this rule, the three chapters (*tripādī*) are not established with respect to the seven chapters and a quarter (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*); furthermore, within the three chapters themselves, a subsequent rule (*para-śāstra*) shall be considered unestablished with respect to a preceding one. External effort (*bāhya-prayatna*), however, is of eleven kinds: open (*vivāra*), closed (*saṃvāra*), breath (*śvāsa*), resonance (*nāda*), voiced (*ghoṣa*), voiceless (*aghoṣa*), weak aspiration (*alpaprāṇa*), strong aspiration (*mahāprāṇa*), acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*). The *yamas* following the *khay* (the five *cavarga* stops), the *svay* (the five *tavarga* stops), *ka*, *pa*, the *visarga*, and the *śar* (the sibilants and *ha*)—these have breath as their secondary effort (*anupradāna*), are voiceless, and involve an open articulation (*vivṛṇvate*).

Other voiced sounds (*ghoṣāḥ*) are produced in the throat and possess resonance (*nādabhāgin*); they are the non-paired members of the classes (*varga*), the semivowels (*yama*), and the *yaṇ* sounds, which are known as having little vitality (*alpāsava*). In the Prātiśākhya, it is well known that within each class (*varga*), when the fifth letter follows, there is an intermediate sound called *yama* (twin) that resembles its predecessor. For example: *palikknīḥ*, *cakhkhnatuḥ*, *agnniḥ*, and *ghaghnanti*. In these cases, following the letters *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *gha* respectively, there are *yamas* that are identical to them.

Among these, the first and second letters of the classes (*vargāḥ*), as well as their corresponding *yamas*, the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya*, the *visarga*, and the letters *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*—these possess wide opening (*vivāraḥ*), aspiration (*śvāsaḥ*), and lack of voicing (*aghoṣaḥ*). For the others, however, there is narrow opening (*saṃvāraḥ*), resonance (*nādaḥ*), and voicing (*ghoṣaḥ*). Among the classes, the first, third, and fifth letters, as well as the first and third *yamas* and the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*, are "unaspirated" (*alpaprāṇāḥ*); the meaning is that the others are "aspirated" (*mahāprāṇāḥ*).

Although external efforts (*bāhyaprayatna*) are not utilized in the definition of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇasaṃjñā*), it should be understood that they will nevertheless be employed in the examination of "nearness" (*āntaratamya*). The consonants from *ka* to *ma* are the stops (*sparśa*). *Ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are the semivowels (*antasthā*). *Śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* are the sibilants (*ūṣman*). The vowels (*ac*) are the tones (*svara*). The sounds preceding *ka* and *pa*—namely, those resembling the half-*visarga*—are the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya*. The *anusvāra* and *visarga* follow the vowels as *aṃ* and *aḥ*. This is the analysis of places of articulation (*sthāna*) and efforts (*prayatna*).

The mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) of the *ṛ* and *ḷ* sounds should be stated. [This is necessary] because, otherwise, mutual homogeneity would result between *a* and *ha*, *i* and *śa*, *ṛ* and *ṣa*, and *ḷ* and *sa*.

SK 13 *nājjhalau* (A 1.1.10): An *ac* vowel accompanied by the letter *ā* and a *hal* consonant—these two are not mutual *savarṇa* (homogeneous) sounds. Therefore, in cases such as *dadhī* followed by *harati*, *śītalam*, *ṣaṣṭham*, or *sāndram*, the substitution of *yaṇ* and so forth does not occur. Otherwise, by the force of the rule governing the inclusion of sounds (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*), the status of being an *ac* vowel would apply to the letters *ha* and others, just as it does to the long vowels and so on. For instance: [text continues]

SK 14: *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (A 1.1.69). That which is understood (*pratīyate*) as being prescribed (*vidhīyate*) is a *pratyaya*. An *aṇ* that is not being prescribed, as well as those marked with *u* (*udit*), shall be the technical term (*saṃjñā*) for their homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sounds. Here, *aṇ* refers to the *a* ending in the *ṇ* of *praṇ* (i.e., *aṇ* = *a, i, u*). *Ku, cu, ṭu, tu,* and *pu* are these *udit* markers. Thus, for example, *a* is the term for eighteen sounds; likewise for *i* and *u*; *ṛ* is the term for thirty; and the same applies to *ḷ*. *E*, *o*, *ai*, and *au* are each the terms for twelve. However, there is no mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between *e* and *ai*, nor between *o* and *au*, because of the force of the commencement of the rule *ai-au-c* (Pāṇini 1.1.2).

Therefore, one should not object that there would thus be twenty-four designations [for the vowels]. Although the prohibition *nājjhalau* applies only to those [sounds] belonging to the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*), nevertheless, the vowel *a* is not a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sound with the letter *h*, because the vowel *a* is also [merely] superimposed (*praśliṣṭa*) upon it. Consequently, in the word *viśvapābhiḥ*, the substitution of *ḍha* by rule *ho ḍhaḥ* does not occur. The letters *ya*, *va*, and *la* are of two kinds, distinguished as nasal (*anunāsika*) and non-nasal (*ananunāsika*). Therefore, those non-nasal ones serve as the designation for each pair [of their respective nasal counterparts].

SK 15: *taparas tatkālasya* (A 1.1.70). That which has *t* followed by *a* (*taḥ paraḥ*) is called *tapara*; such a term shall be the designation for that which has the same duration as its own pronunciation. Therefore, *at*, *it*, and so forth, are designations for six [sounds] each; *ṛt* is the designation for twelve.
SK 16: *vṛddhir ādaic* (A 1.1.1).
The sounds *ā*, *ai*, and *au* (*ādaic*) shall bear the technical designation *vṛddhi*.
SK 17: *adeṅ guṇaḥ* (A 1.1.2). The sounds *a*, *e*, and *o* (*adeṅ*) shall bear the technical designation *guṇa*.
And the vowels a, e, and o shall have the designation "guṇa."
SK 18: *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* (A 1.3.1).
Those beginning with *bhū* that denote action shall be designated as verbal roots (*dhātu*).
SK 19: Under the governing rule *pragṛhyam īśvarān nipātāḥ* (A 1.4.56);
SK 20: *cādayo 'sattve* (A 1.4.57).
And particles such as *ca* and others, when they do not denote a substance, shall be designated as *nipāta*.
SK 21: *prādayaḥ* (A 1.4.58).
Likewise, the particles beginning with *pra* are [indeclinables] when they do not denote a substance (*adravyārtha*).

SK 22: *upasargāḥ kriyāyoge* (A 1.4.59). SK 23: *gatiś ca* (A 1.4.60). When used in connection with a verbal action (*kriyāyoga*), words beginning with *pra* (the *prādayaḥ*) shall bear the technical designation of *upasarga* (preverb) and the designation of *gati* (indeclinable particle). The *prādayaḥ* are as follows: *pra*, *parā*, *apa*, *sam*, *anu*, *ava*, *nis*, *nir*, *dus*, *dur*, *vi*, *āṅ*, *ni*, *adhi*, *api*, *ati*, *su*, *ud*, *abhi*, *prati*, *pari*, *upa*. These are the *prādayaḥ*.
SK 24: *na vā* is the term *vibhāṣā* (A 1.1.44); it shall be the technical designation for both negation and option.
SK 25: *Svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasyāśabdasaṃjñā* (A 1.1.68).
In the science of grammar, a word's own form (*svarūpa*) is the thing designated (*saṃjñin*), except for those words which are technical designations (*saṃjñā*).

SK 26: That which is a qualifier of that which ends in a specific element, by virtue of a rule prescribing an operation for that element, shall be the technical name (saṃjñā) for that which ends in it as well as for its own form. There is an exception in the case of rules prescribing compounds (samāsa) and suffixes (pratyaya), except when the suffix begins with a vowel (ugit) or involves the mention of a phoneme (varṇa).
SK 27: *virāmo 'vasānam* (A 1.4.110).
The absence of phonemes shall be designated as *avasāna* (pause).
SK 28: *paraḥ saṃnikarṣaḥ saṃhitā* (A 1.4.109).
An excessive proximity (*atiśayitaḥ saṃnidhiḥ*) of phonemes shall be designated by the term *saṃhitā*.
SK 29: That which ends in a nominal suffix (*suP*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is called a *pada*.
That which ends in a nominal suffix and that which ends in a verbal suffix shall receive the technical designation *pada*.
SK 30: *halo 'nantarāḥ saṃyogaḥ* (A 1.1.7).
Consonants (*hal*) that are not separated by vowels (*aj*) shall be designated as *saṃyoga* (conjunctions).
SK 31: A short vowel is light (Pāṇini 1.4.10). SK 32: In the presence of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), [a short vowel] is heavy (Pāṇini 1.4.11).
When followed by a conjunct consonant, a short vowel shall bear the designation "heavy."
And long [is the vowel]. SK 33.
And that which is long shall be designated as "heavy."
Thus ends the section on designations.
Chapter Two: On Technical Terms and Conventions.

SK 34 *iko guṇavṛddhī*: Wherever *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are prescribed by means of the words *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, there the word *ikaḥ* (genitive singular of *ik*) stands as a governing term (*upatiṣṭhate*).
SK 35 acaś ca (A 1.2.28):

Wherever an *ac* vowel is prescribed by means of the terms "short" (*hrasva*), "long" (*dīrgha*), or "protracted" (*pluta*), the word *acaḥ* (genitive singular of *ac*) stands as a governing term (*upatiṣṭhate*).
SK 36: *ādyantau ṭakitau* (A 1.1.46).
Those [suffixes] which are stated to be marked with the markers *ṭ* or *k* have, respectively, the first and the last as their constituent parts.

SK 37 mid aco 'ntyāt paraḥ (A 1.1.47): The word *acaḥ* is used in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Among the vowels (*acām*), that which is the final one—after that [vowel], the augment *mit* shall be an internal part (*antāvayava*) of that very [final vowel] alone.
SK 38: *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* (A 1.1.49).
A genitive case ending whose specific relation is not determined should be understood as being connected with "in place of" (*sthāne*). And "place" (*sthāna*) means "occasion" (*prasaṅga*).
SK 39: *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (A 1.1.50).

When there is an occasion [for substitution], the substitute shall be the most similar. Where there is more than one kind of proximity (*āntarya*), proximity by place of articulation (*sthāna*) is stronger.
In the rule "tasminn iti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya" (Pāṇini A 1.1.66),
it should be understood that an operation prescribed by a locative case-indication applies to the preceding element when it is not separated from that [preceding element] by another phoneme.
Therefore, by the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (A 1.1.67),
an operation performed through the mention of the ablative case should be understood as applying to a subsequent element that is not separated by another phoneme.
SK 42: *alo 'ntyasya* (A 1.1.52).
An *ādeśa* shall replace the final *al* (vowel or consonant) that is designated by a genitive case ending.
And regarding the rule *ṅic ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53), this too would apply only to the final [sound]; it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning *sarvasva*.

SK 44: *ādeḥ parasya* (A 1.1.54). That which is prescribed for what follows [an element] should be understood as applying to its beginning. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *alo 'ntyasya*.

SK 45: *anekāl śit sarvasya* (A 1.1.55) is clear. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *alo 'ntyasya*. In cases such as *aṣṭābhya auś*, even the rule *ādeḥ parasya* is superseded by this [present rule] because of its higher status (*paratva*).

SK 46: *svaritenādhikāraḥ* (A 1.3.11). A word-form (*śabdasvarūpa*) endowed with the *svarita* accent is to be understood as governing (*adhikṛta*). Among rules that are respectively subsequent, permanent, internal, and exceptional, each succeeding one is stronger than the preceding. An external operation (*bahiraṅga*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to an internal operation (*antaraṅga*). The followers of Pāṇini do not apply a rule when the conditions for its application have already been disrupted; the meaning is that they do not perform an operation caused by a condition once they see that condition is on the verge of being destroyed. Thus ends the section on the *paribhāṣās*.
Chapter 3: On the Absence of Connection (Acchandhi-prakaraṇa)

SK 47: *iko yaṇ aci* (A 6.1.77). In place of an *ik* vowel, a *yaṇ* semivowel shall occur when followed by a vowel (*ac*) within the domain of *saṃhitā*. When *sudhī upāsya* is established, a *yakāra* replaces the *īkāra* due to positional proximity (*sthāna*). Thus, *sudhy upāsya* arises.
SK 48 *anaci ca* (A 8.4.47): "A *yaṇ* following a vowel may optionally be doubled, but not before a vowel. Thus, there is doubling of the letter *dh*.

SK 49: *sthānivadādeśo 'nalvidhau* (A 1.1.56). A substitute (*ādeśa*) is like the original (*sthānin*), except in a rule that depends on the phoneme (*al*) of the original. On this basis, one should not suspect that the prohibition of doubling by the rule *anaci ca* applies here, by relying on the vowel-nature (*actva*) of the letter *y* through its status as a substitute; for that [prohibition] is excluded by the phrase *analvidhau*.
Pāṇini 1.1.57: *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*.

This rule is for the purpose of [preventing] operations concerning vowels (*alvidhi*). A substitute for a vowel that is caused by something subsequent shall be treated as the original (the *sthānin*) when an operation is to be performed regarding what was seen as preceding that which is the original vowel. Thus, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* having been established...
Pāṇini A 1.1.58: *na padāntadvirvacavareyalopasvarasavarṇānusvāradīrghajaścarvidhiṣu*.

When an operation is to be performed concerning the final element of a word (*padasya caramāvayave*) or concerning reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and so forth, a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśaḥ*) conditioned by what follows (*paranimittaḥ*) is not treated as if it were the original (*na sthānivat*). [Example: The substitution of *da* for *dha* [in *dhukṣīṣṭa*]. Thus is the prohibition of the status of being *sthānivadbhāva*.
SK 52: *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (A 8.4.53). This is clear; thus, [the substitute] would have the designation *lopa* (elision).
SK 53: *adarśanaṃ lopaḥ* (A 1.1.60): the non-appearance of that which was applicable [is called] elision (*lopa*).

SK 54: *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (A 8.2.23). There shall be elision of the final element of a word that ends in a *saṃyoga* (conjunct consonant). Thus, when the elision of *y* is about to occur [by this rule], it is stated: "An exception must be stated for a *yaṇ*. It must be stated that after a *maya* (the letters *m*, *y*, *r*, *l*), there is optionally a doubling of a *yaṇ*. Here, *mayaḥ* is in the ablative case and *yaṇaḥ* is in the genitive case; according to this view, there is also doubling of the letter *y*. Indeed, because of the optional doubling of both the letter *dh* and the letter *y*, there are four forms: *ekadharm-ekayam*, *dvidhaṃ-dviyam*, *dvidhamekayam*, and *ekadhaṃ-dviyam*. [Examples are: *suddhyupāyaḥ*, *maddhvariḥ*, *dhātraṃśaḥ*, *lākṛtiḥ*.

SK 55: *nādrinyākrośe putrasya* (A 8.4.48). The word *putra* does not undergo reduplication when followed by the word *ādinī*, provided that reproach (*ākrośa*) is understood. Example: *putrādinī tvam asi* ("You are a devourer of your son"). Why "when reproach is understood"? Because when stating a fact, reduplication certainly occurs: *puttrādinī sarpiṇī* ("The female serpent devours her own offspring"). And [the rule applies] when that [word *putra*] follows immediately: *putraputrādinī tvam asi pāpe* ("O wicked woman, you are a devourer of your son's son"). Optionally, when followed by *hata* or *jagdha*: *putrahatī* / *puttrahatī*; *putrajagdhī* / *puttrajagdhī*.
According to Śākaṭāyana’s rule (A 8.4.51), when three or more consonants are joined by *y*, doubling may optionally occur. Thus: *inn-d-raḥ* / *indraḥ*; *rāṣ-ṣ-ṭ-r-a-m* / *rāṣṭram*.
According to Śākalya’s view, as stated in Pāṇini 8.4.51, there is no doubling [of the consonant] in all cases: *arkaḥ*, *brahmā*.
SK 58: According to the teachers, there is no doubling [of a consonant] after a long vowel. *dātram* (sickle), *pātram* (vessel). SK 59: A vowel following *ra* or *ha* is doubled. (A 8.4.46)
A consonant (*yara*) following *repha* or *hakāra* that comes after a vowel (*acaḥ*) may optionally be doubled. Examples: *haryyanubhavaḥ*, *nahyy asti*.

SK 60: *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* (A 8.4.64). There is optionally the elision (*lopa*) of a *yam* [consonant] following a *hal* [consonant], when a *yam* [consonant] follows. Thus, in the case where there is elision and in the case where there is no doubling (*dvitva*), the form *ekayam* is identical. However, the purpose of enacting this rule of elision is seen in examples such as *ādityo vedatāsya* and *ādityaṃ haviḥ*. Because the rule *yamāṃ yami* is understood according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), it does not apply here in the word *māhātmyam*.
SK 61: *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ* (A 6.1.78). In place of the *ec* vowels (*e*, *o*, *ai*, *au*), there shall be *ay*, *av*, *āy*, and *āv* respectively, when followed by a vowel (*ac*).

SK 62: *tasya lopaḥ* (A 1.3.9). There should be elision (*lopa*) of that [genitive suffix] *i*. Thus, there is no elision of *y* and *v*, because of the force of their being pronounced [in the rule]. If this is so, then the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) also does not apply here: *haraye*, *viṣṇave*, *nāyakaḥ*, *pāvakaḥ*.

SK 63: *vānto yi pratyaye* (A 6.1.79). When a suffix beginning with the letter *y* follows, *o* and *au* are replaced by *av* and *āv*, respectively. *Gavyam*: "a product of a cow. [This is derived] from the rule *gopayasor yat*. *Nāvyam*: "to be crossed by boat. [This is derived] from the rule *nauvayodharmaviṣamūlamūla... yat*. There is an extension [of this rule] for the substitution of *yū* in the Veda: *goḥ yūtau chandasy upasaṃkhyānam*. Also [there is an extension] regarding the measure of a road: *gavyūtiḥ*. The word *yūti* is established as an irregular formation (*nipātita*) by the rule *ūtiyūtijūtisātiheti...* and so forth.

In the word *vānta*, the letter *va* is elided from the portion preceding [the *au*] in the rule *goḥ pūrvasya yūtāv* by means of the elision rule *lopo vyor vali*; thus, the substitute would end in a heard *va*. This means that the *va* is not elided.

SK 64: *dhātoḥ tannimittasyaiva* (A 6.1.80). When a suffix beginning with *ya* follows, if the substitute *vānta* (*va* or *au*) occurs for an *ec* vowel of a verbal root, it applies only to that *ec* which is caused by that suffix, and not to any other. Examples: *lavyam*, *avaśyalāvyam*. Why does the rule specify "only that which is caused by it"? Consider: *oyate*, *auyata*.

SK 65: *kṣayyajayyau śakyārthe* (Pāṇini 6.1.81). This rule is for the purpose of prescribing the substitution of the vowel *y* [for the final *i*] as a nipātana. That which can be destroyed is *kṣayya*; that which can be conquered is *jayya*. Why "in the sense of being possible"? [Consider: sin that is fit to be destroyed is *kṣeya*; the mind that is fit to be conquered is *jeya*.

SK 66: *krayya* [is used] in the sense of that [purpose] (A 6.1.82). "In the sense of that" (*tadartham*) means for the sake of that which is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). That which is displayed in the marketplace with the intention that "buyers might purchase it" is *krayya*. Anything else is *kreya*. The meaning is "worthy of being purchased."

SK 67: *lopaḥ śākalyasya* (A 8.3.19). There is optionally the elision (*lopa*) of *y* and *v* at the end of a word when preceded by a vowel (*avarṇa*), provided that a vowel other than *a* (*aś*) follows. Because the rule for elision is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the principle *pūrvatrāsiddham*, vowel-sandhi (*svarasaṃdhi*) does not take place. Examples: *hara ehi* / *harayehi*; *viṣṇa iha* / *viṣṇāv iha*; *śriyā udyataḥ* / *śriyāyudyataḥ*; *gurā utkaḥ* / *gurāv utkaḥ*.

In the case of the forms *kāni* and *kau*, the rules for *yaṇ* and *āv* substitution would apply to the elision (*allopa*) of the root *as* by virtue of its being treated as a *sthānivadbhāva*. However, because the rule *na padānta...* prohibits such operations when they concern the status of a word-final (*padānta*), these two substitutions do not take place.
This is stated under the governing rule (adhikāra): "The single [substitute] takes the place of both the preceding and the following" (Pāṇini A 6.1.84).

SK 69 *ād guṇaḥ* (A 6.1.87): When a vowel (*ac*) follows a vowel beginning with *a* (*avarṇa*), a single substitute in the form of a *guṇa* shall take the place of both the preceding and the following sounds, provided they are in *saṃhitā*. Examples: *upendraḥ*, *rameśaḥ*, *gaṅgodakam*.
SK 70: *uraṇ raparaḥ* (A 1.1.51).

It has been stated that *ṛ* is the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for thirty sounds. When *aṇ* occurs in place of that [ṛ], it functions only as being followed by *r*. In that regard, due to the principle of closest similarity (*antaratamatva*), in the word *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ*, *ar* [is substituted], and in *tavalkāraḥ*, *āl* [is substituted]. According to the rule *aco rahābhyām* (8.4.46), there is optionally reduplication (*dvitva*).

SK 71: *jharo jhari savarṇe* (A 8.4.65). After a consonant (*hal*), a *jhara* sound may optionally be elided before a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) *jhara* sound. In the absence of doubling (*dvitva*), when there is elision, there is one form; when there is no elision, there are two forms due to doubling and the absence of elision; and when there is doubling but no elision, there are three forms. Thus: *kṛṣṇardhiḥ*, *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ*, *kṛṣṇardddhiḥ*. On the view that the word *yaṇaḥ* [in A 8.4.47] is in the ablative case and *mayaḥ* is in the genitive case, there is doubling of the letter *ka*. However, for the letter *la*, by the rule *anaci ca* (A 8.4.47), there is doubling. Consequently, in the form *tavalkāraḥ*, there are four possible forms.
The doubling occurs only for *l* or only for *k*, not for both, or for both as well; this fourfold nature [of the doubling] in forms such as *tavalkāra* and others should be understood by the wise.

SK 72 *vṛddhir eci* (A 6.1.88): When *ec* follows, a single substitute *vṛddhi* vowel shall take the place of both [the preceding and following vowels]. This is an exception to *guṇa*. Examples: *kṛṣṇaikatvam*, *gaṅgaughaḥ*, *devaiśvaryam*, *kṛṣṇautkaṇṭhyam*.

SK 73: *ety-edhaty-ūṭhsu* (A 6.1.89). When a vowel (*avarṇa*) precedes and *eti*, *edhati*, or *ūṭh* follows, there shall be a single substitute *vṛddhi*. This is an exception to the rules for *pararūpa* and *guṇa*. Examples: *upaiti*, *upaidhate*, *praṣṭhauhaḥ*. Why "beginning with *e*" (*ejādyoḥ*)? [Counter-examples: *upetaḥ*; *mā bhavān predidhat*. By the principle that an exception (*apavāda*) takes precedence over what precedes it, this *vṛddhi* subverts only the rule *eṅi pararūpam* (A 6.1.94), not the rule *om-āṅoś ca* (A 6.1.95). Therefore, in *avaihī*, the *vṛddhi* is indeed incorrect. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) should be made for *akṣa* before *ūhinī*: *akṣauhṇī* (an army).

[The substitution of *ī* for *e* occurs] before *svādi* and *erinaḥ*. Thus, *svairaḥ*; and because it is his nature (*śīla*) to move according to his own will, he is called *svairī*. (By the *paribhāṣā* regarding words qualified by gender: *svairiṇī*. [The substitution of *ū* for *o* occurs] before *prauḍha*, *pṛḍhya*, *eṣa*, and *eṣya*. Thus, *prauhaḥ*; *prauḍhaḥ*. Because of the rule "when there is the mention of a meaningful element, there is no mention of that which lacks meaning," and because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *vraśca-* where *bhrāj* is mentioned separately from *rāj*, by the mention of *ūḍha* [in the rule], only the word ending in the suffix *kta* is understood, and not a portion of a word ending in *ktavatu*. Thus, *prauḍhavān*; *prauḍhiḥ*.

The root *iṣ* meaning "to desire" belongs to the *tudādi* class; *iṣ* meaning "to go" belongs to the *divādi* class; and *iṣ* meaning "repetition" belongs to the *krayādi* class. With the suffixes *dhañ* and *ṇyat*, these take the forms *eṣaḥ* and *eṣyaḥ*. Since the rule for single-substitute substitution (*pararūpa*) would otherwise apply there, this [rule] prescribes *vṛddhi*: thus, *praiṣaḥ* and *praiṣyaḥ*. However, as for the root *īṣ* meaning "to glean," and the root *īṣ* meaning "to go, to injure, or to see"—because they have a long vowel as their penultimate (*upadhā*), they form *īṣaḥ* and *īṣyaḥ*. There, by the rule for *guṇa* substitution of *at*, we have *preṣaḥ* and *preṣyaḥ*. [The rule applies] also in the case of *ṛta* in a third-case compound: *sukhena ṛtaḥ* (afflicted by pleasure) becomes *sukhārtaḥ*.

Why is "third" mentioned? [To exclude examples like] *paramartaḥ*. Regarding the rule for *pravatsatara-kambala-vasana-arṇa-daśānām ṛṇe*: *prārṇam*, *vatsatarārṇam*, and so forth. That other debt which is incurred for the purpose of clearing a previous debt is called *ṛṇārṇam*. *Daśārṇa* is the name of a country; there is also a river named *daśārṇā*. The word *ṛṇa* refers both to difficult terrain and to water.

SK 74: *upasargād ṛti dhātau* (A 6.1.91). When a verbal root beginning with the vowel *ṛ* follows a prefix ending in an *a*-vowel, a single substitute *vṛddhi* vowel shall take the place of both. Examples: *upārcchati*, *prārcchati*.

SK 75 *antādivac ca* (A 6.1.85): This single-substitute [element] shall be treated as the end of the preceding [element] and as the beginning of the following [element]. Thus, the *repha* (*r*) is considered to be at the end of a word (*padānta*).

SK 76: *kharavasānayor visarjanīyaḥ* (A 8.3.15). When followed by a *khari* sound or at the end of a word (*avasāne*), the *repha* (ṛ) shall become *visarjanīya* at the end of a word. This being the case where *visarjanīya* would have been obtained, there is no *visarjanīya* for the *repha* of a word-final [element] due to its being treated as if it were internal (*antavadbhāva*), because of such indications as *ubhayatharkṣu*, *kartari*, and *carṣidevatayoḥ*. Since the root is already implied by the prefix alone, the mention of "in the root" (*dhātau*) by means of a *yogavibhāga* is for the purpose of prescribing *vṛddhi* again; therefore, even the optional *prakṛtibhāva* prescribed by *ṛtyaka* does not apply here.

SK 77: *vā supy āpiśaleḥ* (A 6.1.92). When a verbal root beginning with *ṛ* follows a prefix ending in *a*, a *vṛddhi* vowel may optionally occur before a *su*-affix. The mention of Āpiśali is for honorific purposes. Examples: *prārṣabhīyati* or *prarṣabhīyati*. Because of phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*), the short *ṛ* includes the long *ṝ*. Examples: *prālkārīyati* or *pralkārīyati*. Because the rule specifies a short vowel by means of a following *t* (*taparatva*), it does not apply to the long vowel: *upaṛkāriyati* or *uparkārīyati*.

SK 78: *eṅi pararūpam* (A 6.1.94). When a verbal root beginning with *eṅ* follows a preposition (*upasarga*) ending in *a*, the single substitute shall be the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). Examples: *prejate*, *upoṣati*. Here, the rule *vā supi* (A 6.1.92) is to be understood as continuing [from the previous sūtra] through a split in the interpretation (*vākyabheda*). Consequently, when a nominal stem (*subanta*) beginning with *eṅ* follows, it is optional: *upeḍakīyati* or *upaiḍakīyati*; *prodhīyati* or *praudhīyati*. [In the case of the particle] *eva*, [the subsequent form is used] except when it expresses restriction (*aniyoga*). Restriction (*niyoga*) means determination (*avadhāraṇa*). Example: *kveva bhokṣyase?* ("Where on earth will you eat?"). Here, the word *eva* expresses impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*). Why "except when it expresses restriction"? Example: *tavaiva* ("only yours").

SK 79: *aco 'ntyādi ṭi* (A 1.1.64). Among vowels (*ac*), that which is the last is the "end" (*antya*); that which has this as its beginning is designated as *ṭi*. In the group beginning with *śakandhu* (*śakandhvādi*), a single substitute in the form of the subsequent sound (*pararūpa*) should be stated; and that [substitute] takes the place of the *ṭi* portion. *śakandhuḥ* (the Śakandhu bird), *karkandhuḥ* (the jujube fruit), *kulaṭā* (an unchaste woman). (Gaṇa-sūtra: *sīmantaḥ* is used in the sense of the arrangement of hair; otherwise, it is *sīmāntaḥ*. *manīṣā* (wisdom), *halīṣā* (the shaft of a plow), *patañjaliḥ* (the name of the sage). *sāraṅgaḥ* refers to certain animals or birds; otherwise, it is *sārāṅgaḥ*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class defined by its general form). *mārtaṇḍaḥ* (the sun). In a compound (*samāsa*), when preceded by a word ending in *u* or *o*, there is optionally [a single substitute in the form of the subsequent sound]. *sthūlotuḥ* or *sthūlautuḥ* (a thick thigh).
*bimboṣṭhaḥ* (lip like the bimba fruit); *bimbauṣṭhaḥ*. Why [is this rule] stated in the context of a compound (*samāsa*)? [Consider: *tavauṣṭhaḥ* (your lip).

SK 80 *omāṅoś ca* (A 6.1.95): When *om* or *āṅ* follows [a vowel], a single substitute of the form of the subsequent sound (*pararūpa*) shall occur. Examples: *śivāya oṃ namaḥ* → *śivāyonamaḥ*; *śiva ehi* → *śivehi*.

SK 81: *avyaktānukaraṇasyāta itau* (A 6.1.98). For an imitation of an indistinct sound, when the syllable *it* follows the vowel *a*, there shall be a single substitute of the form of the subsequent element (*pararūpa*). Example: *paṭat* → *paṭiti*. [Exception: Not so for a word consisting of a single vowel. Example: *śrat* → *śrāditi*.
SK 82: *nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā* (A 6.1.99).

That which was previously stated [regarding the doubling] shall not apply to the *āmreḍita*, but it may optionally apply to the final sound alone, namely the letter *t*. Because of the mention of "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule *ḍāci bahulaṃ dve bhavataḥ*, there is doubling.
SK 83: *tasya paramāmreḍitam* (A 8.1.2).
Of that which is reduplicated, the subsequent form shall bear the technical designation *āmreḍita*. For example: *paṭ-paṭeti*.
SK 84: *jhalāṃ jaśo 'nte* (A 8.2.39). At the end of a word, *jaś*-sounds shall replace *jhal*-sounds. As in *paṭpaṭad*.

SK 85: *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (A 6.1.101). When a vowel (*ac*) homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with a short *ak*-vowel follows, there shall be a single long substitute. Examples: *daityāreḥ*, *śrīśaḥ*, *viṣṇūdayaḥ*. Why "when a vowel follows"? Consider *kumārī śete*. However, the prohibition of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) by the rule *nājjhalau* does not apply to the long vowel and the letter *śa*; for the rule concerning the definition of homogeneity has not yet come into effect prior to the rules prescribing or prohibiting homogeneity. Why "of an *ak*-vowel"? Consider *haraye*. It would have been easier to state simply: "there is a long vowel when followed by an *ak*-vowel. When followed by a homogeneous *ṛ*, there is optionally *ṛ*: *hotṛkāraḥ* or *hotṝkāraḥ*. When followed by a homogeneous *lṛ*, there is optionally *lṛ*.

The *hotṛ* [ending] has the letter *ṛ*; optionally, it may have the letter *ṛ* due to their being homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*). The *hetṛ* [ending] has the letter *ṛ*. Regarding the rules "before *ṛ*, *ṛ* is substituted" and "before *ṛ*, *ṛ* is substituted," as well as "before *ḷ*, *ḷ* is substituted," in both cases the two letters to be prescribed are each of two morae (*dvimātra*). In the first case, there are two *r*-sounds in the middle; one mora belongs to those two, and another mora belongs to the vowel on either side. In the second case, however, there are two *l*-sounds in the middle. The rest is as before. In both instances here, the optional preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ṛtyakaḥ* will be stated.

SK 86 *eṅaḥ padāntād ati* (A 6.1.109): When *ati* follows after an *eṅ* vowel at the end of a word, there shall be a single substitute in the form of the preceding vowel (*pūrvarūpa*). Examples: *hare 'va*, *viṣṇo 'va*. SK 87 *sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ* (A 6.1.122): In all cases, the substitution for *go* is optional.

In both the world (secular usage) and the Veda, the *prakṛtibhāva* (absence of sandhi change) may optionally occur for a word ending in *eṅ* (*e* or *o*) when followed by *go*, at the end of a word. Examples: *goagram* or *go 'gram*. Why "ending in *eṅ*"? Consider *citragvagram*. Why "at the end of a word"? Consider *goḥ*.

SK 88: *avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya* (A 6.1.123). The word *ati* has ceased to apply. When followed by a vowel (*aci*), the substitution of *avaṅ* optionally occurs for *go* at the end of a word (*padānte*). Examples: *gav-agra-grāmaḥ*. Why "at the end of a word"? [Consider] *gavi*. By virtue of the rule of fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), we have *gavākṣaḥ*.
SK 89: In the presence of *indra*, the suffix *avaṅ* should be applied to *go*. [Thus] *gavendraḥ* ("bull-king").
In the absence of sandhi, there is the preservation of the original form (prakṛtibhāva).

SK 90: *plutapragṛhyā aci nityam* (A 6.1.125). It will be stated that *pluta* vowels and *pragṛhya* vowels remain in their original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by a vowel (*ac*), and this shall be obligatory (*nityam*). For example: *ehi kṛṣṇa atra gauś carati*; *harī etau*. Why does it say "obligatory"? [To ensure that] in cases such as *harī etau*, only this specific *prakṛtibhāva* applies, and not the shortening (*hrasva*) prescribed by *iko 'savarṇe śākalyasya* (A 6.1.127).

Pāṇini 6.1.127: *iko ’savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaś ca* (An *ik* vowel at the end of a word remains in its original form when followed by a dissimilar vowel, according to Śākalya; furthermore, it may optionally be shortened). In this rule, since the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is already established by the very force of the prescription for shortening, the Bhāṣya maintains that the particle *ca* (‘and’) need not have been included for the purpose of drawing that [preservation] forward. Examples: *cakri atra* (or *cakry atra*). Why specify “at the end of a word” (*padāntā*)? Consider: *gaur yau*. [The rule does not apply] in a compound (*na samāse*): *vāpyaśvaḥ*. And [the rule applies] after the suffix *sit*: *pārśvam*.

SK 92 *ṛtyakaḥ* (A 6.1.128): Before the vowel *ṛ*, the short vowel *a* remains as before. *brahma ṛṣiḥ* → *brahmarṣiḥ*. This applies only when [the word ending in *a*] is at the end of a word (*padānta*). *ārcchat*. This preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) occurs even in compounds: *saptaṛṣīṇām* or *saptarṣīṇām*. SK 93 *vākyasya ṭeḥ pluta udāttaḥ* (A 8.2.82): At the end of a sentence, the final phoneme (*ṭi*) becomes protracted (*pluta*) and acute-accented (*udātta*).
With reference to this [it is said]:

SK 94: *pratyabhivāde ’śūdre* (A 8.2.83). In the case of a return greeting (*pratyabhivāda*) that does not concern a Śūdra, the final syllable (*ṭi*) of the sentence should be protracted (*pluta*), and it shall be acute (*udātta*). Example: *abhivādaye devadatto ’ham* / *bho āyuṣmānedhi devadatta*. [This does not apply] in the case of a female: *abhivādaye gārgyaham* / *bho āyuṣmatī bhava gārgi*. The protraction is desired only when a personal name or a family name (*gotra*) is employed at the end of the return-greeting sentence; not here: *āyuṣmānedhi*. It should be stated [as an addition to the rule]: "In the case of *bhoḥ*, for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, [the protraction] is optional. Example: *āyuṣmānedhi bho3ḥ* / *bhoḥ*.
Venerable Indravarman, may you live long! Venerable Indrapālita, may you live long!

SK 95 *dūrād dhūte ca* (A 8.2.84): In a sentence used for addressing someone from a distance, the final *ṭi* (the last vowel with its following consonant) shall be protracted (*pluta*). Example: *saktūn piba devadatta 3*.

SK 96: *haiheprayoge haihayoḥ* (A 8.2.22). When these two (*hai* and *he*) are employed in a sentence uttered from a distance to call someone, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs only for *hai* and *he*. Examples: *he 3 rāma* and *rāma hai 3*.

SK 97: According to the Easterners (*prācām*), when a sentence is uttered from a distance (*dūrād dhūte*), there shall be a protracted vowel (*pluta*) for a heavy syllable (*guru*) that is not followed by *ṛ* or *l* (*anṛtaḥ*), even if it is not final (*anantyasya*), provided it occurs singly (*ekaikasya*). For example: *de3vadatta*, *devada3tta*, or *devadatta 3*. Why "heavy syllable" (*guroḥ*)? To prevent [the rule] from applying to the *a* following the *v* in *devadatta*. Why "not followed by *ṛ* or *l*" (*anṛtaḥ*)? As in *kṛṣṇa 3*. The mention of "singly" (*ekaika*) is for the sake of indicating alternation (*paryāyārtha*). Here, the phrase "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) is separated from the rule; therefore, every protracted vowel is made optional.

SK 98: *aplutavad upasthite* (A 6.1.129). When an *it*-word that is not Vedic (*anārṣa*) follows, a protracted vowel (*pluta*) preceding it is treated as if it were non-protracted (*aplutavat*). The meaning is that it undergoes the grammatical operations of a non-protracted vowel, such as *yaṇ*-substitution and so forth. Examples: *suśloka3iti* (or *suśloketi*). Why use the word *vat*? If only *apluta* were stated, then only a non-protracted vowel would be prescribed and the protracted vowel would be prohibited. In that case, when there is *prakṛtibhāva* based on a *pragṛhya*, the protracted vowel would not be heard [as it would be replaced]. Example: *agnī 3 iti*.

According to Cākravarman (A 6.1.130), the *ī3* protracted vowel (*pluta*) followed by a vowel (*aci*) may optionally not behave as if it were not protracted (*aplutavat*). Thus: *cinuhī 3 iti* or *cinu hīti*; *cinu hī 3 idam* or *cinu hīdam*. This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) applicable in both cases.
Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.11: *īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*.

A dual ending (*dvivacana*) that ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *e* is designated as *pragṛhya*. Examples: *harī etau* ("these two Hari-s"), *viṣṇū imau* ("these two Viṣṇu-s"), *gaṅge amū* ("those two Gaṅgā-s"), *pacete imau* ("these two who cook"). However, in the expression *maṇīvoṣṭrasya*, it should be understood that the word *va* or *vā* is used in the sense of *iva* ("like").

SK 101: *adaso māt* (A 1.1.12). The long vowels *ī* and *ū* following this [stem *adas-*] are *pragṛhya*. Examples: *amī īśāḥ*; *rāmakṛṣṇāv amū āsāte*. Why "after *m*" (*māt*)? Consider: *amuke 'tra*. If the mention of *m* were not made, the vowel *e* would also follow from the previous rule.
SK 102 śe (A 1.1.13): This [word *asme*] shall be a *pragṛhya*. Example: *asme indrābṛhaspatī*.

Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.14: *nipāta ekājanāṅ* (An indeclinable consisting of a single vowel, excluding *āṅ*, shall be *pragṛhya*). The particle *i* [expressing] astonishment: *i indraḥ*. The particle *u* [expressing] deliberation: *u umeśaḥ*. Because of the statement "excluding *āṅ*," the form *ā* that is not *āṅ* is indeed *pragṛhya*: *ā evaṃ nu manyase*; *ā evaṃ kila tat*. However, one that is *ṅit* is not *pragṛhya*: *īṣaduṣṇam* (slightly warm), *oṣṇam*. One should know that this *ā* is *ṅit* when it signifies slightness, connection with an action, limit exclusive (*maryādā*), or inclusion (*abhividhi*); it is *aṅit* in the sense of a sentence or recollection.
SK 104 (A 1.1.15): The particle *ot* ending in *-od* shall be *pragṛhya*. For example: *aho īśāḥ*.
SK 105 (A 1.1.16): In the vocative singular, according to Śākalya, the two vowels [of the dual] remain as they are when not part of a Vedic text (*anārṣe*).

The vowel *o*, when caused by a perfective suffix (*saṃbuddhi*), is *pragṛhya* (retains its original form) before the particle *iti*, provided it is not in a Vedic context. Examples: *viṣṇo iti*, *viṣṇa iti*, *viṣṇav iti*. Why "not in a Vedic context"? Because [in the Veda] one says *brahmabandhavity abravīt*.
SK 106 *uñaḥ* (A 1.1.17): Regarding the substitute *uñ*, that which was stated previously applies optionally when followed by *iti*. Thus, [the forms] *u iti* and *v iti*.
In place of *uñ* before the particle *iti*, there may optionally be the substitute *ūṃ*, which is long, nasalized, and a *pragṛhya* vowel. Thus: *ūṃ iti*.

SK 108: *maya uño vo vā* (A 8.3.33). After *maya*, the substitute *va* may optionally replace *uñ* before a vowel. For example: *kimu uktam* or *kimv uktam*. Because the substitution of *va* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of the preceding rule, the anusvāra does not occur.

SK 109: *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe* (A 1.1.19). A word ending in *ī* or *ū* that culminates in the sense of the locative case (*saptamyartha*) shall be *pragṛhya*. Examples: *somo gaurī adhiśritaḥ* ("Soma is placed upon Gaurī") and *māmakī tanū* ("my own body"). Here, the locative case-ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Why is the term "sense" (*artha*) included in the rule? It is so that the rule does not apply when the word has shifted to another meaning in a compound (*vṛtti*). For example, in *vāpyāmaśvo vāpyaśvaḥ* ("a horse belonging to a pond"), the word *vāpī* has shifted its meaning and thus is not *pragṛhya*.

SK 110: *aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* (A 8.4.57). An *aṇ* [vowel] that is not a *pragṛhya*, when occurring at the end of a word (*avasāne*), may optionally take an anusvāra (*anunāsika*). Examples: *dadhiṃ* / *dadhi*. Why "not a *pragṛhya*"? Consider *agnī*.
Thus ends the section on vowel-sandhi (*acsandhi*).
Chapter 5: The Section on Vocal Sandhi (Halsandhiprakaraṇa)
Pāṇini Sūtra 8.4.40: *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ*.

When *s* or the *ta*-class consonants (*tavarga*) are joined with *ś* or the *ca*-class consonants (*cavarga*), *ś* or the *ca*-class consonants are substituted [in place of the former]. Examples: *hariś śete* (Hari lies down), *rāmaś cinoti* (Rāma gathers), *saccit* (existent-consciousness), *śārṅgiñjaya* (O conqueror of Śārṅgin).
SK 112 *śāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.44): After *ś*, there shall not be the substitution of *ścutva* for the following retroflex class (*tavarga*). Examples: *viśvaḥ*, *praśnaḥ*.

SK 113: *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* (A 8.4.41). When *stoḥ* [the sounds *s*, *t*, *th*, *d*, *dh*, *n*] are joined with *ṣṭu* [the sounds *ṣ*, *ṭ*, *ṭh*, *ḍ*, *ḍh*, *ṇ*], they become *ṣṭu*. Examples: *rāmaṣṣaṣṭhaḥ*; *rāmaṣṭīkate*; *peṣṭā taṭṭikā*; *cakriṇḍaukase*.

SK 114: *na padāntāṭ ṭoranām* (A 8.4.42). The word *anām* is a term with its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka*). After a *ṭ*-class consonant (*ṭoḥ*) at the end of a word (*padāntāt*), the *s*-class (*stoḥ*) of the [word] *anām* shall not become a *ṣ*-class (*ṣṭuḥ*). Examples: *ṣaṭ santaḥ*, *ṣaṭ te*. Why "at the end of a word"? [Counter-example: *īṭṭe*. Why "of the *ṭ*-class"? [Counter-example: *sarpiṣṭamam*. It should be stated that this does not apply to *nām*, *navati*, and *nagarī*: *ṣaṇṇām*, *ṣaṇṇavatiḥ*, *ṣaṇṇagaryaḥ*.

When a letter of the *tavarga* (the dental class) is followed by *ṣ*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* does not occur. Example: *sanṣaṣṭhaḥ*. *jhalāṃ jaśo 'nte*: At the end of a word, the *jhaś* sounds (voiced unaspirated stops and nasals) replace the *jhal* sounds (all consonants except semivowels and sibilants). Example: *vāgīśaḥ*, *cidrūpam*.
SK 116: *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (A 8.4.45).

When a nasalized sound (*anunāsika*) follows a *yar* (a consonant other than *h*) at the end of a word, the preceding *yar* may optionally become nasalized. Examples: *etan-murāriḥ* or *etad-murāriḥ*. This rule, which applies to the closest substitute (*antaratama*) in terms of place and effort (*sthāna-prayatna*), finds its scope in the case of a stop (*sparśa*); it does not apply to the letter *r*. Example: *caturmukhaḥ*. However, when followed by an affix (*pratyaya*) in the common language (*bhāṣā*), the substitution is obligatory: *tanmātram*, *cinmayam*. How then is the form *madodagrāḥ kakudmantaḥ* explained? It is due to the specific insertion (*nipātana*) of the letter *d* in the *yavādi* group [of words].

When a letter of the *tavarga* class is followed by *la*, there shall be *parasavarṇa* (homogeneity with the following sound). Examples: *tallayaḥ*; *vidvāṃl likhati*. Here, the nasalized *la* (*anunāsika la*) replaces the *na*.

SK 118: *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya* (A 8.4.61). When *sthā* and *stambh* follow *ud*, there shall be a substitution of the preceding [vowel] with its homogeneous counterpart (*pūrvasavarṇa*). By the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, this applies to the initial [consonant] of the following element. Thus we have *utthānam* and *uttambhanam*. Here, since *s* is voiceless and aspirated (*aghoṣa-mahāprāṇa*), it is replaced by a *th* of the same description. Regarding that [substituted *th*], there is an optional elision (*lopa*) by the rule *jharo jhari*. In the alternative case where elision does not occur, there is the hearing of the *th* itself; however, there is no substitution of *c* for *th* by the rule *khari ca*, because the *th* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) in relation to the application of *cartva*.

SK 119: *jhayo ho ’nyatarasyām* (A 8.4.62). After a consonant of the *jha*-class (*jhayaḥ*), the substitute for *ha* may optionally be a sound homogeneous with the preceding one. For a *ha* that is voiced (*ghoṣavat*), sonorous (*nādavat*), aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*), and produced with the glottis constricted (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭha*), the substitute is specifically the fourth letter of the same class (*vargacaturtha*). Examples: *vāgghariḥ* or *vāghariḥ*.

SK 120: *śaścho ’ṭi* (A 8.4.63). After a final *jhay* consonant, the *ś* that follows may optionally become *ch* before an *aṭ* vowel. Once the *d* has been changed to *j* by the rule of *ścutva*, [the following *ś* becomes *ch*].

SK 121 *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55): When a *khar* sound follows, the *jhal* sounds are replaced by *car* sounds. Thus, the *ja* is replaced by *ca*. *tacchivaḥ* / *tacśivaḥ*. It should be stated that this substitution of *cha* occurs when followed by *amī*. *tacślokena* / *tacchlokena*. Why "when followed by *amī*"? [Consider: *vāk ścyotati*.

SK 122: *mo 'nusvāraḥ* (A 8.3.23). An *anusvāra* shall replace [the final] *m* of a word (*pada*) before a consonant (*hal*). [This applies to] the final letter of the word (*alo 'ntyasya*). Example: *hariṃ vande*. Why does it say "of a word" (*padasya*)? [Consider: *gamyate*.

SK 123: *naś cāpadāntasya jhali* (A 8.4.24). Anusvāra shall be substituted for *n* and *m* when they are not at the end of a word (*apadānta*) and followed by a *jhal* consonant. Examples: *yaśāṃsi*, *ākraṃsyate*. Why "followed by a *jhal*"? Consider: *manyate*.

SK 124: *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (A 8.4.58) is clear. [Examples: *aṅkitaḥ*, *añcitaḥ*, *kuṇṭhitaḥ*, *śāntaḥ*, *gumphitaḥ*. In the case of *kurvanti*, although *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) would have been applicable, because that [substitution] is considered *asiddha* (not yet established), once the *anusvāra* has been substituted and the *parasavarṇa* (homorganic nasal) applied, *ṇatva* does not occur because that [previous stage] is still *asiddha*.
SK 125: *vā padāntasya* (A 8.4.59).

An *anusvāra* at the end of a word may optionally be replaced by a *parasavarṇa* when followed by a *yay* (any consonant except *h*, *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*). Examples: *tvaṅkaroṣi* / *tvaṃkaroṣi*; *saṃyantā* / *saṃyantā*; *saṃvatsaraḥ* / *saṃvatsaraḥ*; *yaṃlokam* / *yaṃlokam*. In this case, the *anunāsika* forms of *y*, *v*, and *l* are optionally substituted for the *anusvāra*.
SK 126: *mo rāji samaḥ kvau* (A 8.2.35). When *kvip* follows *rājati*, the *m* of *sama-* alone is replaced by *ṣ*. Thus: *samrāṭ*.
SK 127: *he mapare vā* (A 8.3.26).

When the letter *ha* followed by *ma* (*mapara*) follows, *ma* may optionally remain as *ma*. [The roots] *hmla* and *hvla* mean "to move. [Examples: *kim hmalayati* / *kiṃ hmalayati*. It should be stated that when *ya*, *va*, or *la* follow (*yavala-pare*), *ya*, *va*, or *la* may optionally take the place of the preceding consonant.

SK 128: *yathāsaṃkhyam anudeśaḥ samānām* (A 1.3.10). A rule involving equal correlates shall apply according to their respective order. Examples: *kiṃhyaḥ* / *kiṃhyaḥ*; *kiṃ hvalayati* / *kiṃ hvalayati*; *kiṃ hlādayati* / *kiṃ hlādayati*. SK 129: *na pare naḥ* (A 8.3.27). [The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur] when followed by *par*.
Before the letter *ha*, the *m* of *kim* may optionally become *n*. Thus: *kin hnute* or *kiṃ hnute*. Regarding Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.28 (*ṅṇoḥ kuk ṭuk śari*):

the augment *kuk* or *ṭuk* is optionally added after the letters *ṅ* and *ṇ* before a sibilant (*śar*). Because *kuk* and *ṭuk* are considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent rules), the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) does not apply. It should be stated that according to Pauṣkarasādi, the second consonants of the *cay* group are substituted before a sibilant. Thus: *prāṅkhṣaṣṭhaḥ*, *prāṅkṣaṣṭhaḥ*, *prāṅṣaṣṭhaḥ*; *sugaṇṭhṣaṣṭhaḥ*, *sugaṇṭṣaṣṭhaḥ*, *sugaṇṣaṣṭhaḥ*.
SK 131: *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ* (A 8.3.28). A *dhuṭ* augment may optionally be added after a *ḍ* sound before the letter *s*. Thus, *ṣaṭtsantaḥ* or *ṣaṭsantaḥ*.

SK 132 *naś ca*: After a word ending in *n*, the augment *dhuṭ* is optionally added before *s*. Examples: *santsaḥ* or *sansaḥ*. SK 133 *śi tuk*: The augment *tuk* is added after a stem ending in *ś* before the nominative plural suffix *śi*.

A *tug* augment may optionally be added to a word-final *n* when followed by *ś*. By the rule *śaś choṭi*, there is an optional substitution of *ch* for *ś*; in the alternative case, there is an elision of *ch* by the rule *jharo jhari*. Thus, there are four forms: *sañchaṃbhuḥ*, *sañcchaṃbhuḥ*, *sañcśabhuḥ*, and *sañśaṃbhuḥ*. These four forms arise here from the optional application of the *tug* augment, the substitution of *ch*, and the elision of *ch*. Specifically, they are derived as *ñ-ch-au*, *ñ-ac-l-au*, *ñ-ac-ś-au*, and *ña-ś-au*.

SK 134 *ḍamo hrasvād aci ṅamuṇnityam* (A 8.3.32): After a word ending in a *ṅam* [nasal] that follows a short vowel, the augment *ṅamuṭ* is always added before a following vowel. Examples: *pratyaṅṅātmā*, *sugaṇṇīśaḥ*, *sannacyutaḥ*. SK 135 *samaḥ suṭi* (A 8.3.5).
The substitute *ru* shall be equal [to the original] when *suṭ* follows; [and it applies] to the final phoneme.
SK 136: *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā* (A 8.3.2).
In this section concerning *ru*, an anusvāra may optionally be substituted for the preceding [sound] of *ru*.
SK 137: *anunāsikāt paro 'nusvāraḥ* (A 8.3.4).

With the exception of the nasalized [consonant], an *anusvāra* augment shall occur after the preceding sound from which the *ru* [substitute] follows. [And: *kharavasānayor visarjanīyaḥ* (A 8.3.15): [The substitute] *visarjanīya* occurs in place of *ru* before a voiceless consonant (*kha*) or at the end of a pause (*avasāna*).

SK 138: *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (A 8.3.34). Before a *khari* sound, the *visarjanīya* should be replaced by *sa*. Since this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the optional *visarga* prescribed by *vā śari*, it is stated that for *saṃ*, *puṃs*, and *kān*, *sa* should be substituted. Thus: *saṃskartā* / *saṃskartā*. Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "some [teachers] say there is elision (*lopa*) of *sam*," since elision also falls within the section on *ru*-substitution, there are two forms with one *sakāra*: one with an *anusvāra* and one with an *anunāsika*. As for the form with two *sakāras*, it has already been explained. In that case, according to the rule *anaci ca*, when there is doubling of the *sakāra*, there are also two forms with three *sakāras*.

Since the reading [of doubling] for the *anusvāra*, *visarga*, *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, and the *yamas*—both when they follow the vowel *a* and when they are among the *śar* consonants—is prescribed as an addition (*upasaṃkhyāta*), the *anusvāra* also possesses the status of being an *ac* (vowel). Thus, for the three [consonants] possessing nasality (*anunāsika*), there are six forms due to the doubling of the *ka* [group] according to the rule *śaraḥ khayaḥ*. For those possessing the *anusvāra*, there are twelve forms due to the doubling of the *anusvāra* itself. When the doubling of the *t* in these eighteen forms occurs, and by another rule there is further doubling, there are fifty-four forms: namely, one *t*, two *ts*, and three *tt*s. When the *aṇ* [vowels] possess nasality, there are one hundred and eight forms.

SK 139: *pumaḥ khayyampare* (A 8.3.6). When followed by a *khay* consonant that is itself followed by an *am* vowel, the word *pum-* undergoes the substitution of *ru*. In the view that [words] are derived (*vyutpattipakṣe*), because of the exclusion of the application of *ṣatva* by the rule *apratyayasya*, the substitutions of *ka* and *pra* would apply. In the view that [words] are not derived (*avyutpattipakṣe*), however, *ṣatva* would apply; thus, by the rule *saṃpuṃkānām*, *sa* is substituted. Examples: *puṃskokilaḥ* / *puṃskokilaḥ*; *puṃsputraḥ* / *puṃsputraḥ*. Why "followed by an *am* vowel"? Consider *puṃkṣīram*. Why "when followed by a *khay* consonant"? Consider *puṃdāsaḥ*. This substitution does not occur when there is the substitute *khyāñ*: *puṃkhyānam*. SK 140: *naś chavy apraśān* (A 8.3.7). [The substitution of *ru* occurs for the final *n* of the word *praśān*] except for *praśān* before a *chav* consonant.

In the presence of a vowel (*am*) followed by *r*, a word ending in *n* becomes *ru*, but not the word *praśān*. [The result is] a visarga; then *satva*; then *ścutva*: *śārṅgiṃ cchindhi* / *śārṅgiṃś chindhi*; *cakriṃstrāyasva* / *cakriṃstrāyasva*. Why "of a word" (*padasya*)? [Because in *hanti*, the final *n* is not part of a complete word. Why "in the presence of a vowel followed by *r*" (*ampare*)? [Because in *santsaruḥ*, which means "the hilt of a sword," the *n* is not followed by *r*. Why "not *praśān*" (*apraśān*)? [Because in *praśāntanoti*, the *n* is part of *praśān*. SK 141: *nṝn pe* (A 8.3.10).
For the word *nṝn*, *ru* may optionally occur before the letter *p*.

SK 142 (A 8.3.37): *kupvoḥ kapau ca*. When a guttural (*kavarga*) or a labial (*pavarga*) follows, the *visarjanīya* is replaced respectively by the *jihvāmūlīya* and the *upadhmānīya*. By the word *ca* ("and"), the *visarga* itself is also retained. According to the maxim *yenanāprāpte*, this rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (A 8.3.34), but not to the rule *śarpare visarjanīyaḥ* (A 8.3.35). Therefore, in forms such as *vāsaḥkṣaumam*, the *visarga* remains. Examples: *nṝṁ pāhi*, *nṝṁ pāhi*, *nṝṁ ḥpāhi*, *nṝṃḥ pāhi*, *nṝn pāhi*. SK 143 (A 8.3.12): *kānāmreḍite*. [The *visarjanīya* of *kān* becomes *saḥ* when followed by a guttural or labial, provided it occurs in a reduplicated form.]
The *ru* substitute shall occur for the word *kāṇ*, when it is followed by its own reduplication (*āmreḍita*). [This is established] by the rule *saṃpuṃkānām*. Alternatively:

SK 144 *kaskādiṣu ca* (A 8.3.48): In these [words] beginning with *kaska*, the visarga following *iṇ* shall become *ṣ*; elsewhere, however, it remains *s*. This is an exception to [the rules concerning] *ka* and *pa*. Thus: *saḥ kāṁskān* or *kāṃskān*; *kaskaḥ*; *kautaskutaḥ*; *sarpiṣkuṇḍikā*; *dhanuṣkapālam*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words).
With reference to the governing rule *saṃhitāyām* (A 6.1.72),
[the sūtra] *che ca* (A 6.1.73) [is stated].

When *cha* follows a short vowel, the augment *tuk* is added in *saṃhitā*. Because the substitution of *ścu* (i.e., *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*) is considered *asiddha*, the dental *da* is first changed to a retroflex by *jaś*-substitution. Then, because the substitution of *car* (i.e., *ca*, *ṭa*, and *ta*) is *asiddha*, the preceding [retroflex] is changed to a palatal by *ścu*-substitution. That [palatal] is then changed to a velar by *car*-substitution. Since the substitution of *ścu* is *asiddha*, the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30) does not apply, and there is no change to a guttural (*ku*). Thus: *svacchāyā*, *śivacchāyā*.

SK 147: *āṅmāṅoś ca* (A 6.1.74). The augment *tuk* is inserted after these two [prefixes, *āṅ* and *māṅ*,] when followed by the suffix *cha*. This is an exception to the optional rule *padāntād vā* (A 6.1.75). Examples: *ācchādayati*, *mācchidat*.
SK 148: After a long vowel, *tuk* is inserted when *cha* follows. This *tuk* belongs to the long vowel, not to *cha*, as evidenced by the rule *senā-surā-cchāyā*. Example: *cecchidyate*. SK 149:
Optionally, [the augment *tuk* is inserted] after a word-final long vowel.

The augment *t* (tuṅ) may optionally be inserted after a long vowel at the end of a word when followed by *ś*. Examples: *lakṣmīcchāyā* or *lakṣmīchāyā*. Thus ends the section on consonant sandhi (*hal-saṃdhi*).
Now begins the section on the euphonic combination of the visarga.
The *visarjanīya* becomes *saḥ*. Viṣṇu is the protector.
SK 150: *śapare visarjanīyaḥ* (A 8.3.35).

When followed by a *khari* consonant that has *ś* as its *para* (subsequent sound), the *visarjanīya* remains as *visarjanīya* and nothing else. As in *kaḥ tsaruḥ* and *ghanāghanaḥ kṣobhaṇaḥ*. In these cases, there is neither *satva* nor the *jihvāmūlīya* according to the rule.

SK 151 *vā śari* (A 8.3.36): When followed by a *śar* consonant, the *visarjanīya* may optionally remain as *visarjanīya*. Thus: *hariḥ śete* or *hariś śete*. It should be stated that when followed by a *śar* consonant in a *khara* (voiceless) environment, there is optionally an elision (*lopa*) of the *visarjanīya*. Thus: *rāmasthātā* or *harisphurati*. In the alternative case where the *visarjanīya* remains or is changed to *s*, there are three forms. *Kupvoḥ ka pau ca* (A 8.3.37): When followed by *k* or *p*, [the *visarjanīya*] becomes *k* or *p* respectively. Thus: *ka karoti* or *kaḥ karoti*; *ka khanati* or *kaḥ khanati*; *ka pacati* or *kaḥ pacati*; *ka phalati* or *kaḥ phalati*.

SK 152: *so 'padādau* (A 8.3.38). The *visarjanīya* becomes *sa* when followed by *ka* or *pa*, provided it does not occur at the beginning of a word. It should be stated that this applies in the presence of the suffixes *pāśa*, *kalpa*, *ka*, and *kāmya*. Examples: *payaspāśam*, *yaśaskalpam*, *yaśaskam*, *yaśaskāmyati*. It should be stated that this rule does not apply to indeclinables (*avyaya*). Thus, here [in the following], there is no substitution: *gīḥ kāmyati*.
SK 153 *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* (A 8.3.39): In the aforementioned contexts, a *ṣakāra* shall replace the *visarga* that follows the root *iṇ*. Examples: *sarpiṣpāśam*, *sarpiṣkalpam*, *sarpiṣkam*, *sarpiṣkāmyati*.
SK 154 *namaspuraso gatyoḥ* (A 8.3.40): [The *ṣatva* rule applies] after *namaḥ* and *puraḥ* when they function as prefixes (*gati*).

In these two cases, *gati* and *saṃjñā*, the *s* of *visarga* becomes *s* when followed by *k* or *p*. In *namaskaroti*, the designation *gati* is optional due to its inclusion in the group beginning with *sākṣāt* when used in conjunction with the root *kṛ*; in the absence of that [option], one says *namaḥ karoti*. In *puraskaroti*, the designation *gati* is obligatory because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) according to the rule *puro 'vyayam*. Because it is not a *gati* here, [the substitution does not apply]: *pūḥ*, *purau*, *puraḥ* are to be entered.
Pāṇini 8.3.41: *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya*.

A *visarga* following a root or stem that has *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter (*upadha*), provided it is not part of an affix (*apratyaya*), is replaced by *ṣ* before the *ka*-series consonants (*ku*) or the *pa*-series consonants (*pu*). Examples: *niṣpratyūham*, *āviṣkṛtam*, *duṣkṛtam*. Why "not part of an affix"? Consider *agniḥ karoti* and *vāyuḥ karoti*. Here, the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply because the *visarga* is caused by a rule for a single substitute (*ekādeśa-śāstra*). This is because the word *bhrātuṣputra* is specifically listed in the *kaska-* group (Pāṇini 8.3.48). Therefore, in this case, there is no *ṣ*: *mātuḥ kṛpā*. There is a prohibition for the word *muhus*: *muhuḥ kāmāḥ*.

SK 156 *tiraso ’nyatarasyām* (A 8.3.42): After *tiras*, the [s] may optionally be substituted [for the initial s of a following word] when followed by *k* or *p*. Examples: *tiraskartā* or *tiraḥkartā*.

SK 157 *dvistriścatur iti kṛtvo ’rthe* (A 8.3.43): For these words occurring in the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas*), the visarga may optionally become *ṣ* before *k* or *p*. Examples include *dviṣkaroti*, etc. Why "in the sense of times"? [Counter-example: *catuṣkapālaḥ*.
SK 158 *isusoḥ sāmarthye* (A 8.3.44): [The visarga of] *is* and *us* becomes *ṣ* before *k* or *p* when there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*).

In these two cases, the *visarga* may optionally become *ṣ* before *k* or *p*. Examples: *sarpiṣkaroti* / *sarpiḥkaroti*; *dhanuṣkaroti* / *dhanuḥkaroti*. Here, "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) means syntactic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). Why is "capacity" specified? [Consider: *tiṣṭhatu sarpiḥ* (Let the clarified butter stand) and *piba tvam udakam* (Drink you water). In these instances, there is no mutual expectancy between the words.
SK 159: *nityaṃ samāse 'nuttarapadasthasya* (A 8.3.45).

In a compound, the visarga of the suffixes *is* and *us*, when not standing at the end of a final member (*anuttarapadastha*), shall always be changed to *ṣ* when followed by *k* or *p*. Examples: *sarpiṣkuṇḍikā*, *dhanuṣkapālam*. Why does it say "not standing at the end of a final member"? [Consider: *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*. The word *sarpiṣkuṇḍikā* is included among the *kaska-* group for the sake of *ṣatva* even in non-compounds where there is no syntactic dependence (*vyapekṣā*); and in cases of syntactic dependence, it is for the sake of making the change obligatory.

SK 160: *ataḥ kṛkami-kaṃsa-kumbha-pātra-kuśā-karṇīṣv-anavyayasya* (A 8.3.46). After the vowel *a*, when followed by the words *kṛ*, *kama*, *kaṃsa*, *kumbha*, *pātra*, *kuśā*, and *karṇī*, provided it is not an indeclinable (*anavyaya*), [the *visarga* becomes *s*], but not when situated within a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*). Examples: *ayaskāraḥ* (iron-worker), *ayaskāmaḥ* (desirous of iron), *ayaskaṃsaḥ* (bronze vessel), *ayaskumbhaḥ* (iron jar), *ayaspātram* (iron vessel), *ayaskuśā* (iron-tipped grass), *ayaskarṇī* (iron-eared). Why "after *a*" (*ataḥ*)? Consider *gīḥkāraḥ* (maker of speech). Why "not an indeclinable" (*anavyayasya*)? Consider *svaḥkāmaḥ* (desirous of heaven). Why "in a compound" (*samāse*)? Consider *yaśaḥ karoti* (he performs fame). Why "not situated in a subsequent member" (*anuttarapadasthasya*)? Consider *paramayaśaḥkāraḥ* (maker of supreme fame).

SK 161: *adhaḥśirasī pade* (A 8.3.47). The substitution of *s* for the *visarga* of these two [words] occurs when followed by the word *pada*. Examples: *adhaspadam*, *śiraspadam*. Only when it is a compound (*samāsa*), as in: *adhaḥpadam*, *śiraḥpadam*. Only when the [word ending in *visarga*] does not stand at the end of a prior member (*anuttarapadastha*), as in: *paramaśiraḥpadam*. Also in the *kaska*-group: *bhāskaraḥ*. Thus ends the section on the euphonic combination of *visarga*.
Now begins the section on the euphonic combinations of *svādi*.
When the *sup* suffix *su* is applied according to "svaujasamauḍ" and the form "śivam arcya" is established, [the rule] "sasajuṣo ruḥ" (A 8.2.66) applies:
"ru" shall be substituted for the final *s* of a word and for the word "sajuṣ. This is an exception to the rule of *jaś*-substitution.

SK 163: *ato roraplutād aplute* (A 6.1.113). After an *at* (short *a*) that is not protracted (*apluta*), the *u* of *ru* shall be substituted for *ru*, provided the following vowel is not protracted. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *yatva* (the change to *y*) prescribed by the rule *bho-bhago-agho...*. However, the fact that the substitution of *rutva* is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the substitution of *utva* does not apply here; for the rule prescribing *utva* has its own force (*sāmarthya*) in restating (*anūdya*) the condition of *rutva*.
SK 164: *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (A 6.1.102).

When an *ac* vowel follows the first or second [vowel] of a group of *ak* vowels, there shall be a single substitution of the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one. This being the case [the following applies]:

SK 165: *nād aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.104). When a vowel (*ac*) follows a short *a*-vowel (*avarṇa*), the long vowel resulting from the substitution of the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) does not occur. [Instead,] *ād guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87) applies: *eṅaḥ padāntād ati* (Pāṇini 6.1.109). Example: *śivo 'rcyaḥ*. Why is the term *ataḥ* (short *a*) specified as having a following *t* (*tapara*)? Consider: *devā atra*. Why is *ati* (long *ā*) specified as having a following *t* (*tapara*)? Consider: *śva āgantā*. Why is it said "not after a protracted vowel" (*aplutāt*)? Consider: *ehi susrota 3 atra snāhi*. Because a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of this rule, the vowel here is subsequent to a short *a*. However, when the condition "not after a protracted vowel" (*aplutāt*) is included as a qualifier, by its very force (*sāmarthya*), the protracted vowel is not considered non-existent. Yet, the inclusion of the *t* in *tapara* has no such force, because its purpose is already fulfilled by the exclusion of long vowels.

Why does it say "not followed by a vowel" (aplute)? [Consider: *tiṣṭhatu paya agnidatta*. Here, the vowel is protracted (*pluta*) because it follows a heavy syllable (*guru*) that is not followed by a vowel.

SK 166 *haśi ca* (A 6.1.114): After a short vowel that is not *pluta*, the substitute *u* shall occur for *ru* before a *haś* sound. Example: *śivo vandyaḥ*. Because of the inclusion of the indicatory letter *u* in the term *ror*, [the substitution does not apply] here: *prātar atra bhrātar gaccha*. When *devās iha* is established, the state of being *ru* (*rutvam*) applies.

Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.17 states: *bho-bhago-aghoad-pūrvasya yo 'śi*. For the *ru* [the substitute for *r*] preceded by *bho*, *bhago*, *aghoad*, or *a*, there shall be the substitution of *ya* when followed by a vowel (*aś*) or a semivowel (*ś*). This non-sandhi is based on a sūtra. The rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* applies: *devā iha* (or *devāyiha*). Why "when followed by a vowel" (*aśi*)? Consider *devāḥ santi*. Even though the visarga is obtained here because the substitution of *ya* is considered *asiddha* (not yet applied) according to P. 8.2.1, nevertheless, due to the status of the visarga as a *sthānivat* (representing its original), it would still possess the quality of *ru*; thus, the substitution of *ya* would occur. This is not a fault, because the rule is not a *m-alvidhi* (a rule concerning a single phoneme); rather, it relies on the form of the entire cluster *ruḥ*. The indeclinables *bhoḥ*, *bhagoḥ*, and *aghoad* end in the letter *s*. When the substitution of *ya* has been applied to their *ru*, [the forms become *bho ya*, *bhago ya*, etc., which then undergo further sandhi].

SK 168: According to Śākaṭāyana, when *aś* follows, the *v* and *y* at the end of a word may optionally be pronounced with less effort (*laghuprayatnatara*). That pronunciation in which laxity arises among the tip, middle, and root of the tongue is called "pronounced with less effort" (*laghūccāraṇa*).

SK 169: According to Gārgya (A 8.3.20), there is always the elision of a *y* that follows an *o* and is at the end of a word (*padānta*) when it is not characterized by light articulation (*alaghuprayatna*). The mention of Gārgya is for the sake of honor. Example: *bho acyata*. In the case of light articulation, it is *bhoy acyata*. Why "at the end of a word"? Consider: *toyam*.

SK 170: *uñi ca pade* (A 8.3.21). There is elision of *y* and *v* at the end of a word when preceded by *a*-vowels, before the word *uñ*. As in *sa u ekāgniḥ*. Why "in a word" (*pade*)? [Consider] *tantrayutam*; this is a form derived from the root *veñ* with *saṃprasāraṇa*. However, if *uñ* were taken as the specific nipāta mentioned in the sūtra, then the mention of "word" (*pada*) would be for the sake of the subsequent rule.

SK 171 *hali sarveṣām* (A 8.3.22): According to the opinion of all [grammarians], there is elision (*lopa*) of the *y* that follows *bho*, *bhago*, *agho*, or *a* as a preceding sound, whether that *y* is pronounced with a short or long duration, when a consonant (*hal*) follows. Examples: *bho devāḥ*; *bho lakṣmi bhovidvadvṛnda*; *bhago namaste*; *agho yāhi*; *devā namyāḥ*; *devā yānti*. Why "when a consonant follows" (*hali*)? [Consider: *devāyiha*.

SK 172: *ro 'supi* (A 8.2.69). The substitution of *r* for *ahar* occurs except when followed by a *sup* (nominal suffix). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *ru*. Examples: *aharahah* ("day after day"), *ahargaṇaḥ* ("a collection of days"). Why "except when followed by a *sup*"? Consider *ahobhyām*; here, the substitution of *ru* applies because of the rule *ahan* [8.2.68]. The substitution of *ru* should be stated [as an option] before the words *rūpa*, *rātri*, and *rathantara*. Examples: *ahorūpam* ("the form of the day"); *gatamahō rātrir eṣā* ("this night whose day has passed")—here, because a modified part is not different from the whole (*ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*), it is called *ahorātraḥ* ("day-and-night"); *ahorathantaram* ("the *Rathantara* chant of the day"). Before words such as *pati* ("lord"), the *r* may optionally replace *ahar* and others. This is an exception to the substitution of *visarga*. Examples: *aharpatiḥ* ("lord of the day"), *gīrpatiḥ* ("lord of speech"), *dhūrpatiḥ* ("lord of the yoke"). In the alternative case, there is either *visarga* or the *upadhmānīya* [aspiration].

SK 173 *ro ri* (A 8.3.14): When *repha* (*r*) follows, there shall be elision of the preceding *repha*. SK 174 *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho ’ṇaḥ* (A 6.3.111): When *ḍha*, *ra*, or *la* are elided, a long vowel takes the place of the preceding *aṇ* vowel.

The rule "one should elide *ḍ* and *r*" means that when those two letters—namely *ḍ* and *r*—follow, there should be a long vowel for the preceding *aṇ*. Examples: *punāramate*, *harīramyaḥ*, *śambhūrājate*. Why "of *aṇ*"? [Consider] *tṛḍhaḥ*; from the roots *tṛhū* (to injure) and *vṛhū* (to lift). The mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) is for the purpose of applying the lengthening to the preceding element alone, even when it is not part of a compound word (*anuttarapada*). Examples: *līḍhaḥ*, *ajarghāḥ*. In the case of *manas-rathaḥ*, once *r* is substituted [for *s*], both the substitution of *u* by the rule *haśi ca* and the elision of *r* by the rule *rori* would apply.

SK 175: *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* (A 1.4.2). When there is a conflict between rules of equal strength, the subsequent rule shall take effect. Thus, when the elision (*lopa*) [of the final vowel] would have applied, [it is prevented by: *pūrvatrāsiddham* (A 6.4.22). Because the rule *rori* (A 8.3.14) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it, only the substitution of *u* (*utvam*) occurs: *manorathaḥ*. SK 176: *etattadoḥ sulopo 'kor anañsamāse hali* (A 6.1.132). The elision of the nominative singular suffix *su* after *eta-* and *tad-*, provided they do not contain the phoneme *k* and are not part of a negative compound (*anañ-samāsa*), occurs before a consonant (*hal*).

The *su* [case-ending] of the words *etad* and *tad*, when they do not contain the letter *k*, is elided before a consonant (*hal*), but not in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). Example: *eṣa viṣṇuḥ* (This is Viṣṇu); *sa śambhuḥ* (He is Śambhu). Why "not containing *k*" (*akoḥ*)? Example: *eṣa ko rudraḥ* (Who is this Rudra?). Why "not in a negative compound" (*anañ-samāse*)? Example: *asaḥ śivaḥ* (He is not Śiva). Why "before a consonant" (*hali*)? Example: *eṣo 'tra* (He here).

SK 177: *so 'ci lope cet pādapūraṇam* (A 6.1.134). There shall be elision (*lopa*) of the *su* of *sas* before a vowel (*aci*), provided that by this very elision the metrical foot (*pāda*) is completed. For example: *semām viḍḍhi prabhṛtiṃ ya īśiṣe*. Vāmana maintains that here only a *ṛk*-verse foot is intended; others hold that, since there is no specification, a *śloka* foot may also be included, as in: *saiṣa dāśarathī rāmaḥ*. Why say "provided [the foot is completed] by elision"? Consider: *sa it kṣeti* or *sa evam uktvā*. The restriction "only when [the foot is completed]" is obtained through the continued application of the term *bahulam* ("frequently") from the preceding rule, *syaś chandasi bahulam*.
Therefore, it does not apply here. "I, who [have been] pure from birth... Thus ends the section on the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) of *sva* and other vowels.
Now begins the section on stems ending in vowels (ajanta-puṃliṅga-prakaraṇa).
(A 1.2.45) Pāṇini Sūtra 178: *arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam*.
Excluding a root (*dhātu*), a suffix (*pratyaya*), and that which ends in a suffix, a meaningful linguistic form shall receive the technical designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem).

SK 179: *kṛt-taddhita-samāsaś ca* (A 1.2.46). Items ending in *kṛt*-suffixes, items ending in *taddhita*-suffixes, and compounds shall receive the designation of *prātipadika*.
