Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *ukhāsrat* (formed with the suffix *kvip*), where the elision of the nasal is effected by the rule *aniditām*. Similarly, it does not apply to *parṇadhvat*. However, it would indeed apply to the root *añc*: *prācī*, *pratīcī*.

SK 456: *vano ra ca* (A 4.1.7). After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *van*, or one that ends in such a [stem], the suffix *ṅīp* shall occur in the feminine, and *ra* shall be the substitute for the final phoneme. The term *van* is a general designation for the suffixes *ṅvanip*, *kvanip*, and *vanip*. When a suffix is mentioned, it refers to what begins with that suffix and ends with it. Thus, because it qualifies the nominal stem, the suffix itself is also understood as ending in it. For example: *atisutvarī* ("one who has surpassed those who press Soma") and *atidhīvarī* ("one who has surpassed those who possess wisdom"). [Also: *śarvarī*. It should be stated: "In the case of *van*, [the substitution of *ra* does not occur] after a [nominal stem] ending in *ha*."

The meaning is that the suffix *ṅīp* and the augment *raṭ* are not applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *van*, nor after one ending in a stem ending in *van*. [The root] *oṇṛ* in the sense of "removing" takes the suffix *vanip*; by the rule *viḍvanoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.41), there is the substitution of *ā* for *o*. Thus, *avāvā brāhmaṇī* ("a Brahmin woman who removes") and *rājayudhvā* ("one who has fought with kings"). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it is optional: *bahudhīvarī* or *bahudhīvā*. In the alternative case, the suffix *ḍāp* will be taught later. Regarding Pāṇini 4.1.8, *pādo 'nyatarasyām*:
after a nominal stem ending in the word *pād-* which has taken a *samāsānta* suffix, the suffix *ṅīp* may optionally occur. Thus, *dvipadī* or *dvipāt*.

SK 458. *ṭāb ṛci* (A 4.1.9): When the word *ṛk* (verse) is to be expressed, the suffix *ṭāp* shall be applied after a stem ending in *pāda*. Examples: *dvipadā ṛk* (a verse of two feet), *ekapadā* (a verse of one foot). *na ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ* (A 4.1.10): [The suffix *ṭāp* is not applied] after the six [numerals] beginning with *svasṛ*. Examples: *pañca*, *catasraḥ*. In the case of *pañca*, although the *n* has been elided, the designation *ṣaṭ* (the name "six") still applies by the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ*; therefore, because the elision of the *n* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of rules concerning case endings (*sup*) and accent (*svara*) according to *nalopaḥ supsvara*, the prohibition *na ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ* applies, and thus the suffix *ṭāp* is not added. SK 459. *manaḥ* (A 4.1.12): [The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after a stem ending in] *man*.
The suffix *ṅīp* is not applied after [a stem ending in] *an*. *sīmā*, *sīmānau*.
According to Pāṇini 4.1.1 (*ano bahuvrīheḥ*), the suffix *ṅīp* is not applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *an*. *bahuyajvā*, *bahuyajvānau*.

SK 461 *ḍāb ubhābhyām anyatarasyām* (A 4.1.13): The suffix *ḍāp* may optionally be applied after both [bases] mentioned in the two preceding rules. Thus: *sīmā*, *sīme*, *sīmānau*; *dāmā*, *dāme*, *dāmāno*. Amara states that *dāmā* is not used in the masculine. Examples: *bahuyajvā*, *bahuyajve*, *bahuyajvānau*. SK 462 *ana upadhālopino ’nyatarasyām* (A 4.1.28): [The suffix *ṅīp*] may optionally be applied after a neuter base ending in *an* when the penultimate vowel is elided.

The suffix *ṅīp* may optionally be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *annat*, provided that the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is elided; in the alternative case, the suffixes *ḍāp* and the prohibition [of *ṅīp*] apply. Thus: *bahurājñī*, *bahurājñau*, *bahurāje*, *bahurājānau*.
(SK 463) According to A 7.3.44, the vowel *a* preceding a *k* belonging to a suffix becomes *i* before a feminine suffix (*āp*), except when that suffix is part of a nominal stem (*sup*).

When *ā* follows, the vowel *i* shall replace the *a* that precedes the letter *ka* situated in an affix (*pratyaya*), provided that this *ā* is not part of a case-ending (*sup*). Examples: *sarvikā*, *kārikā*. Why "after [the *a* of] *ataḥ*"? (Counter-example: *naukā*. Why "situated in an affix"? (Counter-example: *śakā* (from *śaknoti*). Why "not part of a case-ending"? (Counter-example: *bahuparivrājakā nagarī* ("a city with many wandering mendicants"). Why "after *ka*"? (Counter-example: *nandanā*. Why "of the preceding"? (This rule applies to the preceding vowel) so that it does not apply to the following one: *kaṭukā*. Why "followed by *t*" (*tapara*)? (Counter-example: *rākā*. Why "when *ā* follows" (*āpi*)? (Counter-example: *kārakaḥ*. There is an extension of the rule for *māmaka* and *naraka*: *māmikā*.

That which represents men (*narān*) is *narikā*. [The suffix *kan* is applied] after [stems ending in] *tyad*, *tad*, and *adas*: *dākṣiṇātyikā*, *ihatyikā*. A 7.3.45 states: "Not [the substitution of *ya* for *at* occurs] in the case of *yas*. (SK 464)

That [suffix] which would otherwise be applied after *dora* does not occur; namely, *yakā*, *sakā*, *yakām*, and *takām*. There is also a prohibition regarding *tyakan*: *adhityakā*, *upatyakā*. Furthermore, there is no [application of the suffix] after *vun* when expressing a blessing (*āśis*): *jīvakā*, *bhavakā*. Also when there is elision of the final member of a compound (*uttarapadalopa*): *devadattikā*, *devakā*. And in the case of *kṣipakā* and others: *kṣipakā*, *dhruvakā*, *kanyakā*, *caṭakā*. *Tārakā* is used in the sense of "star" (*jyotis*); elsewhere it is *tārikā*. *Varṇakā* is used in the sense of weaving (*tāntava*); elsewhere it is *varṇikā*. *Vartakā* is used in the sense of a bird (*śakuni*) according to the Easterners (*prācām*).

According to the Northern Grammarians (*udīcām*), however, [the suffix] *vartikā* [is formed]. [The word] *aṣṭakā* is used when the deity is the ancestors (*pitṛdaivatye*). Another form is *aṣṭikā*. It should be stated that for the words *sūtakā*, *putrikā*, and *vṛndārakā*, there is an option (*vā*). Here, the division is *vā a*; the meaning is that there is optionally the substitution of the vowel *a* for what precedes *kā*. Consequently, in the word *putrikā*, in the alternative case, the vowel *a* replaces the *ivarṇa* of the suffix *ṅīn*. In other instances, the vowel *a* is substituted for the *a* itself in order to block the substitution of *it* (the *ik*-substitution). Thus we have *sūtakā*, *sūtikā*, and so forth. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 7.3.46: *udīcām ātaḥ sthāne yakapūrvāyāḥ*.

In place of the vowel *a* which follows the suffix *yak* and precedes a feminine suffix, there may optionally be the substitution of *i*, provided that this *a* is preceded by a *ka*-class consonant (*kātpūrva*), when the suffix *āp* follows. By the rule *ke ’ṇaḥ*, the vowel is shortened. Examples: *āryakā* / *āryikā*; *caṭakakā* / *caṭakikā*. Why "after *āt*" (*ātaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *sāṃkāśyikā*, meaning "one who lives in Sāṃkāśya. Why "after *yak*" (*yak*)? [Counter-example: *aśvikā*. Why "feminine suffix" (*strīpratyaya*)? [Counter-example: *śubhaṃyāḥ*, meaning "one who goes toward what is auspicious. *śubhaṃyikā* means "a woman who is not well-known as one who goes toward what is auspicious. However, for the *yak* at the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*), the substitution is obligatory: *sunayikā*, *supākikā*. SK 466: For the words *bhastra*, *eṣā*, *ajā*, *jñā*, *dvā*, *svā*, even when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, [the substitution of *i* is obligatory before *āp*]. (A 7.3.47)

The word ending in *sva* (i.e., *sva*, *svau*, *svas*) is a term with its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka*). For these [words], the *it* augment may optionally occur after the vowel *a*. Since this would already be established by the rule of "application to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*), the phrase "also for those preceded by a negative particle" (*nañ-pūrvāṇām api*) is for the sake of clarity. The mention of *bhastrā* is for the purpose of including it when it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*); for in other cases, it is established by the subsequent rule. However, for these two—*dvā* and *etayoḥ*—when they are preceded by another word, the *it* augment does not occur, because of the prohibition "not after a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix" (*asu-pa*) which relies on the intervening case-suffix. Examples: *aneṣakā*, *paramaiṣakā*; *advake*, *paramadvake*.

The inclusion of the term *sva* is for the sake of [excluding] technical names (*saṃjñā*) and subordinate members (*upasarjana*). For here, the phrase "in place of *āt*" (*ātaḥ sthāne*), which is carried over from a previous rule, is a qualifier of *sva-āt*; it does not qualify *dvai* or *dvyoḥ*, because those two are impossible [in this context], nor does it qualify others, because there is no deviation [from the rule regarding them]. The word *sva*, when it is not a subordinate member, denotes "one's own" and is eligible for the suffix *akac*. However, when it has a different meaning, it is not feminine. But when it functions as a technical name or a subordinate member, it indeed serves as an example [of the rule], because it ends in the suffix *kap*.

And likewise, for *ātmīyā*, there is always the optional form *ātmanīyā* and *paramātmanīyā*. [The forms] *nirbhastrakā* / *nirbhastrikā*, *eṣakā* / *eṣikā* arise because the rule for *kṛṣat* does not apply here; thus there is no option. [Examples: *etikā* / *etike*, *ajakā* / *ajikā*, *jñakā* / *jñikā*, *dvake* / *dvike*, *niḥsvakā* / *niḥsvikā*. A 7.3.48 states: "Also after a word that has not been stated as having a masculine counterpart (*abhāṣitapuṃska*)."

Therefore, in place of the suffix prescribed by this [rule], *ita* or *id* may optionally occur. Examples: *gaṅgakā*, *gaṅgikā*. Because a *bahuvrīhi* compound has already been stated as having a masculine counterpart (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), the suffix prescribed after it occurs invariably. Example: "unknown" = *akhaṭvā*, *akhaṭvikā*. However, when the secondary suffix *kap* is added, there is only optionality. (SK 468) *ādācāryāṇām*: In the scope of the preceding sūtra, *āt* may optionally occur. Examples: *gaṅgākā*, *gāṅgikā*. But from a word that has already been stated as having a masculine counterpart, [the suffix is invariably *āt*]: *śubhrikā*.

SK 469 *anupasarjanāt* (A 4.1.14): This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) extending as far as [the sūtra] *yūnas tiḥ*. This very rule indicates that, regarding feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*), the operation applies to that which ends with [the specified element]. SK 470 *ṭiḍḍhāṇañdvayasajdaghnañmātractayapṭhakṭhañkañkvarapaḥ* (A 4.1.15).

The suffix *ṅīp* shall occur in the feminine after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a letter of the *yaṭ* class (the semi-vowels) that begins with one of those letters, provided it is not a secondary member (*upasarjana*) and ends in the vowel *a*. For example: *kurucarī*. Here, because it is a secondary member, the suffix does not apply: *bahukurucarā*. Regarding the term *nadī*, which is derived from the root *nada-ṭ*: although *ṅīp* would have been applicable here due to the presence of the marker *ṭ* (as in *vakṣyamāṇā*) and the presence of the marker *ṅ* (as in *ugit*), it does not occur. This is because of the metarule: "By virtue of the marker *ṅ* in *yāsuṭ*, it is understood that the grammatical operations dependent on markers do not apply to substitutes (*ādeśa*). Thus, [the suffix] does not apply.

Or rather, because the *śit* designation of the suffix *śānac* indicates that even in certain operations dependent on an *anubandha*, the prohibition "not when [the operation] is prescribed by means of a letter" (*analvidhau*) applies. Examples: *sauparṇeyī*, *aindrī*, *autsī*, *ūrudvayasī*, *ūrudaghnī*, *ūrumātrī*, *pañcayatī*, *ākṣiki*, *lāvaṇikī*, *yādṛśī*, *itvarī*. Even with the *ṇa* suffix used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*), there is the feminine suffix *ṅīp*: *caurī*. There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the suffixes *nañ*, *snañ*, *īkak*, *ūka*, and *yuṃs*, as well as for the words *taruṇa* and *taluna*: *straiṇī*, *pauṃsnī*, *śāktikī*, *āḍhyaṅkaraṇī*, *taruṇī*, *talunī*. SK 471: *yañaś ca* (A 4.1.16). [The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after a word ending in the patronymic suffix *yañ*.]

The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied to a word ending in *yañ* when it denotes a feminine. Once the elision of the vowel *ā* has been performed, [the following rule applies]: SK 472: *halas taddhitasya* (A 6.4.150). There is elision of the *yakāra* that follows a consonant (*hal*) and constitutes the penultimate (*upadhā*) of a *taddhita* suffix, provided that the suffix *ī* follows. Example: *gārgī* (feminine descendant of Garga). The suffix *ṅīp* does not apply to those [suffixes] taught under the heading of *apatya* (descendant). Example: *dvaipyā* (born on an island), from *dvīpa*. Because of the mention of the "heading" (*adhikāra*), it is not applied here in the case of *daivyā*, meaning "the offspring of Deva. For the suffix *yañ* in *devād yañ ñau* belongs to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group, and is not recited under the heading of *apatya*.
SK 473: *prācām ṣpha taddhitaḥ* (A 4.1.17).
After a stem ending in *yañ*, the suffix *ṣpha* may optionally occur in the feminine; and this [suffix] is a *taddhita*.
SK 474: *ṣaḥ pratyayasya* (A 1.3.6). [The letter *ṣ* is the *it* of a suffix.]
The initial *ṣ* of an affix shall be *ṣit*. (Pāṇini 7.1.2) states:

"In place of the phonemes *ph*, *ḍh*, *kh*, *ch*, and *gh* that constitute the beginning of an affix, there shall be the substitutes *āy*, *an*, *īn*, *īy*, and *iy*, respectively. Because it ends in a *taddhita* affix, it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). By virtue of the *ṣit* designation, even though the feminine gender is already expressed by the suffix *ṣpha*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule to be stated later, "ṣid-gaurādibhyaś ca" (Pāṇini 4.1.41). Thus, we have *gārgyāyaṇī*.

SK 476: After all [words] beginning with *lohitādika*—that is, after those beginning with *lohita* and ending with *kata*, which are formed with the suffix *yañ*—the suffix *ṣpha* shall always occur. Examples: *lauhityāyanī*, *kātyāyanī*. SK 477:
And [the suffix *ṣpha* occurs] after *kauravya* and *māṇḍūka*. (A 4.1.19)

From these two [bases], the suffix *ṣpha* shall occur; it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭāp* and *ṅīṣ*. From the group beginning with *kurū-* comes *ṇya*: *kauravyāyaṇī*. From *maṇḍūka* comes *ḍhak*, and by the rule "and *aṇ* from *maṇḍūka*," we have *māṇḍūkāyaṇī*. There is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *āsuri*: *āsurāyaṇī*. SK 478: *vayasi prathame* (A 4.1.20). The suffix *ṅīp* occurs in the feminine after a word ending in short *a* that denotes the first stage of life. Example: *kumārī*. It should be stated that this applies when the age is not the last (*acarama*). Examples: *vadhūṭī*, *ciraṇṭī*. The words *vadhū* and *ciraṇṭa* denote youth. Why "ending in *a*" (*ataḥ*)? Example: *śiśuḥ* (which ends in *u*). Not so in the case of *kanyā*; because of the specific grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) "of *kanyā*, [the substitute] *kanīna* [is applied]."

SK 479 (A 4.1.21): After a *dvigu* compound ending in *a*, the suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied. For example: *trilokī*. Because it belongs to the *ajādi* group, *triphalā* [is formed]. *Tryanīkā* refers to an army. SK 480 (A 4.1.22): The suffix *ṅīp* is not applied after words denoting non-measures (*aparimāṇa*), nor after *bista*, *ācita*, and *kambalya*, when there is no elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix.

The suffix *ṅīp* shall not be applied after a *dvigu* compound ending in a word denoting an immeasurable quantity (*aparimāṇa*) or in *bista*, *ācita*, or *kambalya*, when there is elision (*luk*) of a secondary suffix (*taddhita*). *Pañcabhir aśvaiḥ krītā* ("bought for five horses") results in *pañcāśvā*. [Here,] the suffix *ṭhak* [denoted by] *ārhīyaṣṭhak* is applied, and it is elided by the rule *ardhyadhaḥ*. *Dvau bistau pacati* ("she cooks two *bistas*") results in *dvibistā*; likewise *dvyācitā* and *dvikambalyā*. However, because it ends in a measure of capacity (*parimāṇa*), *dvyāḍhakī* is formed. Why "when there is elision of a secondary suffix"? Consider *pañcāśvī* in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). SK 481: After a *dvigu* ending in *kāṇḍa*, [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied] when referring to a field (*kṣetra*). (A 4.1.23)

In the case of a field (*kṣetra*), when a *dvigu* compound ends in *kāṇḍa*, the suffix *ṅīp* is not applied when there is elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix. For example: "that field-division which has two *kāṇḍas* as its measure" is *dvikāṇḍā kṣetrabhaktiḥ*. This is because the suffix *mātrac* prescribed by the rule *pramāṇe dvayasac-daghnañ-mātracaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.37) undergoes obligatory elision (*luk*) after a *dvigu* when expressing measure, according to the rule *pramāṇe lo dvigor nityam* (Pāṇini 5.2.37). Why say "in the case of a field"? Consider: *dvikāṇḍī rajjuḥ* ("a rope two *kāṇḍas* long").

By the rule *puruṣāt pramāṇe ’nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.24), the suffix *ṅīp* may optionally be applied after a *dvigu* compound ending in *puruṣa* when it expresses measure, provided there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix. For example: "that trench which has two *puruṣas* as its measure" is *dvipuruṣī* or *dvipuruṣā parikhā*.

SK 483 *ūdhaso 'naṅ* (A 5.4.131): For a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ūdhas*, there shall be the substitution of *anaṅ* when [the word] is feminine. When *anaṅ* has been applied, the suffixes *ḍāp*, *ṅīp*, and the prohibition [of *ṅīṣ*] would otherwise apply;
however, SK 484 *bahuvrīher ūdhaso ṅīṣ* (A 4.1.25) [prescribes *ṅīṣ* instead].

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ūdhas* when denoting the feminine. Example: *kuṇḍodhnī* ("having a pail-like udder"). Why "in the feminine"? Example: *kuṇḍodhaḥ* (neuter), meaning "a cow with a pail-like udder. In this case, even the substitution *anaṅ* does not occur, because the rule for that substitution includes the specification "in the feminine" (*striyām*) as an addition. SK 485: After a *bahuvrīhi* beginning with a numeral or an indeclinable, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied;

this is an exception to *ṅīṣ*. Examples: *dvyūdhnī* ("having two udders") and *atyūdhnī* ("exceeding the udder"). The restriction "after a *bahuvrīhi*" is essential: *atyūdhāḥ* ("one who has surpassed the udder") [is not a *bahuvrīhi*, hence no *ṅīp*].

SK 486: *dāmahāyanāntāc ca* (A 4.1.27). The suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound beginning with a numeral and ending in *dāman* or *hāyana*. This rule is stated because, in the case of compounds ending in *dāman*, both *ḍāp* and the prohibition [of *ṅīp*] would otherwise apply; and in the case of those ending in *hāyana*, *ṭāp* would apply. Examples: *dvidāmnī* ("having two neck-ropes"). Because the term *avyaya* ("indeclinable") continues [from the previous rule], in the case of *uddāmā vaḍavā* ("an unbridled mare"), both *ḍāp* and the prohibition [of *ṅīp*] are optionally available. Examples: *dvihāyanī bālā* ("a two-year-old girl"). It should be stated that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the *hāyana* in the words *tri* and *catur*. The suffix *ṅīp* and the substitution of *ṇ* are desired only when *hāyana* denotes age. Examples: *trihāyaṇī*, *caturhāyaṇī*.
In cases other than those denoting age, [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied]. A house that is three years old or four years old is called *tri-hāyanā* or *catur-hāyanā*.

According to A 4.1.29, *nityaṃ saṃjñā-chandasoḥ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *an* which has undergone elision of its penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopin*). For example, there is a city named *surājñī*. In other instances, however, there is only the optionality provided by the previous rule. In the Veda, however, we find *śatamūrdhnī*.

SK 488: After the nine [stems] *kevala*, *āmaka*, *bhāgadheya*, *pāpa*, *apara*, *samāna*, *āryakṛta*, *sumaṅgala*, and *bheṣaja*, the suffix *ṅīp* is invariably applied in the sense of a technical term (*saṃjñā*) or in Vedic literature (*chandas*). For example: *athota indraḥ kevalīr viśaḥ* ("Then Indra [conquered] the exclusive clans"), *māmakī*, *bhāgadheyī*, *pāpī*, *aparī*, *samānī*, *āryakṛtī*, *sumaṅgalī*, *bheṣajī*. Elsewhere, one says *kevalā* and so forth. The inclusion of *māmaka* is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), since the formation would already be established by its ending in the suffix *aṇ*; therefore, in common usage (*loke*), when not a technical term, one says *māmikā*. SK 489: The augment *nuk* is added after the stems *antarvat* and *pativat*. (A 4.1.32)

The suffix *nuk* shall be applied to these two words when used in the feminine. By the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added; however, for the meanings "pregnant" (*garbhiṇī*) and "having a living husband" (*jīvadbhartṛkā*), the original forms of the stems are prescribed as exceptions (*nipātana*). In that regard, in the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) "there is a fetus within her" (*antarastyasyāṃ garbhaḥ*), the word *antaḥ* primarily denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*); therefore, because it lacks grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb *asti*, the suffix *matup* would not otherwise apply, and thus it is prescribed here as an exception. In the case of *pativatnī*, however, the substitution of *v* for *m* is prescribed. Thus: *antarvatnī* ("pregnant") and *pativatnī* ("having a living husband"). But the counter-examples are: *antarastyasyāṃ śālāyāṃ ghaṭaḥ* ("there is a pot in this house") and *patimatī pṛthivī* ("the earth possesses a lord"). [This is governed by] Pāṇini 4.1.33: *patyur no yajñasaṃyoge* ("*n* replaces *t* of *pati* when joined with a sacrifice").

The substitution of *na* for the word *pati* occurs when there is a connection with a sacrifice (*yajña*). For example: *vasiṣṭhasya patnī*. The meaning is: "the enjoyer of the fruit of the sacrifice performed by him," because husband and wife have joint authority (*sahādhikāra*) [in ritual acts].
This is according to A 4.1.34: *vibhāṣā sapūrvasya*.

For a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the word *pati* that is preceded by another member, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally occur. Thus: *gṛhasya patiḥ* (the lord of the house) becomes *gṛhapatiḥ*; [with the optional suffix] *gṛhapatnī*. Although the rule "provided it is not a secondary member" (*anupasarjanasya*) is carried over here for the sake of subsequent rules, it is not a qualifier of *pati* itself, but rather of that which ends in *pati*. Consequently, this applies even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound: *dṛḍhapatnī* (one whose husband is firm) and *dṛḍhapatiḥ*; *vṛṣalapatnī* (the wife of a low-caste man) and *vṛṣalapatiḥ*. If one asks how it is when the words are separated, as in *vṛṣalasya patnī*, the answer is: it is through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), where she is called *patnī* because she is like a *patnī*. Or else: [it is so because the term is applied to her].

The suffix *kvip* is applied after a word ending in the denominative suffix *kvip* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed; and in this view, the forms are *patniyau* and *patniyaḥ*. This is the specific distinction regarding the domain of *iyaṅ*. Why [is it said] "preceded by another word" (*sapūrvasya*)? [Consider: *gavāṃ patiḥ strī* ("a woman who is the mistress of cows").

SK 492: *nityaṃ sapatnyādiṣu* (A 4.1.35). This is an exception to the preceding optional rule. Even when *samāna* undergoes the substitution of *sa*, it is prescribed as such in the case of *sapatnī* and others. She whose husband is the same is *sapatnī*; likewise *ekapatnī* and *vīrapatnī*.

SK 493: Regarding *pūtakratu* and others (A 4.1.36), this set of three sūtras is intended to apply only in the sense of a "connection with a male" (*puṃyoga*). The wife of *Pūtakratu* is *pūtakratāyī*; however, she by whom the *kratu*s (sacrifices) have been purified is simply called *pūtakratu*.
SK 494: Regarding *vṛṣākapi*, *agni*, *kusita*, and *kusida*, [the final vowel] is acute (A 4.1.37).

For these [words], the acute-accented *ai* shall be the substitute, and the suffix *ṅīp* shall also be applied. Thus, the female of *vṛṣākapi* is *vṛṣākapāyī*. According to Amara, "Hara and Viṣṇu are *vṛṣākapī*," and also, "*vṛṣākapāyī* refers to Śrī and Gaurī. Examples are *agnayī*, *kusitāyī*, and *kusidāyī*. The word *kusida* has a short vowel in the middle, not a long one. SK 495: *manor au vā* (A 4.1.38).

For the word *manu*, there is optionally the substitution of the acute-accented *au* and the acute-accented *ai*; by the rule of simultaneous prescription (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭa*), the suffix *ṅīp* is also applied after these two. Thus, the female of *manu* is *manāvī* or *manāyī*. The masculine form is *manuḥ*.

SK 496: *varṇād anudāttāt topadhāt to naḥ* (A 4.1.39). After a non-predominant (*anupasarjana*) nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a word denoting color (*varṇa*), which is anudātta-final and has *t* as its penultimate letter (*topadha*), the suffix *ṅīp* may optionally be applied, and the substitution of *na* for the *t* is also prescribed. Examples: *enī*, *etā*; *rohiṇī*, *rohitā*. According to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* rule "of colors ending in *ta*, *na*, *ti*, or *tā*," these are ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable). The *Gṛhya-sūtra* states: "and with a three-striped porcupine quill" (*tryeṇyā ca śalalyā*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has these three. Why "anudātta"? [Counter-example: *śvetā*. This word is antodātta (accented on the final syllable) by the rule "of *ghṛta* and so forth. The restriction "after *at*" (from A 4.1.38) still applies. [Counter-example: *śitiḥ* (feminine).

The addition of *piśaṅga* [to the list] is required: *piśaṅgī*, *piśaṅgā*. It is not so for *asita* and *palita*: *asitā*, *palitā*. According to some, in the Veda (*chandasi*), the suffix *kna* is applied: *asiknī*, *paliknī*. However, the word *avadāta* does not denote a color, but rather purity; therefore, it remains simply *avadātā*. [Pāṇini 4.1.40: "Elsewhere, *gīṣ* [is applied]."

The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied in the feminine after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting color that ends in an *anudātta* vowel and is not separated by a *taddhita* suffix. Examples: *kalmāṣī*, *sāraṅgī*. These two words are *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable) according to the rule: "In a polysyllabic word, if the final syllable is light, the heavy penultimate syllable is accented. Why "ending in an *anudātta*"? Consider: *kṛṣṇā*, *kapilā*.

By the rule *ṣid-gaurādibhyaś ca* (A 4.1.41), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after stems ending in *ṣit* (those marked with *ṣ* as an it-marker) and after the *gaura*-group. Examples: *nartakī*, *gaurī*. The suffix *ṅīṣ* is optionally applied to *anaḍuh* in the feminine: *anuḍuhī* or *anaḍvāhī*. The group beginning with *pippalī* is also included; this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).

SK 499: *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ* (A 6.4.149). There is elision of the *y* that is in the penultimate position (*upadhā*) of a stem, provided that this *y* is a constituent part of *sūrya*, *agastya*, or *matsya*. [Specifically: for *matsya*, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied; for *sūrya* and *agastya*, when *cha* or *ṅīp* is applied; and for *tiṣya* and *puṣya*, it should be stated that there is elision of *y* when referring to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). *Matsī*: This is established by the fact that the root *mā* is marked with *ṣ* in the rule *mātari ṣic ca*; however, because the word *mātāmahī* is listed in the *gaurādi* group, the application of the *ṅīṣ* suffix after roots marked with *ṣ* is not mandatory. Thus, *daṃṣṭrā* is formed by the *ṅīṣ* suffix.

The suffix *matup* is applied after the following words to denote possession: *jānapada*, *kuṇḍa*, *goṇa*, *sthala*, *bhājana*, *āgaka*, *alana*, *nīla*, *kuśa*, *kāmuka*, and *kabara*; provided that these words do not refer respectively to: a place of residence, a vessel, a field, a natural object, a time, a color, grass, a lover, and a braid of hair; and provided that they do not refer to: a function, a vessel, something artificial, a broth, thickness, a color, a covering, an iron product, a desire for sexual intercourse, and a style of hair. (Pāṇini 5.2.137).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied after these eleven nominal stems (*prātipadika*) in the sense of "occupation" (*vṛtti*) and so forth, respectively: 1. If it is an occupation, [the word] is *jānapadī*; otherwise, it is *jānapadī*. Since it ends in the suffix *añ* due to its being listed in the *utsādi* group, the suffix *ṅīp* applies by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, and it is udātta on the first syllable. 2. If it is a vessel, [the word] is *kuṇḍī*; otherwise, it is *kuṇḍā*. [The root] *kuḍi* means "to burn"; the suffix *ap* is added by the rule *guroś ca halaḥ*. However, as for the word *kuṇḍa* which denotes a human caste—meaning "one born of an adulterer on an unmarried woman"—the suffix *ṅīṣ* certainly occurs there by the characteristic of a genus (*jāti*).

For in the case of *amatra* (a vessel), since it cannot refer to a female, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is prescribed where it was not previously applicable, rather than being restricted. If *goṇī* means a "receptacle for grain," [then *goṇī* is used]; otherwise, it is *goṇā*. If *sthalī* means "uncultivated land," [then *sthalī* is used]; otherwise, it is *sthalā*. If *bhājī* means "boiled food," [then *bhājī* is used]; otherwise, it is *bhājā*. If *nāgī* means "thick," [then *nāgī* is used]; otherwise, it is *nāgā*. The word *nāga*, when denoting an elephant, is used elsewhere as a counter-example because it is applied to something else through its connection with the quality of thickness. If *kālī* refers to a color, [then *kālī* is used]; otherwise, it is *kālā*. If *nīlī* refers to something other than clothing, [then *nīlī* is used]; otherwise, it is *nīlā*.

The meaning is "a garment dyed with indigo. [The suffix] *an* is applied when it is said "it should be smeared with indigo. It is not applied everywhere even when there is no covering; rather, it applies when referring to the medicinal herb *nīlī*, as in *nīlī*; and when referring to an animal, as in *nīlī gauḥ* ("an indigo-colored cow"). When used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), it is optionally so: *nīlī* or *nīlā*. If it refers to a modification of *kuśā* grass, it is *kuśānyā*. If it refers to a woman desiring sexual intercourse, it is *kāmukānyā*. If it refers to the braiding of hair, it is *kabarānyā*; the meaning here is "variegated. According to A 4.1.43, *śoṇāt prācām*: [the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after *śoṇa* according to the Eastern grammarians], resulting in *śoṇī* or *śoṇā*.

SK 502 *voto guṇavacanāt* (A 4.1.44): After a word ending in *u* that denotes a quality (*guṇa*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally be applied. Examples: *mṛdvī* / *mṛduḥ*. Why "ending in *u*" (*utaḥ*)? [Consider] *śuciḥ*. Why "denoting a quality" (*guṇa*)? [Consider] *ākhuḥ*. It is not [applied] after words ending in *kharu* or those having a conjunct consonant as a penultimate element (*saṃyogopadha*). Examples: *kharuḥ* (a maiden choosing her own husband), *pāṇḍuḥ*. SK 503 *bahvādibhyaś ca* (A 4.1.45): [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] also after the group of words beginning with *bahu*.

Or, the suffix *ṅīṣ* may be applied after these [words mentioned previously]. *bahvī*, *bahuḥ*. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix containing the vowel *ī*, provided it does not end in *ktin*. *rātriḥ*, *rātrī*. According to some, [it is applied] after any word that does not signify the action expressed by *ktin*. *śakaṭiḥ*, *śakaṭī*. Why "provided it does not signify the action expressed by *ktin*"? [Consider: *ajananiḥ*. The word *paddhati* is recited in the list [of words taking *ṅīṣ*] for the purpose of a mandatory rule, as its application was not otherwise established due to ending in *ktin*. By the rule *himakāṣihatiṣu ca*, there is the substitution of *pad* [for *pād*]. *paddhatiḥ*, *paddhatī*. A 4.1.48: *puṃyogād ākhyāyām* ("When denoting a woman through her connection with a male").

The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied after a word denoting a male when it is used in the feminine sense due to its connection with a man. For example: *gopasya strī* (the wife of a cowherd) becomes *gopī*. [However, this does not apply] to words ending in *pālaka*: *gopālikā*, *aśvapālikā*. After the word *sūrya*, when it denotes a deity, the suffix *cāp* should be stated: *sūryasya strī devatā* (the female deity Sūrya) becomes *sūryā*. Why "when it denotes a deity"? [Because] *sūrī* refers to Kuntī, who is a human female (*mānuṣī*). SK 505: After *indra*, *varuṇa*, *bhava*, *śarva*, *rudra*, *mṛḍa*, *himāraṇya*, *yavāva*, *vana*, *mātula*, and *ācārya*, the augment *ānuk* is added [before the feminine suffix].

For these [words], there shall be the augment *ānuk* and the suffix *ṅīṣ*. For the six beginning with Indra, as well as for *mātula* (maternal uncle) and *ācārya* (teacher), only the addition of the suffix *puṇ* is desired. In that case, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is already established, only the augment *ānuk* is prescribed. For the remaining four, both [the suffix and the augment] apply. *Indrāṇī*. [The suffix *ānuk* applies] after *himā* and *araṇya* when denoting greatness: great snow is *himānī*; a great forest is *araṇyānī*. [The suffix *ānuk* applies] after *yava* when denoting a defect: defective barley is *yavānī*. [The suffix *ānuk* applies] after *yavana* when denoting a script: the script of the Yavanas is *yavanānī*. After *mātula* and *upādhyāya*, the augment *ānuk* is optional.

*mātulānī*, *mātulī*; *upādhyāyanī*, *upādhyāyī*. However, when she is herself the female teacher (*adhyāpikā*), the suffix *vāṅīṣ* should be stated [as an option]: *upādhyāyī*, *upādhyāyā*. From *ācārya*, there is also the suffix *aṇ*: the wife of an *ācārya* is *ācāryānī*. This is only in the sense of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). When she is herself the female expounder, she is *ācāryā*. From *arya* and *kṣatriya*, the suffix may optionally be used in the same sense (*svārthe*): *aryāṇī*, *aryā*—meaning a mistress or a Vaiśya woman; *kṣatriyāṇī*, *kṣatriyā*. But in the sense of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), they are *aryī* and *kṣatriyī*. How is *brahmāṇī* formed? It means "she who brings or sustains the Brahman," derived from the root with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).

SK 506 (A 4.1.40): After a word ending in *krīta* that has an instrument (*karaṇa*) as its prior member and ends in a short *a*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine. Example: *vastrakrītī* ("bought for a garment"). In some cases, it does not occur: *dhanakrītā* ("bought for wealth"). SK 507 (A 4.1.51): [The suffix *ṅīṣ*] occurs after a word ending in *kta* when it expresses a small quantity.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a feminine noun ending in *kta* derived from a verbal root meaning "to smear" (*lip*), when the sense of "smallness" is to be indicated. Example: *abhraliptī dyauḥ* ("the sky is thinly covered with clouds"). Why is it said "when expressing smallness"? Consider: *candanaliptāṅganā* ("a woman smeared with sandalwood paste").

(A 4.1.52) After a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *kta*, which is oxytone (has the acute accent on the final syllable) and ends in *a*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied in the feminine. It should be stated that this applies when the first member is a genus name (*jāti*). Therefore, it does not apply when preceded by *bahu*, *nañ* (negative particle), words for time, or *sukha*, etc. Examples: *ūrubhinnī* ("one whose thighs are split"). Not here: *bahukṛtā* ("much done"). Not after a word ending in *jāta*: *dantajātā* ("one whose teeth have grown"). [Special rule: *pāṇigṛhītī* is used in the sense of "wife"; otherwise, it is *pāṇigṛhītā*.

SK 509 *asvāṅgapūrvapadād vā* (A 4.1.53). Since the preceding rule would have mandated [the suffix] obligatorily, this present rule provides an option. Examples: *surāpīti* and *surāpītā*. Why [does the sūtra specify] "from that which has an udātta accent on the final syllable"? Consider *vastracchannā*; here, by the prohibition of the udātta [on the final syllable] due to the rule *anācchādanāt*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied even by the preceding rule. SK 510 *svāṅgāc copasarjanād asaṃyogopadhāt* (A 4.1.54).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is optionally applied after a feminine base ending in short *a*, provided that the word is a *svāṅga* (body part) whose penultimate letter is not a *saṃyoga* (conjunct consonant) and which is an *upasarjana* (secondary member of a compound). Examples: *atikeśī* or *atikeśā* ("one who has surpassed her hair"); *candramukhī* or *candramukhā* ("moon-faced"). However, from a base with a *saṃyoga* as the penultimate letter, we have *sugulphā* ("having beautiful ankles"). Why "from an *upasarjana*"? Consider *śikhā* ("crest"), which is not an *upasarjana*. A body part (*svāṅga*) is of three kinds: it must be non-fluid, possess form, reside in a living being, and not be produced by a morbid change. Thus, *susvedā* ("exuding sweat") is not a *svāṅga* because of its fluidity; *sujñānā* ("possessing good knowledge") is not because it lacks form; and *sumukhā śālā* ("a hall with a fine entrance") is not because it does not reside in a living being.

[The suffix *matup*] is applied after words meaning "having a good swelling" because it arises from a modification; and [it is applied] even when that [swelling] is not located there, as seen in the case of *sukeśī* or *sukeśā* "having beautiful hair," since [the term for hair] is seen applied to a living being even though it does not reside in a non-living thing. If, by that [rule], it were thus joined [to the base], then [we have] *sustanī* or *sustanā* "having beautiful breasts," because [the term for breasts] resides in something resembling a living being, just like [the term for] a living being itself.
[And this is taught by: *nāsikodarauṣṭhajaṅghādantakarṇaśṛṅgācca* (Pāṇini 4.1.55).

Or rather, the suffix *ṅīṣ* may be applied after these [words]. In the case of the first two, the prohibition characterized by the presence of many vowels (*bahvac*) and the characteristic of *jvalā* is set aside, according to the maxim of "an exception [applies] before [the general rule]. However, for the five beginning with *oṣṭha*, this statement is made because the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on the rule "from words ending in *asaṃyoga-upadha*" would otherwise apply, according to the maxim of "an exception [applies] in the middle. But the prohibition characterized by the presence of the prefix *saha-* or *nañ* is a sublater of this [present rule], due to its higher status [in the order of rules]. Examples include *tuṅganāsikī* and *tuṅganāsikā*, etc. It does not apply here: *sahanāsikā*, *anāsikā*. Regarding this, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states: "It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after *aṅga*, *atra*, and *kaṇṭha*."

*svaṅgī*, *svaṅgā* and so forth. Some maintain that this should be included by the particle *ca* used in the sense of a collective inclusion (*anuktasamuccaya*) of what has not been explicitly stated. However, the authoritative scholars (*prāmāṇika*) hold that this is not a valid authority because it is not mentioned in the Bhāṣya and other such works. Here are the Vārttikas: *pucchāc ca* (And [the suffix ṅīṣ is applied] after *puccha*). Examples: *supucchī*, *supucchā*. *kabaramaṇiviṣaśarebhyo nityam* (It is obligatory after *kabara*, *maṇi*, *viṣa*, and *śara*). Example: *kabara-pucchī* (a peahen), one whose tail is variegated (*kabara*), and so forth. *upamānāt pakṣāc ca pucchāc ca* (After a word denoting a standard of comparison, the suffix is applied obligatorily after *pakṣa* and *puccha*). The word "obligatorily" (*nityam*) applies here as well. Examples: *ulūka-pakṣī śālā* (a house with an owl-wing roof); *ulūka-pucchī senā* (an army with an owl-tail banner).
*na kroḍādibahvacaḥ* (The suffix is not applied after words beginning with *kroḍa* when they have more than two syllables). (A 4.1.56)

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied after words beginning with *kroḍa* that have more than two syllables when they denote a part of one's own body (*svāṅga*). Examples: *kalyāṇakroḍā* ("one with a beautiful chest"), *aśvānām uraḥ kroḍā* ("the chest of horses"). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); for instance, *sujaghanā* ("one with beautiful hips").

By rule A 4.1.57, *ṅīṣ* is also not applied after words preceded by the three [particles] *sa-* (*saha*), *nañ*, and *vidyamāna*. Examples: *sakeśā* ("having hair"), *akeśā* ("hairless"), *vidyamānanāsikā* ("possessing a nose").

SK 514: After *nakha* and *mukha*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* shall not occur when [the compound] denotes a name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *śūrpaṇakhā*, *gauramukhā*. Why "when it is a name"? Example: *tāmramukhī kanyā* ("a girl with a copper-colored face"). SK 515: After [compounds] where the first member is a cardinal direction (*dik*), the suffix *ṅīp* occurs.

The substitution of *ṅīp* for *ṅīṣ* shall occur after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that has a cardinal direction as its first member and ends in a word denoting a part of the body. Example: *prāṅmukhī* ("facing east"). This word is accented on the first syllable. (SK 516) *vāhaḥ*:

The suffix *ṅīṣ* shall occur after a nominal stem ending in *vāh*. Only *ṅīṣ* is understood here, not *ṅīp*. Example: *dityavāṭ ca me dityauhī ca me* ("May I have a male calf born in two years and a female cow born in two years").

In the rule *sakhyaśiśvīti bhāṣāyām* (A 4.1.62), the word *iti* should be understood as following *bhāṣāyām* in the sense of "in this manner" (*prakāre*). Consequently, [the suffix] occurs even in the Veda (*chandas*) in certain instances: *sakhī*, *aśiśvī*; "let the milch-cows that are not accompanied by their calves (*aśiśvīḥ*) low. SK 518: *jāter astrīviṣayād ayopadhāt* (A 4.1.63).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after a word denoting a genus (*jāti*) that is not restricted to the feminine and does not have *y* as its penultimate letter. "Genus" (*jāti*) refers to that which is grasped by its form; the meaning is that it is manifested by a recurring configuration. Example: *taṭī*. Another definition of genus is: "That which does not possess all genders, and which is to be understood from being taught once. This means that a genus is easily grasped even without being explicitly stated in another individual instance, provided it has been taught once in one instance, on the condition that it does not possess all genders. Example: *vṛṣalī*. Why include the word "existent" (*sat*) [in the definition]? Consider *śuklā* ("white"), which is a quality and not a genus. Why include "once" (*sakṛt*) and so forth? Consider *mṛdvī* ("soft") and *paṭvī* ("clever"). These are qualities that can exist in both masculine and neuter forms (e.g., *mṛduḥ*, *paṭuḥ*), and thus they do not satisfy the condition of not possessing all genders. Therefore, they are not considered genera in this context. *Taṭī*: The bank of a river. *vṛṣalī*: A woman of the lowest caste. *Śuklā*: White. *mṛdvī*: Soft. *Paṭvī*: Clever. *Akṣikī*: A type of bird. *Ākṛtigrahaṇā jātiḥ*: A genus is that which is grasped by its form. *Sakṛdākhyātanirgrāhyā*: It is to be understood from being taught once. *Asarvaliṅgatve sati*: Provided that it does not possess all genders. *Eka-vyaktau kathanād vyaktyantare kathanaṃ vināpi sugrahā*: Because it has been taught in one individual instance, it is easily grasped in another individual instance even without being taught again. (Note: The examples *mṛdvī* and *paṭvī* illustrate that although these words denote qualities, they are excluded because they can take masculine and neuter endings, thus failing the criterion of *asarvaliṅgatva*.)

*Devadattā*. The meaning is that a word ending in a patronymic suffix (*apatya-pratyaya*), which denotes both a lineage (*gotra*) along with its branches of conduct (*caraṇa*) and one who studies a particular Vedic school (*śākhādhyetṛ*), receives the grammatical operation of a genus (*jāti*). Examples are *aupagavī*, *kaṭhī*, *bahvṛcī*, and *brāhmaṇī*; however, in the case of *brāhmaṇī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is superseded by *ṅīn* due to its inclusion in the *śārṅgarava*-group. Why [is the word] "genus" (*jāti*) mentioned? [Consider] *muṇḍā* ("shaven-headed woman"). Why [the condition] "not referring to a female" (*astrīviṣaya*)? [Consider] *balākā* ("crane," which is a feminine species). Why [the condition] "not having *y* as a penultimate letter" (*ayopadha*)? [Consider] *kṣatriyā* ("Kṣatriya woman"). Regarding the prohibition for words having *y* as a penultimate letter, there is no prohibition for the words *hayá-* (horse), *gavaya-* (wild ox), *mukaya-* (a type of fish), *manuṣya-* (human), and *matsya-* (fish). Example: *hayī*.

*gavayī* / *mukayī*: by A 6.4.148 (*halas taddhitasya*), there is the elision of *ya*. *manuṣī*: by A 4.1.63 (*matsyasya ṅyām*). *matsī*. SK 519: *pākakarṇaparṇapuṣpaphalamūlavālottarapadāc ca* (A 4.1.64). After a word ending in *pāka*, *karṇa*, *parṇa*, *puṣpa*, *phala*, *mūla*, or *bāla* as its final member, the suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied, even if the word denotes a genus (*jāti*) or refers specifically to the feminine. Examples: *odanapākī* (one who cooks rice), *śaṅkukarṇī* (having spike-like ears), *śālaparṇī* (a type of plant), *śaṅkhapuṣpī* (conch-flowered), *dāsīphalī* (having the fruit of a slave-girl), *darbhamūlī* (having roots like *darbha* grass), *govālī* (having hair like a cow’s tail). These are conventional designations for specific medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*).

SK 520: After the word *manuṣya* ("human"), the suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied [to form feminine nouns]. Example: *dākṣī* (the daughter of Dakṣa). It is also applied after words having *y* as their penultimate letter (*yopadha*). Example: *audameyī*, meaning "the female descendant of Udameya. Why specify "after *manuṣya*"? [Counter-example: *tittiriḥ* (a partridge). SK 521: The suffix *ūṅ* is applied after a word ending in *u*.

The suffix *ūṅ* shall be applied in the feminine to words denoting a human class (*manuṣyajāti*) that end in the vowel *u* and have *y* as their penultimate letter (*ayopadha*). For example: *kurūḥ*. [Derivation: From *kuru* and similar stems, the suffix *ṇya* is added; this is elided in the feminine by the rule beginning with "for *avanti* etc. Why specify "having *y* as the penultimate letter"? Consider *ṛdhvayuḥ*. There is also an extension of the rule for non-living beings (*aprāṇijāti*), excluding *rajju* and others. Because of the exclusion of *rajju* and so on, [the suffix applies] only to those ending in the vowel *u*. Examples: *alābvā*, *karkandhvā*. Although these two end in a long vowel, the result of the suffix *ūṅ* is the prohibition of the acute accent on the case-ending by the rule "*hoṅdhātvoḥ*". However, for living beings, we have *kṛkavākuḥ*; for *rajju* and its class, we have *rajjuḥ* and *hanuḥ*.

SK 522: After a word ending in *bāhu*, when it denotes a proper name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *ūṅ* shall be applied in the feminine. Example: *bhadrabāhūḥ*. Why "when it denotes a proper name"? Example: *vṛttabāhuḥ*. SK 523: And [the suffix *ūṅ* is applied] after *paṅgu*. (A 4.1.68)

[The suffix] *ūṅ* is applied after [the word] *paṅgu*, and there is also the elision (*lopa*) of the phonemes *u* and *a* of *śvaśura*. By the particle *ca* ("and"), [the suffix] *ūṅ* is also included; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṅīṣ* which is conditioned by connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). By the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding gender-distinct forms), the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) are applied. Thus: *śvaśrūḥ*. Pāṇini A 4.1.69: *ūrūtarapadād aupamye* (after a nominal stem that has *ūru* as its final member, when a word expressing a standard of comparison is the prior member). After a nominal stem whose prior member expresses a standard of comparison and whose final member is *ūru*, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied. Example: *karabhorūḥ* ("she whose thighs are like those of a young elephant").

Pāṇini 4.1.70: *saṃhita-śapha-lakṣaṇa-vāmādeś ca*. This sūtra is for the purpose of excluding cases of comparison (*anaupamyārtham*). *Saṃhitor ūḥ*: "She whose thighs are joined together. Just as *śapha* means "hoof," so too [the term] is applied here metaphorically because of their being closely joined. The word *lakṣaṇa* takes the suffix *ac* according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas* (Pāṇini 5.2.127); thus, *lakṣaṇor ūḥ* means "she whose thighs are marked" (by auspicious signs). *Vāmor ūḥ* means "she whose thighs are beautiful. It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after *sahita* and *saha* as well. *Sahitor ūḥ*: she whose thighs are *sahita*, meaning "joined with what is beneficial" (*hitena saha*). *Sahor ūḥ*: she whose thighs are *saha*, meaning "they endure together" (*sahete*). Alternatively, the word *saha* is used here in its sense of "existing," employed to convey the excellence of the thighs.

SK 526 (A 4.1.72): *saṃjñāyām*—the suffix *ūṅ* shall be applied after *kadru* and *kamaṇḍalu* when they denote a feminine proper name. Examples: *kadrūḥ*, *kamaṇḍalūḥ*. Why "when denoting a proper name"? [Counter-examples: *kadruḥ*, *kamaṇḍaluḥ*. This statement is made for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *ūṅ* in non-Vedic (secular) contexts. SK 527 (A 4.1.73): *śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn*—the suffix *ṅīn* is applied after the *aṇ* suffix [added to the base] *śārṅgarava* and others.

The suffix *ṅīn* shall occur after words belonging to the *śārṅgarava* group that end in the vowel *a* which follows the suffix *añ*, provided they denote a genus (*jāti*). Examples: *śārṅgaravī*, *baidī*. Because the term "genus" (*jāti*) is understood from the previous rule, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs only when expressing a relationship with a male (*puṃyoga*). There is a supplementary rule (*gaṇasūtra*) stating: "In the case of *nṛ* and *nara*, there is also vṛddhi [of the first vowel]. Example: *nārī*. Pāṇini 4.1.74 states: *yaṅś-cāp*. After a word ending in the suffix *yaṅ*, the suffix *cāp* occurs in the feminine. In the expression *yaṅaḥ*, there is a general inclusion of both *ñyaṅ* and *ṣyaṅ*. Examples: *āmbaṣṭhyā*, *kārīṣagandhyā*. It should be stated that *cāp* also occurs after a word ending in *yañ* following a retroflex *ṣ*. Example: *pautimāṣyā*.

SK 529 *āvaṭyāc ca* (A 4.1.75): after this [word], the suffix *āp* shall be applied. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṅīṣ* prescribed by the rule *yañaś ca*. The word *avaṭa* belongs to the *gargādi* group. Thus: *āvaṭyā*.
SK 530 *taddhitāḥ* (A 4.1.73).
This governing rule (*adhikāra*) extends until the end of the fifth book [of Pāṇini’s grammar].

Regarding *yūnastiḥ* (A 4.1.77): the suffix *tiP* is applied after the word *yuvan*; this is a *taddhita* suffix. Although the desired form is established by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the metarule concerning words qualified by gender), the governing rule for *taddhita* suffixes is stated here for the sake of what follows. Thus, we have *yuvatiḥ*. The restriction "provided it is not a subordinate member" (*anupasarjanāt*) still applies. Therefore, in the case of *bahuyuvā*—meaning "a woman who has many young men"—the word *yuvan* is a subordinate member and thus does not take the suffix. However, the form *yuvatī* should be understood as derived from the root *yu* with the present participle suffix *śatṛ*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
Thus end the feminine suffixes. Section on Kārakas, 16.
A 2.3.46: [The nominative case is used] merely to express the meaning of the nominal stem, gender, measure, and number.

The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is that which is invariably present. The word *mātra* (mere/only) is to be construed with each [term]. The nominative case ending shall occur when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem; when there is the addition of mere gender (*liṅga*); mere measure (*parimāṇa*); and mere number (*saṃkhyā*). Examples are: *uccaiḥ* (high), *nīcaiḥ* (low), *kṛṣṇaḥ* (Krishna), *śrīḥ* (Śrī), and *jñānam* (knowledge). These—being either without gender or having a fixed gender—are examples of "merely the meaning of the nominal stem. Those with unfixed genders, however, are examples of the addition of "mere gender": *taṭaḥ* (masculine), *taṭī* (feminine), and *taṭam* (neuter).

In the case of *droṇa* [denoting] a measure of rice (*vrīhi*), the meaning is that the rice is delimited by that measure which has the form of a *droṇa*. The distinction is this: the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)—which is the measure—through a relation of non-difference; however, the meaning of the suffix is a qualifier of the rice through the relation of the delimited and the delimiting. "Number" (*vacana*) refers to count: *ekaḥ* (one), *dvau* (two), *bahavaḥ* (many). Since the purpose [of number] has already been expressed here, the case-ending would not otherwise apply; therefore, its mention is made. By the rule *saṃbodhane ca* (A 2.3.47), the nominative (*prathamā*) should occur here: *he rāma*. Thus, the nominative is applied.
Having introduced the governing rule "with respect to a kāraka" (Pāṇini 1.4.23), [the sūtra] states: "The object is that which is most desired by the agent" (Pāṇini 1.4.49).

The *kāraka* which the agent most desires to reach (*iṣṭatama*) through his action shall be designated as the object (*karman*). Why specify "of the agent"? [Consider: *māṣeṣv aśvaṃ badhnāti* ("He ties the horse among the beans"). Here, the beans are desired by the object [the horse], but not by the agent. What is the purpose of including the superlative suffix *-tamap*? [Consider: *payasā odanaṃ bhuṅkte* ("He eats rice with milk"). Since the term *karman* is understood from the previous rule, the repetition of the word *karman* here is for the purpose of excluding the locus (*ādhāra*). Otherwise, [the designation would apply] only in cases such as *gehaṃ praviśati* ("He enters the house"). This is stated under the governing rule *anabhihite* (A 2.3.1).

SK 537: *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (A 2.3.2). The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) shall occur when the object (*karman*) is not [already] expressed. For example: *hariṃ bhajati* ("he worships Hari"). However, when the object is already expressed, the first case ending alone occurs by the rule *prātipadikārthamātre*. Expression [of the object] generally occurs through finite verbs (*tiṅ*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*). Examples: - *tiṅ*: *hariḥ sevyate* ("Hari is served"). - *kṛt*: *lakṣmyā sevitaḥ* ("served by Lakṣmī"). - *taddhita*: *śatena krītaḥ śatyaḥ* ("bought for a hundred, i.e., worth a hundred"). - *samāsa*: *prāpta ānando yaṃ sa prāptānandaḥ* ("he to whom bliss has been attained is 'one who has attained bliss'"). In some cases, expression occurs through an indeclinable (*nipāta*), as follows:
"Even a poison tree, having been nurtured by oneself, is not fit to be cut down; for the word *sāṃpratam* here means 'it is proper' (*yujyate*).

(SK 538) Furthermore, according to the rule *tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam* (A 1.4.50), a factor of action (*kāraka*) that is connected with the action—even if it is not what is most desired (*anīpsita*)—shall be designated as the object (*karman*), just like that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*). For example: "While going to the village, he touches grass"; "While eating rice, he eats poison."

SK 539: *akathitaṃ ca* (A 1.4.51). A *kāraka* that is not intended to be specified by particular categories such as *apādāna* and so forth shall bear the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *karman*. The meaning is that one must provide an enumeration [of the roots] for which this applies: "For the twelve beginning with *duh* and the four beginning with *nī*, that which is connected with the *karman* [of these verbs] is likewise called the *akathita-karman*. Examples: *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* ("He milks the cow for milk"); *baliṃ yācate vasudhām* ("He begs Bali for the earth").

He asks the undisciplined one for discipline (*vinaya*). He cooks rice-grains into boiled rice (*odana*). He fines the Gargas a hundred [pieces]. He shuts the cow in the pen (*vraja*). He asks the young student (*māṇavaka*) the way. He gathers fruits from the tree. He tells or instructs the young student in the Dharma. He wins a hundred [coins] from Devadatta. He churns the ocean of milk for nectar (*sudhā*). He robs Devadatta of a hundred [coins]. He leads, takes, drags, or carries the goat to the village. This designation is based on the meaning (*artha*).

He begs Bali for the earth; he speaks, expresses, or tells the Dharma to the young student (*māṇavaka*), and so forth. What is the *kāraka*? He asks the father of the young student about the way. It should be stated that when used in connection with roots meaning "to go" (*akarmaka-dhātu*), place (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), and the distance to be traveled (*gantavya-adhvā*) are designated as the object (*karman*). Examples: He sleeps in the Kuru country; he sits for a month; he sits for the duration of milking a cow; he sits for the distance of a *krośa*. Pāṇini A 1.4.52: For roots whose meanings are "motion," "cognition," "eating," those having sound as their object, and those that are intransitive, the agent (*kartṛ*) of the simple verb (*aṇi*) becomes the object (*sa ṇau*) in the causative (*ṇic*).

In the case of roots meaning motion (*gati*) and so forth, those whose object is sound (*śabda-karman*), and those that are intransitive (*akarmaka*), the agent (*kartṛ*) of which [roots] is [the agent] in the *aṇ* (non-causative) state shall become the object (*karman*) in the *ṇi* (causative) state. He caused his enemies to go to heaven; he made his own people know the meaning of the Vedas; he caused the gods to partake of nectar; he caused Brahmā to study the Veda; he caused the earth to rest upon the waters—he who is Śrī Hari, may he be my refuge. Why "meaning motion and so forth"? [Example: He has Devadatta cook the rice. Why "of those ending in *aṇ*" (*aṇyantānām*)? [Example: He causes Devadatta to cook.

Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to go; another employs him [in that action], saying, "Viṣṇumitra causes Yajñadatta to be made to go by Devadatta. The prohibition does not apply to the roots *nī* (to lead) and *vah* (to carry). Examples: *nāyayati* or *vāhayati bhāraṃ bhṛtyena* ("He causes the servant to lead/carry the load"). There is no prohibition for the root *vah* when its agent is a driver (*niyantṛ*). Example: *vāhayati rathaṃ vāhān sūtaḥ* ("The charioteer causes the horses to pull the chariot"). The prohibition does not apply to the roots *ad* (to eat) and *khād* (to chew/eat). Examples: *ādayati* or *khādayati annaṃ baṭunā* ("He causes the boy to eat the food"). The prohibition does not apply to the root *bhakṣ* when it means "to injure" (*ahiṃsārtha*). Example: *bhakṣayaty annaṃ baṭunā* ("He causes the boy to eat the food"). Why specify "when it does not mean to injure"? [Because in cases of injury, the prohibition applies].

[The root *bhakṣ*] "to eat" [is used with the accusative when the object is animate]: he causes the oxen to eat the grain. There is an addition [to the rule] for [roots] such as *jalp* ("to prattle"): Devadatta causes his son to prattle or to speak the Dharma. And [the same applies] to *dṛś* ("to see"): he shows Hari to the devotees. By this it is made known that in the sūtra only roots whose meaning is general cognition (*jñāna*) are included, and not those whose meaning is a specific type of cognition. Therefore, it does not apply to [roots] such as *smṛ* ("to remember") or *ghrā* ("to smell"): he causes Devadatta to remember or to smell. [It also does not apply to] *śabdāy* ("to sound").

In *śabdāyayati devadattena*, there is the application [of the rule for the agentive case] because the object is subsumed within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and thus lacks the status of being an external object (*akarmakatva*). This does not apply even when one intends the object to be expressed by oneself. Therefore, in examples such as *māsam āsayati devadattam*, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) certainly occurs; however, in examples such as *devadattena pācayati*, it does not.
[This is governed by] A 1.4.53: *hṛkror anyatarasyām*.

In the case of the roots *gṛ* ("to seize") and *krī* ("to buy"), that which is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative (*aṇ*) becomes optionally the object (*karman*) in the causative (*ṇic*). For example: *hārayati*, *kārayati* *bhṛtyaṃ* or *bhṛtyena kaṭam*. It should be stated that for the roots *abhivād* ("to salute") and *gṛ* ("to seize") when used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), [the agent becomes the object] optionally. For example: *abhivādayate*, *darśayate* *devaṃ* *bhaktaṃ* or *bhaktena*. *A 1.4.46*: *adhi-śīṅ-sthāsāṃ karma*. For these roots preceded by *adhi*, the locus (*ādhāra*) becomes the object (*karman*). For example: *adhiśete*, *adhitiṣṭhati*, or *adhyāste* *vaikuṇṭhaṃ* *hariḥ* ("Hari rests upon, stands upon, or dwells in Vaikuṇṭha").

SK 543 *abhiniviśaś ca* (A 1.4.47): Following the prefix *abhi-ni*, the locus (*ādhāra*) of the root *viś-* preceded by this [compound] shall be the object (*karman*). One enters the right path (*sanmārgam abhiniviśate*). From the rule *parikrayaṇe saṃpradānam* (A 1.4.44), the phrase *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is carried over here by "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and because a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) is adopted, it does not apply in some cases: "attachment to sin" (*pāpe 'bhiniveśaḥ*). SK 544 *upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ* (A 1.4.48): [The locus of the root *vas-* preceded by the prefixes *upa-, anu-, adhi-,* and *āṅ* is the object.]

The locus (*ādhāra*) of the verb *vasati* (to dwell) preceded by *upa*, *anu*, *adhi*, or *ā* shall be the object (*karman*). For example: *hariḥ vaikuṇṭham upavasati*, *anuvāsati*, *adhivasati*, or *āvasati*. [This rule does not apply] when the meaning is "eating" (*abhukti*); for example: *vane upavasati* (he fasts in the forest). The accusative case is to be employed with the words *ubha* and *sarvatas*, as well as with the three beginning with *dhik* and *upari*, when they are used in reduplication (*āmreḍita*). It is also seen elsewhere than those; for example: *ubhayataḥ kṛṣṇaṃ gopāḥ* (the cowherds are on both sides of Kṛṣṇa), *sarvataḥ kṛṣṇam* (on all sides of Kṛṣṇa), *dhik kṛṣṇābhaktam* (shame on the non-devotee of Kṛṣṇa), *upary upari lokaṃ hariḥ* (Hari is above the world), and *adhy adhi lokam* (over the world).

*Adho-adhaḥ* (lower and lower). Also [the second case ending is used] in connection with *abhitaḥ*, *paritaḥ*, *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, and *hā*. *Abhitaḥ kṛṣṇam* (on both sides of Kṛṣṇa); *paritaḥ kṛṣṇam* (all around Kṛṣṇa); *grāmaṃ samayā* (near the village); *laṅkāṃ nikaṣā* (near Laṅkā); *hā kṛṣṇābhaktam* (alas for the non-devotee of Kṛṣṇa)—the meaning is that he is pitied. *Na pratibhāti kiṃcit bubhukṣitam* (nothing occurs to the hungry one). According to A 2.3.4 (*antarā-antareṇa-yukte*), when joined with these two [words], the second case ending shall be used. *Antarā tvāṃ māṃ hariḥ* (Hari is between you and me); *antareṇa hariṃ na sukham* (without Hari there is no happiness).
Having introduced [the topic] with *karmapravacanīyāḥ* (A 1.4.83),
[it continues with] *anur lakṣaṇe* (A 1.4.84).

When *lakṣaṇa* (mark/indicator) is to be expressed, *anu* shall have the technical designation [of *karmapravacanīya*] previously mentioned. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designations of *gati* and *upasarga*.

By the rule *karmapravacanīyayukte dvitīyā* (A 2.3.8), the second case (*dvitīyā*) shall be used in connection with this [term]. For example: *japam anu prāvarṣat* ("It rained after the recitation"). The meaning is: "The raining was marked by the recitation which served as its cause. Although the third case (*tṛtīyā*) would also apply here by the rule *hetāv* (A 2.3.23), it is superseded by this [second case rule], because the repeated prescription of the technical designation [as *karmapravacanīya*] has the force of overriding that [third case rule], even though the desired result could have been established by the rule *lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna-* (A 1.4.90) and others.

SK 549: When the sense of the third case (instrumental) is to be expressed, *anu* shall receive the aforementioned technical designation (*karmapravacanīya*). Example: *nadīm anv avasitā senā*. The meaning is "the army is situated along with the river" (*nadyā saha sambaddhā*). [The root] *ṣiñ* in the sense of "binding" takes the suffix *kta*. SK 550:
[The term *anu* receives the aforementioned designation] when expressing inferiority (*hīna*). (A 1.4.86)

When inferiority (*hīna*) is to be expressed, *anu* is treated as before [i.e., as a karmapravacanīya]. *Anu hariṃ surāḥ*: the meaning is "the gods are inferior to Hari. (SK 551) *upa*, when expressing superiority (*adhika*) and inferiority (*hīna*), is an indeclinable that receives the aforementioned designation [of karmapravacanīya]. Regarding superiority, the seventh case will be explained later. Regarding inferiority: *upa hariṃ surāḥ*.

SK 552: The prepositions *prati*, *pari*, and *anu* [are used as karmapravacanīyas] in the senses of indication (*lakṣaṇa*), description of a state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), division (*bhāga*), and distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). (A 1.4.90)

In these senses—namely, as objects (*viṣaya*), characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), description of a state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), portion (*bhāga*), and distributive repetition (*vīpsā*)—the words *prati*, *pari*, and *anu* shall receive the technical designation [of karmapravacanīya]. 1. As a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*): *vṛkṣaṃ prati pary anu vā vidyotate vidyut* ("The lightning flashes toward the tree"). 2. In describing a state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*): *bhakto viṣṇuṃ prati pary anu vā* ("He is devoted to Viṣṇu"). 3. As a portion (*bhāga*): *lakṣmīr hariṃ prati pary anu vā*. The meaning is "Lakṣmī is a portion of Hari. 4. In distributive repetition (*vīpsā*): *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati pary anu vā siñcati* ("He waters tree after tree"). Because these do not function as prepositions (*upasarga*) here, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur. Why "in these [senses]"? Consider *pariṣiñcati* ("he sprinkles around"). SK 553: *abhir abhāge* (A 1.4.91). [The term *karmapravacanīya* applies to *abhi* when it does not mean "portion"].

In the sense of "excepting" (*bhāga-varja*), words such as *lakṣaṇa* (mark), etc., shall have the designation *abhi-ukta* (expressed by *abhi*). *harim abhi vartate* (he turns toward Hari); *bhakto harim abhi* (he is devoted to Hari); *devaṃ devam abhi siñcati* (he sprinkles water upon each deity). Why say "excepting the sense of excepting"? [Consider: *yad atra mamābhiṣyāt tad dīyatām* (let that which may accrue to me here be given). *Sūtra 554*: *adhi-parī anarthakau* (A 1.4.93). The words *adhi* and *pari*, when devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*), have the aforementioned designation (*karmapravacanīya*). *kuto 'dhy āgacchati* (whence does he come?); *kutaḥ pary āgacchati*. Because the designation *gati* is superseded [by the designation *karmapravacanīya*], the rule *gatir gatau* (P. 8.1.70) does not apply, and thus there is no elision of the accent (*nighāta*).

SK 555 *suḥ* is used in the sense of praise (A 1.4.94). For example: *susiktam*, *sustutam*. Because it is not a prefix (*anupasarga*), the change to *ṣ* does not occur. What is the purpose of specifying "in the sense of praise"? Consider: *suṣiktaṃ kiṃ tavātra* ("What is well-poured here for you?"). This is an expression of censure (*kṣepa*). SK 556 *ati* is used in the sense of exceeding (*atikramaṇa*) and [praise] (A 1.4.95).

The term *ati* shall be designated as a *karmapravacanīya* when used in the sense of surpassing (*atikramaṇa*) or honoring (*pūjā*). Example: *ati devān kṛṣṇaḥ* ("Kṛṣṇa surpasses the gods" or "Kṛṣṇa honors the gods").

*Sutra A 1.4.96*: *apiḥ padārthasaṃbhāvanānvavasargagarhāsamuccayeṣu*. (The particle *api* [is designated as a *karmapravacanīya*] in the senses of the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), permission (*anvavasarga*), reproach (*garhā*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*).)

When these meanings are to be expressed, the word *api* shall bear the technical designation [of *karmapravacanīya*]. In the example *sarpiṣo ’pi syāt* ("there might even be a drop of clarified butter"), the *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*) does not occur because *anu* is not a prefix (*upasarga*). The potential mood (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). The word *api*, expressing the difficulty of the agent (*kartṛdaurlabhya*) with respect to the occurrence that constitutes the very object of that possibility, is connected with the word *syāt*. As for the genitive case in *sarpiṣaḥ*, it expresses the relationship of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) with the "drop" (*bindu*) which is understood through the force of the word *api*. For this indeed is what is meant by the word *api*'s function of illuminating the meaning of a word (*padārthadyotakatā*).

But the second [case] does not apply here, because it has been stated that there is no connection with even a drop of clarified butter (*sarpiṣaḥ bindunā yogaḥ na tu api*). *api stuyād Viṣṇum*: hyperbole (*atyukti*) used to manifest excellence of capacity (*saṃbhāvanaṃ śaktyutkarṣam*). *api stuhi*: permission for one’s own will (*anvavasargaḥ kāmacārānujñā*). *dhig Devadattam api stuyād vṛṣalam*: censure (*garhā*). *api siñca api stuhi*: conjunction (*samuccaye*). SK 558: *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* (A 2.3.5).

In these cases, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) should occur: *māsaṃ kalyāṇī* (she is auspicious for a month), *māsam adhīte* (he studies for a month), *māsaṃ guḍadhānāḥ* (molasses and grains for a month); *krośaṃ kuṭilā nadī* (the river is winding for a *krośa*), *krośam adhīte* (he studies for a *krośa*), *krośaṃ giriḥ* (the mountain extends for a *krośa*). What is the purpose of the condition "continuous connection" (*atyantasaṃyoga*)? [Consider: *māsasya dvir adhīte* (he studies twice in a month), *krośasyaikadeśe parvataḥ* (the mountain is in one part of a *krośa*). Thus ends the section on the second case.
SK 559: *svatantraḥ kartā* (A 1.4.54).
That meaning which is intended to be expressed as independent with respect to an action shall be the agent (*kartṛ*).
SK 560: *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam* (A 1.4.42). [The most effective means for accomplishing an action is the instrument (*karaṇa*).]

That which is the most effective instrument (*prakṛṣṭopakāraka*) in the accomplishment of an action shall be designated as the *karaṇa* (instrument). Why is the superlative suffix *tamap* used [in the rule]? [Consider: "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).

According to A 2.3.18, *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall be used when the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*) has not already been expressed by another means. For example: "Vālī was killed by Rāma with an arrow" (*rāmeṇa bāṇena hato vālī*). An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) should be made for words such as *prakṛti* and others: - By nature (*prakṛtyā*), he is beautiful. - Generally (*prāyeṇa*), he is a ritualist. - By lineage (*gotreṇa*), he is a Gārgya. - He goes along level ground (*samena eti*). - He goes along uneven ground (*viṣameṇa eti*). - He buys grain for two *droṇas* (*dvidroṇena dhānyam krīṇāti*). - He travels with ease (*sukhena*) or with difficulty (*duḥkhena*), and so forth.

SK 562 *divaḥ karma ca* (A 1.4.43): A *kāraka* that is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the action denoted by the root *div* shall bear the designation *karman*, and furthermore, the designation *karaṇa*. [Examples: *akṣair dīvyati* or *akṣān dīvyati*. SK 563 *apavarge tṛtīyā* (A 1.4.43): When the completion [of an action] is indicated, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is employed.

*Apavarga* means the attainment of the result; when there is an absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) with respect to time or distance in such an attainment, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall be used. Example: *ahnā krośena vānuvāko ’dhītaḥ* ("The lesson was studied in a day or in the distance of a *krośa*"). Why "in the attainment of the result"? Example: *māsam adhīto nāyātaḥ* ("He has studied for a month [but] has not yet mastered it"). In the presence of the word *saha* joined with that which is non-primary (*apradhāna*), the third case ending shall be used. Example: *putreṇa sahāgataḥ pitā* ("The father came together with the son"). The same applies in the case of conjunction with *sākam*, *sārdham*, and *samam*. Even without the word *vinā*, the third case is used, as indicated by the rule *vṛddho yūnā* (Pāṇini 1.2.65), etc.

SK 565 *yenāṅgavikāraḥ* (A 2.3.20): When a modification of a limb (*aṅga*) indicates a modification of the whole (*aṅgin*), the third case ending shall be used for that [limb]. Example: *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ*. The meaning is "distinguished by blindness related to the eye. Why "modification of a limb"? [Counter-example: *akṣi kāṇam asya* ("his eye is blind"). SK 566 *itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe* (A 2.3.21).

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall be used for that which has attained a certain state (*prakāra*). For example: *jaṭābhis tāpasaḥ* ("an ascetic by means of matted hair"). The meaning is: "one characterized by asceticism as made known by matted hair. Regarding *saṃjño ’nyatarasyāṃ karmaṇi* (A 2.3.22):

the third case ending may optionally be used for the object (*karman*) of the verb *jñā* preceded by the prefix *sam*. For example: *pitrā saṃjānīte* or *pitaraṃ saṃjānīte* ("he recognizes [him] as his father").

SK 568 *hetau* (A 2.3.23): The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall occur in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Causality (*hetutva*) is common to substances and so forth, and is independent of [specific] operation (*vyāpāra*). Instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), however, has action alone as its domain and is restricted to [the presence of] operation. For example: *daṇḍena ghaṭaḥ* ("A pot [is produced] by means of a staff"); *puṇyena dṛṣṭo hariḥ* ("Hari was seen because of merit"). Here, even the result (*phala*) is considered a cause; for example: *adhyayanena vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of study"). Even an action that is merely implied (*gamyamāna*) serves as the motivator for a case-ending denoting a factor of action (*kāraka-vibhakti*). *Alaṃ krameṇa* ("Enough with the sequence") means that there is no further goal to be accomplished.

In relation to the act of accomplishment (*sādhanakriyā*), effort (*śrama*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*). [Example: *śatena śatena vatsān pāyayati payaḥ* ("He causes the calves to drink milk by the hundreds"). The meaning is "having distinguished them by the hundreds. In the usage of the unrefined (*aśiṣṭavyavahāra*), when the root *dāṇ* is employed, the third case is used in the sense of the fourth case. [Example: *dāsyā saṃyacchate kāmukaḥ* ("The lustful man gives [himself] to a maidservant"). But in accordance with Dharma, he gives to his wife: *bhāryāyai saṃyacchati*. Thus ends the section on the third case. "A person whom one intends through the object of giving is called the recipient (*saṃpradāna*)" (A 1.4.32).
That person whom one intends through the object (*karman*) of the act of giving shall bear the technical designation "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*). It shall be so.

SK 570: The fourth case (*caturthī*) is used for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). (A 2.3.13) Example: *viprāya gāṃ dadāti* ("He gives a cow to the Brahmin"). Only when not already expressed by another grammatical element (*anabhihita*). Example: *dānīyo vipraḥ* ("The Brahmin is one to whom [something] should be given"). That which one intends to reach through an action is also a recipient. Example: *patye śete* ("She lies down for her husband"). For the root *yaj* ("to sacrifice"), the object receives the technical name "instrument" (*karaṇa*), and the recipient receives the technical name "object" (*karman*). Example: *paśunā rudraṃ yajate*. The meaning is: "He gives the animal to Rudra. SK 571: For verbs having the sense of "pleasing" (*rucy-artha*), the person who is being pleased is the recipient. (A 1.4.33)

When roots meaning "to please" (*ruc*) are employed, that which is being pleased shall be the *saṃpradāna* (recipient). For example: *haraye rocate bhaktiḥ* ("Devotion is pleasing to Hari"). *Ruci* is a desire whose agent is another. In this case, devotion is the agent of the pleasure residing in Hari. Why specify "being pleased"? Consider: *devadattāya rocate modakaḥ pathi* ("The sweetmeat pleases Devadatta on the road"). [Pāṇini A 1.4.34:
*ślāghahnuṅsthāśapāṃ jñīpsyamānaḥ* ("In the case of the roots *ślāgh*, *hnuṅ*, *sthā*, and *śap*, that which is intended to be informed is the *saṃpradāna*").

When these [verbs] are employed, the one intended to be informed shall be the *saṃpradāna*. *Gopī smarāt kṛṣṇāya ślāghate, hnute, tiṣṭhate, śapate vā* ("Out of love, the cowherd girl praises, hides from, stands before, or curses Kṛṣṇa"). What if [the person] is not being made aware? *Devadattāya ślāghate pathi* ("She praises on the road for Devadatta"). *A 1.4.35:
dhārer uttamarṇaḥ* ("In the employment of *dhāri*, the creditor shall have the aforementioned designation").

In the employment of the verb *dhārayati*, the creditor shall receive the technical name (*saṃjñā*) of *saṃpradāna*. *Bhaktāya dhārayati mokṣaṃ hariḥ* ("Hari owes liberation to his devotee"). What if [the person] is not a creditor? *Devadattāya śataṃ dhārayati grāme* ("He owes a hundred in the village to Devadatta").

SK 574 *spṛher īpsitaḥ* (A 1.4.36): When used with the verb *spṛh* (*spṛhayati*), that which is desired shall be the *saṃpradāna*. Example: *puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati* ("he longs for flowers"). Why "desired"? [Counter-example: *puṣpebhyo vane spṛhayati* ("he longs for flowers in the forest"). This designation applies to the mere state of being desired; however, when excellence is intended to be expressed, the designation *karman* takes precedence. Example: *puṣpāṇi spṛhayati* ("he longs for flowers [intensely]"). SK 575 *krudhadruherṣyāsūyārthānāṃ yaṃ prati kopaḥ* (A 1.4.37): For verbs having the sense of anger (*kruddha*), malice (*druh*), envy (*īrṣyā*), or censure (*asūyā*), that person toward whom the anger is directed [shall be the *saṃpradāna*].

When verbs meaning anger (*krudh*) and so forth are employed, that person toward whom the anger is directed shall bear the technical designation [of *saṃpradāna*]. Examples: *haraye krudhyati*, *druhyati*, *īrṣyati*, *asūyati*. Why "toward whom the anger is directed"? [Consider: *bhāryām īrṣyati* ("he is jealous of his wife"), thinking, "Let no other see her. Anger (*krodha*) is intolerance; malice (*droha*) is doing harm; envy (*īrṣyā*) is vexation; censoriousness (*asūyā*) is the revealing of faults in others' virtues. Since *druh* and the others are also understood to arise from anger, the qualification "toward whom the anger is directed" is stated in general terms. (SK 576) *krudhadruhor upasṛṣṭayoḥ karma* (A 1.4.38).
