When these two [roots] are accompanied by prepositions (*upasarga*), the *kāraka* toward whom the anger is directed shall be designated as the object (*karman*). For example: *krūram abhikrudhyati* ("he is angry at the cruel one") and *asidruhyati* ("he bears malice toward the sword").
Regarding the rule *rādhīkṣyor yasya vipraśnaḥ* (A 1.4.39):

when these two [roots] are used, the *kāraka* [toward whom] the inquiry is made shall be the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). That is, it is the person regarding whom a various inquiry is performed. For example: *kṛṣṇāya rādhyati* or *īkṣate*. The meaning is that Garga, being questioned, deliberates upon what is auspicious or inauspicious.

SK 578 *pratyāṅbhyāṃ śruvaḥ pūrvasya kartā* (A 1.4.40): When used in conjunction with these two prefixes (*prati* and *ā*), the agent of the preceding action—the activity consisting of instigation—shall be the *saṃpradāna*. For example: *viprāya gāṃ pratiśṛṇoti* or *āśṛṇoti*. The meaning is that, having been prompted by the Brahmin with the words "Give [the cow] to me," he promises to do so.
SK 579 *anupratigṛṇaś ca* (A 1.4.41): [The agent of the preceding action is also the *saṃpradāna* when used with the root *gṛ* preceded by *anu* and *prati*].

By these two [verbal roots], the agent (*kāraka*) of the root *gṛ* (to praise), who has become the agent of a prior action, shall be designated by the term "released" (*ukta*). For example: *hotre 'nugṛṇāti* or *pratigṛṇāti*. The meaning is that the Hotṛ priest first recites, and the Adhvaryu priest encourages him.
(Pāṇini 1.4.44: *parikrayaṇe saṃpradānam anyatarasyām*—"In the case of hiring, the recipient may optionally be called the *saṃpradāna* [recipient]").

The act of hiring a servant for a fixed period is *parikrayaṇa* (purchase by hire). In that case, the most effective factor (*sādhakatama*) may optionally be designated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). For example: *śatena parikrītaḥ* or *śatāya parikrītaḥ* ("he is hired for a hundred"). The dative case (*caturthī*) should be stated [as optional] when expressing purpose (*tādarthye*). For example: *muktaye hariṃ bhajati* ("he worships Hari for the sake of liberation"). [The dative is also used] with the root *kḷp-* in the sense of "becoming" (*saṃpadyamāne*). For example: *bhaktir jñānāya kalpate*, *saṃpadyate*, or *jāyate* ("devotion leads to, results in, or arises as knowledge," etc.). [The dative is also used] when something is indicated by a portent (*utpātena jñāpite*). For example: *vātāya kapilā vidyut* ("a tawny lightning flash portends wind"). [The dative is also used] in connection with the word *hita*. For example: *brāhmaṇāya hitam* ("beneficial to the Brahmin"). And [the dative is used] for the object of a verb whose subordinate element (*upapada*) expresses the purpose of the action, provided that the primary verb is not present (*sthāninaḥ*). (A 2.3.14) *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ*. For example: *phalebhyo yāti* ("he goes for fruits"), which implies *phalāny āhartuṃ yāti* ("he goes to gather fruits"). Here, the purpose of the action (*yāti*) is expressed by the subordinate element (*phalebhyaḥ*), and the primary verb is absent. Thus, the dative is used for the object of that purpose.

When a word ending in *tumun* (the infinitive suffix) is not explicitly used but is understood as a subordinate element (*upapada*) whose purpose is another action, the fourth case (*caturthī*) shall be employed for its object (*karman*). For example: *phalebhyo yāti* ("he goes for fruits"). The meaning is: "he goes in order to fetch fruits" (*phalāny āhartuṃ yāti*). Similarly: *namaskurmo nṛsiṃhāya* ("we pay homage to Nṛsiṃha"). The meaning is: "in order to propitiate Nṛsiṃha" (*nṛsiṃham anukūlayitum*). The same applies in cases such as *svayaṃbhuve namaskṛtya*.

Furthermore, by the rule *tumarthāc ca bhāvavacanāt* (A 2.3.15), the fourth case shall be employed after a word ending in a suffix that denotes an action (*bhāva*) and has the sense of *tumun*. For example: *yāgāya yāti* ("he goes for the sake of sacrifice"). The meaning is: "he goes in order to sacrifice" (*yaṣṭuṃ yāti*).

SK 583: *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alam-vaṣaṭ-yogāc ca* (A 2.3.16). When used in conjunction with these, the fourth case (*caturthī*) shall be employed. For example: *haraye namaḥ* ("salutation to Hari"). The case ending determined by the syntactic role (*kāraka*) is stronger than that determined by a governing word (*upapada*). Examples: *namaskaroti devān* ("he pays homage to the gods"); *prajābhyaḥ svasti* ("well-being to the subjects"); *agnaye svāhā* ("svāhā to Agni"); *pitṛbhyaḥ svadhā* ("svadhā to the ancestors"). The term *alam* is understood here in the sense of "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*). Therefore, examples such as *daityebhyo harir alam*, *prabhuḥ*, *samarthaḥ*, or *śaktaḥ* ("Hari is sufficient, capable, competent, or powerful against the Daityas") are included. In connection with words like *prabhu* ("master"), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also correct, based on the grammatical rule: *tasmai prabhavati sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ* ("he prevails over him; he is the leader of these").

Thus it is established that [the word *indra*] is used with the fourth case ending when one wishes to express: "May he be the lord of the three worlds. *Vaṣaṭ indrāya*. The particle *ca* serves the purpose of re-enjoining [the rule]. Therefore, when a blessing (*āśis*) is intended to be expressed, even though a sixth case ending might otherwise apply by the rule *parām api caturthīm āśiṣi*, the fourth case ending alone occurs, overriding the sixth. Example: *svasti gobhyo bhūyāt* ("May there be well-being for the cows"). SK 584: *manyakarmaṇy anādare vibhāṣāprāṇiṣu* (A 2.3.17). [The sixth case ending is optionally used] for the object of the verb *man* (to disregard) when expressing disregard, provided the object is not a living being.

When the verb *man* (to consider) takes an object that is not a living being (*aprāṇin*), the fourth case (*caturthī*) may optionally be used in the sense of contempt (*tiraskāra*). For example: *na tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ manye* or *tṛṇāya*. Because of the specific mention of the form *śyan*, this does not apply when the verb is in the *tan*-class (the root *man* in its *tan*-class form is *mān*). Thus, one says: *na tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ manve 'ham*. The rule "not for living beings" (*aprāṇiṣu*) should be removed [from the context], and it should be stated: "except for a boat, food, a parrot, and a jackal. Consequently, in examples such as *na tvāṃ nāvaṃ manye* or *annaṃ manye*, although the objects are not living beings, the fourth case is not used. However, in *na tvāṃ śune manye*, although the object is a living being, the fourth case is indeed used.

Pāṇini 2.3.12: *gatyarthakarmaṇi dvitīyācaturhtyau ceṣṭāyām anadhvan* (A 2.3.12). When there is motion (*ceṣṭā*), these two [case endings], the second and the fourth, occur for the object (*karman*) of verbs meaning "to go," provided it is not a path (*anadhvan*). For example: *grāmaṃ gacchati* or *grāmāya gacchati* ("He goes to the village"). Why "when there is motion"? Consider: *manasā hariṃ vrajati* ("He goes to Hari with his mind"). Why "not a path"? Consider: *panthānaṃ gacchati* ("He goes along the path"). This prohibition applies only when the path is physically traversed by the body. However, when one intends to reach the main path by way of a detour, the fourth case ending does indeed occur: *utpathena pathe gacchati* ("He goes from a wrong path onto the right path"). Thus, the fourth case is used.

SK 586: *dhruvam apāye ’pādānam* (A 1.4.24). Separation (*apāya*) is disjunction; when that is to be accomplished, the stable factor (*dhruva*) serving as the limit (*avadhi*) shall be the *apādāna* (ablative case-relation). SK 587: *apādāne pañcamī* (A 2.3.28). [The fifth case-ending is used] in the sense of the *apādāna*.

"He comes from the village. "He falls from the running horse. What is the *kāraka*? "The leaf of the tree falls. There is an extension [of the rule] for those [roots] meaning "disgust," "cessation," and "negligence": "He feels disgust toward evil"; "he desists"; "he is negligent regarding the Dharma. SK 588: *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ* (A 1.4.25). When used with roots meaning "fear" (*bhī*) or "protection" (*trai*), the cause of fear shall be the *apādāna*. "He fears the thief"; "He protects [himself] from the thief. Why "the cause of fear"? [Because otherwise it would not apply: "He fears or protects himself in the forest."

SK 589 *parājer asoḍhaḥ* (A 1.4.26): When used with the verb *parāji*, that which is "unbearable" (*asoḍha*) shall be the *apādāna*. Example: *adhyayanāt parājayate*. The meaning is "he becomes weary of study. Why say "unbearable"? Consider: *śatrūn parājayate*. The meaning here is "he overcomes the enemies. SK 590 *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* (A 1.4.27): In the case of verbs having the sense of "preventing," that which is desired (*īpsita*) [shall be the *apādāna*].

*Vāraṇa* (prevention) is the obstruction of activity. When roots having the sense of "preventing" are used, that which is desired (*īpsita*) shall be the *apādāna*. Example: *yavebhyo gāṃ vārayati* ("He keeps the cow away from the barley"). Why "desired"? [Counter-example: *yavebhyo gāṃ vārayati kṣetre* ("He keeps the cow away from the barley in the field"). A 1.4.28: *antardhau yenādarśanam icchati* ("In the sense of disappearance, that by means of whom one desires non-perception [is the *apādāna*]").

When there is an intervention, that from which one desires the absence of the self’s perception by the agent shall be the *apādāna*. Example: *mātuḥ nilīyate kṛṣṇaḥ* ("Kṛṣṇa hides from his mother"). Why "in the sense of concealment" (*antardhau*)? [Consider: *caurān na didṛkṣate* ("he does not wish to see the thieves"). Why the inclusion of the word "desires" (*icchatigrahaṇam*)? So that it may apply even when there is actually a perception, provided there is a desire for non-perception. *A 1.4.29: ākhyāta upayoge* ("In the case of instruction, the speaker is designated as such [i.e., *apādāna*]"). When there is the acquisition of knowledge preceded by a formal rule, the speaker shall bear the aforementioned designation. Example: *upādhyāyād adhīte* ("he studies under the teacher"). Why "in the case of instruction" (*upayoge*)? [Consider: *naṭasya gāthāṃ śṛṇoti* ("he hears the song of the actor").
SK 593 *janikartuḥ* (A 1.4.30):
The cause (*hetu*) of that which is being born shall be the ablative (*apādāna*). For example: *brahmaṇaḥ prajāḥ prajāyante* ("Beings are born from Brahman").
SK 594 *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* (A 1.4.31): [The source] of the verb *bhū* ("to be/originate") is the ablative.

*Bhuvana* means the earth (*bhū*). Likewise, *prabhavaḥ* [is used] for the source of the creator of the earth; as in "the Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat," which means she becomes manifest there. [The suffix *ap* occurs] after a word ending in an elided *lyap* (gerund) when it denotes either the object or the locus: *prāsādāt prekṣate* ("he looks out from the palace") and *āsanāt prekṣate* ("he looks out from his seat"). The meaning is that he looks out after having ascended the palace and sat down upon the seat. *Śvaśurāj jihreti* ("she is bashful before her father-in-law") means "having looked at her father-in-law. Even an action that is not explicitly expressed serves as the cause for the case-endings of the factors of action (*kāraka*). Why? "Why are you [standing] by the river? (*kasmāt tvaṃ nadyāḥ*)?

When the creation of distance (*adhvan*) or time (*kāla*) [is expressed], the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used; from that which is connected to it, the first (*prathamā*) and seventh (*saptamī*) cases are used for distance, and the seventh case should also be stated for time. For example: *vanād grāmo yojanam* or *yojane* ("the village is a *yojana* from the forest"); *kārtikyā āgrahāyaṇī māse* ("from the full moon of Kārtika to the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī is a month"). Furthermore, according to A 2.3.29: *anyārāditarartediksabdāñcūttarapadājāhiyukte*, the fifth case is used when joined with *anya*, *ārāt*, *itara*, *ṛte*, words denoting direction (*dik*), *añcu*-prefixed words, words having *uttarapada* as their final member, *āc*, *āhi*, or *yukta*.

The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall occur when these [words] are used in conjunction [with another]. The term *anya* is taken here in its sense (as a general category); the inclusion of *itara* is for the sake of elaboration. Examples: *anyo bhinno vā kṛṣṇāt* ("different from or other than Kṛṣṇa"), *ārād vanāt* ("far from the forest"), *ṛte kṛṣṇāt* ("without Kṛṣṇa"), *pūrvo grāmāt* ("east of the village"). A "direction word" (*dik-śabda*) is a word observed to denote a direction; by that [definition], the rule applies even when the word currently denotes a location or time. Example: *caitrāt pūrvaḥ phālgunaḥ* ("Phālguna is earlier than Caitra"). However, it does not apply when used in conjunction with a word denoting a part of a whole, because of the grammatical instruction: *tasya param āmreḍitam* ("the latter of that is called *āmreḍita*"). Example: *pūrvaṃ kāyasya* ("the front part of the body").

However, although *añcu* has a directional meaning (*dikśabda*) when it forms the final member of a compound, the separate mention [of *añcu*] is intended to override the genitive case prescribed by the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasartha-pratyayena* (Pāṇini 2.3.30). Examples: *prāk grāmāt* ("to the east of the village"), *pratyak grāmāt* ("to the west of the village"), *ā dakṣiṇā grāmāt* ("as far as the south of the village"), *āhi dakṣiṇāhi grāmāt* ("beyond the south of the village"). Regarding the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) with words having the sense of "starting from" (*prabhṛti*), the ablative occurs in connection with such meanings, as evidenced by the usage in the *Mahābhāṣya*: *kārtikyāḥ prabhṛti* ("starting from the full moon of Kārttika"). Examples: *bhavāt prabhṛti* or *ārabhya hariḥ sevyah* ("Hari is to be worshipped starting from the time of Bhava"). The ablative is also used in connection with *bahiḥ* ("outside") based on the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) provided by the rule prescribing compounds for *apa-pari-bahiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.12):
*grāmād bahiḥ* ("outside the village"). Furthermore, according to the rule *apa-parī varjane* (Pāṇini 1.4.88), [the words *apa* and *pari* denote exclusion].
These two are *karmapravacanīya*s when used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*).
A 1.4.89 states: "The prefix *āṅ* [is termed *karmapravacanīya*] when expressing a limit (*maryādā*).
Thus, *āṅ* receives this technical designation when it denotes a limit; because of the inclusion of the word "expression" (*vacana*), it also applies in the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*).
SK 598: *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ* (A 1.4.90).

When used in conjunction with these *karmapravacanīya*s, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be employed. For example: *apa hareḥ pari hareḥ saṃsāraḥ* ("Transmigration is apart from Hari"). Here, *pari* is used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). However, when it signifies a mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, one says *hariṃ pari*. Similarly, *ā* [is used] up to what has been mentioned: *ā sakalād brahma* ("Brahman extends up to everything"). SK 599: *pratiḥ pratinidhipratidānayoḥ* (A 1.4.92). [The term *prati* is a *karmapravacanīya* when used in the senses of representation (*pratinidhi*) and exchange (*pratidāna*).]

The term *prati* shall have the designation *ukta* when used with these two senses. According to A 2.3.11 (*pratinidhipratidāne ca yasmāt*), the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be used in connection with *karmapravacanīyas*. For example: *pradyumnaḥ kṛṣṇāt prati* ("Pradyumna is a substitute for Kṛṣṇa") and *tilebhyaḥ pratiyacchati māṣān* ("He gives beans in exchange for sesame seeds").

SK 601: *akartary ṛṇe pañcamī* (A 2.3.24). When a debt that is not the agent serves as the cause, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be used after it. Example: *śatād baddhaḥ* ("bound because of a hundred [debt]"). Why "not the agent"? Example: *śatena bandhitaḥ* ("caused to be bound by a hundred"). SK 602: *vibhāṣā guṇe 'striyām* (A 2.3.25). [The fifth case ending is optionally used] when a quality (*guṇa*) other than a feminine noun serves as the cause.

When expressing a cause that is a quality (*guṇa*) and not feminine in gender, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) may optionally be used. For example: *jāḍyāj jāḍyena vā baddhaḥ* ("bound because of dullness"). Why "when a quality"? Consider: *dhanena kulam* ("the family [is established] by wealth"). Why "not feminine"? Consider: *baddhyā muktaḥ* ("released from bondage"). Because of the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) by the word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*), it sometimes occurs even when not a quality or when feminine: *dhūmād agnimān* ("there is fire because of smoke") and *nāsti ghaṭo 'nupalabdheḥ* ("the jar does not exist because it is not perceived"). SK 603: With *pṛthak*, *vinā*, and *nānā*, the third case is optionally used. (A 2.3.32)

In connection with these [words], the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall occur, as well as the fifth (*pañcamī*) and the second (*dvitīyā*). The mention of *anyatarasyām* is for the purpose of inclusion (*samuccaya*). The [terms] *pañcamī* and *dvitīyā* are carried over [from the previous rule]. For example: *pṛthag rāmeṇa*, *rāmāt*, or *rāmam*. The same applies to *vinā* and *nānā*. SK 604: *karaṇe ca stokālpakṛcchrakatipayasyāsattvavacanasya* (A 2.3.33). In the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the third and fifth case endings occur after these words—*stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya*—when they do not denote a substance (*adravyavacana*). For example: *stokena* or *stokād muktaḥ* ("released with little effort"). However, when denoting a substance, one says *stokena viṣeṇa hataḥ* ("killed by a small amount of poison").

SK 605: *dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca* (A 2.3.35). After words meaning "far" (*dūra*) or "near" (*antika*), the second case (*dvitīyā*) shall also [be used], and optionally the fifth (*pañcamī*) and third (*tṛtīyā*). This rule applies when there is merely the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Examples: *grāmasya dūram*, *dūrāt*, or *dūreṇa*; *antikam*, *antikāt*, or *antikenā*. Because the phrase "when not denoting a substance" (*asattvavacanasya*) is understood [from the previous rule], it does not apply here in the case of *dūraḥ panthāḥ* ("a distant path"), where the fifth case is used. SK 606: *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (A 2.3.50). The sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the remaining relations (*śeṣe*).

The *śeṣa* (remainder) is a relationship such as that between owner and owned which is distinct from the meanings of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the case-roles (*kāraka*). In that case, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall occur. For example: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"). Even for [grammatical roles] such as the object (*karman*), when there is a desire to express merely the general relation, the sixth case alone is used: *satāṃ gatam* ("the going of the virtuous"), *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he knows [how to use] ghee"), *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers his mother"), *edho dakasyopaskurute* ("the fuel improves the water"), *bhaje śambhoś caraṇayoḥ* ("I worship the two feet of Śambhu"), *phalānāṃ tṛptaḥ* ("satisfied with fruits"). SK 607: *ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge* (A 2.3.26). When the word *hetu* ("cause") is employed and the cause is to be indicated, the sixth case shall occur. Example: *annasya hetor vartate* ("he lives for the sake of food").

SK 608: *sarvanāmnas tṛtīyā ca* (A 2.3.27). When a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) or the word *hetu* ("cause") is employed to indicate the sense of "cause" (*hetu*), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) shall be used, as well as the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For example: *kena hetunā vasati* ("For what reason does he dwell? or *kasya hetoḥ*. When words synonymous with *nimitta* ("occasion," "cause") are employed, all cases are generally observed. For example: *kiṃ nimittaṃ vasati*, *kena nimittena*, *kasmai nimittāya*, and so forth. Similarly: *kiṃ kāraṇam*, *ko hetuḥ*, *kiṃ prayojanam*, and so forth. Because of the inclusion of the term "generally" (*prāyas*), the first and second cases do not occur when the word is not a pronoun.

Hari is to be served for the sake of knowledge (*jñānena nimittena*), [or] for the purpose of knowledge (*jñānāya nimittāya*), and so forth. According to A 2.3.30, *ṣaṣṭhy atasarthapratyayena*, the genitive case shall be used in connection with suffixes having the sense of *atas-arthāḥ*. The rule *dikśabda* [A 2.3.29] is an exception to the ablative case. Examples: *grāmasya dakṣiṇataḥ* (to the south of the village), *puraḥ* (in front of), *purastāt* (in front of), *upari* (above), *upariṣṭāt* (above).

SK 610: *enapā dvitīyā* (A 2.3.31). In connection with a word ending in the suffix *enap*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) shall be used. Because of the syntactical split (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule *enapā*, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) may also be used. For example: *dakṣiṇena grāmam* or *grāmasya*. Likewise for *uttareṇa*. SK 611: *dūrāntikārthaiḥ ṣaṣṭhy anyatarasyām* (A 2.3.34). With words having the sense of "far" or "near," the sixth case may optionally be used.
In connection with these [words], the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as well as the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) may occur. For example: *dūraṃ nikaṭaṃ grāmasya* or *grāmāt*.
(SK 612) Regarding the rule *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe* (A 2.3.51):

when the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the verb *jñā* (to know), provided it does not mean "to recognize," is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatvena*), the sixth case-ending shall occur. Example: *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee").

SK 613: *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* (A 2.3.52). For these [roots] meaning "to remember" (*adhi-i*), "to pity" (*day*), and "to rule" (*īś*), the genitive case ending shall be used for the object when it is treated as a residual relation (*śeṣe*). Examples: *mātuḥ smaraṇam* ("the remembering of the mother"); *sarpiṣo dayanam* or *īśanam* ("pitying" or "ruling over the clarified butter").
SK 614: *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne* (A 2.3.53). [The genitive case ending is used for the object of the root *kṛ* ("to do/make") when it denotes improvement or restoration.]

When a verb meaning "to do" (*kṛñ*) is used in the sense of imparting a quality (*guṇādhāna*), the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be employed for the object (*karman*) when it is treated as residual (*śeṣa*). Example: *edho dakasyopaskaraṇam* ("the fuel's preparation with water"). Regarding A 2.3.54, *rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanānām ajvareḥ*: When verbs meaning "to afflict" (*rujārtha*) denote a state (*bhāva*) and have an agent that is a state (*bhāvakartṛka*), the sixth case ending shall be used for the object when it is treated as residual, provided the root *jvari* (to fever) is excluded. Example: *caurasya rogasya rujā* ("the affliction of the thief by disease"). It should be stated: "excluding *jvari* and *saṃtāpi*. Examples: *rogasya caurajvaraḥ* or *caurasaṃtāpaḥ*. The meaning is: the fever or the affliction belonging to the thief, which has the disease as its agent.

SK 616 *āśiṣi nāthaḥ* (A 2.3.55): When the verb *nāth* has the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), the sixth case ending shall be used for the remaining object. Example: *sarpiṣo nāthanam* ("the blessing for [the obtainment of] clarified butter"). Why "in the sense of a benediction"? Example: *māṇavaka-nāthanam*. This means a request related to that [object]. SK 617 *jāsiniprahaṇanāṭakrāthapiṣāṃ hiṃsāyām* (A 2.3.56): [The sixth case ending is used for the remaining object] of the verbs *jas*, *ni-pra-han*, *naṭ*, *krath*, and *piṣ* when they denote injury (*hiṃsā*).

For these roots meaning "injury," the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for the remaining object (*śeṣe karmaṇi*). For example: *caurasyojjāsanam* ("the extermination of the thief"). In the case of *ni* and *pra*, whether they are joined together, reversed, or separated: *caurasya niprahaṇanam*, *praṇihananam*, *nihananam*, or *prahaṇanam*. The root *naṭ* in the sense of "leaping upon" belongs to the *curādi* group: *caurasyonnāṭanam*. Also: *caurasya krāthanam* ("the throttling of the thief") and *vṛṣalasya peṣaṇam* ("the grinding of the low-born"). Why "in the sense of injury"? Consider: *dhānāpeṣaṇam* ("the grinding of parched grain"). [Pāṇini 2.3.57: *vyavahṛpaṇoḥ samarthayoḥ* ("In the case of *vyavahṛ* and *paṇ* when they have the same meaning...").

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for the remaining object [of the verbs *div* "to gamble" and *vyavahṛ* "to deal"]. In gambling and in the business of buying and selling, these two [verbs] have the same meaning. Examples: *śatasya vyavaharaṇam* or *paṇanam* ("dealing with or betting on a hundred"). Why [specify] "when they are synonymous"? Consider *śalākā-vyavahāraḥ* ("dealing with counting-sticks"); this means "counting. *brāhmaṇa-paṇamam*; this means "praising. [Rule A 2.3.58: *divas tadarthasya*. The genitive case shall be used for the object of the verb *div* when it has that meaning—that is, when it means "gambling" or "the business of buying and selling. Example: *śatasya dīvyati* ("he gambles or deals with a hundred"). Why [specify] "having that meaning"? Consider *brāhmaṇaṃ dīvyati*; this means "he praises."

SK 620 *vibhāṣopasarge* (A 2.3.59): This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. [Examples: *śatasya* or *śataṃ pratidīvyati*. SK 621 *preṣyabruvor haviṣo devatāsaṃpradāne* (A 2.3.61): [The genitive is used] with the verbs *pra-iṣya-* and *brū-* when the oblation (*havis*) is being offered to a deity as the recipient.

When the words *preṣya* and *brūhi* are used in the sense of an offering to a deity, the sixth case ending shall be employed after a word denoting the object—that is, a specific oblation (*havis*)—of such an offering. For example: *agnaye chāgasya haviṣo vapāyā medasaḥ preṣya* or *anubrūhi* ("Command [the Hotṛ] to offer the omentum and fat of the goat-oblation to Agni," or "Recite [the invitatory verse]").

In the application of words expressing frequency (*kṛtvas-arthānām*), when a word denoting time is used as the locus (*adhikaraṇe*), the sixth case ending shall be employed in the sense of a remainder (*śeṣe*). For example: *pañcakṛtvo 'hno bhojanam* ("Eating five times a day") or *dvirahno bhojanam* ("Eating twice a day"). Why say "in the sense of a remainder"? Consider: *dvirahany adhyayanam* ("Studying twice on a day"). Here, the seventh case is used because it denotes the locus, not a remainder.

SK 623 *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (A 2.3.65): When used in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be employed for both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). Example: *kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ* ("the act of Kṛṣṇa"); *jagataḥ kartā kṛṣṇaḥ* ("Kṛṣṇa is the creator of the world"). It is also desired [to apply] when there is a subordinate action (*guṇakarman*): *netā aśvasya srughnasya* or *srughnam* ("the leader of the horse to Srughna"). Why "when a *kṛt*-suffix"? To prevent it from applying to a *taddhita* suffix: *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"). SK 624 *upayapprāptau karmaṇi* (A 2.3.66): When the suffix *upaya* is used in the sense of attainment, the sixth case is employed for the object.

Where there is a *kṛt* suffix and the application of both [the sixth case and the third case] occurs, the sixth case should be used only for the object. For example: *āścaryo gavāṃ doho ’gopena* ("The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is wonderful"). This restriction does not apply to feminine suffixes that do not contain the sounds *ka* or *ā*. For example: *bhedikā bibhitsā vā rudrasya jagataḥ* ("Rudra’s breaking or desire to break the world"). Regarding the "remainder" (*śeṣe*), there is an option (*vibhāṣā*). Some say this applies only to feminine suffixes; for example: *vicitrā jagataḥ kṛtir hareḥ hariṇā vā* ("Hari’s wonderful creation of the world"). Some, however, desire this option without distinction; for example: *śabdānām anuśāsanam ācāryeṇa ācāryasya vā* ("The teaching of words by the Teacher"). (Pāṇini 2.3.67: *ktasya ca vartamāne*) [Note: The provided text contains a portion of the commentary on Pāṇini’s rules regarding the use of the genitive case with *kṛt* participles.]

When used in connection with a *kta*-suffix denoting present time, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be employed. This is an exception to the prohibition [stated in A 2.3.69], "not after words listed in the *loka* group," etc. Example: *rājñāṃ mataḥ*, *buddhaḥ*, or *pūjitaḥ* ("respected, understood, or honored by kings").

A 2.3.68: *adhikaraṇavācinaś ca*. When used in connection with a *kta*-suffix expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the sixth case shall be employed. Example: *idam eṣām āsitam*, *śayitam*, *gatam*, or *bhuktam* ("this is where they sat, lay, went, or ate").

SK 627: *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* (A 2.3.69). When these are used, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall not occur. 1. Substitutes for *l* (present participles): *hariḥ sṛṣṭiṃ kurvan* or *kurvāṇaḥ* (Hari, creating the world). 2. *u*: *hariṃ didṛkṣuḥ* (desirous of seeing Hari) or *alaṃkariṣṇuḥ* (desirous of adorning). 3. *uka*: *daityān ghātuko hariḥ* (Hari is the slayer of the Daityas). *Exclusion of the prohibition for the root √kam:* *lakṣmyāḥ kāmuko hariḥ* (Hari is the lover of Lakṣmī). 4. Indeclinable (*avyaya*): *jagat sṛṣṭvā* (having created the world); *sukhaṃ kartum* (to do something easily). 5. Past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*): *viṣṇunā hatā daityāḥ* (the Daityas were slain by Viṣṇu); *daityān hatavān viṣṇuḥ* (Viṣṇu has slain the Daityas). 6. Words having the sense of the *khal* suffix (*khalartha*): *īṣatkaraḥ prapañco hariṇā* (the world was easily made by Hari).

*tṛn* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term) beginning with the word *tṛ* from the rule *śatṛśānacau* and ending with the *n* of *tṛn*. [The following are examples: *śatṛ*: *somaṃ pavamānaḥ* ("purifying the Soma"); *cānaś*: *ātmānaṃ maṇḍayamānaḥ* ("adorning himself"); *śatṛ*: *vedaṃ adhīyan* ("studying the Veda"); *tṛn*: *kartā lokān* ("one who will create the worlds"). [Regarding the rule] *dviṣaḥ śatur vā* ("after the root *dviṣ*, the genitive may optionally be used with the present participle suffix *śatṛ*"): *murasya muraṃ vā dviṣan* ("hating Muru or the son of Muru"). This entire prohibition concerns the genitive case of the *kāraka* (participant in an action). However, the "residual" (*śeṣa*) genitive would certainly still apply: *brāhmaṇasya kurvan* ("doing for a Brahmin"), *narakasya jiṣṇuḥ* ("conqueror of Naraka").
[A 2.3.70] *akenor bhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ* ("With the future passive participles *akenoḥ*, the genitive is prohibited when expressing future time or debt").

In the case of the word *bhaviṣyat* ("future") joined with a word having the sense of "debt" (*ṛṇa*) or "indebtedness" (*adhamarṇya*), the sixth case ending would not occur [if this rule were not stated]. For example: *sataḥ pālaka avatirati* ("the protector of the virtuous descends"), *vrajaṃ gāmī* ("going to the cow-pen"), and *śataṃ dāyī* ("one who owes a hundred").
Regarding the suffixes called *kṛtya*, the agent may optionally take the sixth case ending (A 2.3.71).

Or else, the genitive case may be used: *mayā* or *mama sevyaḥ hariḥ* ("Hari is to be served by me"). Why [is it said] "when the agent is expressed"? Consider: *geyaḥ māṇavakaḥ sāmnām* ("the boy is to sing the Sāman hymns"). Because the suffix *yat* is prescribed in the sense of the agent by the rule *bhavyageya-*, the object is not already expressed [by the suffix]. Here, the rule is divided: *kṛtyānām*. The phrases *ubhayaprāptau* and *na* are carried over [from previous rules]. Therefore: *netavyā vrajaṃ gāvaḥ kṛṣṇena* ("the cows are to be led to the cow-pen by Kṛṣṇa"). Then: *kartari vā*. The meaning has been stated. A 2.3.72: *tulyārthair atulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyāntarasyām* ("With words having the sense of 'equal', except for *atula* and *upama*, the third case ending is optionally used instead of the sixth").

When joined with words having the same meaning as *tulya*, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) shall optionally be used, and in the alternative, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For example: *tulyaḥ*, *sadṛśaḥ*, or *samaḥ* [is] of Kṛṣṇa, or by Kṛṣṇa (*kṛṣṇasya* or *kṛṣṇena*). Why [mention] *atula* and *upama*? [Because they do not have the same meaning]: there is no equal (*tulā*) or comparison (*upamā*) of Kṛṣṇa.
In a benediction (*āśis*), the fourth case (*caturthī*) is also used along with [the sixth], when joined with *āyuṣya*, *madra*, *bhadra*, *kuśala*, *sukha*, *artha*, and *hita*. (A 2.3.73)

When joined with words having these meanings, there shall optionally be either the fourth case (*caturthī*) or, in the alternative, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). For example: *āyuṣyaṃ ciraṃjīvitaṃ kṛṣṇāya kṛṣṇasya vā bhūyāt* ("May long life be for Kṛṣṇa"). Likewise: *madraṃ bhadraṃ kuśalaṃ nirāmayaṃ sukhaṃ śaṃ arthaḥ prayojanaṃ hitaṃ pathyaṃ vā bhūyāt* ("May there be welfare, prosperity, well-being, health, happiness, peace, purpose, benefit, or what is salutary"). Why "in the sense of a benediction"? [Consider: *devadattasyāyuṣyam asti* ("Devadatta has long life"). Because of the explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*), the term "meaning" (*artha*) is understood everywhere. Since *madra* and *bhadra* are synonyms, only one of them need be recited. Thus ends the section on the sixth case. SK 632: The locus (*ādhāra*) is the locus-case (*adhikaraṇa*). (A 1.4.45)

The locus (*ādhāra*) of an action residing therein, by way of the agent or the object, shall be designated as the *adhikaraṇa* (locus) kāraka. [This is expressed by] Pāṇini 2.3.36: *saptamy adhikaraṇe ca*.

The locative case (*saptamī*) shall be used for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). By the word "and" (*ca*), [the locative] is also used after words meaning "near. The locus (*ādhāra*) is threefold: contact-based (*aupaśleṣika*), situational (*vaiṣayika*), and pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*). Examples: *kaṭe āste* ("He sits on a mat"); *sthālyāṃ pacati* ("He cooks in a pot"); *mokṣe icchāsti* ("There is a desire for liberation"); *sarvasminn ātmāsti* ("The Self exists in everything"). *vanasya dūre antike vā* ("Far from or near the forest"). Thus, including the three cases [instrumental, ablative, and locative] for words meaning "far" and "near," four cases are established here. There is an extension [of the rule] regarding the object of a verbal noun ending in *ktin* when it refers to a field of study: *adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("One who has studied grammar").

In the analysis *adhītam anena* ("this has been studied by him"), the suffix *inaṅ* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *iṣṭādibhyaś ca*. [The rule] *sādhvasādhuprayoge ca* [is also mentioned]. "Kṛṣṇa is good toward his mother"; "he is bad toward his maternal uncle. Regarding the rule *nimittāt karmayoge*: here, "cause" (*nimitta*) refers to the result; "connection" (*yoga*) consists of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*). [As stated in the Bhāṣya: "One kills the leopard for its skin; one kills the elephant for its two tusks; one kills the yak for its hair; the musk deer is killed for its scent-gland. Since the instrumental case would have applied here by virtue of the cause (*hetu*), this [rule] is intended to prevent that.

*sīmāṇḍakośaḥ* (the sheath of the border); *puṣkalakaḥ* (a musk deer), [which is] *gandhamṛgaḥ* (a fragrant deer). [Question: What [is the purpose of the word] *yogaviśeṣe* (in the case of a specific connection)? [Answer: He reaps grain for wages (*vetanena*). **SK 634:** *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (A 2.3.37).

When another action is characterized by the action of something else, the locative case shall be used after that [thing]. Example: *goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ* (He went while the cows were being milked). [This applies] when those who are worthy are the agents and those who are unworthy are not the agents, or in the opposite case. Examples: *satsu taratsu asanta āsate* (While the virtuous are crossing over, the wicked remain behind); *asatsu tiṣṭhatsu santas taranti* (While the wicked remain behind, the virtuous cross over); *satsu tiṣṭhatsu asantas taranti* (While the virtuous remain behind, the wicked cross over); *asatsu taratsu santas tiṣṭhanti* (While the wicked are crossing over, the virtuous remain behind).

SK 635: *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare* (A 2.3.38). When there is a characteristic of an action (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*) involving an excess of disregard (*anādara*), both the sixth and seventh case endings are used. For example: *rudati rudato vā prāvrājīt*. The meaning is: "He went forth into homelessness, disregarding his son and others who were weeping. SK 636: *svāmīśvarādhipatidāyādasākṣipratibhūprasūtaiś ca* (A 2.3.39). [The sixth case ending is used with these words when they denote the relationship of ownership. Thus: *rājñaḥ svāmī*, *rājña īśvaraḥ*, *rājño 'dhipatiḥ*, *rājño dāyādaḥ*, *rājñaḥ sākṣī*, *rājñaḥ pratibhūḥ*, *rājñaḥ prasūtaḥ*. (Note: The word *sākṣin* is optionally declined in the genitive or locative; *pratibhū* is always in the genitive.)

In connection with these seven [words], the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and seventh (*saptamī*) case endings occur. Since the sixth case would have applied alone, this rule is stated to provide for the optional seventh case. For example: *gavāṃ goṣu vā svāmī* ("the owner of cows") or *gavāṃ goṣu vā prasūtaḥ* ("born for the cows"). The meaning is: "born in order to experience the cows themselves. Pāṇini 2.3.40 states: *āyuktakuśalābhyāṃ cāsevāyām* ("And with *āyukta* and *kuśala*, when there is intentness"). In connection with these two, the sixth and seventh cases occur when the sense is that of intentness (*tātparya*). *Āyukta* means "employed" or "engaged. Examples: *āyuktaḥ kuśalo vā haripūjane haripūjanasya vā* ("intent on the worship of Hari"). Why "when there is intentness"? Consider: *āyukto gauḥ śakaṭe* ("the ox is yoked to the cart"); the meaning here is "only slightly yoked."

SK 638: *yataś ca nirdhāraṇam* (A 2.3.41). "Selection" (*nirdhāraṇa*) is the separation of one part from a whole by means of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or name (*saṃjñā*). When selection occurs, the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and seventh (*saptamī*) case endings are used. Examples: among men (*nṛṇām* or *nṛṣu*), the non-Brāhmaṇa is the best; among cows (*gavām* or *goṣu*), the black one yields much milk; among those walking (*gacchatām* or *gacchatsu*), the running one is the fastest; among students (*chātrāṇām* or *chātreṣu*), Maitra is the cleverest. SK 639: *pañcamī vibhakte* (A 2.3.42). [The fifth case ending is used when there is a distinction.]

*Vibhāga* means "distinction" (*vibhaktam*). Where there is a distinction of that which is being singled out (*nirdhāryamāṇa*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) should be used. Example: *māthurāḥ pāṭaliputrakebhya āḍhyatarāḥ* ("The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra"). SK 640: *sādhunipuṇābhyām arcāyāṃ saptamy aprateḥ* (A 2.3.43). When used in conjunction with these two words, the seventh case (*saptamī*) should be employed to express honor (*arcā*), provided that *prati* is not used. Example: *mātari sādhunipuṇo vā* ("He is good or skillful toward his mother"). Why "to express honor"? Example: *nipuṇo rājño bhṛtyaḥ* ("The servant is skillful toward the king")—here, the intent is merely to state a fact. It should be stated that [the rule applies] when [words] such as *prati* are not used. Example: *sādhur nipuṇo vā mātaraṃ prati pary anu vā* ("He is good or skillful toward his mother").

SK 641: *prasita-utsukābhyāṃ tṛtīyā ca* (A 2.3.44). When used in conjunction with these two words, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall be employed, and optionally the seventh case (*saptamī*) as well. For example: *prasitaḥ* or *utsukaḥ hariṇā* or *harau*. SK 642: *nakṣatre ca lupi* (A 2.3.45). [The third case ending is also used] when a word denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is present, provided that the nominal suffix (*pratyaya*) has been elided (*lup*).

When [the suffix] denoting the sense of the base itself is elided by the technical term *lup* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), [the locative and ablative case endings] occur: "one should invoke the Goddess under Mūla" (*mūlena*) or "one should dismiss her under Śravaṇa" (*śravaṇena*). Or one may say "under Mūla" (*mūle*) or "under Śravaṇa" (*śravaṇe*). Why mention *lup*? [Consider: "Saturn is in Puṣya" (*puṣye śaniḥ*). (A 2.3.7:
The seventh and fifth cases occur when there is an interval between two *kārakas*.)

Between the two powers (*śakti*), there are the two paths of time (*kāla-adhvan*); by means of these, these [cases] occur: "Having eaten today, he will eat in two days" or "after two days. This is the time between the two powers of the agent and the action. "Standing here, he would pierce the target at a *krośa* or from a *krośa*"—this is the space between the two powers of the agent and the object (*karman*). The seventh and fifth cases are desired when used in conjunction with the word *adhika* ("more than"), because of the rule-indication in the *sūtras*: *tad asminn adhikam* and *yasmād adhikam*. In common usage: "Hari is more than the world" (*loke* / *lokāt* *bādhiko hariḥ*). [This is governed by] *adhir īśvare* (Pāṇini 1.4.97).

In the relation of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), the term *adhi* shall be designated as a *karmapravacanīya*. According to A 2.3.9, "the locative case is used for that which is superior (*adhika*) and for that which expresses lordship (*īśvara*)," the locative case shall be employed when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. For example: *upa parārdhe harer guṇāḥ* ("The qualities of Hari exceed the highest number"). The meaning is "superior to the highest number. Regarding lordship, however, the locative case is used alternatively for both the owner and the owned: *adhi bhuvi rāmaḥ* ("Rāma is over the earth") or *adhi rāme bhūḥ* ("the earth is under Rāma"). But in the case of compounding according to the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ*, [the form] is *rāmādhīnā* ("dependent on Rāma"), with the suffix *kha* applied by the rule *aṣaḍakṣa-* etc.
SK 646: *vibhāṣā kṛñi* (A 1.4.98).

The prefix *adhi*, when used with the root *kṛ* in the sense of "lordship" (*īśvara*), may optionally be designated as a *gati*. For example: *yad atra mām adhikariṣyati*. The meaning is "he will employ me here. In this case, the lordship of the employer is understood. Because it is not a *gati* [in the technical sense], and because of the rule *tiṅi codāttavati* (Pāṇini 8.1.28), there is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent). Thus ends the section on the locative case.
Thus ends the section on kārakas.
Section 17: The Section on Avyayībhāva Compounds.
SK 647: *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (A 2.1.1): A grammatical operation (*vidhi*) concerning words (*pada*) should be understood as being dependent upon semantic competency (*samartha*).
SK 648: *prākkaḍārāt samāsaḥ* (A 2.1.3): [The category of] compound (*samāsa*) begins from [the rule] *kaḍāra*.

From the rule *kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye* (SK 649) onwards, the heading "compound" (*samāsa*) is in force. The rule *saha supā* (A 2.1.4) is divided into two separate rules: *saha* and *supā*. 1. *Saha*: A word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is compounded with a word that has the same meaning (*samartha*). Since this division of the rule is for the purpose of establishing desired results, this compound includes certain words ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) as its final members; however, such compounds occur only in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Examples: *paryabhūṣat*, *anuvyacalat*. 2. *Supā*: A word ending in a case-suffix is compounded with another word ending in a case-suffix. Because it is a compound, it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

SK 650 *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (A 2.3.71): There shall be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) which is a member of these two—namely, a verbal root (*dhātu*) or a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The word *bhūta* is placed first [in the compound] because of the rule *bhūtapūrve caraṭ* (Pāṇini 4.2.69). That which existed previously is *bhūtapūrva*. [The example] *jīmūtasyeva* is a compound with *iva*, and there is no elision of the case-ending.
SK 651 *avyayībhāvaḥ* (A 2.1.5): This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).

SK 652 *avyayaṃ vibhaktisamīpasamṛddhivyṛddhyarthābhāvātyayāsaṃpratiśabdaprādurbhāvapaścādyathānupūrvyayaugapadyasādṛśyasaṃpattisākalyāntavacaneṣu* (A 2.1.6): An indeclinable (*avyaya*) [is compounded with a following noun] in the sense of case-inflection (*vibhakti*), proximity (*samīpa*), prosperity (*samṛddhi*), adversity (*vyṛddhi*), non-existence (*arthābhāva*), passing away (*atyaya*), "not now" (*asaṃprati*), the appearance of a word (*śabdaprādurbhāva*), "after" (*paścāt*), "according to" (*yathā*), sequence (*anupūrvya*), simultaneity (*yaugapadya*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), attainment (*saṃpatti*), totality (*sākalya*), and limit (*anta*).
The rule *avyayam* is analyzed as a separate yoga. An indeclinable (*avyaya*) is compounded with a word that is semantically connected to it; that [compound] is called *avyayībhāva*.
According to A 1.2.43, *prathamānirdiṣṭaṃ samāsa upasarjanam*:
in a rule concerning compounds, that which is designated by the first case ending shall bear the technical designation *upasarjana* (subordinate member).
SK 654: *upasarjanaṃ pūrvam* (A 2.2.30).
In a compound (*samāsa*), the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) must be placed first.
SK 655: *ekavibhakti cāpūrvanipāte* (A 1.2.44). A word that has a single case-ending is also called *upasarjana*, except when it is not to be placed first in the compound.
In a compound (vigraha), that which has a fixed case-ending shall be designated as an upasarjana, but it does not necessarily undergo prior placement (pūrvanipāta).

SK 656 *gostriyor upasarjanasya* (A 1.2.48): When the word *go* is an upasarjana, and when a nominal stem ending in a feminine suffix is an upasarjana, the final vowel of that nominal stem shall be shortened. By the rule *avyayībhāvaś ca*, [the compound] acquires the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). SK 657 *nāvyayībhāvād ato 'm tv apañcamyāḥ* (A 2.4.83): After an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) ending in *a*, the suffix *am* is used [in place of the case endings], except for the fifth case.

After an indeclinable *avyayībhāva* compound ending in a consonant, there is no elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*), but rather its replacement by *am*, with the exception of the fifth case (*pañcamī*). For example: *apadiśam* (between the two directions). Regarding this, Amara states: "The neuter indeclinable *apadiśam* means between two directions; [the feminine] *vidik* means intermediate direction. (Amarakośa). Furthermore, according to A 2.4.84, *tṛtīyāsaptamyor bahulam* ("the third and seventh cases are optionally retained").

After an indeclinable (*avyayībhāva*) compound ending in *adanta* (ending in *a*), there is optionally the substitution of *am* for the third and seventh case endings. Thus: *apadiśam*, *apadiśena*; *apadiśam*, *apadiśe*. Because of the mention of "optionally" (*bahulagrahaṇāt*), in cases such as *sumadram* and *unmattagaṅgam*, the substitution of *am* for the seventh case is obligatory. This is the meaning of the rule beginning with "vibhakti": an indeclinable (*avyaya*) denoting the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*) and so forth is compounded with a word ending in a case suffix (*subanta*); that is an *avyayībhāva* compound. First, regarding the case ending itself: *harau* [denoting location] becomes *adhihari*.

In this context, *adhi* is merely an indicator (*dyotaka*) of the sense of the locative case. The colloquial analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is *hari ṅi adhi*. Although the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is already expressed by the particle (*nipāta*), the locative case ending occurs here by virtue of the power of the explicit rule.
[This is governed by] A 2.4.18: *avyayībhāvaś ca*.

This [term] would be neuter. [The rule] *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* [states that] the final vowel of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) becomes short when it is neuter. One who protects (*gopāyati*) or guards cows (*gāḥ pāti*) is a *gopā*. [The form] *adhigopam* is formed with the word *tasmin* [meaning "near" or "in the vicinity of"]. It means "in the vicinity. *Upakṛṣ�ṇam* means "the vicinity of Kṛṣṇa. However, in the cases of *samayā grāmam*, *nikaṣā laṅkām*, and *ārād vanāt*, there is no *avyayībhāva* compound; this is because of the force of the rules prescribing the second (*dvitīyā*) and fifth (*pañcamī*) case endings for the words *abhitaḥ*, *paritaḥ*, and *anyārāt*. *Sumadram* means "the prosperity of the Madras. *Duryavanam* means "the misfortune of the Yavanas."

*Vigata-ṛddhi-vyṛddhiḥ*: the passing away of prosperity. *Nirmakṣikam*: the absence of flies. *Atihimam*: the passing of the cold; *atyaya* means destruction. *Atinidram*: sleep is not appropriate at this time. *Itihari*: the manifestation of the word "Hari. *Anuviṣṇu*: after Viṣṇu. However, this is not a compound with the word *paścāt*; for there is a usage in the Bhāṣya: *tataḥ paścāt sraṃsyate* ("after that, he will fall"). The meanings of *yathā* are fitness, repetition (*vīpsā*), going beyond the meaning of the word (*padārthātivr̥tti*), and similarity. *Anurūpam*: according to form.

The meaning is "suitable for form" (*rūpasya yogyam*). *Pratyartham* means "with respect to each object" (*artham arthaṃ prati*). Because of the power of the rule prescribing that the word *prati* is designated as a *karmapravacanīya* when used distributively (*vīpsā*), there is also a sentence containing the accusative case when it is joined with it. *Yathāśakti* means "not exceeding one's capacity. *Sahari* means "similarity to Hari," according to the rule to be stated later: "the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-*. *Anujyeṣṭham* means "in order of seniority," [derived from] "after the eldest" (*jyeṣṭhasyānupūrvyeṇa*). This occurs in the analysis (*vigraha*) of "simultaneously with the wheel" (*cakreṇa yugapat*). According to A 2.1.6 and A 2.1.7, this forms an *avyayībhāva* compound. By A 6.3.81, *avyayībhāve cākāle*, the *sa-* is substituted for *saha-* when not referring to time.

In an *avyayībhāva* compound, the word *saha* becomes *sa-* except when denoting time. Examples: *sacakram* (together with the wheel); but when denoting time, *sahapūrvāhṇam* (along with the forenoon). In *sasakhi* (accompanied by a friend), the form is established simply by the sense of "according to the object" (*yathārthatvena*); however, the explicit mention of "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is for the purpose that the rule should apply even when similarity is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). Examples: *sakṣatram* (the prosperity of the Kṣatriyas); *ṛddhi* is abundance or excess, while *saṃpatti* is a state of being in accordance [with one's nature]—this is the distinction. Example: *satṛṇam atti* (he eats [even] the grass, not leaving even a blade behind).

The meaning is "in its entirety. However, there is no intention here [to imply] the eating of grass. At the end: one who studies up to the section on fire is called "Sāgni" (one who has studied the Agni section).

SK 661 *yathāsādṛśye* (A 2.1.7): The word *yathā* is compounded only when it does not signify similarity (*asādṛśye*). Therefore, in the example "as Hari is, so is Hara" (*yathā haris tathā haraḥ*), there is no compound; here the word *yathā* indicates that Hari is the object of comparison (*upamāna*). Thus, what would otherwise have been obtained by the rules *sādṛśye* or *yathārthe* is prohibited. SK 662 *yāvadavadhāraṇe* (A 2.1.8): [The word *yāvat* is compounded] when it signifies limitation (*avadhāraṇe*).

As many verses as there are, so many prostrations to Acyuta, verse by verse. (SK 663) *sup* with *prati* is used in the sense of "measure" (A 2.1.9): *śākaprati*, meaning "a small portion of vegetable. Why "in the sense of measure"? [Consider: *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut* ("The lightning flashes toward every tree").

SK 664 (A 2.1.10): *akṣa-śalākā-saṃkhyāḥ pariṇā*. In the context of gambling (*dyūta-vyavahāra*), this compound denotes only defeat. For example: *akṣapari* ("defeated by the die"), *śalākāpari* ("defeated by the counter"), *ekapari* ("defeated by one").
SK 665 (A 2.1.11): *vibhāṣā*. [The following rule applies optionally.]

This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). By the force of this very rule, the preceding [compounds] are necessarily compounds (*nityasamāsa*). However, the rule *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) does not constitute a necessary compound, because there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the formative rules for compounds such as *avyayam* (Pāṇini 2.1.6).

A 2.1.12: *apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* ("The words *apa*, *pari*, *bahiḥ*, and those ending in *añcu* [i.e., *prāñc*, *pratyañc*, etc. form compounds with a word ending in the fifth case-suffix"). Examples:

*apaviṣṇu saṃsāraḥ* (the cycle of existence is outside Viṣṇu), *apa viṣṇoḥ*; *pariviṣṇu* (around Viṣṇu), *pari viṣṇoḥ*; *bahirvanam* (outside the forest), *bahir vanāt*; *prāgvanam* (east of the forest), *prāg vanāt*.

SK 667 *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ* (A 2.1.13): With these two senses—limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*)—the prefix *āṅ* is optionally compounded with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), and the resulting compound is an *avyayībhāva*. Examples: *āmukti saṃsāraḥ* ("the cycle of existence until liberation") = *ā mukteḥ*; *ābālaṃ haribhaktiḥ* ("devotion to Hari from [including] children") = *ā bālebhyaḥ*. SK 668 *lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye* (A 2.1.14): When expressing direction toward something (*ābhimukhya*), the words *abhi* and *prati* are compounded with a word denoting a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

The prefixes *abhi* and *prati*, which indicate directionality (*ābhimukhya*), form compounds with words denoting a mark (*cihna*) as previously stated [in A 2.1.14]. For example: *abhyagni śalabhāḥ patanti* ("moths fall toward the fire") or *agnim abhi*; *pratyagni* ("toward the fire") or *agniṃ prati*. Regarding *anu* [in A 2.1.15]: *anur yatsamayā*. The prefix *anu* is compounded with that word by which proximity (*samayā*) to a certain object is indicated; that compound is an *avyayībhāva*. For example: *anuvanam aśanirgataḥ* ("the thunderbolt struck near the forest"). The meaning is: "it went into the vicinity of the forest" (*vanasya samīpaṃ gataḥ*).

SK 670 *yasya cāyāmaḥ* (A 2.1.16): The prefix *anu* is compounded with that word by which its length (*āyāma*)—that is, its extension—is indicated as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). For example, *anugaṅgaṃ vārāṇasī* ("Vārāṇasī along the Gaṅgā"). The meaning is: "along the Gaṅgā," characterized by a length similar to the length of the Gaṅgā.
SK 671 *tiṣṭhadguprabhṛtīni ca* (A 2.1.17): The compounds beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu* are also [irregularly formed].

These [forms] are irregularly derived (*nipātyante*). When cows stand, that time is *tiṣṭhadguḥ*, meaning "the time of milking. *Āyatīgavam* and so forth. Here, the substitution of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), the absence of the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), and the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) are irregularly prescribed.
[Furthermore, by A 2.1.18: *pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā* ("*pāra-* and *madhya-* optionally [form a compound] with a word in the genitive case").

The words *pāra* and *madhya* may optionally be compounded with a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), and the final *e* is substituted for their final vowel as a formal irregularity (*nipātana*). In the alternative, they form a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. Examples: *pāregaṅgād ānaya* ("bring from across the Gaṅgā") or *gaṅgāpārāt*; *madhyegaṅgāt* or *gaṅgāmadhyāt*. By virtue of the *mahāvibhāṣā*, the analytical sentence is also permitted: *gaṅgāyāḥ pārāt* or *gaṅgāyā madhyāt*. (Pāṇini 2.1.11) *saṃkhyā vaṃśyena*: A numeral may be compounded with a word denoting a member of a lineage (*vaṃśya*).

Lineage (*vaṃśa*) is twofold: by learning (*vidyā*) and by birth (*janman*). One who belongs to such a lineage is *vaṃśya*. A numeral may optionally be compounded with a word expressing that [lineage]. Two sages belonging to the lineage [of grammar] are *dvimuni*; [the study of] grammar [belonging to] three sages is *trimuni*. When there is an intention not to distinguish between the science and its possessor, [one says] *trimuni* for grammar. Twenty-one [stanzas belonging to] Bhāradvāja is *ekaviṃśati-bhāradvājam*. (A 2.1.20) "And with words denoting rivers": a numeral is compounded with words denoting rivers as previously stated. This [compound] is also desired in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*): *saptagaṅgam*, *dviyamunam*.

SK 675: *anyapadārthe ca saṃjñāyām* (A 2.1.21). A nominal ending (*subanta*) occurring as the meaning of another word is always compounded with feminine river names (*nadī*) when it denotes a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Although the governing rule of optionality (*vibhāṣā*) applies here, because the proper name cannot be understood through a loose syntactical phrase (*vākya*), this is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*). Examples: *unmattagaṅgam* (the region named Unmattagaṅgā), *lohitagaṅgam*. SK 676: *samāsāntāḥ* (A 5.4.68). [The following rules concern] suffixes added at the end of compounds (*samāsānta*).
With reference to this [topic], [Pāṇini] states: *avyayībhāve śaratprabhṛtibhyaḥ* (A 5.4.107).

In an *avyayībhāva* compound, the suffix *ṭac* shall be applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) after words beginning with *śarad*. Examples: *upaśaradam* (near autumn); *prativipāśam* (along the Vipāś river). The list of words beginning with *śarad* is: *śarad*, *vipāś*, *anas*, *manas*, *upānah*, *div*, *himavat*, *anaḍuh*, *diś*, *dṛś*, *viś*, *cetas*, *catur*, *tyad*, *tad*, *yad*, *kiyat*. Regarding *jarā*: the substitution of *jaras* for *jarā* also occurs [before the suffix]. Example: *upajarasam* (near old age). Regarding *akṣan*: after the prefixes *prati*, *para*, *sama*, and *anu*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied to *akṣan*. By the rule *yasyeti ca*, the final vowel and its following consonant are elided. Example: *pratyakṣam* (before the eyes).

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "beyond the eye" (*akṣṇaḥ param*), it is an *avyayībhāva* compound by virtue of the rule prescribing the final element of the compound (*samāsānta*). The substitution of the vowel *au* for *para-* occurs due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule "the *liṭ* [perfect] is used for what is beyond the senses" (*parokṣe liṭ*). Thus, we have *parokṣam*; and forms such as *parokṣā kriyā* are derived by adding the suffix *ac* in the sense of possession (*arśa-ādi*). *samakṣam* and *anvakṣam*.
By the rule *anaś ca* (A 5.4.108), the suffix *ṭac* is added after an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in *an*.
SK 679 *nastaddhite* (A 6.4.144): In a *taddhita* suffix, there shall be elision of the final phoneme (*ṭi*) of a *bha*-stem ending in *n*. Examples: *uparājam*, *adhyātmam*.
SK 680 *napuṃsakād anyatarasyām* (A 5.4.109): [The suffix *cha* is applied] optionally after a neuter [base].

The suffix *ṭac* may optionally follow an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in a neuter word that has no other final vowel (*annanta*). Examples: *upacarmam* or *upacarma*. (SK 681) The suffix *ṭac* may optionally follow compounds ending in *nadī*, *paurṇamāsī*, and *āgrahāyaṇī*:
*upanadam* or *upanadi*; *upapaurṇamāsam* or *upapaurṇamāsi*; *upāgrahāyaṇam* or *upāgrahāyaṇi*.

SK 682 *jñayaḥ* (A 5.4.111): The suffix *ṭac* is optionally added after an indeclinable compound ending in a word formed with the suffix *jña*. Examples: *upasamidham* or *upasamit*. SK 683 *gireś ca senakasya* (A 5.4.112): According to Senaka, the suffix *ṭac* is also added after the word *giri* when it forms an indeclinable compound. Examples: *adrigatam* or *adri*.

After an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in "giri," that [suffix] may optionally be applied. The mention of Senaka is for the sake of honor. Thus, *upagiram* and *upagiri* are examples of *avyayībhāva*.
The Section on Tatpuruṣa Compounds 18.
SK 684 *tatpuruṣaḥ* (A 2.1.22): This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*) extending up to [the rule for] *bahuvrīhi*. SK 685 *dviguś ca* (A 2.1.23).

A *dvigu* compound should also bear the designation of *tatpuruṣa*. This rule could be dispensed with; for by reading the rule as "that which has a numeral as its first member is a *dvigu*, and [it is also a *tatpuruṣa*]," it would be easy to state the co-occurrence of both designations by the force of the particle *ca*. The purpose [of the designation *tatpuruṣa*] is to apply the suffixes at the end of compounds (*samāsānta*). For example: *pañcarājam*. SK 686: A word ending in the second case is compounded with *śrita*, *atīta*, *patita*, *gata*, *atyasta*, *prāpta*, and *āpanna* (A 2.1.24).

A word ending in the second case is optionally compounded with words such as *śrita* (resorted to) that end in case-terminations; this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. For example: *kṛṣṇaṃ śritaḥ* (one who has resorted to Kṛṣṇa) becomes *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ*; *duḥkham atītaḥ* (one who has transcended suffering) becomes *duḥkhātītaḥ*. There is an extension of this rule to include words such as *gamī* (going): *grāmaṃ gamī* (going to the village) becomes *grāmagamī*; *annaṃ bubhukṣuḥ* (desirous of eating food) becomes *annabubhukṣuḥ*.

In SK 687, *svayaṃ ktena* (A 2.1.25), the rule "the second case [ending]" (*dvitīyā*) does not apply because it is unsuitable; thus, *svāyaṃkṛtiḥ* means "the offspring of one who has made himself. In SK 688, *khaṭvā kṣepe* (A 2.1.26).

A word ending in the second case, having *khaṭvā* as its base, is compounded with a word ending in a *su*-affix that has a past passive participle (*ktānta*) as its base, when contempt is expressed. For example: *khaṭvārūḍho jālmaḥ* ("the wretch who has mounted the couch"). This is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), for the sense of contempt cannot be understood through a loose sentence (*vākya*).
[Pāṇini 2.1.27] *sāmi*: *sāmikṛtam*.

SK 690 *kālāḥ* (A 2.1.28): [The word *kālāḥ*] is governed by the rule *ktena* alone. This statement is for the purpose of excluding absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). Example: *māsam uṣitaḥ pratipaccandraḥ*. The meaning is: "He has begun to measure a month," i.e., the new moon has been visible for one month. SK 691 *atyantasaṃyoge ca* (A 2.1.29).
It is simply *kālāḥ* [time-words]. This statement is for the purpose of including those ending in *-akta*. *Muhūrtaṃ sukham* (happiness for a moment) becomes *muhūrtasukham*.

According to Pāṇini 2.1.30, *tṛtīyā tatkṛtārthena guṇavacanena*, the word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) is compounded with a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) that denotes something produced by that [instrumental factor], where the third case marker is elided (*luptatṛtīyāka*). Thus, a word ending in the third case is compounded with a word expressing a quality produced by the meaning of the third case, as well as with the word *artha* (purpose), in the same manner as before. Examples: *śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ* (broken by a wedge) becomes *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ*; *dhānyenārthaḥ* (wealth by means of grain) becomes *dhānyārthaḥ*. Why say "produced by that" (*tatkṛta*)? [Counter-example: *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* (blind in one eye)—[here the blindness is not produced by the eye itself, but is a pre-existing condition].

SK 693: *pūrva-sadṛśa-sama-ūna-artha-kalaha-nipuṇa-miśra-ślakṣṇaiḥ* (A 2.1.31). A word ending in the third case is compounded with these [words], as previously stated. *māsapūrvaḥ* ("preceded by a month"). *mātṛsadṛśaḥ* ("resembling his mother"). *pitṛsamaḥ* ("equal to his father"). In the sense of "deficient" (*ūna-artha*): *māṣonaṃ kārṣāpaṇam* ("a kārṣāpaṇa deficient by one māṣa"). *māṣavikalam* ("lacking one māṣa"). *vākkalahaḥ* ("a quarrel of words"). *ācāranipuṇaḥ* ("skilled in conduct"). *guḍamiśraḥ* ("mixed with molasses"). *ācāraślakṣṇaḥ* ("gentle in conduct"). When the word *miśra* is mentioned, that which has a prefix (*sopasarga*) is also included, because of the mention of "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) in the rule *miśraṃ cānupasargam asandhau*. *guḍasaṃmiśrā dhānāḥ* ("parched grains mixed with molasses"). An addition should be made for the word *avara* ("inferior"): *māsenāvaro māsāvaraḥ* ("inferior by a month").

SK 694: *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (A 2.1.32). When the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*) is expressed, the third case ending is used extensively (*bahulam*) with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, as previously stated. Examples: *hariṇā trātaḥ* → *haritrātaḥ* ("saved by Hari"); *nakhair bhinnaḥ* → *nakhabhinnaḥ* ("split by the claws"). When a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned [in a rule], that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is also included. Example: *nakhanirbhinnaḥ*. What is the purpose of saying "agent or instrument"? Consider: *bhikṣābhir uṣitaḥ* ("dwelt because of alms"). Here, this third case is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*). The inclusion of the term "extensively" (*bahulam*) is for the purpose of showing deviation from all such conditions. Therefore, it does not apply in cases such as *dātreṇa lūnavān* ("he has reaped with a sickle"). Why specify "with a *kṛt* suffix"? Consider: *kāṣṭhaiḥ pacatitarām* ("he cooks very well with wood"). Here, although wood is the instrument, it is not a *kṛt*-derived word.

SK 695 *kṛtyair adhikārthavacane* (A 2.1.33): An explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) whose fruit is praise or censure is called an "explanatory statement of additional meaning" (*adhikārthavacana*). In that case, the third case ending is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), as before, with *kṛtya* suffixes. Example: *vātacchedyaṃ tṛṇam* ("the grass is to be cut by the wind"); *kākapeyā nadī* ("the river is drinkable even by crows"). SK 696 *annena vyañjanam* (A 2.1.34).

The third-case ending word denoting a substance that effects a transformation is compounded with *anna* as before: *dadhnā odanaḥ* becomes *dadhyodanaḥ* (rice with curd). Here, the semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) is established through the intermediate action of sprinkling (*upaseka*).
By [the rule] *bhakṣyeṇa miśrīkaraṇam* (A 2.1.35), [a word in the third case] is compounded with a word for food when there is mixing:
*guḍena dhānāḥ* becomes *guḍadhānāḥ* (parched grain mixed with molasses). Here, the semantic connection is established through the intermediate action of mixing.

SK 698: *caturthī tadarthārthabalihitasukharakṣitaiḥ* (A 2.1.36). A word ending in the fourth case optionally forms a compound with words expressing that which is for the sake of what is denoted by the fourth-case-ending word, as well as with the words *artha*, etc., according to the previous rule. By the word *tadartha*, only the relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) is understood, based on the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the inclusion of the words *bali* and *rakṣita*. Examples: *yūpāya dāru* → *yūpadāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post"). Not here: *randhanāya sthālī* ("a pot for cooking"). However, compounds such as *aśvaghāsa* ("grass for horses") are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). It should be stated that with the word *artha*, there is an obligatory compound and it takes the gender of the qualified object (*viśeṣya-liṅgatā*). Examples: *dvijāyāyaṃ dvijārthaḥ sūpaḥ* ("this soup is for the Brahmin"); *dvijārthā yavāgūḥ* ("the gruel is for the Brahmin").

*Milk for the sake of the twice-born* (*dvijārthaṃ payaḥ*); *an offering to the spirits* (*bhūtabaliḥ*); *for the welfare of the cow* (*go hitam*); *the happiness of the cow* (*gosukham*); *protected by the cow* (*gorakṣitam*).

[SK 699] "The fifth case [is compounded] with *bhaya* (fear). *Fear of a thief* (*corād bhayam* → *corabhayam*). It should be stated that [compounding occurs] with *bhaya*, *bhīta*, *bhīti*, and *bhī*. *Afraid of a wolf* (*vṛkabhītaḥ*); *the fear of a wolf* (*vṛkabhītiḥ*); *the dread of a wolf* (*vṛkabhīḥ*).

SK 700: *apetāpoḍhamuktapatitāpatrastair alpaśaḥ* (A 2.1.38). With these words—*apeta*, *apoḍha*, *mukta*, *patita*, and *apatrasta*—the word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is optionally compounded when it signifies "a small amount" (*alpaśas*); this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Examples: *sukhāpetaḥ* ("devoid of happiness"), *kalpanāpoḍhaḥ* ("free from conceptual construction"), *cakramuktaḥ* ("escaped from the wheel"), *svargapatitaḥ* ("fallen from heaven"), *taraṅgāpatrastaḥ* ("terrified by the waves"). Why say "when signifying a small amount"? [Counter-example: *prāsādāt patitaḥ* ("fallen from the palace"). SK 701: *stokāntikadūrārthakṛcchrāṇi ktena* (A 2.1.39). Words expressing "smallness" (*stoka*), "nearness" (*antika*), "distance" (*dūra*), and those having the sense of "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*), when used as adjectives, are compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix (*kta*). [Examples follow.]

"Released from a little," "released from a small amount," "come from nearby," "come from close at hand," "come from afar," "come from a distance," "come with difficulty. [In these cases] there is no elision (*aluk*) due to the rule *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.31).
The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*): "the king's man" is *rājapuruṣaḥ*.

SK 703: By means of these words beginning with *yājaka* (A 2.2.9), a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is compounded. This is an exception (*pratiprasava*) to the rule A 2.2.15, *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari*. Examples: *brāhmaṇayājakaḥ* ("one who sacrifices for Brahmins"), *devapūjakaḥ* ("one who worships the gods"). It should be stated that when [a word] ending in *tarap* expresses a quality (*guṇa*), there is a compound with it and the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *tarap*. This is an exception to the prohibitions found in A 2.2.10, *na nirdhāraṇe*, and A 2.2.11, *pūraṇaguṇa-*. Examples: *sarvaśvetaḥ* ("the whitest of all"), *sarvamahān* ("the greatest of all").
It should be stated that the genitive case ending used in connection with a *kṛt* suffix is compoundable. For example: *idhmasya vraścanaḥ* becomes *idhmavraścanaḥ*. (SK 704) *na nirdhārane*:

A genitive used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is not compoundable. For example: *nṛṇāṃ dvijaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ* ("Among men, the twice-born is the best"). It should be stated that a genitive prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*) is not compoundable. For example: *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee").

SK 705: [A word ending in the sixth case] is compounded with words meaning "fullness" (*pūraṇa*), with words expressing a "quality" (*guṇa*), with words having the sense of "satisfied" (*suhita*), with the word *sat*, with indeclinables (*avyaya*), and with words in the gerundive (*tavya*) when they are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). (A 2.2.11)

The genitive case is not compounded with words meaning "full" (*pūrṇa*) and so forth, nor with words meaning "good" (*sat*) and so forth. Regarding [the prohibition] for ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa*): *ṣaṣṭhaḥ satām* ("the sixth among the virtuous"). Regarding [the prohibition] for qualities (*guṇa*): *kākasya kārṣṇyam* ("the blackness of a crow") and *brāhmaṇasya śuklāḥ* ("the white [teeth] of a Brahmin"). This is an example when the qualified object, "teeth," is understood through context or other means. This prohibition regarding quality is non-obligatory (*anitya*), because of such rules as *tadaśiṣyaṃ saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt* ("that need not be taught, because the name is the authority"). By this, expressions such as *arthagauravam* ("weightiness of meaning") and *buddhimāndyam* ("slowness of intellect") are established. Words meaning "satisfied" (*suhita*) have the sense of being satiated.

[The word] *suhita* [is used] with fruits (*phalānām*). However, a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) may indeed occur; there is merely a difference in accent (*svara*). For example: *dvijasya kurvan* or *kurvāṇaḥ*, meaning "acting as a servant" (*kiṅkara*). [Regarding] an indeclinable (*avyaya*): *brāhmaṇasya kṛtvā*. Because of the association with what precedes and follows, only an indeclinable *kṛt*-suffix is understood here. By this, forms such as *tadupari* are established; thus says Rakṣita. [In the case of] the suffix *-tavya*: *brāhmaṇasya kartavyam*. But with the suffix *-tavyat*, it certainly occurs: *svakartavyam*. There is a difference in accent. [This applies] when combined with a word in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

[This refers to] the snake Takṣaka. Here, a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) does not apply because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* [in Pāṇini’s rules]. In examples such as *goḥ dhenoḥ*, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would have been applicable—since compounds like *poṭāyuvati* are already established with different case endings—and that too is prevented by this [rule]. By the rule *ktena ca pūjāyām* (A 2.2.12), a word ending in a *kta* suffix prescribed by the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaś ca* (A 3.2.188) is not compounded with a genitive. For example: *rājñāṃ mato buddhaḥ pūjito vā* ("respected, known, or honored by kings"). However, in cases such as *rājapūjitaḥ*, there is a third-case compound (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) with a word ending in a *kta* suffix denoting the past (*bhūte*).

SK 707: A word ending in a *kta* suffix denoting the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is not compounded with a genitive case-ending word. For example: *idam eṣām āsitam*, *gatam*, or *bhuktam* ("this is the place where they sat, went, or ate").

SK 708 *karmaṇi ca* (A 2.2.14): When there is the possibility of [the genitive] applying to both [agent and object], the genitive that applies to the object is not permitted. Example: *āścaryo gavāṃ doho ’gopena* ("It is wonderful, the milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd"). SK 709 *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* (A 2.2.15).

There is no compound with a word ending in the sixth case [the genitive] when it is joined with a word ending in *tṛ*, *tṛc*, or *aka* that denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). Examples: *apāṃ sraṣṭā* ("the creator of waters"), *vajrasya bhartā* ("the wielder of the thunderbolt"), *odanasya pācakaḥ* ("the cooker of rice"). Why "denoting the agent"? Consider *ikṣūṇāṃ bhakṣaṇam ikṣubhakṣikā* ("the eating of sugarcane, a sugarcane-eating"). However, the word *bhartṛ* meaning "husband" does form a compound because it belongs to the *yājakādi* group: *bhūbhartā* ("the lord of the earth"). How then is the expression *ghaṭānāṃ nirmātuḥ tribhuvanavidhātuś ca kalahaḥ* ("the quarrel between the maker of pots and the creator of the three worlds") explained? Kaiyaṭa says it is a compound with a genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). [This is governed by] A 2.2.16: *kartari ca*.

There is no compound of a genitive case ending in the sense of the agent with a word ending in *akan*. For example: *bhavataḥ śāyikā* ("your lying down"). Here, the suffix *tṛc* does not recur [from the previous rule], because when that is joined, the agent is already expressed [by the verbal suffix], and thus the genitive of the agent does not occur.

SK 711: *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* (A 2.2.17). In these two senses—play (*krīḍā*) and livelihood (*jīvikā*)—a genitive is always compounded with a word ending in *akan*. Examples: *uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā* ("the plucking of Uddālaka flowers")—this is the name of a particular game; here, the suffix *ṇvul* is used in the sense of an action (*bhāve*) by the rule *saṃjñāyām*. For livelihood: *dantalekhakaḥ* ("one who carves ivory"). Regarding those, since there was an option for play and a prohibition by the rule *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* (A 2.2.15) regarding livelihood, this statement [of the sūtra] is made.
Pāṇini 2.2.1: *pūrvāparādharottaram ekadeśinaikādhikaraṇe*.

Words such as *pūrva* ("front," "eastern") are compounded with a word denoting a whole (*ekadeśin*) when they share the same substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*), provided that the whole is qualified by the number one. This is an exception to the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Examples: *pūrvaṃ kāyasya* becomes *pūrvakāyaḥ* ("the front part of the body"); *aparakāyaḥ* ("the hind part of the body"). Why "with a word denoting a whole"? Consider: *pūrvaṃ nābheḥ kāyasya* ("the front part of the body from the navel"). Why "when sharing the same substratum"? Consider: *pūrvaś chātrāṇām* ("the first among the students"). Every part (*ekadeśa*) is compounded with the word *ahar* ("day"), according to the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *saṃkhyā-visāya-*. Examples: *madhyāhnaḥ* ("midday"); *sāyāhnaḥ* ("evening").

Some, however, say that every single part [of a compound] is compounded with *kāla* (time), and not only with *ahar* (day); for the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) applies generally. By this, forms such as *madhyarātraḥ* ("midnight") and *upāratāḥ paścimarātragocarāḥ* ("those who have ceased from the sphere of the final night") are established.
(SK 713: *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*, A 2.2.2)

The word *ardha*, when denoting an equal portion, is always neuter; it is treated as before [i.e., like a *pūrvapada*]. The rule regarding a single case-ending applies except for that which ends in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). This prohibition of the designation *upasarjana* concerns the domain of *ekadeśisamāsa* compounds. By this, forms such as *pañcakhaṭvī* are established. Examples include *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ* (half of a long pepper), which becomes *ardhapippalī*. Why "in the neuter"? Consider *grāmārdhaḥ* (half of a village). It occurs only when there is a unity of substance (*dravyaikya*). An example where there is no unity of substance is *ardhaṃ pippalīnām* (half of several long peppers). SK 714: *dvitīyatṛtīyacaturthaturyāṇy anyatarasyām* (A 2.2.3). [In the domain of *ekadeśisamāsa*, these words are optionally *upasarjana*.]

These [compounds] may optionally form a *tatpuruṣa* with a word denoting a part (*ekadeśin*), as previously stated; otherwise, they are *karmadhārayas*. The second example is *bhikṣāyā dvitīyam*, "the second portion of alms. Why specify "with a word denoting a part"? Consider *bhikṣāyā bhikṣukasya dvitīyam*, "the second [portion] of the alms of the beggar. By the force of the inclusion of the option (*anyatarasyām*), the prohibition [of the sixth-case compound] by the rule *pūraṇaguṇa-* is set aside, and thus a sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is optionally formed: *bhikṣādvitīyam*. SK 715: *prāptāpanne ca dvitīyayā* (A 2.2.4). [The words *prāpta* and *āpanna* form a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a word in the second case.]

In one alternative, there is the compound *dvitīyā-śrita* [meaning "that which has a second case ending followed by *śrita*"]. *Prāptajīvikaḥ* means "one who has obtained a livelihood"; likewise *jīvikāprāptaḥ*, *āpannajīvikaḥ*, and *jīvikāpannaḥ*. In this rule (*sūtra*), having split it as *dvitīyayā a*, the vowel *a* is also prescribed. By that, a woman who has obtained a livelihood is *prāptajīvikā* or *āpannajīvikā*. SK 716: *kālāḥ parimāṇinā* (A 2.2.5). [This prescribes a compound of time-denoting words with a word denoting the thing measured.]

Times (*kāla*) are compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix that expresses a limit (*pariccheda*). For example, *māsajātaḥ* ("born after a month") means "one for whom a month has passed since birth. *Dvyahajātaḥ* ("born after two days"): the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one for whom two days have passed since birth," where *dvyahaḥ* is the collective compound (*samāhāra*) of two days (*dvayoḥ ahnoḥ*).
