To ensure the formation of a *dvigu* compound with a subsequent member denoting a measure (*parimāṇin*), there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of this rule to *tatpuruṣa* compounds involving multiple members. Thus, *dvyahnajātaḥ* ("born after two days") is formed; here, the substitution *ahna-* (for *ahar-*) will be taught later by the rule *ahno 'hnaḥ*.
However, in the previous case (*māsajātaḥ*), the prohibition applies according to the rule *na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhāre*.

SK 717: *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ* (A 2.1.40). A word ending in the seventh case may optionally form a compound with words beginning with *śauṇḍa*, as previously described. *akṣeṣu śauṇḍaḥ* → *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ* ("skilled at dice"). The word *adhi* is included here [in the list of *śauṇḍa* etc.]. By the rule *adhyuttarapadāt khaḥ* (A 5.4.7), the suffix *kha* is applied: *īśvarādhīnaḥ* ("dependent on the Lord"). SK 718: *siddhaśuṣkapakvabandhaiś ca* (A 2.1.41). [A word ending in the seventh case forms a compound] also with *siddha*, *śuṣka*, *pakva*, and *bandha*.

With these [words], a word ending in the seventh case is compounded as before. Examples: *sāṃkāśyasiddhaḥ* ("perfected in Sāṃkāśya"), *ātapaśuṣkaḥ* ("dried in the sun"), *sthālīpakvaḥ* ("cooked in a pot"), *cakrabandhaḥ* ("bound by a wheel").

SK 719: *dhvāṅkṣeṇa kṣepe* (A 2.1.42). A word ending in the seventh case is compounded with a word denoting a crow (*dhvāṅkṣa*) when expressing censure. Example: *tīrthe dhvāṅkṣa iva* = *tīrthadhvāṅkṣaḥ* ("a crow at a sacred bathing place"); *tīrthakākaḥ* ("a crow at a sacred bathing place").

SK 720: *kṛtyair ṛṇe* (A 2.1.43). A word ending in the locative case is compounded with words ending in *kṛtya* suffixes, as previously stated, when necessity (*āvaśyaka*) is implied. Example: *māse deyam ṛṇam* ("a debt to be paid within a month"). The mention of "debt" (*ṛṇa*) is intended to indicate "obligation" (*niyoga*) in general. Example: *pūrvāhṇe geyam sāma* ("a Sāman to be sung in the forenoon"). SK 721: *saṃjñāyām* (A 2.1.44). [A word ending in the locative case is compounded with a word ending in a *kṛtya* suffix when it forms a proper name.]

A word ending in the seventh case (*saptamyanta*) is compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*), as previously stated, when it forms a name (*saṃjñā*). Since a name cannot be understood through a loose sentence (*vākya*), this is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). Examples: *araṇyetilakāḥ* ("sesame plants in the forest"), *vanekaserukāḥ* ("kaseruka plants in the forest"). The elision (*luk*) of the locative suffix does not occur because of the rule *haladantāt saptamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.9). **SK 722:** Words denoting parts of a day or night (*ahorātrāvayavāḥ*) [ending in the seventh case] are compounded with a word ending in the suffix *kta*, as previously stated.

Parts of *ahan* (day) and *rātri* (night) ending in the seventh case are compounded with a word ending in *kta*. Examples: *pūrvāhṇakṛtam* ("done in the forenoon"), *apararātrakṛtam* ("done in the latter part of the night"). Why is the mention of "parts" (*avayavagrahaṇam*) necessary? [To exclude cases like: *ahni dṛṣṭam* ("seen during the day").

SK 723: In that context, the word *tatra*, ending in the locative case, forms a compound with a word ending in the suffix *kta* according to the previous rule. Example: *tatra bhuktam* ("eaten there"). SK 724: When used in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*). [The same applies.]

A word ending in the seventh case [locative] is compounded with a word ending in *kta*, as previously stated, when expressing censure. (Pāṇini 2.1.48) *pātresamitādayaś ca*: these are also prescribed as irregular compounds (*nipātana*) when used in a derogatory sense. Examples: *pātresamitāḥ* (“those who meet only at the dining table,” i.e., those who associate only during mealtime and not for any other purpose); *geheśūraḥ* (“a hero only in the house”); *gehenardī* (“one who roars only in the house”). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). The particle *ca* serves the purpose of restriction; by virtue of this, these words do not enter into other compounds as constituent members. For example: *paramāḥ pātresamitāḥ* (“the most excellent among those who meet only at the dining table”).

Pāṇini 2.1.49: *pūrvakāla-eka-sarva-jarat-purāṇa-nava-kevalāḥ samānādhikaraṇena* (The words beginning with *pūrvakāla* [words denoting prior time], *eka*, *sarva*, *jarat*, *purāṇa*, *nava*, and *kevala* [when compounded] with a word in grammatical apposition). This rule is formulated for two purposes: first, although the general rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa* (Pāṇini 2.1.57) already establishes that these words may be compounded with a word in apposition, this sūtra serves to restrict their position as the first member (*pūrvanipāta*). Second, it is intended to override the restriction imposed by Pāṇini 2.1.50, *diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām* (Directional words and numerals are compounded with a word in apposition only when they form a proper name). Examples: *snātānuliptaḥ* ("one who has first bathed and subsequently anointed himself"). *ekanāthaḥ* ("the sole lord"). *sarvayājñikāḥ* ("all the ritualists"). *jaranneyāyikāḥ* ("the aged Naiyāyikas"). *purāṇamīmāṃsakāḥ* ("the ancient Mīmāṃsakas"). *navapāṭhakāḥ* ("the new reciters"). *kevalavaiyākaraṇāḥ* ("the exclusive grammarians"). Pāṇini 2.1.50:
*diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām* (Directional words and numerals are compounded with a word in apposition only when they form a proper name).

The phrase "with a word in grammatical apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇena*) is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) that extends until the end of the chapter. The rule [Pāṇini 2.1.49] is for the purpose of restriction, meaning it applies only when a name (*saṃjñā*) is being formed. Examples: *pūrveṣukāmaśamī* ("the eastern Eṣukāmaśamī"), *saptarṣayaḥ* ("the seven sages"). But not here: *uttarā vṛkṣāḥ* ("northern trees") or *pañca brāhmaṇāḥ* ("five Brahmins"). [Next is] Pāṇini 2.1.51: *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* ("and also when the sense of a secondary derivative suffix, a subsequent member of a compound, or a collective aggregate is expressed").

When a secondary derivative (taddhita) meaning is intended, or when a subsequent word follows, or when a collective sense (samāhāra) is to be expressed, the terms for direction and number (*dik-saṃkhye*) are optionally treated as before. In the case of "one who exists in the eastern hall" (*pūrvasyāṃ śālāyāṃ bhavaḥ*), the form is *paurvaśālaḥ*. Once the compound is formed, the suffix *ñ* is applied according to the rule "after a directional term as the first member, when not a proper name" (*dikpūrvapadād asaṃjñāyāṃ ñaḥ*). There is masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) for a pronoun in all compound formations. In the case of a three-word *bahuvrīhi* such as "one for whom the eastern hall is dear" (*pūrvā śālā priyā yasya*), once the *bahuvrīhi* is formed with the word *priyā* as the final member, a *tatpuruṣa* is formed between the first two members. Consequently, the vowel *ā* in the word *śālā* becomes acute-accented (*udātta*).

[The rule] *saṃkhyāyās taddhitārthe* [applies]. From *ṣaṇṇāṃ mātṛṇām apatyam*, [we derive] *ṣāṇmāturaḥ*. Regarding the three-word *bahuvrīhi* "one whose wealth consists of five cows" (*pañca gāvo dhanaṃ yasya*), since an optional internal *tatpuruṣa* would otherwise apply, there is the statement that for a *dvandva* or a *tatpuruṣa*, the compound is obligatory when followed by a final member. By *gor ataddhitaluki* (A 5.4.92), the suffix *ṭac* occurs as a compound-final affix after a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *go*, provided there is no elision of a *taddhita* suffix; thus, [we have] *pañcagavadhanaḥ*.
SK 730: A *dvigu* compound is that which has a numeral as its first member (A 2.1.52).
The threefold rule stated under the heading "for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning" applies here: a *dvigu* is that which has a numeral as its prior member.
SK 731: A *dvigu* compound takes the singular number (A 2.4.1).

A *samāhāra* (collective) compound denoting a double meaning shall be treated as a singular. By the rule "that [compound] is neuter," it takes the neuter gender. For example, the collection of five cows is *pañcagavam*. SK 732: *kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ* (A 2.1.53). Things being censured may be compounded with the words expressing that censure, according to the previous rules. Examples: *vaiyākaraṇakhasūciḥ* (a grammarian who is a "bad needle" [i.e., one who does not produce anything useful]), *mīmāṃsakadurdurūḍhaḥ* (a Mīmāṃsaka who is "badly stuck" [i.e., one who is stubborn or dull-witted]).

SK 733 *pāpāṇake kutsitaiḥ* (A 2.1.54): This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. Examples: *pāpanāpitaḥ* ("a bad barber"), *āṇakakulālaḥ* ("a wretched potter"). SK 734 *upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ* (A 2.1.55).

*Ghanaśyāmaḥ* means "dark as a cloud," being dark like wealth (*dhana*). Here, the word *iva* is employed in the popular analysis (*laukikavigraha*) to indicate that the first member of the compound is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote something similar to it. This sūtra is intended to establish a rule regarding the mandatory placement of the first member. [Pāṇini 2.1.56] states: "That which is compared with tigers and the like [forms a tatpuruṣa compound], provided that a common attribute is not expressed. (SK 735).

When the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is not employed, as in the previous [rules], the object of comparison (*upameya*) is used with words such as *vyāghra* (tiger), etc.; this rule is for the purpose of ensuring that the qualified noun (*viśeṣya*) is placed first. Examples: *puruṣavyāghraḥ* (a tiger among men), *nṛsomaḥ* (a moon among men). The group beginning with *vyāghra* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). Why "when the common attribute is not employed"? Example: *puruṣo vyāghra iva śūraḥ* (the man is brave like a tiger). Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.57: *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (a qualifier is frequently compounded with the thing qualified).

A qualifier is frequently compounded with its coreferential qualificand, as previously stated. For example, *nīlam utpalam* becomes *nīlotpalam*. Because of the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulagrahaṇāt*), in some cases it is obligatory, as in *kṛṣṇasarpaḥ*. In other cases, it does not apply, as in *rāmo jāmadagnyaḥ*.
And [the words] *pūrva*, *apara*, *prathama*, *carama*, *jaghanya*, *samāna*, *madhya*, *madhyama*, and *vīra* [are also compounded in this way]. (A 2.1.58)

This [rule] is for the purpose of establishing a restriction regarding the initial placement [of words]. Examples: *pūrvavaiyākaraṇaḥ* ("a former grammarian"), *aparādhyāpakaḥ* ("a latter teacher"). It should be stated that the form *paśca-* occurs in place of *apara-* when it means "half": *aparaś cāsāv ardhaś ca* = *paścārdhaḥ* ("the latter half"). How is [the compound] *ekavīraḥ* ("a solitary hero") formed? Since this rule would override the rule *pūrvakālaika-* (Pāṇini 2.1.49) due to its higher status, the compound would instead result in *vīraikaḥ*. [Answer: It will occur by virtue of the mention of the term *bahulam* ("diversely"). SK 738: *śreṇyādayaḥ kṛtādibhiḥ* (A 2.1.59).
Regarding the group beginning with *śreṇi*, a statement concerning the sense of the suffix *cvi* must be made: non-rows (*aśreṇayaḥ*) made into rows (*śreṇayaḥ*) are "made into rows" (*śreṇīkṛtāḥ*).

SK 739: *ktena nañviśiṣṭenānañ* (A 2.1.60). A word ending in a *kta*-suffix that does not itself contain the negative particle *nañ* is compounded with another word ending in a *kta*-suffix that is qualified by *nañ*. For example: *kṛtaṃ ca tad akṛtaṃ ca* = *kṛtākṛtam* ("done and undone"). To account for compounds such as *śākapārthiva*, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the rule regarding the elision of the middle member (*uttarapadalopa*). Thus, *śākapriyaḥ pārthivaḥ* = *śākapārthivaḥ* ("the king who loves vegetables"), and *devabrahmaṇaḥ* ("a Brahmin who is like a god"). SK 740: *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (A 2.1.69). The words *sat*, *mahat*, *parama*, *uttama*, and *utkṛṣṭa* are compounded with words denoting those who are being honored.

By means of words denoting excellence (*sadvadyaiḥ*). The form [of the compound] is as will be explained: *mahāvaiyākaraṇaḥ* ("a great grammarian"). By what is it being honored? It means "an excellent ox," that is, one who has been pulled out from the mud.

(SK 741) Regarding the rule *vṛndārakanāgakuñjaraiḥ pūjyamānam* (A 2.1.62): *govṛndārakaḥ* ("an ox that is like a chief"). Since this is already established by the fact that the *vyāghrādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, this statement is for the sake of including general applications.

SK 742 *katarakatamau jātiparipraśne* (A 2.1.63): *katarakaṭhaḥ* ("Which [of the two] is a Kaṭha?"); *katamakalāpaḥ* ("Which [of the many] is a Kalāpa?"). Because a lineage (*gotra*) is associated with Vedic schools (*caraṇa*), it possesses the nature of a genus (*jāti*). SK 743 *kiṃ kṣepe* (A 2.1.64): [The compound *kiṃ-kāraṇam* is formed when *kim* expresses censure.]

A contemptible king is a *kiṃrājā* (a "what-king"), one who does not protect. (SK 744) The genus [is compounded] with *poṭā*, *yuvati*, *stoka*, *katipaya*, *gṛṣṭi*, *dhenu*, *vaśā*, *vehad*, *baṣkayaṇī*, *pravaktṛ*, *śrotriya*, *adhyāpaka*, and *dhūrta*. (A 2.1.65) A *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have a common referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is a *karmadhāraya*. (A 1.2.42)
Pāṇini A 6.3.42 states: *puṃvat karmadhāraya-jātīya-deśīyeṣu*.

When followed by a *karmadhāraya* compound, or by the suffixes *-jātīya* or *-deśīya*, that which precedes [the feminine word] is treated like the masculine (*puṃvat*) provided that it is of such a nature that the suffix *-ūṅ* does not occur after it when it is a word that has already expressed the masculine gender (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). By this rule, the application of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment), which would otherwise not apply in the case of ordinal numbers (*pūraṇī*) or words beginning with *priyā*, is prescribed. Examples include: *mahānavamī* (the great ninth day), *kṛṣṇacaturdaśī* (the dark fourteenth day), and *mahāpriyā* (the very dear one). Likewise, the prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* for words ending in *ka* and others, which applies in *karmadhāraya* compounds and the like, is here restated as an exception: *pācakastrī* (a woman who is a cook), *dattabhāryā* (a wife given [in marriage]), *pañcamabhāryā* (a fifth wife), and *sraughnabhāryā* (a wife from Sraughna).

The wife of Sukeśa; the wife of a Brāhmaṇa; likewise, one who is of the class of cooks (*pācakajātīyā*), one who resembles a cook (*pācakadeśīyā*), and so forth. A female elephant-calf (*ibhapoṭā*); a *poṭā* is a woman possessing the characteristics of both sexes. A young female elephant (*ibhayuvati*). A small fire (*agnistoka*); a little buttermilk (*udaśvitkatipaya*). A cow that has calved once is a *gṛṣṭi*; a cow that has calved once is a *gogṛṣṭi*. A cow that has recently calved is a *dhenu*; a cow that has recently calved is a *godhenu*. A barren cow is a *vaśā*; a barren cow is a *govāśā*. A cow that miscarries is a *vehat*; a cow that miscarries is a *go-vehat*. A cow with a young calf is a *baṣkayaṇī*; a cow with a young calf is a *gobaṣkayaṇī*. One who recites the *Kaṭha* texts is a *kaṭhapravaktā*; a learned scholar of the *Kaṭha* school is a *kaṭhaśrotriya*; a teacher of the *Kaṭha* school is a *kaṭhādhyāpaka*; a rogue of the *Kaṭha* school is a *kaṭhadhūrta*.

SK 747: *praśaṃsāvacanaiś ca* (A 2.1.66). When combined with these words denoting praise, a genus-word (*jāti*) is compounded as previously stated. Examples: *gomatallikā*, *gomacarcikā*, *goprakāṇḍam*, *gavoddhaḥ*, *gotallajaḥ*. The meaning is "an excellent cow. Words such as *matallikā* have fixed genders and are not dependent on the gender of the noun they qualify (*viśeṣyanighna*). Why specify "genus-word"? [Counter-example: *kumārī matallikā* ("an excellent young girl"). SK 748: *yuvā khalatipalitavalinajaratībhiḥ* (A 2.1.67). [The word] *yuvan* ("young") is compounded with *khalati* ("bald"), *palita* ("grey-haired"), *valina* ("wrinkled"), and *jaratī* ("old woman").

This *sūtra* is for the purpose of establishing a rule regarding the obligatory initial placement [of the first member]. By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning words qualified by gender, the word *yuvati-* is also compounded: *yuvā khalatiḥ* → *yuvakhalatiḥ*; *yuvatiḥ khalatī* → *yuvakhalatī*; *yuvajaratī*. There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because the qualities of an old woman are perceived in the young woman itself, leading to the superimposition of that form [upon her].
SK 749: Words denoting gerundives (*kṛtya*) or things equal (*tulyākhyā*) may be compounded with a word that is not a genus-term (*ajātyā*).

Examples: *bhojyoṣṇam* ("hot food"), *tulyaśvetaḥ* ("equally white"), *sadṛśaśvetaḥ* ("similarly white"). Why "not a genus-term"? Example: *bhojya odanaḥ* ("rice that is to be eaten"). Due to the force of this prohibition, even the qualifier-compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) does not apply here.

SK 750: A word denoting color (*varṇa*) [is optionally placed first] when compounded with another word denoting color that stands in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), as previously stated. Example: *kṛṣṇasāraṅgaḥ* ("black-spotted"). SK 751: Words beginning with *kaḍāra* [are optionally placed first] in a *karmadhāraya* compound. (A 2.2.38)

Words beginning with *kaḍāra* may optionally be placed first in a *karmadhāraya* compound: *kaḍārajaiminiḥ* or *jaiminikaḍāraḥ*. According to A 2.1.70, *kumāraḥ śramaṇādibhiḥ*, [the word] *kumāra* is optionally placed first when compounded with words such as *śramaṇā*:

*kumārīśramaṇā* or *kumāraśramaṇā*. In this list (*gaṇa*), feminine forms such as *śramaṇā*, *pravrajitā*, and *garbhiṇī* are recited. This should be understood as the very indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the *paribhāṣā* rule concerning "words qualified by gender" (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*).

SK 753 *catuṣpādo garbhiṇyā* (A 2.1.71): A word denoting a four-footed genus forms a compound with the word *garbhiṇī* according to the previous rule. Example: *gogarbhiṇī* ("a cow that is pregnant"). SK 754 *mayūravyaṃsakādayaś ca* (A 2.1.72): And [the compounds] beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka* [are also formed as indeclinable compounds].

These are irregularly formed (nipātana). *Mayūra-vyaṃsaka*: a peacock that deceives; here *vyaṃsaka* means a rogue. *Uccāvacam*: both high and low. *Niścapracam*: both determined and accumulated. *Aliñcanaḥ*: one who has nothing at all. When a verb is compounded with another verb to express continuous action (*kriyāsātatya*), as in *aśnīta-pibatā*—where it is constantly expressed as "eat and drink"—and *pacata-bhṛjjatā*, *khādta-modatā*. In the case of *ehīḍā* and similar forms, they denote a different referent (*anyapadārtha*).

The term *ehīḍam* refers to that action [expressed] by "come and play" (*ehīḍa*). [Examples include: *ehipacam* ("come and cook"). *Uddharotsṛjā* refers to that action [expressed] by "take out from the granary and give away" (*uddhara koṣṭhād utsṛja dehīti*). *Uddhamavidhamā*. This reading here is for the sake of non-continuity (*asātatyārtham*). The word *jahī* is frequently compounded with an object when expressing frequency (*ābhīkṣṇye*), and it denotes the agent. The meaning is that the word *jahī* is frequently compounded with an object when frequency is to be understood, and by means of the compound, the agent is expressed. Examples are *jahijoḍaḥ* ("one who repeatedly kills the *joḍa*") and *jahistambaḥ* ("one who repeatedly strikes the pillar").
One for whom there is no fear from anywhere is "akutobhaya" (fearless from all sides). Another king is "rājāntara" (another king). Consciousness alone is "cinmātra" (pure consciousness).

According to Pāṇini SK 755 (*īṣadakṛtā*), [the suffix *ka* is applied] as in "īṣattviṅgalaḥ" (slightly lame). It should be stated that [this applies] when combined with a quality-word (*guṇavacana*), as in "īṣadraktaḥ" (slightly red).
*nañ* is compounded with a *sup*-ending word.
SK 757 *nalopo nañaḥ* (A 6.3.73): there is elision of the *n* of *nañ*.

The *na* of the negative particle *nañ* is elided when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). For example: *na brāhmaṇaḥ* = *abrāhmaṇaḥ*. By the rule *tasmān nuḍ ati* (A 6.4.74), the augment *nuṭ* is added to a subsequent member beginning with a vowel that follows the *nañ* whose *n* has been elided. For example: *anaśvaḥ*. In the sense of "absence of meaning" (*arthābhāve*), this [formation] is optionally treated as an *avyayībhāva* compound. This is because of the usage in the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika*: *rakṣohāgamalaghvasaṃdehāḥ prayojanam* ("The purpose is the preservation [of the text], the removal [of errors], the addition [of omissions], brevity, and absence of doubt") and *adru tāyām asaṃhitam* ("in the case of non-rapid recitation, there is no *saṃhitā*"). By this, forms such as *anupalabdhiḥ*, *avivādaḥ*, and *avighnam* are established. The *n* of *nañ* is elided before a finite verb (*tiṅ*) when used in a reproachful sense (*kṣepe*). For example: *apacasi tvaṃ jālma* ("You cook poorly, you fool!").

In "naikadhā" and similar forms, however, there is a *sup-supa* compound with the word *na*. According to Pāṇini A 6.3.75: "In *nabhrāj*, *naptṛ*, *naptṛ*, *veda*, *anas*, *atyana*, *mucina*, *kulina*, *khana*, *puṃsaka*, *nakṣatra*, *nakra*, and *nāka*, [the initial vowel] remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*)."

*pād* ends in the suffix *śatṛ*; *vedāḥ* ends in the suffix *asun*. *Na satyāḥ* means "not true," which becomes *asatyāḥ*; *na asatyāḥ* becomes *nāsatyāḥ*. That which does not release (*muñcati*) is *namuciḥ*. That which has no family (*kulam*) is *nakulam*; that which has no sky (*kham*) is *nakham*. *Napuṃsakam* means "neither female nor male. The neuter state for the pair "female and male" occurs by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). That which does not flow away (*kṣarati*) is *nakṣatram*; from the roots *kṣarati* or *kṣīyati*, the form *kṣatram* is irregularly derived. That which does not move (*krāmati*) is *nakraḥ*; the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *kram*. That in which there is no suffering (*akam*) is *nākaḥ*. [Pāṇini 6.3.77] states: "In the case of non-living beings, *naga-* may optionally [be used]."

In the case of *naga*, the negative particle *nañ* is optionally treated as its own base form (*prakṛti*). Thus, *nagāḥ* means "non-mountains" or "mountains. Why [is it said] "not for non-living things"? Consider: *ago vṛṣalaḥ śītena* ("the low-born man is cold"). While the word *nityam* (always) continues from the rule *nityaṃ krīḍā-* (SK 761), the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (A 2.2.18) states that these—*ku*, *gati*, and *prādi*—are always compounded with a compatible word. For example: *kutsitaḥ puruṣaḥ* becomes *kupuruṣaḥ*. And while the word *gati* continues [from the previous rule]:

SK 762 *ūryādicviḍācaś ca* (A 1.4.61): These, when used in connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), shall be designated as *gati*s. Examples: *ūrīkṛtya*, *urarīkṛtya*, *śuklīkṛtya*, *paṭapaṭākṛtya*. There is an addition [to the rule] regarding the word *kārikā*: *kārikā* means "action" (*kriyā*); thus, *kārikākṛtya*. SK 763 *anukaraṇaṃ cānitiparam* (A 1.4.62): An imitation (*anukaraṇa*) [of a sound] is also [a *gati*], provided it is not followed by the word *iti*.
Having made the sound *khāṭ*; what is the meaning of *anitiparam*? Having made the sound *khāḍ*, he spat. According to A 1.4.63, *sadasatī* [are used] in the sense of respect and disrespect:
*satkṛtya* (having honored); *asatkṛtya* (having dishonored).

SK 765 *alam* [is used as a *gati*] in the sense of "adornment" (A 1.4.64). Example: *alaṃkṛtya* ("having adorned"). Why say "in the sense of adornment"? Example: *alaṃ kṛtvā odanaṃ gataḥ* ("having finished with the rice, he left"). The meaning is "sufficiently. The group of three sūtras beginning with *anukaraṇam* (A 1.4.62–64) naturally have *kṛñ* as their scope. SK 766 *antar* [is used as a *gati*] in the sense of "not taking possession" (A 1.4.65).

*Antarhatya* means having killed in the midst; that is, having struck down. What is the meaning of *aparigrahe*? *Antarhatvā gataḥ* means he has gone after taking hold of what was killed. SK 767: *kaṇemanasī śraddhāprātighāte* (A 1.4.66).

*Kaṇehatya payaḥ pibati* (he drinks milk until his thirst is satisfied); *manohatya*. The word *kaṇe* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) resembling a locative case-ending, used in the sense of an excess of desire. The word *manaḥ* is used in this very same sense.
SK 768 *puro ’vyayam* (A 1.4.67): [the indeclinable] *puras* [is a karmapravacanīya]; e.g., *puraskṛtya*.
SK 769 *astaṃ ca* (A 1.4.68): [the indeclinable] *astam* [is also a karmapravacanīya].
The indeclinable *astaṃ*, ending in the letter *m*, shall be designated as a *gati*. [Examples: *astaṃgatya* (having gone to rest/set). SK 770:

*accha* [is a *gati*] in connection with verbs meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*) and "to speak" (*vad*) [and others]. [The rule] "an indeclinable" (*avyayam*) applies here as well. [Examples: *acchagatya* (having approached), *acchodya* (having spoken). The meaning is: having gone toward [someone] and having spoken [to them]. Why "indeclinable"? [Counter-example: *jalaṃ acchaṃ gacchati* (he goes to clear water).
SK 771 *ado ’nupadeśe* (A 1.4.70):
*adaḥkṛtya*, *adaḥkṛtam*. When it is not an instruction directed toward another, this is the counter-example: *adaḥkṛtvā*. SK 772 *tiro ’ntardhau* (A 1.4.71).
Having disappeared;
[by] *vibhāṣā kṛñi* (A 1.4.72): *tiraḥkṛtya*, *tiraskṛtya*, *tiraḥkṛtvā*.

SK 774: *upāje* and *anvāje* are optionally designated as *gati*s before the root *kṛ*. [Examples: *upājekṛtya*, *upājekṛtvā*; *anvājekṛtya*, *anvājekṛtvā*. The meaning is: "having provided strength to one who is weak. SK 775: *sākṣāt* and the following items [are also optionally designated as *gati*s].

The terms designated as *gati* may optionally be so when used with the root *kṛ* (*kṛñ*). It should be stated that this applies to the sense of the suffix *cvī*. Examples: *sākṣātkṛtya* / *sākṣātkṛtvā*; *lavaṇaṃkṛtya* / *lavaṇaṃ kṛtvā*. The ending in *-m* [in *sākṣātkṛtya*, etc. is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). A 1.4.75: *urasimanasī anatyādhāne*. [The words *uras* and *manas* are *gati* when used with *kṛ*] except in the sense of "placing upon" (*atyādhāna*). Examples: *urasikṛtya* / *urasi kṛtvā*; the meaning is "having accepted. *manasikṛtya* / *manasi kṛtvā*; the meaning is "having resolved. In the case of "placing upon," which means "contacting" (*upaśleṣaṇa*), it is not so: *urasi kṛtvā pāṇiṃ śete* ("he lies down having placed his hand on his chest").

SK 777: *madhye*, *pade*, and *nivacane* (A 1.4.76)—these may optionally be designated as *gati*s when used with the root *kṛ*, provided they do not signify "placing upon. Examples: *madhyekṛtya* / *madhye kṛtvā*; *padekṛtya* / *pade kṛtvā*; *nivacanekṛtya* / *nivacane kṛtvā*. The meaning is "having restrained one's speech. SK 778: *haste* and *pāṇau* are always [designated as *gati*s] when used with *kṛ* in the sense of "taking in marriage" (A 1.4.77).

With the root *kṛ* [the following apply]: *upayamana* means "marriage"; others say it means "mere acceptance. [Examples: *hastekṛtya*, *pāṇaukṛtya*. Regarding *prādhvam* in the sense of "binding" (*bandhane*) [A 1.4.78]: *prādhvam* is an indeclinable; [thus] *prādhvaṃkṛtya*. The meaning is "having made favorable by means of binding. However, when making someone favorable through entreaty and so forth, one says *prādhvaṃ kṛtvā*.

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.1.79: *jīvikopaniṣadāv aupamye* (The words *jīvikā* and *upaniṣad* [form a compound with a following word] when used in the sense of comparison). Examples: *jīvikām iva kṛtvā* = *jīvikākṛtya*; *upaniṣadam iva kṛtvā* = *upaniṣatkṛtya*. Why "in the sense of comparison"? Example: *jīvikāṃ kṛtvā* (having made a livelihood). The inclusion of the term *prādi* ("prepositions and the like") is for the purpose of including those that do not signify motion (*agati*). Example: *supuruṣaḥ* (a good man). Regarding this, there are Vārttikas: 1. Words beginning with *pra* form a compound with a word in the first case when they signify "gone" (*gata*) and so forth. Example: *pragata ācāryaḥ* = *prācāryaḥ* (a teacher who has departed). 2. Words beginning with *ati* form a compound with a word in the second case when they signify "transcended" (*krānta*) and so forth. Example: *atikrānto mālām* = *atimālaḥ* (one who has surpassed a garland). 3. Words beginning with *ava* form a compound with a word in the third case when they signify "cried out to" (*kruṣṭa*) and so forth. Example: *avakruṣṭaḥ kokilayā* = *avakokilaḥ* (one called out to by a cuckoo).

The group beginning with *pari* [forms a compound] with a word in the fourth case when meaning "exhausted by" (*glāna*) and so forth; e.g., *pariglāno ’dhyayanāya* → *paryadhyayanaḥ* ("exhausted by study"). The group beginning with *nis* [forms a compound] with a word in the fifth case when meaning "departed from" (*krānta*) and so forth; e.g., *niṣkrāntaḥ kauśāmbyāḥ* → *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("departed from Kauśāmbī"). There is a prohibition [of compounding] for *karmapravacanīyas*; e.g., *vṛkṣaṃ prati*. SK 781: *tato ’papadaṃ saptamīstham* (A 3.1.92).

A word denoting a jar (*kumbha*) or the like, which stands as the object (*karman*) and so forth to be expressed and resides in a word ending in the seventh case, shall be designated as an *upapada*. And only when that exists, the suffix to be mentioned [later] occurs.

SK 782: *upapadam atiṅ* (A 2.2.19). An *upapada*, being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), is always compounded with a word that is semantically related to it. Furthermore, this compound does not end in a verbal suffix (*atiṅ*). For example: *kumbhaṃ karoti* ("he makes a pot") becomes *kumbhakāraḥ* ("pot-maker"). Here, the non-standard analytical sentence (*alaukika-prakriyāvākya*) is *kumbha as kāra*. Why "not ending in a verbal suffix" (*atiṅ*)? [Consider: *mā bhavān bhūt*. Because of the rule *māṅi luṅ* (A 3.3.175), which specifies the locative case (*saptamī-nirdeśāt*), *māṅ* is an *upapada*. The mention of *atiṅ* indicates that the term *sup* (from A 2.1.4) does not carry over here. In the previous rule as well, the mention of *gati* was separated, and the mention of *atiṅ* is drawn back into it.

And [the rule] *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* has been set aside. Thus it is established that "there is a statement regarding the compounding of a verb root (*kṛt*), a case-role (*kāraka*), or a subordinate word (*upapada*) with [a word ending in] a *kṛt*-suffix prior to the arising of the nominal suffix (*sup*). Examples: *vyāghrī*, *aśvakrītī*, *kacchapī*.
[Now follows: *amaivāvyayena* (A 2.2.20).

Only that which has the same rule of formation (*tulyavidhāna*) as the *am*-ending suffix is compounded with an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Examples: *svāduṃkāram* ("having made sweet"). Not here: *kālaḥ*, *samayaḥ*, or *velā bhoktum* ("it is time, the occasion, or the hour to eat"), because of the rule *kālasamayavelāsu tumun*. Why specify "only with the *am*-suffix"? Consider: *agre bhojam* ("eating before") and *agre bhuktvā* ("having eaten before"). Here, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* apply by the rule *vibhāṣāgreprathamapūrveṣu*. This [compounding] is prescribed equally with both the *am*-suffix and other [suffixes]. *A 2.2.21: tṛtīyāprabhṛtīny anyatarasyām* ("The words beginning with the third case [are optionally compounded]").

Words such as *upadaṃśa* in the rule *upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.30) may optionally form a compound with an indeclinable ending in *am*. Examples: *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats with a radish as a side-dish) or *mūlakopadaṃśam* (eating with a radish as a side-dish). SK 785: *ktvā ca* (A 2.2.22).

Words beginning from the third case (*tṛtīyā*) onwards, when used as *upapadas*, may optionally form a compound with a word ending in the suffix *ktvā*. Examples: *uccairkṛtya* or *uccaiḥkṛtvā* (having done so loudly). The suffix *ktvā* is applied here by the rule *avyaye ’yathābhipretākhyāne kṛñaḥ ktvā* (A 7.2.56). Why specify "beginning from the third case"? Consider these examples: *alaṃ kṛtvā* (having done enough) and *khalu kṛtvā* (having indeed done). These do not form compounds.

SK 786: *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ* (A 5.4.86). For a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *aṅguli* that begins with a numeral or an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the suffix *ac* is added at the end of the compound. Example: *dvyaṅgulam dāru* ("wood measuring two finger-breadths"), where *dve aṅgulī pramāṇam asya*. Example: *niraṅgulam*, where [something] has gone out from the fingers (*nirgatam aṅgulibhyaḥ*). SK 787: *ahaḥsarvaikadeśasaṃkhyātapuṇyāc ca rātreḥ* (A 5.4.87). [The suffix *ac* is added] after *rātri* when it follows *ahan*, *sarva*, a word denoting a part (*ekadeśa*), a numeral, *āpta*, or *puṇya*.

The suffix *ac* shall be applied after these [words] when preceded by a numeral or an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and also after the word *rātri*. The mention of *ahan* is for the sake of forming a *dvandva* compound: *ahan* and *rātri* form *ahorātraḥ*. *Sarvā rātriḥ* forms *sarvarātraḥ*. *Pūrvā rātreḥ* forms *pūrvarātraḥ*. *Saṃkhyātā rātriḥ* forms *saṃkhyātarātraḥ*. *Puṇyā rātriḥ* forms *puṇyarātraḥ*. The collection of two nights (*dvayo rātryoḥ samāhāraḥ*) forms *dvirātram*. That which has passed beyond the night (*atikrānto rātrim*) forms *atirātraḥ*.

By the rule *rājahaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* (A 5.4.91), the suffix *ṭac* shall be applied to a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in these [words]. *Paramo rājā* forms *paramarājaḥ*. *Atikrāntā rājñīm* forms *atirājī*. *Kṛṣṇasya sakhā* forms *kṛṣṇasakhaḥ*.

SK 789: The elision of the suffix *ṭi* occurs only after [compounds ending in] *ahan*, and not elsewhere. Examples: *uttamāhaḥ* ("the last day"); *dvyahīnaḥ kratuḥ* ("a sacrifice lasting two days"). [In this case], there is a *dvigu* compound for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Under the governing rule *tam adhīṣṭo...* (Pāṇini 5.1.80), with the continuation of the option *dvigor vā* (5.1.82), the suffix *kha* is applied by the rule *rātryahaḥsaṃvatsarāc ca*. Because the *paribhāṣā* regarding "words qualified by gender" (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) is not universally applicable, it does not apply here: *madrāṇāṃ rājñī* becomes *madrarājñī* ("queen of the Madras"). SK 790: For these [words beginning with *madrarāja-*, etc.], the substitute *ahn* is used in place of *ahan* [before a suffix beginning with a vowel]. (Pāṇini 5.4.88)

The word *ahan* following words beginning with *sarva* is replaced by *ahna* when a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) follows. (SK 791) By A 8.4.7, *ahna*, the *n* of the substitute *ahna* becomes *ṇ* when it follows a *r* situated in a preceding member ending in *a*. Examples: *sarvāhṇaḥ*, *pūrvāhṇaḥ*, *saṃkhyātāhnaḥ*. [Derivation: "That which exists in two days" (*dvayor ahnor bhavaḥ*). By [A 4.3.11] *kālāt ṭhañ*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied. By [A 4.1.88] *dvigor lug anapatye*, there is elision (*luk*) of *ṭhañ*. Result: *dvyahnaḥ*. In the feminine, because it ends in *a*, *ṭāp* is added: *dvyahnā*. *dvyahnapriyaḥ*. *atyahnaḥ*.

SK 792: *kṣubhnādiṣu ca* (A 8.4.39). In these [words], the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* shall not occur. For example: *dīrghāhnī prāvṛṭ*. Thus, for this purpose, the laborious effort of treating *ahnaḥ* as an imitation of a stem ending in *-a* need not be undertaken; for it is necessary to include [the word *ahnā*] in the *kṣubhnādi* list in order to prevent the application of *ṇatva* by the rule *prātipadikānta-* (A 8.4.14). Because of the specification *adantāt* (after a stem ending in -a) with the *tapara* marker, [the rule does not apply here]: *parāhṇaḥ* (the latter part of the day), from *parāgatam ahaḥ*. SK 793: *na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhāre* (A 5.4.89). [The suffix *taddhita* *aṇ* is not applied after a compound beginning with a numeral when it denotes a collective.]

For a word beginning with a numeral that occurs in a collective compound (*samāhāra*), the substitution of *ahan* [for *ahar*] would not take place. The phrase "beginning with a numeral" (*saṃkhyādeḥ*) is for the sake of clarity. The collection of two days is *dvyahaḥ*; [the collection of three days is] *tryahaḥ*. A 5.4.90: *uttamaikābhyāṃ ca* ("Also after *uttama* and *eka*"). After these two, the substitution of *ahan* does not occur. The word *uttama* means "last. It refers to the word *puṇya*. It would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as *puṇyaikābhyām*. Examples: *puṇyāham* ("an auspicious day"), *sudināham* ("a fair day"). The word *sudina* denotes something praiseworthy. *ekāhaḥ* ("a single day"). Some say that the mention of *uttama* is intended to include the penultimate (*upāntya*) as well. Example: *saṃkhyātāhaḥ* ("a counted day").
SK 795: The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied after the word *uras* when it follows a word denoting "foremost" (*agrākhya*). For example, *aśvoraśam*, meaning "the foremost horse.
SK 796: The suffix *ṭac* is applied after words ending in *an*, as well as after *aśman*, *ayas*, and *saras*, when they denote a genus (*jāti*) or a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

The suffix *ṭac* occurs after [the word *upānat*] when denoting a genus (*jāti*) or a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Examples for genus: *upānaham*, *amṛtāśmaḥ*, *kālāyasam*, *maṇḍūkasarasam*. Examples for proper names: *mahānasam*, *piṇḍāśmaḥ*, *lohitāyasam*, *jalasarasam*. SK 797: After *grāma* and *kauṭa*, [the suffix *ṭac* is added] to *takṣan*.
*Grāmasya takṣā* becomes *grāmatakṣaḥ*; the meaning is "one who is common [to the village]. *Kuṭyāṃ bhavaḥ* becomes *kauṭaḥ*, meaning "independent"; such a person is a carpenter, hence *kauṭatakṣaḥ*.
SK 798 *ateḥ śunaḥ* (A 5.4.96):
*atiśvo varāhaḥ* ("a boar that surpasses a dog"); *atiśvī senā* ("an army that surpasses dogs").
SK 799 *upamānād aprāṇiṣu* (A 5.4.97).

The suffix *ṭac* is applied after the word *śvan* when it expresses a comparison with something that is not a living being (*aprāṇin*). For example: *ākarṣaśvaḥ* ("a dog-like puller"). Why "not a living being"? Consider: *vānaraśvā* ("a monkey-like dog," where the comparison is with a living being). SK 800: The suffix *ṭac* is also applied after *sakthi* preceded by *uttara*, *mṛga*, or *pūrva*, as well as after an *upamāna* (standard of comparison). Examples: *uttarasaktham* ("the hind leg"), *mṛgasaktham* ("deer-thigh"), *pūrvasaktham* ("front leg"), and *phalasaktham* ("a thigh like a board").

SK 801 *nāvo dvigoḥ* (A 5.4.99): The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied after a *dvigu* compound ending in the word *nau*, but not when there is elision (*luk*) of a *taddhita* suffix. For example: *dvināvarūpyaḥ* ("brought by two boats"). Because the word *aci* is drawn back [from the previous rule] into the rule *dvigor luganapatye* (A 4.1.88), there is no elision for a stem beginning with a consonant. Examples: *pañcanāvapriyaḥ*, *dvināvam*, *trināvam*. Why say "not when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix"? Consider: *pañcanauḥ* ("purchased for five boats"), where the suffix *ṭhan* is elided. SK 802 *ardhāc ca* (A 5.4.100): [The suffix *ṭac* is applied after *ardha* when it forms a *dvigu*].

The suffix *ṣṭac* may optionally be applied after the word *nau* [meaning "boat"] when it follows *ardha*. Examples: *nāvo 'rdham* ("half a boat") becomes *ardhanāvam*. Its neuter gender is established by common usage.

According to Pāṇini 5.4.100 (*khāryāḥ prācām*), the suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied after *khārī* following a *dvigu* compound or after *ardha*, according to the Eastern grammarians. Examples: *dvikhāram* or *dvikhāri*; *ardhakhāram* or *ardhakhāri*.

SK 804: After *dvi* and *tri*, the suffix *ṭac* may optionally be applied to *añjali* when it forms a *dvigu* compound. Examples: *dvyañjalim* or *dvyañjali*. This applies only when there is no elision of a *taddhita* suffix (*ataddhitaluki*). For instance, that which is purchased for two *añcalis* is called *dvyañjaliḥ*. SK 805: The word *brahman* takes the feminine suffix *ṅīp* when it denotes a place-name (*jānapadākhyāyām*). (A 5.4.104)

The suffix *ṭac* shall be applied after the word *brahman* when it occurs at the end of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, provided that the compound expresses the status of being a member of a particular region (*jānapada*). For example: *surāṣṭre brahmā* = *surāṣṭrabrahmaḥ*.

According to A 5.4.105, *kumahadbhyām anyatarasyām*, the suffix *ṭac* may optionally be applied after the word *brahman* when preceded by *ku* or *mahat* in a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Thus: *kutsito brahmā* = *kubrahmaḥ* or *kubrahmā*.
Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.46: *ānmahataḥ samānādhikaraṇajātīyayoḥ*.

The substitution of the vowel *ā* for the final [phoneme] of *mahat* occurs when followed by a co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) subsequent word or by the suffix *jātīya*. Examples: *mahābrāhmaṇaḥ*, *mahābrahmā*, *mahādevaḥ*, *mahājātīyaḥ*. Why "co-referential"? Consider *mahataḥ sevā* ("the service of the great one"), which results in *mahatsevā*. If one were to argue that, setting aside technical definitions, only the specific compound mentioned in the rule—namely *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.61)—is intended here, then *mahābāhuḥ* would not be valid. Therefore, the paribhāṣā "between a term defined by a general rule and one mentioned specifically, the specifically mentioned prevails" does not apply here.

[The substitution of *ā* occurs] by virtue of the inclusion of the term "in grammatical apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Alternatively, the substitution of *ā* occurs through the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) beginning with *ād*, or because of the specific mention [in the sūtra] of "prior to eleven" (*prāg ekādaśabhyaḥ*). Thus: *ekādaśa*. When the masculine form is applied to the word *mahatī* according to the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye*, the substitution of *ā* occurs: *mahājātīyā*. Regarding the substitution of *ā* for *mahat*, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) [of this rule] to the words *ghāsa*, *kara*, and *viśiṣṭa*, as well as the application of the masculine form. This is for the purpose of including cases where there is no grammatical apposition (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*): *mahato mahatyā vā ghāsaḥ* = *mahāghāsaḥ*; *mahākaraḥ*; *mahāviśiṣṭaḥ*.

In the case of the word *aṣṭan* [ending in the nominative singular], when followed by *kapāla* in the sense of an oblation (*havis*), the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel is prescribed; thus, we have *aṣṭākapālaḥ*. Furthermore, when the word *go* follows in the sense of "yoked" (*yukta*), the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of *aṣṭan* must be stated when the meaning "yoked" is to be understood. Thus, *aṣṭāgavaṃ śakaṭam* ("a cart yoked to eight oxen"). Regarding the form *aṣṭagavam*, although the rule *ac-praty-anv-ava-* (Pāṇini 5.4.75) applies to compounds beginning with *prati*, *anu*, *ava*, and *ni*, the term *ac* is here separated as a distinct *yogavibhāga* (rule-splitting), which allows for the suffix *ac* even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Alternatively, *aṣṭagavam* may mean "a collection of eight oxen," and because the cart is yoked to those, it is called *aṣṭāgavam*. SK 808: *dvyaṣṭanaḥ saṃkhyāyām abahuvrīhyaśītyoḥ* (A 6.3.47). [The substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of *dvi* and *aṣṭan* occurs before a word denoting a number, provided it is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound and does not end in *aśīti*.]

From here on, [the following applies]: *dvi* (two) and *daśa* (ten) make *dvādaśa* (twelve), or alternatively, *deśa* with *dvi* prefixed makes *dvādaśa*. *Dvāviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-two), *aṣṭādaśa* (eighteen), *aṣṭāviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-eight). Why is it not so in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound or when followed by *aśīti* (eighty)? [Examples: *dvitrāḥ* (two or three), *dvyaśītiḥ* (eighty-two). It should be stated that this applies "prior to one hundred" (*prāk śatāt*). Not here: *dviśatam* (two hundred), *dvisahasram* (two thousand). SK 809: *trestrayaḥ* (A 6.3.48). [In the place of *tri*, *trayaḥ* is substituted.]

In the aforementioned context, the word *tri* becomes *traya-* [before a following *daśan*, etc.]: *trayodaśa* (thirteen), *trayoviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-three). However, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it remains *tri-*: *trir daśa* (ten times three), *tridaśāḥ* (the thirty [gods]). A *bahuvrīhi* is used here in the sense of "good" (*su-artham*). But before *aśīti* (eighty), it remains *tri-*: *tryaśītiḥ* (eighty-three). This applies only up to one hundred: *triśatam* (three hundred), *trisahasram* (three thousand). According to A 6.3.49, *vibhāṣā catvāriṃśatprabhṛtau sarveṣām*: [The substitution of *traya-* for *tri*] is optional before forty and so on for all [words].

Before the word *catvāriṃśat* and others, the forms previously mentioned—namely *dvi-aṣṭa-nau* and *tri*—may optionally occur. Thus: *dvicatvāriṃśat* or *dvācatvāriṃśat*, *aṣṭacatvāriṃśat* or *aṣṭācatvāriṃśat*, and *tricatvāriṃśat* or *trayaścatvāriṃśat*. The same applies to *pañcāśat*, *ṣaṣṭi*, *saptati*, and *navati*.
Furthermore, according to A 6.3.76, *eka* and other numerals may optionally take the form *ekā-* before *eka-* [when followed by another numeral]. Thus: *ekādaśa* or *ekadaśa*.

The word *eka* and others [beginning with *dvi*] remain in their original form (*prakṛti*) when combined with the negative particle *nañ*, and the augment *ad-ū* is added to *eka*. When a compound is formed with *nañ* together with the word *viṃśati*, the compound is formed with the word *eka* by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) from the rule *tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.30). There is an option regarding the nasalization [of the final vowel]. Thus: *ekānnaviṃśatiḥ*, *ekānnaviṃśatiḥ*, *ekādanaviṃśatiḥ*; the meaning is "one less than twenty" (*ekonaviṃśati*). It should be stated that in the case of *ṣaṣ*, there is a change to *u* before the words *datṛ*, *daśan*, and *dhā*, and that the first letter of the subsequent member becomes *ṣṭu* before the words *dhā*, optionally. Thus: *ṣōḍan*, *ṣoḍaśa*, *ṣōḍḥā*, *ṣaḍdhā*. SK 812: For a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the gender is that of the final member (*paravalliṅga*). (A 2.4.26)

In these two cases, the gender would be that of the subsequent member [of the compound]: *imau kukkuṭamayūrau* ("these two, a cock and a peahen") and *imau mayūrīkukkuṭau* ("these two, a peahen and a cock"). [The rule applies] to compounds with *ardha-*, *dvigu*, *prāpta-*, *āpanna-*, *alam-pūrva*, and *gati* compounds; however, a prohibition must be stated for these: *pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ pañcakapālaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* ("a sacrificial cake prepared in five vessels"), *prāpto jīvikāṃ prāptajīvikaḥ* ("one who has obtained a livelihood"), *āpannajīvikaḥ* ("one who has fallen into a livelihood"), *alaṃ kumāryai alaṃkumāriḥ* ("sufficient for a maiden"). It is precisely because of this [usage] that it is known that a compound is formed [with *alaṃ*]. [Examples include: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("one who has departed from Kauśāmbī"). SK 813: *aśvavaḍavau pūrvavat* (A 2.4.27). "The words *aśva-* and *vaḍava-* are as before.
