These two types of compounds—dvandva and tatpuruṣa—ending in [the word] *anta* are masculine only. Because it is an internal rule (*antaraṅga*), this [rule] also sets aside the subsequent rule regarding the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*), and by virtue of being a later rule, it overrides the neuter gender of the collective compound (*samāhāra*). Examples: *ahorātraḥ* (day and night); *pūrvarātraḥ* (the first part of the night); *pūrvāhṇaḥ* (forenoon); *dvyahaḥ* (two days). When preceded by a numeral, the word *rātri* is neuter: *dvirātram*, *trirātram*, *gaṇarātram*. According to A 2.4.29: *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi* (The words *rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* are masculine).

These two types of compounds—dvandva and tatpuruṣa—ending in [the word *anta*] are exclusively masculine. Because this rule is internal (*antaraṅga*), it serves as an exception to the general rule of taking the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*); furthermore, by virtue of its own priority, it overrides the neuter gender of collective compounds (*samāhāra*). Examples: *ahorātraḥ* (a day and night). *Pūrvarātraḥ* (the first part of the night), *pūrvāhṇaḥ* (the forenoon). *Dvyahaḥ* (two days). When preceded by a numeral, the word *rātra* is neuter: *dvirātram*, *trirātram*, *gaṇarātram*. SK 815: *apathaṃ napuṃsakam* (A 2.4.30).

This applies specifically to a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Otherwise, however, *apathaḥ* means "a region without a path. Because the form is specified with the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) applied, it does not apply here: *apanthāḥ* (a bad path).

SK 816 *ardharcāḥ puṃsi ca* (A 2.4.31): Words beginning with *ardharca* may be used in both the masculine and the neuter genders. For example: *ardharcaḥ* (masculine) or *ardharcam* (neuter); *dhvajaḥ* (masculine) or *dhvajam* (neuter). Likewise: *tīrtha*, *śasīra*, *maṇḍa*, *pīyūṣa*, *deha*, *aṅkuśa*, *kalaśa*, and so forth. SK 817 *jātyākhyāyām ekasmin bahuvacanam anyatarasyām* (A 1.2.58): When a genus (*jāti*) is being denoted, the plural number may optionally be used for a single individual.

Even a single object may take a plural form: *brāhmaṇāḥ pūjyāḥ* ("Brahmins are to be honored") or *brāhmaṇaḥ pūjyaḥ* ("a Brahmin is to be honored"). According to A 1.2.59, *asmado dvayoś ca*, when singularity or duality is intended, the plural may optionally be used for the pronoun *asmad* ("we"): *vayaṃ brūmaḥ* ("we say"), or alternatively, *ahaṃ bravīmi* ("I say") or *āvāṃ brūvaḥ* ("the two of us say"). This option is prohibited when the pronoun has a qualifier: *paṭur ahaṃ bravīmi* ("I, being clever, say").

SK 819: In the case of the asterisms *phalgunī* and *proṣṭhapadā*, when they are used in the dual number, the grammatical operation conditioned by the plural may optionally take place. Examples: *pūrve phalgunyau* / *pūrvāḥ phalgunyaḥ*; *pūrve proṣṭhapade* / *pūrvāḥ proṣṭhapadāḥ*. Why "in the case of an asterism"? [Consider: *phalgunyau māṇavike* ("two girls named Phalgunī"). SK 820:
In a *dvandva* compound of asterisms consisting of *tiṣya* and *punarvasu*, the dual number necessarily replaces the plural. (A 1.2.63)

The plural number occurs as it does for the dual. *Tiṣya* and *Punarvasū* [form] *tiṣyapunarvasū*. Why [is it specified that they are] *tiṣya*? [To exclude cases such as] *viśākhānurādhāḥ*. Why [is it specified that they are] *nakṣatra* (asterisms)? [To exclude cases such as] *tiṣyapunarvasavo māṇavakāḥ* ("the boys Tiṣya and Punarvasu"). SK 821: That [compound] is neuter. (A 2.4.17)

In a collective compound (samāhāra), both *dvigu* and *dvandva* shall be neuter; this is an exception to the rule regarding the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅga*). Examples: *pañcagavam* (five cows), *dantoṣṭham* (teeth and lips). A *dvigu* whose final member ends in *a* is desired to be feminine: *pañcamūlī* (five roots). Or it may end in *ā*: *pañcakhaṭvī* or *pañcakhaṭvam* (five beds). In a *dvigu*, a feminine form ending in *an* optionally drops its *n*: *pañcatakṣī* or *pañcatakṣam* (five carpenters). This does not apply to compounds ending in *pātra* and so on: *pañcapātram* (five vessels), *tribhuvanam* (the three worlds), *caturyugam* (the four ages). After the words *puṇya* and *sudina*, the word *ahan* is desired to be neuter: *puṇyāham* (an auspicious day), *sudināham*.

*Puṇyāham* ("an auspicious day") and *sudināham* ("a fair day"). Regarding *pathaḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*: the meaning is that the word *patha*, when followed by a numeral or an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and having the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) applied, is neuter. For example: *tripatham* ("the path of three" or "a place where three roads meet"), and *vipatham* ("a bad road"). Because the rule specifies the form with the compound-final suffix applied, this does not apply here: *supanthāḥ* ("a good road") and *atipanthāḥ* ("a very long road"). [In these cases,] the neuter gender is used in the sense of a general quality: *mṛdu pacati* ("he cooks softly") and *prātaḥ kamanīyam* ("it is pleasant in the morning"). *Tatpuruṣo 'nañkarmadhārayaḥ* (A 2.4.19): This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).

SK 823 *saṃjñāyāṃ kanthośīnareṣu* (A 2.4.20): A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *kanthā* shall be neuter if it is a name (*saṃjñā*) of a rag-robe (*kanthā*) produced in the land of the Uśīnaras. For example: the descendants of Suśama are the Sauśamas; their rag-robe is *sauśamikantham*. Why "if it is a name"? [Counter-example: *vīraṇakanthā* (a mat made of *vīraṇa* grass). Why "in the land of the Uśīnaras"? [Counter-example: *dākṣikanthā* (the rag-robe of Dakṣi). SK 824 *upajñopakramaṃ tadādyācikhyāsāyām* (A 1.4.21): A compound beginning with *upajñā* or *upakrama* is a neuter singular when there is a desire to express that it was first known or begun by that person.

A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *upajñā* or *upakrama* shall be neuter, provided that the beginning (*ādi*) or the commencement (*prārambha*) of those two—the thing first known (*upajñāyamāna*) or the thing first undertaken (*upakramyamāṇa*)—is intended to be expressed. For example: *pāṇiny-upajñaṃ granthaḥ* ("the work first known by Pāṇini"), *nandopakramaṃ droṇaḥ* ("the battle commenced by Nanda").
[Also, a word for] "shadow" (*chāyā*) [is neuter] when it denotes multiplicity (A 2.4.22).

A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *chāyā* shall be neuter when there is an abundance of the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*). For example: *ikṣucchāyam* ("the shade of sugarcane"). This is an exception to the optional rule [A 2.4.25] beginning with *vibhāṣā senā*. However, in the expression *ikṣucchāyāniṣādinyaḥ* ("those sitting in the shade of sugarcane"), one should understand that the prefix *āṅ* is elided, as it means "sitting all around" (*ā samantān niṣādinyaḥ*). [A 2.4.23] *sabhā* [is feminine], except when preceded by a word denoting a king or a non-human being.

A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in a synonym for "king" (*rāja-paryāya*) or the word "non-human" (*amanuṣya*), when preceded by [another word], shall be neuter when referring to an assembly (*sabhā*). *inasabham* ("the assembly of the lord"); *īśvarasabham* ("the assembly of the master"). This is desired only when [the first member] is a synonym; not here: *rājasabhā* ("the king's assembly") or *candraguptasabhā* ("Candragupta’s assembly"). The word *amanuṣya* refers by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) to *rakṣas*, *piśāca*, and so forth. *rakṣaḥsabham* ("the assembly of demons"); *piśācasabham* ("the assembly of *piśācas*"). SK 827: *aśālā ca* (A 2.4.24).

A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *sabhā* which has the sense of a "congregation" (*saṃghāta*) and does not mean a "house" (*śālā*) shall be neuter. *strīsabham*; the meaning is "a congregation of women. Why say "not a house"? [Consider: *dharmasabhā*; the meaning is "a hall of justice" (*dharmaśālā*).

SK 828: *vibhāṣā senāsurācchāyāśālāniśānām* (A 2.4.25). A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in these [words] may optionally be neuter. *brāhmaṇasenam* / *brāhmaṇasenā* (Brahmin-army); *yavasuram* / *yavasurā* (barley-liquor); *kuḍyacchāyam* / *kuḍyacchāyā* (wall-shadow); *gośālā* (cow-stall); *śvaniśam* / *śvaniśā* (dog-night). Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "a *tatpuruṣa* other than one with *nañ* or a *karmadhāraya" [is neuter], this does not apply here: *dṛḍhaseno rājā* (the king Dṛḍhasena), *asenā* (no army), *paramasenā* (supreme army).
Thus ends the section on the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
The Section on Bahuvrīhi Compounds 19.

SK 829 *śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ* (A 2.2.23): This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). The meaning is that the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to those [compounds] for which a specific compound formation has not been stated by the rules beginning with *dvitīyā-śrita-* (A 2.1.24), and which consist of words ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*). SK 830 *anekam anyapadārthe* (A 2.2.24).

Several words ending in the nominative case (*prathamā*), when functioning in the sense of another word, may be compounded; this is *bahuvrīhi*. It follows that *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of a case other than the nominative and that the members must be in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Examples: *prāptodako grāmaḥ* ("the village to which water has come"); *ūḍharatho 'naḍvān* ("an ox that has drawn a chariot"); *upahṛtapaśū rudraḥ* ("Rudra to whom an animal has been offered"); *uddhṛtaudanā sthālī* ("a pot from which rice has been taken out"); *pītāmbaro hariḥ* ("Hari who wears yellow garments"); *vīrapuruṣako grāmaḥ* ("a village whose men are heroes"). However, it does not occur in the sense of the nominative: *vṛṣṭe deve gataḥ* ("he went when the god [rain] had rained").

Nor [is the elision] of words that have different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). For example: *pañcabhir bhuktam asya* ("five were eaten by him"). The elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*) may optionally be stated after prefixes such as *pra-* when followed by a word derived from a verbal root (*dhātujasya*). For example: *prapatitaparṇaḥ* becomes *praparṇaḥ*. The elision of the final member may optionally be stated after the negative particle *nañ* when followed by words having the sense of "to exist" (*astyartha*). For example: *avidyamānaputraḥ* becomes *aputraḥ*. The word *asti* here is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that resembles a case-ending. For example: *astikṣīrā gauḥ* ("a cow that has milk"). Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.34: In the feminine, a word ending in a suffix other than *ūṅ*, which has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), takes the masculine form (*puṃvat*) when it is in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with another feminine word, provided it is not a word denoting a ordinal number (*apūraṇī*) or one of the class beginning with *priya* (*apriyādiṣu*). *SK* stands for *Siddhāntakaumudī*. (Note: The text provided contains fragments of Sanskrit grammatical rules and examples related to compound formation and the elision of members.)

The term *uktapuṃskāt* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that in which there is an absence (*abhāva*) of *ūṅ* after [a stem] that has already expressed the masculine. Due to a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the fifth case-ending and elision (*luk*) of the sixth case-ending. When the cause for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is identical, for a feminine-denoting word that follows one which has already expressed the masculine and in which there is such an absence of *ūṅ*, its form shall be like that of the masculine-denoting word, provided the following member (*uttarapada*) is a feminine noun in grammatical apposition; however, this does not apply when a *pūraṇī* (ordinal) or a word beginning with *priya* follows. By the rule *gostriyoḥ*, the final vowel is shortened.

In the worldly analytical statement (*laukika-vigraha*), "one whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya*); in the non-worldly analytical statement (*alaukika-vigraha*), *citrā as go as*. [The resulting compound is] *citraguḥ*. Similarly, *rūpavadbhāryaḥ*. In the analytical statement "one whose cow is variegated and old" (*citrā jaratī gaur yasya*), a *bahuvrīhi* may be formed even with many members because it expresses more than one [quality]. Regarding this, some say: *citrājaratīguḥ* or *jaratīcitrāguḥ*. Likewise, *dīrghātanvījaṅghaḥ* or *tanvīdīrghājaṅghaḥ*. In a three-word *bahuvrīhi*, the first member does not undergo the masculine form (*puṃvat*) because the final member is separated by the middle member.

The second [member] also does not become like the masculine (*puṃvat*), because it lacks the status of being a *pūrvapada* (prior member). For they say that the word *uttarapada* is conventionally established as the final constituent of a compound, whereas the word *pūrvapada* is conventionally established as the first constituent. However, in reality, the prior member is not implied here, just as in the rule *ānaṅ ṛtaḥ*. Therefore, the penultimate [member] indeed becomes like the masculine, as in *citrā-ajarad-guḥ* and so forth. For this very reason, even in a compound containing a *dvandva*, such as "one whose cows are a brindled female and an old female," the *Bhāṣya* states *citrā-ajarad-guḥ*.

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, however, when the final member is a feminine word, [the suffix *ṅīp* is replaced by *ṅīṣ*], as in *citrajaradgavīkaḥ*. Why "of a feminine word" (*striyāḥ*)? [Consider] *grāmaṇidṛṣṭiḥ*, meaning "one whose view is that of a village headman. Why "from a word that has a corresponding masculine form" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*)? [Consider] *gaṅgābhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is the Gaṅgā"). Why "not ending in *ūṅ*" (*anūṅ*)? [Consider] *vāmorūbhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife has beautiful thighs"). Why "in a coreferential compound" (*samānādhikaraṇe*)? [Consider] *kalyāṇīmātā*, meaning "the mother of a beautiful woman. Why "in the feminine" (*striyām*)? [Consider] *kalyāṇīpradhānaḥ*, meaning "one for whom a beautiful woman is the primary [object]. But in the case of ordinal numbers (*pūraṇī*), [the rule is governed by]: *appūraṇīpramāṇyoḥ* (A 5.4.116).

The suffix *ap* is added after a feminine word ending in a *pūraṇī* (ordinal) suffix and after a feminine word ending in *pramāṇī* (standard of measure*) when these form part of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For example: *kalyāṇī-pañcamā rātrayaḥ* ("the nights of which the fifth is auspicious"); *strī-pramāṇaḥ* ("one for whom a woman is the standard"). The prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) and the addition of the suffix *ap* apply only when the *pūraṇī* is the principal member (*pradhāna*). In the examples cited above, the night (*rātri*) is both the *pūraṇī* and the expressed meaning (*vācyā*), and thus it is the principal member. However, in other cases, [the rule applies] according to *A 5.4.143*: *nady-ṛtaś ca*. *(Note: The term *pramāṇī* here refers to a feminine noun used as a standard of measurement or authority.)*

The suffix *kap* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose final member is a word meaning "river" (*nadī*) or whose final member ends in the vowel *ṛ*. There is also the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).
When [the rule] *ke 'ṇaḥ* (A 7.4.13) applies—stating that a short vowel shall replace a non-ṇatva vowel (*aṇ*) when followed by the suffix *ka*—[the following is obtained].

SK 835: *na kapi* (A 7.4.14). When the suffix *kap* follows, the short vowel [of the first member] shall not occur. Example: *kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ* ("the fortnight having the auspicious fifth day"). Here, because the fortnight (*pakṣa*)—whose internal divisions are obscured—is the referent of the external compound (*anyapadārtha*), the night (*rātri*) is subordinate. Example: *abhukartṛkaḥ*. In what cases does this not apply when [the first member] is among those beginning with *apriya*? Examples: *kalyāṇīpriyaḥ*, *priyā*, *manojñā*, *kalyāṇī*, *subhagā*, *durbhagā*, *bhaktiḥ*, *sacivā*, *svasā*, *kāntā*, *kṣāntā*, *samā*, *capalā*, *duhitā*, *vāmā*, *abalā*, *tanayā*. [Note: A neuter form is used for the general sense.
One whose devotion is firm is *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ*; however, when the feminine gender is intended, it is *dṛḍhābhaktiḥ*. This is according to Pāṇini 6.3.35: *tasil-ādiṣv ā-kṛtvasucaḥ*.

When suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending in *kṛtvasuc* follow, the feminine form should become masculine (*puṃvat*). A specific enumeration (*parigaṇana*) must be made to avoid both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*). The following suffixes are included: *tratasau*, *taraptamapau*, *caraḍjātīyarau*, *kalpabdeśīyarau*, *rūpappāśapa*, *thāl*, *tilthyanau*. Examples: *bahvīṣu* → *bahutra*; *bahutaḥ*; *darśanīyatarā*; *darśanīyatamā*. Regarding *gharūpa-*, the shortening (*hrasva*) to be mentioned later takes precedence over the masculine transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*). Examples: *paṭvitarā*; *paṭvitamā*.

*Paṭucarī*: one who is clever, of a clever nature, resembling one who is clever, having the appearance of one who is clever, possessing the form of one who is clever, having the allure of one who is clever; or one who is many-sided, excellent—a female wolf (*vṛkī*), a she-wolf (*vṛkati*). *Ajathyā*: beneficial for goats. Regarding the suffix *śas*, it should be stated that there is the substitution of the masculine form for a word meaning "many" or "few": give to many in many ways (*bahuśaḥ*); give to few in few ways (*alpaśaḥ*). Regarding the suffixes *tva* and *tal*, [the substitution of the masculine form occurs] after a quality-word (*guṇavacana*): the state of being white is "whiteness" (*śuklatvam*) or "whiteness-ness" (*śuklatā*). Why "after a quality-word"? [Because in the following case it does not occur: the state of being an agent is "agency" (*kartrītvam*).

In examples such as *śaradaḥ kṛtārthatā*, the neuter gender is used for the general category (*sāmānya*). [The rule] *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* [applies]: a collection of female elephants is *hāstikam*. Why "not before a suffix beginning with a vowel" (*aḍhe*)? Consider *rauhiṇeyaḥ*; here, the suffix *ḍha* is understood from the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*. However, the suffix *ḍhak* from the rule *agner ḍhak* remains masculine. For example: "This sacrificial oblation (*sthālīpāka*) has Agnāyī as its deity" is *āgneyaḥ*. The word *sapatnī* is threefold: one form is derived from the word *sapatna* meaning "enemy," with the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* because it belongs to the *śārṅgarava*-class.

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "she whose husband is the same" (*samānaḥ patir yasyāḥ*), the second [type of *sapatnī*] is a word that is invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*), based on the word *pati* as used in the context of marriage. The third [type] is a word that has undergone masculine inflection (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), using the word *pati* as a synonym for "master" (*svāmin*). In the case of the first two, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *śivādyaṇ*. Thus, the offspring of a *sapatnī* is *sāpatnaḥ*. However, from the third type, by the technical rule regarding gender-distinction (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), only the suffix *ṇya*—characterized by having *pati* as its final member—is applied, and not *aṇ*. This is because the rule *śivādau* refers only to those words that are established (*rūḍhi*) in that sense. Thus, [the offspring] is *sāpatyaḥ*. [The suffix *aṇ* is also applied] after [stems ending in] *ṭhak* and *chas*.

Your students are *bhāvatkāḥ* or *bhavadīyāḥ*. This Vārttika and the rule *ekataddhite ca* need not be formulated, because their purpose is already served by the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra that "in all derivative formations (*vṛtti*), a pronoun undergoes masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*). Thus: *sarvamayaḥ*, *sarvakāmyati*, *sarvakabhāryaḥ* (one whose wife is *sarvikā*), *sarvapriyaḥ*, and so forth. This [masculine substitution] applies only to the former [type of formation], as indicated by the rule *bhastraiṣājājñād vā*. Therefore, it does not apply in the case of *akac* or in the formation of *ekaśeṣa*; hence, [the forms remain] *sarvikā*.

All [of these apply] to the eggs and so forth of hens and others: *kukkuṭyā aṇḍam* becomes *kukkuṭāṇḍam* (the egg of a hen); *mṛgyāḥ padam* becomes *mṛgapadam* (the track of a doe); *mṛgakṣīram* (the milk of a doe); *kākaśāvaḥ* (the chick of a crow). By rule A 6.3.36, *kyaṅ* and *nāninoḥ*: *śyenīvācarati* becomes *śyenāyate* (he acts like a hawk). *darśanīyamāninī* refers to one who considers some woman other than herself to be beautiful. *Darśanīyamānī caitraḥ* refers to Caitra who considers a beautiful woman to be beautiful [himself].

SK 838: *na kopadhāyāḥ* (A 6.3.37). A feminine word having *k* as its penultimate letter (*kopadhā*) does not undergo the masculine form (*puṃvat*). Examples: *pācikābhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a cook"), *rasikābhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a connoisseur"). *madrikāyate* ("she acts like Madrikā"), *madrikāmāninī* ("one who considers herself Madrikā"). Regarding the prohibition concerning words with a penultimate *k*, the term *taddhita* is understood [to include] *vu*. Therefore, this does not apply here: *pākabhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a cooking [act]"). SK 839: *saṃjñāpūraṇyoś ca* (A 6.3.38). [The masculine form is also prohibited for] proper names (*saṃjñā*) and ordinal numbers (*pūraṇī*).

In these two cases, the masculine form is not applied (*na puṃvat*): *dattābhāryaḥ* and *dattāmāninī*. Since this [term] is a name (*saṃjñā*) for both the female and the male based on the act of giving (*dānakriyā*), it possesses the quality of having been previously used in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*). [Examples: *pañcamībhāryaḥ*, *pañcamīpāśā*.

[And] regarding a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) whose cause is a vowel increment (*vṛddhi*), provided it does not denote a colored product or a transformation (*araktavikāre*), [the feminine is formed by adding *ṅīṣ*]. (A 6.3.39)

A feminine word ending in a *taddhita* suffix that causes a *vṛddhi* vowel (as prescribed by the term "vṛddhi") and does not signify a colored substance or a modification [of the material] is treated like the masculine (*pumvat*). Examples: *sraughnī-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is from Sraughna"), *māthurīyate* ("she acts like a woman from Mathurā"), *māthurīmāninī* ("she considers herself a woman from Mathurā"). Why "causing a *vṛddhi* vowel"? Consider *madhyama-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is of middle stature"). Why "a *taddhita* suffix"? Consider *kāṇḍalāva-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a reaper of stalks"). Why "by the term *vṛddhi*"? Consider *tāvat-bhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is so much"). However, in the case of a colored substance, as in *kāṣāyī kanthā yasya sa kāpāyakanthaḥ* ("he who has a saffron-colored shawl"), it is not treated as such.

In the case of a derivative (*vikāra*), however, one who has a golden ring is called *haimamudrikaḥ*. Because the word expressing increase (*vṛddhi-śabda*) does not contribute toward the result [of the compound] with respect to the increase itself, it is treated as masculine here: *vaiyākaraṇabhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a grammarian") and *sauvaśvabhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a descendant of Suvaśva"). SK 841: *svāṅgāc cetaḥ* (A 6.3.40).

A feminine word ending in the vowel *ī* following a word denoting a limb of the body (*svāṅga*) is not treated as masculine. Example: *sukeśībhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife has beautiful hair"). Why "from a limb of the body" (*svāṅgāt*)? Example: *paṭubhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is clever"). Why "ending in *ī*" (*ītaḥ*)? Example: *akeśabhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is hairless"). It should be stated that this does not apply to words ending in *-māninī*: *sukeśamāninī* ("one who considers herself to have beautiful hair").

SK 842 *jāteś ca* (A 6.3.41): That which ends in a feminine suffix following a word denoting genus (*jāti*) is not treated as masculine (*na puṃvat*). Examples: *śūdrābhāryaḥ*, *brāhmaṇībhāryaḥ*. This prohibition applies only to [feminine suffixes] prescribed in the sūtras. Therefore, in the case of *hastinīnāṃ samūho hāstikam* ("a collection of female elephants"), the rule *bhasyāḍhe* (Pāṇini 1.4.18) does indeed apply.

SK 843 *saṃkhyayāvyayāsannādūrādhikasaṃkhyāḥ saṃkhyeye* (A 2.2.25): A numeral, an indeclinable (*avyaya*), *āsanna* ("near"), *adūra* ("not far"), *adhika* ("more than"), or a numeral itself [forms a compound] with a word denoting the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*).

Numerals expressing a countable object are compounded with words such as *avyaya* (indeclinables), and that compound is a *bahuvrīhi*. Those which are near ten are called *upadaśa*; the meaning is "nine" or "eleven. In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* denoting a countable object, the suffix *ḍac* will be prescribed [by the rule *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍac*];
and by the rule *ti viṃśater ḍiti* (A 6.4.142), the final syllable of *viṃśati* is elided when followed by a suffix beginning with *ḍ*.

The word *ti* of the word *viṃśati* is elided before a suffix beginning with *ḍ*. *Āsannaviṃśāḥ*: meaning "near twenty. *Adūratriṃśāḥ*: "not far from thirty. *Adhikacatvāriṃśāḥ*: "more than forty. *Dvitrāḥ*: "two or three. *Dvidaśāḥ*: ten repeated twice; that is, twenty. SK 845: *diṅnāmāny antarāle* (A 2.2.26). Names of directions are compounded as previously described when an intermediate direction is to be expressed. *Dakṣiṇāpūrvā*: the intermediate direction between the south and the east. Because of the mention of the word "name" (*nāma*), this does not apply to derivative terms. [Example: the intermediate direction between the direction of Indra (*aindrī*) and the direction of Kubera (*kauberī*).
Regarding Pāṇini 2.2.27 (*tatra tenedam iti sarūpe*):

when two words of identical form (*sarūpe*) occur—one ending in the locative case within the scope of "grasping" (*grahaṇa*), and the other ending in the instrumental case within the scope of "weapon" (*praharaṇa*)—they are compounded in the sense that "this battle has commenced," provided that a reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*) is to be expressed; this is a *bahuvrīhi*. From the word *iti*, this specific scope is obtained. The suffix *ic* will be stated as the final element of the compound. Because [the form] is read among the *tiṣṭhadgu*-type compounds with the suffix *ac*, it is an *avyayībhāva* and thus indeclinable. The lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*.

Having seized each other by the hair, this battle proceeded; thus, *keśākeśi*. Having struck each other with sticks, this battle proceeded; thus, *daṇḍādaṇḍi*. *Muṣṭīmuṣṭi*. [By] Pāṇini 6.4.146, there is *guṇa* substitution for a *bha*-stem ending in the vowel *u* before a *taddhita* suffix. There is the substitution of *ava* [for *u*]. Thus, *bāhūbāhavi*. Although one could have simply stated *oroḥ*, the mention of *guṇa* is intended to indicate that "a rule conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not universally obligatory" (*anitya*); by this, forms such as *svāyambhuvam* are established. Why does [the sūtra] say "when the members are similar" (*sarūpe*)? [Consider: *halena musalena* ("with a club and a mace").
SK 848: *tena saha* (A 2.2.28).

When expressing equality of connection (*tulyayoga*), the word *saha*, occurring in that sense, is compounded with a word ending in the third case, as previously stated. SK 849: *vopasarjanasya* (A 6.3.82). [The substitution of *sa* for *sa-*] may optionally occur for the word *saha* when it is an *upasarjana*.

The *s* of the word *saha*, when it is a member of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, may optionally become *sa*. For example: *saputraḥ* or *sahaputraḥ āgataḥ* ("he has come with his son"). The rule concerning the expression of simultaneous connection (*tulyayoga*) is generally applicable (*prāyika*). Examples: *sakarmakaḥ* ("having an object"), *salomakaḥ* ("having body hair"). SK 850: *prakṛtyāśiṣi* (A 6.3.83). In expressions of benediction (*āśis*), the word *saha* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). Example: *svasti rājñe sahaputrāya sahāmātyāya* ("May there be prosperity for the king, together with his sons and ministers"). It should be stated that this does not apply to *go*, *vatsa*, and *hala*. Examples: *sagave*, *savatsāya*, *sahalāya*.

SK 851: *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍaj-abahugaṇāt* (A 5.4.73). The suffix *ḍac* shall be applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound that denotes a numeral (*saṃkhyeya*). Examples: *upadaśāḥ* ("nearly ten"). Why "not after *abahu* or *gaṇa*"? Example: *upabahavaḥ* ("nearly many"), *upagaṇāḥ* ("nearly a group"). Here there is a difference in accent (*svara*). For a numeral in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the suffix *ḍac*] must be stated [as an exception]. Example: *nirgatāni triṃśato nistriṃśāni varṣāṇi caitrasya* ("thirty years have passed for Caitra"); *nirgatas triṃśato 'ṅgulibhyo nistriṃśaḥ khaḍgaḥ* ("a sword thirty finger-breadths long"). SK 852: *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac* (A 5.4.113). The suffix *ṣac* is applied after the words *sakthi* and *akṣi* when they denote a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*) within a *bahuvrīhi* compound. [Example: *dīrghasakthaḥ*, *viśālākṣaḥ*].

The genitive case is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). The suffix *ṣac* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *sakthi* or *akṣi* when they denote one's own limbs (*svāṅga*). For example: *dīrghasakthaḥ* ("one whose two thighs are long") and *jalajākṣī* ("one whose eyes are like lotuses"). Why "one's own limbs" (*svāṅgāt*)? [Consider: *dīrghasakthi śakaṭam* ("a cart with long poles") and *sthūlākṣā veṇuyaṣṭiḥ* ("a bamboo staff with thick nodes"). In these cases, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *akṣṇo 'darśanāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.76). Furthermore, the suffix *ac* is applied after *aṅguli* when referring to wood (according to A 5.4.114).

The suffix *ṣac* is added after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *aṅguli* when the meaning is "wood. For example, *pañcāṅgulam dāru* ("wood with five finger-breadths") refers to a wooden measure for scattering grain that has parts resembling fingers. Why say "after a *bahuvrīhi*"? [Consider: *dvyaṅgulā yaṣṭiḥ* ("a staff two fingers long"); here, because it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound expressing a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) sense, the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ*. Why say "when the meaning is wood"? [Consider: *pañcāṅguliḥ hastaḥ* ("a hand with five fingers"). SK 854: After *dvi* and *tri*, the suffix *ṣa* is added to *mūrdhan*. (A 5.4.115)

The suffix *ṣa* (which results in *an*) is applied after the word *mūrdhan* in a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed with these two [words *dvi* and *tri*]. Examples: *dvimūrdhaḥ*, *trimūrdhaḥ*. In the case of the word *netṛ* when referring to a constellation (*nakṣatra*), the suffix *ap* should be stated [as the substitute for *ṣa*]. Examples: those nights of which the deer is the leader are *mṛganetrā rātrayaḥ*; likewise, *puṣyanetrāḥ*. By A 5.4.117, the suffix *ap* is applied after the word *loman* in a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed with the words *antar* and *bahiḥ*. Examples: *antarlomaḥ*, *bahirlomaḥ*.

SK 856: *añ nāsikāyāḥ saṃjñāyāṃ nasaṃ cāsthūlāt* (A 5.4.118). The suffix *ac* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *nāsikā* when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*), and the word *nāsikā* is replaced by *nasa*; however, this does not apply if *sthūla* precedes it. SK 857: *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* (A 8.4.3). [The rule regarding the doubling of a consonant applies] after a word other than *go* that stands as the first member (*pūrvapada*) of a compound, when the compound is a proper name.

After a cause (*nimitta*) situated in the first member of a compound, the *n* of the following [member] becomes *ṇ*, provided it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), but not when there is an intervention by the letter *g*. Example: *druṇasaḥ* ("one whose nose is like a tree"), *svaraṇasaḥ*. Why "not after *aga*"? Example: *ṛgayanam* ("a study of the *ṛc* verses"). In the *Mahābhāṣya*, the mention of *aga* is rejected on the grounds that the rule *aṇṛgayanādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.73) is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) which assumes the absence of *ṇatva*. Why "not after *sthūla*"? Example: *sthūlanāsikaḥ* ("thick-nosed"). After *khura* and *khara*, *nas* optionally becomes *ṇas*: *khuraṇāḥ*, *kharaṇāḥ*. In this case, the suffix *ac* is also desired: *khuraṇasaḥ*, *kharaṇasaḥ*. SK 858: *upasargāc ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.14).

After a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *nāsikā* that begins with a prefix (*prādi*), the suffix *ac* is applied, and *nāsikā* is replaced by *nas*. This rule is stated for the purpose of excluding cases where it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). For example, one whose nose is prominent is *unnasaḥ*. The author of the *Bhāṣya*, having set aside the rule "after a prefix, except when followed by *anot* or *para*" (*upasargād anotparaḥ*), says:
"After a prefix, [the substitution of *nas* for *nāsikā* occurs] diversely" (*upasargād bahulam*). (SK 859)

After a cause that is situated in a prefix (*upasarga*), the *ṇ* of the *nas* [root] may optionally become *ṇ*. For example: *praṇasaḥ*. It should be stated that after the prefix *vi*, there is *g* [in place of the *s*]. For example: one whose nose has departed is *vigraḥ*. And also after *khyā*: *vikhyaḥ*. How then is the Bhaṭṭi [verse] to be explained: *vinasā hatabāndhavā* (BhK 5.8)? It should be explained as "characterized by a departed nose" (*vigatayā nāsikayopalakṣitā*).
SK 860: *suprāta-suśva-sudiva-śāri-kukṣa-caturaśra-eṇīpad-ajapada-proṣṭhapadāḥ* (A 5.4.120). [These are irregularly formed compounds ending in *pada*.]

These are irregularly formed (*nipātana*) *bahuvrīhi* compounds ending in the suffix *-ac*. One whose morning is beautiful is *suprātaḥ*. One whose tomorrow is beautiful is *suśvaḥ*. One whose day is beautiful is *sudivaḥ*. One whose belly is like that of a *śārī* bird is *śārikukṣaḥ*. One whose four corners are [well-formed] is *caturaśraḥ*. One whose feet are like those of a female antelope (*eṇī*) is *eṇīpadaḥ*; likewise, *ajapadaḥ*. A *proṣṭha* is not a cow; one whose feet are like those of such a [beast] is *proṣṭhapadaḥ*. SK 861: After the negative particle *nañ*, and after *duḥ* and *su*, the suffix *-ac* is optionally applied to *halin* and *sakthi*. (A 5.4.121)

There may be [the forms]: *ahalaḥ*, *ahaliḥ*; *asakthaḥ*, *asakthiḥ*. Likewise with *duḥ* and *su*. There is another reading, *śaktyoḥ*: *aśaktaḥ*, *aśaktiḥ*. SK 862: *nityam asic prajāmedhayoḥ* (A 5.4.122). [The suffix] *asic* is applied after *nañ*, *duḥ*, and *su* [before the words *prajā* and *medhā*]. Thus: *aprajaḥ*, *duṣprajaḥ*, *suprajaḥ*; *amedhāḥ*, *durmedhāḥ*, *sumedhāḥ*.

Pāṇini 5.4.124 states: *dharmād anic kevalāt*. The suffix *anic* is applied to a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *dharma*, provided that this word follows an uncompounded (*kevala*) first member. For example: *kalyāṇadharmā* ("one whose nature is auspicious"). Why "uncompounded"? To prevent the application of the suffix in a three-membered *bahuvrīhi* such as *paramaḥ svo dharmo yasya* ("for whom his own dharma is supreme"), because here the word *sva-* is not merely the first member, but is relative due to its intermediate position. However, in cases such as *saṃdigdhasādhyadharmā* ("one whose property to be proven is doubtful"), it is a *bahuvrīhi* with a *karmadhāraya* as its first member; thus, *paramasvadharmā* would likewise be correct.

This is like [the compounds] *nivṛttidharma* ("having the nature of cessation") and *anucchittidharma* ("having the nature of non-annihilation"), where the preceding member is implied by a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Regarding *jambhā suharitatṛṇasomebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini A 5.4.125):

the form *jambha*, having the *samāsānta* suffix applied, is established as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). *Jambha* means "food" and "tooth. *Sujambha* ("having beautiful teeth") is one whose *jambha* is excellent; *haritajambha* ("having green teeth"). *Tṛṇajambha* ("grass-toothed") refers to one for whom grass is food, or one whose teeth are like grass. *Somajambha* ("moon-toothed"). Why [is it not applied] after words beginning with *pati*? For example: *patitajambhaḥ* ("one whose teeth have fallen out").
SK 865 *dakṣiṇermā lubdhayoge* (A 5.4.126):

One whose right side (*dakṣiṇe*) has a wound (*īrma*, i.e., a scar) is called *dakṣiṇermā*, referring to a deer. The meaning is: "one who has been wounded by a hunter. SK 866 *ic karmavyatihāre* (A 5.4.127).

The suffix *ic* shall be applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) after that *bahuvrīhi* which involves the mutual striking of actions (*karmavyatihāra*). Examples: *keśākeśi* ("by seizing each other by the hair"), *musalāmusali* ("with clubs against clubs").

By rule A 5.4.128, *dvidaṇḍyādibhyaś ca*: this suffix *ic* shall also be applied for the sake of establishing these forms, even though they do not denote the purpose of the fourth case (*tādarthya*). For the sake of their derivation, the suffix *ic* occurs. An instrument of attack in which two sticks are used is *dvidaṇḍi-praharaṇam*. Similarly: *dvimusali*, *ubhāhasti*, *ubhayāhasti*.

SK 868 *prasaṃbhyāṃ jānunor jñuḥ* (A 5.4.129): When these two [prefixes] precede, the word *jānu* undergoes the substitution of *jñu* in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For example: one whose knees are extended is *prajñuḥ*; *saṃjñuḥ*. SK 869 *ūrdhvādivibhāṣā* (A 5.4.130): [The substitution of *jñu* for *jānu* occurs] optionally when preceded by *ūrdhva*, etc.
*ūrdhvajñuḥ* / *ūrdhvajānuḥ*. According to Pāṇini 5.4.132 (*dhanuṣaś ca*), the word-final *dhanus* in a bahuvrīhi compound undergoes the substitution of *anaṅ*. Example: *śārṅgadhanvā*.
Or [the substitution of *an* for *a*] occurs before a word denoting a name:
*śatadhanvā* or *śatadhanuḥ*. The suffix *niṅ* is substituted for the final vowel of *jāyā*: *jāniḥ*.

In place of the word *jāyā* at the end of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there shall be the substitution of *niṅ*. By the rule *lopo vyor vali* (A 6.1.66), there is the elision of the phonemes *v* and *y* before a *val* suffix. There is also the application of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment). Thus, "one whose wife (*jāyā*) is a young woman (*yuvatī*)" is *yuvajāniḥ*.

SK 874 *gandhasyedutpūtisusurabhibhyaḥ* (A 5.4.135): After these [words], the substitute *ik* is applied to the end of the word *gandha*. Examples: *udgandhiḥ*, *pūtigandhiḥ*, *sugandhiḥ*, *surabhigandhiḥ*. Regarding the substitution of *it* for *gandha*, there is the requirement that it be "exclusive" (*ekānta*). The meaning of "exclusive" is that it is perceived as if it were a single part (*ekadeśa*), without being divided. Examples: *sugandhi puṣpaṃ salilaṃ ca* ("fragrant flower and water"); *sugandhir vāyuḥ* ("fragrant wind"). It is not the case here in: *śobhanā gandhā dravyāṇy asya sugandha āpaṇikaḥ* ("this merchant has beautiful fragrances as his goods; he is a 'sugandha' merchant"). SK 875 *alpākhyāyām* (A 5.4.136): [The suffix *kan* is added after *gandha*] when expressing a small amount.

That food in which there is even a trace of the smell of soup is called *sūpagandhi*; likewise, *ghṛtagandhi*. According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *gandha* [is used] in the senses of fragrance, a trace, connection, and pride.
[Furthermore, by the rule] *upamānāc ca* (A 5.4.137): that which has a smell like a lotus is *padmagandhi*.

SK 877: *pādasya lopo ’hastyādibhyaḥ* (A 5.4.138). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the word *pāda* when it follows a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), provided that [the comparison] is not from the class beginning with *hastin*. This is a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) by way of substitution (*sthānin*). Example: one whose feet are like those of a tiger is *vyāghrapāt*. Why "not from *hastin* and so on"? Example: *hastipādaḥ* (elephant-footed), *kusūlapādaḥ* (granary-footed). SK 878: *kumbhapadīṣu ca* (A 5.4.139). [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a word ending in *pāda*] in the case of [words such as] *kumbhapadī* and others.

In the case of *kumbhapadī* and similar forms, the elision of *pāda* and the suffix *ṅīp* are prescribed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) when the feminine gender is intended; [the rule] *pādaḥ pat* [applies]. *Kumbhapadī*. Why "in the feminine"? [Answer: *kumbhapādaḥ*. (Pāṇini 5.4.139) In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there shall be elision of *pāda*, as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*), when it is preceded by a numeral or the word *su*. *Dvipāt*. *Supāt*.

SK 880 *vayasi dantasya datṛ* (A 5.4.141): For the word *danta*, the substitute *datṛ* shall occur when age (*vayas*) is indicated, provided that it is preceded by a numeral or the word *su*. Examples: *dvidan* ("two-toothed"), *caturdan* ("four-toothed"), *ṣoḍan* ("six-toothed" [from *ṣaṣ*]), *sudat* ("having beautiful teeth"). Regarding feminine forms: *sudatī*. Why "when age is indicated"? [Counter-examples: *dvidantaḥ karī* ("a two-toothed elephant"), *sudantaḥ* ("having beautiful teeth"). SK 881 *striyāṃ saṃjñāyām* (A 5.4.143).

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *datṛ* is substituted for *danta* as a final member of the compound. Examples: *ayodatī* ("having iron teeth"), *phāladatī* ("having plough-shaped teeth"). Why "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*)? Consider *samadantī* ("having even teeth").

SK 882: *vibhāṣā śyāvārokābhyām* (A 5.4.144). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, *datṛ* is optionally substituted for *danta* after the words *śyāva* and *aroka*. Examples: *śyāvadan* or *śyāvadantaḥ* ("having dark teeth"); *arokadan* or *arokadantaḥ* ("having lusterless teeth").

SK 883: *agrānta-śuddha-śubhra-vṛṣa-varāhebhyaś ca* (A 5.4.145). After these [words], the substitution of *datṛ* for *danta* is optional: *kuḍmalāgradan* or *kuḍmalāgradantaḥ*. SK 884: *kakudasyāvasthāyāṃ lopaḥ* (A 5.4.146). In the sense of a particular state (*avasthā*), there is the elision (*lopa*) of the word *kakuda*.
*ajātakakut* (one whose hump has not yet appeared), *pūrṇakakut* (one whose hump is full).

According to Pāṇini 5.4.147 (*trikakutpūrvate*), the form *trikakud* is derived from *trīṇi kakudāny asya* ("he who has three humps"). This is a proper name for a specific mountain; any other [being] with three humps is simply called *trikakuda*.

SK 886: After the prefixes *ud-* and *vi-*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the word *kākuda*. Examples: *utkākut* and *vikākut*. *Kākuda* refers to the palate (*tālu*). SK 887: After the prefix *pūrṇa-*, the elision is optional (*vibhāṣā*).

*pūrṇakākut*, *pūrṇakākudaḥ*. SK 888: *suhṛddurhṛdau mitrāmitrayoḥ* (A 5.4.150). When preceded by *su-* and *dur-*, the substitution of *hṛt* for *hṛdaya* is prescribed as a nipātana. *Suhṛt* means a friend; *durhṛt* means an enemy. In other cases, one says *suhṛdayaḥ* and *durhṛdayaḥ*.

SK 889: *uraḥ-prabhṛtibhyaḥ kap* (A 5.4.141). [The suffix] *kap* is added after words beginning with *uras*. Examples: *vyūḍhoraskaḥ* (one with broad chest), *priyasarpiṣkaḥ* (one fond of ghee). Here, words such as *pumān*, *anaḍvān*, *payaḥ*, *nauḥ*, and *lakṣmīḥ* are listed in their singular forms. However, when they appear in dual or plural forms, the suffix *kap* is applied optionally according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. Examples: *dvipumān* or *dvipuṃskaḥ* (two men). [SK 889 continued: After the word *artha*, [the suffix *kap* is added] after the negative particle *nañ*. Example: *anarthakam* (meaningless). Why "after *nañ*"? [Counter-example: *apārtham* or *apārthakam* (pointless). SK 890: *inaḥ striyām* (A 5.4.152). [The suffix *kap* is added] after a word ending in *in* when it denotes a feminine. Example: *bahuvṛtrahāṇī senā* (an army that has slain many Vṛtras). Why "when denoting a feminine"? [Counter-example: *bahuvṛtrahā senā* (an army that has slain many Vṛtras). Why "after *in*"? The city is *bahudaṇḍikā*. The rules regarding the inclusion of the suffixes *ini*, *na*, *as*, *man*, and *g* apply to a formation ending in those suffixes, whether they are meaningful or meaningless. Thus we have *bahuvāggmikā*. Why "in the feminine"? [Consider] *bahudaṇḍī*; *bahudaṇḍikaḥ* refers to a village. SK 891: *śeṣād vibhāṣā* (A 5.4.154).

The suffix *kap* may optionally be added to a *bahuvrīhi* compound that falls under the scope of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) rule and for which no other *samāsānta* suffix has been prescribed. Examples: *mahāyaśaskaḥ* or *mahāyaśāḥ*. Why is it said "for which no other [suffix] has been prescribed," etc.? Consider: *vyāghrapāt*, *sugandhiḥ*, *priyapathaḥ* (which take specific suffixes). Why "falling under the scope of the remainder rule"? Consider: *upabahavaḥ*, *uttrapūrvā*, *saputraḥ* (which do not fall under the *śeṣa* category). The word *śeṣa* here, by virtue of its technical application, refers to two meanings. SK 892: *āpo 'nyatarasyām* (A 7.4.15).
When the suffix *kap* follows, the final vowel *ā* of a stem ending in *āp* may optionally be shortened. Examples: *bahumālākaḥ* or *bahumālakaḥ*; but in the absence of *kap*, it is *bahumālaḥ*.

SK 893: *na saṃjñāyām* (A 5.4.143). The suffix *kap*, which would otherwise apply by the rule *śeṣāt* [A 5.4.154], shall not occur when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Example: *viśve devā asya* → *viśvedevaḥ*.
SK 894: *īyasaś ca* (A 5.4.146). [The suffix *kap* is also prohibited after a word ending in the comparative suffix *īyas*.]

The suffix *kap* is not added after a word ending in a comparative suffix (*īyasun*) as the final member [of a bahuvrīhi]. For example: *bahuśreyaḥ* ("one who has many superiors"). When the rule "of the feminine *go* and a feminine noun" (*gostriyoḥ*) would require shortening of the vowel, it is stated: "In a bahuvrīhi containing a comparative suffix, [shortening] does not occur. For example: *bahuśreyasī* ("one who has many superior women"). Why specify "in a bahuvrīhi"? Consider: *atiśreyasiḥ* ("one who has an excellent superior"). [Also: *vandine bhrātuḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.147).

The suffix *kap* is not applied after a word ending in *bhrātṛ* when that word denotes something praised (*pūjita*). For example, one whose brother is praised is called *praśastabhrātā*. It will be stated later that the prohibition "not after a word denoting praise" (*na pūjanāt*) applies only prior to the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ* (A 5.4.113). Why say "when praised"? [Consider: *mūrkhabhrātṛkaḥ* ("one who has a foolish brother"). SK 896: *nāḍītantryoḥ svāṅge* (A 5.4.159). [The suffix *kap* is optionally applied after *nāḍī* and *tantrī* when they denote a part of the body.]

The suffix *kap* shall not be applied after the words *nāḍī* and *tantrī* when they denote parts of one's own body (*svāṅga*). *bahunāḍiḥ kāyaḥ* ("a body with many veins"); *bahutantrīr grīvā* ("a neck with many strings"). Since *tantrī* means "artery" (*dhamanī*), the vowel is not shortened because it does not end in a feminine suffix. Why "parts of one's own body"? [Counter-examples: *bahunāḍīkaḥ stambhaḥ* ("a pillar with many tubes"); *bahutastrīkā vīṇā* ("a lute with many strings"). SK 897: *niṣpravāṇiś ca* (A 5.4.160). Here, the absence of *kap* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). From the root *ve* preceded by *pra*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied: *pravāṇī* means "the shuttle of a weaver. *Niṣpravāṇiḥ paṭaḥ* ("a cloth whose shuttle has been removed") means a cloth that has finished being woven; it means "new."

Pāṇini 2.2.37 (*saptamīviśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau*): In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that which ends in the seventh case (*saptamī*) and that which is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) should be placed first. Examples: *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("one whose throat is black," i.e., Śiva). Precisely because of this [rule] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), there exists a *bahuvrīhi* with non-co-referential members (*vyadhikaraṇapada*). Examples: *citraguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows") and *dviśuklaḥ* ("twice white"). When these two [types of qualifiers] are compounded with each other, the numeral comes first, by virtue of the "prohibition of the subsequent" (*śabdaparavipratiṣedha*). Example: *dvyanyaḥ* ("other than two"). [In the case of a numeral followed by another numeral,] the smaller numeral comes first: *dvitrāḥ* ("two or three"). This also applies in a *dvandva* compound: *dvādaśa* ("twelve"). Optionally, the word *priya* may come first: *guḍapriyaḥ* ("fond of molasses") or *priyaguḍaḥ*. In the case of words beginning with *gaḍu*, the seventh-case member comes last: *gaḍukaṇṭhaḥ* ("one with a goiter on the neck").
In some cases, it is not so; for example, *vahegaḍuḥ*. SK 899: *niṣṭhā* (A 2.2.36).

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that which ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix should stand first. Examples: *kṛtakṛtyaḥ* ("one who has accomplished his task"). It should be stated that a *niṣṭhā* suffix follows words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth. Examples: *sāraṅgajagdhī* ("eaten by a deer"), *māsajātā* ("born after a month"), *sukhajātā* ("born in happiness"). However, this is only a general rule (*prāyika*). Counter-examples include *kṛtakaṭaḥ* ("one who has made a mat") and *pīnodakaḥ* ("one whose water is abundant").

SK 900: In the group beginning with *āhitāgni* (Pāṇini 2.2.37), we have *āhitāgniḥ* ("one who has established the sacred fires") and *agnyāhitaḥ*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). When words meaning "a weapon" precede, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) and the locative case (*saptamī*) follow: *abhyudyataḥ* ("with a raised weapon") and *daṇḍapāṇiḥ* ("staff-in-hand"). In some cases, this does not occur: *vivṛtāmiḥ* ("with the fire uncovered"). Thus ends the section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds.
Chapter 20: On Dvandva Compounds.

SK 901: *cārthe dvandvaḥ* (A 2.2.29). Several *sub*-ending words occurring in the sense of *ca* (*cārthe*) may be compounded; that is a *dvandva*. The meanings of *ca* are: conjunction (*samuccaya*), sequential mention (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), and collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). Conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the connection of several things, independent of one another, with a single [action]. Sequential mention (*anvācaya*) occurs when one of them is subordinate (*anuṣaṅgikatva*). Mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*) is the connection of things joined together. Collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) is a collection. Among these, in the case of conjunction, as in "Worship both the Lord and the Teacher" (*īśvaraṃ guruṃ ca bhajasva*).

In the case of *anvācaya* (conjunction), there is no compound in such expressions as *bhikṣām aṭa gāṃ cānaya* ("Go for alms and bring the cow"), because of a lack of semantic fitness (*asāmarthya*). Examples include *dhavakhadirau* ("the Dhava and Khadira trees"), *saṃjñāparibhāṣam* ("technical terms and rules of interpretation"), and *hotṛpotṛneṣṭodgātāraḥ* ("the Hotṛ, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Udgātṛ priests")—this last being formed by the mention of "many" [in Pāṇini’s rule]. However, if one first forms a *dvandva* compound of each pair and then forms a final *dvandva*, the result is *hotāpotāneṣṭodgātāraḥ*. According to A 2.2.31, *rājadantādiṣu param*, in the *rājadanta*-type group, the subsequent member [is placed first].

Among these, that which is most worthy of priority [should stand first]. *Rājadantaḥ* ("the king of teeth") means the front tooth; there is no fixed rule regarding words such as *dharma* and the like: *arthadharmau* or *dharmārthau*; *dampatī*, *jampatī*, or *jāyāpatī*. The substitution of *jam* for the word *jāyā* (wife) or its substitution by *dam* is optionally prescribed. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). SK 903: *dvandve ghi* (A 2.2.32).

In a *dvandva* compound, that which bears the designation *ghi* (ending in short *i* or *u*, or ending in long *ī* or *ū*) should stand first. For example: *hariś ca haraś ca* → *hariharau*. When several [words] could potentially occupy the first position, the restriction applies to one specific case, while there is no restriction in the remaining cases: *hariguruharāḥ* or *hariharaguravaḥ*.

SK 904 *ajādyadantam* (A 2.2.33): In a *dvandva* compound, this [member] beginning with a vowel other than *a* and ending in *a* should stand first. For example: *īśakṛṣṇau* (Īśa and Kṛṣṇa). When there are many members, there is no fixed rule: *aśvarathendrāḥ* (horse, chariot, Indra) or *indrāśvarathāḥ* (Indra, horse, chariot). A member ending in *dhi* takes precedence over one beginning with a vowel other than *a* and ending in *a*, by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*): *indrāgnī* (Indra and Agni). SK 905 *alpāctaram* (A 2.2.34): That which has fewer syllables should stand first.

Śiva and Keśava; [the names of] the seasons and the lunar mansions, when they have the same number of syllables, are placed in their natural order: *hemanta-śiśira-vasantāḥ* (winter, cool season, spring); *kṛttikā-rohiṇyau* (Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī). Why "of equal syllables"? [Answer: *grīṣma-vasantau* (summer and spring). That which has fewer syllables comes first: *kuśa-kāśam* (Kuśa grass and Kāśa grass). And that which is more venerable comes first: *tāpasa-parvatau* (the ascetic and the mountain). [The names of] the social classes (*varṇa*) are placed in their natural order: *brāhmaṇa-kṣatriya-viṭ-śūdrāḥ* (Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras). [The name] of the elder brother [comes first]: *yudhiṣṭhira-arjunau* (Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna). SK 906: A *dvandva* compound consisting of parts of living beings, musical instruments, or an army is singular. (A 2.4.2)

The *dvandva* compound of these [members] shall be treated as a singular. Examples: *pāṇipādam* (hand and foot), *mārdaṅgikapāṇavikam* (the drummers and the lute-players), *rathikāśvāroham* (the charioteers and the horsemen). Since the singularity is already established by the fact that the collective (*samāhāra*) is one, this section is for the purpose of restriction: so that for parts of living beings and the like, it may be used only in the sense of a collective. SK 907: *anuvāde caraṇānām* (A 2.4.3). The *dvandva* compound of Vedic schools (*caraṇa*) shall be treated as a singular when there is a restatement of something already established. It should be stated: "after the roots *sthā* and *i*, when *luṅ* follows. Examples: *udagāt kaṭhakālāpam* (the Kaṭha and Kālāpa schools have emerged), *pratyaṣṭhāt kaṭhakauthumam* (the Kaṭha and Kauthuma schools have been established).

SK 908: *adhvaryukraturanapuṃsakam* (A 2.4.4). A *dvandva* compound consisting of words denoting sacrifices (*kratu*) prescribed in the Yajurveda that are not neuter in gender shall be singular. Example: *arkāśvamedham*. Why "sacrifice prescribed by the Adhvaryu"? [Consider: *iṣuvajrau*, which are prescribed in the Sāmaveda. Why "not neuter"? [Consider: *rājasūyavājapeye*. [The rule applies to] *ardharcādi* [words]. SK 909: *adhyayanato 'viprakṛṣṭākhyānām* (A 2.4.5). [A *dvandva* compound] consisting of names of those who are not separated [in space] based on their study [of the same Veda shall be singular].

Those whose names are closely associated with the study [of the Veda] form a *dvandva* compound that is treated as singular. *Padaka-kramakam*. SK 910: *Jātir aprāṇinām* (A 2.4.6). A *dvandva* compound consisting of words denoting classes (*jāti*) of non-living things is treated as singular. Example: *dhānā-śaṣkulī* (fried grain and fried cakes). However, for living beings, it is not so; e.g., *viṭ-śūdrau* (the Vaiśya and the Śūdra). This applies only to classes of substances (*dravya-jāti*). It does not apply here: *rūpa-rasau* (color and taste), or *gamana-ākuñcane* (going and contracting). This singular treatment occurs only when the class (*jāti*) is predominant. But when there is an intention to express specific individual substances (*dravya-viśeṣa*), it is plural: *badarāmalakāni* (jujube fruits and myrobalans).

SK 911: *viśiṣṭaliṅgo nadīdeśo ’grāmāḥ* (A 2.4.7). In a collective *dvandva* compound, words denoting rivers or regions that have different genders—provided they do not denote villages—shall be singular. For example: *uddhyā ca irāvatī ca* → *uddhyerāvati*; *gaṅgā ca śoṇaś ca* → *gaṅgāśoṇam*; *kuravaś ca kurukṣetraṃ ca* → *kurukurukṣetram*. Why "having different genders"? [Counter-example: *gaṅgāyamune* (both feminine); *madrakekayāḥ* (masculine). Why "not villages"? [Counter-examples: *jāmbavaṃ nagaram* (a city); *śālūkinī grāmaḥ* (a village); *jāmbavaśālūjinyau* (a city and a village, both singular). SK 912: *kṣudrajantavaḥ* (A 2.4.8). [Words denoting] small creatures [form a singular collective *dvandva*].

In the case of their collective grouping (*samāhāra*), a *dvandva* compound shall be treated as singular. Examples: *yūkālikṣam* ("lice and nits"). Creatures smaller than a mongoose (*nakula*) are considered "small animals" (*kṣudrajantu*). According to Pāṇini 2.4.9, "And those that are in eternal enmity," these [small animals] follow the previous rule [of being singular in a *samāhāra-dvandva*]. Examples: *ahinakulam* ("snake and mongoose"), *govyāghram* ("cow and tiger"), *kākolūkam* ("crow and owl"). In such cases, although the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) prescribed by the rule *vṛkṣamṛga-* would otherwise apply due to its subsequent position in the rules, it is set aside by the presence of the particle *ca*.

SK 914: For Śūdras who are not excluded—that is, for Śūdras who have not been cast out—the rule is as before. [The compound] *takṣāyaskāram* [is an example]. However, for those excluded from the company of vessels, such as Caṇḍālas and corpse-carriers, [the rule does not apply]. SK 915: And [the compounds] beginning with *gavāśva* (cow and horse), etc. [are also examples].
So that the words may be correctly pronounced as they are uttered: *gavāśvam*, *dāsīdāsam*, and so forth.
[Pāṇini 2.4.12] The compound of *vṛkṣa*, *mṛga*, *tṛṇa*, *dhānya*, *vyañjana*, *paśu*, *śakuni*, *aśva-vaḍavā*, and *pūrva-apara-adharottara* is optional (vibhāṣā).

There is an optional *dvandva* (copulative compound) for the seven beginning with "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), as well as for the three *dvandvas* beginning with "horse and mare" (*aśvavaḍavā*), according to the previous rule. In the case of the [seven] beginning with "tree," only specific varieties are included. Examples: *plakṣanyagrodham* / *plakṣanyagrodhāḥ* (the *Plakṣa* and *Nyagrodha* trees). *rurupṛṣatam* / *rurupṛṣatāḥ* (the *Ruru* and *Pṛṣata* deer). *kuśakāśam* / *kuśakāśāḥ* (the *Kuśa* and *Kāśa* grasses). *vrīhiyavam* / *vrīhiyavāḥ* (rice and barley). *dadhighṛtam* / *dadhighṛte* (curd and ghee). *gomahiṣam* / *gomahiṣāḥ* (cows and buffaloes). *śukabakam* / *śukabakāḥ* (parrots and cranes). *aśvavaḍavam* / *aśvavaḍavau* (horses and mares). *pūrvāparam* (the former and the latter).

The compounds *pūrvāpara*, *adharottara*, and *adharottare* are established as exceptions. It should be stated that a *dvandva* compound consisting of multiple members remains singular when it denotes fruits, armies, parts of the body, trees, wild animals, birds, small creatures, darkness, or grass. For example: *badarāṇi cāmalakāni ca* (jujubes and myrobalans) becomes *badarāmalakam*. This singularity occurs by the rule "a genus [denoting] non-living things" (*jātir aprāṇinām*). However, it does not apply here: *badarāmalake* (the jujube and the myrobalan), *rathikāśvārohau* (the charioteer and the horseman), *plakṣanyagrodhau* (the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha* tree), and so forth.

In the *Vibhāṣāvṛtti*, regarding the rule "the term *jāti* [is used] for non-living beings" (*aprāṇinām*), the mention of those that are not living beings serves to provide an option where a compulsory application would otherwise have occurred. The mention of "animals" (*paśu*) is for the purpose of restricting the case where a compulsory application would have occurred for elephants, horses, and so forth, because they are parts of an army (*senāṅga*). The mention of "wild animals" (*mṛga*) and "birds" (*śakuni*) is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): that a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of wild animals must be formed with wild animals alone, and of birds with birds alone; whereas with others, there is only mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). The same applies to the expression "prior and posterior," "lower and upper."

The mention of *aśva-vaḍavau* is for the purpose of ensuring the neuter gender in certain cases; otherwise, due to its higher status [in the order of rules], it would result in the form *pūrvavad-aśvavaḍavau*. (SK 917) And that which expresses a contradiction does not denote a substratum (*anadhikaraṇavācin*). (A 2.4.13)

A *dvandva* compound consisting of words with contradictory meanings that do not denote substances may optionally be singular. Examples are *śītoṣṇam* (cold and heat) or *śītoṣṇe* (cold and heat). This rule is intended as a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the optional *samāhāra-dvandva* obtained by the sūtra *cārthe dvandvaḥ*: if such a *dvandva* occurs for words with contradictory meanings, it must be only for those that do not denote substances. Consequently, for words denoting substances, there is only the *itaretarayoga* (mutual connection) type. Example: *śītoṣṇe udake staḥ* (cold and heat exist in the water). What is meant by "contradictory" (*vipratiṣiddha*)? *Nandakapāñcajanyau* (the sword Nandaka and the conch Pāñcajanya)—here the optional *samāhāra-dvandva* certainly does occur.

SK 918: And *dadhi-payas* and so forth do not take the singular ending (*naikavat*). Examples: *dadhipayasī* (curd and milk), *idhmābarhiṣī* (fuel and sacrificial grass); [in these] the long vowel [of the first member] occurs by way of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*). [Also: *ṛksāme* (Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda), *vāṅmanase* (speech and mind). SK 919: And [the singular is used] when the sense is that of a collective locus (*adhikaraṇa-etāvatva*).

If the number of substances were understood [from the compound], there would be no restriction that it must always be in the singular, as in "ten teeth-and-lips" (*daśa dantoṣṭhāḥ*). According to A 2.4.16, *vibhāṣā samīpe* ("optionally when near"), there might instead be a restriction such that when the quantity of the substratum is determined by proximity, it must be a collective compound (*samāhāra*) alone, as in "near ten teeth-and-lips" (*upadaśaṃ dantoṣṭham*) or "nine or eleven teeth-and-lips" (*upadaśā dantoṣṭhāḥ*).

SK 921 *ānaṅ ṛto dvandve* (A 6.3.25): In a *dvandva* compound, for words ending in *ṛt* that denote a relationship based on knowledge (*vidyā*) or biological origin (*yoni*), the substitution *ānaṅ* occurs when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *hotā-potārau* (the Hotṛ and Potṛ priests); *hotṛ-potṛ-neṣṭṛ-udgātāraḥ* (the Hotṛ, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Udgātṛ priests); *mātā-pitarau* (mother and father). SK 922 *devatādvandve ca* (A 6.3.26): And [the substitution *ānaṅ* occurs] in a *dvandva* compound of deities.

In this context, when the following word begins with *uttara-pada*, the substitution *ānaṅ* occurs [for the final vowel and consonant of the preceding member]. Examples: *mitrāvaruṇau*. There is a prohibition when the word *vāyu* is employed: *agnivāyū*, *vāyvagnī*. The repetition of the term "dvandva" (copulative compound) is for the purpose of including only those whose association is well-known (*prasiddha-sāhacarya*). Therefore, in cases such as *brahmaprajāpatī*, there is no *ānaṅ* substitution; for this [pair] is neither heard in the Veda as sharing a single sacrificial oblation (*eka-havis-bhāgitva*) nor is their association well-known in common worldly usage. [Regarding the rule] *īd-agneḥ soma-varuṇayoḥ* (A 6.3.27): [The substitution of] *īt* for the final vowel of *agni* occurs before *soma* and *varuṇa* in a dvandva of deities (*devatā-dvandve*). SK 924 *agneḥ stutstomasomāḥ* (A 8.3.82): In a compound, the *s* of these words following *agni* becomes *ṣ*. Examples: *agniṣṭut*, *agniṣṭomaḥ*, *agnīṣomau*, *agnīvaruṇau*. SK 925 *idvṛddhau* (A 6.3.28): [The substitute *iṭ* is applied] when there is *vṛddhi*.

When the second member of a *devatā-dvandva* compound has a *vṛddhi*-strengthened vowel, the word *agni* undergoes the substitution of *id*. For example: *agnāmarutau devate asya* [these two, Agni and Marut, are its deities] results in *āgnimārutam karma* [the rite dedicated to Agni and Marut]; *agnīvaruṇau devate asya* [these two, Agni and Varuṇa, are its deities] results in *āgnivāruṇam*. In the case of a *devatā-dvandva*, there is *vṛddhi* strengthening of both members by the rule *devatādvandve ca*. In the unformed (*alaukika*) sentence, the substitution of *ānaṅ* and the change to the long *ī* are superseded by this rule. Why "when there is *vṛddhi*"? Consider *āgnendraḥ*; here, by the rule *nendrasya parasya*, the *vṛddhi* of the second member is prohibited. It does not apply when *viṣṇu* follows: *āgnāvaiṣṇavam*. (Pāṇini 6.3.29) *divo dyāvā* [the word *div* becomes *dyāvā*].

In a *devatā-dvandva* compound, when the second member (*uttarapada*) follows, [the form is as follows]: *dyāvābhūmī*, *dyāvākṣāmā*. Because of the particle *ca*, *dyāvā* is also included. The vowel *a* is pronounced in this substitute (*ādeśa*) so that the *s* does not undergo the change to *r* (*rutva*). Thus: *dyauś ca pṛthivī ca* becomes *divas pṛthivyau*, and then *dyāvāpṛthivyau*. In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), one follows the forms as they are observed. As in *dyāvā cidasmai pṛthivī*; and in *divaspṛthivyor aratim*, the makers of the *pada-pāṭha* read the visarga (*visargaṃ paṭhanti*).

*Mātāpitarau* ("mother and father"). Why [specify] "of the northerners"? [Because otherwise it would be *mātāpitarau*]. SK 930: *dvandvāc cudaṣahāntāt samāhāre* (A 5.4.106).

The suffix *ṭac* shall be added after a *dvandva* compound ending in *c*, *ṣ*, or *h*, when it denotes a collective (*samāhāra*). Examples: *vāk ca tvak ca* → *vāktvacam*; *tvaksrajam*; *śamīdṛṣadam*; *vāktviṣam*; *chatropānaham*. Why "when denoting a collective"? [Counter-example: *prāvṛṭśaradau* ("the rainy season and autumn").
Thus ends the section on copulative compounds (*dvandva*).

Now, the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one): [Pāṇini 1.2.64] "Of those that have the same form (*sarūpa*)—[the singular remains]. For example: *rāmau*, *rāmāḥ*. [Also: "Of those that have different forms (*virūpa*) but the same meaning. For example: *vakradaṇḍaś ca kuṭiladaṇḍaś ca* results in *vakradaṇḍau* or *kuṭiladaṇḍau*. [A 1.2.65] "When an elder (*vṛddha*) is mentioned together with a youth (*yuvan*), if the difference between them consists solely of that [suffix], the term denoting the elder lineage (*gotra*) is retained. When a youth is mentioned in conjunction with [an elder], the word expressing the *gotra* is retained, provided that the entire disparity between the two consists only of the suffixes denoting the *gotra* and the youth. For example: *gārgyaś ca gārgyāyaṇaś ca* results in *gārgyau*. Why "elder" (*vṛddha*)? [Counter-example: *bhāgavittibhāgavittikau*. Why "entire" (*kṛtsna*)? [Counter-example: *gārgyavātsyāyanau*.

SK 932 *strī puṃvac ca* (A 1.2.66): When a feminine and a masculine [term] are mentioned together with a youth (*yuvan*), the feminine term that denotes an elder (*vṛddha*) remains, and its meaning is treated like the masculine. For example, *gārgī* and *gārgyāyaṇau* become *gargāḥ*. While the rule *astriyām* ("not when feminine") is being carried over, the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* are elided by *yaññoś ca*. Thus, *dākṣī* and *dākṣāyaṇaḥ* become *dākṣī*. SK 933 *pumān striyā* (A 1.2.67): When a masculine and a feminine [term] are mentioned together, the masculine remains.

When a male and a female are mentioned together, the male alone remains, provided that the specific characteristic of the male applies to both. For example: *haṃsī ca haṃsaś ca* (the female swan and the male swan) results in *haṃsau*.
According to A 1.2.68, *bhrātṛputrau svamṛduhitṛbhyām*:
*bhrātā ca svasā ca* (brother and sister) results in *bhrātarau*; *putraś ca duhitā ca* (son and daughter) results in *putrau*.

Pāṇini A 1.2.69: *napuṃsakam anapuṃsakenaikavac cāsyānyatarasyām*. When a neuter noun is mentioned together with a non-neuter noun, the neuter remains; and it may optionally be treated as a singular, provided that the distinction between them is based solely on their grammatical gender. Examples: *śuklaḥ paṭaḥ* (a white cloth), *śuklā śāṭī* (a white garment), *śuklaṃ vastram* (a white cloth); *tad idaṃ śuklam* (this is white), *tānīmāni śuklāni* (these are white). Pāṇini A 1.2.70: *pitā mātrā*. [The word *pitṛ* remains when in co-utterance with *mātṛ*.]

When mentioned together with the mother, the father may optionally remain [as the sole survivor]. *Mātā ca pitā ca* becomes *pitarau* or *mātāpitarau*. (Pāṇini 1.2.71) When mentioned together with the mother-in-law, the father-in-law may optionally remain [as the sole survivor], provided that there is no distinction in their respective characteristics. *Śvaśrūś ca śvaśuraś ca* becomes *śvaśurau* or *śvaśrūśvaśurau*.

SK 938: *tyadādīni sarvair nityam* (A 1.2.72). When there is a co-utterance (*sahokti*) with all [other words], those beginning with *tyad* are always retained. For example: *sa ca devadattaś ca tau* ("He and Devadatta—those two"). When those beginning with *tyad* are co-uttered with one another, that which follows is retained. For example: *sa ca yaś ca yau* ("He and who—those two"). The *Mahābhāṣya* states: "The retention of the preceding is also observed. For example: *sa ca yaś ca tau*. Regarding the gender and number [of the remainder]: after those beginning with *tyad*, the gender and number follow the masculine or neuter [precedent]. For example: *sā ca devadattaś ca tau* ("She and Devadatta—those two"); *tac ca devadattaś ca yajñadattaś ca tāni* ("That and Devadatta and Yajñadatta—those").

However, between a masculine and a neuter [word], the neuter remains because it is subsequent [in the order of listing]. And that [is the case for] *devadattaś ca te* ("Devadatta and she"). It should be stated: "This does not apply to *dvandva*s, *tatpuruṣa*s, or qualifiers. [Examples: *kukkuṭamayūryāv ime* ("this rooster and peahen"); *mayūrīkukkuṭav imau* ("this peahen and rooster"). *tac ca sā ca ardhapiṣpalyau te* ("that and she are two half-pepper-corns").
A feminine [word] remains in a group of domestic animals when they are not young (A 1.2.73).

Among these, when there is a desire to express them together, the feminine remains; this is an exception to the rule *pumān striyā* ("the masculine [remains] after the feminine"). Example: *imā gāvaḥ* ("these cows"). Why say "domestic animals" (*grāmya*)? Example: *ime ruravaḥ* ("these ruru deer"). Why include the term "animals" (*paśu*)? Example: *brāhmaṇāḥ* ("Brahmins"). Why say "in groups" (*saṅgheṣu*)? Example: *etau gāvau* ("these two cows"). Why say "not young" (*ataraṇeṣu*)? Example: *ime vatsāḥ* ("these calves"). It should be stated that this applies to "those with non-divided hooves" (*anekaśapheṣu*). Example: *ime aśvāḥ* ("these horses"). In all these cases, once the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) has been applied, a *dvandva* (copulative compound) does not occur because there is no longer more than one inflected word (*subanta*).

Therefore, in cases such as *śirasī* and *śirāṃsi*, the final udātta accent prescribed by the rule *samāsasya* does not apply, nor does the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) occur because these are parts of living beings. In cases such as *panthānau* and *panthānaḥ*, the suffix added at the end of a compound (*samāsānta*) does not occur.
Thus ends the section on *ekaśeṣa*.
Chapter 22: The Section on the Remainder of All Compound Formations (Sarvasamāsaśeṣaprakaraṇa)

There are five types of *vṛtti* (grammatical formations): nominal derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), elliptical formations (*ekaśeṣa*), and verbal formations with prefixes and suffixes (*sanādyanta-dhātu*). *Vṛtti* is the expression of a meaning for the sake of another [word]. A sentence (*vākya*) that expresses the meaning of a *vṛtti* is an analysis (*vigraha*). It is of two kinds: worldly (*laukika*) and non-worldly (*alaukika*). That which is grammatically correct (*sādhu*) because it is fully established is worldly; that which is unfit for usage and is incorrect (*asādhu*) is non-worldly. For example: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s man); [its non-worldly analysis is] *rājan as*, *puruṣa su*. An analysis-less compound is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), or one whose analysis is not in its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*).

The statement that "compounds are of four kinds" is merely a general rule (*prāyovāda*), because compounds are prescribed even for those elements outside the governing rules (*adhikāra*) for *avyayībhāva*, *tatpuruṣa*, *bahuvrīhi*, and *dvandva* by the rule *saha supā*. Furthermore, the traditional assertion of the ancients—that "the *avyayībhāva* is predominant in the meaning of the first member; the *tatpuruṣa* is predominant in the meaning of the final member; the *bahuvrīhi* is predominant in the meaning of a word other than the members; and the *dvandva* is predominant in the meaning of both members"—is likewise a general intention (*prāyo'bhiprāya*).

Because [the suffix *samāsānta*] is absent in the avyayībhāva compound such as *sūpaprati unmattagaṅgam*, in the tatpuruṣa compounds beginning with *atimāla*, in the bahuvrīhi compounds such as *dvitrāḥ*, and in the dvandva compounds such as *dantoṣṭham*. A *karmadhāraya* is a specific type of *tatpuruṣa*; a *dvigu* is a specific type of that [karmadhāraya]. Multitude of words (*anekapadatva*) occurs only in *dvandva* and *bahuvrīhi* compounds; it was stated that for the *tatpuruṣa*, it occurs only in certain instances. Furthermore: [The rule] "of *sup*s with *sup*, with *tiṅ*, with a noun (*nāman*), or with a verbal root (*dhātu*)," and "of *tiṅ*s with *tiṅ*."

It should be understood that compounds ending in *sub*-suffixes are known by the wise to be of six kinds: 1. *Sub* with *sub*: *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man). 2. With a *tiṅ* (verbal suffix): *paryabhūṣat* (he adorned completely). 3. With a noun (*nāman*): *kumbhakārāḥ* (pot-makers). 4. With a verbal root (*dhātu*): *kaṭaprūḥ* (one who makes a mat); *ajasram* (unceasingly). 5. *Tiṅ* with *tiṅ*: *pibatasvādatā* (those drinking and tasting); *svādatamodatā* (those tasting and rejoicing). 6. *Tiṅ* with *sub*: *kṛntavicakṣaṇā*—that action in which there is "cutting and looking on. Compounds such as *ehīḍā* ("come and play") and others are included because they are listed in the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. Thus ends the section on the remainder of all compound formations.
