[To exclude cases like: "a rope twice that long" (*dvis tāvatī*), "a rope three times that long" (*tris tāvatī*). SK 953: *upasargād adhvanaḥ* (A 5.4.85). [The suffix *ac* is added after the word *adhvan* when preceded by a prefix. Example:
*pragato 'dhvānam* → *prādhvo rathaḥ* ("a chariot that has gone beyond the road").

SK 954 *na pūjanāt* (A 5.4.69): No compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) shall apply after words used in the sense of praise. Examples: *surājā* ("good king"), *atirājā* ("excellent king"). This restriction applies only after *su-* and *ati-*. Hence, not here: *paramarājaḥ* ("supreme king"). Why "after praise"? Consider: *gām atikrānto 'tigavaḥ* ("one who has surpassed a cow"). This prohibition occurs precisely prior to the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ* (A 5.4.113). Therefore, not here: *susakthaḥ* ("having beautiful thighs"), *svakṣaḥ* ("having beautiful eyes"). SK 955 *kimaḥ kṣepaḥ* (A 5.4.70): [The suffix *kan* is applied] after the word *kim* when it expresses censure.

When the interrogative *kim* follows [a word] used in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*), then after that [compound], the suffixes at the end of a compound (*samāsānta*) shall not occur. *kusito rājā* → *kiṃrājā*; *kiṃsakhā*; *kiṃgauḥ*. Why "in the sense of censure"? *kiṃrājaḥ*; *kiṃsakhaḥ*; *kiṃgavaḥ*.

[By the rule] *nañas tatpuruṣāt* (A 5.4.71), there is no compound-ending suffix after a *tatpuruṣa* compound beginning with *nañ*: *arājā*; *asakhā*. Why "after a *tatpuruṣa*"? [Counter-example: *adhuraṃ śakaṭam* ("a cart without a pole").

SK 957 *patho vibhāṣā* (A 5.4.72): After the word *pathin*, when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) is optionally applied. Examples: *apatham* or *apanthāḥ*. [The rule applies] only after a *tatpuruṣa* compound; thus, *apatho deśaḥ* ("a region without a path") and *apathaṃ vartate* ("it proceeds without a path").
This concludes the section on compound-final suffixes.
The Section on Compounds with Elided Case-endings (Aluk-samāsa) 24.
SK 958 *aluguttarapade* (A 6.3.1):

The governing heading for *aluk* (non-elision) extends prior to [the rule concerning] *ānaṅ*; however, the governing heading for *uttarapada* (subsequent member of a compound) extends until the end of the chapter (*āpādasamāpteḥ*).
SK 959 *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ* (A 6.3.2).

The ablative case (*pañcamī*) shall not be elided (*aluk*) before a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) when following these [words]: *stoka* (a little), as in *stokānmuktaḥ* ("released with little effort"). Likewise, this applies to words having the sense of "near" (*antika*) or "far" (*dūra*), and the word *kṛcchra* (difficulty). Why mention "before a subsequent member"? Consider *nistokaḥ*, meaning "one who has emerged from a little," where the ablative is elided. There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the compound *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*. The ritual recitations (*śastra*) prescribed in the *Brāhmaṇas* are metaphorically called "Brāhmaṇas"; one who recites them is a *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, a specific type of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). This is due to the very extension of the ablative case to express the sense of the accusative. SK 960: After the words *ojas*, *sahas*, *ambhas*, and *tamas*, the ablative case (*tṛtīyā*) is not elided before a subsequent member. (A 6.3.3)

"Ojasākṛtam," and so forth. There is an extension [of the rule] for *añjas*. *Añjasākṛtam* means "done with straightforwardness"; that is, done with honesty. Also, *puṃsānujaḥ* and *januṣāndhaḥ*. He whose elder brother is male is *puṃsānujaḥ*. *Januṣāndhaḥ* means blind from birth; that is, congenitally blind.
According to Pāṇini 6.3.4, *manasaḥ saṃjñāyām*, [the suffix *ṭac* is applied after *manas* when forming a name]:
*manasāguptā*.

And [the suffix *ini*] is applied after the word *manas* when it means "one who knows" (*ājñāyin*), provided that the word *manas* itself is used [in the compound]. One whose nature is to know with the mind is *manasājñāyī*.
And [the suffix *ini* is applied] after the word *ātman* [when it means "one who knows"].

There shall be no *aluk* (non-elision) of the third case ending of the word *ātman*. It should be stated that this applies when a "pūraṇa" [ordinal] follows; that is to say, when the final member (*uttarapada*) ends in a pūraṇa suffix. Examples include *ātmāpañcamaḥ* ("with oneself as the fifth"). However, in the case of *janārdana ātmacaturtha eva*, it should be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Why specify "pūraṇa"? Consider *ātmakṛtam* ("done by oneself"). SK 964: In the designation of a grammarian, the fourth case [is used for *ātman*]. (A 6.3.7) The word *ātman* is understood from the previous rule. Examples: *ātmanepadam* ("middle voice"), *ātmanebhāṣāḥ* ("verbs spoken for oneself"). This fourth case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). The compound is formed through the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding the fourth case.
SK 965: *parasya ca* (A 6.3.8): [The suffixes] *parasmaipada* [are used for roots] whose speech is directed toward another (*parasmaibhāṣā*). SK 966:

*haladantāt saptamyāḥ saṃjñāyām* (A 6.3.9): [The elision of the case-ending] of a locative case ending occurs after a word ending in a consonant or the letter *a*, when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

There is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending after a word ending in *hal* or *ad*, when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*). *tvacisāraḥ*. By A 8.3.95, *gaviyudhibhyāṃ sthiraḥ*: after these two, the *s* of *sthira* becomes *ṣ*. *gaviṣṭhiraḥ*. In this case, the non-elision (*aluk*) occurs precisely because of the mention of *gavi*. *yudhiṣṭhiraḥ*. *araṇyetilakāḥ*. Here, by the rule "when it is a proper name," there is a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*). Also [there is no elision] after *hṛd* and *div*. *hṛdispṛk*. *divispṛk*.

SK 968: *kāraṇāmni ca prācāṃ halādau* (A 6.3.10). In the name of a place belonging to the Easterners (*prācām*), when it is the name of a tax-base (*kāraṇāman*) and the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) begins with a consonant (*hal*), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending after a stem ending in *hal*. Examples: *mukuṭekārṣāpaṇam* ("a kārṣāpaṇa coin [paid] at Mukuṭa"), *dṛṣadimāṣakaḥ* ("a māṣaka coin [paid] at Dṛṣadi"). Since this was already established by the preceding rule, this is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*): [the elision occurs] only when it is the name of a tax-base, only in the Eastern region, and only when the subsequent member begins with a consonant. Why "name of a tax-base"? Example: *abhyāhitapaśuḥ* ("an animal brought near [for sacrifice]"). This is the name of something to be given other than a tax. Why "of the Easterners"? Example: *yūthapaśuḥ* ("an animal from a herd"). Why "beginning with a consonant"? Example: *avikaṭoraṇaḥ* ("a hurdle for sheep"). Why "ending in *hal*"? Example: *nadyāṃ doho nadīdohaḥ* ("milking in the river").
SK 969: After *madhya* [the suffix *ka* is applied] when *guru* follows:
*madhyeguruḥ*. Also after *anta*: *anteguruḥ*. SK 970:
After a word denoting a limb of the body (*svāṅga*), except for *mūrdhan* and *mastaka*, [the suffix *ka* is applied] when not meaning "desire" (*akāme*).

*kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("the one with black [hair] on the neck"), *urasilomā* ("the one with hair on the chest"). Why say "not from *mūrdhan* or *mastaka*"? [Examples: *mūrdhaśikhaḥ*, *mastakaśikhaḥ*. Why say "when not meaning desire" (*akāme*)? [Example: *mukhakāmaḥ* ("one whose desire is for the mouth"). SK 971: *bandhe ca vibhāṣā* (A 6.3.13). There is optionally no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending after a word ending in a consonant or the letter *a*, when followed by *bandha*. [Examples: *hastebandhaḥ* or *hastabandhaḥ*. Why say "after a word ending in a consonant or the letter *a*" (*haladantāt*)? [Counter-example: *guptibandhaḥ*.
SK 972: In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, before a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, [the first member] frequently retains its original accent (A 6.3.14).

Examples: *stamberamaḥ* ("an elephant"), *karṇejapaḥ* ("a slanderer"). In some cases, it does not: *kurucaraḥ* ("one who wanders in the Kurus"). SK 973: Before the suffix *-ja*, [the first members] *prāvṛṣ*, *śarat*, *kāla*, and *divas* [retain their original accent] (A 6.3.15).

*prāvṛṣijaḥ*, *śaradijaḥ*, *kālejaḥ*, *divijaḥ*. This is an elaboration of the preceding [rule]. According to A 6.3.16, *vibhāṣā varṣakṣaraśaravarāt*, there is optionally no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending before the suffix *ja* after these words: *varṣejaḥ* or *varṣajaḥ*; *kṣarejaḥ* or *kṣarajaḥ*; *śarejaḥ* or *śarajaḥ*; *varejaḥ* or *varajaḥ*.

SK 975 *ghakālataneṣu kālanāmnaḥ* (A 6.3.17): After a word denoting time, there is optional elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending before words ending in the suffix *gha*, and before *kāla* and *tana*. Examples: *pūrvāhṇe-tare* / *pūrvāhṇa-tare*; *pūrvāhṇe-tame* / *pūrvāhṇa-tame*. Before *kāla*: *pūrvāhṇe-kāle* / *pūrvāhṇa-kāle*. Before *tana*: *pūrvāhṇe-tane* / *pūrvāhṇa-tane*. SK 976 *śayavāsavāsiṣv akālāt* (A 6.3.18): [The elision of the locative case ending] does not occur after a word that is not a term for time, when followed by *śaya*, *vāsa*, or *vāsin*.

*kheśayaḥ* / *khaśayaḥ* / *grāmevāsaḥ* / *grāmavāsaḥ* / *grāmevāsī* / *grāmavāsī*. [The rule] "after a word ending in a consonant or the letter *a*" (*haladantāt*) applies here as well: *bhūmiśayaḥ*. In the case of words containing the element *ap*, before the suffixes *yoni*, *yat*, and *matup*, [the elision of the final vowel of *ap* does not occur]. For example: one whose birth or origin (*yoni*) is in the waters is *apsuyoniḥ*; that which exists in the waters is *apsavyaḥ*; the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are *apsumantau*. SK 977: *nen-siddha-bandhiṣu ca* (A 6.3.19). The elision of the locative case-ending (*saptamyā aluk*) does not occur before words ending in *in*, nor before *siddha* and *bandhin*. Examples: *sthaṇḍilaśāyī* (one who sleeps on the bare ground), *sāṅkāśyasiddhaḥ* (one perfected at Sāṅkāśya), *cakrabandhaḥ* (a binding with a wheel).

SK 978 *sthe ca bhāṣāyām* (A 6.3.20): In the case of the word *stha*, there is no elision (*aluṅ*) of the locative case ending when used in common speech (*bhāṣā*). Example: *samasthaḥ*. Why "in common speech"? [Counter-example: *kṛṣṇo 'syākhareṣṭhaḥ*. SK 979 *ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe* (A 6.3.21): In the case of the genitive case ending, there is no elision when used in an expression of abuse (*ākrośa*).

The compound *caurasya kulaṃ* (the clan of a thief) is a genitive-tatpuruṣa. [Question: What about when it refers to an insult? [Answer: *brāhmaṇakulaṃ* (the Brahmin clan). [The rule] *vāgdikpaśyadbhyo yuktidaṇḍahareṣu* applies: *vācoyuktiḥ* (a clever speech), *diśodaṇḍaḥ* (a punishment directed toward a quarter), *paśyatoharaḥ* (one who steals while being watched). Also, there are the forms *āmuṣyāyaṇa*, *āmuṣyaputrika*, and *āmuṣyakulika*. *Āmuṣyāyaṇaḥ* means "the offspring of such-and-such" (*amuṣya apatyam*); the suffix *phak* is applied because it belongs to the *naḍādi* group. *Āmuṣyaputrikā* means "the state of being the son of such-and-such"; the suffix *vuñ* is applied because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group. Similarly, there is *āmuṣyakulika*. And the term *devānāṃpriyaḥ* is used for a fool; otherwise, it is simply *devapriyaḥ* (beloved of the gods).
In the case of *śeṣa*, *puccha*, and *lāṅgūla*, [the sixth case ending] of *śvan* [is elided]. *śunaḥśeṣaḥ*, *śunaḥpucchaḥ*, *śunolāṅgūlaḥ*. Also for *div* before *dāsa*: *divodāsaḥ*.

(SK 980) Regarding *putra*, optionally (anyatarasyām): when *putra* follows, the sixth case ending may optionally not be elided (*aluk*) if there is censure (*nindā*). *dāsyāḥputraḥ* or *dāsīputraḥ*. Why "if there is censure"? [Example: *brāhmaṇīputraḥ*.

SK 981: *ṛto vidyāyonisaṃbandhebhyaḥ* (A 6.3.23). There is no elision (*aluk*) of the sixth case ending after a word ending in *ṛt* that denotes a relationship through learning (*vidyā*) or procreation (*yoni*). Examples: *hotur-antevāsī* (the pupil of the Hotṛ priest), *hetuḥ-putraḥ* (the son of the cause), *pitur-antevāsī* (the pupil of the father), *pituh-putraḥ* (the son of the father). Regarding "relationships through learning and procreation," there is a requirement to include both the preceding and following members of the compound. Thus, it does not apply here: *hotṛ-dhanam* (the wealth of the Hotṛ). SK 982: *vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ* (A 6.3.24). [The elision of the sixth case ending] is optional before the words *svasṛ* (sister) and *pati* (husband). [Examples: *svasuḥ-svasā* or *svasuḥ-svasā*, *patyuḥ-patiḥ* or *patyuḥ-patiḥ*.]

The sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is optionally not elided after a stem ending in *ṛ* when followed by the words *svasṛ* or *pati*. (SK 983) According to A 8.3.85, *mātuḥpiturbhyām anyatarasyām*, the *s* of *svasṛ* may optionally become *ṣ* after these two [words] within a compound. Thus: *mātuḥsvasā* or *mātuḥṣvasā*; *pituḥsvasā* or *pituḥṣvasā*. However, in the case where the elision (*luk*) applies:

SK 984: In a compound, the *s* of the word *svasṛ* following these two—*mātṛ* and *pitṛ*—becomes *ṣ*. Thus: *mātṛṣvasā* ("mother's sister") and *pitṛṣvasā* ("father's sister"). However, in a non-compound, it remains *mātuḥ svasā* and *pituḥ svasā*.
This concludes the section on compounds with elision (*aluk*).
Chapter 25: The Section on Rules Dependent on Compounds (Samāsāśrayavidhi)

In the case of *ghara*, *upakalpa*, *cela*, *ḍbruvan*, *gotra*, *mata*, and *hata*, the suffix *ḍya* is applied [to form a feminine noun], and for a stem with more than one vowel (*anekāc*), the vowel is shortened. (A 6.3.43)

The short vowel [substituted] for a stem ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī* which has a corresponding masculine form, provided it consists of more than one syllable, occurs when the suffixes *gha*, *rūpa*, *kalpa* follow, or when *celaṅ* and others are the subsequent members (*uttarapada*). Examples include: *brāhmaṇitarā*, *brāhmaṇitamā*, *brāhmaṇirūpā*, *brāhmaṇikalpā*, *brāhmaṇicalī*, *brāhmaṇibruvā*, *brāhmaṇigotrā*, and so forth. In the case of *bruvā*, the suffix *ac* is added after the root *brū* (in the sense of "one who calls himself"), and the absence of *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* substitutions is prescribed as a grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*). The items beginning with *celaṅ* denote contempt (*kutsana*) within the scope of a compound; thus, the compound is formed according to the rule: "A word denoting the object of contempt is compounded with words expressing the contempt itself."
What is the meaning of *ṅyaḥ*? [It means] "after a word ending in a feminine suffix marked by *ṅ*. What is the meaning of *bhāṣitapuṃskāt*? [The example is] *āmalakītarā*, *kuvalītarā*.

SK 986: *nadyāḥ śeṣasyānyatarasyām* (A 6.3.44). After a feminine stem ending in *ṅī*, and after a monosyllabic (*ekāc*) stem ending in *ṅī*, there may optionally be a short vowel before suffixes such as *gha* and others. [Examples: *brahmabandhutarā* / *brahmabandhūtarā*; *stritarā* / *strītarā*. [Note: This does not apply to a feminine stem formed with a *kṛt* suffix: *lakṣmītarā*.

SK 987 *ugitaś ca* (A 6.3.45): When a feminine stem ending in a vowel that is designated as *ugit* follows, there may optionally be a short vowel for that which ends in such a stem before suffixes beginning with *gha*. Examples: *viduṣitarā*; however, in the alternative where the shortening does not occur, the rule *tasilādiṣu* applies, resulting in the masculine form: *vidvattarā*. In works such as the *Vṛtti*, *viduṣītarā* is also cited, but that is without foundation. SK 988 *hṛdayasya hṛllakhayadaṇalāseṣu* (A 6.3.50): The substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* occurs before the suffix *lac*, before the suffix *ya*, before the suffix *aṇ*, and before the word *lāsa*.

*hṛllekhaḥ* means "one who scratches the heart. *Hṛdyam* means "dear to the heart. *Hārdam* means "belonging to the heart. *Hṛllāsaḥ* [is another example]. The form *lekha-* is taken here as ending in the suffix *aṇ*. However, with the suffix *ghañ*, it would be *hṛdayalekhaḥ*. The very mention of *lekha-* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, under the governing rule concerning the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), there is no application of the principle of including the final member (*tadantavidhi*). Regarding *vā śokaṣyañrogeṣu* (A 6.3.51): *hṛcchokaḥ* / *hṛdayaśokaḥ*; *sauhārdyam* / *sauhṛdayyam*; *hṛdrogaḥ* / *hṛdayarogaḥ*. There is also a word *hṛt* which is a synonym for the word *hṛdaya*. Since the forms are already established by that, this [rule] is stated for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*).

SK 990: *pādasya padājyātigopahateṣu* (A 6.3.52). When the words *aji*, *āti*, *ga*, or *upahata* follow as subsequent members, the word *pāda* shall undergo the substitution of *pada* ending in a long vowel (*ā*). Thus: *pādābhyām ajati iti padājiḥ* ("one who moves by means of his feet"), *padātiḥ*. The suffix *iṇ* is applied according to the rule *arjyānabhyāṃ pāde ca*; the absence of the augment *jarvya* is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Examples: *padagaḥ* ("going on foot"), *padipahataḥ* ("struck down by the feet"). SK 991: *padyatyatadarthe* (A 6.3.53). [The substitution of *pada* for *pāda* occurs] before the root *pad*, provided that the sense of "foot" itself is not intended.

The word *pāda* becomes *pad* when followed by the suffix *yat*, provided it does not mean "for the sake of that" (*atadarthe*). Examples: *padyāḥ śarkarāḥ* ("pebbles that strike the feet"). Why "provided it does not mean for the sake of that"? Consider *pādārtham udakam pādyam* ("water for the feet"); here the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *pādārghābhyāṃ ca*. There is an extension [of this rule] for the suffix *ika* in the sense of "moving on. Example: *pādābhyāṃ carati padikaḥ* ("one who moves on foot"); here the suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied because the word belongs to the *parpādi* group. SK 992: *himakāṣihatiṣu ca* (A 6.3.54). Examples:
*paddhimam* ("snow on the feet"), *patkāṣī* ("one who scrapes with the feet"), *paddhatiḥ* ("a path").

SK 993: *ṛcaḥ śe* (A 6.3.55). When *śas* follows, the word *pāda* becomes *pad* after the word *ṛc*. Example: *gāyatrīṃ pacchaḥ śaṃsati* ("he recites the Gāyatrī verse foot by foot"). [The suffix] *śas* expresses "in parts" (*pādaṃpādam*). Why say "after *ṛc*"? [Counter-example: *pādaśaḥ kārṣāpaṇaṃ dadāti* ("he gives a kārṣāpaṇa coin by the foot"). SK 994: *vā ghoṣamiśraśabdeṣu* (A 6.3.56). [The substitution of *pad* for *pāda* occurs optionally] when words denoting sounds mixed with noise follow.

*Pada* becomes *pad* [before certain suffixes]: *paddhoṣaḥ*, *pādaghoṣaḥ*, *panmiśraḥ*, *pādamiśraḥ*, *pacchabdaḥ*, *pādaśabdaḥ*. It should be stated that this also applies before *niṣka*: *panniṣkaḥ*, *pādaniṣkaḥ*. SK 995: In a name (*saṃjñā*), *udaka* becomes *uda*: *udameghaḥ*. It should be stated that this also applies to the final member of a compound (*uttarapada*): *kṣīrodaḥ*.

SK 996: *peṣam-vāsa-vāhana-dhiṣu ca* (A 6.3.58). *upapeṣam* [he grinds]; *udavāsaḥ* [dwelling in water]; *udavāhanaḥ* [carrying water]; *udadhir ghaṭaḥ* [a jar that holds water]. In the case of the ocean (*samudra*), however, it is established by the previous rule. SK 997: *ekahalādau pūrayitavye 'nyatarasyām* (A 6.3.59). [The elision of the case-ending is optional] when a word beginning with a single consonant follows, provided it denotes something to be filled.

*udakumbhaḥ* / *udakakumbhaḥ*. Why [is it said] "when it means 'one' (*eka*)"? [Answer: *udakasthālī*. Why [is it said] "when it is to be filled (*pūrayitavya*)"? [Answer: *udakaparvataḥ*. And in the case of *mantha*, *odana*, *saktu*, *bandu*, *vajra*, *bhāra*, *hāra*, *vīvadha*, and *gāha* [the word *uda-* is optionally substituted for *udaka-*]. *udamanthaḥ* / *udakamanthaḥ*; *udaudanaḥ* / *udakaudanaḥ*.

SK 999: *iko hrasvo 'ṅyo gālavasya* (A 6.3.61). For a stem ending in an *ik* vowel that ends in a feminine suffix (*aṅ*), there may optionally be a short vowel before a subsequent word (*uttarapada*), according to Gālava. Examples: *grāmaṇiputraḥ* or *grāmaṇīputraḥ*. Why "ending in an *ik* vowel" (*ikaḥ*)? [Consider] *ramāpatiḥ*. Why "ending in a feminine suffix" (*aṅya*)? [Consider] *gaurīpatiḥ*. The mention of Gālava is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*), because the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood from the previous rule. It should be stated that this does not apply to indeclinables (*avyaya*) that undergo the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*: [examples] *śrīmadaḥ*, *bhrūbhaṅgaḥ*, *śuklībhāvaḥ*. It should be stated: "Except for *bhru-kuṃsa* and others. [Examples: *bhrukuṃsaḥ*, *bhrukutiḥ*; *bhrūkuṃsaḥ*, *bhrūkutiḥ*.

Another interpretation is that the vowel *a* is prescribed by this [rule]. Examples: *bhrakuṃsaḥ*, *bhrakuṭiḥ*. One who has *bhruvā kuṃsaḥ*—where *kuṃsaḥ* means speaking or beauty—is a dancer wearing female attire. *Bhruvaḥ kuṭiḥ* is the crookedness of the eyebrows. Regarding *ekataddhite ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.62):
the short vowel [substituted] for the word *eka* occurs before a *taddhita* suffix and in a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *ekasyā āgatam* → *ekarūpyam*; *ekakṣīram*.

SK 1023 *eti saṃjñāyām agāt* (A 8.3.99): A cerebral [substitute] is substituted for the *s* [of the second member] when preceded by *eti* (the root *i*), provided it forms a name (*saṃjñā*) and does not begin with the letter *g*. In the case of a compound name, a dental *n* is optionally changed to a retroflex *ṇ* after a word ending in *a*, provided it is not preceded by *a*. Examples: *rohiṇīpeṇaḥ* or *rohiṇīsenaḥ*. The suffix *guṇa* (i.e., the augment *a*) is added to the word *anya* when followed by *āśis*, *āśā*, *āsthā*, *āsthita*, *utsuka*, *ūti*, *rāga*, *īya*, and so forth. (1) In the case of words denoting directions, the suffix *tīra* may optionally become *tāra*.

In the words *dūḍāś*, *dūṇāś*, and *dūḍabha*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the initial letter of the second member (*uttarapadādi-ṣṭutvam*), as well as the substitution of *u* for *duḥ*. It is difficult to offer sacrifice (*duḥkhena dāśyate*)—thus *dūḍāśaḥ*. It is difficult to destroy (*duḥkhena nāśyate*)—thus *dūṇāśaḥ*. It is difficult to deceive (*duḥkhena dabhyate*)—thus *dūḍabhaḥ*. The suffix *khal* is applied after these three; the elision of the nasal (*n*) in the root *dambh* is irregularly prescribed (*nipātita*). It meditates with difficulty (*duḥkhena dhyāyati*)—thus *dūḍhyaḥ*; the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ātaś ca*. A *bṛsī* is that on which those speaking sit; there is the substitution of *bṛ* for the word *bruvat*, and the suffix *ḍaṭ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*) from the root *sad*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). This is an *adhiṅāra* (a supplementary rule) under *saṃhitāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.114).

**SK 1036:** When the word *karṇa* follows, a long vowel is substituted for a word denoting a physical mark (*lakṣaṇa*), provided it is not among those beginning with *viṣṭa*, nor *aṣṭa*, *pañca*, *maṇi*, *bhinna*, *chinna*, *chidra*, *sruva*, or *svastika*. Example: *dviguṇākarṇaḥ* ("having ears marked by two lines"). Why "denoting a mark"? Example: *śobhanakarṇaḥ* ("having beautiful ears"). Why exclude those beginning with *viṣṭa*? Examples: *viṣṭakarṇaḥ*, *aṣṭakarṇaḥ*, *pañcakarṇaḥ*, *maṇikarṇaḥ*, *bhinnakarṇaḥ*, *chinnakarṇaḥ*, *chidrakarṇaḥ*, *sruvakarṇaḥ*, *svastikakarṇaḥ*. **SK 1037:** [The long vowel is substituted] before the suffixes *kvip* and *kvun* following the roots *nah* (to bind), *vṛt* (to turn), *vṛṣ* (to rain/impregnate), *vyadh* (to pierce), *ruc* (to shine/delight), *sah* (to endure), and *niṣu* (the prefix *nis*). (A 6.3.116)

When these [suffixes] ending in *kvip* follow, the first member of the compound takes its long vowel (*dīrgha*). Examples: *upānat*, *nīvṛt*, *prāvṛṭ*, *marmāvit*, *nīruk*, *abhīruk*, *ṛtīṣaṭ*, *parītat*. Why "ending in *kvip*"? Consider *pariṇahanam*. From the rule *vibhāṣā puruṣe* (Pāṇini 6.3.126), the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is carried over here by "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*), and that optionality is restricted (*vyavasthitā*). Therefore, it applies only when the preceding word is a *gati* or a *kāraka*. It does not apply here: *paṭuruk*, *tigmaruk*. SK 1038:
In the case of names (*saṃjñā*), the long vowel is applied to words such as *koṭara* and *kiṃśulaka* when followed by *vana* and *giri*. (A 6.3.117)

The long vowel [of the final syllable] occurs in the case of *vana* when it follows *koṭara*, etc., in the sense of "another forest," and when it follows *kiṃśuluka*, etc., in the sense of "another mountain," provided that the compound forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
[Pāṇini 6.3.123] *vanaṃ puragā-miśrakā-sidhrakā-sārikā-koṭarāgrebhyaḥ* (A 8.4.4).

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs in the word *vana-* when it is the final member [of a compound] only after these [specific words], and not after others. Here, the five words ending in *koṭara*—namely, *miśrakā*, *sidhrakā*, *sārikā*, *koṭara*, and *agra*—should be understood as being intended for the rule prescribing the lengthening of the vowel (*dīrghavidhi*). The mention of those [words] with their vowels already lengthened in the rule prescribing the *ṇ*-substitution serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). However, the mention of the word *agra* is for the purpose of prescribing the rule itself (*vidhyartha*). Examples: *puragāvaṇam* (the forest of Puraga), *miśrakāvaṇam* (the Miśraka forest), *sidhrakāvaṇam* (the Sidhraka forest), *sārikāvaṇam* (the Sārika forest), *koṭarāvaṇam* (the Koṭara forest). Why "only after these"? Consider *asipatravanam* (the sword-leaf forest). Also, *agrevaṇam* (the forest at the front).

In the case of *rājadanta* and similar compounds, the elision of the locative case-ending (*aluk*) occurs by virtue of specific grammatical injunctions (*nipātana*). The nominative case is used in the sense of the nominal stem alone (*prātipadikārthamātre*). For example: *kiṃśulukāgiriḥ*.
According to A 6.3.118, *vale*:
when the suffix *vala* follows, a long vowel (*dīrgha*) shall occur in the case of a technical name (*saṃjñā*). For example: *kṛṣīvalaḥ*.
SK 1041: In the case of *matau* [the suffix *matup*], the long vowel is substituted for the final vowel of words with more than two syllables, except for those beginning with *ajira* (A 6.3.119).

Examples: *amarāvatī*. Why say "except for those beginning with *ajira*"? Consider: *ajiravatī*. Why say "of words with more than two syllables"? Consider: *vrīhimatī*. This applies only when it is a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*). Not here: *valayavatī*. SK 1042: And also for words beginning with *śara* (A 6.3.120).

*Śarāvatī*. [Pāṇini 6.3.121] *iko vahe ’pīloḥ*: A vowel ending in *ik* (i, u, ṛ, ḷ) becomes long before the word *vaha*, except when it is *pīlu*. Example: *ṛṣīvaham*. Why “ending in *ik*”? [Counter-example: *piṇḍavaham*. Why “except for *pīlu*”? [Counter-example: *pīluvaham*. It should be stated that this applies to words other than *pīlu* and its like: [example: *dāruvaham*.

SK 1044 *upasargasya ghañy amanuṣye bahulam* (A 6.3.122): When a *ghañ*-affix follows, the vowel of a prefix (*upasarga*) is optionally lengthened, provided it does not refer to a human being. Examples: *parīpākaḥ* or *paripākaḥ*. Why "not referring to a human being"? Consider *niṣādaḥ*. SK 1045 *ikaḥ kāśe* (A 6.3.123): [The vowel of a prefix ending in] an *ik* vowel is lengthened before the word *kāśa*.
The long vowel [ā] shall replace the final *i* or *u* of a preposition (*upasarga*) before the word *kāśa*. For example: *vīkāśaḥ*. Why "of *ika*" (*ikaḥ*)? [Consider: *prakāśaḥ*.

(Pāṇini 6.3.124) In a compound where there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the long vowel [ā] replaces the final vowel of *aṣṭan* when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*). For example: *aṣṭāpadam*. Why "in a proper name" (*saṃjñāyām*)? [Consider: *aṣṭaputraḥ*. (Pāṇini 6.3.125)
SK 1047: Before the suffix *kapi*, [the final vowel of] *citi* is replaced by *kapi*:
*ekacitīkaḥ*.
SK 1048: Before the word *nara-*, when used as a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*), [the final vowel of *citi* is replaced by *kapi*].

*Viśvānaraḥ*. According to Pāṇini A 6.3.130, *mitre carṣau*, [the vowel lengthening occurs] when *viśva* is followed by *mitra* if the latter refers to a seer (*ṛṣi*). Why "if a seer"? [Consider: *viśvamitraḥ māṇavakaḥ* ("Viśvamitra the boy"). Regarding the word *śvan* ("dog"), lengthening is to be stated before the words *danta*, *daṃṣṭrā*, *karṇa*, *kunda*, *varāha*, *puccha*, and *pada*. Thus: *śvādantaḥ* ("dog-tooth") and so forth.

SK 1050: *pranirantaḥśarekṣuplakṣāmrakārṣyakhadirapīyūkṣābhyo ’sañjñāyām api* (A 8.4.5). The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs after these [prefixes] when followed by the word *vana*, even if it does not form a technical name (*asañjñā*). Examples: *pravaṇam*, *kārṣyavaṇam*. In this case, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs because it follows a retroflex sibilant (*ṣ*). SK 1051: *vibhāṣauṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ* (A 8.4.6). The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* after these [prefixes] when followed by names of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*) or trees (*vanaspati*) is optional.

The substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the word *vana* may optionally occur after these [words]: *dūrvāvaṇam* / *dūrvāvanam*; *śirīṣavaṇam* / *śirīṣavanam*. This occurs only after words consisting of two or three syllables; not here: *devadāruvanam*. A prohibition must be stated for words such as *irikā*: *irikāvanam*, *mirikāvanam*. SK 1052: *vāhanam āhitāt* (A 8.4.8). The substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the word *vāhana* following a cause situated in the sense of "that which is carried after being mounted" occurs. The meaning is: "a vehicle belonging to Indra. The *vṛddhi* strengthening in *vahana-* (from the root *vah*) occurs by virtue of this very rule being an archaic irregularity (*nipātana*).
SK 1053 *pānaṃ deśe* (A 8.4.9):

When "country" (*deśa*) is implied, the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of *pāna* occurs after a cause (a letter of the *nimitta*-class) situated in the preceding member of the compound. For example: *kṣīrapāṇā uśīnarāḥ* ("the Uśīnaras, whose drink is milk") and *surāpāṇāḥ prācyāḥ* ("the Easterners, whose drink is liquor"). Here, *pānam* means "that which is drunk," formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).
SK 1054 *vā bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (A 8.4.10): [The substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of *pāna*] is optional when the suffix denotes either the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The same applies to *pāna*. Examples: *kṣīrapāṇam* or *kṣīrapānam*. For *giri-nadī* and similar compounds, there is optionally [the substitution of *ṇ*]: *giriṇadī* or *girinadī*; *cakranitambā* or *cakranitambā*.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.11 states: "Also before the final vowel of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), before the augment *num*, and before case-endings."

After a cause (nimitta) situated in the preceding member (*pūrvapada*), the *n* of a suffix situated in these [subsequent members] may optionally become *ṇ*. 1. At the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*): *māṣavāpiṇau* ("two who sow beans"). 2. In the presence of the augment *num*: *vrīhivāpāṇi* ("those which sow rice"). 3. In a case-ending (*vibhakti*): *māṣavāpeṇa* ("by means of sowing beans"). In the alternative, *māṣavāpinau*, and so forth. The substitution of *ṇ* occurs only for that which belongs to the end of the nominal stem that constitutes the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). It does not apply here: *gargabhaginī* ("the sister of the Gargas"), because the entire compound *gargāṇām bhaginī* is the subsequent member. For this very reason, the mention of *num* was made [in the rule]; since *num* is prescribed as belonging to the *aṅga* (the inflective base), it is indeed a part of that, but not a part of the subsequent member itself. Furthermore:

In examples such as *prahiṇvan*, the mention of *num* [in the rule] is intended to ensure the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* after *num*; however, in examples such as *prenvanam*, the substitution does not occur because the root belongs to the *kṣubhna*-class (*kṣubhnādi*), nor does it occur after roots beginning with *y*. For example: *ramyayūnā* and *paripakvāni*. When a monosyllabic word precedes a compound member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is obligatory, as has been stated. For example: *vṛtrahaṇau*. In the sense of "honoring Hari," we have *harimāṇī*. When *num* follows, as in *kṣīrapāṇi*; when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows, as in *kṣīrapeṇa* and *ramyaviṇā*. SK 1056: *kumati ca* (A 8.4.13). When a compound member containing the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) follows, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs as previously mentioned. For example: *harikāmiṇau*, *harikāmāṇi*, and *harikāmeṇa*.

SK 1057: Even when there is an intervention by a *pada* (A 8.4.38), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* shall not occur even when there is separation by a word, as in *māṣakumbhavāpena* and *caturaṅgayogena*. It should be stated that this does not apply when it is not a *taddhita* suffix: e.g., *ārdragomayeṇa*, *śuṣkagomayeṇa*. SK 1058: *kastumburūṇi* is a genus (*jāti*) [A 6.1.143].

In this context, *suṇ* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). *Kuskumbhuru* means *dhānyāka* (coriander). The neuter gender is not restrictive. Why [is *jāti* mentioned]? As in *kutumburūṇi*, which means "wicked *tinduka* fruits. (SK 1059) *Aparasparāḥ* is prescribed as a nipātana in the sense of continuity of action (A 6.1.144): *aparasparāḥ sārthā gacchanti* ("the caravans go one after another"). The meaning is that they go continuously without interruption. Why [is *kriyā* mentioned]? As in *aparaparā gacchanti*, which means "they go once each, some behind and some ahead."

SK 1060: *goṣpada* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) used in the senses of "frequented," "not frequented," and "measure. The suffix *suṭ* is added, and the *s* of *suṭ* undergoes the change to *ṣ*. In the sense of "frequented": a place where cows are found is "frequented by cows" (*gobhiḥ sevitaḥ*), hence it is called *goṣpada*. In the sense of "not frequented": "wildernesses that are not *goṣpada*" (*agoṣpadāny araṇyāni*). In the sense of "measure": "a field measuring a *goṣpada*" (*goṣpadamātraṃ kṣetram*). Why [specify] "frequented" and so forth? [Otherwise, one would get] *gopada*, meaning simply "the foot of a cow. SK 1061: *āspada* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the sense of "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*). [The *suṭ* is added, and the *s* changes to *ṣ*.]

The augment *suṭ* is applied after the preverb *ā* when it means "a place for staying" (*ātmayāpanāya*). Example: *āspadaṃ*. Why say "after *pra*"? [Counter-example: *āpad āpadam*. *Sūtra 1062:* *āścaryam anitye* (A 6.1.147). The augment *suṭ* is applied after *ā* when expressing something wonderful (*adbhuta*) that is not permanent (*anitya*). Example: *āścaryaṃ yadi sa bhuñjīta* ("It would be a wonder if he were to eat"). Why say "not permanent"? [Counter-example: *ācaryaṃ karma śobhanam* ("The work is wonderfully beautiful").
SK 1063: *avaskaraḥ* is used in the sense of *varcaska* (A 6.1.148).

*Varcaska* is contemptible excrement; it is the impurity of food. The suffix *suṭ* is applied in this sense. It is called *avaskara* because it is scattered (*ava-kṛ*). Why "in the sense of *varcaska*"? [Counter-example: *avakara*. SK 1064: *apaskaraḥ* is a part of a chariot (A 6.1.149).
Another [example] is *apakaraḥ*.

Regarding *viṣkiraḥ* in the sense of a bird (*śakuni*), [Pāṇini 6.1.150 states] "or *vikiraḥ*. Since the optional application of the augment *suṭ* would already be established by the very mention of the word "option" (*vāvacana*), the inclusion of the term *vikira*—intended to prevent its use in any sense other than "bird"—is not correct according to the *Vṛtti*, because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*.

SK 1066: *pratiṣkaśaś ca keśaḥ* (A 6.1.152). From the root *kaś* in the sense of "going" or "commanding," another form of the same root preceded by *prati* takes the suffix *ac* (in the *pacādi* class), with the augment *suṭ* being applied irregularly (*nipātana*) and the change of *s* to *ṣ*. A companion or one who goes ahead is called *pratiṣkaśa*. Why [is the rule] stated as *keśaḥ*? Consider *pratikaśo 'śvaḥ* ("a horse that has reached the whip"). Even though the word *kaśā* ("whip") is derived from the very same root *kaś*, the mention of the root *kaś* here is for the purpose of including the prefix *prati*; therefore, it does not apply to prefixes belonging to other roots. SK 1067: *praskaṇvahariścandrāvṛṣī* (A 6.1.153). [The forms *praskaṇva* and *hariścandra* are derived with the augment *suṭ* when they denote sages (*ṛṣi*).]

The mention of *hariścandra* is for the sake of excluding those who do not intend the meaning [of the specific technical term]. Why say "a seer" (*ṛṣi*)? [To exclude: *prakaṇva* as a place; *haricandra* as a young brahmin student (*māṇavaka*). SK 1068: *maskara-maskariṇau veṇu-parivrājakayoḥ*.

The word *makara* is an underived (*avyutpanna*) term; its *suṭ* augment and the suffix *ini* are prescribed [as substitutes] for it. Why say "bamboo" (*veṇu*)? [To exclude: *makara* as a crocodile; *makarī* as the ocean.

SK 1069: In the case of the city name *kāstīra* and *ajastunda* (A 6.1.155), [the suffix *aṇ* is applied]. A city named *kāstīra* is so called because it has a slight (*īṣat*) bank (*tīra*). A city named *ajastunda* is so called because its protrusion (*tuṇḍa*) is like that of a goat (*aja*). Why say "in the case of a city"? [Counter-examples: *kātīra*, *ajatunda*. SK 1070:
*Kāraskara* is a tree (A 6.1.156). [The suffix *aṇ* is applied to form the name of a specific tree.]
Because it produces fruit (*kāraṃ karoti*), it is called *kāraskara*, a tree; elsewhere it is *kārakara*. However, some read this in the *kaskādi* group and not in the sūtras.
[This is because of the rule: "And *pāraskara* and so forth are [correctly formed] when they are proper names" (*pāraskaraprabhṛtīni ca saṃjñāyām*, A 6.1.157).

These [words] are cited as examples for the name [Pāraskara]: *pāraskaraḥ*, *kiṣkindhā*. Regarding *tadbṛhatoḥ karapatyoś coradevatayoḥ suṭ talopaś ca*: in the case of *tat* and *bṛhat*, the letters *d* and *t* are elided; in the case of *kara* and *pati*, the augment *suṭ* is added. The phrase "of the thief (*cora*) and the deity (*devatā*)" is a condition applied to the whole compound. Thus: *taskaraḥ* (thief), *bṛhaspatiḥ* (the deity Bṛhaspati). Regarding *prāyasya citticittayoḥ*: *prāyaścittaḥ* (one who effects atonement), *prāyaścittam* (atonement). *Vanaspatiḥ* (lord of the forest), and so forth. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words).
This concludes the section on the rules for patronymics within the chapter on secondary suffixes (*taddhita*).

SK 1072: *samarthānāṃ prathamād vā* (A 4.1.82). These three words are governed [as an adhikāra] up to *prāg diśaḥ*. "Capability" (*sāmarthya*) means being fully established; that is to say, having undergone the operations of sandhi. SK 1073: *prāgdīvyato ’ṇ* (A 4.1.83).
The suffix *aṇ* is governed from this point forward, prior to [the rule] "one plays with that" (*tena dīvyati*).

By the rule *aśvapatyādibhyaś ca* (A 4.1.84), the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after words such as *aśvapati* and others in the senses falling before "that which pertains to [a person]" (*prāgdīvyatīya*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇya* which is about to be mentioned.

SK 1075: *taddhiteṣv acāmādeḥ* (A 7.2.117). When a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* follows, there shall be *vṛddhi* substitution for the vowel at the beginning of the vowels (*ac*) [of the base]. SK 1076: *kiti ca* (A 7.2.118). [Vṛddhi substitution also occurs] when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *k* follows.

The same applies in the case of *taddhita* suffixes: from *aśvapati*, the derivatives for offspring and so forth are *āśvapatam* and *gāṇapatam*. However, the form *gāṇapatyaḥ* as a mantra is merely an error.
[Pāṇini 4.1.85: After *diti*, *aditi*, *āditya*, and words ending with *patī*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied.

The suffix *ṇya* shall be applied after words beginning with *diti*, as well as after a word ending in *pati*, in the sense of "descended from" (*prāgdīvya*) and similar meanings; it is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*. Examples: *daityaḥ*; *ādityaḥ* (from *aditi* or *āditya*); *prājāpatyaḥ*. According to the *Kāśikā*, [the suffix applies] also after *yama*: *yāmyaḥ*. After *pṛthivī*, the suffixes *ña* and *añ* are applied: *pārthivā*, *pārthivī*. After *deva*, the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* are applied: *daivyam*, *daivam*. After *bahiṣ*, there is elision of the final syllable and the suffix *yañ* is applied: *bāhyaḥ*. The suffix *īkak* may also be applied: *bāhīkaḥ*. After *sthāman*, the suffix *a* is applied: *asthāmaḥ*. [In this case], due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the *s* is changed to *t*.

However, in the sense of *bhava* (originating from), elision (*luk*) should be stated: *aśvatthāmā*. Regarding the suffix *a* after *loman* when there are many descendants: the suffix *a* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule for] *iñ* after *bāhu* and so on. Examples: *uḍulomāḥ*, *uḍulomān*. Why "when there are many"? Consider *auḍulomiḥ*. When *go* is followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), *yat* applies: *gavyam*. Why "beginning with a vowel"? Consider *gorūpyam* (derived from *go* as a cause) and *gomayam*. SK 1078: After *utsa* and others, the suffix *añ* is applied (A 4.1.86):

*autsaḥ*. The suffix *ḍhak* should be stated after *agni* and *kali*: *āgneyam* (meaning "offspring" etc. of Agni) and *kāleyam*. Thus end the suffixes common to meanings ranging from "offspring" to "modification."

SK 1079: *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañsnañau bhavanāt* (A 4.1.87). Before the word *bhavana* in the rule *dhānyānāṃ bhavane*, the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* are respectively applied after the words *strī* and *pums* in the sense of "belonging to" (*prāgartheṣu*). Examples: *straiṇaḥ* ("belonging to women"), *pauṃsnaḥ* ("belonging to men"). The suffix *vat* is not used in this sense; this is known from the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *strī puṃvac ca*. Examples: *strīvat*, *puṃvat*. SK 1080: *dvigor luganapatye* (A 4.1.88). The elision (*luk*) of the suffix [denoting descent] occurs after a *dvigu* compound when it does not denote a descendant (*anapatye*).

The *luk* elision of a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel other than *a*, which is not in the sense of "progeny" (*apatya*) and belongs to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group, occurs when it is caused by a *dvigu* compound. For example: *pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* ("a sacrificial cake prepared in five potsherds") becomes *pañcakapālaḥ*. Why specify "caused by a *dvigu*"? Consider *pañcakapālasyedaṃ khaṇḍaṃ pāñcakapālam* ("a fragment of this five-potsherd [cake]"). Why specify "beginning with a vowel other than *a*" (*ajādi*)? Consider *pañcagargarūpyam* ("silver purchased for five gargara coins"). Why specify "not in the sense of progeny"? Consider *dvayor mitrayor apatyaṃ dvaimitriḥ* ("the offspring of two Mitrās"). [This rule applies] when the suffix is *añ* in the sense of a *gotra* lineage, according to A 4.1.89.

When a suffix belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group is intended to follow a word beginning with a vowel other than *a*, there shall be no elision (*aluk*) of the *gotra* suffix. For example: *gargāṇāṃ chātrāḥ* ("the pupils of the Gargas"). [By rule A 4.2.114] *vṛddhāc chaḥ*, the suffix *cha* is applied.

By A 6.4.151, *āpatyasya ca taddhite 'nāti*, the *y* of a patronymic suffix is elided when a *taddhita* suffix follows, provided it is not *ā*; however, this does not apply before the suffix *ā*. Thus: *gārgīyāḥ*. Why "belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group"? Consider: *gargebhyo hitam gārgīyam* ("beneficial for the Gargas"), where the suffix *cha* is not *prāgdīvyatīya*. Why "before a vowel"? Consider: *gargebhya āgatam gargarūpyam* ("come from the Gargas"), where the suffix *rūpya* begins with a consonant.

SK 1083 *yūni luk* (A 4.1.90): When a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group is intended to be applied, there shall be elision (*luk*) of the *yuvan*-suffix. For example: *glucuka* has a descendant in the *gotra* lineage named *glucukāyaniḥ* [formed by the suffix *phin*, which will be mentioned later]. From that, the *yuvan*-suffix *aṇ* is added, resulting in *glaucukāyanaḥ*. A student (*chātra*) of that person is also called *glaucukāyanaḥ*. Because the *aṇ* suffix has been elided, the condition of being "elderly" (*vṛddha*) no longer applies; therefore, the suffix *cha* is not applied. SK 1084 *pailādibhyaś ca* (A 2.4.59): [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the names] beginning with *paila*.

From these [names], there is *luk* elision of the *yuvan*-suffix. From *pīlā*, by the rule *vā* [in the case of the suffix] *aṇ*, there is *aṇ*. From that, by the rule *aṇo dvyacaḥ*, there is *phiñ*; of that, there is *luk*. Thus, *pailaḥ* applies to both father and son. By the rule *tadrājāc cāṇaḥ*, from the word *āṅga*—which ends in *aṇ* by the rule *dvyañmagadha-*—there is *luk* of the *phiñ* by the rule *aṇo dvyacaḥ*. Thus, *āṅgaḥ* applies to both father and son. (SK 1085) *iñaḥ prācām* (A 2.4.60).

The suffix *iñ* is elided after a *gotra* [patronymic] stem ending in that [suffix], provided that the *gotra* belongs to the Easterners (*prācām*). [Example: The descendant of *Pannāgāra*. [The derivation is as follows: *iñ* is applied by the rule *ata iñ*; then *phak* is applied by the rule *ñañiñoś ca*. There is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. Thus, *pānnāgāriḥ* applies to both the father and the son. Why "of the Easterners"? [Counter-example: *dākṣiḥ* is the father; *dākṣāyaṇaḥ* is the son. SK 1086: *na taulvalibhyaḥ* (A 2.4.61). There shall be no elision of the *yuvan* suffix following stems such as *taulvali*. This was applicable by the preceding rule. [Example: *Tulvala*. From this, *iñ* is applied, then *phak*. Thus, *taulvaliḥ* is the father; *taulvalāyanaḥ* is the son.

SK 1087 *phakphiñor anyatarasyām* (A 4.1.91): This sūtra provides an option (*vikalpa*) where a compulsory elision (*nitye luki*) of *phak* and *phiñ* would otherwise apply by the rule *yūni luk*. Examples: *kātyāyanasya chātrāḥ* ("the pupils of Kātyāyana")—namely, *kātīyāḥ* or *kātyāyanīyāḥ*. [Derivation: From *yaḥ*, "whose offspring," comes *yāskaḥ* ("descendant of Yakṣa"), formed with the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *śivādyaṇ*. His youthful descendant (*tasyāpatyaṃ yuvā*) is *yāskāyaniḥ*, formed with *phiñ* by the rule *aṇo dvyac*. The pupils of that person are *yāskīyāḥ* or *yāskāyanīyāḥ*. SK 1088 *tasyāpatyam* (A 4.1.92): [The suffixes taught from this point onward denote] "his offspring."

After a word ending in the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhyanta), following the application of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*), the suffixes already mentioned or those yet to be mentioned may optionally occur in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*). For example: *upagoḥ apatyam* becomes *aupagavaḥ*. The initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) supersedes both the final and penultimate *vṛddhi*. This would have been done for the purpose of superseding [the rule] *tasyedaṃ* even in the case of offspring; however, that [rule *tasyedaṃ*] remains a general rule (*utsarga*) for the remainder, while the present rule serves as the specific exception (*apavāda*) for words beginning with a *vṛddhi* vowel. But by means of a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), [we get]: *bhānoḥ apatyam* becomes *bhānavaḥ*. Why "following the application of euphonic combination"? Consider *sautthitiḥ*.

Let this [application of the] *paribhāṣā* "that which has not undergone *vyūha*" not take effect; let it not apply here by virtue of the *paribhāṣā* "that which is capable. [Example: *vastram upagor apatyaṃ caitrasya* ("the cloth and the offspring of Upagu, belonging to Caitra"). Why say "from the first"? [It is to ensure that] it does not apply in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when the word for "offspring" (*apatya*) follows. Because of the mention of the option (*vā*), there is also the sentence form. Because the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is carried over from the rule *daivayajñi-* (Pāṇini 4.1.85), there is also the compound form: *upagvapatyam*. Due to its being a genus (*jāti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied: *aupagavī*. [Other examples: *āśvapataḥ*, *daityaḥ*, *autsaḥ*, *straiṇaḥ*, *pauṃsnaḥ*. SK 1089: *apatyaṃ pautraprabhṛti gotram* (Pāṇini 4.1.162): "Offspring beginning with the grandson is called *gotra*."
That which is intended to be expressed as offspring, such as a grandson and so forth, shall be designated as *gotra*. However, according to A 4.1.163, *jīvati tu vaṃśye yuvā*:

while an ancestor (*vaṃśya*), such as a father and so forth, is living, the offspring of a grandson and so forth—beginning with the fourth generation—is designated only as *yuvan* (younger descendant), not as *gotra*.
SK 1091: And when an elder brother is living—when the eldest brother is living, the younger brother, being fourth or subsequent in order of birth, shall be called *yuvan*.
SK 1092: Or, when another *sapiṇḍa* who is more venerable (*sthaviratara*) is living.

When a brother’s other *sapiṇḍa* who is older is living, the offspring of a grandson or later descendant shall be designated as "yuvan" (junior) even while that elder is alive. One mention of the word "living" (*jīvati*) is an attribute of the offspring; the second is an attribute of the *sapiṇḍa*. The use of the comparative suffix *-tara* is for the purpose of indicating superiority in both cases. [This applies] when a paternal uncle, maternal grandfather, or brother is superior by position or age. For example, the offspring of Gārgya may be called Gārgyāyaṇa or simply Gārgya. Why [is the word] "elder" (*sthavira*) used?

In cases where there is a deficiency in place (*sthāna*) or age (*vayas*), it is *Gārgya* alone [that is used]. Why say "while he is living"? Because when he is dead, or even while he is dead, it is still *Gārgya* alone. It should be stated that this applies to an elder (*vṛddha*) for the sake of respect (*pūjā*). For the Easterners (*prācām*), the designation "elder" (*vṛddha-saṃjñā*) applies only to the *gotra*. When respect is intended, the designation "younger" (*yuva-saṃjñā*) applies to the *gotra*. Example: *tatrabhavān Gārgyāyaṇaḥ* ("the venerable Gārgyāyaṇa"). Why say "for the sake of respect"? Because otherwise it is simply *Gārgya*. It should be stated that the designation "*gotra*" applies to the "younger" (*yuvan*) when contempt (*kutsā*) is intended. Example: *gārgyo jālmaḥ* ("the wretched Gārgya"). Why say "contempt"? Because otherwise it is *Gārgyāyaṇaḥ*. SK 1093: *eko gotre* (A 4.1.93). [This rule states that] in the *gotra* lineage, only one [patronymic] is used.

If [the suffix] were applied only once to the *gotra*, there would be a single suffix indicating the descendant: from *upagu* comes *aupagavaḥ*; likewise *gārgyaḥ* and *nāḍāyanaḥ*. [If it were applied repeatedly], there would be a succession of suffixes in the *gotra* numbering one less than itself; or else, the undesirable consequence (an-iṣṭotpatti) of producing [forms] numbering two less than itself would follow. (1) The offspring would belong only to the father, and not even to those prior to him. This sūtra and the subsequent one are intended to prevent that [undesirable result] according to different opinions. (2)

For if one holds the position that "a descendant is [identical] to the father," then when the third generation from Upagu is to be expressed, the suffix *iñ* would be applied after *aupagava*. But when the fourth generation is to be expressed—provided the eldest ancestor is living and the lineage member is deceased—the suffix *phak* would be applied after *aupagavi*. In this way, through the succession of *phak* and *iñ*, there would be ninety-nine suffixes in the hundredth *gotra* from the root ancestor.

In the primary view (*mukhyapakṣa*), where it is stated that [the suffixes] apply even to the grandfather and so forth, although the desired form is established by adding *aṇ* to Upagu in the third generation, and then *iñ* after the stem ending in *aṇ*, and then *phak* in the fourth generation—thus, in this succession of *phak* and *iñ*, there would be ninety-eight undesired suffixes in the hundredth generation. Therefore, this rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). The same should be inferred for the subsequent rule as well. SK 1094: *gotrād yūny astriyām* (A 4.1.94).

In the case of a young descendant (*yūnyapatya*), the suffix should be added only after a word ending in a *gotra* suffix. However, for a female descendant, there is no designation as "young" (*yuvasaṃjñā*). For example, the young descendant of Garga is Gārgyāyaṇa; in the feminine, because it is a *gotra*, there is only one suffix. *ata iñ* (A 4.1.95):
After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *a*, the suffix *iñ* shall be applied in the sense of a descendant, provided that the stem ends in the genitive case. Example: Dākṣi.

SK 1096: And [the suffix *iñ* is applied] after [words beginning with] *bāhu* etc. (A 4.1.96): *bāhaviḥ*, *auḍulomiḥ*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). SK 1097: After *sudhātṛ*, the suffix *akaṅ* is also applied [along with *iñ*]. (A 4.1.97)
And [the suffix] *iñ* [is applied]. The offspring of Sudhātṛ is Saudhātakiḥ. It should be stated that this applies to Vyāsa, Varuḍa, Niṣāda, Caṇḍāla, and Bimba as well (SK 1098).
Regarding Pāṇini 7.3.3, *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyāṃ pūrvau tu tābhyām eva*:

there is no *vṛddhi* substitution for a vowel following final *y* or *v* at the end of a word; rather, the augments *ai* and *au* respectively are inserted before those two. Thus, from Vyāsa we derive Vaiyāsakiḥ, from Varuḍa, Vāruḍakiḥ, and so forth.

Pāṇini 4.1.98: *gotre kuñjādibhyaś caphañ* (the suffix *caphañ* is added after words beginning with *kuñja* when denoting a lineage). Pāṇini 5.3.113: *vrātacphaṇor astriyām* (after words expressing a *vrāta* and after those ending in *caphañ*, the suffix *ñya* is applied in the sense of the base itself, but not in the feminine). The suffix *ñya* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*) after words denoting a *vrāta* and after those ending in *caphañ*, provided it is not in the feminine. For example: *kauñjāyanyaḥ*. In the plural, the elision (*luk*) will be taught because these are *tadrāja* [names of kings]. Similarly: *brādhnāyanyaḥ*. In the feminine: *kauñjāyanī*; here, because it is a genus (*jāti*) by virtue of being a lineage (*gotra*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. In the sense of an immediate descendant (*anantarāpatya*), the form is *kauñjiḥ*.

SK 1101: After [stems] beginning with *naḍa*, the suffix *phak* is applied (A 4.1.99), provided that [the context is] "gotra" (lineage). Examples: *nāḍāyanaḥ*, *cārāyaṇaḥ*. The immediate [derivative] is *nāḍiḥ*.
SK 1102: After [stems] beginning with *harita*, the suffix *añ* is applied (A 4.1.100).

The suffix *phak* is applied after these [names] ending in *yañ* and *iñ* when a younger generation (*yūni*) is to be expressed. For example: *hāritāyanaḥ*. Although this occurs under the heading of *gotra* (lineage), it applies to the younger generation here by virtue of its specific force; for there is no *gotra*-suffix other than those derived from a *gotra*. The group beginning with *harita* is included within the sub-group beginning with *bidādi*. By the rule *yañiñoś ca* (A 4.1.101), *phak* shall be applied after a word ending in *yañ* or *iñ* that denotes a *gotra*. Because it is stated "not preceded by *ā*" (*anāt*), the elision of *ya* prescribed by the rule *āpatyasya ca taddhite* does not take place. Examples: *gārgyāyaṇaḥ*, *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*.

SK 1104: After *śaradvat*, *śunaka*, and *darbha*, the suffix *phak* is applied when [the patronymic] refers to the lineages (*gotra*) of Bhṛgu, Vatsa, and Agrāyaṇa respectively. This is an exception to the suffixes *añ* and *iñ*. The first two [names] belong to the *bidādi* group. If he is a descendant of Bhṛgu, [the form is] *śāradvatāyana*; otherwise, [it is] *śāradvata*. If he is a descendant of Vatsa, [the form is] *śaunakāyana*; otherwise, [it is] *śaunaka*. If he is an Agrāyaṇa, [the form is] *dārbhāyaṇa*; otherwise, [it is] *dārbhi*. SK 1105: After *droṇa*, *parvata*, and *jīvant*, [the suffix *phak* is applied] optionally. (A 4.1.103)

From these [names], *phak* is optionally applied in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*). [Examples: *Dauṇāyanaḥ* / *Drauṇiḥ*; *Pārvatāyanaḥ* / *Pārvatiḥ*; *Jaivantāyanaḥ* / *Jaivantiḥ*. Here, Droṇa is not a *ṛṣi* (seer); however, the term is used figuratively because Aśvatthāman follows immediately after him. Regarding the rule *A 4.1.108*: "After *bidādi* [names], *ac* [is applied] when there is no immediate succession of a *ṛṣi*. From these [names], *añ* is applied in the sense of a lineage. However, for those among them who are not *ṛṣis*, it is applied to the immediate descendant. In the rule, *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). The offspring of Bidu in the lineage is *Baidaḥ*. The immediate descendant is *Baidiḥ*. Because the *bāhvādi* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), *iñ* is applied. The offspring of a son is *Pautraḥ*; [the offspring of a daughter is] *Dauhitraḥ*.

SK 1107: After *garga* and the following, the suffix *yañ* is applied [to form patronymics], provided that the meaning is "lineage" (*gotra*). Examples: *gārgyaḥ*, *vātsyaḥ*. SK 1108: [The elision of the suffixes] *yañ* and *añ* [is applied before a taddhita suffix beginning with a vowel or *y*].

If, in the context of a *gotra* [patronymic], there is an affix *añ* and an affix *añ*, there shall be elision (*luk*) of these two when they form a plural number derived from that [affix], but not in the feminine. Examples: *gargāḥ*, *vatsāḥ*, *bidāḥ*, *ūrvāḥ*. Why "derived from that"? Consider *priyagārgyaḥ* (one who has a dear Gārgya). Why "in the feminine"? Consider *gārgya-striyaḥ* (Gārgya women). Why "in the context of a *gotra*"? Consider *daipyāḥ* and *autsāḥ*. Here, "gotra" refers to what is well-known from the *Pravarādhyāya* [the list of ancestral lineages]; therefore, it does not apply here: *pautrāḥ* (grandsons) and *dauhitrāḥ* (daughters' sons). SK 1109: After *madhu* and *babhru*, there is elision of the *añ* affix when the descendants are respectively Brāhmaṇas and Kauśikas. (A 4.1.106)

In the case of a *gotra* [name], [the suffix] *yañ* is applied: *mādhavyaḥ* for a Brāhmaṇa, but *mādhaviḥ* for another; *bābhravyaḥ* for the Ṛṣi Kauśika, but *bābhraḥ* for another. Although this is established by the inclusion of the word *babhru* in the *gargādi* group, this rule is for the sake of restriction (*niyama*). The result of its inclusion in the *gargādi* group, however, is the application of the rules pertaining to the *lohitādi* group: *bābhravyāyaṇī*. SK 1110: After *kapi* and *bodha*, [the suffix] *yañ* is applied when referring to a descendant of Aṅgiras (*āṅgirasa*) who is a *gotra*. Thus: *kāpyaḥ* and *baudhyaḥ*. Why "when [referring to] Aṅgiras"? [Because otherwise: *kāpeyaḥ* and *baudhiḥ*.

SK 1111 *vataṇḍāc ca* (A 4.1.108): [The suffix *yañ* is applied] only when [the patronymic refers to] an Āṅgirasa. Thus, *vātaṇḍyaḥ*. However, if he is not an Āṅgirasa, since [the name *vataṇḍa*] is listed among the *garga*-group and the *śiva*-group, the suffixes *yañ* and *aṇ* apply respectively. Thus, *vātaṇḍyaḥ* and *vātaṇḍaḥ*. SK 1112 *luk striyām* (A 4.1.102): [The suffix *yañ* is elided] in the feminine.

There shall be *luk* (elision) of the suffix prescribed after *vataṇḍa* when used in the feminine. Because it belongs to the *śārṅgarava*-class, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied: *vataṇḍī*. However, if he is not of the lineage of Aṅgiras, it is *vātaṇḍyāyanī*, because it belongs to the *lohita*-class and thus takes the suffix *ṣpha*. But when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, it is *vātaṇḍī*. Since he is a seer (*ṛṣi*), the suffix *ṣyaṅ* which will be mentioned later does not apply. SK 1113: After words beginning with *aśva*, the suffix *phañ* is added in the sense of a *gotra* (lineage). Thus: *āśvāyanaḥ*. The word "in the masculine" (*puṃsi*) refers to the specific qualifier of the base form (*prakṛti*). The *gotra*-descendant of one born (*jāta*) is *jātāyanaḥ*. Why "in the masculine"? [To exclude: the descendant of one who is born (feminine) is *jāteyaḥ*.

SK 1114: After *bharga*, when denoting a descendant in the *traigarta* lineage, the suffix *phañ* is applied. [Examples: *bhārgāyaṇaḥ* (a Traigarta), *bhārgiranyaḥ*. SK 1115: After words beginning with *śiva*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. (A 4.1.112)

The term *gotra* is excluded [from this context]. *Śaivaḥ* means "the offspring of Śiva. *Gāṅgaḥ* [is formed with the suffix *aṇ*]. Alternatively, by virtue of belonging to the *tikādi* group, the suffix *phiñ* is applied: *gāṅgāyaniḥ*. By virtue of belonging to the *śubhrādi* group, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied: *gāṅgeyaḥ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.113:
*avṛddhābhyo nadīmānuṣībhyas tannāmikābhyaḥ*) [The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after names of rivers and female humans that do not have an initial *vṛddhi* vowel.]

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after [names of] rivers that do not begin with a *vṛddhi* vowel and after names of human females; this is an exception to the suffix *ḍhak*. Examples: *yāmunaḥ* (descendant of Yamunā), *nārmadaḥ* (descendant of Narmadā). The offspring of Cintitā is *caintitaḥ*. Why "after those not beginning with a *vṛddhi* vowel"? Consider: *vāsavadatteyaḥ* (offspring of Vāsavadattā). Why "rivers and so forth"? Consider: *vainateyaḥ* (offspring of Vinatā). Why "after those whose names are such"? Consider: the offspring of Śobhanā is *śobhaneyaḥ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.114): And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the names of sages (*ṛṣi*), the Andhakas, the Vṛṣṇis, and the Kurus.

The seers (*ṛṣi*) are the seers of the mantras: Vāsiṣṭha, Vaiśvāmitra; from the Andhakas, Śvāphalka; from the Vṛṣṇis, Vāsudeva and Aniruddha. In the case of *Śauri*, however, the suffix *iñ* is applied because the word belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group. From the Kurus, Nākula and Sāhadeva; this [suffix *iñ*] is an exception to [the general rule for patronymics], according to the principle that "an intermediate exception [sets aside] a preceding [general rule]. However, after the word *atri*, the suffix *ḍhak* applies because it is subsequent [in the rules]: *Ātreya*. (SK 1118) [Pāṇini 4.1.115:
After the word *mātṛ*, when preceded by a numeral, *sam*, or *bhadra*, [the suffix *ḍhak* is applied].

For a word preceded by a numeral, there shall be the substitution of *mātr̥* for the word *mātṛ*, and the suffix *aṇ*. Examples: *dvaimāturaḥ* ("having two mothers"), *ṣāṇmāturaḥ* ("having six mothers"), *sāṃmāturaḥ* ("having all mothers"), *bhādramāturaḥ* ("having auspicious mothers"). This statement is for the purpose of prescribing the substitution; the suffix, however, is established by the general rule (*utsarga*). The mention of the feminine gender is with reference to the meaning; therefore, it does not apply to *dhānyamātur* ("one whose mother is grain"). Why "preceded by a numeral"? Consider *saumātraḥ* ("son of Sumātr̥"). [In this case,] *vaimātreyaḥ* is formed because [the base] belongs to the *śubhra*-class. (Pāṇini 4.1.116: *kanyāyāḥ kanīna ca*) [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *kanyā*, and the form *kanīna* is also substituted.]

The suffix *ḍhak* is an exception [to the general rule], and by its very application, the substitution of *kanīna-* occurs. Thus, Vyāsa and Karṇa are called *kānīna*. The meaning is: "the offspring of one who has not yet been married. Pāṇini 4.1.117 states:

*vikarṇa-śuṅga-chagalāt vatsa-bharadvāja-atriṣu* (the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *vikarṇa*, *śuṅga*, and *chagala* when the descendants Vatsa, Bharadvāja, and Atri are respectively indicated). Examples: *Vaikarṇa-* refers to a descendant of Vatsa; another [descendant] is *vaikarṇi*. *Śauṅga-* refers to a descendant of Bharadvāja; another [descendant] is *śauṅgi*. *Chāgala-* refers to a descendant of Atri; another [descendant] is *chāgali*. Some, however, read *śuṅga* as ending in the long vowel *ā* (*śuṅgā*). For them, the counter-example would be with the suffix *ḍhak*: *śauṅgeya*.

SK 1121: Regarding *pīlā*, since the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by [A 4.1.117] for those whose names end in that word is set aside, and since the suffix *ḍhak* would apply by virtue of the rule "for words with two syllables" [A 4.1.115], this [suffix *aṇ*] is prescribed as an alternative. The offspring of *Pīlā* is *Pailaḥ* or *Paileyaḥ*.
SK 1122: And *ḍhak* [is applied] after *maṇḍūka*. [A 4.1.119]
And [the suffix] aṇ [is applied]; optionally, iñ [is applied]: Māṇḍūkeyaḥ, Māṇḍūkaḥ, [and] Māṇḍūkiḥ.

SK 1123 *strībhyo ḍhak* (A 4.1.120): The suffix *ḍhak* shall be applied after words ending in feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*). [Examples: *vaidateyaḥ*; by virtue of belonging to the *bāhv-ādi* group, *saumitriḥ*; by virtue of belonging to the *śiva-ādi* group, *sāpatnaḥ*. SK 1124 *dvyacaḥ* (A 4.1.121): [The suffix *ḍhak* is applied] after a word consisting of two syllables [ending in a feminine suffix].

The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after a two-syllable stem ending in a feminine suffix to denote offspring; this is an exception to the *aṇ* prescribed by the rule for names of villages (*tannāmikāṇ*). Examples: *dātteyaḥ*, *pārthaḥ*. However, in the case of *pārthaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam* (A 4.3.120). Furthermore, by the rule *itaś cāniñaḥ* (A 4.1.122), the suffix *ḍhak* shall be applied after a two-syllable stem ending in *i* to denote offspring, provided that the stem does not end in the suffix *iñ*. Examples: *dauleyaḥ*, *naidheyaḥ*.
SK 1126: After [words] such as *śubhra*, the suffix *ḍhak* shall be applied. The descendant of *śubhra* is *śaubhreyaḥ*.
SK 1127: In the case of the suffix *ḍha*, [the substitution of *ai* for the final vowel and the preceding consonant] occurs for *pravāhaṇa*.

When the suffix *ḍha* follows, there is optionally a *vṛddhi* strengthening of the first vowel of the first member, while for the suffix following the word *pravāhaṇa* as the second member, there is *vṛddhi* of the first vowel among the vowels [of that second member]. The descendant of *Pravāhaṇa* is *Prāvāhaṇeyaḥ* or *Pravāhaṇeyaḥ*.

By the rule *tatpratyayasya ca* (A 7.3.29), when a suffix beginning with *ḍha* follows, there is *vṛddhi* of the first vowel of the second member *pravāhaṇa*, while for the first member there is optionally [the same]. The descendant of *Pravāhaṇeya* is *Prāvāhaṇeyiḥ* or *Pravāhaṇeyiḥ*. This rule is formulated because a *vṛddhi* caused by an external *taddhita* suffix cannot be overridden by the optional rule dependent on *ḍha*.

SK 1129: After *vikarṇa* and *kuṣītaka*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied [to form patronymics] when derived from *kāśyapa*. Thus: *vaikarṇeyaḥ* and *kauṣītakeyaḥ*. Otherwise, the forms are *vaikarṇiḥ* and *kauṣītakiḥ*. SK 1130: After *bhru*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied, and the augment *vuk* is added as well. [Thus: *bhrūṇām apatyam* = *bhrauveyaḥ*].

The suffix *ḍhak* [is applied after words beginning with *kalyāṇī*]. [The result is] *bhrauveyaḥ*. According to A 4.1.126, for words such as *kalyāṇī*, there is the substitution of *inaṅ* [for the final vowel and following consonant], and *ḍhak* [is also applied]. Thus: *kālyāṇineyaḥ*; *bāndhakineyaḥ*.

SK 1132: *kulatāyā vā* (A 4.1.127). Only the suffix *inaṅ* is optionally prescribed here; however, the suffix *ḍhak* is obligatory by the preceding rule [A 4.1.126]. Thus, we have *kaulaṭineyaḥ* and *kaulaṭeyaḥ*. In this context, the term *kulaṭā* refers to a virtuous woman who has become a mendicant (*bhikṣukī*). However, for a woman who wanders among families for the sake of sexual misconduct, the suffix *ḍhrak* applies optionally by the rule *kṣudrābhyo vā* (A 4.1.131), resulting in *kaulaṭeraḥ*.

SK 1133: *hṛdbhagasindhvante pūrvapadasya ca* (A 7.3.19). [In these cases, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* occurs not only for the final syllable of the second member but also for the corresponding syllable of the first member.]

In the case of *hṛd* and others, when followed by suffixes marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k*, there is *vṛddhi* substitution for the first vowel of the preceding and following members. The offspring of *suhṛd* is *sauhārdaḥ*. The offspring of *subhagā* is *saubhāgineyaḥ*. Rivers (*sindhavaḥ*) where *saktu* is predominant are called *saktusindhavaḥ*; that which originates in them is *sāktusaindhavaḥ*. [By rule A 4.1.128: *airak* is the suffix after *caṭakā*.

It should be stated that [the suffix] applies to *caṭaka*. By the rule concerning the inclusion of forms distinguished by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), it also applies to the feminine: the offspring of a male *caṭaka* or a female *caṭakā* is *cāṭakairaḥ*. It should be stated that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix in the case of the offspring of the feminine: the offspring of those two when female is *caṭakā*; [here] *ṭāp* is applied because it belongs to the *ajādi* group. SK 1135: After *godhā*, the suffix *ḍhrak* [is applied]. [The offspring] is *daudheraḥ*. Optionally, by virtue of belonging to the *śubhrādi* group, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied: *gaudheyaḥ*.

SK 1136: After *āragudī*, [the suffix] *añ* is applied (A 4.1.130). [Examples: *gaudheraḥ*; alternatively, by virtue of belonging to the *śubhrādi* group, the suffix *ḍhak* is optionally applied: *gaudheyaḥ*. SK 1137: After feminine words denoting low-caste women (*kṣudrā*), [the suffix *ḍhak*] is optionally applied (A 4.1.131).

The suffix *ḍhrak* (or optionally *ḍhak*) is applied after words meaning "deficient in limbs," "deficient in moral conduct," or "mean" (*kṣudra*). Examples: *kāṇeraḥ* / *kāṇeyaḥ*; *dāseraḥ* / *dāseyaḥ*. By A 4.1.132, the suffix *chaṇ* is applied after the word *pitṛṣvasṛ* ("paternal aunt"), superseding the suffix *aṇ*. Example: *paitṛṣvastreyaḥ*.

SK 1139 *ḍhaki lopaḥ* (A 4.1.133): Before the suffix *ḍhak*, there is elision of the final vowel and the consonant following it (*y*) in the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*. By this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), the suffix *ḍhak* is applied [to form] *paitṛṣvaseyaḥ* (the son of a father’s sister). SK 1140 *mātṛṣvasuś ca* (A 4.1.134): [The same applies] after *mātṛṣvasṛ*.

What is stated for the daughter of the father’s sister applies to this as well: *mātṛṣvasrīyaḥ* and *mātṛṣvaseyaḥ*. [Pāṇini 4.1.135] states: “The suffix *ḍhañ* is added after words ending in *catuṣpād*.
[Pāṇini 6.4.147] states: “In the presence of the suffix *ḍha*, there is elision [of the final vowel and consonant] except in the case of *kadrū*.”

There is elision of the final vowel and the following consonant of *kadrū* when followed by the suffix *ḍha*. [Example: *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*. The word *kamaṇḍalu* refers to a specific species of four-footed animal. (Pāṇini 4.1.136) The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after the group beginning with *gṛṣṭi*; this is an exception to the suffixes *aṇ* and *ḍhak*. [Examples: *gārṣṭeyaḥ*; "the offspring of *mitrayu*. Since the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* would otherwise apply, *ḍhañ* is used here.

SK 1144: *kekaya-mitrayu-pralayānāṃ yāder iyaḥ* (A 7.3.2). For these [words], when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* follows, the substitute *iya* shall replace the initial vowel *a*. Thus, when the substitution of *iya* was about to take effect, [the following sūtra applies]: SK 1145: *dāṇḍināyana-hāstināyana-ātharvaṇika-jaihmāśineya-vāsināyani-bhrauṇahatya-dhaivata-sāravāika-ikṣvāka-maitreya-hiraṇmayāni* (A 6.4.174). [The forms *dāṇḍināyana*, *hāstināyana*, *ātharvaṇika*, *jaihmāśineya*, *vāsināyani*, *bhrauṇahatya*, *dhaivata*, *sāravāika*, *aikṣvāka*, *maitreya*, and *hiraṇmaya* are established as such by nipātana.]
These are treated as *nipātas* (irregularly formed words), and thus there is elision of the suffix *-yu*. For example: *maitreyaḥ*, *maitreyau*.

According to A 2.4.63, *yaskādibhyo gotre*, there shall be elision (*luk*) of the patronymic suffix after these [names] when plurality is produced by that very suffix, but not in the feminine. For example: *mitrayavaḥ*.

SK 1147 (A 2.4.65): After *atri*, *bhṛgu*, *kutsa*, *vasiṣṭha*, *gotama*, and *aṅgiras*, there shall be elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix denoting a lineage (*gotra*), when plurality is produced by that [suffix], but not in the feminine. Examples: *atrayaḥ*, *kutsāḥ*, *vasiṣṭhāḥ*, *gotamāḥ*, *aṅgirasaḥ*. SK 1148 (A 2.4.66): After a secondary suffix *iñ* that contains more than two syllables, there is elision of the suffix when plurality is produced by it, provided the lineage belongs to the Easterners (*prācya*) or the Bharatas.
The suffix *iñ* that follows a polysyllabic stem and occurs in a Prācya lineage or a Bharata lineage shall be elided (*luk*). Examples: *pānnāgārāḥ*, *yudhiṣṭhirāḥ*.

(A 2.4.67) *na gopavanādibhyaḥ*: The elision of the gotra-suffix shall not occur after [the stems] beginning with *gopavana*. This is a sub-group (*gaṇa*) included within the *bidādi* group. Examples: *gaupavanāḥ*, *śaigravāḥ*.

SK 1150 (A 2.4.68): *tikakitavādibhyo dvandve* — after these [names], there shall be elision (*luk*) of the patronymic suffix (*gotrapratyaya*) when they form a plural *dvandva* compound. For example: *taikāyanayaḥ* and *kaitavāyanayaḥ*; the suffix *phiñ* applied to *tika* and others is elided, resulting in *tikakitavāḥ*. SK 1151 (A 2.4.69): *upakādibhyo ’nyatarasyām advandve* — after [names] beginning with *upaka*, the elision of the patronymic suffix is optional (*anyatarasyām*) when not forming a *dvandva* compound.

In these cases, when there is a plurality of *gotra* suffixes, their elision (*luk*) may optionally occur in both *dvandva* and non-*dvandva* compounds. *Upakāyanāḥ* and *Lāmakāyanāḥ*: from *naḍa* and others, the suffix *phak* is applied; its elision occurs, resulting in *upakalamakāḥ*. Alternatively: *aupakāyanalāmakāyanāḥ*. *Bhrāṣṭrakāḥ* and *Kapiṣṭhalāḥ*: [resulting in] *bhrāṣṭrakakapiṣṭalāḥ*; alternatively: *bhrāṣṭrakikāpiṣṭalayaḥ*. *Lamakāḥ* and *Lāmakāyanāḥ*. SK 1152: For *Āgastya* and *Kauṇḍinya*, [the forms] *Agasti* and *Kuṇḍina* [are substituted]. (A 2.4.70)

In these two cases, there shall be elision (*luk*) of the *aṇ* and *yañ* suffixes which convey the sense of lineage (*gotra*) when they occur in the plural; for the remaining stem portion, there shall be the respective substitutes *agasti* and *kuṇḍinac*. Thus: *agastayaḥ*, *kuṇḍināḥ*. [Pāṇini 4.1.137] *rāja-śvaśurād yat*: it should be stated that the suffix *yat* is applied to *rājan* only when denoting a species (*jāti*).

SK 1154: In the presence of a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *ya*, the stem remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) when it does not denote an action or an object (*abhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), but not when it denotes an action or an object. Examples: *rājanyaḥ* (son of a king), *śvaśuryaḥ* (son of a father-in-law). Because the term "jāti" (caste/class) is specified [in the rule], one born from a *śūdra* woman and so forth is called *rājanaḥ*.
SK 1155: [The suffix] *an* [is applied according to A 6.4.167].

The suffix *aṇ* shall remain in its original form (*prakṛtyā*); thus, there is no elision of the *ṭi* portion [of the stem]. Why say "not when expressing an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*)"? Consider *rājyam*, which means "the activity or state of a king. (Pāṇini 6.4.166) *saṃyogādiś ca*: A word beginning with a conjunct consonant shall remain in its original form when followed by the suffix *in*. For example, the offspring of a *cakrin* is *cākriṇaḥ*.

SK 1157: *na mapūrvo ’patye ’varmaṇaḥ* (A 6.4.170). A word preceded by *m* does not retain its original form (*anprakṛtyā*) before the patronymic suffix *aṇ*. Example: *bhādrasāmaḥ*. Why "preceded by *m*"? Example: *sautvanaḥ*. Why "in the sense of a descendant (*apatye*)"? Example: *carmaṇā parivṛtaś cārmaṇo rathaḥ* ("a chariot covered with leather"). Why "not preceded by *varman*"? Example: *cakravarmaṇo ’patyaṃ cākravarmaṇaḥ*. It should be stated that this applies optionally to the name *hitanāman*: the descendant of *hitanāman* is either *haitanāmaḥ* or *haitanāmanaḥ*. SK 1158: *brāhmo ’jātau* (A 6.4.171). [The word *brahman* retains its original form] before the suffix *aṇ* when it does not denote a caste (*ajātau*). [Example: *brāhmaṃ dānam*]. When denoting a caste, [the form is *brāhmaṇaḥ*].

In this case, a formal separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*) must be made. First: "The form *brāhma* is established as a substitute for *brahman* when the suffix *aṇ* does not denote a descendant. For example: *brāhmaṃ haviḥ* ("an oblation belonging to Brahmā"). Then: "Except when it denotes a genus. When the suffix *aṇ* denotes a descendant and refers to a genus, there should be no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of *brahman*. For example: *brahmaṇo 'patyaṃ brāhmaṇaḥ* ("the offspring of Brahmā is a Brāhmaṇa"). Why say "when it denotes a descendant"? Consider: *brāhmī auṣadhiḥ* ("a medicinal herb belonging to Brahmā"). SK 1159: *aukṣam anapatye* (A 6.4.173). When the suffix *aṇ* does not denote a descendant, the elision of the *ṭi* is established as a formal exception (*nipātyate*). For example: *aukṣaṃ padam* ("a footprint of a bull"). Why say "when it does not denote a descendant"? Consider: *ukṣṇo 'patyam* ("the offspring of a bull").

SK 1160: *ṣapūrvahandhṛtarājñām aṇi* (A 6.4.135). When the suffix *aṇ* follows, there is elision of the vowel *a* belonging to a stem that begins with *han* or *dhṛtarājan*, provided it is preceded by a word ending in a *ṣ*-sound (*ṣapūrva*), and this applies when the stem is in the *bha*-state. Examples: *aukṣṇaḥ* (from *ukṣan*), *tākṣṇaḥ* (from *takṣan*), *bhrauṇaghnaḥ* (from *bhrūṇahan*). *Dhṛtarājño 'patyam* becomes *dhārtarājñaḥ*. Why "preceded by a *ṣ*-sound"? Consider *sāmno 'patyam*, which becomes *sāmanaḥ* (where the stem does not begin with a *ṣ*-sound). Why "when *aṇ* follows"? Consider *tākṣaṇyaḥ* (which takes the suffix *ṇya*). SK 1161: *kṣatrāddhaḥ* (A 4.1.138). The suffix *dha* is applied after the word *kṣatra* [to denote a descendant].
*kṣatriyaḥ* [is formed with *yañ*] by the rule *jātau* alone; another [word] is *kṣātriyaḥ*.

By *kulāt khaḥ* (A 4.1.139), [we have] *kulīnaḥ*. This suffix is applied even after a compound ending in *kula*, because of the indicator *apūrvapadāt* in the subsequent sūtra; for example, *āḍhyakulīnaḥ*.

SK 1163: After a word beginning with *apūrva-*, the suffixes *yañ*, *ḍhak*, and *añ* are optionally applied [to form derivatives meaning "belonging to that family"]. This applies specifically when the word is *kula*. In the alternative case, the suffix *kha* is applied. Examples: *kulyaḥ*, *kauleyakaḥ*, *kulīnaḥ*. Why is the word *pada-* mentioned [in the rule]? [To exclude cases like] *bahukulyaḥ*, *bāhukuleyakaḥ*, *bahukulīnaḥ*. SK 1164: After the word *mahākula-*, the suffixes *añ* and *khañ* are applied [to form derivatives meaning "belonging to that great family"].
The term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood [from the previous rule]. In the alternative case, the suffix *kha* is applied. Thus: *māhākulaḥ*, *māhākulīnaḥ*, *mahākulīnaḥ*.
According to A 4.1.142, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied after *duṣkula*;
as before, in the alternative case, *kha* is applied. Thus: *dauṣkuleyaḥ*, *duṣkulīnaḥ*.
SK 1166: After *svasu*, the suffix *cha* [is applied] (A 4.1.143);
[the derivative is] *svasrīyaḥ*.
SK 1167: After *bhrātṛ*, [the suffixes] *vyat* and *cha* [are applied] (A 4.1.144).
