*cha* replaces [the suffix *aṇ*] after *bhrātṛ*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*. Examples: *bhrātṛvyaḥ*, *bhrātrīyaḥ*.

By A 4.1.145, *vyat* is substituted for *bhrātṛ* when a descendant is denoted, provided that the combination of base and suffix expresses an enemy (*śatru*). Example: *bhrātṛvyaḥ* as "an enemy. However, the expression *pāpmanā bhrātṛvyeṇa* ("by a sinful enemy") occurs through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
SK 1169: *revatyādibhyaṣ ṭhak* (A 4.1.146). SK 1170: *ṭhasyekaḥ* (A 7.3.50).
There shall be the substitution of *ikā* for *ṭha* that follows an *aṅga*. [Thus: *raivatikaḥ*.

SK 1171: *gotrastriyāḥ kutsane ṇa ca* (A 4.1.147). From a word denoting a woman belonging to a *gotra*, the suffixes *ṇa* and *ṭhak* occur when contempt is expressed; by implication, this refers to a descendant (*yuvan*). Thus, the offspring of a *gārgī* is *gārgaḥ* or *gārgikaḥ* if he is a wretch (*jālmaḥ*). By the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* [which prescribes] *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine stem substitution) before a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a non-*āḍha* vowel, the suffixes *ṇa* and *ṭhak* are applied to the form *gāryya*. There is elision of the final vowel and its following consonant (*yasyeti ca*); there is elision of *ya* by the rule *āpatyasya ca taddhite ’nāti* [when it begins with a vowel]. SK 1172: *vṛddhāṭ ṭhak sauvīreṣu bahulam* (A 4.1.148). The suffix *ṭhak* is diversely applied after a *vṛddha* [stem] to denote a descendant among the Sauvīras.

The *sauvīras* are those born in the land of the *suvīras*. After a *vṛddha* [patronymic] belonging to the *sauvīra* gotra, the suffix *ṭhak* is frequently applied to denote a younger generation when contempt is implied. From *bhāgavitti*, we have *bhāgavittikaḥ*; optionally, by the suffix *phak*, we have *bhāgavittāyanaḥ*. According to A 4.1.149 (*pheś cha ca*), the suffix *cha* is also applied after a stem ending in *phiṣ*.

After a patronymic ending in *phiñ* that does not belong to the Sauvíra lineage, the suffixes *cha* and *ṭhak* are added when contempt is implied. For example, the descendant of Yāmunda is *Yāmundāyaniḥ*; because [the base] belongs to the *tikādi* group, *phiñ* is applied. His descendant is *Yāmundāyanīyaḥ* or *Yāmundāyanikaḥ*. Why "when contempt is implied"? Because *Yāmundāyaniḥ* [is formed with the regular suffix *aṇ*, which is elided by the rule *ṇyakṣatriya-*. Why "Sauvíra"? Because *Taikāyaniḥ* [is formed from a non-Sauvíra base]. A 4.1.150: After *Phāṇṭāhṛti* and *Mimata*, the suffixes *ṇa* and *phiñ* are added.

In the case of *sauvīreṣu*, there is no correspondence according to the respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) here; the author of the Vṛtti states this because of the indication that the word with fewer syllables is placed later. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is established that there is indeed a correspondence according to the respective order. *phaṇṭāhṛtaḥ* / *phāṇṭāhṛtāyaniḥ* / *maimataḥ* / *maimatāyaniḥ*. By rule A 4.1.151, *kurvādibhyo ṇyaḥ*: the suffix *ṇya* is applied to form patronymics. Thus, *kauravyāḥ brāhmaṇāḥ* ("Brāhmaṇas who are descendants of Kurv"), *vāvadūkyāḥ*. The suffix *ṇya* is applied after *samrāj* when referring to a Kṣatriya: *sāmrājyaḥ*. Any other [descendant] is *sāmrājaḥ*.

SK 1176: After *senānta*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *kārin*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied. By the rule *eti saṃjñāyām*, the *s* is changed to *ṣ*. Examples: *hāriṣeṇyaḥ*, *lākṣaṇyaḥ*. From *kārin* meaning "an artisan," we have: *tān tuvāyyaḥ*, *kaumbhakāryaḥ*, *nāpityaḥ*. SK 1177: According to the Northern Grammarians (*udīcām*), the suffix *iñ* is applied [after these].

Hāriṣeṇiḥ, lākṣaṇiḥ, tāntuvāyiḥ, kaumbhakāriḥ. However, in the case of *nāpita*, because it is subsequent [in the rules], only *phiñ* applies: *nāpitāyaniḥ*. There is an addition [to the rule] for *takṣan* with the suffix *aṇ*: due to the rule "when preceded by *ṣa*," there is elision of the vowel *a* in *ana*; thus, *tākṣṇaḥ*. Optionally, *tākṣṇyaḥ*. According to A 4.1.154, *tikādibhyaḥ phiñ*: *taikāyaniḥ*.

SK 1179: By the rules *kauśalyakārmāryābhyām ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.155), the suffix *phiñ* is applied after the words *kauśalya* and *karmārya* to denote offspring; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *iñ*. This [suffix] is desired only after the ultimate base form (*paramaprakṛti*). The base form is irregularly substituted (*nipātita*) in conjunction with the suffix. The offspring of *kuśala* is *Kauśalyāyaniḥ*; the offspring of *karmāra* is *Kārmāryāyaṇiḥ*. It is also [applied] after *chāga* and *vṛṣa*: *Chāgyāyaniḥ*, *Vārṣyāyaṇiḥ*. SK 1180: After a word ending in the suffix *aṇ* that consists of two syllables [the suffix *phiñ* is applied]. (Pāṇini 4.1.156)

The suffix *phiñ* is applied after a word denoting a descendant (*apatya*), as an exception to *iñ*. Example: *kārtrāyaṇiḥ*. Why [is it said] "after [a word ending in] *aṇ*"? Example: *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*. Why "after a word consisting of two syllables" (*dvyacaḥ*)? Example: *aupagaviḥ*. It should be stated that *phiñ* optionally applies to the words beginning with *tyad* (the pronouns). Examples: *tyādāyaniḥ* or *tyādaḥ*. By the rule *udīcāṃ vṛddhād agotrāt* (A 4.1.157), [the suffix *phañ* is applied] after a word denoting a descendant that is *vṛddha* (containing a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable) but not a family name (*gotra*). Example: *āmraguptāyaniḥ*. However, according to the Easterners (*prācām*), it is *āmraguptiḥ*. Why "after a *vṛddha* word"? Example: *dākṣiḥ*. Why "not a family name" (*agotrāt*)? Example: *aupagaviḥ*.

SK 1182: *vākinādīnāṃ kuk ca* (A 4.1.158). For [the words] beginning with *vākin*, the suffix *phiñ* may optionally be applied to denote a descendant (*apatya*), and the augment *kuk* is added. The descendant of *vākinas* is *vākinakāyaniḥ* or *vākiniḥ*.
SK 1183: *putrāntād anyatarasyām* (A 4.1.159). [The suffix *phiñ*] may optionally be applied after a word ending in *putra* to denote a descendant.

Alternatively, since the suffix *phiñ* is established after this [word], when that [suffix] follows, the augment *kuk* is optionally prescribed for a word ending in *putra*. Examples: *gārgīputrakāyaṇiḥ*, *gārgīputrāyaṇiḥ*, *gārgīputriḥ*.
According to Pāṇini 4.1.160 (*prācām avṛddhāt phiñ bahulam*), the form *glucukāyaniḥ* is derived.

SK 1185: After the word *manu*, when the suffix *añ* follows, there is also the augment *ṣuk*. The meaning of the whole is "descendant of Manu": *mānuṣaḥ* / *manuṣyaḥ*. SK 1186: From a word denoting a country (*janapada*), when it refers to a Kṣatriya, the suffix *añ* is applied.

The suffix *añ* occurs after words denoting a *janapada* (country) or a *kṣatriya* (warrior-noble) to form a patronymic. In the word *dāṇḍināyana*, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) is due to a specific grammatical injunction (*nipātana*) in the rule. Examples: *aikṣvākaḥ* (descendant of Ikṣvāku), *aikṣvākau* (the two descendants of Ikṣvāku). From a *janapada* that has the same name as a *kṣatriya*, the suffix is applied to denote its king, just as in the case of a patronymic; this is because of the force of the etymological definition (*anvartha-saṃjñā*) of "tadrāja" (king of that [country]). Example: the king of the *pañcālas* is *pāñcālaḥ*. The suffix *aṇ* should be stated for *pūru*: *pauravaḥ* (descendant of Pūru). The suffix *ṅyaṇ* is applied after *pāṇḍu*: *pāṇḍyaḥ* (descendant of Pāṇḍu). Also, [the suffix *aṇ* applies] after *sālveya* and *gandhāri*: *sālveyaḥ* and *gāndhāraḥ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.169).

The suffix *añ* is applied after these two [names] when forming a word for a descendant; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ñyaṅ* prescribed by the rule *vṛddhet*. Examples: *sālveyaḥ*, *gāndhāraḥ*. The same applies when denoting the king thereof.

By the rule *dvyañmagadhakaliṅgasūramasād aṇ* (A 4.1.170), the suffix *aṇ* is applied after names consisting of two syllables ending in *añ*, as well as after *magadha*, *kaliṅga*, and *sūramasa*; this is an exception to *añ*. Examples: *āṅgaḥ*, *vāṅgaḥ*, *sauhmaḥ*, *māgadhaḥ*, *kāliṅgaḥ*, *sauramasaḥ*. The same applies when denoting the king thereof.

SK 1189: The suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied after [words ending in] *vṛddhi* vowels, as well as after *it*, *kosala*, and *aja*. Examples: from *ambaṣṭha*—*āmbaṣṭhyaḥ*; from *sauvīra*—*sauvīryaḥ*; from *it*—*āvantyaḥ*; from *kosala*—*kausalyaḥ*; the offspring of *ajada* is *ājadyaḥ*. SK 1190: The suffix *ṇya* is applied after [words beginning with] *kuru* and *naḍa*.

*Kauravyaḥ*, *naiṣadhyaḥ*, and *sa naiṣadhasyārthapateḥ*—in such cases, however, the suffix *aṇ* is applied as a secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffix. By the rule *sālvāvayavapratyagrathakalakūṭāśmakād iñ* (A 4.1.173), the suffix *iñ* is applied after [names of] parts of the *sālva* country, after *udumbara* and others, and after the three beginning with *pratyagratha*. This is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*. Examples: *audumbariḥ*, *prātyagrathi*, *kālakūṭiḥ*, *āśmakiḥ*. The same applies when referring to the king (*rājanya*).

SK 1192: Those [patronymics] beginning with *añ* which denote a king (*tadrāja*) shall receive this designation (*etatsaṃjñā*). SK 1193: When these *tadrāja* [patronymics] occur in the plural, provided they do not denote a feminine, [the suffix *taddhita* is elided by] that very same rule.

The suffix of the *tadrāja* [type] is elided (*luk*) when plurality is expressed for the sake of that [kingdom], but not in the feminine. Examples include *ikṣvākavaḥ* and *pañcālāḥ*. How then is one to explain *kauravyāḥ paśavaḥ* ("Kuru cattle") and *tasyām eva raghoḥ pāṇḍyāḥ*? This is to be resolved by understanding that the forms *kauravya* and *pāṇḍya* are used here in their proper sense [without elision]. As for the statement, "I shall describe the lineage of the Raghus, who were somehow obstructed by the Yadus," the words *raghu* and *yadu* are used there figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to denote their descendants. [The rule: *kambojāl luk* (A 4.1.175). [This prescribes the elision of the suffix after the name Kamboja.]

From this [sūtra], there is elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix. [Examples: *kambojau*. It should be stated that [this applies] after *kamboja* and others: *colaḥ*, *śakaḥ*. There is elision of the *aṇ* suffix characterized by having two syllables: *keralaḥ*, *yavanaḥ*. There is elision of the *añ* suffix: the reading *kambojāḥ samare* is easy to understand. However, in the reading beginning with the long vowel (*dīrghādi*), the meaning is "those for whom *kamboja* is their native land" (*abhijana*). The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *sindhu-takṣaśilādibhyo ’ṇ-añ-au*. SK 1195: After *avanti*, *kunti*, and *kuru*, as well as after a *tadrāja* suffix, there shall be elision (*luk*) when a feminine suffix is applied. [Examples: *avantī*, *kuntī*, *kurūḥ*.

And therefore, by [Pāṇini 4.1.177], there is elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix after a *tadrāja* stem ending in the vowel *a*. Examples: *śūrasenī*, *bhadrī*. How is it that we have the expression *mādrīsuta* ("the two sons of Mādrī")? Haradatta maintains that the reading should simply be with a short vowel (*hrasva*). Alternatively, one may assume that [the name] belongs to the *bharga*-class. [By Pāṇini 4.1.178:
There is no elision after Eastern [tribes] or those beginning with *bharga* or *yaudheya*.

The *luk* elision of the *tadrāja* suffix does not apply after these: *pāñcālī*, *vaidarbhī*, *āṅgī*, *vāṅgī*, *māgadhī*; these are Easterners (*prācyāḥ*). However, in the case of *bhārgī*, *kārūśī*, *kaikeyī*, and *kekayī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies because they denote a woman through her relation to a man (*puṃyoga*), characterized by the relationship between wife and husband. From *yudhā* and *śukrā*, the suffix *ḍhak* applies according to the rule "after a word with two syllables. Then, for the sake of expressing the same meaning, the suffix *añ* applies according to the rule "after *pārśva*, *yaudheya*, etc. [yielding *yaudheya* and *śaukreya*]. From this, the suffix *ṅīn* applies according to the rule "after words ending in *añ* such as *śārṅgarava*. If, however, there were *luk* elision by the rule "after a feminine suffix," then because the word would end in *ḍhak*, the *ṅīp* suffix would apply, resulting in the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent of the disappearance of the acute). Thus: *yaudheyī*, *śaukreyī*.

The suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied after a *gotra* [patronymic] stem that does not end in *aṇ* or *iṇ*, provided that the penultimate syllable is heavy (*guru*) and the word is not a Vedic archaism (*anārṣa*).

The last among the suffixes beginning with *try* is called "ultimate" (*uttama*); that which is near it is "penultimate" (*upottama*). When the suffixes *aṇ* or *iñ* have been prescribed after a nominal stem belonging to a lineage (*gotra*) that is not a Vedic name (*anārṣa*), provided that the penultimate syllable of that stem is heavy (*guru*), there shall be the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* for the feminine. Because the rule states that substitutions apply only to what is explicitly mentioned, this applies only to *aṇ* and *iñ*. The markers *ṣ* and *ṅ* are indicatory (*it*): [the marker *ṣ* indicates] the addition of *āp*, and [the marker *ṅ* indicates] the addition of *yaṅ*. Examples: *kaumudagandhyā* (feminine) = the female descendant of *kumudagandhi*; *vārāhyā* (feminine). Why "not Vedic names"? Examples: *vāsiṣṭhī*, *vaiśvāmitrī*. Why "with a heavy penultimate syllable"? Example: *aupagavī*.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied when [the word] denotes a genus (*jāti*). What is the purpose of the condition "in the case of a lineage (*gotra*)"? Consider *āhicchatrī*, meaning "born in Ahicchatra. SK 1199: *gotrāvayavāt* (A 4.1.79). From a word denoting a branch of a lineage—that is, from a family name regarded as part of a lineage—the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* prescribed for a lineage are replaced by *ṣyaṅ* in the feminine. This rule is commenced for the sake of cases where the penultimate syllable is not heavy (*agurūpottama*). Examples: *pauṇikyā*, *bhauṇikyā*.

SK 1200: After [patronymics] beginning with *krauḍi*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied in the feminine. This rule is formulated to include cases where the penultimate syllable is not heavy (*agurūpottama*) and to cover instances where the suffixes *aṇ* or *iñ* do not apply. Examples: *krauḍyā*, *vyāḍyā*. When referring to a young woman, after *sūta*: *sūtyā*. SK 1201: After *daivayajñi*, *śaucivṛkṣi*, *sātyamugri*, and *kāṇḍeviddhi*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is optionally applied in the feminine.

The suffix *ṣyaṅ* is optionally applied after these four [words]. This [rule] is intended for cases where the word does not denote a lineage (*agotra*); however, even when denoting a lineage, it applies because it is a subsequent rule. In the alternative case, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule "after this [word ending in *i*, it denotes a human" (*ito manuṣyaḥ*). Examples include *daivayajñyā* and *daivayajñā*, and so forth. Thus ends the section on descendants (*apatya*).
Among the secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), these are the words with four meanings (*cāturarthika*). 27.

SK 1202: *tana raktaṃ rāgāt* (A 4.2.1). That by which something is dyed is called *rāga*. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words denoting a dyeing substance. "Dyed with *kaṣāya*" is *kāṣāya*; likewise *māñjiṣṭha*. Why say "from a dyeing substance"? [Counter-example: "Cloth dyed by Devadatta. SK 1203: *lākṣārocanāṭ ṭhak* (A 4.2.2). [The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *lākṣā* and *rocana* when they denote a dyeing substance.]

*lākṣikaḥ* (dyed with lac), *raucanikaḥ* (dyed with red arsenic). There is an addition [to the rule] regarding *śakala* and *kardama*: *śākalikaḥ* (dyed with wood-shavings), *kārdamikaḥ* (dyed with mud). According to the author of the Vṛtti, there is also the suffix *aṇ* after these two: *śākalaḥ*, *kārdamaḥ*. After *nīlī*, the suffix *an* [is applied]: that which is dyed with indigo is *nīlam*. After *pīta*, the suffix *kan* [is applied]: *pītakam* (yellow). After *haridrā* and *mahārajana*, the suffix *añ* [is applied]: *hāridram* (dyed with turmeric), *māhārajanam* (dyed with saffron). SK 1204:
Time joined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) [takes the suffix *aṇ*]. That which is joined with the constellation Puṣya is *pauṣamahaḥ* (the Puṣya day), *pauṣī rātriḥ* (the Puṣya night).

SK 1205 (A 4.2.4): *lub aviśeṣe* (there is elision of the suffix when no specific [subdivision] is understood). There shall be elision (*lup*) of that which was prescribed by the preceding rule, provided that no internal subdivision of the time consisting of sixty *daṇḍas* is perceived. For example: "Today is Puṣya. [Objection: How then is it explained that "the full moon day joined with Puṣya is *pauṣī*"? [Response: Because the statement *vibhāṣā phālgunī-śravaṇā-kārtikī-caitrībhyaḥ* indicates that this elision does not apply to the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). However, from the word *śravaṇa*, the forms are derived through irregular derivation (*nipātana*): *śrāvaṇī*. SK 1206 (A 4.2.5): *saṃjñāyāṃ śravaṇā-śvatthābhyām* (when it is a name, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *śravaṇā* and *aśvattha*).

This undertaking is for the sake of a specific meaning. *Śravaṇā* is a night; *aśvattha* is a muhūrta. [Question: What is the purpose of the term *saṃjñāyām*? [Answer: *śrāvaṇī*, *āśvatthī*. (A 4.2.6) *Dvandvāc chaḥ*:

After a *dvandva* compound of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the suffix *cha* shall be applied when denoting a specific time, whether such a specific distinction exists or not. Examples: *tiṣyapunarvasavīyam ahaḥ* (the day belonging to Tiṣya and Punarvasu); *rādhānurādhīyā rātriḥ* (the night belonging to Rādhā and Anurādhā).

SK 1208: [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after a word meaning "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) when it is accompanied by the word "by him" (*tena*). For example: *vasiṣṭhena dṛṣṭaṃ sāma* = *vāsiṣṭhaṃ sāma* ("the Sāman seen by Vasiṣṭha"). In this sense, it should be stated that the suffix *aṇ* optionally takes the marker *ḍit*. Thus: *uśanasā dṛṣṭam* = *auśanam* or *auśanasam*. SK 1209: [The suffix] *ḍhak* is applied after the word *kali*. (A 4.2.8)
The *sāman* seen by Kāleya is called *kāleya*.

By [Pāṇini 4.2.9], *vāma-eva-aḍ-ḍyaḍ-ḍyau*, the *sāman* seen by Vāmadeva is *vāmadevyam*. Since the elision of *yasya* (by Pāṇini 6.4.148) would have already established the form, for what purpose are *ḍya* and *ḍya* prescribed with the marker *ḍ*? The *Mahābhāṣya* states: "The mention [of the suffixes] is for the sake of preventing [the application of] the accent of the negative particle (*nañ*) to *vāmadevyasya*. (SK 1210).

SK 1211 *parivṛto rathaḥ* (A 4.2.10): A chariot covered with cloths is called a *vāstra-ratha*. Why "chariot" (*ratha*)? [Because the rule applies only to this: a body covered by a cloth (*vastra*). "Covered" (*parivṛta*) means surrounded on all sides; therefore, it does not apply here: a chariot surrounded by students (*chātra*). SK 1212 *pāṇḍukambalādiniḥ* (A 4.2.11).

*Pāṇḍukambalī* means "covered with a white woolen blanket" (*pāṇḍukambalena parivṛtaḥ*). The word *pāṇḍukambala* denotes a king or a woolen blanket used for covering. Although the suffix *matup* would have sufficed to express this meaning, the explicit statement [of the suffix *aṇ*] is for the purpose of excluding it.
SK 1213: *dvaipavaiyāghrād añ* (A 4.2.12).
*Dvaipa* is the derivative from *dvīpin* (leopard); that which is covered by it is a *dvaipa* chariot. Likewise, *vaiyāghra*.

SK 1214 *kaumāra-apūrvavacane* (A 4.2.13): The term *kaumāra-* is cited here without a case-ending (*avibhaktika-nirdeśaḥ*). This is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) used in the sense of "not having had [another] husband before" (*apūrvatve*). A husband who has approached a maiden who has not had a previous husband is called a *kaumāra-pati*. Alternatively, a maiden who has not had a previous husband and has approached a husband is called a *kaumāra-bhāryā*. SK 1215 *tatroddhṛtam amatrebhyaḥ* (A 4.2.14): [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after words denoting vessels (*amatra*) in the sense of "taken out from that."]

*śarāva-uddhṛtaḥ* means "rice removed from a shallow dish" (*śarāva-odanaḥ*). Here, the root *ud-dhṛ* refers to placing [something] after first removing it; therefore, the locative case is used. The meaning is "having been removed, it was placed [there].

Regarding *sthaṇḍilāc chayitari vrate* (A 4.2.15), the word *tatra* is understood. If the observance (*vrata*) is understood through the whole expression, [the suffix *cha* is applied]. One who sleeps on a bare ground (*sthaṇḍila*) is a *sthāṇḍila* mendicant.

SK 1217 *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* (A 4.2.16): The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after a word ending in the locative case in the sense of "prepared," provided that what is prepared consists of edible foods (*bhakṣa*). For example: *bhrāṣṭre saṃskṛtāḥ* → *bhrāṣṭrā yavāḥ* ("barley grains prepared on a frying pan"); *aṣṭasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ* → *aṣṭākapālaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* ("a sacrificial cake prepared on eight potsherds"). SK 1218 *śūlokhād yat* (A 4.2.17): The suffix *yat* is applied after the words *śūla* and *ukhā* [in the same sense]. For example: *śūle saṃskṛtam* → *śūlyam* ("prepared on a spit"); *ukhāyāṃ saṃskṛtam* → *aukhyam* ("prepared in a cooking pot").
This is an exception to the [rule for] *aṇ*. That which is prepared on a spit is *sūlya* meat. An *ukhā* is a specific type of vessel; that which is prepared in it is *ukhya*.
By the rule *dadhnaṣṭhak* (A 4.2.18), that which is prepared in curds is *dādhika*.

SK 1220: After *udaśvit*, the suffix *ṭhak* may optionally be applied; in its alternative, *aṇ* is applied. SK 1221: After a stem ending in *i*, *u*, *s*, or *uk*, the suffix *ka* is applied [to form the feminine].

After the suffixes *is* and *us*, when they follow [a nominal stem] ending in *u*, the substitute *ka* shall take the place of the suffix *ṭha*. For example: that which swells or increases by means of water (*udakena*) is called *udaśvit* (curdled milk). That which is prepared therein is *audaśvitkaḥ* or *audaśvitaḥ*. Because the rule specifies the explicit mention (*pratipadokta*) of the suffixes *is* and *us*, this substitution does not apply here: one who acts with a blessing (*āśiṣā*) is *āśiṣikaḥ*; one who acts with dawn (*uṣasā*) is *auṣikaḥ*. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) should be made for the word *doṣa*: one who acts with the arms (*dorbhyām*) is *dauṣkaḥ*.

SK 1222 *kṣīrāḍ ḍhañ* (A 4.2.20): here, only the word *saṃskṛtam* ("prepared") is connected [to the suffix], and not *bhakṣāḥ* ("edibles"). Therefore, it also occurs in the case of barley-gruel (*yavāgū*): *kṣaireyī*. SK 1223 *sāsmin paurṇamāsīti* (A 4.2.21).

From the word *iti* [in the rule], it is understood that this applies when forming a name (*saṃjñā*). *Pauṣī* is the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) of the month of Puṣya; the month containing that is *pauṣa*. By the rule *āgrahāyaṇyaśvatthāṭ ṭhak* (A 4.2.22), [the suffix *ṭhak* is added]. That which has its year (*hāyana*) beginning with this [full moon] is *āgrahāyaṇī*. Since the group beginning with *prajñā* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. By the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* (A 8.4.3), there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. The month in which the *āgrahāyaṇī* full moon occurs is *āgrahāyaṇika*. The full moon joined with the *aśvattha* [nakṣatra] is called *aśvattha*. Due to a formal exception (*nipātana*), the elision (*lup*) of the suffix also occurs here despite the reference to the full moon. Thus, we have *āśvatthika*.

SK 1225 *vibhāṣā phālgunī-śravaṇā-kārttikī-caitrībhyaḥ* (A 4.2.23): After these [words], the suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied; in the alternative case, *aṇ*. Thus: *phālgunikaḥ* / *phālgunaḥ* māsah ("the month Phālguna"); *śrāvaṇikaḥ* / *śrāvaṇaḥ*; *kārtikikaḥ* / *kārtikaḥ*; *caitrikaḥ* / *caitraḥ*. SK 1226 *sāsya devatā* (A 4.2.24): [The suffixes previously mentioned] are applied after a word denoting a deity when it means "this has that as its deity."

"Indra is its deity"—thus it is an *aindra* oblation; likewise, a *pāśupata* or *bārhaspatya* one. The deity is the specific object intended with respect to the substance being relinquished, as indicated by the praise in the mantra. [For example: "The mantra is *aindra*"; or "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed *āgneya* by deity," where the suffix *ḍhak* is applied everywhere for the secondary (*śaiṣika*) sense, [yielding] *agni-ḍhak*. By the rule *kasyet* (A 4.2.25), the word *ka-* undergoes the substitution of *id-* in conjunction with the suffix. Because this occurs after the elision [of the final vowel and consonant] by the rule *yasya*, the initial *vṛddhi* strengthening takes precedence. [Thus: "Brahmā is its deity"—it is a *kāya* oblation. "Śrī is its deity"—it is a *śrāya* [oblation].
SK 1228: After *śukra*, the suffix *dhan* [is applied] (A 4.2.26): *śukriya*. SK 1229:
After *aponaptr̥* and *ānnaptr̥*, the suffix *gha* [is applied] (A 4.2.27).

*aponaptriyam*, *apānnaptriyam*; *aponapāt*, *apānnapāt*—these two deities [are referred to by these names]. The stated forms are established as *nipātana*s (irregularly prescribed forms) in connection with the suffixes [cha and gha]. For this very reason, there is the injunction (*praiṣa*): "Recite for Aponapāt" and "Recite for Apānnapāt. [The sūtra] *cha ca* (A 4.2.28) involves a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) for the purpose of preventing the application of the respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). Thus we have *aponaptrīyam* and *apānnaptrīyam*. From *śatarudra*, [the suffixes] *gha* and *cha* [are applied]. Because of the word *ca*, [the suffix] *cha* is also included. That of which the hundred Rudras are the deity is *śatarudriyam* or *śatarudrīyam*. Due to the force of the specific prescription of the suffixes *gha* and *cha*, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye* does not take place.

SK 1231: After *mahendra*, [the suffixes] *dhāṇ* and *cha* are applied (A 4.2.29). From *cha*, [the feminine suffix] *ī* is added: *mahendriyaṃ haviḥ* ("an oblation for Mahendra"), *māhendram*, and *mahendrīyam*. SK 1232: After *soma*, the suffix *ṭthaṇ* is applied (A 4.2.30).
*Saumya*. Because it ends in *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied: *saumī* (a verse belonging to Soma). According to Pāṇini 4.2.31, *vāyvṛtupitruṣaso yat*:
*vāyavyam* (belonging to Vāyu), *ṛtavyam* (belonging to the seasons).

SK 1234 *rīṅ ṛtaḥ* (A 7.4.27): When a non-*kṛt* suffix beginning with the letter *y* that is not a *sārvadhātuka*, or when the suffix *cv-* follows, the substitute *rīṅ* occurs for a stem ending in *ṛ*. Thus, [by the rule] *yasyeti ca*, we have *pitryam* and *uṣasyam*. SK 1235 *dyāvāpṛthivī-śunāsīra-marutvad-agnīṣoma-vāstoṣpati-gṛhamedhāc cha ca* (A 4.2.32): After the compounds *dyāvāpṛthivī*, *śunāsīra*, *marutvat*, *agnīṣoma*, *vāstoṣpati*, and *gṛhamedha*, the suffix *cha* is also applied [in addition to *aṇ*].
And [the suffix] *yat* is applied: *dyāvāpṛthivīyam*, *dyāvāpṛthivyam*, *śunāsīrīyam*, *śunāsīryam*;
by *agner ḍhak* (A 4.2.33), [we have] *āgneyam*.
SK 1237: After words denoting time, [the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] as in the case of *bhava*;
e.g., *māsikaṃ* and *prāvṛṣeṇyam*.
SK 1238: After the words *mahārāja* and *proṣṭhapada*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; e.g., *māhārājikaḥ* and *proṣṭhapadikaḥ*.

*māhājārikam* / *prauṣṭhapadikam*. According to Pāṇini 7.3.21, *devatādvandve ca*, there shall be vṛddhi of the initial vowel of both the preceding and following members when followed by a suffix marked with Ñ, Ṇ, or K. For example: *āgnimārutam*.
SK 1240 *nendrasya parasya* (A 7.3.22):

The vṛddhi substitute shall not occur for the word *indra* when it follows [another word]. Example: *saumendraḥ*. Why "when it follows"? Example: *aindrāgnaḥ*. SK 1241 *dīrghāc ca varuṇasya* (A 7.3.22): [The vṛddhi substitute shall not occur] for the word *varuṇa* when it follows a long vowel.

There is no *vṛddhi* substitution for the vowel following [the word] *varuṇa* when it follows a long vowel. For example: *aindrāvaruṇam*. Why "after a long vowel"? Consider: *āgnivāruṇīm anaḍvāhīm ālabheta* ("one should sacrifice a cow dedicated to Agni and Varuṇa"). The rule "that which occurs in this" (*tad asmin vartate*) requires an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for words such as *navayajña*: *nāvayajñikaḥ kālaḥ* ("the time of the new sacrifice"); *pākayajñikaḥ* ("the time of the cooked sacrifice"). The suffix *aṇ* should be stated [after the word] *pūrṇamāsa*: because a full moon (*pūrṇa-māsa*) occurs on this day, it is called *paurṇamāsī*, the lunar day (*tithi*).
SK 1242: *pitṛvyamātulamātāmahapitāmahāḥ* (A 4.3.26). [These forms are derived with the suffix *vyat* after the respective bases.]

These [words] are derived through irregular derivation (*nipātana*). From *pitṛ* (father) with the suffix *vyat* when referring to a brother: *pitṛvyaḥ* (paternal uncle). From *mātṛ* (mother) with the suffix *ḍulac*: *mātulaḥ* (maternal uncle). From *mātṛ* and *pitṛ* with the suffix *ḍāmahac* when referring to a father: *mātāmahaḥ* (maternal grandfather); *pitāmahaḥ* (paternal grandfather). When referring to a mother, there is also the suffix *ṣic*: *mātāmahī* (maternal grandmother); *pitāmahī* (paternal grandmother). Regarding *avi* (sheep), the suffixes *soḍha*, *dūsa*, *marīsa*, and *aca* should be stated; because of the presence of the letter *s* in the root, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. From *piñjara* (reddish-brown), the suffixes *piñja* and *peja* are applied: *tilapiñjaḥ* (barren sesame); *tilapejaḥ* (barren sesame)—the meaning is "barren sesame. In the Veda, from *piñjara* there is also the suffix *ḍit*: *tilpiñjaḥ*.
SK 1243: "The collection of that" (A 4.2.37).
A collection of crows is *kākam*; a collection of cranes is *bākam*.
SK 1244: The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *bhikṣā* (A 4.2.38).

The collection of *bhikṣā* (alms) is *bhaikṣam*; the collection of *garbhiṇī* (pregnant women) is *gārbhiṇam*. Here, since the masculine form has been applied by the rule *bhasyāḍhe* [Pāṇini 7.1.89], the rule *inaṇyanapatye* [Pāṇini 6.4.164] applies, stating that when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) beginning with *aṇ* follows—provided it does not denote offspring—the stem *in* remains unchanged. Consequently, by the rule *naśca taddhite* [Pāṇini 6.4.143], the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) does not occur. Thus, the collection of *yuvatī* (young women) is *yauvanam*. From the present participle ending in *śatṛ*, the suffix *añ* is added because it begins with an *anudātta* vowel, resulting in *yauvatam*.

SK 1246: *gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhrarājanyarājaputravatsamanuṣyājād vuñ* (A 4.2.39). The suffix *vuñ* shall be applied after these [words] when forming a collective (*samūha*). Here, "lineage" (*gotra*) refers to the worldly sense, which is simply offspring (*apatya*). SK 1247: *yuvor anākau* (A 7.1.1). [In place of the *yū* and *vū* suffixes, the substitutes *an* and *ak* are applied respectively.]

In place of these two *anunāsika* sounds, *ana* and *aka* are respectively the substitutes. Thus, *glucukāyanīnāṃ samūhaḥ* (the collection of Glucukāyanīs) becomes *glaucukāyanakam*; likewise, *aukṣakam*, and so on. When the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) is about to occur by the rule *āpatyasya ca* [SK 1079], it is stated: "The forms *akerāja*, *manuṣya*, and *yuvan* remain in their original form (*prakṛtyā*). Thus, *rājanyakam* and *mānuṣyakam*. It should be stated that this applies after a *vṛddha* [stem] as well; thus, *vārdhakam*. SK 1248: After *kedāra*, the suffix *yañ* is applied, and by the word "and" (*ca*), *vuñ* is also included. Thus, *kaidāryam* and *kaidārakam*. It should be stated that *yañ* is applied after *gaṇikā*; thus, *gāṇikyam*.

SK 1249: And [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after words ending in *kavaca* (A 4.2.41); and because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is also applied after *kedāra*. A collection of those wearing armor (*kavacin*) is *kāvacikam*; [a collection of fields] is *kaidārīkam*. SK 1250: The suffix *yat* is applied after *brāhmaṇa*, *māṇava*, and *vāḍava* (A 4.2.42).

*brāhmaṇyam*, *māṇavyam*, *vāḍavyam*. An addition [to the rule] is made for *pṛṣṭha*: *pṛṣṭhyam*. By A 4.2.43 (*grāma-anubandhubhyas tal*), [the suffix] *tal* is applied: *grāmatā*, *janatā*, *bandhutā*. It should be stated that [the suffix *tal* is also applied] after *gaja* and *sahāya*: *gajatā*, *sahāyatā*. The suffix *kha* is applied after *ahan* when referring to a sacrifice (*ṛtu*): *ahīnaḥ*. The meaning is: a sacrifice consisting of a series of days (*ahargaṇa*) characterized by Soma-pressings (*sutyā*). Why "when referring to a sacrifice"? [Consider] *āhnaḥ*; here, the suffix *añ* is applied because [the word *ahan*] belongs to the *khaṇḍika*-class. Due to the restriction "only after *ahan* [the suffixes] *ṭa* and *kha*" apply, there is no elision of the final *n*. It should be stated that the suffix *ṇas* is applied after *parśu*.

When a suffix marked with *s* follows, the preceding element shall be designated as a *pada*. Because it does not end in *ab*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. A collection of ribs (*parśu*) is *pārśvam*.
SK 1253 *anudāttāder añ* (A 4.2.44): [The suffix] *añ* is applied [to form a collective noun] after a word that has an *anudātta* accent on its first syllable.
*Kāpotam* (a flock of pigeons), *māyūram* (a flock of peacocks).
According to Pāṇini 4.2.45, *khaṇḍikādibhyaś ca*, the suffix *añ* shall be applied. A collection of *khaṇḍikas* is *khāṇḍikam*.
SK 1255: After words meaning "feet," [the suffix *aṇ*] is applied as in the case of *dharma* (A 4.2.46); e.g., *kāṭhakam*, *chāndogyam*. SK 1256:
After words that do not denote a mind (*acitta*), and after *hastin* and *dhenu*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied (A 4.2.47).

*sāktukam*, *hāstikam*, *dhainukam*. According to A 4.2.48, *keśa* and *aśva* optionally take the suffixes *yañ* and *cha*; in the alternative case, they take *ṭhak* and *aṇ*: *kaiśyam*, *kaiśikam*, *aśvīyam*.
SK 1258: After *pāśa* and the following words, the suffix *ya* [is applied]. Examples:
*pāśyā*, *tṛṇyā*, *dhūmyā*, *vanyā*, *vātyā*. SK 1259: After *khala* and *go*, the suffix *tha* [is applied].

*khalyā*, *gavyā*, *rathyā*. According to A 4.2.51, *initrakaṭyac-ś-ca*, the suffixes *ini*, *tra*, and *kaṭyac* are applied respectively after the words *khala* and the others: *khalinī*, *gotrā*, *rathakaṭhyā*. It should be stated that the suffix *ini* is also added after *khala* and the others: *ḍākinī*, *kuṭumbinī*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).
SK 1261 *viṣayo deśe* (A 4.2.52):

Suffixes such as *aṇ* and others shall be applied after a word ending in the genitive case when it denotes a "domain" (*viṣaya*) that has been thoroughly mastered, provided that this domain is a geographical region (*deśa*). For example: the domain thoroughly mastered by the Śibis is *śaiba*. Why "geographical region"? [Consider: Devadatta’s domain is a section of the Veda (*anuvāka*).
SK 1262 *rājanyādibhyo vuñ* (A 4.2.53): The suffix *vuñ* is applied after words beginning with *rājanya* [in the same sense].

*rājanyakaḥ* / [SK 1263] *bhaurikyādyaiṣukāryādibhyo vidhalbhatkalau* (A 4.2.54): the region that is the domain of the Bhaurikas is *bhaurikividha*; *bhaulikividha*; *aiṣukāribhakta*; *sārasāyanabhakta*.

SK 1264: By the rule *so 'syādir iti cchandasaḥ pragātheṣu* (A 4.2.55), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. For example, because the *paṅkti* meter is its beginning, it is called a *pāṅkta* *pragātha*. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is made for the sake of the word itself: *triṣṭubh* itself is *traiṣṭubham*. SK 1265: [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after words denoting the purpose or the combatants in relation to a battle (*saṃgrāma*).

The phrase "so 'sya" (this belongs to him) is understood [to apply here]. One for whom Subhadrā is the purpose (*prayojana*) of this battle is *saubhadra*. One for whom the Bharatas are the combatants (*yoddhṛ*) of this battle is *bhārata*.
Regarding the rule *tad asyāṃ praharaṇam iti krīḍāyāṃ ṇaḥ* (A 4.2.57): in the sense that "this is the weapon (*praharaṇa*) used in this game," the suffix *ṇa* is applied;
thus, a game in which a staff (*daṇḍa*) is the weapon is *dāṇḍā*, and one in which a fist (*muṣṭi*) is the weapon is *mauṣṭā*.

SK 1267: *ghañaḥ sāsyāṃ kriyeti ñaḥ* (A 4.2.58). After a word ending in *ghañ* that denotes an action and is in the nominative case, the suffix *ñ* occurs in the feminine gender in the sense of the locative "in this [time]" (*asyām*). Because the mention of *ghañ* includes the inclusion of *kṛt*-suffixes, it applies even to words preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. SK 1268: *śyenatilasya pāte ñe* (A 6.3.71). [In the compound *śyenatilapāta*, the elision of the middle term occurs] when the suffix *ñ* follows *pāta*.

The augment *mum* is added to the words *śyena* and *tila* when followed by the word *pāta* as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) in which the suffix *ya* occurs. In the sense of "hunting in which the swoop of a hawk (*śyenapāta*) occurs," there is *śyainaṃpātā*. In the sense of "the funeral offering (*svadhā*) in which the falling of sesame seeds (*tilapāta*) occurs," there is *tailaṃpātā*. Why [is it] *śyena* and *tila*? [Consider: "the day on which the falling of a staff (*daṇḍapāta*) occurs" is *dāṇḍapātā tithiḥ*.
[The rule] *tadadhīte tadveda* (A 4.2.59) [states]: one who studies or knows that [subject] is called a *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* (grammarian), if he studies or knows grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

SK 1270: *kratūkthādisūtrāntāṭ ṭak* (A 4.2.60). Here, only those [words] denoting specific sacrifices (*kratu*) are taken. From these, when used in their primary sense, the suffix applies to one who knows [the sacrifice]; when they refer to the texts that expound them, it applies to one who studies them. Examples: *āgniṣṭomikaḥ* (one who knows the Agniṣṭoma), *vājapeyikaḥ* (one who knows the Vājapeya). The word *uktha* refers to a specific Sāman; by metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to a specific text characterized by that [Sāman]. One who studies or knows that is called *aukthikaḥ*. However, from the word *uktha* in its primary sense, the suffixes *ṭak* and *aṇ* are not desired. Examples: *nyāyam*, *naiyāyikaḥ* (one who knows the Nyāya); *vṛttim*, *vārtikaḥ* (one who knows the Vṛtti).

*Lokāyata* and *laukāyatika*, and so forth. However, according to the Sūtrānta, [the suffix] is desired only after *kalpa* and the like; thus, one who belongs to the *Sāṃgraha-sūtra* is a *sāṃgrahasūtrika*. After what [words] other than *kalpa* and the like? After *kalpasūtra*: a *kālpasūtra*. It should be stated that [the suffix] also follows words ending in *vidyā*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *kalpa*: a *vāyasavidyika* (one who knows the science of crows), a *gaulakṣaṇika* (one who knows the characteristics of cows), an *āśvalakṣaṇika* (one who knows the characteristics of horses), and a *pāraśarakalpika* (one who knows the ritual manual for the Pāraśara). It should be stated that [the suffix] does not follow words ending in *vidyā* preceded by *aṅga*, *kṣatra*, *dharma*, or *tri*: *āṅgavidyā*; one who studies or knows that is a *traividya*.

And [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after the words *ākhyāna*, *ākhyāyikā*, *itihāsa*, and *purāṇa*. An *ākhyāna* composed concerning Yavakrīta is, by metaphorical usage, called "Yavakrīta"; one who studies or knows that is a *yāvakrītikaḥ*. An *ākhyāyikā* composed concerning Vāsavadattā is "Vāsavadattā. In the sense of "a work composed concerning [a person]," the suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in a long vowel; this [suffix] is then elided by the rule "there is frequent elision (*lup*) of [the suffixes] *cha* and *ṭhak* after *ākhyāyikā*. From that, by this [present rule], *ṭhak* is applied: *vāsavadattikaḥ*. Similarly, *aitihāsikaḥ* and *paurāṇikaḥ*.

It should be stated that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix after [compounds] beginning with *sarva* and those beginning with *sa*. *Sarvavedaḥ*: one who has studied all the Vedas. *Sarvatantraḥ*: one who has mastered all systems. *Savārtikaḥ*: one who has mastered [the work] together with the Vārtikas. By the rule "elision of the suffix after a *dvigu*," there is elision: *dvitantraḥ*. After [words ending in] *ikan*, *pada* as the final member, and [words ending in] *śata* and *ṣaṣṭi*, the suffix *ṣikan* is applied to form words meaning "one who studies" (*pathin*). *pūrvapadikaḥ*: one who studies the *Pūrvapada*. *uttarapadikaḥ*: one who studies the *Uttarapada*. *śatapathikaḥ*: one who studies the *Śatapatha*. *śatapathikī*: a female student of the *Śatapatha*. *ṣaṣṭhipathikaḥ*: one who studies the *Ṣaṣṭhipatha*. *ṣaṣṭhipathikī*: a female student of the *Ṣaṣṭhipatha*. SK 1271: The suffix *vun* is applied after [words] such as *krama*. *kramakaḥ*: one who studies the *Krama-pāṭha*. The *kramādi* group consists of: *krama*, *pada*, *śikṣā*, *mīmāṃsā*, etc.

SK 1272 *anubrāhmaṇādiniḥ* (A 4.2.62): In the sense of "one who studies that" or "one who knows that. A text similar to a *brāhmaṇa* is an *anubrāhmaṇa*; one who studies that is an *anubrāhmaṇī*. Although this would be established by the suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*), this rule is for the purpose of precluding the suffix *aṇ*. SK 1273 *vasantādibhyaṣ ṭhak* (A 4.2.63): [The suffix] *ṭhak* [is applied] after words beginning with *vasanta*.

One who studies the Vāsantika [text] is a *vāsantika*. One who studies the *Atharvan* is an *ātharvaṇika*; here, due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) prescribed in the rule for *dāṇḍināyana*, there is no elision of the suffix *ṭi*. SK 1274: *proktāl luk* (A 4.2.64). There shall be elision (*luk*) of the suffix denoting the student or knower (*adhyetṛ-veditṛ-pratyaya*) following a suffix that conveys the sense of "taught by" (*prokta*). The act of bargaining is *paṇaḥ*. The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the suffix *ghañ* according to the rule *ghañ-arthe ka-vihānam*. That which possesses this [bargaining] is *paṇī*; the lineage descendant (*gotrāpatya*) of that *paṇī* is *pāṇinaḥ*.

SK 1275: *gāthividathikeśigaṇipaṇinaś ca* (A 6.4.165). These [words] remain in their original form (*prakṛtyā*) before the suffix *aṇ*. Thus, there is no elision of the *ṭi* portion. Thereafter, the suffix *iñ* is added for the younger generation (*yūni*): *pāṇiniḥ*. SK 1276: *ṇyakṣatriyārṣañito yūni lug aṇiñoḥ* (A 2.4.58). For the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* derived from *ṇya*, *kṣatriya*, *ārṣa*, and those ending in *añ*, there is elision (*luk*) when applied to the younger generation.

There shall be elision (*luk*) of the *aṇ* and *iñ* suffixes when they follow a word ending in a *ṇya*-suffix, a *gotra*-suffix denoting a *kṣatriya* lineage, a *gotra*-suffix denoting a *daṃṣṭrin* (snake) name, or a suffix marked with *ñ*, provided these suffixes denote a younger descendant (*yuvan*). Examples: *Kauravyaḥ* is the father; *Kauravyaḥ* is the son. *Śvāphalkaḥ* is the father; *Śvāphalkaḥ* is the son. *Vāsiṣṭhaḥ* is the father; *Vāsiṣṭhaḥ* is the son. *Taikāyaniḥ* is the father. From that [name], the suffix *iñ* is applied: *Kauhaḍiḥ* is the son. Why "denoting a younger descendant" (*yūni*)? Consider: the pupils of Vāmarathya are *Vāmarathāḥ*. (In this case, there is no elision.)

Thus, the elision (*luk*) of the *aṇ* suffix does not occur here, because by the mention of "Vedic" (*ārṣa*), only that *aṇ* which is explicitly prescribed for seers (*ṛṣi*) is intended. [In the case of] "proclaimed by Pāṇini" (*pāṇininā proktam*), the suffix is *cha* according to [Pāṇini 4.3.101] *vṛddhāc chaḥ*; the *aṇ* suffix [of 4.3.102] does not apply, because it will be stated later [under 4.3.128] that [the suffix *cha* applies] after a word ending in *iñ* that denotes a lineage (*gotra*). From that [word ending in *cha*], there is elision of the *aṇ* suffix denoting one who studies or knows [the work]. There is a difference regarding accent and the feminine form: [it becomes] *pāṇinīyaḥ* and *pāṇinīyā*. [The rule] *sūtrāc ca kopadhāt* (A 4.2.65) [also applies].

There shall be elision (*luk*) of the suffixes denoting one who studies or knows [a work] when that work is designated by a *sūtra* and its penultimate letter is *ka*. This rule is commenced for the sake of cases not previously covered. For example: *aṣṭakaṃ pāṇineḥ sūtram*, meaning "the Sūtra of Pāṇini consists of eight chapters. Those who study or know it are called *aṣṭakāḥ*. According to A 4.2.66: "The *Chandas* [Vedic texts] and the *Brāhmaṇas* are also [designated by the number of their sections], provided they refer to that [subject]."

The *chandas* (Vedic texts) and the *brāhmaṇas*, when ending in suffixes denoting "proclaimed by," should have that [person] as their scope; the meaning is that they are not to be used without a suffix denoting the student or the knower. For example: *kaṭhāḥ* ("the Kaṭhas") refers to those who study what was proclaimed by Kaṭha. [The formation is as follows: from the word *vaiśampāyana*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied because he is a pupil of Vaiśampāyana (*vaiśampāyanāntevāsī*). By the rule "after *kaṭha* and *caraka*," there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. Then the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and by the rule "after a word denoting what has been proclaimed (*prokta*)," there is elision of that [suffix *aṇ*].

SK 1279: [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] in the sense that "it exists in this," when the name refers to a place; for example, *audumbara*, meaning "there are *udumbara* trees in this place. SK 1280: [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] in the sense of "produced by means of that" (*tena nirvṛttam*).
The city Kauśāmbī was founded by Kuśāmba; [the suffix -aṇ is applied] in the sense of "his residence" (A 4.2.69). The country that is the residence of the Śibis is called Śaiba.

SK 1282 *adūrabhavaś ca* (A 4.2.70): "Not far from Vidisā" is a city; thus, the city not far from Vidisā is called Vaidiśa. By the word *ca* ("and"), the three previously mentioned meanings are brought together. Consequently, it is established that the suffixes to be mentioned hereafter possess the fourfold meaning (*cāturarthikatva*). SK 1283 *ar añ* (A 4.2.71).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*. [Examples: *kakṣatu*, *kākṣatavam*. However, in the case of a river name, *matup* applies because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]: *ikṣumatī*. [A 4.2.72] *matoś ca bahvajaṅgāt*: After a word ending in *matup* whose stem (*aṅga*) contains many vowels (*bahvac*), the suffix *añ* is applied instead of *nāṇ*. [Example: *saidhrakāvatam*. Why does [the rule] say "having many vowels" (*bahvac*)? [Counter-example: *āhimatam*. The mention of "stem" (*aṅga*) is for the purpose of qualifying that [term "many vowels"].
SK 1285 *bahvacaḥ kūpeṣu* (A 4.2.73): This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. A well constructed with a long rope is called *dairghavaratraḥ kūpaḥ*.
SK 1286 *udak ca vipāśaḥ* (A 4.2.74): [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word ending in *udaka*, except when it refers to the river Vipāś.]

The suffix *añ* is applied after words denoting wells (*kūpa*) located on the northern bank of the Vipāś river, provided that the undertaking was not for the sake of many people. A well completed by Datta is called *dātta*. Why "water" (*udaka*)? [Because the rule applies only to wells containing water; on the southern bank of the Vipāś, only the suffix *aṇ* is applied. (SK 1287) Regarding the rule *saṅkalādibhyaś ca*: the phrase "in the case of wells" (*kūpeṣu*) is no longer operative here. That which is completed by Saṅkala is *sāṅkalam*; likewise, *pauṣkalam*.

SK 1288 (A 4.2.76): When feminine names of the countries Sauvīra, Sālva, and Prācya are to be expressed, the suffix *añ* is applied. For example: in Sauvīra, a city established by Dattāmitra is called *Dāttāmitrī*; in Sālva, *Vaidhūmāgnī*; in Prācya, *Mākandī*. SK 1289 (A 4.2.77): From [the group of countries] beginning with Suvāstu, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the previous rule]. *Sauvāstavam* means "located not far from Suvāstu. *Vārṇavam* means "belonging to the class (*varṇa*). The mention of the suffix *aṇ* is for the purpose of superseding the suffix *matup* when applied to a river name; thus, *sauvāstavī*. SK 1290: *roṇī* (A 4.2.78). From the word *roṇī* and from words ending in it, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; this is an exception to the suffix *añ* used after the word *kūpa*. Thus, *rauṇaḥ* ("produced from a cave") and *ajakaroṇaḥ* ("produced from a goat-cave").

SK 1291 *kopadhāc ca* (A 4.2.79): The suffix *aṇ* [is applied after a word ending in *ka* as a penultimate letter]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *añ*. Examples: *kārṇacchidrakaḥ kūpaḥ* ("a well belonging to Karṇacchidra"), *kārkavākavam*, *traiśaṅkavam*. SK 1292 *vuñ-chaṇ-kaṭhac-ila-senira-aḍ-ṇya-y-ay-pha-kphiñ-iñ-ñya-kak-ṭhak*: [The following suffixes are applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*tasyedam*): *vuñ*, *chaṇ*, *kaṭhac*, *il*, *senira*, *aḍ*, *ṇya*, *y*, *ay*, *phak*, *phiñ*, *iñ*, *ñya*, *kak*, *ṭhak*.

[The suffix *cha* is applied after the following words: rīhaṇa, kṛśāśva, ṛśya, kumuda, kāśa, tṛṇa, prekṣā, aśmasakhin, saṅkāśa, bala, pakṣa, karṇa, sutaṅgama, pragadina, varāha, kumuda, and so forth. (Pāṇini 4.2.80)

From these seventeen [bases], seventeen suffixes follow in order to express the four meanings [beginning with "produced from"]: 1. *vuñ* after *arīhaṇa* and others: *ārīhaṇaka* (produced by Arīhaṇa). 2. *chaṇ* after *kṛśāśva* and others: *kārśāśvīya*. 3. *ila* after *ṛśya* and others: *kāśila*. 4. *sa* after *tṛṇa* and others: *tṛṇasa*. 5. *ini* after *prekṣā* and others: *prekṣī*. 6. *ra* after *aśman* and others: *aśmara*. 7. *ḍhañ* after *sakhi* and others: *sākheya*. 8. *ṇya* after *saṅkāśa* and others: *sāṅkāśya*. 9. *ya* after *bala* and others: *balya*.

*Phak* is added after *pakṣa* and others: *pākṣāyaṇaḥ*. After *pathin*, [the suffix *phak* is added] and *pathin* is replaced by *pantha*: *pānthāyanaḥ*. *Phiñ* is added after *karṇa* and others: *kārṇāyaniḥ*. After *sutaṅgama* and others, *iñ* is added: *sautaṅgamiḥ*. After *pragadin* and others, *ñya* is added: *pragadin*, *prāgadyaḥ*. After *varāha* and others, *kak* is added: *vārāhakaḥ*. After *kumuda* and others, *ṭhak* is added: *kaumudikaḥ*. (SK 1293) *janapade luk*:
when a country (*janapada*) is to be expressed, there shall be elision (*luk*) of the suffixes having fourfold meanings (*cāturarthika*).

SK 1294: *lupi yuktavad vyaktivacane* (A 1.2.51). When *lup* occurs, the gender and number are like those of the base (*prakṛti*). For example: "The country which is the dwelling place of the Pañcālas" is called *pañcālāḥ*; likewise, *kuravaḥ*, *aṅgāḥ*, *vaṅgāḥ*, and *kaliṅgāḥ*. SK 1295: *tadaśiṣyaṃ saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt* (A 1.2.53). That [gender and number] need not be prescribed, because the name itself is the authority.
A statement [of derivation] as if it were logically justified (*yuktavat*) should not be made, because names (*saṃjñā*) are authoritative in themselves.
According to the rule *lubyogāprakhyānāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.54),
even the elision (*lub*) [of the suffix] should not be applied, since the meaning of the constituent parts (*avayavārtha*) is not perceived here.
SK 1297: And if it were based on the authority of *yoga*, then in its absence there would be no perception [of the meaning] (A 1.2.55).
For if this [word] were to convey its meaning through the power of *yoga* (etymological derivation), then it would not be perceived when that [yoga] is absent.
SK 1298: The statement regarding the meaning of the primary suffix is made because the meaning [of the word] is established by other means of valid cognition (A 1.2.56).

Even a statement of the form "the meaning of the suffix is primary" is not something that requires an explicit rule (*aśiṣya*). Why? Because the meaning is established through common worldly usage alone. (SK 1299) The same applies to "time" and "subordinate element" (*upasarjana*) [as defined by A 1.2.57]:

a day is called "of today" (*adyatana*) when it is joined with the latter half of the past night and the former half of the coming night. Regarding the technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) formulated by previous teachers—that "a qualifier is a subordinate element" (*viśeṣaṇam upasarjanam*)—and so forth, the fact that it does not require an explicit rule is likewise the same, because it is well-known in the world.
Pāṇini 1.2.52: *viśeṇānāṃ cājāteḥ* (And for qualifiers, when there is elision [of the suffix], the gender and number of those [qualifiers] are the same as that [base], with the exception of genus).

Even for qualifiers of that which has its suffix elided (*lub-artha*), the gender and number are like those [of the base], provided they do not denote a genus (*ajāteḥ*). Examples: *pañcālā ramaṇīyāḥ* ("The Pañcālas are pleasant"); *godau ramaṇīyau* ("The two Godau [rivers] are pleasant"). Why "with the exception of genus"? Consider: *pañcālā janapadaḥ* ("The Pañcāla country"); *godau grāmaḥ* ("The Godau village"). In the case of *harītakī* and similar words, the individual instance is denoted: *harītakyāḥ phalāni harītakyaḥ* ("The fruits of the *harītakī* tree are *harītakyaḥ* [plural]"). In the case of *khalatika* and similar words, the number is denoted: *khalatikasya parvatasyādūrabhavāni khalatikaṃ vanāni* ("The forests situated not far from Mount Khalatika are *khalatikaṃ* [neuter plural]"). There is a prohibition regarding the elision of the suffix after a word denoting a human being (*manuṣya-lupi*).

The meaning is that when the suffix *lup* is applied in the sense of "characteristic of a human" (*manuṣyalakṣaṇa*), the rule does not apply to the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), but it does apply to the word ending in *lup*. Example: *cañcā abhirūpaḥ* ("a handsome puppet"). And from the rule *varaṇādibhyaś ca* (A 4.2.82): this rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding the designation of a "country" (*janapada*). A city situated near the Varaṇā river is called *varaṇāḥ*.

SK 1302: After the word *śarkarā*, there may optionally be elision (*lup*) of the suffixes expressing the four meanings [of place]. SK 1303: Furthermore, the suffixes *ṭhak* and *cha* [may also be elided].

These two suffixes (*ṭhak* and *ka*) apply after the word *śarkarā*. Because of its inclusion in both the *kumuda* and *varāha* groups, there is optionally the suffix *aṇ* by virtue of the force of the rule's formulation; and because of the explicit mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*), there is also the general suffix *aṇ*, for which the elision (*lub-vikalpa*) is optional. Thus, there are six forms: *śarkarā*, *śārkaram*, *śārkarikam*, *śarkarīyam*, *śarkarikam*, and *śārkarakam*. The suffix *matup* is applied after a river name to express the four meanings [of place, proximity, etc. (Pāṇini 4.2.85). For example: *ikṣumatī*.

SK 1305: After *madhu* and the others, the suffix *matup* occurs with the fourfold meaning (*cāturarthika*). This rule is commenced for the sake of meanings other than those already covered [by previous rules]. Examples: *madhumān*. SK 1306: After *kumuda*, *naḍa*, and *vetasa*, the suffix *ṅmatup* occurs.

*kumudvān*, *naḍvān*, *vetasvān*. In the first two cases, [the suffix] *matup* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in a consonant of the *jhay* class" (*jhayaḥ*), and in the last case, it is applied by the rule to be stated later, "after a word ending in *m* or having *m* as its penultimate letter" (*mād upadhāyāḥ*). It should be stated that [the suffix is also applied] after *mahiṣa*: *mahiṣmān* is the name of a country. By the rule *naḍa-śādāḍ ḍvalac* (A 4.2.88), from *naḍa* we get *naḍvalaḥ*. *Śāda* means a swamp or grass; from *śāda* we get *śādvalaḥ*.
SK 1308: By [the rule] *śikhāyā valac* (A 4.2.81), [we derive] *śikhāvalam*.
SK 1309: By [the rule] *utkarādibhyaś chaḥ* (A 4.1.90), [we derive the suffix *cha*].
*utkarīyaḥ*. According to A 4.2.91, *naḍādīnāṃ kuk ca*:
*naḍakīyam*. For *kruñcā*, there is shortening [of the vowel]: *kruñcakīyaḥ*. For *takṣan*, there is the elision of *n*: *takṣakīyaḥ*.

SK 1311: *bilvakādibhyaś chasya luk* (A 6.4.153). For those words beginning with *bilvaka* that are included among the *naḍādi* group, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cha* when a *taddhita* suffix follows. For example: "that in which *bilva* trees exist" is *bilvakīyā*; "those who live in it" are *bailvakāḥ*. Similarly, *vetrakīyāḥ* and *vaitrakāḥ*. Why mention *cha*? So that there may be elision of the suffix *cha* itself, and not the removal of the *kuk* augment. Otherwise, by the rule *saṃniyogaśiṣṭānām*, the *kuk* would also have been removed. The explicit mention of *luk* is for the purpose of total elision; otherwise, there would be mere *lopa* (deletion) of the final phoneme. Thus end the suffixes having four meanings (*cāturarthika*).
Among the secondary suffixes (taddhita), those beginning with Śaiṣika [are now treated].

SK 1312 *śeṣe* (A 4.2.52): "The remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to any meaning other than those beginning with "offspring" (*apatya*) and ending with the four senses of the suffixes; in such cases, the suffixes *aṇ* and others shall apply. That which is perceived by the eye is *cākṣuṣaṃ rūpam* (visible form); sound is *śrāvaṇaḥ śabdaḥ* (audible sound); the person [discussed] in the Upaniṣads is *aupaniṣadaḥ puruṣaḥ*. Flour ground on a grinding stone is *dārṣadāḥ saktavaḥ* (flour ground on a stone); barley-gruel crushed in a mortar is *aulūkhalo yāvakaḥ* (gruel crushed in a mortar). A chariot carried by horses is *āśvo rathaḥ*; a cart drawn by four [oxen] is *cāturaṃ śakaṭam*; a demon seen on the fourteenth day is *cāturdaśaṃ rakṣaḥ*. The term *śeṣe* serves both as a defining rule (*lakṣaṇa*) and as a governing heading (*adhikāra*).
The section on the "remainder" (*śeṣādhikāra*) begins from the point before the rule *tasya vikāraḥ* (SK 1313).

Regarding the rule *rāṣṭrāvārapārāddhakhau* (A 4.2.93): the suffixes *dha* and *kha* are applied respectively after these two words in the sense of the "remainder. Thus, *rāṣṭriyaḥ* ("belonging to the kingdom") and *avārapārīṇaḥ* ("one who has gone from this shore to the other"). It should be stated that [the suffixes apply] even when the compound *avārapāra* is analyzed or reversed: *avārīṇaḥ*, *pārīṇaḥ*, and *pārāvārīṇaḥ*. In this section, suffixes beginning with *dha* and ending with *ṭya*, *uṭya*, and *ul* are taught according to specific bases; their specific meanings, such as "born there," and their governing case endings will now be explained.

SK 1314: After the word *grāma*, the suffixes *yak* and *khañ* are applied [to denote one who belongs to that]. Examples: *grāmyaḥ*, *grāmīṇaḥ*. SK 1315: After words such as *kattra*, the suffix *ḍhakañ* is applied.

The three contemptible ones are the *kat-trayaḥ*. One born therefrom and so forth is a *kāttreyakaḥ*; a *nāgareyakaḥ*; and, because of the continued application of the rule "from *grāma*," a *grāmeyakaḥ*.
(A 4.2.96) *Kula*, *kukṣi*, and *grīvā* [take the suffix *ḍhañ*] in the sense of a dog, a sword, and an ornament respectively:
a *kauleyakaḥ* is a dog; another is *kaulaḥ*. A *kaukṣeyakaḥ* is a sword; another is *kaukṣaḥ*. A *graiveyakaḥ* is an ornament; another is *graivaḥ*.
SK 1317: After words such as *nadī* ("river"), the suffix *ḍhak* is applied [to form adjectives denoting "originating from" or "belonging to"]. Examples:

*nādeyam*, *māheyam*, *vārāṇaseyam*. SK 1318: After the words *dakṣiṇā*, *paścāt*, and *puras*, the suffix *tyak* is applied [with the same meanings]. Examples: *dākṣiṇātya*, *pāścāttya*, *paurastya*.

*dakṣiṇā* ending in *ā* is an indeclinable [used as a base]. [Examples: *dākṣiṇātyaḥ*, *pāścāttyaḥ*, *paurastyaḥ*. According to A 4.2.99, *kāpiśyāḥ śphak*: [the suffix] *śphak* is applied after *kāpiśī*. [Examples:
honey produced in *kāpiśī* is *kāpiśāyanaṃ madhu*; the grape [produced there] is *kāpiśāyanī drākṣā*.

SK 1320: After *raṅku*, when not denoting a human being, the suffixes *aṇ* and [the others] apply; by the word "and" (*ca*), *ṣphak* also applies. Examples: *rāṅkavaḥ gauḥ* (a Rāṅku ox); *rāṅkavāyaṇaḥ*. Why "not a human being"? Example: *rāṅkavakaḥ manuṣyaḥ* (a human being from Raṅku). SK 1321: After *dyu*, *prāc*, *apāc*, *udac*, and *pratīc*, the suffix *yat* applies.
Divya, prācya, apācya, udīcya, pratīcya.
SK 1322: *kaṇṭhāṭ ṭhak* (A 4.2.102); *kānthikaḥ*.

SK 1323: *varṇau vuk* (A 4.2.103). After the word *kaṇṭhā*, which denotes a region near the river *varṇu*—*varṇu* being a river—the suffix *vuk* is applied when the word refers to that region. For example: *kānthakam* "produced in the Himavat mountains. SK 1324: *avyayāt tyap* (A 4.2.104). [The suffix *tyap* is applied after an indeclinable.]

[The suffix *tyaC* is applied] after *am*, *iha*, and *kva-tas-ita-tra*, [respectively] in the senses of "being near" (*amāntika*) and "together with" (*sahārtha*). Examples: *amātyaḥ* ("one who is at home"), *ihatyah* ("belonging here"), *kvatyaḥ* ("belonging where"), *tatastyaḥ* ("belonging from there"), *tatratyaḥ* ("belonging there"). Why is this an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*)? [To exclude: *upariṣṭād bhava aupariṣṭaḥ* ("located above"). There is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of indeclinables (*avyaya*) when any *bha*-suffix follows. This [elision rule] is not universal, because of the specific prescription for the elision of the *ṭi* of *bahiṣ*. Therefore, it does not apply here: *ārātīyaḥ* ("situated nearby"). It should be stated that [the suffix *tyaC* is applied] after *dhruva* with the marker *tyap*: *nityaḥ* ("constant"). [The suffix *tyaC* is applied] after *nis* in the sense of "gone. SK 1325: [There is elision of the *ṭi* of a stem ending in a short vowel] before a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *t*. (A 8.3.101).

The *s* of a word ending in a short vowel followed by *iṇ* becomes *ṣ* before a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) beginning with *t*. *Nirgataḥ* from the *varṇas* and *āśramas* forms *niṣṭyaḥ*, meaning one such as a *caṇḍāla*. From *araṇya* comes the suffix *ṇa*: *āraṇyāḥ sumanasaḥ* ("wild flowers"). From *dūra* comes *etya*: *dūretyaḥ*. From *uttara* comes *āhañ*: *auttarāhaḥ*. SK 1326: *eṣamo hyaḥśvaso ’nyatarasyām* (A 4.2.105). From these, the suffix *tyap* is optionally applied. In its absence, the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* will be mentioned later. *aiṣamastyam* / *aiṣamastanam*; *hyastyam* / *hyastanam*; *śvastyam* / *śvastanam*. In the alternative case, *śauvastikam* will be mentioned.

SK 1327: After a compound ending in *tīra* or *rūpya*, the suffixes *añ* and *ñi* are applied respectively (A 4.2.106). For example: *kākatīram*, *pālvalatīram*, *śaivarūpyam*. It is not stated that the compound must end in *tīra* or *rūpya*; [this is so] lest [the suffixes apply] after a compound preceded by *bahu*, as in *bāhurūpyam*. SK 1328: After a compound whose first member is a cardinal direction (*dik*), the suffix *ña* is applied when it is not a proper name (A 4.2.107).

The suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form patronymics] after [the word] *paurvaśāla*. Why is it said "provided it is not a name"? It is so that [the suffix] does not apply when the base is a proper name. For example, from *pūrveṣukāmaśamī*, the form *pūrvaiṣukāmaśamaḥ* is derived; here, by the rule *prācāṃ grāmanagarāṇām*, there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member.

By the rule *madrebhyo ’ñ* (A 4.2.108), [the suffix *añ* applies] specifically when preceded by a directional term (*dik*). Because of the exclusion of the *madra* countries in the rule *diśo ’madrāṇām*, there is vṛddhi of the initial syllable. Thus, we have *paurvamadraḥ* and *āparamadraḥ*.
SK 1330: After a name of a village in the north that consists of more than two syllables and has an udātta accent on the final syllable, the suffix *añ* shall be applied. Example: Śaivapuram.
SK 1331: The suffix *aṇ* is applied after names ending in *prastha*, those beginning with *palady-*, and those having *ka* as their penultimate element.

*Māhikiprasthaḥ*, *pāladaḥ*, *nailīnakaḥ*. According to A 4.2.111, *kaṇvādibhyo gotre*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after these [names] which end in a *gotra* suffix. *Kaṇva* belongs to the *garga-ādi* group. The students of *Kaṇva* are called *kāṇvāḥ*.

SK 1333 *iñaś ca* (A 4.2.112): After a word ending in the suffix *iñ* that denotes a *gotra*, the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied. Example: *dākṣāḥ*. Why "denoting a *gotra*"? [Consider: this belongs to Sautangama, hence *sautaṅgamīyam*. Here, "lineage" (*gotra*) refers to the technical sense used in this grammatical system, not the common worldly sense. Therefore, it does not apply here: *pāṇinīyam*. SK 1334 *na dvyacaḥ prācyabharateṣu* (A 4.2.113): The suffix *aṇ* is not applied after a two-syllable word denoting a *gotra* when the patronymic refers to people of the Eastern region (*prācya*) or the Bharatas.

The suffix *iña* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*. [Examples: *prāṣṭhīyāḥ*, *kāśīyāḥ*. Although the Bharatas are Easterners (*prācya*), their separate mention here is an indicator (*liṅga*) that they are not included under the term "Easterners" in other rules.
SK 1335: *vṛddhir yasyācāmādis tadvṛddham* (A 1.1.73).
That collection of vowels for which the first among them is a *vṛddhi* vowel shall be designated as *vṛddha*.
SK 1336: The words beginning with *tyad* (i.e., the pronouns) shall have the designation *vṛddha*.
SK 1337: The suffix *cha* is applied after a *vṛddha* [stem].

*śālīyaḥ*, *mālīyaḥ*, *tadīyaḥ*. Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.75 states: *eṅ prācāṃ deśe*. A word beginning with *eṅ* (e or o) among the vowels of the easterners (*prācām*) is optionally designated as *vṛddha* when it denotes a place. Examples: *eṇīpacanaḥ*, *gaunardīyaḥ*, *bhojakaṭīyaḥ*. In the alternative case, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied: *aiṇīpacanaḥ*, *gaunardaḥ*, *bhaujalaṭaḥ*. Why "beginning with *eṅ*"? Consider: *āhicchatraḥ*, *kānyakubjaḥ*. It should be stated that the designation *vṛddha* is optional for proper names (*nāmadheya*). Examples: *daivadattaḥ*, *devadattīyaḥ*.

SK 1339 *bhavataṣṭhakchasau* (A 4.2.115): These two suffixes, *ṭhak* and *cha*, occur after the word *bhavat* when it is a *vṛddha* [patronymic] stem. Thus: *bhāvatkaḥ*. By the rule for the substitution of *jaś* [to *c*], we have *bhavadīyaḥ*. Because the term "after a *vṛddha*" is understood to carry over, only *aṇ* occurs after the present participle form (*śatṛn*) [of *bhavat*]: *bhāvatāḥ*. SK 1340 *kāśyādibhyaṣṭhañ-ñiṭhau* (A 4.2.116): The suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* occur after [the group of words] beginning with *kāśi*.

The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. *Kāśikī*, *kāśikā*; *baidikī*, *baidikā*. [The suffixes *ṅīṣ* and *ṅīp* are applied] after a word ending in a temporal term (*kālānta*) that has *āpad* or similar words as its prior member (*pūrvapada*). *Āpad-ādi* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). Examples: *āpatkālikī*, *āpatkālikā*. A 4.2.117: *vāhīkagrāmebhyaś ca* ("And after names of Vāhīka villages").

After words denoting Vāhīka villages that contain a *vṛddhi*-strengthened vowel in the first syllable, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* are optionally applied. Examples: *saudarśanikī*, *saudarśanikā*, *saudarśanīyā*.

SK 1343: *deśe ṭhañ* (A 4.2.119). The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a word denoting a place that ends in *u*. Examples: *niṣādakarṣūḥ*, *naiṣādakauṣukaḥ*. [In the latter,] the short vowel is substituted by *ke'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.13). Why "denoting a place"? [Consider: *paṭoś chātrāḥ pāṭavāḥ* ("the students of Paṭu"). The mention of *ṭhañ* is for the purpose of excluding *ñiṭhan*. Because it is subsequent in order, this [suffix *ṭhañ*] supersedes *cha* prescribed after a *vṛddha* [place-name]. Example: *dākṣikarṣukaḥ*. SK 1344: *vṛddhāt prācām* (A 4.2.120). [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after a *vṛddha* [place-name] belonging to the Easterners (*prāc*).

This sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that [the suffix *aṇ*] occurs only after a *vṛddha* word denoting a place in the east. Examples: *āḍhakajambukaḥ*, *śākajambukaḥ*. Here, it does not apply: *mallavāstu*, *māllavāstava*. SK 1345: *dhanvayopadhād vuñ* (A 4.2.121).

The suffix *vuñ* shall occur after a *vṛddha* word denoting a place that is either a specific desert (*dhanvan*) or has *ya* as its penultimate letter (*upadha*). Example: *airāvataṃ dhanva* → *airāvatakaḥ*. The words *sāṅkāśya* and *kāmpilya* end in *ṇya* by the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-ādi-sūtra*; thus: *sāṅkāśyakaḥ*, *kāmpilyakaḥ*.

SK 1346: After a word denoting a region that ends in *prastha*, *pura*, or *vaha* and is *vṛddha* (containing a long vowel in the first syllable), the suffix *vuñ* shall be applied. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *cha*. Examples: *mālāprasthakaḥ*, *nāndīpurakaḥ*, *pailuvahakaḥ*. The inclusion of the term *purānta* is for the sake of excluding [the application of this rule to] words ending in *pura* that are not from the East (*aprāgdeśa*). In the case of regions to the east (*prāgdeśa*), however, the desired form is established by the subsequent rule. SK 1347: After a word denoting a region of the Easterners (*prācām*) that has *ra* as its penultimate letter (*ropadha*) or ends in *ita*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied.

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after a word denoting a place in the eastern region (*prāgdeśa*) that begins with a dental nasal (*ropadhāt*) or ends in the vowel *ī*, provided it is a *vṛddha* stem. Examples: *pāṭaliputrakaḥ*; from a stem ending in *ī*: *kākandakaḥ*. SK 1348: *janapadatadavadhyoś ca*.
The suffix *vuñ* occurs after a *vṛddha* stem denoting a country (*janapada*) or its boundary (*tadavadhi*). Examples: *ādarśakaḥ*; *traigartakaḥ*.
SK 1349: *avṛddhād api bahuvacanaviṣayāt* (A 4.2.125).

The suffix *vuñ* shall be applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a country (*janapada*) or its boundary (*tadavadhi*), whether it is non-*vṛddha* or *vṛddha*, provided that it occurs in the plural. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ* after a non-*vṛddha* country and to *cha* after a *vṛddha* country. Examples: - From a non-*vṛddha* country: *āṅgakaḥ*. - From a non-*vṛddha* boundary of a country: *ājamīḍhakaḥ*. - From a *vṛddha* country: *dārvakaḥ*. - From a *vṛddha* boundary of a country: *kālañjarakaḥ*. Why is the term "plural" (*viṣaya*) mentioned? [It is] so that [the suffix] does not apply when plurality is expressed through *ekaśeṣa* (e.g., *aṅgāḥ*). Thus, it should not occur in such cases.

*vartanī*, *vartanī*, *vartanī*—these are *vartanyaḥ*. That which exists in them is *vārtanaḥ*. According to Pāṇini A 4.2.126, *kacchāgnivaktravartottarapadāt*, the suffix *vuñ* shall be applied after place-names ending in *kaccha*, *agni*, *vaktra*, or *varta*, whether they are *vṛddha* or *avṛddha*. Examples: *dārukacchakaḥ*, *kāṇḍāgnakaḥ*, *saindhuvaktrakaḥ*, *bāhuvartakaḥ*.
SK 1351: After words denoting place, such as *dhūma* ("smoke") and others, the suffix *vuñ* is applied [to form a patronymic]. Examples: *dhaumakaḥ*, *tairthakaḥ*.
SK 1352: After the word *nagara* ("city"), [the suffix *vuñ* is applied] in the sense of contempt or proficiency.

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after the word *nagara* when contempt or proficiency is to be understood. For example: *nāgarakaś cauraḥ* (“a thief who is a city-dweller”) or *nāgarakaḥ śilpī* (“a craftsman who is a city-dweller”). Why say “when contempt [or proficiency]”? [Consider: *nāgarā brāhmaṇāḥ* (“city Brahmins”). By rule A 4.2.129 (*araṇyān manuṣye vuñ*), *vuñ* is applied after *araṇya* when referring to a human being; this is an exception to the rule *araṇyāṇ ṇaḥ*. It should be stated that [the suffix applies] when the referents are a path, a chapter (*adhyāya*), a method (*nyāya*), a pleasure grove (*vihāra*), a human, or an elephant. Examples: *āraṇyakaḥ panthāḥ*, *adhyāyaḥ*, *nyāyaḥ*, *vihāraḥ*, *manuṣyaḥ*, or *hastī*. Alternatively, [the suffix applies] when referring to cow-dung (*gomaya*). Examples: *āraṇyakāḥ* or *āraṇyāḥ gomayāḥ* (“cow-dung from the forest”).

SK 1354: After *vibhāṣā* [the suffixes] *kurū-* and *yugaṃdhara-* [the suffix] *vuñ* [is applied]. Examples: *kauravakaḥ* / *kauravaḥ*; *yaugaṃdharakaḥ* / *yaugaṃdharaḥ*. SK 1355: After *madra-* and *vṛji-* [the suffix] *kan* [is applied].
The suffix *vuñ* is used for [names of] regions (*janapada*). One born in the Madra country is a *Madraka*; likewise, a *Vṛjika*. By rule A 4.2.132, *kopadhād aṇ*, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied:
a *Māhiṣika*.

SK 1357: *kacchādibhyaś ca* (A 4.2.133). The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words denoting regions beginning with *kaccha*; it is an exception to *vuñ* and other such suffixes. Examples: *kācchaḥ*, *saindhavaḥ*. SK 1358: *manuṣyatatsthayor vuñ* (A 4.2.134). [The suffix *vuñ* is applied] after a word denoting a region when it signifies a human being or something situated therein.

This is an exception to [the suffix] *yaṇ* after *kaccha*. A person born in *kaccha* and so forth is a *kācchaka*; laughter is *kacchakam*. Why does [the rule] specify "a person"? [To exclude: a *kāccha* ox. Regarding the rule *apadātau sālvāt* (A 4.2.135):

since the suffix *vuñ* is already established for the word *sālva* because it belongs to the *kacchādi* group, this [rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). It means: only when not referring to a foot-soldier (*apadāti*). An example is: a *sālva* Brahmin. Why does it say "not a foot-soldier"? [To exclude: a *sālva* foot-soldier is walking.

SK 1360 *goyavāgvoś ca* (A 4.2.136): After the word *sālva*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied [to denote a product]. This is an exception to the suffix *yaṇ* prescribed after words ending in *kaccha*. Examples: *sālvakaḥ gauḥ* ("a cow from Sālva"), *sālvikā yavāguḥ* ("barley-gruel from Sālva"). Any other [product] is called *sālvam*. SK 1361 *gartottarapadāc chaḥ* (A 4.2.137): After a compound whose final member is *garta*, the suffix *cha* is applied [to denote a product].
In the sense of place, this is an exception to [the suffix] *aṇ*. *vṛkagartīyam*. The mention of "the latter member" (*uttarapada*) is for the purpose of excluding those preceded by *bahu*.
A 4.2.138: *gahādibhyaś ca* ("and after *gaha* and so forth").

The suffix *cha* may be applied [to words ending in *mukha* and *pārśva*, with the elision of the final phoneme]. Thus: *mukhatīyam*, *pārśvatīyam*. This [rule] is intended to indicate that the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) after indeclinables (*avyaya*) is not universal before all *bha*-suffixes. The suffix *ka* is applied to *jana* and to *para*. Thus: *janakīyam*, *parakīyam*. The suffix *ka* is also applied to *deva*. Thus: *devakīyam*. The suffix *ka* is also applied to *sva*. Thus: *svakīyam*. The suffix *chaṇ* should be stated [after the group beginning with] *veṇuka*. Thus: *vaiṇukīyam*, *vaitrakīyam*, *auttarapadakīyam*. [The suffix *chaṇ* is applied] after words beginning with *kaṭa* when they denote regions of the easterners (*prācām*). (A 4.2.139)

The suffix *cha* shall be applied after words such as *kaṭa*, which denote places in the eastern region (*prāgdeśa*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. Examples: *kaṭanagarīyam*, *kaṭaghoṣīyam*, *kaṭapalvalīyam*.
Regarding the rule *rājñaḥ ka ca* (A 4.2.140):

since the suffix *cha* is already established for words denoting a place belonging to a king (*rājan*) that end in a *vṛddhi* vowel, this rule merely prescribes the substitution of *ka* in conjunction with that suffix. Example: *rājakīyam*.
SK 1365 *vṛddhād akekāntakhopadhāt* (A 4.2.141):

The suffix *cha* shall be applied after a word denoting a region that is *vṛddha* (containing a long vowel in the first syllable), ending in *aka*, *ika*, or having *kha* as its penultimate letter (*upadhā*). For example: *brāhmaṇakīyaḥ*, meaning "born in the region named Brāhmaṇaka, where the Brāhmaṇas live by the profession of arms"; *śālmalikīyaḥ*; *āyomukhīyaḥ*. SK 1366 *kanthāpaladanagaragrāmahradottarapadāt* (A 4.2.142): [The suffix *cha* is applied] after a *vṛddha* word denoting a region that has *kanthā*, *palada*, *nagara*, *grāma*, or *hrada* as its final member.

The suffix *cha* shall be applied after a word denoting a place that ends in one of the five words beginning with *kantha*, provided that it is a *vṛddha* [word]. This is an exception to [the application of] *ṭhañ*, *ñiṭha*, and so forth. Examples: *dākṣikanthīyam*, *dākṣipaladīyam*, *dākṣinagarīyam*, *dākṣigrāmīyam*, *dākṣihradīyam*.
According to Pāṇini 4.2.143, *parvatāc ca*:
*parvatīyaḥ*.

SK 1368 *vibhāṣāmanuṣye* (A 4.2.144): When the meaning is other than "human," the suffix *cha* may optionally occur after *parvata*, and in its alternative, the suffix *aṇ*. Thus, *parvatīyāni* or *pārvatāni* phalāni ("fruits from the mountain"). Why say "other than human"? [Observe: *parvatīyo manuṣyaḥ* ("a human from the mountain"). SK 1369 *kṛkaṇaparṇād bhāradvāje* (A 4.2.145): [The suffix *cha* occurs] after *kṛkaṇa* and *parṇa* when [the patronymic] Bhāradvāja is meant.

The suffix *cha* is applied after these two words, *bhāradvāja* and *deśa*. Examples: *kṛkaṇīyam*, *parṇīyam*. Why "after *bhāradvāja*"? [Counter-example: *kārkaṇam*, *pārṇam*. By rule A 4.3.1, *yuṣmadasmadoḥ anyatarasyāṃ khañ ca*, the suffix *khañ* is optionally applied after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; and because of the word *ca* ("and"), the suffix *cha* is also applied. In the alternative case, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Examples: *yuvayoḥ* or *yuṣmākam* ayam iti *yuṣmadīyaḥ*; *asmadīyaḥ*.

SK 1371: In that [context], when the suffix *khañ* or *yaṇ* follows, *yuṣmākā* and *asmākā* are the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. [Examples: *yauṣmākīṇaḥ*, *āsmākīnaḥ*; *yauṣmākaḥ*, *āsmākaḥ*. KS 1372: When used in the singular, *tavaka* and *mamaka* are the substitutes [for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*].

The forms *tavaka* and *mamaka* replace *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, which denote a single referent, when the suffix *khañ* or the suffix *aṇ* follows. Thus: *tāvakīnaḥ*, *tāvakaḥ*; *māmakīnaḥ*, *māmakaḥ*. However, when the suffix *cha* follows, [the following applies]: A 7.2.98 states that when a suffix or a subsequent member of a compound follows, the forms *tvam* and *mau* replace *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in *map* provided they denote a single referent. Thus: *tvadīyaḥ*, *madīyaḥ*.
SK 1374: After *ardha*, [the suffix] *yat* is applied [to form a taddhita derivative];
thus, *ardhya*. SK 1375: [The suffix *yat* is also applied] after compounds preceded by *para*, *avara*, *adhama*, or *uttama*.

*parārdhya*, *avarārdhya*, *adhamārdhya*, *uttamārdhya*. According to Pāṇini 4.3.6, *dikpūrvapadāt ṭhañ ca*: the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a word denoting a direction as the first member [of a compound], and by the word "ca" (*and*), the suffix *yat* is also applied. Thus: *paurvārdhika* and *pūrvārdhya*.

SK 1377. *grāmajanapadaikadeśād añ-ṭhañ-au* (A 4.3.7). The suffixes *añ* and *ṭhañ* are applied after words denoting a part of a village (*grāma*) or a part of a country (*janapada*), provided they are preceded by a word denoting direction (*dik*) and end in *ardha*. For example: *ime 'smākaṃ grāmasya janapadasya vā paurvārdhāḥ* ("these belong to the eastern half of our village or country") or *paurvārdhikāḥ*. [The analysis is: "those which exist in the eastern half of the village" (*grāmasya pūrvasmin ardhe bhavāḥ*). This is a compound formed for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning. The explicit mention of *ṭhañ* is for the sake of clarity; otherwise, if only *añ* were mentioned, one might suspect that *ya* is also being carried over [from the previous rule]. SK 1378. *madhyān maḥ* (A 4.3.8). The suffix *ma* is applied after the word *madhya*.
