*prāk krītāc chaḥ* (A 5.1.1). The suffix *cha* is governed from the point "purchased with that" (*tena krītam*) onwards.

SK 1662 *ugavādibhyo yat* (A 5.1.2): This rule applies up to the word *krīta*. The suffix *yat* shall be added after words ending in *u* and after the group beginning with *go*; it is an exception to the suffix *cha*. For the word *nābhi*, there is the substitution of *nabha*. Thus: *nabhyo 'kṣaḥ* ("an axle fit for the nave") and *nabhyam añjanam* ("ointment for the nave"); this [suffix] occurs only when referring to the nave of a chariot wheel. After the word *śvan*, there is optionally vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and lengthening of the vowel. Thus: *śūnyam* or *śunyam*. After the word *ūdhas*, the suffix *naṅ* is added. Thus: *ūdhanyaḥ*. SK 1663 *kambalāc ca saṃjñāyām* (A 5.1.3).
That which [is made from] it: *kambalya* refers to one hundred palas of wool. Why say "in the sense of a name"? [Otherwise, it would apply to] *kambalīyā ūrṇā* ("wool for a blanket").
A 5.1.4 states: *vibhāṣā havirapūpādibhyaḥ*. [Examples:
*āmikṣyaṃ* or *āmikṣīyaṃ dadhi* ("curd for curds"); *puroḍāśyās* or *puroḍāśīyās taṇḍulāḥ* ("rice grains for a sacrificial cake"); *apūpyam* or *apūpiyam* ("flour for a cake").
SK 1665: The suffix *cha* (ya) is applied in the sense of "beneficial for that" (*tasmai hitam*).

For example: *vatsīyaḥ* ("beneficial for calves") refers to a cowherd; *śaṅkavyam* ("beneficial for a stake") refers to wood. Also: *gavyam*, *haviṣyam*. SK 1666: The suffix *yat* is applied after a word denoting a part of the body (*śarīrāvayava*) [in the sense of "beneficial for that"].

Dental (*dantyam*); guttural (*kaṇṭhyam*); nasal (*nas*) [comes] from *nāsikā*; nasalized (*nasvam*); umbilical (*nābhyam*). Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.7 (*ye ca taddhite*): When a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *y* follows, the word *śiras* undergoes the substitution *śīrṣan*. Example: *śīrṣaṇyaḥ* ("belonging to the head"). Why "in a *taddhita* suffix"? [Consider: *śirasyati* ("he desires a head"). [The rule applies] optionally when referring to hair: *śīrṣaṇyāḥ* or *śirasyāḥ* hairs. It should be stated that the substitution *śīrṣa* occurs before a vowel-initial [suffix]. Thus, before a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel, *śiras* is replaced by *śīrṣa*. Example: *sthaulaśīrṣam* ("belonging to one who has a thick head"; derived from *asthūlaśirasaḥ*).

Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.7: *khalayavamāṣatilavṛṣabrahmaṇaś ca*. The suffix *ya* (forming adjectives meaning "beneficial for") is applied after these words: *khala*, *yava*, *māṣa*, *tila*, *vṛṣa*, and *brahman*. Thus:

*khalyam* (beneficial for threshing floors), *yavyam* (beneficial for barley), *māṣyam* (beneficial for beans), *tilyam* (beneficial for sesame), *vṛṣyam* (beneficial for bulls), and *brahmaṇyam* (beneficial for Brahmins). [The sūtra also includes] *cādrathyāḥ*. Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.8: *ajāvibhyāṃ thyan*. The suffix *thyan* (forming *īya*) is applied after the words *aja* and *avi* (meaning "beneficial for goats" and "beneficial for sheep," respectively). Thus: *ajāyya* and *avīyya*.
*ajathyā* means "not belonging to the herd"; *avithyā*.

[Pāṇini 5.1.9] The suffix *kha* is applied after words ending in *ātman*, *viśvajana*, or a word denoting enjoyment (*bhoga*) as the final member of a compound. [Pāṇini 6.4.169] In the case of this suffix *kha*, the forms *ātman* and *adhvan* undergo substitution [with *ātmanīya* and *ādhvanya* respectively].

These two [suffixes, *cha* and *khañ*,] occur by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*) in the sense of "beneficial for" (*ātmane hita*). [The suffix *cha* occurs after: *ātmanīna* (beneficial for oneself). *viśvajanīna* (beneficial for all people). This is desired only after a *karmadhāraya* compound; after a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* or a *bahuvrīhi*, only *cha* occurs: *viśvajanīya*. There is an extension [of the rule] for *pañcajana*: *pañcajanīya*. After *sarvajana*, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *khaś* occur: *sārvajanikaḥ* and *sarvajanīnaḥ*. After *mahājana*, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs: *māhājanikaḥ*. *mātṛbhogīṇaḥ*, *pitṛbhogīṇaḥ*, *rājabhogīṇaḥ*. After *ācārya*, there is also the substitution of *aṇ* for *cha*: *ācāryabhogīnaḥ*.

SK 1672: After the words *sarva* and *puruṣa*, the suffixes *ṇa* and *ḍhañ* [are applied]. It should be stated that after *sarva*, *ṇa* is optionally [applied]. That which is beneficial for all (*sarvasmai hitam*) is *sārva-* or *sarvīya-*. After *puruṣa*, [the suffixes are applied] in the senses of "killing," "modification," "collection," and "done by him. Because of the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya, the word *tena* ("by him") is inserted in the middle of the *dvandva* compound [of the four senses]. The killing of a person (*puruṣasya vadhaḥ*) is *pauruṣeyaḥ*; since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply by the rule *tasyedam* ("belonging to this"), [this sūtra provides an exception]. A modification of a person (*puruṣasya vikāraḥ*) is *pauruṣeyaḥ*; since the suffix *añ* would otherwise apply by the rule *prāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ* ("after words denoting living beings, *rajata*, etc., the suffix *añ* is applied"), and since the suffix *aṇ* would also apply in the sense of a collection, [this sūtra provides the exceptions].

Māgha says that even when alone, one is as if surrounded by attendants (*pauruṣeya*). The distinction is this: when the suffix *aṇ* would apply to a work composed by him, it does not apply to non-works such as palaces (*prāsāda*) and the like.
Regarding the rule *māṇavacarakābhyāṃ khañ* (A 5.1.11):
"beneficial for a young student" (*māṇava*) is *māṇavīna*; "beneficial for a guard" (*caraka*) is *cārakīṇa*.

SK 1674: *tadarthaṃ vikṛteḥ prakṛtau* (A 5.1.12). When a modification (*vikṛti*) is intended for the sake of something else (*tadartha*), the suffix *cha* shall be applied after a word denoting that modification which ends in the fourth case, provided that the material cause (*prakṛti*) is to be expressed. Examples: *aṅgārebhya etāni aṅgārīyāṇi kāṣṭhāni* ("these are the wood-sticks for the purpose of charcoal"); *prākārīyā iṣṭakāḥ* ("bricks for the purpose of a wall"); *śaṅkavyaṃ dāru* ("wood for the purpose of a stake"). SK 1675: *chadir-upadhi-baler ḍhañ* (A 5.1.13). The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after the words *chadi*, *upadhi*, and *bali* [in the same sense].

*chādiṣeya* refers to grass for covering; *bāleya* refers to rice grains for an elephant. After the word *upadhi*, the suffix *cha* is desired in its own sense (*svārthe*): that which is placed upon (*upadhīyate*) is an *upadhī*, namely a part of a chariot, and that itself is *aupadheya*.

According to A 5.1.14, *ṛṣabhopānahor ñyaḥ*, the suffix *ñya* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *cha*: *ārṣabhya* refers to a calf; *aupānahya* refers to *muñja* grass. This same suffix *ñya* is also applied after the word *carman* by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*): *aupānahyam carma* (leather for a sandal).

SK 1677: *carmaṇo ’ñ* (A 5.1.15). The suffix *añ* shall be applied after a word denoting a modification of leather (*carman*). For example: this leather for a shield is *vārdhraṃ carma*; leather for a plow is *vāratraṃ carma*. SK 1678: *tad asya tad asmin syād iti* (A 5.1.16). [The suffixes previously mentioned are applied] when the sense is "this belongs to him" or "this exists in it."

The phrase "prākāra āsām iṣṭakānāṃ syāt" means "these bricks would constitute a wall," resulting in the term *prākārīyā iṣṭakāḥ* ("bricks for a wall"). *Prāsādīyaṃ dāru* means "wood for a palace. *Prakāro 'smin syāt* means "there would be a rampart in this place," resulting in *prākārīyo deśaḥ* ("a region with a rampart"). The word *iti* indicates that one follows common worldly usage; therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *prāsādo devadattasya syāt* ("the palace would belong to Devadatta").
By the rule *parikhāyā ḍhañ* (A 5.1.17), from *parikhā* we derive *pārikheyī bhūmiḥ* ("land for a moat"). This concludes the section on the suffixes *cha* and *ya*.
For those [rules] beginning with that, the suffixes prescribed for the arha- category apply. 33.
SK 1680: *prāgvateṣ ṭhañ* (A 5.1.18).
Since he will teach the suffix *vati* in the sense of "satisfied by that" (*tena tuṣyam*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is here prescribed as governing the rules prior to that.
SK 1681: *ārhādagopucchasaṃkhyāparimāṇāṭ ṭhak* (A 5.1.19). [The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words ending in *ārhāt*, excluding *gopuccha*, numerals, and measures.]

The suffix *ṭhak* is introduced as an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ* within the governing rule for *ṭhañ*, extending up to the word *arhati* (Pāṇini 5.1.19), with the exception of words such as *gopuccha*.

(SK 1682) The rule *niṣkādibhyaḥ* (A 5.1.20), "from *niṣka* and so forth," governs the seventeen sūtras beginning with *ārhāt* (5.1.19) up to *tena krītam* (5.1.37). Thus, *ṭhak* occurs after *niṣka* and other such words when they are not in a compound, in the sense of "worth" (*ārhīya*). For example: *naiṣkikam* ("worth one *niṣka*"). However, in a compound, *ṭhañ* is used.

SK 1683: *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ* (A 7.3.17). There shall be vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member when a suffix beginning with *ñi* follows, provided the word ending in a measure (*parimāṇa*) is not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*) or the word *śāṇa*. Example: *paramanaiṣkikaḥ*. Why "not a technical name"? Consider: *pañca kalāpāḥ parimāṇam asya* ("five bundles are its measure"), resulting in *pāñcakalāpikam*. Here, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *tad asya parimāṇam*. The mention of "non-compound" (*asamāsa*) in the preceding rule is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the rule of "taking what ends in [the specified term]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies prior to this point. Therefore, we have forms such as *sugavyam* and *yavāpūpyam*. However, from this point onward, the inclusion of what ends in [the specified term] (*tadantagrahaṇa*) is desired for words preceded by a numeral, up to the rule *prāgvateḥ*, and this applies even when the elision of the suffix (*luk*) has occurred. Example: *pārāyaṇikaḥ*.

*dvaipārāyaṇikaḥ* ("one who has studied two *pārāyaṇas*"). Why say "not ending in *luk*"? [Consider: *dviśūrpam* ("bought for two *śūrpa*s"). In the sense of "bought for two *śūrpa*s," let there not be the suffix *añ* after *śūrpa*, but rather *ṭhañ*: *dviśaurpikam*. SK 1684: *ardhāt parimāṇasya pūrvasya tu vā* (A 7.3.26).

When a suffix beginning with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* follows, there is optionally the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the initial vowel of the second member which denotes a measure, and of the preceding member. *ārdhadrauṇikam* ("bought for half a *droṇa*") or *ardhadrauṇikam*.
SK 1685 (*nātaḥ parasya*, A 7.3.27):

When a word denoting a measure follows *ardha-*, the substitution of *vṛddhi* does not occur for the subsequent [member], but it may optionally occur for the first member (*pūrvapada*) when a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ñi* follows. Examples: *ārdhaprasthikam* (formed with obligatory *vṛddhi*) and *ardhaprasthikam* (formed with optional *vṛddhi*). Why "after *ataḥ*" (*ataḥ kim*)? Consider *ārdhakauḍavikam* (where the vowel is short). Why "with *t* as an indicator" (*taparaḥ kim*)? Consider *ardhakhārībhāryaḥ*, derived from *ardhakhāryām bhavā* ("born in half a khārī"). In this case, the prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) by the rule *vṛddhinimittasya...* would not apply if the *t* were not present. SK 1686 (*śatāc ca ṭhanyatāvaśate*, A 5.1.21): The suffixes *ṭhan* and *yat* are added after *śata-* to form words meaning "worth a hundred," provided that the sense is not "not a hundred. (Note: This sūtra provides the basis for the forms *śatikaḥ* and *śatyaḥ*.)

That which is bought for a hundred is *śatikaṃ* or *śatyam*. Why say "not when it is not a hundred"? [Consider: a group whose measure is a hundred is *śatakaḥ saṅghaḥ*. Here, the meaning of the suffix does not in fact differ from the meaning of the base; therefore, the suffixes *ṭhan* and *ṭi* do not apply, but rather only *kan*. This applies only when there is no compound. That which is bought for two hundred is *dviśatakam*. [Rule A 5.1.22: *kan* is added after a numeral that does not end in *ati* or *śad*.

The suffix *kan* is applied to a numeral in the sense of "purchased for that price," but not to one ending in *tya* or *śad*. For example: *pañcabhiḥ krītaḥ* ("bought for five") becomes *pañcakaḥ*; *bahukaḥ* ("bought for many"). However, for a numeral ending in *tya*, it is *sāptatikaḥ*; for one ending in *śad*, it is *cātvāriṃśatkaḥ*. SK 1688: *vatoriḍvā* (A 5.1.23).
After a word ending in *vat*, the augment *iṭ* may optionally be added to the suffix *kan*. Thus: *tāvatikaḥ* or *tāvatkaḥ*.

SK 1689: *viṃśatitriṃśadbhyāṃ ḍvunasaṃjñāyām* (A 5.1.24). A split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) should be made. From these two [stems], the suffix *kan* shall apply; however, when not used as a name (*asaṃjñā*), *ḍvun* shall apply as an exception to *kan*. Examples: *viṃśakaḥ*, *triṃśakaḥ*. But when used as a name (*saṃjñā*), [the forms are] *viṃśatikaḥ*, *triṃśatkaḥ*. SK 1690: *kaṃsāṭ ṭiṭhan* (A 5.1.25). [The suffix *ṭiṭhan* is applied after the word *kaṃsa*.]

The suffix *ṭhaÑ* has the meaning of "worth" (*mūlyārtha*). The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. Examples: *kāṃsikaḥ*, *kāṃsikī*. It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after the word *ardha*: *ardhikaḥ*, *ardhikī*. It should be stated that after the word *kārṣāpaṇa*, the suffix *ṭiṭhan* is applied, and there is optionally the substitution of *prati* [for *kārṣāpaṇa*]: *kārṣāpaṇikaḥ*, *kārṣāpaṇikī*; *pratikaḥ*, *pratikī*. Sūtra 1691: After *śūrpa*, the suffix *añ* is optionally applied. Examples: *śaurpam*, *śaurpikam*.

SK 1692: After *śatamāna*, *viṃśatika*, *sahasra*, and *vasana*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form a word denoting "purchased with"]. This is an exception to the suffixes *ṭhañ*, *ṭhak*, and *kan*. *Śatamānena krītam* ("purchased with a *śatamāna*") becomes *śātamānam*; likewise, *vaiṃśatikam* and *sāhasram*. From *vasana*, we have *vāsanam*. SK 1693:
After a *dvigu* compound whose first member is *adhyardha*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix, provided it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*).

The suffix *ṭhañ* (which forms words meaning "worth" or *arhīya*) following a *dvigu* compound or the word *adhyardha* shall be elided (*luk*). Examples: *adhyardhakaṃsa*, *dvikaṃsa*. However, when used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), it is *pāñcakalāpika*. (Pāṇini 5.1.28).

By the rule *vibhāṣā kārṣāpaṇasahasrābhyām* (A 5.1.29), the elision may optionally occur after *kārṣāpaṇa* and *sahasra*. Examples: *adhyardhakārṣāpaṇa*, *adhyardhakārṣāpaṇika*; *dvikārṣāpaṇa*, *dvikārṣāpaṇika*. There is also elision of the *ṭiṭhan* suffix added by the supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*). In the alternative case: *adhyardhapratika*, *dvipratika*; *adhyardhasahasra*, *adhyardhasāhasra*; *dvisahasra*, *dvisāhasra*.

SK 1695: After a word preceded by *dvi*, the suffix *niṣka* may optionally undergo elision (*lug*). Examples: *dviniṣkam* or *dvinaiṣkikam*; *triniṣkam* or *trinaiṣkikam*. It should be stated that this also applies when preceded by *bahu*: *bahuniṣkam* or *bahunaiṣkikam*. SK 1696: Also after *bista*.

The suffix *luk* may optionally be applied to a word ending in *viṣṭi* preceded by *dvi*, *tri*, or a numeral greater than these, when followed by a word denoting a price (*ārhīya*). Examples include *dvibiṣṭam* and *dvibaistikam*, and so forth.
According to A 5.1.32, the suffix *kha* is added after *viṃśatika* when preceded by *adhyardha* or a numeral (as a *dvigu* compound). Examples include *adhyardhaviṃśatikīnam* and *dviviṃśatikīnam*.
SK 1698: After *khārī*, the suffix *īkan* is applied [to denote a measure]. Examples:

*adhyardhakhārīkam* ("one and a half *khārīs*"), *dvikhārīkam* ("two *khārīs*"). It should be stated that this applies even when the word is used alone: *khārīkam*. SK 1699: After *paṇa*, *pāda*, *māṣa*, and *śata*, the suffix *yat* is applied [to denote a measure].

*adhyardhapaṇyam*, *dvipaṇyam*; *adhyardhapādyam*, *dvipādyam*. Here, the substitution of *pat* for *pāda-* does not occur, because of the status as a *sthānivat* of the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule *yasya...*. Nor does the rule *padyatyatadarthe* apply, because in that context only the meaning of "a limb of a living being" is intended. By the rule *śāṇād vā* (A 5.1.35), the suffix *yat* may optionally apply; in the alternative case, *ṭhañ* applies, which is then elided (*luk*). Thus: *adhyardhaśāṇyam* or *adhyardhaśāṇam*.

SK 1701: *dvitripūrvād aṇ ca* (A 5.1.36). [The rule] "after *śāṇa*" applies here as well. Because of the word *ca*, there is also *yat*. Thus, there are three forms. Due to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ*, there is only initial *vṛddhi*. Therefore: *dvaiśāṇam*, *dviśāṇyam*, and *dviśāṇam*. Here, thirteen suffixes beginning with *ṭhañ* have been introduced; their governing case-endings (*samarthavibhakti*) and meanings were required, and they are now stated. SK 1702: *tena krītam* (A 5.1.37). [That by which something is bought.]

The suffix *ṭhañ* [is applied]: *gopucchena krītam* (bought for a cow's tail) becomes *gaupucchikam*; *sāptatikam* (bought for seventy); *prāsthikam* (bought for a *prastha*). The suffix *ṭhak* [is applied]: *naiṣkikam* (bought for a *niṣka*). [Pāṇini 5.1.18] *idgoṇyāḥ* (A 1.2.40): the vowel *i* is substituted for the final syllable of *goṇī* when a *taddhita* suffix is elided; this is an exception to the general elision (*luk*). *pañcabhir goṇībhiḥ krītaḥ paṭaḥ* (a cloth bought for five bundles of grass) becomes *pañcagoṇiḥ*.

SK 1704: *tasya nimittaṃ saṃyogotpātau* (A 5.1.38). *Saṃyoga* means connection; *utpāta* means an omen indicating good or evil fortune. [Examples: *śatikaḥ* or *śatyaḥ* refers to a connection with the Lord of Wealth (*dhanapati*). *Śatikaṃ* or *śatyaṃ* refers to the throbbing of the right eye; the meaning is "the cause of a hundred [coins]. There should be an addition to the rule for *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* regarding their pacification (*śamana*) and provocation (*kopana*): *vātasya śamanaṃ kopanaṃ vā vātikam*; likewise, *paittikam* and *ślaiṣmikam*. It should also be stated that this applies to *saṃnipāta*: *sāṃnipātikam*.

SK 1705: *godvyaco 'saṃkhyāparimāṇāśvāder yat* (A 5.2.39). The suffix *yat* is applied after a word beginning with *go*, provided it is a compound of two syllables (*dvyac*), and not a number (*asaṃkhyā*), a measure (*parimāṇa*), or a word beginning with *aśva*. *Gavyaḥ*: that which is the cause, conjunction, or portent (*utpāta*) of a cow. Examples of two-syllable words: *dhanyaḥ*, *yaśasyaḥ*, *svargyaḥ*. Why "after a word beginning with *go* and consisting of two syllables"? Consider *vijayasya vaijayikaḥ*. Why "not a number" and so forth? Consider *pañcānām pañcakam*, *saptakam*, *prāsthikam*, *khārīkam*. The group beginning with *aśva*: *āśvikam*, *āśmikam*. An addition [to the rule] for *brahmavarcasa*: *brahmavarcasyam*.

SK 1706: After the word *putra*, the suffixes *cha* and (by the word *ca*, also *yan*) [are applied]. Examples: *putrīyaḥ*, *putryaḥ*. SK 1707: After the words *sarvabhūmi* and *pṛthivī*, the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* [are applied respectively].

The term *sārvabhauma*—meaning "belonging to the whole earth"—refers to a sign, a conjunction, or an omen pertaining to the entire earth (*sarvabhūmi*). The word *sarvabhūmi* is listed among the *anuśatikādi* group [of compounds].
According to Pāṇini 5.1.42 (*tasyeśvaraḥ*), and 5.1.43 (*tatra viditaḥ*), [the suffix -aṇ is applied to form *sārvabhauma*].

One who is the lord (*īśvara*) of all lands, or one who is known throughout all lands, is a *sārvabhauma* king. According to Pāṇini A 5.1.44, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after the words *loka* and *sarvaloka* in the sense of "known therein. Thus, from *loka* we have *laukika*, and from *sarvaloka* we have *sārvalaukika*; in both cases, there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of both members of the compound because they belong to the *anuśatikādi* group.

SK 1711 *tasya vāpaḥ* (A 5.1.45): "vāpa" means that in which something is sown; it refers to a field. The sowing of a *prastha* is *prāsthika*; likewise, *drauṇika* and *khārīka*. SK 1712 *pātrāt ṣṭhan* (A 5.1.46).

The sowing of a vessel is a "vessel-field" (*pātrika*); a division of a field belonging to a vessel is "vessel-portion" (*pātrikī*). [Pāṇini 4.3.75] *tadasmin vṛddhyāyalābhaśulkopadā dīyate*: "That [rate] is given in this [place] as interest, profit, gain, toll, or a gift. (A 4.1.47)

In the sequence beginning with "interest (*vṛddhi*) is given," the singular number is used because each term is connected individually. That in which five percent interest, profit (*āya*), gain (*lābha*), toll (*śulka*), or a bribe (*upadā*) is given is called *pañcaka*. [Similarly,] *śatika*, *śatya*, *sāhasra*. Interest (*vṛddhi*) is that which is to be taken by the creditor in excess of the principal. Profit (*āya*) is the portion to be taken by the owner in villages and other such places. Gain (*lābha*) is that which is to be taken by the seller in excess of the price. Toll (*śulka*) is the king’s share consisting of the fee for protection. A bribe (*upadā*) is a secret gift.

An addition [to the rule] is required for the sense of the fourth case (*caturthy-artha*). For example: *pañcako devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta owes five [units of interest]"), meaning that five units of interest and so forth are given to him. Alternatively, there is an intention to express the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as in the expression *samam abrāhmaṇe dānam* ("giving equally to one who is not a Brahmin"). [The sūtra] *pūraṇārdhāṭ ṭhan* (A 5.1.48) prescribes the suffix *ṭhan*; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *ṭhak* and *ṭiṭhan* respectively. For example: *dvitīyikaḥ* ("one to whom a second [unit of interest] is given"), *tṛtīyikaḥ*, and *ardhikaḥ*. The word *ardha* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of half a *rūpaka* coin.

SK 1715: *bhāgād yañ ca* (A 5.1.49). The suffix *ṭhan* is added after *cāṭ*. The word *bhāga* is also conventionally used to mean "half of a *rūpaka*. When the sense is that a portion such as interest (*vṛddhi*) and so forth is given in this [amount], we have *bhāgyaṃ* or *bhāgikaṃ śatam* ("a hundred [coins] with a portion [of interest]"). *Bhāgyā* or *bhāgikā viṃśatiḥ* ("twenty [coins] with a portion").

SK 1716: *taddharati vahatyāvahati bhārād vaṃśādibhyaḥ* (A 5.1.50). [The suffix *ṭhan* is added after words beginning with *vaṃśa* when they denote a load (*bhāra*), provided they signify that one carries, bears, or brings it.]

The meaning is: from a nominal stem ending in the word *bhāra* which follows words such as *vaṃśa*, [the suffix *ṭhan* is added]. For example: one who carries, bears, or brings a load of bamboo is a *vāṃśabhārikaḥ*; an *aikṣubhārikaḥ*. Regarding the rule *bhārād vaṃśādibhyaḥ*, there is another interpretation: "from bamboo and the like that have become a load. Thus, one who carries bamboo that has become a load is a *vāṃśikaḥ*; an *aikṣukaḥ*. SK 1717: After the words *vasna* and *dravya*, the suffixes *ṭhan* and *kan* [are added respectively]. (A 5.1.51)

They occur according to their respective order. One who takes, carries, or brings a price (*vasna*) is called *vasnika*; likewise, one who deals in goods is *dravyaka*. Regarding the rule "it contains, it brings, it cooks" (A 5.1.52):

that which contains a *prastha* is *prāsthika*, as in "a cooking pot (*kaṭāha*) containing a *prastha*. The meaning is that it causes a *prastha* to be placed within itself. A *brāhmaṇī* woman is *prāsthikī*, meaning she brings or cooks a *prastha*. Regarding the expression "he cooks that": from the word *droṇa*, there is the suffix *aṇ* and also *ṭhañ*. One who cooks a *droṇa* is *drauṇī* (with *aṇ*) or *drauṇikī* (with *ṭhañ*).

SK 1719: After *āḍhaka*, *ācita*, and *pātra*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is optionally applied (A 5.1.53). In the alternative case, [the suffixes *khañ* and *ṭhañ* are applied]. [Examples: That which contains, brings forth, or cooks one *āḍhaka* is called *āḍhakīnā* or *āḍhakikī*. [Similarly: *ācitīnā* or *ācitikī*; *pātrīṇā* or *pātrīkī*. SK 1720: After a *dvigu* compound, the suffix *ṣṭhan* is also applied (A 5.1.54). [In addition to the previously mentioned suffixes.]

"From *āḍhaka*, *ācita*, and *pātra*," and so forth. After a *dvigu* compound ending in *āḍhaka* and the others, the suffixes *ṭhan* and *kha* optionally occur in the senses beginning with "possible" (*saṃbhavati*). In the alternative case, *ṭhañ* is used; by the rule *adhyardha-* etc., there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. Because it is marked with *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied: *dvyāḍhakikī*. Alternatively, *dvyāḍhakīnā*. By the rule *dvigoḥ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied: *dvyāḍhakī*. Similarly, *dvyācitikī*, *dvyācitīnā*, and *dvyācitā*; because of the prohibition of *ṅīp* by the rule *aparimāṇa-*, [only *ṅīp* applies]. *dvipātrikī*, *dvipātrīṇā*, and *dvipātrī*. SK 1721: *kulijāl lukkhau ca* (A 5.1.55). After *kulija*, there is elision (*luk*), as well as *ṭhan* and *kha*.

After a *dvigu* compound ending in *kulija*, there is optionally the elision (*luk*) or the suffix *ṭhan* in the senses beginning with "produced therein" (*saṃbhavati*). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), there is also the suffix *ṣṭhan*. In the absence of elision, there is the audible form of the suffix *ṭhañ*. Examples: *dvikulijī*, *dvaikulijikī*, *dvikulijīnā*, *dvikulijikī*. SK 1722: *so 'syāṃśavasnabhṛtayaḥ* (A 5.1.56).
"Share" (*aṃśaḥ*) means a portion; "price" (*vasnam*) means value; "wages" (*bhṛtiḥ*) means salary. Example: that which has five as its share, price, or wages is called *pañcakaḥ*.

SK 1723: *tad asya parimāṇam* (A 5.1.57). [The suffix *ṭhan* is added after a word denoting a measure when it signifies "this is its measure. Example: *prasthaṃ parimāṇam asya prāsthiko rāśiḥ* ("a heap whose measure is a *prastha*"). SK 1724: *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃjñāsaṅghasūtrādhyayaneṣu* (A 5.1.58). [The suffix *ṭhan* is added after a numeral when it denotes a name, a collection, a sūtra, or a lesson.]

The preceding sūtra is carried over. In that context, a suffix should be stated in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) when forming a name (*saṃjñāyām*). Alternatively, as in the case of *dvyeka-* (Pāṇini 1.4.22), since the word functions merely as a number, the suffix is applied to the possessor of the measure (*parimāṇin*). Examples include: *pañcakāḥ śakunayaḥ* ("five [birds]"), meaning "those whose measure is five"; or *pañcakaḥ saṅghaḥ* ("a group of five"). Regarding the word *sūtra*, there is *aṣṭakaṃ pāṇinīyam* ("the eight [chapters] of Pāṇini"). Since the word *saṅgha* is conventionally restricted to a collection of living beings, "sūtra" is mentioned separately. An example is *pañcakam adhyayanam* ("a study consisting of five [sections]"). Regarding the *stoma*, the rule for the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed.

That which has fifteen mantras as its measure is *pañcadaśaḥ*; likewise, *saptadaśaḥ* and *ekaviṃśaḥ*. In Soma sacrifices, the hymn of praise performed by the *chandoga*s, known by names such as *pṛṣṭhya* and so forth, is called a *stoma*.

According to Pāṇini A 5.1.59, these words—*paṅkti*, *viṃśati*, *triṃśat*, *catvāriṃśat*, *pañcāśat*, *ṣaṣṭi*, *saptati*, *aśīti*, *navati*, and *śata*—are established as conventional (*rūḍhi*) terms through irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
SK 1725: Optionally, when *pañcan* occurs before *daśati* in a compound denoting a class (*varga*), [the suffix *kan* is applied].

*Pañca* is its measure: *pañcadvargaḥ* / *daśat*. In the alternative, [the suffixes *kan* and *kan* respectively apply]: *pañcakaḥ* / *daśakaḥ*. SK 1727: When *triṃśat* and *catvāriṃśat* denote a proper name (*saṃjñā*) referring to a Brāhmaṇa, the suffix *ḍaṇ* is applied.

The measure of these Brāhmaṇas is thirty chapters; thus they are called *traiṃśāni* Brāhmaṇas. Regarding the sense "he deserves" or "he is fit to obtain" that [object], suffixes such as *vañ* and others occur after a word ending in the second case. For example: one who deserves a white umbrella is *śvaitacchatrikaḥ*.

SK 1729 *chedādibhyo nityam* (A 5.1.64): The word *nityam* here means "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇyam*). That which constantly deserves cutting is called *chaidika*, as in the case of the reed (*vetasa*), because it grows back after being cut. [The words] *virāga* and *viraṅga* [are also included]. That which constantly deserves discoloration is *vairāgika*; [that which constantly deserves disfigurement is] *vairaṅgika*. SK 1730 *śīrṣacchedād yac ca* (A 5.1.65).

One who deserves decapitation always [is called] *śīrṣacchedya*, *śairṣacchedika*. By the application of the suffix *yaṭṭhak*, the substitution of *śīrṣa-* for *śiras-* is prescribed. According to A 5.1.66, *daṇḍādibhyo yat*, the suffix *yat* occurs after these [words]: one who deserves a staff is *daṇḍya*; one who deserves food is *agdhya*; one who deserves death is *vadhya*.

SK 1732: After *pātra*, the suffixes *dhañ* and *yat* are applied in the sense of "one who deserves that" (*tadarhati*). Examples: *pātriyaḥ*, *pātryaḥ*. SK 1733: After *kaḍaṅkara* and *dakṣiṇā*, the suffix *cha* is also applied [along with *dhañ* and *yat*].

And regarding *yat*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) of "that which makes fodder" (*kaḍaṃ karoti*), the suffix *khac* is applied precisely because of this specific irregularity (*nipātana*). Thus, *kaḍaṅkara* refers to the wood of beans, mung beans, and so forth; a cow that deserves such fodder is called *kaḍaṅkarīya*. [The form] *kaḍaṅkaryaḥ* [is also used]. One who deserves a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is *dakṣiṇīya*; [the form] *dakṣiṇyaḥ* [is also used]. According to A 5.1.70, *sthālībilāt*:
rice grains that deserve being cooked in a pot (*sthālībila*) are *sthālībilīya*; [the form] *sthālībilyāḥ* [is also used]. The meaning is "fit for cooking."

SK 1735: After the words *yajña* and *ṛtvij*, the suffixes *gha* and *khañ* respectively [are applied] (A 5.1.71). Thus, one who deserves the sacrifice (*yajña*) or the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is called *yajñiyaḥ*; the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is called *ārtvijīnaḥ*. There is an extension [of the rule]: after *yajña* and *ṛtvij*, these suffixes are applied when [the word refers to] that which deserves their function (*tatkarmārhati*). Thus, a place worthy of sacrifice is *yajñiyaḥ*; an officiating priest is *ārtvijīnaḥ*. This marks the end of the twelve suffixes beginning with *ṭhak* used in the sense of "deserving" (*ārhīya*). From here on, only the suffix *ṭhañ* applies. This concludes the section on *ṭhañ* among the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*). 34.

SK 1736 *pārāyaṇa-turāyaṇa-cāndrāyaṇaṃ vartayati* (A 5.1.72): He performs the *pārāyaṇa*; a student who does so is a *pārāyaṇika*. *Turāyaṇa* is a specific sacrifice; one who performs it is a *taurāyaṇika* sacrificer. A *cāndrāyaṇika*. SK 1737 *saṃśayam āpannaḥ* (A 5.1.73): One who has fallen into doubt.

An object that has become the subject of doubt is *sāṃśayika*. [By the rule] *yojanaṃ gacchati* (Pāṇini 5.1.74), one who goes a *yojana* is called *yaujanika*. There is an extension of the application [of this rule] to the cases of *krośaśata* and *yojanaśata*. One who goes a hundred *krośas* is *krauśaśatika*; one who goes a hundred *yojanas* is *yaujanaśatika*. It should also be stated: "one who deserves to go there from that [place]. A monk who deserves to come from a distance of a hundred *krośas* is *krauśaśatika*; a teacher who [deserves to come] from a hundred *yojanas* is *yaujanaśatika*.
SK 1739: *pathaḥ ṣkan* (A 5.1.75). The suffix *ṣ* is for the purpose of [triggering] *ṅīṣ*. One who goes to a path (*panthānam*) is a *pathikaḥ* or *pathikī*.
SK 1740: *pantho ṇa nityam* (A 5.1.76). [The suffix *ṇa* is applied] invariably after *panth-* [to form *pathin*].
A traveler (*pāntha*) constantly goes along a path; [the feminine form is] *pānthī*.
(SK 1741) Regarding the rule *uttarapathenāhṛtam ca* (A 5.1.77):

that which is brought by way of the northern route (*uttarapatha*) is *auttarapathika*; one who goes by way of the northern route is *auttarapathika*. In the section concerning "brought" (*āhṛta*), there is an extension of the rule for compounds preceded by *vāri*, *jaṅgala*, *sthala*, and *kāntāra*: *vāripathika*.
SK 1742: From *kālāt* (A 5.1.78), this is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*) prior to the rule *vyuṣṭādibhyo ’ṇ* (A 5.1.87).
SK 1743: *tena nirvṛttam* (A 5.1.79).
That which is accomplished by the day is "daily" (āhnika).

SK 1744: *tam adhīṣṭo bhṛto bhūto bhāvī* (A 5.1.80). *Adhīṣṭaḥ* means employed with due honor; *bhṛtaḥ* means hired for wages; *bhūtaḥ* means that which has occupied a period of time by its own existence; *bhāvī* means exactly such a thing [occupying a period] in the future. Examples: *māsam adhīṣṭo māsiko 'dhyāpakaḥ* (a teacher commissioned for a month); *māsaṃ bhṛto māsikaḥ karmakaraḥ* (a laborer hired for a month); *māsaṃ bhūto māsiko vyādhiḥ* (a disease lasting for a month); *māsaṃ bhāvī māsika utsavaḥ* (a festival lasting for a month). SK 1745: *māsād vayasi yatkhañau* (A 5.1.81). [The suffixes *yat* and *khañ* are applied after *māsa* when expressing age.]
*abhūtaḥ* [become], *māsyaḥ*, *māsīnaḥ*.
According to Pāṇini 5.1.82, *yap* follows a *dvigu* compound;
the rule *māsād vayasī* (Pāṇini 5.1.83) continues to apply. Thus, one who has existed for two months is *dvimāsyaḥ*.
SK 1747: *ṣaṇmāsāṇ ṇyac ca* (A 5.1.83). The word *vayas* (age) continues to apply here as well, and *ca* (and) brings forward *ṭhañ*. Thus, we have *ṣaṇmāsyaḥ* and *ṣāṇmāsikaḥ*.
SK 1748: *avayasi ṭhañ ca* (A 5.1.84). [The suffixes *ṇyat* and *ṭhañ* are applied after *ṣaṇmāsa*] when it does not refer to age.

And [the suffix] *ṇyat*. A disease lasting six months is *ṣāṇmāsyaḥ*. According to Pāṇini 5.1.85, *samāyāḥ khaḥ*: one who is commissioned for, hired for, has existed for, or will exist for a year is *samīnaḥ*.

SK 1750: *dvigor vā* (A 5.1.86). For a *dvigu* compound ending in *samā*, the suffix *kha* is applied; thus, the suffixes [ending in *īna* and *ika*] are applied in the five senses beginning with "completed" (*nirvṛtta*), prior to [the rule for] *parijayya*. Examples: *dvisamīnaḥ*, *dvaisamikaḥ*. SK 1751: *rātryahaḥsaṃvatsarāc ca* (A 5.1.87). [The suffix *kha* is also applied after *rātri*, *ahan*, and *saṃvatsara* when forming a *dvigu*.]

The rule *dvigoḥ* applies here as well: *dvirātrīṇaḥ*, *dvairātrikaḥ*, *dvyahīnaḥ*, *dvaiyahnikaḥ*. Because the rule for adding a compound-final suffix (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not universally obligatory, the suffix *ṭac* is not applied. *Dvisaṃvatsarīṇaḥ*. [This is governed by] A 7.3.15: *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsara-saṃkhyasya ca*.

There shall be *vṛddhi* substitution for the final vowel of a numeral when followed by a word beginning with *ñit* or *ṇit*. Examples: *dvisāṃvatsarikaḥ* ("lasting two years"); *dviṣāṣṭikaḥ* ("hired for sixty-two [pieces]"). Although the rule would have been established simply by saying "of a numeral ending in a measure-word" (*parimāṇāntasya*), the specific mention of *saṃvatsara* is intended to ensure that measures of time (*kālaparimāṇa*) are not included under the term "measure-word. Consequently, in *dvaisamikaḥ*, there is no *vṛddhi* substitution in the second member. **SK 1753:** *varṣāl luk ca* (A 5.1.88).

After a *dvigu* compound ending in the word *varṣa*, the suffix *kha* is optionally applied; alternatively, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied, or else there is elision (*luk*) of both. This results in three forms: *dvivarṣīṇo vyādhiḥ* ("a disease lasting two years"), *dvivarṣaḥ* ("two years old"), and [the form with *ṭhañ*: *dvivārṣikaḥ*].

SK 1754: *varṣasyābhaviṣyati* (Pāṇini 7.3.16). There shall be Vṛddhi substitution for the final vowel of the second member [of a compound ending in *varṣa*]. For example: *dvivārṣikaḥ manuṣyaḥ* ("a person two years old"). However, when [the sense] is "future," it is *dvaivarṣikaḥ*. The prohibition [of Vṛddhi] by the rule *adhīṣṭabhṛtayor abhaviṣyati* does not apply here. For in that case, although future time is understood, it is not the meaning expressed by the secondary suffix (*taddhita*). Thus, a person who has been requested (*adhīṣṭa*) or hired (*bhṛta*) for two years to perform work is called *dvivārṣikaḥ*. Regarding a word ending in a measure (*parimāṇa*), except for a technical name (*saṃjñā*) or the word *śāṇa*: *dvau kuḍavau parimāṇam asya* ("its measure is two *kuḍava*s") results in *dvikauḍavikaḥ*.

That which is purchased for two gold coins is *dvisauvarṇika*; [it is also] *dvinaiṣkika*. Why "not a name" (*asaṃjñā*)? [Consider: that whose measure is five bundles is *pāñcakalāpika*; this is a name ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). [Also] *dvaiśāṇa*. Some also read the word *kulija*: *dvaikulijika*. SK 1755: *cittavati nityam* (A 5.1.89).

After a *dvigu* compound ending in the word *varṣa*, there is always elision (*luk*) of the suffix when the meaning of the suffix refers to a sentient being (*cetana*). [Example: *dvivarṣo dārakaḥ* ("a two-year-old boy").

SK 1756: *ṣaṣṭikāḥ* [means] "those that ripen in sixty nights" (A 5.1.90). The plural number is not restrictive; it refers to a specific type of grain. The suffix *kan* is prescribed after a word ending in the third case, and the elision of the word *rātra* is also prescribed by rule.
SK 1757: [The suffix *khañ* is applied] after a word ending in the third case to express "conquerable by that," "obtainable by that," "to be done by that," or "easy to do by that" (A 5.1.93).

A monthly illness can be overcome through mastery within a month; a task that is obtainable or easy to perform within a month is called *māsika*. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *māsa*] when it means "his period of religious studentship" (*brahmacarya*). (A 5.1.94)

A suffix shall be added after a word denoting time ending in the second case (accusative) in the sense of "belonging to this" (*asya*). The second case is used here because of absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). For example: *māsaṃ brahmacaryam asya* ("his period of celibacy lasts for a month") = *māsikaḥ brahmacārī* ("a month-long celibate"); likewise, *ārdhamāsikaḥ*. Alternatively, the suffix may be added after a word ending in the first case (nominative) in the sense of "belonging to this": *māso 'sya* ("this belongs to a month") = *māsikaṃ brahmacaryam* ("a month-long period of celibacy"). There is also an extension [of the rule] to words such as *mahānāmnī*, which end in the sixth case (genitive). The *mahānāmnīs* are the verses beginning with *vidā maghavan*, etc.

Their *brahmacarya* is called *māhānāmnika*. Haradatta, however, says that because of the rule regarding the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*)—namely, *bhasyāḍhe*—it should be *māhānāmika*. The suffix *ṇya* is applied after the word *caturmāsa* in the sense of "occurring therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*). Thus, the sacrificial rites occurring in four months are the *Cāturmāsyas*. The suffix *aṇ* is used for a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*). That which occurs in four months is the *Cāturmāsī*, namely the full moon day of Āṣāḍha. Because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
And its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is derived from words denoting sacrifices [with the suffix *aṇ*], according to A 5.1.95.

The *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice is called *dvādaśāhikī*. Because the specific name is mentioned, [the suffix applies] even when not referring to time: *āgniṣṭomikī*, *vājapeyikī*.
And in that context, [the suffixes] *bhava-vat* apply for what is given or what is to be done (*kārya*):
*prāvṛṣeṇyam* (given or to be done in the rainy season), *śāradam* (autumnal). Under the heading of *ṭhañ*, the scope of the section on time is complete.

SK 1761: *vyuṣṭādibhyo ’ṇ* (A 5.1.97). The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words such as *vyuṣṭa*. For example, that which is given or performed at dawn (*vyuṣṭa*) is called *vyaṣṭam*. The *vyuṣṭa*-group includes: *vyuṣṭa*, *tīrtha*, *saṃgrāma*, *pravāsa*, and so forth. There is an extension [of this rule] for words beginning with *agnipada*: that which is given or performed at the place of fire (*agnipada*) is called *āgnipadam*; likewise, *pailumūlam*. SK 1762: *tena yathākathāca hastābhyāṃ ṇayatau* (A 5.1.98). The suffixes *ṇa* and *yat* are applied after the word *yathākathāca* and the word *hasta* when used with the sense of "by means of that. (Note: *yathākathāca* is indeclinable; *yathākathācena* = "in whatever manner"; *hastena* = "by the hand").

From the indeclinable compound *yathākathāc* ending in the third case, and from the word *hasta*, the suffixes *ṇa* and *yat* respectively are applied. However, a corresponding application (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not intended for the two meanings [of "giving" and "doing"]. That which is given or done in a casual manner is *yāthākathātvam*; the meaning is that it is something to be given or done without regard. That which is given or done with the hand is *hastyam*.

(SK 1763) The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the sense of "accomplished by means of" (*saṃpādini*). This follows from the rule "by means of that" (*tena*). An ornament accomplished by means of ear-rings is *kārṇaveṣṭakikaṃ mukham*; the meaning is that the face necessarily shines because of the ear-ornaments.
SK 1764: *karmaveṣād yat* (A 5.1.100).

That which is accomplished through action is "actionable" (*karmaṇyam*), such as valor. That which is accomplished by dress is "dress-related" (*veṣya*), such as an actor; dress (*veṣaḥ*) is an artificial appearance. SK 1765:
*tasmai prabhavati saṃtāpādibhyaḥ* (A 5.1.101). [The suffix *yat* is applied after words such as *saṃtāpa* when meaning "capable of that."]

That which is capable of causing distress is *sāṃtāpika*; likewise, *sāṃgrāmika*. According to Pāṇini 5.1.102, from the word *yoga*, both the suffixes *yat* and *ṭhañ* are applied: that which is capable for yoga is *yogya* or *yaugika*.

SK 1767: By the rule *karmaṇa ukañ* (A 5.1.103), [the suffix *ukañ* is added after a word denoting an object] to form *kārmukam*, meaning "that which is capable for the purpose of the object" (i.e., a bow).
SK 1768: By the rule *samayas tad asya prāptam* (A 5.1.104), [the suffix *ṭhañ* is added after a word denoting time to form a derivative meaning] "this has reached that [time]."
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [words ending in] *samaya* when the sense is "this has reached its time": *samayaḥ prāpto 'sya sāmayikam*.

By A 5.1.105 (*ṛtor aṇ*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *ṛtu* when the sense is "this has reached its season": *ṛtuḥ prāpto 'sya ārtavam*. There is an extension of this rule to words such as *upavasta*: *upavastā prāpto 'sya aupavastram*; *prāsitā prāpto 'sya prāsitram*.

SK 1770: *kālād yat* (A 5.1.107). The suffix *yat* is applied after a word denoting time when it signifies that which has arrived at that time. Example: *kālyaṃ śītam* ("the cold that has arrived at its [proper] time").
SK 1771: *prakṛṣṭe ṭhañ* (A 5.1.108). The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied [after a word denoting time] when it signifies excellence.

[The suffix *ṭhañ*] occurs after [a word denoting] time (*kāla*), and also after [a word denoting] "that is its" (*tad asya*). An enmity whose duration is long and extended is called *kālikam* (lasting).

[The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs] after [a word denoting] a purpose (*prayojana*), and [the rule] "that is its" (*tad asya*) applies. That which has the festival of Indra (*indramahaḥ*) as its purpose is *aindramahikam*. Purpose (*prayojana*) means both result (*phala*) and cause (*kāraṇa*).

SK 1773: *viśākhāṣāḍhādaṇ manthadaṇḍayoḥ* (A 5.1.110). The suffix *aṇ* is applied after these two words in the sense of "having this as its purpose," specifically when the meanings are respectively *mantha* (churning stick) and *daṇḍa* (staff). *Viśākhā* is the purpose of this: *vaiśākhaḥ manthaḥ* (a churning stick for the Viśākhā festival). *Āṣāḍhaḥ daṇḍaḥ* (a staff for the Āṣāḍhā festival). There is an extension of the rule to include *cūḍā* and others: *cūḍā*, *cauḍam*; *śraddhā*, *śrāddham*. SK 1774: *anupravacanādibhyaś chaḥ* (A 5.1.111). The suffix *cha* (which becomes *īya*) is applied after the group beginning with *anupravacana*.
That for which recitation (*anupravacana*) is the purpose is *anupravacanīya*. According to Pāṇini 5.1.112, *samāpanāt sapūrvapadāt*,
that for which the completion of grammar (*vyākaraṇasamāpana*) is the purpose is *vyākaraṇasamāpanīya*.

SK 1776: The suffix *aikāgārika* is added [to *ekāgāra*] in the sense of "a thief" (A 5.1.113). One whose purpose is a single, solitary house (*ekam asahāyam agāram*) is a thief who intends to plunder; he is called *aikāgārika*. SK 1777: The suffix *ākālika* is added [to *ākalika*] when expressing the meaning of "lasting from beginning to end" (A 5.1.114).

*Ākālika* means that whose beginning and end are simultaneous; it is a substitute (*ādeśa*) for *samānakāla*. The meaning is "perishing quickly," or rather, "arising at midday or the like on one day and perishing at that very same time on the following day. From *ākāla*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is also applied: *ākālikā vidyut* ("lightning that lasts only a moment"). The full scope of *ṭhañ* ends here. The section concerning the *nañ* and *snañ* suffixes among the secondary nominal derivatives (*taddhita*) begins [at this point]. [Now follows: "When there is an action, the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of 'equal to that' (Pāṇini 5.1.115)."

"Like a Brāhmaṇa" means he studies like a Brāhmaṇa (*brāhmaṇavad adhīte*). Why specify "if it is an action"? [So that the suffix does not apply] when there is equality of quality: "He is as fat as his son" (*putreṇa tulyaḥ sthūlaḥ*).
In that context, by the rule *tatra tasyeva* (A 5.1.116), [the suffix *vati* is applied]:
"The manner in Srughna is like that in Mathurā" (*mathurāyām iva mathurāvat srughne prakāraḥ*); "Maitra’s cows are like Caitra’s" (*caitrasyeva caitravan maitrasya gāvaḥ*).

SK 1780 *tadarham* (A 5.1.117): [The suffix *vat*] is added after a word meaning "he deserves that" (*arhati*) to form an adverbial expression meaning "in accordance with that" (*vidhivat*). It is completed [by the addition of *vat*]. The mention of "action" (*kriyā*) is understood here by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) [i.e., skipping intervening rules]. Therefore, it does not apply here: *rājānam arhati chatram* ("He deserves a parasol for the king").
SK 1781 *tasya bhāvas tvatalau* (A 5.1.119): The suffixes *tva* and *tal* are added after a word to denote its abstract state (*bhāva*).

In a cognition produced by a *prakṛti* (base), that which serves as the qualifier (*prakāra*) is the *bhāva* (abstract state). For example, from *go*, we have *gotva* (cowness) or *gotā*. A word ending in *-tva* is neuter, while one ending in *-tā* is feminine.

SK 1782: *ā ca tvāt* (A 5.1.120). From this point up to the rule *brahmaṇas tvaḥ* (A 5.1.138), the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are governed. This is for the purpose of allowing them to co-occur with exceptions (*apavāda*) and for the purpose of prescribing them after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) and others in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). The particle *ca* is included so that they may also co-occur with *nañ* and *srañ*. The state of being a woman (*strī*) is *sraiṇam*, *strītvam*, or *strītā*. The state of being a man (*pumān*) is *pauṃsnam*, *puṃstvam*, or *puṃstā*. SK 1783: *na nañpūrvāt tatpuruṣād acaturasaṃgatalavaṇavaṭayudhakatarasalasebhyaḥ* (A 5.1.121). The suffix *tva* is not applied after a *tatpuruṣa* compound beginning with *nañ*, except for those ending in *catura*, *saṃgata*, *lavaṇa*, *vaṭa*, *yudha*, *katara*, *salasa*, and *sala*.

From this point forward, those suffixes denoting abstract states (*bhāvapratyaya*) shall not be applied after *nañ-tatpuruṣa* compounds, with the exception of those beginning with *catur*. Examples: *apatitvam* (the state of not being fallen), *apaṭutvam* (the state of not being clever). Why "after [a compound] preceded by *nañ*"? Consider *bārhaspatyam* (the state of Bṛhaspati). Why "from a *tatpuruṣa*"? Consider *apaṭuḥ* (one who does not possess cleverness); the state of that person is *āpaṭavam*. Why "except for those beginning with *catur*"? Consider *ācaturyam*, *āsaṅgatyam*, *ālavaṇyam*, *āvaṭyam*, *āyudhyam*, *ākatyam*, *ārasyam*, *ālasyam*. Regarding *pṛthvādibhya imanij vā* (Pāṇini 5.1.122):
the mention of "optionally" (*vā*) is for the purpose of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the suffixes beginning with *aṇ*.
SK 1785: *ra ṛto halāder laghoḥ* (A 6.4.161). For a light *ṛ*-vowel that begins with a consonant, *ra* is substituted [for *ṛ*] before the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *īyasun*, and *imanic*.
SK 1786: *ṭeḥ* (A 6.4.155). [The final phoneme] of the base (*bhas*) is elided [before those same suffixes].

The *ṭi* portion of this [base] shall be elided before the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *īyasun*, and *imanic*. The state of being broad (*pṛthu*) is *prathimā*; [with *aṇ*: *pārthavam*. *Bhradimā*; *mārdavam*. SK 1787:

After words denoting color (*varṇa*) and after *dṛḍha* etc., the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied, and by the word "and" (*ca*), also *imanij*. *Śauklyam*; *śuklimā*. *Dārḍhyam*. In the case of *pṛthu*, *mṛdu*, *bhṛśa*, *kṛśa*, *dṛḍha*, and *parivṛḍha* only, there is the substitution of *ra* for the final vowel. *Drāḍhimā*. The *ṣ* [in *ṣyañ*] is for the purpose of [triggering] *ṅīṣ*. *Aucitī*; *yāthākāmī*.

SK 1788: *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ karmaṇi ca* (A 5.1.124). By the word "ca" (and), [the suffix] is also used in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*). The action or state of one who is dull (*jaḍa*) is *jāḍyam*. The state or action of one who is deluded (*mūḍha*) is *mauḍhyam*. *Brāhmaṇyam*. After the word *arhat*, there is also the suffix *tun*. The state or action of an *arhat* is *ārhantyam* or *ārhantī*. *Brāhmaṇādi* is a class-based group (*ākṛtigaṇa*). SK 1789: *yathātathāyathāpurayoḥ paryāyeṇa* (A 7.3.31). [The substitution of *ām* for the final vowel and following consonant occurs] alternatively after *yathātathā* and *yathāpura*.

When these two words follow the negative particle *nañ*, the first vowel (*ac*) of either the preceding or the following member optionally receives *vṛddhi* before an affix beginning with *ñ* or *ṅ*. Examples: *ayathātathya* (the state of not being as it is) or *ayāthātathya*; *āyathāpurya* or *ayāthāpurya*. Up to the end of this section on feet, the governing topic is "state" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*). An addition is made for *caturvarṇa* and similar compounds to express their own meaning (*svārtha*): *cāturvarṇya* (the four castes), *cāturāśramya* (the four stages of life), *traisvaryam* (the three accents), *ṣāḍguṇyam* (the six political expedients), *sainyam* (an army), *sāṃnidhyam* (proximity), *sāmīpyam* (nearness), *aupamyam* (similarity).

"Trailokyam," and so forth. "All Vedas" (*sarvavedāḥ*); one who studies them is a *sarvavedaḥ*. By the rule *sarvādeḥ*, there is elision (*luk*) [of the suffix]. He himself is a *sārvavaidyaḥ*. For the word *caturveda*, there is vṛddhi in both members [of the compound]: one who studies four Vedas is a *caturvedaḥ*; he himself is a *cāturvedyaḥ*. There is an alternative reading *caturvidya*. One who possesses four branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) is indeed a *cāturvaidyaḥ*. According to A 5.1.125, *stenādyannalopaś ca*: [the suffix *ṇya* is added after words beginning with *stena*, and there is elision of the final *an*].

"Not so," [says the author], for there is a reference to a collective group (*saṃghāta*). The word *stena* means "theft" (*caurya*), derived from the root *stṛ* with the suffix *ac* in the sense of the action (*pacādyac*). *Steya* is the state or the act of a thief (*stena*). Some also accept the form *stainya*, ending in the suffix *ṣyañ*, by dividing the rule as *stenāt*.
(Pāṇini 5.1.126: *sakhyur yaḥ*)

The state (*bhāva*) or action (*karman*) of a friend is *sakhyam*. [The suffix *yañ* is applied] after the words *dūta* and *vaṇij* as well. The state or action of a messenger is *dūtyam*; according to the *Kāśikā*, it is *vaṇijyam*. However, Mādhava states that the word *vaṇijyā* is feminine by its very nature; furthermore, he asserts that this suffix denotes only the state (*bhāva*) and not the action (*karman*). In the *Bhāṣya*, however, the rule "after *dūta* and *vaṇij*" does not exist at all. Alternatively, *vāṇijyam* is formed because [the word *vaṇij*] belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class (Pāṇini 5.1.124).
According to A 5.1.127, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied after *kapi* and *jñāti*: *kāpeyam* and *jñāteyam*.

SK 1793: *patyantapurohitādibhyo yak* (A 5.1.128). *maitrāpaityam*; *paurohityam*. Regarding *rājāse*: the meaning is that the word *rājan* takes the suffix *yak* when not in a compound. Thus, the state or activity of a king is *rājyam*. However, in a compound, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇādi* group; hence, *ādhirājyam*. SK 1794: *prāṇabhṛjjātivayovacanodgātrādibhyo 'ñ* (A 5.1.129). [The suffix *añ* is applied after words denoting species of living beings, words expressing age, and the class beginning with *udgātṛ*.]

Regarding the genus of living beings (*prāṇabhṛjjāti*): *āśvam* ("belonging to a horse"), *auṣṭram* ("belonging to a camel"). Regarding words denoting age (*vayovacana*): *kaumāram* ("youthful"), *kaiśoram* ("adolescent"), *audgātram* ("pertaining to the Udgātṛ priest"), *aunnetram* ("pertaining to the Unnetṛ priest"), *sauṣṭavam* ("pertaining to excellence"), *dauṣṭavam* ("pertaining to wickedness").
By rule A 5.1.130, *hāyanāntayuvādibhyo 'ṇ*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after words ending in *hāyana* and after the group beginning with *yuvan*. Examples:

*dvaihāyanam* ("two-year-old"), *traihāyanam* ("three-year-old"), *yauvanam* ("youthfulness"), *sthāviram* ("old age"). [In the case of] *śrotriya*, there is also elision of the *y*: *śrautram* ("pertaining to one learned in the Vedas"). The words *kuśala*, *capala*, *nipuṇa*, *piśuna*, *kutūhala*, and *kṣetrajña* are listed both among the *yuvādi* (beginning with *yuvan*) and the *brāhmaṇādi* (beginning with *brāhmaṇa*) groups. Examples: *kauśalyam* ("skillfulness"), *kauśalam* ("skill"), and so forth.

SK 1796: And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after a stem ending in *i* or *u*, provided that the preceding syllable is light. From the root *śuc*: the state or action of being pure is *śaucam*. *Maunam* [is derived from *muni*]. How is *kāvyam* [formed]? It is because the word *kavi* belongs to the *brāhmaṇādi* group, and thus the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied. SK 1797: The suffix *vuñ* is applied after a stem having *y* as its penultimate (*yopadha*) and having a heavy vowel (*guru*) in the penultimate-to-penultimate position (*gurūpottama*).
*rāmaṇīyakam* / *ābhidhānīyakam* / or from *sahāya*: *sāhāyyam* / *sāhāyakam*. According to Pāṇini 5.1.133, *dvandva* and *manojña* etc.:
*śaiṣyopādhyāyikā* / *mānojñakam*.

SK 1799: *gotracaraṇāc chāghātyākāratadaveteṣu* (A 5.1.134). *Atyākāra* means insult; *tadaveta* refers to the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the action (*karman*) pertaining to lineage (*gotra*) or school (*caraṇa*), or one who has understood them. [Examples: *gārgikayā ślāghate*—the meaning is that he boasts by way of being a descendant of Garga (*gārgyatvena vikatthate*). *gārgikayātyākurute*; *gārgikāmavetaḥ*. SK 1800: *hotrābhyaś chaḥ* (A 5.1.135). [The suffix *cha* is applied after words denoting the names of officiating priests.]

The word *hotrā* is feminine and denotes an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Due to the plural ending, specific [priestly roles] are understood. *Ācchāvākīyam* means the state or function of the *acchāvāka*. *Maitrāvaruṇīyam* [is formed similarly]. SK 1801: *brahmaṇas tvaḥ* (A 5.1.136). The suffix *tva* should occur after the word *brahman* when it denotes an officiating priest. This is an exception to [the general rule for] the suffix *cha*. Thus, *brahmatvam*. Although one could have simply said "not [the suffix *cha*]," the explicit mention of *tva* is for the purpose of overriding the suffix *tal*. However, from the word *brahman* as a synonym for *brāhmaṇa*, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* both apply: *brahmatvam* and *brahmatā*.
The section concerning *nañ* and *snañ* is completed.
36. Among the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), those expressing the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
A 5.2.1: "The suffix *khañ* is applied after words for grains to denote the field where they grow.
"Field" (*bhavana*) means that in which something grows. A field where mung beans (*mudga*) grow is called *maudgīna*.
SK 1803: After *vrīhi* and *śāli*, the suffix *ḍhak* [is applied] (A 5.2.2). Examples: *vraiheyam*, *śāleyam*. SK 1804: After *yava*, *yavaka*, and *ṣaṣṭika*, the suffix *yat* [is applied] (A 5.2.3).
The field that is the place of growth for barley is *yavya* or *yavakya*. [Similarly: *ṣaṣṭikya*.

According to A 5.2.4, *vibhāṣā tilamāṣomābhaṅgāṇubhyaḥ*, the suffix *yat* may optionally be used, or else *khañ* may be applied; thus: *tilya* or *tailīna*; *māṣya* or *māṣīṇa*; *umya* or *aumīna*; *bhaṅgya* or *bhāṅgīna*; *aṇavya* or *āṇavīna*.

SK 1806: *sarvacarmaṇaḥ kṛtaḥ khakhañau* (A 5.2.5). Even though there is a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), the compound is formed by virtue of this specific rule (*nipātana*). "Made entirely from leather" is *sarvacarmīṇaḥ* or *sārvacarmīṇaḥ*.
SK 1807: *yathāmukhasammukhasya darśanaḥ khaḥ* (A 5.2.6). [The suffix *kha* is applied after the compounds *yathāmukha* and *sammukha* when followed by the word *darśana*.]

*Yathāmukham* is a reflection that resembles the face; it is an *avyayībhāva* compound by virtue of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) signifying resemblance. *Saṃmukham* means the entire face equally; here, the elision of the final syllable of the word *sama* is an irregular formation. *Yathāmukhīnaḥ* is one whose appearance is according to the face. *Saṃmukhīnaḥ* is one who faces every face. SK 1808: *tatsarvādeḥ pathyaṅgakarmapatrapātraṃ vyāpnoti* (Pāṇini 5.2.7). The suffix *kha* occurs after a word beginning with *sarva* and ending in *pathin*, *aṅga*, *karman*, *patra*, or *pātra*, provided it is in the accusative case and signifies "pervading" [that]. *Sarvapathīnaḥ* is one who pervades all paths. *Sarvāṅgīṇaḥ*. *Sarvakarmīṇaḥ*.

SK 1809 *āprapadaṃ prāpnoti* (A 5.2.8): The tip of the foot is *prapada*; that which reaches as far as that limit is *āprapadam*. An *āprapadīna* garment is one that reaches down to the tips of the feet.

SK 1810 *anupadasarvānnāyānayaṃ baddhābhakṣayatineyeṣu* (A 5.2.9): [The suffix *khañ* is applied after the words *anupada*, *sarva*, and *anna*] when combined with the words *āya*, *anaya*, *baddha*, *abhakṣayati*, and *neya* respectively.

The suffix *īna* is applied after *anu*, *rāya*, and *sādṛśya*. *Anupadīnā upānat*: a sandal fastened to the heel. *Sarvānnīno bhikṣuḥ*: a mendicant who eats all kinds of food. *Ayānayaḥ* is a particular place; *āyānayīnaḥ śāraḥ* is an arrow that can be carried to and from that place.
(A 5.2.10) *Parovaraparamparaputrapautram anubhavati*: he experiences [the lineage] of father, son, grandson, and great-grandson.

One who experiences those higher (*parān*) and lower (*avarān*) is called *parovarīṇaḥ*; here, the substitution of *u* for the vowel of *avara-* is an irregularity (*nipātana*). One who experiences those higher and even those beyond them (*paratarān*) is *paramparīṇaḥ*; here, the state of being *parampara-* is an irregularity applied to the base. One who experiences sons and grandsons is *putrapautrīṇaḥ*. However, the word *paramparā* is another independent word (*śabdāntaram*) not derived [from *para-para*], feminine in gender; from that very word, with the suffix *ṣyañ* in its own sense (*svārthe*), we have *pāramparyam*. How then is [the form] *pārovaryavat* explained? This is indeed incorrect, because the irregularity *parovara-* is prescribed specifically in conjunction with the suffix *khak*.

SK 1812: *avārapārātyantānukāmaṃ gāmī* (A 5.2.11). One who goes to both banks (*avārapāraṃ gāmī*) is called *avārapāriṇaḥ*, *avāriṇaḥ*, *pāriṇaḥ*, or *pārāvārīṇaḥ*. One who goes to the end (*atyantaṃ gāmī*) is called *atyantīnaḥ*; the meaning is "one who goes very far. One who goes according to desire (*anukāmaṃ gāmī*) is called *anukāmīnaḥ*; the meaning is "one who goes as he pleases. SK 1813: *samāṃsamāṃ vijāyate* (A 5.2.12). [The suffix *khā* is applied after *samāṃsamām* when it means "giving birth every year."]

The elision of *ya* and the non-elision (*aluk*) of the remaining case-ending in the first member of the compound are prescribed as irregularities. *Samāṃsamīnā gauḥ* ("a cow that calves every year"): this refers to a cow that gives birth every year. It should be stated that when the suffix *kha* does not occur, there is optionally an elision of *ya*: *samāṃsamāṃ vijāyate* ("she gives birth every year") or *samāyāṃ samāyāṃ*. Regarding *adyaśvīnāvaṣṭabdhe* (A 5.2.13):

*adyaśvīnā vaḍavā* ("a mare about to foal") means she will give birth today or tomorrow; the meaning is "one whose delivery is imminent. Some, however, do not carry forward the word "gives birth" (*vijāyate*). Thus, *adyaśvīnaṃ maraṇam* ("death imminent") means it is near.

SK 1815 *āgavīnaḥ* (A 5.2.14): The suffix *kha* is irregularly prescribed after the word *go* preceded by *āṅ*, in the sense of a laborer. One who performs work until the return of the cow is called *āgavīna*. SK 1816 *anugvalaṃgāmī* (A 5.2.15).
The cowherd who goes to follow after the cow is called *anugavīnaḥ*. Regarding the rule *adhvano yat-khau* (A 5.2.16):

one who goes sufficiently along the road is called *adhvanyaḥ* or *adhvanīnaḥ*. By the two rules *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ* and *ātmādhvānau khe*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāvaḥ*).

SK 1818: *abhyamitrāc cha ca* (A 5.2.17). Because of the word "ca" (and), [the suffixes] *yat* and *kha* are also applied. *abhyamitrīyaḥ*, *abhyamitryaḥ*, *abhyamitrīṇaḥ*. The meaning is: "one who goes well toward the enemy. SK 1819: *goṣṭhāt khañ bhūtapūrve* (A 5.2.18). [The suffix] *khañ* is applied after *goṣṭha* when expressing that something previously existed there.
*Goṣṭha* means "formerly a cow-pen"; *gauṣṭhīna* refers to a place [that was formerly a cow-pen].
According to A 5.2.19, *aśvasyaikāhagamaḥ*:
that which is traversed in one day (*ekāhena gamyate*) is called *ekāhagama*; thus, *āśvīna* refers to a road.
SK 1821: *śālīna* and *kaupīna* [are used] in the senses of "timid" and "that which should not be done" respectively (A 5.2.20).

One who deserves entry into the house (*śālā*) is *śālīna*, meaning timid. That which deserves falling into a well (*kūpa*) is *kaupīna*, meaning sin; because it is the means for that [fall], or because it is to be concealed like that [sin], the male organ is also so called; and by association with that, the garment which covers it is also so called. SK 1822: [The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in] *vrāta* when [the sense is] "one who lives by means of that" (A 5.2.21).
One who lives by means of a *vrāta*—that is, through physical labor and not through the excellence of his intellect—is a *vrātīna*.
Regarding the rule *sāptapadīnaṃ sakhyam* (Pāṇini 5.2.22): friendship is obtained by seven steps; thus it is called *sāptapadīna*.

SK 1824 *haiyaṅgavīnaṃ saṃjñāyām* (A 5.2.23): In the sense of a derivative (*vikāra*), the substitution of *hiyaṅgu* for *hyogodoha* is prescribed, and the suffix *khañ* is also applied as an irregularity (*nipātana*). *Doha* means that which is milked, i.e., milk. *Haiyaṅgavīna* is the derivative of the milk of a cow that has just calved; it refers to fresh butter (*navanīta*). SK 1825 *tasya pākamūle pīlvādikarṇādibhyaḥ kuṇabjāhacau* (A 5.2.24): After words belonging to the *pīlvādi* group and after those beginning with *karṇa*, the suffixes *kuṇap* and *jāhac* are respectively added [to form derivatives denoting the cooking or the root of that thing].
The ripening of *pīlu* fruits is *pīlukuṇa*. The root of the ear is *karṇajāha*.
According to A 5.2.25, *pakṣāt tiḥ*, only the mention of the word *mūla* is carried over [from the previous rule]. The root of a wing (*pakṣa*) is *pakṣati*.

SK 1827: *tena vittaścuñcupcaṇapau* (A 5.2.26). Since the letter *y* is indicated as elided at the beginning of the two suffixes, it does not receive the designation *it*. One who is known by means of knowledge is *vidyācuñcuḥ* or *vidyācaṇaḥ*. SK 1828: *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau nasah* (A 5.2.27). [The suffixes *na* and *āna* are applied after the words *vi* and *nañ*, respectively, with the substitution of *na* for the final phoneme.]

The suffixes *vinā* and *nānā* are applied in their own sense (*svārthe*) to the roots *vi* and *pra*, which here function in the sense of "separation" (*asahārthe pṛthagbhāve*). [Pāṇini 5.2.27 states: *vinā* and *nānā*. [Pāṇini 5.2.28 states: *veḥ śālacchaṅkaṭacau*.
These suffixes are applied in their own sense to words denoting an instrument (*sādhana*) qualified by an action (*kriyāviśiṣṭa*). Examples: *vistṛtam*, *viśālam*, *viśaṅkaṭam*.

SK 1830: *saṃ-pra-ud-aś* with *kaṭac* (A 5.2.29). From these prefixes, the suffix *kaṭac* is applied: *saṅkaṭam*, *prakaṭam*, *utkaṭam*. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), [the suffix is also applied after] *vikaṭam*. There is an extension [of this rule] for dust (*rajas*) derived from *alābū*, *tila*, *umā*, and *bhaṅgā*: *alābūnāṃ rajaḥ* = *alābūkaṭam*; *tilakaṭam*. The suffixes *goṣṭha-jā* and others are applied to names of animals in the sense of "place" (*sthāna*) and so forth: *gavāṃ sthānam* = *gogoṣṭham*. The suffix *kaṭac* is applied in the sense of a "collection" (*saṃghāta*): *avīnāṃ saṅghātaḥ* = *avikaṭaḥ*. The suffix *paṭac* is applied in the sense of "extent" (*vistāra*): *avipaṭaḥ*. The suffix *goyugac* is applied in the sense of "pair" (*dvitva*): two camels = *uṣṭragoyugam*. The suffix *ṣaṅgavac* is applied in the sense of "six" (*ṣaṭtva*): six horses = *aśvaṣaḍgavam*.

In the sense of "oil," [the suffix *cha*] is applied after the word *sneha*: *tailac*, as in *tilataila* ("sesame oil") and *sarṣapataila* ("mustard oil"). In the sense of "growing in" (*bhavana*), [the suffixes *cha* and *kan*] are applied after *kṣetra*: *śākaṭa* and *śākina*, as in *ikṣuśākaṭa* ("a field of sugarcane") and *ikṣuśākina*. According to A 5.2.30, *avāt kuṭārac ca*: after the prefix *ava*, the suffix *kuṭārac* is applied, and by the word *ca* ("and"), the suffix *kaṭac* is also applied. Thus, *avācīna* becomes *avakuṭāraḥ* and *avakaṭaḥ*.

SK 1832: After *nata* [meaning] "bent," when expressing a relationship with the nose (*nāsikā*), the suffixes *ṭīṭan*, *nāṭac*, and *bhraṭac* are applied (A 5.2.31). This applies only after words beginning with *ava*. *Nata* means "bending. The nose being bent is *avaṭīṭam*, *avanāṭam*, or *avabhraṭam*. Due to connection with that [state], the nose is called *avaṭīṭā*; the person as well is *avaṭīṭaḥ*. SK 1833: After *ni*, the suffixes *biḍac* and *birīsac* are applied (A 5.2.32).

*nibiḍam* / *nibirīsam*. By A 5.2.33, *inac*, *piṭac*, and *ci* [are added] after the prefix *ni-*; this applies specifically to *ni-*. When the meaning is "bent nose," the suffixes *inac* and *piṭac* are applied, and the base [of the prefix] undergoes the substitutions *cik* and *ci*, etc. It should also be stated that the suffix *ka* is applied and *cik* is substituted for the base. Thus: *cikinam*, *cipiṭam*, *cikkam*. [The suffixes] *cil* and *pill* are added to *klinna-* ("moist"), and its eyes are [so described]. One whose eyes are moist is *cillaḥ* or *pillaḥ*. Also, with the suffix *cul*: *cullaḥ*.

SK 1835: *upādhibhyāṃ tyakann āsannāruḍhayoḥ* (A 5.2.34). The term *saṃjñāyām* ("in the sense of a name") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. *Upatyakā* is the ground near a mountain; *adhityakā* is the ground ascended upon [a mountain]. SK 1836: *karmaṇi ghaṭo ’ṭhac* (A 5.2.35). [The suffix] *aṭhac* is applied after the word *ghaṭa* when it occurs in the objective case (*karman*).

*Ghaṭa* means "that which strives" (*ghaṭate*), derived from the root *ghaṭ* with the suffix *ac* according to the rule *pacādyac*. It is used in the sense of the object: "the starry sky strives toward him. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words).

According to the rule *tad asya saṃjātaṃ tārakādibhya itac* (Pāṇini 5.2.36), the suffix *itac* is added after words such as *tāraka*; thus, "stars have appeared for him" is expressed as *tārakitaṃ nabhaḥ* ("the sky is starred").

Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.37: *pramāṇe dvayasaj-daghnañ-mātracaḥ*. The phrase "tad asya" ("that is its") is understood here. When the thigh (*ūru*) is the measure of something, it is called *ūrudvayasam*, *ūrudaghnam*, or *ūrumātram*. The suffix *la* is used when the measure is a *śama*, *diṣṭi*, or *vitasti*. After a *dvigu* compound, these suffixes are obligatory: for example, that which has two *śamas* as its measure is *dviśamam*. Regarding uncertainty, the suffix *mātraC* should be stated after a number as well as after a measure or a measure-word: *śamamātram*, *prasthamātram*, *pañcamātram*. After a word ending in *vat*, the suffixes *dvayasaC* and *mātraC* are applied diversely in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
That much, that very amount; [it is] two-fold. SK 1839:

*puruṣahastibhyām aṇ ca* (A 5.2.38). That for which a man (*puruṣa*) is the measure is *pauruṣam*; [or] *puruṣadvayasam*. [That for which] an elephant (*hastin*) is the measure is *hāstinam*; [or] *hastidvayasam*.
SK 1840: After the words *yad*, *etad*, and others, the suffix *vatup* is added in the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*). [Examples:
that which is its measure is *yāvān*, *tāvān*, or *etāvān*. SK 1841: After the words *kim* and *idam*, the suffix *gha* replaces *va*. [Resulting forms: *kiyat* and *iyat*.]
The suffix *vatup* occurs after these two [words *kim* and *idam*], and for this [suffix], *gha* is substituted. *Kiyān* / *iyān*.

(Pāṇini 5.2.41) "After *kim*, when expressing a numerical measure, there is also *ḍati*; and because of the word 'also' (*ca*), there is *vatup*. And for that *va* of *vatup*, *gha* shall be substituted. Those whose number is how much? *Kati*. *Kiyantaḥ*.

SK 1843: The suffix *taya* is added to a numeral to denote a part (*avayava*). Example: *pañcāvayavā asya pañcatayaṃ dāru* ("this wood has five parts; it is fivefold"). SK 1844: After the words *dvi* and *tri*, the suffix *taya* may optionally be replaced by *aya*. (A 5.2.43)

Two (*dvaya*), a pair (*dvitaya*), three (*traya*), a triad (*tritaya*). According to A 5.2.44, *ubhād udātto nityam*, the suffix *tayap* after the word *ubha* becomes *ayac*, and this [suffix] is always accented on its first syllable: *ubhayam*.

SK 1846: *tadasminn adhikam iti daśāntāḍḍuḥ* (A 5.2.45). [The suffix] *ḍa* is applied after a word ending in *daśan* to form a bahuvrīhi meaning "this has more than that. For example, *ekādaśa adhikā asmin ekādaśam* ("eleven are in excess in this," i.e., eleven). This is desired only when referring to a hundred (*śata*) or a thousand (*sahasra*). It does not apply here: *ekādaśa adhikā asyāṃ viṃśatau* ("eleven are in excess in this twenty"). It is also desired only when the base (*prakṛti*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) belong to the same genus (*samānajātīyatva*). It does not apply here: *ekādaśa māṣā adhikā asmin suvarṇaśate* ("eleven māṣas are in excess in this hundred gold coins"). SK 1847: *śadantaviṃśateś ca* (A 5.2.46). [The suffix *ḍa* is applied] also after a word ending in *śat* and after *viṃśati*.
The suffix *ḍaḥ* occurs in the sense of "stated. For example: *triṃśaṃ śatam* ("a hundred [in which] thirty are added") and *viṃśam*.
According to A 5.2.47, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied after a numeral when it denotes a multiplier (*guṇa*) in the sense of a measure (*nimāna*).

The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs after a word denoting a number, ending in the nominative case, when it signifies a portion (*bhāga*) that serves as the price (*nimāna*), provided it stands in the sense of the genitive case. Example: *yavānāṃ dvau bhāgau nimānam asya udaśvid-bhāgasya* → *dvimayam udaśvid yavānām* ("two parts of barley are the price for this one part of buttermilk"). Why say "of a quality" (*guṇasya*)? Consider: *dvau vrīhi-yavau nimānam asya udaśvitaḥ* ("two [measures] of rice and barley are the price for this buttermilk"). Here, rice and barley are substances, not qualities. Why say "when it is the price" (*nimāne*)? Consider: *dvau guṇau kṣīrasya ekaḥ tailasya* → *dviguṇaṃ kṣīraṃ pacyate tailena* ("there are two qualities of milk and one of oil; the milk is cooked with double the amount of oil"). Here, "quality" refers to the measure, not the price. SK 1849: The suffix *ḍaṭ* occurs in the sense of "filling that" (*tasya pūraṇe*). Example: *ekādaśānāṃ pūraṇaḥ* → *ekādaśaḥ* ("the eleventh, which completes eleven").

SK 1850: *nāntād asaṃkhyāder maṭ* (A 5.2.49). After a word ending in *n*, but not beginning with a numeral (*asaṃkhyādi*), the augment *maṭ* is added to the suffix *ḍaṭ*. For example, that which completes five is *pañcamaḥ*. Why "after a word ending in *n*"? Consider *viṃśaḥ* (twentieth). Why "not beginning with a numeral"? Consider *ekādaśaḥ* (eleventh). SK 1851: *ṣaṭkatikatipayacaturāṃ thuk* (A 5.2.51). The augment *thuk* is added after the words *ṣaṣ*, *kati*, *katipaya*, and *catur*.

The suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied after these [words] to denote an ordinal (*thugāgamaḥ*). For example: *ṣaṣṇām pūraṇaḥ* = *ṣaṣṭhaḥ* ("the sixth among six"); *katithaḥ*. Even though the word *katipaya* is not a numeral, the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied to it by this very rule as an indicator (*jñāpaka*): *katipayathaḥ*. *Caturthaḥ* ("the fourth"): after the word *catur*, the suffixes *cha* or *tha* are applied, with the elision of the first syllable; thus, *turīyaḥ* or *turyaḥ*. SK 1852: After the words *bahu*, *pūga*, *gaṇa*, and *saṅgha*, the augment *tithuk* is added when *ḍaṭ* follows. Although *pūga* and *saṅgha* are not numerals, the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied to them by this very rule: *bahutithaḥ*, and so forth.
SK 1853: After *vati*, the suffix *ithuk* is applied [to form ordinal numbers] (A 5.2.53); [the rule] "after *ḍaṭ*" remains in force. Example: *yāvatithaḥ*. SK 1854:
After *dvi*, the suffix *tīya* is applied (A 5.2.54). Example: *dvitīyaḥ*.
The suffix *ḍaṭ* is an exception [to the previous rule]. That which completes two is *dvitīyaḥ*.
According to A 5.2.55, *tri-* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*, resulting in *tṛtīyaḥ*.

SK 1856 *viṃśatyādibhyas tamaḍ anyatarasyām* (A 5.2.56): After these [words beginning with] *viṃśati*, the augment *tamaṭ* may optionally be added to the suffix *ḍaṭ*. Examples: *viṃśatitamaḥ* or *viṃśaḥ*; *ekaviṃśatitamaḥ* or *ekaviṃśaḥ*. SK 1857 *nityaṃ śatādimāsārdhamāsasaṃvatsarāc ca* (A 5.2.57): [The suffix *ḍaṭ*] is always [added] after [words] beginning with *śata*, as well as after *māsa*, *ardhamāsa*, and *saṃvatsara*.

The ordinal suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied to [numerals] beginning with "hundred" (*śata*) by this very rule: *śatasya pūraṇaḥ* = *śatatamaḥ*; *ekaśatatamaḥ*. From [numerals] beginning with "month" (*māsa*), the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied for the same reason: *māsatamaḥ*.
By A 5.2.58, *ḍaṭ* is also applied to [numerals] beginning with "sixty" (*ṣaṣṭi*) provided they do not begin with a cardinal number (*asaṃkhyādi*):

*ṣaṣṭitamaḥ*. However, for those beginning with a cardinal number such as "twenty" (*viṃśati*), there is only an option (*vikalpa*) according to the rule *viṃśatyādibhyaḥ*: *ekaṣaṣṭaḥ* or *ekaṣaṣṭitamaḥ*.

SK 1859: *matau chaḥ sūktasāmnoḥ* (A 5.2.59). The suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) after the words *sūkta* and *sāman*. For example: *acchāvākīyam sūktam* ("a hymn containing the word *acchāvāka*") and *vāravantīyam sāma* ("a chant containing the word *vāravant*"). SK 1860: *adhyāyānuvākayor luk* (A 5.2.60). [The suffix *cha*] is elided (*luk*) when referring to an *adhyāya* or an *anuvāka*.

[The suffix] *cha* [is applied] in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Precisely because of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), the suffix *cha* occurs there; and by virtue of the power of its specific prescription (*vidhāna-sāmarthya*), there is optionally (*vikalpena*) elision (*luk*). Examples: *gardabhāṇḍaḥ* and *gardabhāṇḍīyaḥ*. SK 1861: *vimuktādibhyo ’ṇ* (A 5.2.61).

The suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthe ’ṇ*) for the names of chapters (*adhyāya*) and sections (*anuvāka*). For example: the word *vimukta* exists in this [chapter/section], hence it is called *vaimukta*; likewise, *daivāsuraḥ*.
SK 1862: The suffix *vun* is added after words such as *goṣada* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), when referring to an *adhyāya* or an *anuvāka*. [Examples: *goṣadakaḥ*, *iṣetvakaḥ*. SK 1863:
The suffix *pathaḥ* is added after the word *kuśala* in the sense of "skilled in that. [Example: *pathaḥ-kuśalaḥ*.
The suffix *vuñ* may be used: one skilled on a path is a *pathika*. According to A 5.2.64, *kan* is added after words such as *ākarṣa*:
one skilled at *ākarṣa* is an *ākarṣaka*. Regarding the rule "after *ākaṣa*-etc.," the primary reading is without the letter *r*; *ākaṣa* refers to a touchstone.

SK 1865: *dhanahiraṇyāt kāme* (A 5.2.65). *Kāma* means desire. *Dhanakaḥ* refers to Devadatta’s desire for wealth; *hiraṇyakaḥ* [likewise]. SK 1866: *svāṅgebhyaḥ prasite* (A 5.2.66). [The suffix *kan* is applied after words denoting one's own limbs when they signify being attached to them.]

*Keśakaḥ* means one who is intent upon hair; that is to say, one who is devoted to its arrangement. Regarding the rule *udarāṭ ṭhag ādyūne* (A 5.2.67): the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *udara* when the person is not seeking to win over others (*avijigīṣau*). This is an exception to the suffix *kan*. For example, one who is excessively tormented by hunger and intent upon his belly is called *audarikaḥ*. Why specify "not seeking to win over others"? Consider *udarakaḥ*: this refers to one who is occupied with such things as rubbing the belly—that is, one who is addicted to such activities.

SK 1868: *sasyena parijātaḥ* (A 5.2.68). The suffix *kan* is prescribed here, not *ṭhak*. The word *sasya* denotes a quality (*guṇa*), not grain (*dhānya*). There is an alternative reading, *śasyena*. That which is thoroughly produced (*parijāta*) or connected with a quality (*sasya*) is correctly called *sasyaka*.
SK 1869: *aṃśaṃ hārī* (A 5.2.69).

In *hārīti*, the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). For this very reason, the genitive case is not employed when it is joined with that [word]. In *aṃśake dāyādaḥ* ("an heir to a share"), [the genitive is likewise absent].

According to A 5.2.70, *tantrāt* is used in the sense of "recently removed from the loom" (*acirāpahṛta*); thus, *tantrakaḥ paṭaḥ* means "a cloth recently [taken] from the loom," that is, one that is fresh.

SK 1871 *brāhmaṇakoṣṇike saṃjñāyām* (A 5.2.71): A region where Brāhmaṇas subsist as warriors is called *brāhmaṇaka*. A thin gruel (*yavāgū*) in which there is little food is called *uṣṇikā*; here, the substitution of *uṣṇa* for the word *anna* is prescribed by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). SK 1872 *śītoṣṇābhyāṃ kāriṇi* (A 5.2.72): [The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa* when they mean "one who acts accordingly"].
