One who makes cold is *śītaka*, meaning lazy; one who makes warm is *uṣṇaka*, meaning one who acts quickly. According to Pāṇini 5.2.73, the suffix *kan* is added to the word *adhyārūḍha* preceded by *adhika*, with the elision of the final member of the compound.

SK 1874: *anukābhikābhīkaḥ kamitā* (A 5.2.74). The suffix *kan* is added after the prefixes *anu-* and *abhi-* [when joined with the verb root *kam*]. After *abhi-*, there is optionally a lengthening of the vowel. One who desires following is *anukaḥ*; one who desires intensely is *abhikaḥ* or *abhīkaḥ*. SK 1875: *pārśvenānvicchati* (A 5.2.75). [The suffix *kan* is added after *pārśva-* when it means "to seek out."]
One who seeks [something] by an indirect means is called *pārśvaka*.
According to Pāṇini 5.2.76 (*ayaḥśūladaṇḍājinābhyāṃ ṭhak-ṭhañau*), the suffixes *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ* are applied.

One who employs a harsh means is an *ayaḥśūla*; one who seeks [his goal] by such means is *āyaḥśūlika*—that is, a reckless person. *Daṇḍājina* refers to hypocrisy; one who seeks [his goal] by such means is *dāṇḍājinika*.

SK 1877: *tāvatithaṃ grahaṇam iti lug vā* (A 5.2.77). The suffix *kan* may optionally be added [to a word ending in an ordinal number], and there is also optional elision (*luk*) of the ordinal suffix itself. For example: *dvitīyakaṃ* or *dvikaṃ grahaṇaṃ devadattasya* ("Devadatta’s second time of taking"). The meaning is "taking in the form of a second [instance]. It should be stated that the suffix *kan* is added after an ordinal number when the sense is "he takes [something] by means of that many times," and the elision of the ordinal suffix is obligatory. For example: *ṣaṣṭhena rūpeṇa gṛhṇāti* → *ṣaṭko devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta takes [it] six times"); *pañcakaḥ* ("takes five times"). SK 1878: *sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ* (A 5.2.78). [The suffix *kan* is added to a word denoting a person] who is the leader (*grāmaṇī*) among these [people]. (Note: This rule provides the basis for forms such as *daśakaḥ* "leader of ten" or *viṃśatkaḥ* "leader of twenty.")
Those for whom Devadatta is the chief are *devadattakāḥ*; likewise, *tvatkāḥ* and *matkāḥ*.
According to Pāṇini A 5.2.79, when a chain (*śṛṅkhala*) is the means of binding for a young camel (*karabha*), it is called *śṛṅkhalakaḥ karabhaḥ*.

SK 1880: *utka* means "eager" (*unmanāḥ*) [Pāṇini 5.2.80]. From the word *ucchā*, which denotes the activity of an uplifted mind (*udgatamanaskavṛtti*), the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Thus, *utkaḥ* means "longing" (*utkaṇṭhitaḥ*). SK 1881: [The suffix *kan* is added] after words denoting time or purpose when referring to a disease [Pāṇini 5.2.81].

The suffix *kan* is applied after words expressing time (*kāla*) and words expressing purpose (*prayojana*) when referring to a disease (*roga*). An example of [time]: *dvitīyako jvaraḥ* ("a fever occurring on the second day"). An example of [purpose]: *viṣapuṣpakaḥ* ("a disease caused by poisonous flowers"), where the cause or the fruit of the disease is expressed. An example of [purpose]: *uṣṇakaḥ* ("one for whom heat is the effect [of the disease]"). Why "when referring to a disease"? [Counter-example: *dvitīyo divaso 'sya* ("the second day belongs to him"). [This concludes the section on] *tad asminn annaṃ prāye saṃjñāyām* (A 5.2.82).

The suffix *kan* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case in the sense of the locative, provided that the nominative-ending word refers to food that constitutes the principal part [of a meal]. For example: *guḍāpūpāḥ prāyeṇānnam asyām* ("In this [day], sweetmeat cakes are generally the food") results in *guḍāpūpikā paurṇamāsī* ("the full-moon day on which sweetmeat cakes are the main food"). It should be stated that the suffix *ini* is used after *vaṭaka*: *vaṭakinī*. According to A 5.2.83, the suffix *añ* is used after *kulmāṣa*:
*kulmāṣāḥ prāyeṇānnam asyām* ("In this [day], boiled grains are generally the food") results in *kaulmāṣī*.

SK 1884: One who has studied the *chandas* is called a *śrotriya* (A 5.2.84). Because the word "or" (*vā*) is understood [from the previous rule], there is also the form *chāndasa*. SK 1885: The suffixes *-in* and *-iṣṭhan* are applied [to the word *śrāddha*] when it means "one by whom a *śrāddha* has been eaten" (A 5.2.85).
*śrāddhī*, *śrāddhikaḥ*. According to Pāṇini 5.2.86 (*pūrvādiniḥ*), the suffix *ini* is applied after *pūrva*: one by whom [something] was done previously is called *pūrvī*.
SK 1887: And [the suffix *ini*] is applied after a word preceded by *pūrva-* (A 5.2.87), as in *kṛtapūrvī*.
SK 1888: And [the suffix *ini* is applied] after words such as *iṣṭa-* (A 5.2.88).

*Iṣṭī* means "one who has sacrificed," and *adhītī* means "one who has studied. According to Pāṇini 5.2.89, *paripanthin* and *pariparin* are used in the Vedic language (*chandasi*) to denote one who stands in the way;
however, in common worldly usage (*loke*), the word *paripanthin* is not strictly correct [according to that rule].

SK 1890: *anupady-anveṣṭā* (A 5.2.90). One who searches for a track is *anupadī*, as in *anupadī gavaḥ* ("one who tracks the cows"). SK 1891: *sākṣāt-draṣṭari saṃjñāyām* (A 5.2.91). [The suffix *ṇini* is applied after *sākṣāt*] in the sense of "a witness," when it is a proper name.
A witness (*sākṣin*) is one who sees directly (*sākṣāt draṣṭā*).

Regarding *kṣetriya*—as in "one to be treated in another's field" (*parakṣetre cikitsyaḥ*, A 5.2.92)—a *kṣetriya* disease is one that must be treated in another body; the meaning is that it is incurable.

SK 1893: *indriya* [is derived] from "the mark of Indra," "seen by Indra," "created by Indra," "enjoyed by Indra," or "given by Indra" (Pāṇini 5.2.93). Here, *indra* means the Self (*ātman*); it is its "mark" (*liṅga*) because the agent is inferred through the instrument. The word *iti* has the sense of "in this manner. Alternatively, *indriya* means that which is difficult for Indra to conquer. SK 1894: The suffix *matup* [is applied] in the sense of "that belongs to him" or "that exists in this" (Pāṇini 5.2.94).

One who has cows in this [place] or who possesses them is *gomān* ("cow-possessing"). The suffixes *matup* and others occur when there is abundance (*bhūman*), censure (*nindā*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), constant connection (*nityayoga*), excellence (*atiśāyana*), association (*saṃsarga*), or when the existence [of the quality] is intended to be expressed (Pāṇini 5.2.94).

And after *rasa* and so on, the suffix *matup* is applied (A 5.2.95): *rasavān*, *rūpavān*. This statement is for the purpose of excluding other suffixes expressing possession (*matvarthīya*). [The words are: *rasa*, *rūpa*, *varṇa*, *gandha*, *sparśa*, *śabda*, *sneha*. [The suffix *matup* occurs] after a word denoting a quality (*guṇa*) that consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*): *svavān*. The mention of "quality" (*guṇa*) serves as a qualifier for *rasa* and the others.

SK 1896 *tasau matvarthe* (A 1.4.19): A stem ending in *-ta* or *-sa* receives the designation *bha* when followed by a suffix expressing possession (*matvartha*). [Vt.]: There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel in *vasu*. Example: *viduṣmān* ("one who possesses knowledge"). [Vt.]: The elision (*luk*) of the possessive suffix *matup* is desired after words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*). Example: "that which has the quality of white" → *śuklaḥ paṭaḥ* ("a white cloth"); likewise, *kṛṣṇaḥ* ("black"). SK 1897 *mādupadhāyāś ca mator vo 'yavādibhyaḥ* (A 8.2.9): The final *m* of the possessive suffix *matup* is replaced by *v*, provided it follows a word ending in *m* or *u*, or one having *m* or *u* as its penultimate letter, excluding words such as *yava*. (Note: This rule applies to the formation of the word *śuklavān* etc., though the specific example for this particular sūtra is not provided in the source text).

The *m* of the suffix *matup* following a word ending in *m* or *v*, or having *m* or *v* as its penultimate (*upadhā*) letter—provided it is not preceded by *ya* or similar sounds—is replaced by *v*. Examples: *kiṃvān*, *jñānavān*, *vidyāvān*, *lakṣmīvān*, *yajñasvān*, *bhāsvān*. However, in the case of *yava* and others, we have *yavamān*, *bhūmimān*.

[SK 1898] *jñayaḥ*: The *m* of *matup* following a word ending in *jña* is replaced by *v*. Because this is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*), the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) does not apply. Example: *vidyutvān*.

SK 1899 (A 8.2.11): In the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), the *m* of the suffix *matup* shall be replaced by *v*. Examples: *ahīvatī*, *munīvatī*. [Note: The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *śarādīnāṃ ca*.
SK 1900 (A 8.2.12): [The forms] *āsandīvat*, *aṣṭhīvat*, *cakrīvat*, *kakṣīvat*, *rumaṇvat*, and *carmaṇvatī* [are established as names].

These six are irregularly formed (nipātita) in the sense of possession (*saṃjñā*). The word *āsana* becomes *āsandī*: *āsandīvān grāmaḥ* ("a village possessing a chair"); elsewhere, it is *āsanavān*. The word *asthi* becomes *aṣṭhī*: *aṣṭhīvān* is the name of a seer (*ṛṣi*); elsewhere, it is *asthimān*. The word *cakra* becomes *cakrī*: *cakrīvān* is the name of a king; elsewhere, it is *cakravān*. There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of *kakṣyā*: *kakṣīvān* is the name of a seer; elsewhere, it is *kakṣyāvān*. The word *lavaṇa* becomes *rumaṇ*: *rumaṇvān* is the name of a mountain.

Elsewhere, it is *lavaṇavat*. In the case of *carman*, there is an absence of the elision of *n* and the substitution of *ṇ*; thus, *carmaṇvatī* is the name of a river (*madī*), whereas elsewhere it is *carmavat*.

SK 1901 *udanvān* is used for *udadhi* (ocean) and [in the sense of] *matau* (the suffix -mat); there is the substitution of *udan-* for *udaka-* in the word *udadhi* and when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). *Udanvān* refers to the ocean and also to a ploughman. SK 1902 *rājanvān* is used in the sense of good governance (*saurājya*).

The earth possesses a king (*rājanvatī bhūḥ*), but elsewhere it is *rājavān*. According to A 5.2.96, *prāṇisthād āto laj anyatarasyām*, [the suffix] *lac* is optionally applied after a word ending in long *ā* that denotes something residing in a living being. Examples: *cūḍālaḥ* / *cūḍāvān*. Why "residing in a living being"? [Consider: *śikhāvān dīpaḥ* ("a lamp with a flame"). Why "ending in long *ā*"? [Consider: *hastavān*. [The suffix applies] only after a word denoting a limb of a living being; not here: *meghavān* ("possessing clouds"). Since the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is already established by the accent of the suffix itself, the particle *ca* in the rule is for the purpose of overriding the circumflex (*svarita*) accent prescribed by the rule *svarito vānudātte padādau* in cases such as *cūḍālo 'si*.

SK 1904 *sidhmādibhyaś ca* (A 5.2.97): The suffix *lac* may optionally be applied after [the words] beginning with *sidhma*. Thus, *sidhmalaḥ* or *sidhmavān*. The mention of *anyatarasyām* is for the purpose of including the suffix *matup*, and not for the purpose of providing an option regarding the suffix itself. Consequently, the suffixes *ini* and *iṣṭhan* do not apply after words ending in *akāra*. Furthermore, for the words *vāta*, *danta*, *bala*, and *lalāṭa*, the feminine suffix *ūṅ* is also applied. Thus, *vātūlaḥ*. SK 1905 *vatsāsābhyāṃ kāmabale* (A 5.2.98).

From these two [words, *kāma* and *bala*], the suffix *lañ* occurs respectively when the meanings are "possessing desire" (*kāmavat*) and "possessing strength" (*balavat*). Thus: *vatsalaḥ* ("affectionate") and *aṃsalaḥ* ("strong"). According to A 5.2.99, *phenād ilac ca*, the suffix *ilac* also occurs after *phena*. Furthermore, the mention of *anyatarasyām* (optionally) continues here for the purpose of including the suffix *matup*. Thus: *phenilaḥ*, *phenalaḥ*, and *phenavān* ("foamy").

SK 1907: *lomādipāmādipicchādibhyaḥ śanelacaḥ* (A 5.2.100). From *loman* and the following, the suffix *śa* is applied: *lomaśaḥ*, *lomavān*; *romaśaḥ*, *romavān*. From *pāman* and the following, the suffix *na* is applied: *pāmanaḥ*. After *aṅga*, [the suffix *na* is applied] in the sense of "beautiful": *aṅganā*. After *lakṣmī*, the suffix *ac* is also applied: *lakṣmaṇaḥ*. In the case of *viṣvak*, there is elision of the final member of the compound, with the sandhi not having been applied: *viṣuṇaḥ*. From *piccha* and the following, the suffix *ilac* is applied: *picchilaḥ*, *picchivān*; *urasilaḥ*, *urasvān*. SK 1908: *prajñāśraddhārcābhyo ṇaḥ* (A 5.2.101). The suffix *ṇa* is applied after *prajñā*, *śraddhā*, and *arcā*.
*Prājña-* from *pra-ajña*, *prājñā*; *śrāddha-*; *ārca-*; and from *vṛt*: *vārta-*. SK 1909: *tapas-sahasrābhyāṃ vinīnī* (A 5.2.102).

The vowel *i* in *vin* and *in* is for the purpose of protecting the letter *n*. Thus: *tapasvī* and *sahasrī*. Although [the suffixes] would have been established by virtue of being *asan* (not having *an*) and ending in *a*, the rule is stated again so that they may not be superseded by *aṇ*. However, in the case of *sahasra*, it is also for the purpose of superseding *ṭhan*.

SK 1910 *aṇ* ca (A 5.2.103). This separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. Examples: *tāpasaḥ*, *sāhasraḥ*. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is made for words beginning with *jyotsnā*: *jyautsnaḥ*, *tāmisraḥ*. SK 1911 (A 5.2.104).

A jar made of sand; [a place] consisting of gravel. According to Pāṇini 5.2.105, *deśe lub-ilac-au ca* ("In the sense of 'place,' there is elision (*lub*), as well as *ilac* and *aṇ*, and also *matup*"), [the forms are derived as follows]: because there are sands (*sikatāḥ*) in this place, it is called *sikatāḥ*, *sikatilaḥ*, *saikataḥ*, or *sikatāvān*. The same applies to *śarkarā* and so forth.
SK 1913 *danta-unnata-urac* (A 5.2.106): The suffix *urac* is applied after *danta* and *unnata*. One who has protruding teeth is called *danturaḥ*.
SK 1914 *ūṣa-suṣi-muṣka-madho raḥ* (A 5.2.107): The suffix *raḥ* is applied after *ūṣa*, *suṣi*, *muṣka*, and *madhu*.

*Ūṣaraḥ* (salt-waste); *suṣiraḥ* (hollow); *muṣkaḥ* means the testicle, hence *muṣkaraḥ*; *madhu* means sweetness, hence *madhuraḥ*. In the section on the suffix *ra*, there is an addition for *kha*, *mukha*, and *kuñja*: *kharaḥ* (donkey); *mukharaḥ* (talkative); *kuñjaḥ* means the jaw of an elephant, hence *kuñjaraḥ* (elephant). Also [the suffix *ra* is added] after *naga*, *pāṃsu*, and *pāṇḍu*: *nagaraḥ* (city); *pāṃsuraḥ* (dusty); *pāṇḍuraḥ* (pale). However, the word *pāṇḍura* is itself un-derived (*avyutpanna*). After *kacchu*, there is also shortening [of the vowel]: *kacchuraḥ* (scabby). A 5.2.108: after *dyu* and *dru*, the suffix *ma* is added: *dyumaḥ* (heavenly); *drumaḥ* (tree).

SK 1916: *keśād vo ’nyatarasyām* (A 5.2.109). Since the suffix *matup* is already established by the previously mentioned option (*anyatarasyām*), its mention again is for the purpose of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of both *ini* and *thañ*. Examples: *keśavaḥ*, *keśī*, *keśikaḥ*, *keśavān*. It is also seen after other words: *maṇivaḥ* (a specific type of serpent); *hariṇyavaḥ* (a specific type of treasure). [After the word *arṇas*,] there is also elision (*lopa*): *arṇavaḥ*. SK 1917: *gāṇḍyajagāt saṃjñāyām* (A 5.2.110). [The suffix *va* occurs after *gāṇḍī* and *ajaga* when they denote a proper name.]

The short and long forms [of the suffixes] are indicated by *yaṇ* substitution according to the principle of *tantra*. *Gāṇḍiva* and *gāṇḍīva* refer to the bow of Arjuna; *ajagava* refers to the *pināka* bow. According to Pāṇini 5.2.111, *kāṇḍāṇḍād īrannīracau*, the forms *kāṇḍīraḥ* and *āṇḍīraḥ* are derived.

SK 1919: *rajaḥ-kṛṣi-āsuti-pariṣada-valac* (A 5.2.112). *rajasvalā* (a woman in her menses); *kṛṣīvalaḥ* (a farmer). [The suffix] *valac* takes the long vowel [in the preceding stem], as in *āsutīvalaḥ* (a distiller), i.e., a vintner; *pariṣadvalaḥ*. There is an alternative reading *parṣad*, as in *parṣadvalam*. It is also seen after other [words]: *bhrātṛvalaḥ* (one who has many brothers), *putravalaḥ* (one who has many sons), *śatruvalaḥ* (one who has many enemies). In the rule for *valac*, because the term *saṃjñāyām* ("when it is a name") is understood [from the previous sūtra], the long vowel does not apply here [in these examples]. SK 1920: *danta-śikhāt saṃjñāyām* (A 5.2.113). [The suffix *valac* is applied after the words *danta* and *śikha* when they form a name.]
*Dantāvalaḥ* means an elephant; *śikhāvalaḥ* means a peacock. [SK 1921] *Jyotsnātamisrāśṛṅgiṇorjasvinnūrjasvalagominmalinamalīmasāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.114).

The suffix *in* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). From *jyotis*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) and the suffix *na*. Thus: *jyotsnā* (moonlight). From *tamas*, the penultimate vowel is changed to *i* and *ra* is added. Thus: *tamisrā* (darkness). The feminine gender is not mandatory; thus: *tamisram* (neuter). From *śṛṅga*, the suffix *ini* is added: *śṛṅgiṇaḥ* (horned). From *ūrjas*, the suffix *balac* is added. This is so that the [suffix *in*] might not be superseded by it; therefore, *vin* is also used: *ūrjasvī* and *ūrjasvalaḥ*. As for the statement in the *Vṛtti* that "there is the augment *asug* after *ūrjas*," this is to be reconsidered, since the form is accounted for by the suffix *asun* itself, as in *ūrjasvatī*. From the word *go*, the suffix *min* is added: *gomī* (possessing cattle). From the word *mala*, the suffix *ini* is added: *malinaḥ* (dirty). And from [the same base], the suffix *īmasa* is also added: *malīmasaḥ*.
SK 1922 *ata iniṣṭhanau* (A 5.2.115):
*daṇḍī*, *daṇḍikaḥ*. SK 1923 *vrīhyādibhyaś ca* (A 5.2.116).

*vrīhī*, *vrīhikaḥ*. However, the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan* are not desired after all [bases] such as *vrīhi*; rather, *ini* is applied after *śikhā*, *mālā*, *saṃjñā*, and so forth; *ika* is applied after *yava*, *khada*, and so forth; and both are applied after others.
Furthermore, by A 5.2.117, *ilac* is also applied after *tuṇḍa* and so forth.

The suffixes *ca*, *ini*, *ṭhan*, and *matup* [are applied after words denoting a bodily limb when that limb is increased]. Examples: *tundilaḥ*, *tundī*, *tundikaḥ*, *tundavān*. [The same applies to] *udara*, *picaṇḍa*, *yava*, and *vrīhi*. When a word denoting a bodily limb (*svāṅga*) is qualified by increase (*vivṛddhi*), the suffixes *ilac*, etc., may be applied. One whose ears are increased is *karṇilaḥ*, *karṇī*, *karṇikaḥ*, or *karṇavān*. SK 1925: After a word preceded by *eka* or *go*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is always applied [in the sense of "possessing"].

Example: one who possesses one hundred cows is *aikasahasrikaḥ*; one who possesses one thousand cows is *aikasahasrikaḥ*; one who possesses a hundred cows is *gauśatikaḥ*; one who possesses a thousand cows is *gausahasrikaḥ*.

SK 1926: After a nominal stem ending in *niṣka* followed by *śata* or *sahasra*, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Examples: *naiṣkaśatikaḥ* ("possessing one hundred *niṣkas*") and *naiṣkasahasrikaḥ* ("possessing one thousand *niṣkas*").
SK 1927: After the word *rūpa*, the suffix *yap* occurs in the sense of "struck" (*āhata*) or "praised" (*praśaṃsā*). [Examples: *rūpyam āhatam* and *rūpyaḥ praśastaḥ*].

That which has struck (*āhata*) form is *rūpya*, such as a silver coin (*kārṣāpaṇa*); that which possesses excellent form is *rūpya*, such as a fine cow. Why say "struck"? [To exclude cases like] *rūpavān* ("possessing form"). It is also seen after other [words]: *himyāḥ parvatāḥ* ("snowy mountains") and *guṇyā brāhmaṇāḥ* ("virtuous Brahmins"). Pāṇini 5.2.121 states: *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* ("the suffix *vini* is applied after words ending in *as*, *māyā*, *medhā*, and *sraj*").

*vaśasvī*, *yaśasvān*, *māyāvī*, *māyāvān*. Because of their inclusion in the *vrīhy-ādi* group, the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan* are applied: *māyī*, *māyikaḥ*. Because it ends in the *kvip* suffix, [the word *sraj*] becomes *ku*: *sragvī*. There is an addition of *āmaya* [to the list], and there is lengthening [of the vowel]: *āmayāvī*. From *śṛṅga* and *vṛnda*, the suffix *ārakan* is applied: *śṛṅgārakaḥ*, *vṛndārakaḥ*. From *phala* and *barha*, the suffix *inac* is applied: *phalinaḥ*, *barhiṇaḥ*. After *hṛdaya*, the suffix *āluc* is optionally applied; [otherwise] *ini*, *iṭhan*, and *matup* are applied: *hṛdayāluḥ*, *hṛdayī*, *hṛdayikaḥ*, *hṛdayavān*.

The suffix *ālu* is applied after *śīta*, *uṣṇa*, and *tṛpra* when there is an inability to endure them. One who does not endure cold is *śītāluḥ*; one who does not endure heat is *uṣṇāluḥ*. The suffix *rak* is added by the rule *sphāyitañci* [Uṇādi Sūtra 184]. *Tṛpra* refers to a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). One who does not endure it is *tṛprāluḥ*. Mādhava states that *tṛpra* means suffering (*duḥkha*). After *hima*, the suffix *elū* is applied: one who does not endure cold is *himeluḥ*. After *bala*, the suffix *ūla* is applied: one who does not endure strength is *balūlaḥ*. After *vāta*, the suffix *ūla* is applied in the sense of "not enduring" or "a collection": one who does not endure wind, or a collection of winds, is *vātūlaḥ*. After *tarpa*, *avama*, and *marut*, [the suffix *ūla* is applied]: *parvataḥ* ("mountain") and *maruttaḥ* ("name of a king"). By the rule *ūrṇāyā yus* (A 5.2.123), the suffix *yus* is applied after *ūrṇā*.

Because it is a *pada*, [the *ū* of] *ūrṇāyuḥ* [becomes long]. Here, some maintain that the rule *chandasi* (in Vedic) is to be supplied; and this is correct. Otherwise, one would have included the mention of *ūrṇā* right there in the rule *ahaṃśubhamoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.88).
[From the rule] *vāco gminiḥ* (A 5.2.124), [we derive] *vāggmī*.

SK 1931: The suffixes *ālaj* and *āṭac* are applied [to the word *bahu*] when it means "one who speaks much" (*bahubhāṣin*). It should be stated that this applies when it is used in a derogatory sense (*kutsita*). One who speaks excessively in a contemptible manner is called *vācālaḥ* or *vācāṭaḥ*. However, one who speaks much correctly is simply called *vāggmī*. SK 1932: The suffix *svāmin* is applied in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

From the word *sva*, which denotes sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), the suffix *āmin* is added in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) to form *svāmī*. According to Pāṇini A 5.2.127, *arśa-ādibhyo 'c*, the suffix *ac* is added after words such as *arśas*; thus, one who has hemorrhoids (*arśāṃsi*) is called *arśasaḥ*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words).

SK 1934: *dvandvopatāpagarhyāt prāṇisthād iniḥ* (A 5.2.128). The suffix *ini* is applied after a compound (*dvandva*), a word denoting a disease (*upatāpa*), or a censurable quality (*garhya*), provided it refers to something residing in a living being (*prāṇistha*). Examples: *kaṭakavalayinī* ("possessing bracelets and bangles"); *śaṅkhanūpuriṇī* ("possessing anklets"). *Disease*: *kuṣṭhī* ("suffering from leprosy"); *kilāsī* ("suffering from white leprosy"). *Censurable*: *kakudāvartī* ("having a hump and a curl on the neck"); *kākatālukī* ("having a palate like a crow's"). Why "residing in a living being"? Consider: *puṣpaphalavān ghaṭaḥ* ("a pot possessing flowers and fruit")—here the suffix is not applied because it does not refer to a living being. Why "not [after] a limb of a living being"? Consider: *pāṇipādavatī* ("possessing hands and feet")—here the suffix *ini* is not applied. The rule applies only after words ending in *at*. Consider: *citrakalalāṭikāvatī* ("possessing a variegated forehead-mark"). Since the suffix was already established by the previous rule, its restatement here is for the purpose of excluding suffixes such as *ṭhan*.

SK 1935: *vātātīsārābhyāṃ kuk ca* (A 5.2.129). After the words *vāta* ("wind/dysentery") and *atisāra* ("diarrhea"), the suffix *ini* is applied, and the augment *kuk* is added. Examples: *vātakī* ("suffering from wind-disorder"); *atisārakī* ("suffering from diarrhea").

The suffix *ini* is applied after words beginning with *vāta*. Thus: *vātakī* ("suffering from wind-disorder") and *atīsārakī* ("suffering from dysentery"). This is intended [only] in the sense of a disease; it is not used here in *vātavatī guhā* ("a cave full of wind"). [The suffix *ini* is also applied] after *piśāca*: *piśācakī*. SK 1936: After ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa*), the suffix *ini* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) when age is to be indicated. For example: *pañcamī uṣṭraḥ* ("a camel that has reached its fifth year"), meaning "a camel for whom the fifth month or year exists. This rule is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *ṭhan*. Why "when age"? Consider *pañcamavān grāmaḥ* ("a village having five [parts]"). Here, it does not refer to the age of a living being.

SK 1937: *sukhādibhyaś ca* (A 5.2.131). The suffix *ini* is added in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) after words such as *sukha*. Examples: *sukhī*, *duḥkhī*. [The suffix *ini* is also applied] in the sense of a garland (*mālā*) when it implies a reproach (*ākṣepa*). Example: *mālī*. SK 1938: *dharmaśīlavarṇāntāc ca* (A 5.2.132). [The suffix *ini* is applied] after words ending in *dharma*, *śīla*, or *varṇa*.

The suffix *ini* is added after words such as *dharma* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). Examples: *brāhmaṇadharmī*, *brāhmaṇaśīlī*, *brāhmaṇavarṇī*. According to A 5.2.133, *hastin* is formed from *hasta* when referring to a genus (*jāti*). Why "when referring to a genus"? [Answer: *hastavān puruṣaḥ* ("a man with hands").
SK 1940: After the word *varṇa*, [the suffix *ini*] is applied when [the compound] refers to a religious student (*brahmacārin*); [thus] *varṇī*.
SK 1941: After words such as *puṣkara*, [the suffix *ini* is applied] when [the compound] refers to a place (*deśa*).

The suffix *ini* is applied after the words *puṣkara* and *padma* when they denote a location. Why "when denoting a location"? [Counter-example: *puṣkaravān karī* ("a lotus-bearing elephant"). [The suffix *ini* is applied] after a word ending in *bala* that has *bāhu* or *ūru* as its prior member: *bāhubalī* ("strong-armed") and *ūrubalī* ("strong-thighed"). It is also applied after words beginning with *sarva*: *sarvadhanī* ("possessing all wealth") and *sarvabījī* ("possessing all seeds"). And it is applied after the word *artha* when it does not mean "present": *arthī* ("needy"). But when it means "present," it is *arthavān*. And it is applied after a compound ending in those [words mentioned above]: *dhānyārthī* ("needy of grain") and *hiraṇyārthī* ("needy of gold").
By rule A 5.2.136, *matup* may optionally be used after *bala* and others: *balavān* or *balī*, *utsāhavān* or *utsāhī*.

SK 1943: *saṃjñāyāṃ manmābhyām* (A 5.2.137). The suffix *ini* is applied after words ending in *man* and *mā* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), provided they form a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *prathiminī*, *dāminī*, *hominī*, *sominī*. Why "provided it is a proper name"? Consider *somavān*. SK 1944: *kaṃśaṃbhyāṃ babhayustitutayasaḥ* (A 5.2.138). The words *kaṃśam* end in the suffix *mān*. *Kam* is used in the senses of water and happiness; *śam* is used in the sense of happiness. From these two, seven suffixes (*yu*, *si*, *as*, etc. may occur. The *s* in *yus* and *as* is for the purpose of establishing their status as *pada*s. *kaṃbaḥ*, *kaṃbhaḥ*, *kaṃyuḥ*, *kaṃtiḥ*, *kaṃtuḥ*, *kaṃtaḥ*, *kaṃyaḥ*; *śaṃbaḥ*, *śaṃbhaḥ*, *śaṃyuḥ*, *śaṃtiḥ*, *śaṃtuḥ*, *śaṃtaḥ*, *śaṃyaḥ*. (A 5.2.139)

*Vṛddhā* means having a protruding navel; *tundī* means having a large belly. Mādhava states that this [suffix] has *mūrdhan* as its upadhā. Thus: *tuṇḍibhaḥ*, *valibhaḥ*, *vaṭibhaḥ*. Because it belongs to the *pāmādi* group, it is also applied to *valin*. Regarding the rule *ahaṃśubhamor yus* (A 5.2.140):

*aham* is an indeclinable ending in *m* used in the sense of ego (*ahaṅkāra*); *śubham* is used in the sense of auspiciousness (*śubha*). *Ahaṃyuḥ* means "possessing ego"; *śubhaṃyuḥ* means "endowed with auspiciousness."
Thus end the suffixes expressing possession (*matvarthīya*).
This concludes section 37 on the *taddhita* suffixes beginning with those derived from the quarters (*prāgdiśīya*).

SK 1947 *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (A 5.3.1): The suffixes to be mentioned hereafter, prior to [the rule concerning] words denoting direction (*dikśabda*), shall bear the technical designation *vibhakti*. SK 1948 *kiṃsarvanāmabahubhyo 'dvyādibhyaḥ* (A 5.3.2): [The suffixes beginning with *tasil* are applied] after the word *kim*, pronouns (*sarvanāman*), and the word *bahu*, provided they are not among the group beginning with *dvi*.
The rule *kimaḥ sarvanāmno bahuśabdāc ca* is governed by the heading *prāgdiśaḥ*; furthermore, *idama iś* (A 5.3.3) applies when a suffix belonging to the *prāgdiśīya* group follows.

Because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it is a substitute for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*). *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.7): "There is elision of the *n* at the end of a nominal stem. *sarvasya so 'nyatarasyāṃ di* (A 5.3.6):

"Before an affix beginning with *d* that belongs to the *prāgdiśīya* group, *sa-* may optionally be substituted for *sarva-*.**" *(Note: In the original Sanskrit text, the rule *sarvasya so 'nyatarasyāṃ di* is cited from A 5.3.6, which governs the substitution of *sa-* for *sarva-* before certain *prāgdiśīya* suffixes beginning with *d*.)**

SK 1953: *pañcamyās tasil* (A 5.3.7). The suffix *tasil* may optionally occur after words such as *kim* when they end in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). SK 1954: *ku tihoḥ* (A 7.2.104). [The substitution of *ku* occurs for *kim*] before the suffixes *ti* and *ha*.

And by A 5.3.8 (*taseś ca*), there shall be the substitution of *tasil* for *tas* following *kim*, pronouns (*sarvanāman*), and *bahu*. This statement is made for the sake of the accent and for the sake of the case-ending.

SK 1956 *paryabhibhyāṃ ca* (A 5.3.9): The suffix *tasil* is added after these two [prepositions] *pari* and *abhi*, but only when they have the sense of "all" (*sarva*) or "both" (*ubhaya*). *Paritas* means "on all sides" (*sarvatas*); *abhitas* means "on both sides" (*ubhayatas*). SK 1957 *saptamyās tral* (A 5.3.10): The suffix *tral* is added in place of the locative case ending (*saptamī*).
In what place? *kutra*; in that place, *yatra*; in that place, *tatra*; in many places, *bahutra*.
According to A 5.3.11, *idam* takes the substitute *ha* before the suffix *tra*, which is an exception to [the rule for] *tral*; thus, *iha*.

SK 1959: The mention of *vā* ("optionally") from A 5.3.13 is drawn back [to this rule]. After the word *kima-* ending in the seventh case, *ad* may optionally occur; in the alternative, *tral* occurs.
The substitute *kva* may optionally take the place of *kimaḥ* before the suffix *ati*. Examples: *kva*, *kutra*.
According to A 5.3.13, *vā ha ca chandasi*, [the substitute *kva* also occurs] in the Vedic language:
*kuha sthaḥ*, *kuha jagmathuḥ*.

SK 1962: *etadastratasostratasau cānudāttau* (A 2.4.33). When used in the context of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), the substitute *aś* shall replace *etad*, and it shall be unaccented (*anudātta*) when followed by *tratas* or *tratasau*; these two suffixes also become unaccented. For example: *etasmin grāme sukhaṃ vasāmaḥ / atho 'trādhīmahe / ato na gantāsmaḥ* ("We live happily in this village; therefore we study here; for that reason we will not go"). Because of the inclusion of the word "seen" (*dṛśi*), they occur only in connection with *bhavat* and others: *sa bhavān*, *tato bhavān*, *tatra bhavān*; *taṃ bhavantam*, *tato bhavantam*, *tatra bhavantam*. Likewise: *dīrghāyuḥ*, *devānāmpriyaḥ*, *āyuṣmān*. [Pāṇini A 5.3.15:
After *sarva*, *eka*, *anya*, *kiṃ*, *yad*, and *tad*, the suffix *dā* is added in the sense of time.

The suffix *dā* shall be applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) after these words ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) which denote time. Examples: *sarvasmin kāle* → *sadā*; *sarvadā*; *ekadā*; *anyadā*; *kadā*; *yadā*; *tadā*. Why "denoting time"? [Counter-example: *sarvatra deśe* ("in every place"). By rule A 5.3.16, *hil* is applied after a word ending in the locative case denoting time. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ha*. Example: *asmin kāle* → *etarhi*. Why "denoting time"? [Counter-example: *iha deśe* ("in this place").

SK 1966 (A 5.3.17): The suffix *adhunā* shall be added in its own sense (*svārthe*) after the word *idam* when it ends in the seventh case and denotes time. [The substitution of] *i* occurs; by the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is elision [of the final vowel and consonant]. Thus: *adhunā*. Now:

by *SK* 1968, *tado dā ca* (*A* 5.3.19), [the forms] *tadā* and *tadānīm* [are derived]. The mention of *dā* after *tada-* is redundant, because [the suffix *dā*] has already been prescribed [by a previous rule].
SK 1969: *anadyatane rhil anyatarasyām* (A 5.3.21). [The suffix] *rhil* is optionally used for these:
*karhi*, *kadā*, *tarhi*, *yadā*, *tadā*, and *etarhi* (meaning "at this time").

SK 1970: *sadyaḥ parut parāryauṣamaḥ paredyavyadyapūrvedyuranyedyuranyataredyuritaredyuraparedyuradharedyurubhayedyuruttaredyuḥ* (A 5.3.22). [These are the forms derived with the suffixes *dyu* and *dya* for various temporal meanings.]

These are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs when combined with *dya-* to form a word meaning "on the same day": *samāne 'hani* → *sadyaḥ*. When combined with *para-* and *udāra-* to mean "in the year," the forms are derived from *pūrva-* and *pūrvatara-*: *pūrvasmin saṃvatsare* → *parut*; *pūrvatare saṃvatsare* → *parāri*. With *idam-* meaning "in the year," the suffix *samaṣ* is added and *iś* is substituted: *asmin saṃvatsare* → *aiṣamaḥ*. From *para-* to mean "on the next day," the suffix *edyavi* is added: *parasminn ahani* → *paredyavi*. For *idam-* meaning "on this day," *aś* is substituted and *dya-* is added: *asminn ahani* → *adya*.

The suffix *edyus* is applied after the eight words beginning with *pūrva* when referring to a day: *pūrvedyuḥ*, *anyedyuḥ*, *uttaredyuḥ*, *adharedyuḥ*, *aparedyuḥ*, *paredyuḥ*, *ubhayedyuḥ*, and *sarvedyuḥ*. It should be stated that the word *dyu* is also added after *ubhaya*: *ubhayadyuḥ*.

By rule A 5.3.23, *thāl* is used in the sense of expressing a manner (*prakāra*). The suffix *thāl* occurs in its own meaning after words such as *kim* when they function to express a manner. [Examples: *tena prakāreṇa* = *tathā*; *yathā*.

SK 1972 *imadas thamuḥ* (A 5.3.24): This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *thāl*. It should also be stated that [the suffix *thamu*] applies after *etad* as well: by this manner or by that manner—*ittham*.
SK 1973 *kimaś ca* (A 5.3.25).
In what manner? How? The full limit for the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of those [suffixes] belonging to the *prāg-diś* group has been reached.

Among the *taddhita* suffixes, those beginning with *pra* are treated as such; specifically, by the rule: "After words denoting direction, the suffix *astāti* is applied in the sense of the seventh, fifth, and first case endings, when direction, place, or time is intended" (A 5.3.27).

The suffix *astāti* occurs in its own sense after words denoting direction, place, or time that are established [as such] and end in the seventh case (*saptamī*) or other case endings. According to A 5.3.39, *pūrvādharāvarāṇām asipurdhavaś caiṣām*, the suffix *asip* occurs in the sense of *astāti* after these [words], and when joined with it, there shall be the substitutes *pura*, *adha*, and *ava* for them respectively.

SK 1976 *astāti ca* (A 5.3.40): When *asti* follows, the words beginning with *pura-* are substituted for the words beginning with *pūrva-*. For example: *pūrvasyāṃ pūrvasyāḥ pūrvā vā dik* becomes *puraḥ*, *purastāt*, *adhaḥ*, *adhastāt*, *avaḥ*, or *avastāt*. SK 1977 *vibhāṣāvarasya* (A 5.3.41): [The substitution of *pura-* etc. is optional when *avara-* follows.

The suffix *astāti* is optionally applied after the word *avara*. [Examples: *avastāt* or *avarastāt*. The same applies when referring to direction (*diś*) or time (*kāla*). Why [is it said] "after words denoting established directions" (*digirūḍhebhyaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *aindryāṃ vasati* ("He dwells in the eastern quarter"). By the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *astāti ca*, the suffix *asi* does not supersede *astāti*.

SK 1979: By [the rule] *vibhāṣā parāvarābhyām* (A 5.3.29), [the suffixes] *parataḥ*, *avarataḥ*, *parastāt*, and *avarastāt* are formed. SK 1980:
By [the rule] *añcer luk* (A 5.3.30), there is elision (*luk*) [of the suffix].

in the scope of *astāti*, the word *ūrdhva* is substituted by *upa*, and the two suffixes *ril* and *riṣṭātil* are also applied. Thus, one dwells, has come, or [something] is delightful above—either *upari* or *upariṣṭāt*.
SK 1982: After [the word] *paścāt* (A 5.3.32), there is the substitution of *paśca-* for *apara-*, and the suffix *āti*. [The forms are] *adharāt* and *dakṣiṇāt*.
SK 1983: After *uttara-*, *adhara-*, and *dakṣiṇa-*, the suffix *āti* [is applied] (A 5.3.34).
From the north, from the south, from the east, from the west.

Here, some teachers, without following the rule for "north" and the others, state that *enap* is applied after any mere directional term (*dik-śabda*). SK 1985: After *dakṣiṇa*, [the suffix *āc* is applied] when *astāti* follows (A 5.3.36). Example: *dakṣiṇā vasati* ("he dwells to the south"). Only provided that it is not in the fifth case (*pañcamī*): example, *dakṣiṇād āgataḥ* ("come from the south"). From *dakṣiṇa*, [the suffixes] *dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca* (A 2.3.34) apply: *dakṣiṇāhi*, *dakṣiṇā*. Also from *uttara*:

According to A 5.3.44, *ekāddho dhyamuñ anyatarasyām*, the forms *aikadhyam* and *ekadhā* are derived.

In two ways / In three ways. According to Pāṇini A 5.3.47, the suffix *pāśap* is used in the sense of "deserving of being bound" (*yāpye*). An example is *bhiṣakpāśaḥ*, meaning "a contemptible physician."
SK 1994: After a word ending in *pūraṇa* (a ordinal number), when it denotes a part (*bhāga*), the suffix *tīya* is applied [by A 5.3.48].

Before the number eleven (*ekādaśan*), [the suffix *tīya* is applied] except in Vedic usage (*acchandasi*). [A 5.3.49]

The suffix *an* is added after a word ending in a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) to denote a part. Thus: *caturthaḥ* ("the fourth") and *pañcamaḥ* ("the fifth"). SK 1998: *ekādākiniccāsahāye* (A 5.3.52). [The suffix *kan* applies after *eka-* when expressing "alone," and the suffix *ākinic* also applies.]
And [the suffixes] *kan* and *luka*: *ekaḥ*, *ekākī*, *ekakaḥ*. [Vārttika:
The suffix *caraṭ* is applied in the sense of "having previously been" (*bhūtapūrve*). One who was previously wealthy is called *āḍhyacaraḥ*.

SK 2000: *ṣaṣṭhyā rūpya ca* (A 5.3.54). After a word ending in the genitive case, when the sense is "formerly belonging to," the suffixes *rūpya* and *caraṭ* may be applied. SK 2003: *taraptamapau ghaḥ* (A 1.1.22). These two [suffixes], *taraP* and *tamap*, bear the technical designation *gha*.

[The suffix] *ām* is added after words ending in *kim*, *et*, *tiṅ*, or indeclinables (*avyaya*), as well as after words with the *gha*-designation, provided that they do not denote a substance (*adravya*) and express excellence (*prakarṣa*).

[Pāṇini 5.3.57: The suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* occur when a dual or a word expressing division (*vibhajya*) is the attendant word (*upapada*).

When two things are to be distinguished by the superiority of one over the other, these two suffixes (*tara* and *tamap*) occur after words ending in *sup* or *tiṅ*; they are exceptions to the two preceding rules. *laghutaraḥ* ("lighter") or *laghīyān* ("lighter") [is used] when it is said that "this one is lighter than those two. *paṭutarāḥ* ("more clever") or *paṭīyāṃsaḥ* ("more clever") [is used] when it is said that "the people of the North are more clever than the people of the East. [Pāṇini 5.3.60] *praśasyasya śraḥ*: for the word *praśasya*, there shall be the substitute *śra* before the suffixes beginning with vowels.
SK 2010: *prakṛtyaikāc* (A 6.4.163).

In the list beginning with *iṣṭa*, that which consists of a single vowel remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *śreṣṭhaḥ*, *śreyān*. SK 2011: *jya ca* (A 5.3.61). [The substitute *jyā* is applied for the word *praśasya* when forming the superlative and comparative degrees.]

In place of *praśasya* (praiseworthy), there shall be the substitution of *jya* before the suffixes *iṣṭha* and *īyas*. Thus, *jyeṣṭhaḥ*. By A 6.4.160, *jyādādīyasaḥ*, the initial *pra* of *praśasya* is replaced by *jya*; hence, *jyāyān*.
SK 2013: In place of *vṛddha*, the substitute *jya* shall occur before the [comparative] suffixes *īyasun* and *iṣṭhan*. Examples: *jyeṣṭhaḥ*, *jyāyān*. SK 2014:
In place of *antika* and *bāḍha*, the substitutes *neda* and *sādhu* [respectively] occur before the same suffixes.

*ajādyoḥ* / *nediṣṭhaḥ* / *nedīyān* / *sādhiṣṭhaḥ* / *sādhīyān*. Pāṇini A 6.4.156 states: *sthūladūrayuvahrasvakṣiprakṣudrāṇāṃ yaṇādiparaṃ pūrvasya ca guṇaḥ*. In these words, when suffixes such as *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* follow, the *yaṇ*-class vowels and subsequent sounds are elided, and the preceding vowel undergoes *guṇa* substitution. Thus: *sthaviṣṭhaḥ*, *daviṣṭhaḥ*, *yaviṣṭhaḥ*, *hrasiṣṭhaḥ*, *kṣepiṣṭhaḥ*, *kṣodiṣṭhaḥ*. Similarly for *īyasun*: *hrasimā*, *kṣepimā*, *kṣodimā*—these being derived from the *pṛthu*-group (*pṛthvādi*).

Pāṇini A 6.4.157: *priyasthirasphirorubahulaguruvṛddhatṛpradīrghavṛndārakāṇāṃ prasthasphavarbaṃhigarvarṣitrapdrāghivṛndārāḥ*. For the words beginning with *priya*, the substitutes beginning with *pra* occur respectively when suffixes such as *iṣṭhan* are applied. Thus: *preṣṭhaḥ*, *stheṣṭhaḥ*, *spheṣṭhaḥ*, *variṣṭhaḥ*, *baṃhiṣṭhaḥ*, *gariṣṭhaḥ*, *varṣiṣṭhaḥ*, *trapiṣṭhaḥ*, *drāghiṣṭhaḥ*, *vṛndiṣṭhaḥ*. Similarly with the suffix *īyasun*: *preyān*. For *priya*, *uru*, *bahula*, *guru*, and *dīrgha*, the suffix *imanic* is applied because they belong to the *pṛthu* group; thus: *preman* and so forth.
SK 2017 *bahor lopo bhū ca bahoḥ* (A 6.4.158): There is elision of the suffixes *imaN* and *īyasUN* when they follow *bahu*, and *bahu* is replaced by *bhū*. Examples: *bhūmā*, *bhūyān*.
SK 2018 *iṣṭhasya yiṭ ca* (A 6.4.159): [The augment *yiṬ* is added] after the suffix *iṣṭha*.

There shall be the elision of the final portion of *bahu* when followed by *iṣṭha*, and the augment *yiṭ* is added: *bhūyiṣṭhaḥ*. By the rule *yuvālpayoḥ kan anyatarasyām* (A 5.3.64), the substitute *kan* may optionally take the place of these two (*yuvan* and *alpa*) before the suffixes *iṣṭha* and *īyas*. Thus: *kaniṣṭhaḥ* and *kanīyān*; in the alternative case: *yaviṣṭhaḥ* and *alpiṣṭhaḥ*, and so forth.

SK 2020: *vin-matupor luk* (A 5.3.65). There is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *matup* before the superlative suffixes *iṣṭha* and *īyas*. [Examples: One who is most possessed of garlands is *srajiṣṭhaḥ*; one who is more possessed of garlands is *srajīyān*. One who is most possessed of skin is *tvaciṣṭhaḥ*; one who is more possessed of skin is *tvacīyān*. SK 2021: *praśaṃsāyāṃ rūpap* (A 5.3.66). The suffix *rūpaP* is added after a word to express praise.

[The suffix *rūpa* is added] after a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) and after a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). [Examples: *praśastaḥ paṭuḥ* → *paṭurūpaḥ*; *praśastaṃ pacati* → *pacatirūpam*. SK 2022: *īṣadasamāptau kalpab-deśya-deśīya-raḥ* (A 5.3.67). When there is slight incompleteness (*īṣadasamāpti*), the suffixes *kalpa*, *deśya*, *deśīya*, and *ra* are applied.
[Examples: *īṣadūnaḥ vidvān* → *vidvatkalpaḥ*; *yaśaskalpam*; *yajuḥkalpam*; *dvivaddeśyaḥ*; *vidvaddeśīyaḥ*; *pacatikalpam*.

SK 2023: *vibhāṣā supo bahuc parastāt* (A 5.3.68). When the sense is that of being slightly incomplete, the suffix *bahuc* may optionally be added after a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*), and it must be placed before [the stem], not after it. For example: *īṣadūnaḥ paṭuḥ* ("slightly less clever") becomes *bahupaṭuḥ*; likewise, *paṭukalpaḥ*. Why "after a word ending in a case-suffix"? Consider *yajatikalpam* ("like a sacrifice"). SK 2024: *prakāravacane jātīyar* (A 5.3.69). The suffix *jātīyar* is used when expressing a class or type.
And this [suffix] occurs when there is a possessor of a quality (*prakāravat*). The suffix *thāl* occurs merely to denote a type (*prakāramātra*); for example, *paṭuprakāraḥ* or *paṭujātīyaḥ*.
From the rule *prāgivāt kaḥ* (A 5.3.70), up to the rule *ive pratikṛtau*, the section governing the suffix *ka* applies.
SK 2026: *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ* (A 5.3.71). The phrase *tiṅaś ca* is understood [from the previous rule]. SK 2027: *kasya ca daḥ* (A 5.3.72).
In place of the final letter of *kānta* and *avyaya*, there shall be the substitution of *da*, and *akac* [is also added].

(SK 2028) Regarding the unknown (*ajñāte*): of whom is this horse? *aśvakaḥ*. *uccakaiḥ*. *nīcakaiḥ*. *sarvake*. *viśvake*. When a case-ending (*sup*) beginning with *o*, *sa*, or *bha* follows, *akac* is inserted before the elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). *yuvakayoḥ*. *āvakayoḥ*. *yuṣmakāsu*. *asmakāsu*. *yuṣmakābhiḥ*. *asmakābhiḥ*. Why "beginning with *o*" etc.? [Because it does not apply here: *tvayakā*. *mayakā*. In the section on *akac*, it should be stated that *kām* is added after *tūṣṇīm*. Because it has the marker *m*, it is placed after the final vowel. *tūṣṇīkām āste*. The suffix *ka* is added in the sense of habit (*śīla*), and *malāp* is also [added].
*tūṣṇīṃśīlaḥ* means "one who is habitually silent" (*tūṣṇīkaḥ*). [The suffix *kan* is applied after the following: *pacataki*, *jalpataki*, *dhakit*, *hirakut*. According to Pāṇini 5.3.74, *kutsite*:
when expressing contempt, as in *aśvakaḥ* ("a contemptible horse").

SK 2030 *saṃjñāyāṃ kan* (A 5.3.75): The suffix *kan* shall be applied in the sense of contempt (*kutsita*), provided that a name (*saṃjñā*) is understood by means of the word ending in it. Examples: *śūdrakaḥ*, *rādhakaḥ*. This statement is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). SK 2031 *anukampāyām* (A 5.3.76): [The suffix *kan* is applied] in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*).
*Putrakaḥ*: this means a son who is pitied (*anukampita*). [Pāṇini 5.3.77] *nītau ca tadyuktāt*:

when "policy" (*nīti*)—meaning a method such as conciliation or bribery—is understood, the suffix *kap* occurs after a word joined with pity. Examples: *hanta te dhānakāḥ* ("Oh, these grains for you!"), *guḍakāḥ* ("little balls of molasses!"), *ehaki*, *addhaki*. The distinction is that by the previous rule [5.3.76], the suffix occurs after a word expressing the object of pity, whereas by this rule, it occurs even when there is an indirect connection.
SK 2033: The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a polysyllabic word that is not a human name, in the scope of the two preceding rules.
SK 2034: The suffixes *ghan*, *ilac*, and *ca* are also applied [in the same scope].
In that very same context, *Pāṇini* 5.3.83 states: *ṭhājādāv ūrdhvaṃ dvitīyād acaḥ*.

In this section, when a suffix beginning with *ṭha* or one beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) follows, everything after the second vowel of the base (*prakṛti*) is elided. Examples: *Devadatta*, when treated with compassion, becomes *devikaḥ*, *deviyaḥ*, *devilaḥ*, or *devadattakaḥ*. *Vāyudatta*, when treated with compassion, becomes *vāyudattakaḥ*. The mention of the suffix *ṭhak* is for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *ka* when it occupies the position of the second [suffix in the list]. Examples: *vāyukaḥ*, *pitṛkaḥ*. It should be stated that there is optionally an elision of what follows the fourth vowel.

*Bṛhaspatidatta* becomes *bṛhaspatika*; [the suffix *ka*] is applied after *anaja* (vowels other than *a*) and so forth, and its elision is optionally stated. Thus, *devadattaka* and *devaka*. There is also elision of the preceding member: *dattika*, *dattiya*, *dattila*, and *dattaka*. Even without the suffix, the optional elision of either the preceding or the following member should be stated: *devadatta*, *datta*, and *deva*. [Similarly,] *satyabhāmā* becomes *bhāmā* and *satyā*. After a vowel ending in *u*, *la* is substituted for *il* (the suffix *ila*): *bhānudatta*.

After a word beginning with *an* [meaning "near" or "inferior"], there is elision (*lopa*) of the first member [of the compound] when the suffix *apratyaya* follows; likewise, after a word ending in *u*, the *il* [portion] is elided. According to the Easterners (*prācām*), the term *la* is a technical designation for elision. Pāṇini’s rule A 5.3.80 states: *prācām upāder aḍajvucau ca*.

From a nominal stem preceded by the word *upa*, in the aforementioned scope, the suffixes *uḍac* and *vuc* occur. By the particle *ca*, that which is otherwise applicable [by other rules] also applies. The mention of "the Easterners" (*prācām*) is for the sake of honor. Examples of a person named Upendradatta who is treated with compassion: *upaḍaḥ*, *upakaḥ*, *upikaḥ*, *upiyaḥ*, *upilaḥ*, and *upendradattakaḥ*. These are the six forms.

SK 2037: *kan* is added after a word denoting a genus (*jāti*) that is also a human name (A 5.3.81). This applies specifically to words for genus that are names of humans; *kan* shall be added to such a word to express compassion or to denote a rule (*nīti*). Examples: *siṃhakaḥ*, *śarabhakaḥ*, *rāsabhakaḥ*. If the word begins with a diphthong (*saṃdhyakṣara*), it should be stated that the initial portion [of the second vowel] is elided. Example: one who is pitied, *kahoḍaḥ*, becomes *kahikaḥ*. It should be stated that for words whose prior member consists of a single syllable, the subsequent member is elided. Example: *vāgāśīrdattaḥ* becomes *vācikaḥ*. How is it that *ṣaḍaṅgulidattaḥ* becomes *ṣaḍikaḥ*? It is established by the rule concerning the sixth case-ending and words beginning with *ajādi*.

SK 2038: *śevala-supa-ri-viśāla-varuṇa-aryaman*-etc. (A 5.3.84). For these names of humans, when a suffix beginning with *ṭha* or *añ* follows, there shall be elision of everything after the third vowel. This is an exception to the preceding rule (*pūrvāpavāda*). An object of compassion who is named Śevaladatta becomes *śevalikaḥ*, *śevaliyaḥ*, or *śevalilaḥ*. Similarly: *suparikaḥ*, *viśālikaḥ*, *varuṇikaḥ*, *aryamikaḥ*. SK 2039: *ajināntasyottarapadalopaś ca* (A 5.3.82). [When a suffix beginning with *ṭha* or *añ* follows], there is also the elision of the final member (*uttarapada*) of a name ending in *ajina*.

The suffix *kan* is applied after a word ending in *ajina* that denotes a human being, in the sense of "pity," and there is the elision of the final member of the compound. One who is pitied for his tiger-skin is called *vyāghrakaḥ*; [one who is pitied for his lion-skin is] *siṃhakaḥ*. According to A 5.3.85, *alpe*: a small amount of oil is *tailakam*.
When [the meaning] is "small," [the suffix *ka* is added]: *vṛkṣa* becomes *vṛkṣaka*.
SK 2042: *saṃjñāyāṃ kan* (A 5.3.87). [The suffix *kan* is added] when it is a name.

The suffix *kan* is applied when a notion based on a short [measure] is to be understood; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. Examples: *vaṃśakaḥ*, *veṇukaḥ*. By A 5.3.88, *kuṭī-śamī-śuṇḍābhyaḥ raḥ*: the suffix *ra* is applied after these words when they denote something small.
Examples: *kuṭīraḥ* (a small hut), *śamīraḥ* (a small *śamī* tree), *śuṇḍāraḥ* (a small trunk).

SK 2044: By the rule *kutvā ḍupac* (A 5.3.89), from the word *kutū-* with a short vowel, the form *kutupa-* is derived. A *kutū-* is a vessel for oil made from split bamboo; when it is short, that same object is called *kutupa*, which is masculine. SK 2045: By the rule *kāsūgoṇībhyāṃ ṣṭarac* (A 5.3.90), [the suffix *ṣṭarac* is added after the words *kāsū-* and *goṇī-*].
*Kāsū* is a specific type of weapon; *kāsūtari* is a small one. [Similarly] *goṇītari*. According to A 5.3.91, *vatsokṣāśvarṣabhebhyaś ca tanutve*:

*vatsataraḥ* means having reached the second stage of life; *ukṣataraḥ*; *aśvataraḥ*; *ṛṣabhataraḥ*. This suffix applies only when there is a diminution (*tanutva*) in the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*).

SK 2047: After *kim*, *yat*, and *tad*, when there is a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) from two [of many], the suffix *ḍatarac* is applied (A 5.3.92). Examples: *anayoḥ kataro vaiṣṇavaḥ* ("Which of these two is a Vaiṣṇava?"), *kataraḥ*, *itarah*, *taraḥ*. By the great option (*mahāvibhāṣā*), [the forms] *kaḥ*, *yaḥ*, and *saḥ* [are also used]. SK 2048: When there is a question regarding a genus (*jāti*) among many, the suffix *ḍatamac* is optionally applied (A 5.3.93).

When selecting one from among many, the suffix *ḍatamac* may optionally be used. The rule *jātiparipraśne* has been rejected in the original treatise (*ākara*). Examples: *katamo bhavatāṃ kaṭhaḥ?* ("Which among you is the Kaṭha?"); *yatamaḥ*; *tatamaḥ*. The mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is for the sake of including the *akac* suffix: *yakaḥ*; *sakaḥ*. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, [the forms] *yaḥ* and *saḥ* are also used. In this context, the suffix *ḍatarac* is also applied after *kim*: *kataraḥ*. SK 2049: *ekāc ca prācām* (A 5.3.94). After a stem consisting of a single vowel, the suffixes *ḍatarac* and *ḍatamac* may be added according to the Eastern grammarians. Examples: *anayor ekataraḥ maitraḥ* ("Of these two, one is Maitra"); *eṣām ekatamaḥ*.
SK 2050: *kan* is added [after a word] in the sense of disparagement (*avakṣepa*). For example:

*vyākaraṇakena garvitaḥ* → *vyākaraṇakaḥ* ("one who is proud because of his grammar"). That which is used here to disparage another is the example; however, when the object itself is inherently contemptible, the rule *kutsite* (Pāṇini 5.3.74) applies. This concludes the limit for the suffixes beginning with *prāg-iv* (i.e., those taught from Pāṇini 5.1.18 onwards). Now, among the secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*), the section on royal designations (*tadrāja*) begins. 39.

SK 2051: The suffix *kan* shall be applied after [the word *iva*] when it signifies a "likeness" (*pratikṛti*). For example: *aśva iva pratikṛtiḥ* → *aśvakaḥ* ("a likeness of a horse"). Why "when it signifies a likeness"? [Consider: *gaur iva vatsaḥ* ("a calf like a cow"). SK 2052: And [the suffix *kan* is applied] when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

The suffix *kan* occurs in the sense of "like" (*iva*), provided that the entire compound is understood as a technical name (*saṃjñā*). This rule is commenced to prevent [the application of] the sense of "an image" (*apratikṛti*). It is the name for something resembling a horse: *aśvakaḥ*; [likewise] *uṣṭrakaḥ*. Pāṇini A 5.3.98 states:

*lummanuṣye* ("there is elision when a human being is to be expressed"). There is elision (*lup*) of the suffix *kan* prescribed in the sense of a name when a human being is to be denoted. *Cañcā* is a man made of straw; a man who is like a *cañcā* is called *cañcā*. [Likewise] *vardhrikā*.

SK 2054 *jīvikārthe cāpaṇye* (A 5.3.99): When that which is not for sale and is used for the sake of livelihood is to be expressed, there shall be the elision (*lup*) of the suffix *kan*. Examples: Vāsudeva, Śiva, Skanda. This refers to images of deities belonging to temple-priests (*devalaka*) used for their livelihood. Why "not for sale"? Example: He sells little elephants (*hastikān*). SK 2055 *devapathādibhyaś ca* (A 5.3.100).
The suffix *lup* may optionally apply [to a word ending in *kan*]. Examples: *devapathaḥ*, *haṃsapathaḥ*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). SK 2056:

After the word *vasti*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied. The term *iva* (as if) continues to apply from the previous rule, while *pratikṛtau* (in the sense of "representing") has ceased to apply. Examples: *vāsteyam* (like a bladder), *vāsteyī* (a female like a bladder).

SK 2057: *śilāyā ḍhaḥ* (A 5.3.102). From the word *śilā*, the suffix *ḍha* [is applied]. As in *śileva śileyam* ("like a stone, thus stony"). According to some, because of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the suffix *ḍhañ* is also [applied]; thus *śaileyam*. SK 2058: *śākhādibhyo yaḥ* (A 5.3.103). From words beginning with *śākhā*, the suffix *ya* [is applied].
Like *śākha*, [the suffix *yat* forms] *śākhya*; *mukhya*. Like *jaghana*, [the suffix *yat* forms] *javanya*; *agrya*; *śaraṇya*.
According to A 5.3.104, *dravya* is used when it means "suitable for" (*bhavya*):
this Brāhmaṇa is a *dravya* [i.e., worthy of the gift].
Pāṇini 5.3.105: *kuśāgrāc chaḥ* — from the word *kuśāgra*, the suffix *cha* is added [to form a comparative sense].
For example: *kuśāgrīyā buddhiḥ* ("an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass").
Pāṇini 5.3.106: *samāsāc ca tadviṣayāt* — the same suffix is added after a compound that has that [same] scope.

The suffix *cha* shall occur after a compound whose meaning is based on the sense of "like" (*iva*). For example: *kākatālīyo devadattasya vadhaḥ* ("Devadatta’s death was like the fall of the palm fruit upon the crow"). Here, the meaning of the compound is that the encounter with the thief is similar to the encounter between the crow and the palm fruit; however, the meaning conveyed by the suffix is that it resulted in Devadatta's death in a manner similar to the death of the crow. Another example is *ajākṛpāṇīyaḥ*, which results in the sense of "unexpectedly encountered. According to A 5.3.107, *śarkarādibhyo 'ṇ*: after words such as *śarkarā*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Thus, *śarkareva śārkaram*.
SK 2063: The suffix *ṭhak* is added after words such as *aṅguli*.
For example: like a finger (*aṅgulī*) is an *āṅgulika*; like a *bharuja* is a *bhārujika*. SK 2064: The suffix *ṭhañ* is optionally added after the word *ekaśālā*. (A 5.3.109)
Just as with the word *ekaśālā* and others, the suffix *ṭhañ* is optionally applied, and in the alternative case, *ṭhak*. Thus, *ekaśālā* itself becomes *ekaśālikaḥ* or *aikaśālikaḥ*.
According to A 5.3.110, *karkalohitādīkak*:
like a *karka*, which is a white horse, [one who is like it] is *kārkīkaḥ*; a crystal that is red is *lauhītīkaḥ*.

SK 2066 *pūgāññyo 'grāmaṇīpūrvāt* (A 5.3.112): The sense of *iva* ("like") has ceased [to apply]. From a word denoting a *pūga*—a group consisting of people of various castes, of indefinite conduct, and primarily devoted to wealth and pleasure—the suffix *ñya* occurs in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Examples: *lauhityadhvajyaḥ*. Regarding *vrāta* and *cphañ*: "In the masculine, not in the feminine. *Vrāta*: *kāpotapākyaḥ*. *cphañ*: *kauñjāyanyaḥ*, *brādhnāyanyaḥ*. SK 2067 *āyudhajīvisaṅghāñ ñyaḍvāhīkeṣv avrāhmaṇarājanyāt* (A 5.3.114): After words denoting a guild (*saṅgha*) of those who live by arms, the suffix *ñyaṭ* occurs when referring to the Vāhīkas, provided the word does not denote a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya.

The suffix *ñyaṭ* is applied after a word denoting a group (*saṅgha*) of weapon-bearers (*āyudhajīvin*) among the Vāhīkas, in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Examples: *kṣaudrakyaḥ*, *mālavyaḥ*. Because of the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added: *kṣaudrakī*. Why "weapon-bearers"? [Consider: *mallāḥ* ("wrestlers"). Why "group"? [Consider: *samrāṭ* ("emperor"). Why "among the Vāhīkas"? [Consider: *śabarāḥ* ("Śabaras"). Why "not Brāhmaṇas" (*abrāhmaṇa*)? [Consider: *gopālakāḥ* ("cowherds") and *śālaṅkāyanāḥ* ("descendants of Śālaṅka"); for regarding Brāhmaṇas, specific types are intended, whereas regarding Kṣatriyas (*rājanya*), the actual form is intended. SK 2068: After *vṛka*, the suffix *ṭeṇyaṇ* is applied in the sense of the base itself, provided it denotes a group of weapon-bearers. Example: *vārkeṇyaḥ*. Why "weapon-bearers"? To prevent it from applying to words denoting mere species (*jātiśabda*).

SK 2069: *dāmany-ādi-trigarta-ṣaṣṭhāc chaḥ* (A 5.3.116). The suffix *cha* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*) after the group beginning with *dāmani* and those ending with *trigarta*, which denote corporations of weapon-bearers (*āyudhajīvi-saṅgha*). Those for whom the Trigartas constitute the sixth [group] are called *trigarta-ṣaṣṭhāḥ*. They say that the *trigarta-ṣaṣṭhāḥ* consist of Kauṇḍoparatha, Dāṇḍakī, Krauṣṭuki, Jālamāni, Brahmagupta, and Jālaki. Examples: *dāmanīyaḥ*; *dāmanīyau*; *dāmanayaḥ*. *Aulapi*: *aulapīyaḥ*. *Trigarta*: *trigartīyaḥ*. *Kauṇḍoparatha*: *kauṇḍoparathīyaḥ*. *Dāṇḍakī*: *dāṇḍakīyaḥ*.

SK 2070: *parśvādiyaudheyādibhyo ’ṇañau* (A 5.3.117). From these [groups of words] denoting communities (*saṅgha*) of those who live by arms, the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* respectively occur in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*). Examples: *pārśavaḥ*, *pārśavau*, *parśavaḥ*; *yaudheyaḥ*, *yaudheyau*, *yaudheyāḥ*. SK 2071: *abhijidvidabhṛcchālāvacchikhāvacchamīvadūrṇāvacchrumadaṇo yañ* (A 5.3.118). From the suffix *aṇ* following *abhijit*, *vidabhṛt*, *śālāvat*, *śikhāvat*, *śamīvat*, *ūrṇāvat*, and *śrumat*, the suffix *yañ* occurs in the sense of the base itself.

The suffix *yañ* occurs in its own sense after [names] beginning with *abhijit* that end in the suffix *aṇ*. For example: the descendant of *abhijit* is *ābhijityaḥ*; likewise, *vaidabhṛtyaḥ*, *śālāvatyaḥ*, *śaikhāvatyaḥ*, *śāmīvatyaḥ*, *aurṇāvatyaḥ*, and *śraumatyaḥ*.

SK 2072: *ñyādayas tadrājāḥ* (A 5.3.119). Those [suffixes] beginning with *ñya*—starting from the rule *pūgāññyaḥ*—are designated as *tadrāja*. Consequently, there is elision (*luk*) when referring to many [members] in the non-feminine gender. Examples include: *lohitadhvajāḥ*, *kapotapākāḥ*, *kauñjāyanāḥ*, and *brādhnāyanāḥ*.

A 5.4.1: *vun* is added after a word beginning with a numeral such as "pāda" or "śata" when there is distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), and there is elision (*lopa*) [of the final syllable]. The mention of "elision" is for the purpose of indicating that it is not conditioned by anything else; therefore, it does not behave like the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*). [By A 6.4.130] *pāda* becomes *pat*. When the compound is formed according to A 2.1.51 (*taddhitārthe*), the suffix is added. That which ends in *vun* occurs only in the feminine gender. [Examples: "He gives two feet each" → *dvipadikām*; "two hundred each" → *dviśatikām*. The explicit mention of *pāda* and *śata* is redundant, because [the suffix] is seen elsewhere as well: e.g., *dvimodakikām* ("two sweetmeats each"). A 5.4.2: And [the suffix *vun* is added] after [a word ending in] *daṇḍa* in the sense of "giving away" (*vyavasarga*).

*vun* should be [stated]. This is for the purpose of excluding the sense of distributive repetition (*avīpsā*). *dvipadikām*, *dviśatikām*: he fines with two feet, or two hundred; the meaning is that he releases or gives.
(Pāṇini 5.4.3) *kan* is added after words such as *sthūla* in the sense of expressing a manner (*prakāra*);

it is an exception to *jātīyar*. Examples: *sthūlakaḥ*, *aṇukaḥ*. There is a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *cañcat* and *bṛhat*: *cañcatkaḥ*, *bṛhatkaḥ*. After *surā* in the sense of a snake (*ahi*): a snake having the color of wine is *surakaḥ*.
SK 2076: After a *kta* suffix [denoting] non-finality, [the suffix *kan* is added]. Examples: *chinnakam*, *bhinnakam*, *abhinnakam*.
SK 2077: Not so when a word expressing a part [of a whole] (*sāmivacana*) is present.

When *sāmi* occurs as an accompanying word (*upapada*), the suffix *kan* is not applied after a word ending in *kta*. Examples: *sāmikṛtam* ("half-done"), *ardhakṛtam* ("half-done"). Since the meaning here is expressed by the base form itself due to the sense of "not being completely finished," the application of *kan* by the previous rule was not applicable. This very prohibitory rule indicates that *kan* is also used in its ultimate sense of expressing the same meaning as the base (*svārthika*). Example: *bahutarakam* ("more than much"). SK 2078: After *bṛhatī*, the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of "a garment. Two equal lengths of cloth for an upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*) are called *bṛhatikā*. Why "in the sense of a garment"? [Answer: *bṛhatī* [is a name for] a meter (*chandaḥ*).
The suffix *kha* is applied after a compound whose final member is *aṣaḍakṣa*, *āśitaṅgu*, *alaṃkarma*, *alaṃpuruṣa*, or *adhi*. (A 5.4.7)

In the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*): *aṣaḍakṣīṇo mantraḥ* ("a counsel not for six eyes"); the meaning is that it was made by only two people. *Āśitā gāvo 'smin* ("the cows have eaten in this place") results in *āśitaṅgavīnam araṇyam* ("a forest where the cows have eaten"); the *mum* augment of the preceding [vowel] occurs due to a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). *Alaṃ karmaṇe* ("sufficient for the task") results in *alaṃkarmīṇaḥ*; *alaṃpuruṣīṇaḥ*. *Īśvarādhīnaḥ* ("dependent on the Lord"). This suffix *kha* is compulsory (*nitya*), because the subsequent rule contains the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*). Other suffixes added in the sense of the base word itself are also held to be compulsory: those beginning with *tamap* up to before *kan*; those beginning with *ñya* up to before *vun*; those beginning with *ām* up to before *mayaṭ*. As stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Those ending in *bṛhatī*, those ending in a genus name (*jāti*), and compound-ending suffixes (*samāsānta*)."

SK 2080: *vibhāṣāñcer adikstriyām* (A 5.4.8). After a nominal stem ending in the suffix *añc*, which denotes a direction (*adiś*) or a feminine (*strī*), the suffix *kha* may optionally occur in its own sense (*svārthe*). Examples: *prāk* (east), *prācīnam*; *pratyak*, *pratīcīnam*; *avāk*, *avācīnam*. [Note: *nikṛṣṭa*, *pratikṛṣṭa*, *arva*, *repha*, *yāpya*, *avama*, *adhama* are synonyms for "low" or "inferior. That which faces toward a horse (*arvantam añcati*) is *arvāk* or *arvācīnam*. Why "not denoting a direction or a feminine"? [Counter-example: *prācī dik* (the eastern direction); *udīcī dik* (the northern direction). Why the mention of "direction" (*dig*)? [Counter-example: *prācīnā brāhmaṇī* (an eastern Brahmin woman). Why the mention of "feminine" (*strī*)? [Counter-example: *prācīnaṃ grāmād āmrāḥ* (mango trees to the east of the village). SK 2081: *jātyantāc cha bandhuni* (A 5.4.9). After a nominal stem ending in *jāti*, the suffix *cha* occurs when the word refers to a kinsman (*bandhu*).

[The word] *brāhmaṇajātīyaḥ* [is formed with the suffix -īya]. Why [is the condition] *bandhuni* [stated]? [Consider: *brāhmaṇajātiḥ śobhanā* ("an excellent Brāhmaṇa caste"). A substance (*dravya*) that manifests a genus (*jāti*) is a *bandhu*. SK 2082: If [the condition] "optionally when preceded by a different locative" (*sthānāntād vibhāṣā sasthānena*) is stated, the meaning is: if [the word] ending in a locative (*sthānānta*) is meaningful (*arthavat*) and is equal (*tulya*) to the locative (*sasthānena*). [Examples: *pitṛsthānīyaḥ* ("standing in the place of a father"), *pitṛsthānaḥ*. Why [is the condition] *sasthānena* [stated]? [Consider: *goḥ sthānam* ("the place of a cow").
SK 2083: The suffix *ṭhak* is added after *anugādin* (A 5.4.13).
One who follows along is an *anugādī*; he himself is an *ānugādika*. SK 2084:
The suffix *ṭhak* is added after *visārin* when referring to a fish (A 5.4.16).

The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied [after the word *visārin*]. For example: *vaisāriṇaḥ* ("a fish"). Why specify "in the sense of 'fish'"? [Because otherwise] *visārī devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta who wanders") would also be so formed. (A 5.4.17) *kṛtvasuc* is added after a numeral when counting the repetition of an action (*kriyābhyāvṛtti*). "Repetition" (*abhyāvṛtti*) means birth (*janma*). The suffix *kṛtvasuc* occurs in its own meaning (*svārthe*) after a numeral word that functions to count the births of an action. Example: *pañcakṛtvo bhuṅkte* ("he eats five times"). Why specify "after a numeral"? [Because otherwise] *bhūrivārān bhuṅkte* ("he eats many times") would not be formed.

SK 2086 *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc* (A 5.4.18): This is an exception to *kṛtvasuc*. [The suffix *suc* is added after these words to form adverbs. *dviḥ* "twice," *triḥ* "thrice. [In the case of *catuḥ*,] *s* is substituted for *t*. *catuḥ* "four times. SK 2087 *ekasya sakṛc ca* (A 5.4.19): [The suffix *suc* is added after *eka*,] and *sakṛt* is also [the resulting form]. *sakṛt* "once."

The substitute *sakṛt* should occur [in place of *bahus*], and furthermore, the suffix *suc* is also applied. In *sakṛd bhuṅkte*, there is the elision of *suc* by the rule *saṃyogāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.23), but not by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68). This is because, just as with the suffix *sic* in *abhaitsīt*, the application of that [rule] is excluded for *suc* here.

SK 2088: *vibhāṣā bahor dhāviprakṛṣṭakāle* (A 5.4.20). "Not distant" (*aviprakṛṣṭa*) means "near" (*āsanna*). [Examples: *bahudhā divasasya bhuṅkte* ("He eats many times during the day"). Why "when the time is near"? [Counter-example: *bahukṛtvo māsasya bhuṅkte* ("He eats many times during the month").

SK 2089: *tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ* (A 5.4.21). "That which is introduced as the primary subject" (*prakṛta*) means that which is presented in abundance; "the expression of that" (*vacana*) means its representation. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used either in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). In the first case [of the action], it refers to the food that is the primary subject: *annamayaḥ* ("consisting of food"), *apūpamayaḥ* ("consisting of cakes"), *yavāgūmayī* ("consisting of gruel"). In the second case [of the locus], it refers to that in which the food is the primary subject: *annamayo yajñaḥ* ("a sacrifice consisting mostly of food"), *apūpamayaṃ parva* ("a festival consisting mostly of cakes"). SK 2090: *samūhavac ca bahuṣu* (A 5.4.22). And [the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied] in the sense of a collection when many [items] are involved.

The collective suffixes *cha*, *an*, and *mayaṭ* are extended [to this rule]. When *modaka* is the base, we have *maudakikam*, *modakamayam*; likewise, *śāṣkulikam*, *śuṣkulīmayam*. In the second sense [of "consisting of"], we have *maudakiko yajñaḥ* ("a sacrifice consisting of sweetmeats") and *modakamayaḥ*.
By the rule *anantāvasathetihabheṣajāñ ñyaḥ* (A 5.4.23):
*ananta* itself is *ānantyam*; *āvasatha* itself is *āvasathyam*. *Iti-ha* is a collection of particles; from it comes *aitihyam*. *Bheṣaja* itself is *bhaiṣajyam*.

SK 2092: *devatāntāt tādarthye yat* (A 5.4.24). *Tādarthya* means "being for that purpose. The suffix *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense [to form the abstract noun]. For example: *agnidevatāyai idam* (this is for the deity Agni) becomes *agnidevatyam*; likewise, *pitṛdevatyam*. SK 2093: *pādārghābhyāṃ ca* (A 5.4.25). [The suffix *yat* is applied after the words *pāda* and *argha* in the sense of being for that purpose.]

Water for the feet is *pādya*; [water] for the guest-offering is *arghya*. For the word *nava* ("new"), the substitute *nū* is prescribed, and the suffixes *tṇap*, *tanap*, and *sva* should be stated [after it]: *nūtnam*, *nūtanam*, *navīnam*. And after the word *pra*, when it signifies "ancient" (*purāṇa*), the suffix *na* should be stated; and by the word "and" (*ca*), the previously mentioned suffixes [are also included]. Thus: *praṇam*, *pratnam*, *pratanam*, *prīṇam*. After words meaning "portion" (*bhāga*), "form" (*rūpa*), and "name" (*nāman*), the suffix *dheya* is applied: *bhāgadheyam*, *rūpadheyam*, *nāmadheyam*. After the words *āgnīdhra* and *sādhāraṇa*, the suffix *añ* is applied: *āgnīdhram*, *sādhāraṇam*. In the feminine, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied: *āgnīdhrī*, *sādhāraṇī*.
SK 2094 *atither ñyaḥ* (A 5.4.26): [The suffix] *ñya* is applied in the sense of "for the purpose of that" (*tādarthye*). Example: *ātithyam* ("hospitality"), meaning "this is for the guest.
SK 2095 *devāt tal* (A 5.4.27): [The suffix] *tal* is applied after the word *deva*.
*deva* itself is *devatā*. According to A 5.4.28 (*aveḥ kaḥ*), *aviḥ* itself is *avikaḥ*.

SK 2097: The suffix *kan* is applied after words such as *yāva* (A 5.4.29). Thus, *yāva* itself becomes *yāvakaḥ*; likewise, *maṇikaḥ*. SK 2098: [The suffix *kan* is applied] after the word *lohita* when referring to a gem (A 5.4.30).
The word *lohitaka* refers to a red gem;

[according to Pāṇini 5.4.31,] it also denotes a color that is impermanent, as in "he is red with anger. Alternatively, there is a sublation of the gender [of the base word], so that *lohitakā* and *lohinikā* mean "red with anger."

SK 2100: After the word *lohita* when it means "dyed with lac and so forth" (*rakte*), the suffix *kan* shall be applied; or rather, it is simply for the purpose of subverting the gender. [Examples: *lohitikā*, *lohinikā* [as in] *śāṭī* (a red garment).
SK 2101: And also after the word *kāla*. (A 5.4.33)

In the case of *varṇa*, the two [terms] "impermanent" (*anitya*) and "red" (*rakta*) follow. *Kālaka-mukha* means having a dark face due to embarrassment; *kālaka-paṭa* means a black cloth; *kālikā-śāṭī* means a black garment.
By the rule *vinayādibhyaṣ ṭak* (A 5.4.34), from *vinaya* etc., the suffix *ṭak* is applied:
*vinaya* itself is *vainayika*; *sāmayika*. There is also shortening of the vowel in *upāya*: *aupayika*.

SK 2103: After the word *vāc* when it signifies a message (*vyāhṛta-artha*)—that is, speech containing a communicated meaning—the suffix *ṭhak* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*). Thus, *saṃdeśa-vāc* becomes *vācikam*. SK 2104: After a word denoting an action (*karman*) connected with that [message], the suffix *aṇ* occurs.

*Kārmaṇa* is simply *karman*. The meaning is: action performed by resorting to speech (*vācika*). [In the rule] *oṣadher ajātau* (A 5.4.37), the suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). [Example: *auṣadhaṃ pibati* ("he drinks medicine"). Why "not when it is a genus" (*ajātau*)? [Counter-example: *oṣadhayaḥ kṣetre rūḍhāḥ* ("medicinal plants grown in the field").

SK 2106 *prajñādibhyaś ca* (A 5.4.38): From [the group beginning with] *prajña*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Thus, *prājñaḥ* means "one who possesses wisdom. The feminine form is *prājñī*. Examples: *daivataḥ*, *bāndhavaḥ*.
SK 2107 *mṛdastikan* (A 5.4.39): The suffix *tikan* is applied after the word *mṛd*. Thus, *mṛttikā*.

*mṛd* is the same as *mṛttikā*. According to A 5.4.40, *rasna* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*); it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *rūpa*. Thus, excellent earth is *mṛtsā* or *mṛtsnā*. Because of the inclusion of the word *anyatarasyām* in the subsequent sūtra, this [application of *rasna*] is obligatory (*nitya*).

SK 2109: *bahvalpārthāc chas kārakād anyatarasyām* (A 5.4.42). From words expressing "much" (*bahu*) or "little" (*alpa*), when they function as a *kāraka*, the suffix *śas* is optionally added. Examples: *bahuśo dadāti* ("he gives much"), *alpaśo dadāti* ("he gives little"). The mention of "words expressing much or little" is for the purpose of specifying auspicious or inauspicious contexts; it does not apply here [in the following case]: *bahūni dadāty aniṣṭeṣu* ("he gives much in regard to undesirable things") and *alpaṃ dadāty ābhyudayikeṣu* ("he gives little in regard to festive occasions"). SK 2110: *saṃkhyaikavacanāc ca vīpsāyām* (A 5.4.43). And [the suffix *śas* is added] after numerals and words having the sense of a singular, when distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is intended.

He gives two by two; he gives them in pairs. *māṣam māṣam* means "bean by bean" (*māṣaśaḥ*); *prasthaśaḥ*. In a compound, words denoting measure have only a single referent. Why [is it said] "from a numeral or a word in the singular"? [Answer: *ghaṭaṃ ghaṭaṃ dadāti* ("he gives pot after pot"). Why [is it said] "in the sense of repetition" (*vīpsā*)? [Answer: *dvau dadāti* ("he gives two"). Only when [the word denotes] a *kāraka* [is this rule applied]. [Counter-example: *dvayor dvayoḥ svāmī* ("the owner of two each"). (Pāṇini 5.4.44:
*pratiyoge pañcamyās tasiḥ*—"The suffix *tasi* occurs after a word in the fifth case in connection with *prati*").

The suffix *tasi* shall occur after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) prescribed in connection with the *karmapravacanīya* particle *prati*. Example: *pradyumnaḥ kṛṣṇataḥ prati* ("Pradyumna is a match for Kṛṣṇa"). There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) [of this rule] to words such as *ādi*: *ādau* → *āditaḥ*; *madhyataḥ*; *pṛṣṭhataḥ*; *pārśvataḥ*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Examples: *svareṇa* → *svarataḥ*; *varṇataḥ*. SK 2112: *apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ* (A 5.4.45).

The suffix *tasi* shall occur after a word ending in the fifth case prescribed in the sense of the *apādāna* (ablative) relation, except when used with the roots *hī* (to depart) or *ruh* (to descend). Example: *grāmād āgacchati* ("He comes from the village") → *grāmataḥ*. Why "except when used with *hī* or *ruh*"? Example: *svargād dhīyate* ("He falls from heaven"); *parvatād avarohati* ("He descends from the mountain").

SK 2113: *atigrahāvyathanakṣepeṣv akartari tṛtīyāyāḥ* (A 5.4.46). The suffix *tasi* may optionally occur after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) when it does not denote the agent (*akartari*), provided that the sense is "surpassing" (*atigraha*), "not wavering" (*avyathana*), or "censure" (*kṣepa*). *Atigraha* means "surpassing. Example: *cāritreṇātigṛhyate* / *cāritrato 'tigṛhyate*. The meaning is: he conducts himself by surpassing others through his conduct (*cāritra*). *Avyathana* means "not wavering," i.e., "not moving. Example: *vṛttena na vyathate* / *vṛttato na vyathate*. The meaning is: he does not waver from his conduct; he does not deviate from his conduct. In the sense of "censure" (*kṣepa*): Example: *vṛttena kṣiptaḥ* / *vṛttataḥ kṣiptaḥ*. The meaning is: he is censured on account of his conduct; he is reproached because of his conduct. Why is it said "when not denoting the agent" (*akartari*)? [To exclude cases where the agent is expressed.]
[The suffix] *tasi* is optionally added after a word ending in the third case, provided it denotes that which is inferior or evil, when used with a verb other than *kṣip* ("to throw").

Because of the rule *hīyamānapāpayogāc ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.47), *tasi* is added after a word in the third case ending in a term signifying something inferior or evil, provided it does not denote the agent (*akarta*). Examples: *vṛttena hīyate* ("he is deficient in conduct") *vṛttena pāpaḥ* ("evil in conduct") *vṛttena pāpaḥ* ("evil in conduct") *vṛttataḥ* ("by way of conduct") This [application of *tasi*] occurs when the sense of "throwing" (*kṣepa*) is not intended. However, when "throwing" is intended, the form is already established by the previous rule. Why specify "not denoting the agent"? Consider: *devadattena hīyate* ("Devadatta is being left behind"). Here, Devadatta is the agent, so *tasi* is not applied.

SK 2115: *ṣaṣṭhyā vyāśraye* (A 5.4.48). The suffix *tasi* may optionally occur after a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when there is a reliance on different sides. *devā arjunato 'bhavan* (the gods were on Arjuna's side); *ādityāḥ karṇato 'bhavan* (the Ādityas were on Karṇa's side). The meaning is "on the side of Arjuna. Why "when there is a reliance on different sides"? [Consider: *vṛkṣasya śākhā* (the branch of the tree). SK 2116: *rogāc cāpanayane* (A 5.4.49). [The suffix *tasi* occurs] after the word *roga* (disease) in the sense of removal.

The suffix *tasi* is optionally used after a word denoting a disease ending in the genitive case, when medical treatment is intended. For example: *pravāhikātaḥ kuru*. The meaning is: "Perform a remedy for this [disease]. Why is it said "in the sense of removal"? [Consider: *pravāhikāyāḥ prakopanam karoti* ("he causes an aggravation of dysentery").
