In the first rule prescribing the *loṭ* suffix, the verbal root that serves as the base for that *loṭ* must be employed as the subsequent verb (*anuprayoga*).
According to A 3.4.5, "in the case of a conjunction [of actions], [the root] expressing the general [action] [is to be used]. *SK* 2828.

In the rule prescribing the *loṭ* suffix for the sense of "conjunction" (*samuccaya*), there should be the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of a verbal root in its general sense. Following that subsequent application, the *laṭ* suffixes and the *tiP*-class suffixes (*tib-ādayaḥ*) occur according to their respective rules. From that, there is the manifestation of number, tense, and the specific meaning of person. When the repetition of an action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*) is to be expressed, the word is doubled; for example, *yāhi yāhi iti yāti*. The meaning of the root *yā-* here is going repeatedly or with intensity. The word *yāti* expresses going performed by a single agent in the present time.

The word *iti*, however, indicates the intention (*tātparya*) regarding non-differentiation in the connection [of actions]. For example: "He has gone thus" (*evaṃ yātaḥ*); "they go thus" (*yānti*); "you go thus" (*yāsi*); "you two go thus" (*yāthaḥ*); "you all go thus" (*yātha*); "you cause them to go thus" (*yātayata*); "you all go thus" (*yūyaṃ yātha*). [In the case of repetition: "Go! Go! implies "he went" (*ayāsīt*) or "he will go" (*yāsyati*). "Instruct! Instruct! implies "he studies" (*adhīte*). Regarding the domain of the suffix *-dhvam*, in one alternative it is "study! study! (*adhīdhvam adhīdhvam*), meaning "you all study" (*yūyam adhīdhve*). In the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*), however: "Drink the barley-meal; eat the parched grains! implies "he consumes them. "Eat the food; taste the curd-sauce! implies "he consumes it."

In the case of *tad-dhva-mas*, however, [the forms] *pibata* ("drink"), *svādatta* ("taste"), and *abhyavaharatha* ("consume") are used; [likewise], *bhuṅdhvam* ("eat"), *āsvādayadhvam* ("taste"), and *abhyavaharadhve* ("consume") are used. In these instances, the suffixes *hi* and *sva* are optionally employed. Here, there is a non-differentiation through connection with a general sense for the purpose of subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) regarding the specific items being conjoined. Optionally, one says: *saktūn pibati* ("he drinks barley meal"), *dhānāḥ svādati* ("he tastes roasted grains"), *annaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats food"), or *dādhikam āsvādayate* ("he tastes curd"). By this [same principle], one explains: "Raid the city, cut down the Nandana grove, steal the jewels, and carry off the celestial nymphs! (Raghuvamśa 13.50).

The powerful one, having engaged in conflict with the enemy of Namuci, brought about this state of ill-health day after day; thus has it been explained. The meaning is that there was an action of ill-health—consisting of forms such as leaping upon and cutting down—which occurred in the remote past (bhūtānadyatana-parokṣa) and had a single agent. However, the interpretation that "here [the sense is] 'he leaped again and again' and so forth" is rooted solely in error, because of the recurrence of the term *kriyāsamabhihāra* ("intensification of action") from the second sūtra, and because it would result in the doubling of the verb ending in the imperative (*loṭ*).

The notion held by some that *avaskandesi* and so forth are examples of the second person singular is merely an error, because it has been stated here that the designations "person" (*puruṣa*) and "number" (*vacana*) do not apply [to the substitutes of *l*].
Thus ends the section on the meaning of the *lakāras*.
Thus ends the section on verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) in the Uttarārdha of the *Siddhāntakaumudī* composed by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita.
The Section on Primary Derivatives (Kṛdanta): 63 / SK 2829.

This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) extending until the end of the third book [of Pāṇini’s grammar]. In this context, that which stands in the locative case is the *upapada*. *kṛt* [suffixes] are those that are not *atiṅ* [i.e., not finite verb endings].

SK 2830: *vāsarūpo 'striyām* (A 3.1.94). This is a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*). Within this section concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*), a suffix that is an exception (*apavāda*) and is dissimilar in form (*asarūpa*) may optionally supersede the general rule (*utsarga*), with the exception of those [suffixes] prescribed in the section concerning feminine formations (*stryadhikāra*). SK 2831: *kṛtyāḥ* (A 3.1.95).

This is the governing rule for the suffix *ṇvul* prior to [SK 2832]. Since it was established that "a *kṛt* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent" (A 3.4.67), and thus *kṛtya* suffixes would also occur in the sense of the agent, [this rule is stated].

SK 2833: The suffixes having the sense of *kṛtya* and *khal* occur only after [roots] expressing the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). SK 2834: The suffixes *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar* [occur after roots expressing the sense of the action or the object].

These suffixes occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*). The letters *t* and *r* are for the sake of the vowel accent. [Examples: *edhitavyam* (it must be increased); *edhanīyam* (it is to be increased) by you. In the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), the default singular number and neuter gender apply. [Example: *cetavyaḥ* or *cayanīyaḥ* dharmaḥ (the duty is to be performed) by you. After the root *vas*, the suffix *tavyat* occurs, and the causative (*ṇic*) also applies. [Example: "he dwells" (*vasati*) thus he is a resident (*vāstavyaḥ*). There is an addition [to the rule] regarding *kelimara*: *pacelimā māṣāḥ* (the beans are to be cooked); [equivalent to] *paktavyāḥ*. *bhidelimāḥ saralāḥ* (the *sarala* trees are to be split); [equivalent to] *bhettavyāḥ*. This suffix occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*).
However, the author of the *Vṛtti* says that this [suffix] is also desired in the sense of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*), but that contradicts the *Bhāṣya*.

SK 2835 *kṛtyacaḥ* (A 8.4.29): Following a cause situated in a prefix (*upasarga*), there shall be the substitution of *ṇ* for a *n* belonging to a *kṛt*-suffix that follows a vowel. Example: *prayāṇīyam*. Why "following a vowel" (*acaḥ*)? Consider *pramagnaḥ*. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is made for *nirviṇṇa*: this statement is necessary because the rule would otherwise not apply due to the absence of a vowel following [the *n*]. There is *ṇatva* for the subsequent [letter] and *ṣṭutva* for the preceding one. Result: *nirviṇṇaḥ*. SK 2836 *ṇer vibhāṣā* (A 8.4.30): [The substitution of *ṇ* for *n*] after the affix *ṇi* is optional.

After a cause (nimitta) standing in an *upasarga*, the *ṇ* that is optionally substituted for the *n* of a *kṛt* suffix prescribed after a causative (*ṇi*)-stem may occur. For example: *prayāpaṇīyam* / *prayāpanīyam*. Why is it necessary to specify "prescribed" (*vihita*)? So that [the substitution] occurs even when there is an intervention by *yak*. Example: *prayāpyamāṇaṃ paśya*. It has been stated that in the case of the substitution of *ṇ*, *dus* does not have the status of an *upasarga*. Examples: *duryānam* / *duryāpanam*. (SK 2837) *Halaś cej upadhāt* (A 8.4.31).

After a root beginning with a consonant (*hal*) that has *ij* as its penultimate letter, the *ṇatva* (replacement of *n* by *ṇ*) may optionally apply to a *kṛt*-suffix *na*, provided it follows a vowel other than *a*. Examples: *prakopaṇīyam* or *prakopanīyam*. Why "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*)? Consider *prohaṇīyam*. Why "having *ij* as its penultimate letter" (*ijupadhāt*)? Consider *pravacaṇīyam*. Pāṇini A 8.4.32: *ijādeḥ sanumaḥ* ("The *ṇatva* applies after a root beginning with *ij* or having the augment *num*").

If there is *num*, then [the substitution of *ṇ*] applies only to that which is prescribed after a root beginning with *ij* and ending in a consonant (*hal*), when it is situated within a *kṛt* suffix. Example: *preṅkhaṇīyam*. Why "beginning with *ij*" (*ijādeḥ*)? Consider *magi* in the sense of "creeping": *pramaṅganīyam*. The mention of *num* is for the purpose of indicating the *anusvāra*; this is also the case in the rule *aṭkupvāṅ...* (Pāṇini 8.4.2). Therefore, it does not apply here: *pranvanam*. But it would certainly apply here: *prombhaṇam*. SK 2839: *vā niṃsanikṣanindām* (A 8.4.33). For these roots—*niṃs*, *nikṣ*, and *nind*—the *n* may optionally become *ṇ* when followed by a *kṛt* suffix. Examples: *praṇiṃsitavyam* / *praniṃsitavyam*.

SK 2840: *na bhābhūpūkamigamipyāyīvepām* (A 8.4.34). After these roots, the *ṇ* of a *kṛt* suffix is not [substituted for *n*]. Examples: *prabhānīyam*, *prabhavanīyam*. Here, only the root *pūñ* (to purify) is intended to be included; however, from *pūṅ* (to swell), we have *prapavaṇīyaḥ somaḥ*. There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the causative forms of *bhā* and the others: *prabhāpanīyam*. It has been stated that for the root *khyā* with the suffix *khaś*, the *ś* may optionally become *y*. This should be understood as being overridden by the present section on *ṇatva*. Because the substitution of *y* is considered *asiddha*, there is no *ṇatva* due to the intervention of the letter *ś*: *prakhyānīyam*. SK 2841: *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (A 3.3.113). The *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes are applied diversely.
That by which one bathes is *snānīya* powder; that to whom something is given is a *dānīya* Brahmin. (SK 2842) *aco yat*:

the suffix *yat* shall occur after a verbal root ending in a vowel. Thus: *ceyam*, *jeyam*. The mention of "vowels" (*aj*) could have been omitted; the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) would likewise be possible, because *yat* is easily understood even within the context of *tavyat* and the other suffixes.

SK 2843 (A 6.4.65): *īdyati*—when *yati* follows, *ī* shall be substituted for *ā*. [Thus] *guṇa* [is applied]. *deyam*, *gleyam*. It should be stated that *yad* follows the roots *tak*, *śas*, *cat*, *yat*, and *jan*. [Examples: *takyam*, *śasyam*, *catyam*, *yatyam*, *janyam*. The rule for *yad* after *jan* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). Since the form is established even from the causative (*ṇyantā*) root, there is no risk of *vṛddhi*; this is because of the prohibition [stated in A 7.3.35]: *janivadhyoś ca*. It should be stated that *yad* optionally follows *han*, and it is replaced by *vadha*. [Examples: *vadhyaḥ*. In the alternative case, *ṇyat* is applied as will be mentioned later: *ghātyaḥ*. SK 2844 (A 3.1.98):
*por adupadhāt*—[the suffix *yat* is added] after a root ending in *p* with a light penultimate vowel (*adupadhāt*).

The suffix *yat* shall occur after a root ending in a consonant of the *pa*-group (*pavarga*) that has *a* as its penultimate vowel; this is an exception to the rule for *ṇyat*. Examples: *śapyam*, *labhyam*. The fact that a root lacks similarity (*asārūpya*) due to an *anubandha* does not prevent the application of *ṇyat*. Therefore, *ṇyat* does not apply here, but *tavyat* and other suffixes certainly do. Regarding Pāṇini 7.1.65, *āṅo yi*:

the augment *num* is added to the root *labh* when it follows the prefix *āṅ* and a suffix beginning with *y* is intended to follow. Once *num* is applied, the root no longer has *a* as its penultimate vowel; consequently, *ṇyat* applies instead. Example: *ālambhyaḥ gauḥ* ("the ox to be touched").

SK 2846 *upāt praśaṃsāyām* (A 7.1.66): In the sense of praise, [the suffix -ya is applied after the root √labh following the prefix *upa*. Example: *upalambhyaḥ sādhuḥ* ("praiseworthy"). Why "in the sense of praise"? [Counter-example: *upalabhyaḥ* meaning "capable of being perceived. SK 2847 *śakisahoś ca* (A 3.1.99): [The suffix -ya is also applied after roots ending in -śak or -sah.]

The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *sah*, *gam*, *mad*, *car*, and *yam*, provided they are not preceded by a prefix. (A 3.1.100) *Śakyam* and *sahyam*. (SK 2848) *Gadamadacarayaṃś cānupasarge*. (A 3.1.100)

*gadyam* / *madyam* / *caryam*. After the root *car*, [the suffix *yat* is applied] when preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, provided it does not mean "to go. Thus, *ācarya* means "a region"; the sense is "that which is to be traversed. Why "provided it does not mean 'to go'"? [To answer: *ācārya* means "a teacher. The rule for the root *yam* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), so that [the suffix] does not occur after [the root *yam*] with a prefix; thus, *prayāmyam*. However, it should indeed occur after [the root *yam*] preceded by *ni*; hence, from the usage in the Vārttika, "therefore, *viniyamyam* would not occur there," it follows that this is not an improper application. The statement "Surely you are to be restrained by one with divine vision," and so forth, is explained by this. Alternatively, [the suffix *yat* is applied] in the sense of "one who is skilled in restraint" (*niyame sādhur*).
The words *avadya*, *paṇya*, and *varya* are used in the senses of "blameworthy," "to be sold," and "prohibited," respectively. (A 3.1.101)

When *nañ* is the upapada, by the rule *vader āśīr-ācchādane kyap* (Pāṇini 3.1.106), the suffixes *yat* and *kyap* would otherwise apply; however, this is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) for both purposes to indicate that it occurs only in the sense of censure (*garhā*). Thus, *avadyam* means "sinful" or "blameworthy. Why "in the sense of censure"? Consider *anudyaṃ gurunāma* ("the name of a teacher is not to be uttered"). For that [name] is neither blameworthy nor fit to be uttered. According to the traditional law (*smṛti*): "One who desires his own welfare should not utter his own name, the name of a teacher, the name of one who is extremely wretched, or the names of his eldest child and wife. *Paṇyā gauḥ*: "A cow for sale"; the meaning is "to be traded. *Pāṇyam* is something else [not for sale].

The meaning is "worthy of praise. *Anirodha* means "unobstructed"; the suffix *yat* is applied to the root *vṛñ* in that sense [of being unimpeded]. An example is *śatena varyā kanyā* ("a maiden to be chosen for a hundred [pieces of gold]"); another is *vṛtyā* ("by means of livelihood"). Regarding *vahyaṃ karaṇam* (A 3.1.102):
*vahyam* means "a cart," in the sense of "that by which one carries" (*vahanty anena*). Why specify *karaṇam* ("instrument")? [To exclude cases like] *vāhyam*, which means "to be carried."

SK 2851: *aryaḥ* is used for a master (*svāmin*) or a Vaiśya (Pāṇini 3.1.103). [The root] *ṛ* means "to go. From this, the suffix *yat* is applied; it is an exception to *ṇyat*. Thus, *aryaḥ* means a master or a Vaiśya. Why [is it said] "of these two"? [Consider: *āryaḥ* as a Brāhmaṇa; the meaning is "one who is to be attained" (*prāptavya*). SK 2852: *upasaryā* is used in the sense of "fit for breeding" (*kālyā prajane*) (Pāṇini 3.1.104).

The meaning is: "if the time for conception has arrived. *Upasaryā* refers to a cow; the meaning is that she is fit to be approached by a bull for the purpose of impregnation. Why [is the word] *prajane kālyā* mentioned? [Consider: *upasāryā kāśī*; the meaning is "to be reached" [not for procreation].
SK 2853: *ajaryaṃ saṃgatam* (A 3.1.105).

The suffix *yat* is applied after the root *jṛ* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, when it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), provided that the word is connected with a qualifier (*viśeṣya*). Thus, "that which does not age" is *ajarya*. Therefore, Bhaṭṭi says: *tena saṃgatam āryeṇa rāmājaryaṃ kuru drutam* (BhK 6.54), meaning "quickly make [this] agreeable to the noble Rāma. However, in the verse: *mṛgair ajaryaṃ jarasopadiṣṭam adehabandhāya punar babandha*, the qualifier *saṃgatam* must be supplied [as the object]. Why [is it necessary]? Because in *ajaritā kambalaḥ* ("an undecaying woolen blanket"), it refers to the agent. But in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), even when the agent is one who has come together (*saṃgata-kartṛka*), only the suffix *ṇyat* is used: *ajāryaṃ saṃgatena*. SK 2854: *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (A 3.1.106). The suffix *kyap* is also applied after the root *vad* when a nominal stem (*sup*) follows.

From the subsequent sūtra, the word *bhāve* ("in the sense of an action/state") is drawn over here. After the root *vad*, the suffix *kyap* occurs in the sense of an action (*bhāve*), and optionally *yat* as well, provided there is no prefix (*anupasarge*) and a nominal stem (*sup*) is present as an upapada. Examples: *brahmodyam* and *brahmavadyam*. The meaning is "the speaking of the *brahman*"; that is, the *brahman* is the Veda, and its speaking is what is intended. Some maintain that these two suffixes occur in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). However, when there is a prefix (*upasarge*), only the suffix *ṇyat* occurs: *anuvādyam*, *apavādyam*. SK 2855: After the root *bhū*, the suffix *kyap* occurs in the sense of an action (*bhāve*). Example: *brahmaṇo bhāvaḥ* = *brahmabhūyam*. [The condition] "provided there is a nominal stem (*sup*) as an upapada" still applies. Example: *bhavyam*. [The condition] "only when there is no prefix" (*anupasarga eva*) applies. Example: *prabhavyam*.
SK 2856: *hanasta ca* (A 3.1.108).

When a nominal beginning with a vowel (*sup*) that is not a prefix (*anupasarga*) is present as an upapada, the suffix *kyap* shall be applied to the root *han* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), and the letter *t* shall be substituted for its final [nasal]. For example: *brahmaṇo hananam* becomes *brahmahatyā*. The feminine gender is established by common usage (*lokāt*).
SK 2857: *etistuśāsvṛdṛjuṣaḥ kyap* (A 3.1.09). The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *i*, *stu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ* [in the sense of an abstract state].

The suffix *kyap* occurs after these [roots]. By the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* (Pāṇini 6.1.71), the augment *tuk* is added: *stutyaḥ*. By the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, [the root *śās* becomes *śis*]: *śiṣyaḥ*. Regarding the mention of *vṛ*: this refers to the root *vṛñ* (to choose), not *vṛṅ* (to choose as a bride). Thus, *vṛtyaḥ*. However, from *vṛṅ* we have *vāryā ṛtvijaḥ* (the officiating priests are to be chosen). *Ādṛtyaḥ*. *Juṣyaḥ*. The repetition of the mention of *kyap* is for the purpose of supplanting even the subsequent suffix *ṇyat*. Thus: *avaśyastutyaḥ*. According to the *Kāśikā*, there is an option after the roots *śaṃs*, *duh*, and *guh*: *śasyam* or *śaṃsyam*; *duhyam* or *dohyam*; *guhyam* or *gohyam*.

The form *śrā* [from the root *śaṃs*] is established by the force of two rules: *praśasyasya śraḥ* and *īḍavandavṛśaṃsaduhāṃ ṇyataḥ*. However, the source for the other two [forms] must be sought. Regarding the addition [of the suffix *kyap*] to the root *añj* preceded by *āṅ* when a name (*saṃjñā*) is formed: the root *añj* is used in the sense of manifesting, smearing, and so forth. By virtue of the rule of multiplicity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *kyap* is added in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). There is elision of the nasal (*n*) according to the rule *aniditām...* [Pāṇini 6.4.24]. Thus, *ājyam*. [Pāṇini 3.1.110 states: "Also after a root with *ṛ* as its penultimate letter, except for *kṛp* and *cṛ*."

*vṛt* / *vṛtyam*; *vṛdh* / *vṛdhyam*. But for *klṛp* and *cṛt*: *kalpyam*, *cartyam*. Why is the *tapara* marker used? [To exclude] *kṝt* / *kīrtyam*. Since the *cur*-class verbs are not necessarily *ṇic*-ending, the suffix *ṇyat* applies in the absence of *ṇic*; however, when *ṇic* is present, only *yat* applies. (SK 2860) *ī ca svanaḥ* (A 3.1.111):
because of the word "ca," there is also *kyap*. *ād guṇaḥ* [applies]. *kheyam*. It is easier to read [the rule] as *i ca* for the sake of the short vowel.

SK 2861: *bhṛño 'saṃjñāyām* (A 3.1.112). *Bhṛtyāḥ* means "servants" (*karmakarāḥ*), that is, those who are to be supported (*bhartavyāḥ*). This is a word denoting an action (*kriyāśabda*) and not a proper name (*saṃjñā*). [The rule] *samaś ca bahulam* [is also applied]. Thus we have *saṃbhṛtyāḥ* and *saṃbhāryāḥ*. This Vārttika is for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*) specifically when it is not a proper name. Why is it specified "when it is not a proper name"? [Consider: *bhāryā nāma kṣatriyāḥ* ("the Kṣatriyas called Bhāryā"). But how then is *bhāryā* used in the sense of "bride" (*vadhū*)? For in this case, since it is a proper name, the suffix *kyap* [prescribed by A 3.1.104, *samaja-nigama-ādhama-paṇya-bhṛtaḥ*] ought to apply. However, the exclusion of proper names has its utility in the masculine gender. True.

From the root *bhṛ* ending in a long vowel (*bibharti*), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, either because it belongs to the *kry-ādi* group or by specific rule; however, the suffix *kyap* applies only to the root *bharati*. This is due to the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*): "When a term with a specific marker (*anubandha*) is mentioned, it does not include a term lacking that marker.
According to A 3.1.113, *mṛjer vibhāṣā*:
after the root *mṛj*, the suffix *kyap* may optionally be applied, and in its absence, *ṇyat* is used. Thus, the form *mṛjyaḥ* is derived.

Pāṇini 7.3.52: *cajoḥ ku ghiṇyatoḥ*. When the suffixes *ghi* or *ṇyat* follow, the substitution of a guttural (*kutva*) occurs for the letters *c* and *j*. It should be stated that this applies when the suffix is not followed by the *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) affixes, provided the root is not *aniṭ*. Therefore, it does not apply here: *garjyam*. [In the case of] *mṛj*, there is *vṛddhi*: *mārgyaḥ*. Pāṇini 7.3.53: *nyaṅkvādīnāṃ ca*. [The guttural substitution also applies to the words beginning with *nyaṅku*.]
There would be the suffix *kvip*. [Examples: *nyaṅkuḥ* (a kind of deer). The suffix *u* is applied by the rule "not after the root *vañc*" (*nāvañceḥ*).
A 3.1.114 states: *rājasūya-sūrya-mṛṣodya-rucya-kupya-kṛṣṭapacya-avyathyāḥ*.

These seven forms ending in *kyap* are derived as irregular formations (*nipātana*). *Rājasūya*: [The sacrifice] is to be pressed (*sotavya*) by the king (*rājñā*) through the means of extraction (*abhiṣava*), that is, it is to be accomplished; or else, King Soma, who consists of the creeper, is pressed (*sūyate*) or crushed (*kaṇḍyate*) therein—thus, the suffix *kyap* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*). By irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the vowel is lengthened. Hence, *rājasūyaḥ*; [also] *rājasūyam*, belonging to the *ardharcādi* group. *Sūrya*: He moves (*sarati*) in the sky (*ākāśe*). The suffix *kyap* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). By irregular derivation, the change to *u* (*utva*) occurs. Or else, from the root *ṣū* (meaning "to impel") belonging to the *tudādi* class: he impels (*suvati*) the world toward its activity. The suffix *kyap* is added with the augment *ruṭ*.

After the root *vad* preceded by the prefix *mṛṣā*, the suffix *kyap* is always used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Example: *mṛṣodyam*. This word is variable according to its gender when it modifies another noun (*viśeṣyanighna*). Example: "The qualities of height and beauty are false" (*mṛṣodyāḥ*). After the root *ruc*, the suffix *kyap* is used; example: *rucyaḥ*. After the root *gup*, there is a change of the initial *g* to *k* when forming a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Example: "Wealth other than gold and silver is base metal" (*kupyaṃ*); anything else is *gopyam*. When [grain] ripens by itself on ploughed land, they are called *kṛṣṭapacyāḥ*; this refers to the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*). But when the object (*karman*) alone is intended, they are *kṛṣṭapākyāḥ*. That which does not suffer is *avyathyaḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.1.115: *bhidyoddhyau nade* ("The words *bhidya* and *udhya* are used in the sense of a river").

The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *bhid* and *ujjh*. Furthermore, for the root *ujjh*, the verbal root status (*dhātutva*) is also [retained]. *bhinatti kūlam* (he breaks the bank) → *bhidyaḥ*; *ujjhaty udakam* (he abandons the water) → *uddhyaḥ*. Why "in the sense of a river" (*nade*)? [Counter-example: *bhettā* (a breaker), *ujjitā* (one who has abandoned). Regarding *puṣyasiddhyau nakṣatre* (A 3.1.116): the suffix *kyap* is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātita*) when the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). *puṣyanti asmin arthāḥ* (meanings flourish in this) → *puṣyaḥ*; *siddhyanti asmin* (things are accomplished in this) → *siddhyaḥ*.
SK 2868: After the roots *pū* (to purify), *nī* (to lead), and *ji* (to conquer), the suffix *kyap* is applied when followed by the words *muñja*, *kalka*, and *hali*.

The suffix *kyap* is added after *pū*, *nī*, and *ji*. *vipūya* refers to *muñja* grass; the meaning is that it must be purified for the purpose of making ropes and the like. *vinīya* refers to *kalka*; the meaning is a ground medicinal substance, or alternatively, "sin. *jitya* refers to *hali* (a plough); the meaning is that which is to be drawn by force—a large log used for leveling the furrowed land. In other cases, however, the forms are *vipavyam*, *vineyam*, and *jeyam*. SK 2869: The suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *grah* (to seize) when preceded by the prefixes *prati* and *apa*. (A 3.1.118)
It should be stated that [the suffix *ghya*] occurs in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Thus: *pratigṛhyam* and *apigṛhyam*. But in common usage (*loka*), it is *pratigrāhyam* and *apigrāhyam*.
A 3.1.119: [The suffix *ghya* is applied] also in the sense of "foot," "not independent," "external," and "belonging to a faction."

*Avagṛhyam* / *pragṛhyaṃ padam* / *asvairī paratantraḥ* / *gṛhyakāḥ śukāḥ*; the meaning is that they have been rendered dependent by being bound in cages and the like. *Bāhyāyām*: *grāmagṛhyā senā*; the meaning is that the army is situated outside the village. Because of the specification of the feminine gender, [the suffix does not apply] to the masculine or neuter. *Pakṣe bhavaḥ pakṣyaḥ*; [the suffix] *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. *Āryair gṛhyate āryagṛhyaḥ*; the meaning is one who has taken refuge in their faction. SK 2871: *vibhāṣā kṛvṛṣoḥ* (A 3.1.120); the suffix *kyap* may optionally be applied after the roots *kṛ* and *vṛṣ*. Thus: *kṛtyam*, *vṛṣyam*; or, in the alternative case: [other forms].
SK 2872: *ṛhalor ṇyat* (A 3.1.124).
The suffix *ṇyat* shall be applied after a verbal root ending in an *ṛ*-vowel or a consonant (*hal*). [Examples: *kāryam*, *varṣyam*. SK 2873:
*yugyaṃ ca patre* (A 3.1.121). [The suffix *ṇyat* is also applied] after the root *yuj* when the meaning is "a vehicle" (*patra*). [Example: *yugyam*.
*Patra* means a vehicle; *yugya* means an ox. Here, the suffix *kyap* is applied and the change to *k* (*kutva*) is prescribed by irregular derivation (nipātana).
[Pāṇini 3.1.122] *Amāvāsyā* may optionally [be formed].

The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after the root *vas* when preceded by the indeclinable *amā*, provided it denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). When the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) has occurred, a short vowel is optionally substituted by nipātana. Because the moon and sun dwell together (*amā saha vasataḥ*) in this [night], it is called *amāvasyā* or *amāvāsyā*. [In the case of *amāvāsyā*,] the suffix *ṇyat* is applied after roots ending in *ṛ* or *hal*; by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* for the *j*. Thus, *pākyam*. The suffix *ṇyat* should be stated after the root *sṛj* when preceded by *pāṇi*; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *kyap* which would otherwise apply because the root has *ṛ* as its penultimate letter. A rope that is released by the two hands is called *pāṇisargyā rajjuḥ*. [The suffix *ṇyat* is also applied] after [the root *sṛj*] preceded by *sam-ava*. Thus, *samavasargyā*. SK 2875: [The suffix *ṇyat* is not applied] after roots beginning with *kvā*. (A 7.3.59)

The substitution of *k* for the *c* and *j* of roots beginning with *kvā* does not occur; thus, [the form] is *garjyam*. However, the author of the Vārttikas, having supplemented the rule *cajoḥ* with the phrase "not before the suffix *niṣṭhā* when it is without the augment *iṭ*" (*niṣṭhāyām aniṭaḥ*), rejected the rule *na kvādeḥ* and so forth. Consequently, there is no substitution of *k* for roots such as *arji* and *tarji*, because they take the augment *iṭ* before the suffix *niṣṭhā*. But for roots such as *gruci* and *gluñcu*, even though they belong to the *kvādi* class, the substitution of *k* must indeed occur. According to the view of the original Sūtra, although the opposite result would have been obtained, nevertheless, among the sages, authority rests with each subsequent one.
SK 2876: The substitution of *ku* does not occur for the roots *aj* and *vraj*. [Examples: *samājaḥ*, *parivrājaḥ*. SK 2877:
The forms *bhujam* and *nyubjam* are used respectively in the sense of "hand" and "affliction. (A 7.3.61)

These two are *nipātana*s (irregularly formed words). That by which one enjoys is "bhuja," meaning the hand; [the suffix] *ghañ* is applied according to the rule *halaś ca*. That in which things are bent down is "nyubja. "Upatāpa" means disease. [The rule applies] in the sense of "hand" and "disease"; why [is it not so in other cases]? [In those cases, we have] *bhoga* ("enjoyment") and *samudga* ("a casket"). SK 2878: *prayāja-anuyājau yajñāṅge* (A 7.3.62). These two are *nipātana*s when they refer to parts of a sacrifice. "Five *prayājas*" and "three *anuyājas*. Why [only] when referring to parts of a sacrifice? [Otherwise, we have] *prayāga* ("a place of pilgrimage") and *anuyāga* ("a secondary sacrifice").

SK 2879: In the sense of "going" (*gatau*), there is no *kutva* [change of *c* to *k*] for the root *vañc*. Thus, *vañcayam*. Why "in the sense of going"? Consider *vaṅkyam kāṣṭham*; the meaning is "made crooked. SK 2880: In the sense of "dwelling" (*oke*), there is *kutva* for the root *uc* before the suffix *ke*. [Thus, *ukka*].

The substitutions *u* for *ū* and *ca* for *ka* are prescribed as *nipātana* when the suffix *ka* follows. Examples are *okaḥ* (abode) and *śakunta-vṛṣalau*. The suffix *ka* is applied here by virtue of the rule regarding roots ending in *i* or *u* (*igupadhala-kṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*). Although the form could have been established by the suffix *ghañ*, this rule is intended to ensure that the word is *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable).
By the rule *ṇya āvaśyake* (A 7.3.65), the substitution of *ku* does not apply; thus, we have *avaśyapācyam*.

SK 2882: *yajayācarucapravacarcaś ca* (A 7.3.66). The suffix *ṇyaT* is applied, and there is no substitution of *ku* [for the *ca* of *yaja*]. Examples: *yājyam*, *yācyam*, *rocyam*, *pravācyam* (referring to a specific type of literary work), *ṛc*, *arcyam*. Even though these roots have *ṛt* as their penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*), the suffix *ṇyaT* is applied precisely because of this very *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence). And from the root *tyaj*: *tyājyam*. According to the *Kāśikā*, the rule is *tyajipūjyoś ca*; however, the inclusion of *pūj* therein is questionable, as it is not mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*. Indeed, the *Bhāṣya* states that there is an *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition) of *tyaj* within the section on *ṇyaT*. SK 2883: *vaco 'śabdasaṃjñāyām* (A 7.3.67). [The substitution of *uT* for the final vowel of *vac* occurs when followed by *ṇyaT*, provided it does not form a technical grammatical term.]

It should be stated that "vākya" refers to what is expressed by words; however, in the context of grammar, it refers to a sentence. Regarding the rule *prayojyaniyojyau śakyārthe* (A 7.3.68): one who can be employed is a *prayojya*; one who can be directed is a *niyojya*, such as a servant.

SK 2885: *bhojya* is used in the sense of "that which is to be eaten" (*bhakṣye*); otherwise, it means "that which is to be enjoyed" (*bhogya*). In the section concerning the suffix *ṇyat*, it should be stated that [the suffix applies] after the roots *lap* and *dambh*: *lāpya*. Although the root *dambh* is not listed among the verbal roots (*dhātu*), it must be accepted on the strength of this Vārttika. *dābhya*. SK 2886: Or, [the suffix *ṇyat* applies] in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyake*).

The suffix *ṇyat* occurs after a verbal root ending in the vowel *u* when the sense of "necessity" (*avaśyambhāva*) is to be expressed. Examples: *lāvyam*, *pāvyam*. [By rule A 3.1.126: *āsuyuvapirapitrapicamaśca*:

from the root *ṣuñ* (to press), *āsāvyam*; from *yu* (in the sense of mixing), *yāvyam*; from *vā* (to weave), *vāpyam*; from *rā* (to give), *rāpyam*; from *trā* (to protect), *trāpyam*; from *cam* (to sip), *cāmyam*.

SK 2888: *ānāyya* is formed when preceded by *āṅ* (A 3.1.127). From the root *nī*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, and the substitution of *āya* is prescribed as a *nipātana*. This refers specifically to a particular *dakṣiṇāgni* fire. For that fire is brought (*ānīyate*) from the *gārhapatya* fire, and it is "not constant" (*anitya*) because it does not burn perpetually. Other things such as jars are "to be brought" (*āneya*), and the *dakṣiṇāgni* is also [so called] when it is brought from the house of a Vaiśya or similar source.
SK 2889: *praṇāyya* is used in the sense of "approved" (*saṃmata*) (A 3.1.128).

*Saṃmati* is the state of becoming an object of affection; its verbal function (*karmavyāpāra*) is such. Likewise, *saṃmati* also refers to regard for enjoyments. *Praṇāyya* means a thief; the meaning is "one unworthy of affection. *Praṇāyya* also means a pupil; the meaning is "one who is detached. *Praṇeya* has another meaning. [The rule] *pāyyasānnāyyanikāyyadhāyyā mānahavirnivāsasāmidhenīṣu* (A 3.1.129) [applies].

That by which something is measured is *pāyya*, a measure; [the suffix] *ṇyat* is applied, and there is the substitution of *p* for the initial of the root. By the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ*, the augment *yuk* is added. That which is led together toward the fire for the sake of an oblation is *sānnāyya*, a specific type of sacrificial offering (*havis*); [the suffix] *ṇyat* is applied, the *ā* of the prefix *sam* is substituted for *āy*, and the lengthening of *sam* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). That in which grain and so forth are piled up is *nikāya*, an abode; [the suffix] *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of a locus, and the substitution of *k* for the initial of the root is prescribed as an irregularity. That verse by which fuel is placed is *dhāyyā*, a *ṛc*; [this is taught by] Pāṇini 3.1.129. Regarding the seasonal sacrifices, *kuṇḍapāyya* and *saṃcāyya* [are formed with *ṇyat*]; (A 3.1.130).

In this [rite], Soma is drunk from a *kuṇḍa* [vessel]; thus it is the *kuṇḍapāyya* sacrifice. That which is gathered together is the *saṃcāyya*. Regarding the rule *agnau paricāyyopacāyyasamūhyāḥ* (A 3.1.131): these [words] are correct when referring to specific places for maintaining the fire; otherwise, however, one has *pariceyam*, *upaceyam*, and *saṃvāhyam*.

SK 2893: *cityāgnicitye ca* (A 3.1.132). That which is piled up (*cīyate*) is the "piled fire" (*cityo 'gniḥ*). The piling of the fire is "fire-piling" (*agnicityā*). The suffixes *kṛtya* are also used in the senses of command (*praiṣa*), permission (*atisarga*), and the arrival of the proper time (*prāptakāla*). Examples: *tvayā gantavyam*, *gamanīyam*, *gamyam*. This rule for *kṛtya* suffixes is stated again so that it may not be sublated by the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix. Furthermore, it indicates that after the section on feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*), the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply in some cases. By this, it is established that [the *vāsarūpa* rule] does not apply in the case of *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tusun*, and suffixes having the sense of *khala*. The *kṛtya* suffixes and *tṛc* are also used in the sense of fitness (*arha*). Example: one who is fit to praise is "praiseworthy" (*stutyaḥ*), meaning the object of praise.
The *stotṛ* is the one who performs the praise. By means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), there is the rule for the kṛt-affixes *kṛtya* and *tṛc* so that there may be no sublation [of the meaning];
this is according to A 3.4.68: *bhavyageyapravacanīyopasthānīyajanyāplāvyāpātyā vā*.

These [suffixes] ending in *kṛtya* are optionally prescribed when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed; alternatively, according to the rule *tayor eva*, they should be understood as expressing the object (*karman*) when used with a transitive verb, and the state (*bhāva*) when used with an intransitive verb. For example: *bhavyaḥ* means "he who becomes" (*bhavati*), or "that which is to be become by him" (*bhavyam anena*). *Geyaḥ* means "this one who sings the Sāmans" (*gāyati*), or "the Sāman to be sung by him" (*geyaṃ sāmānena*), and so forth. Regarding the rule *śaki liṅ ca*: because of the word *ca*, the *kṛtya* suffixes are also included. Thus, *voḍhavyaḥ* (or *vahanīyaḥ*, *vāhyaḥ*) means "capable of being carried" (*voḍhuṃ śakyaḥ*). The mention of the *kṛtya* suffixes here is to prevent the application of the *liṅ* (optative) suffix.

Since it is possible to convey this meaning by this very rule due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the inclusion of "kṛtya" in the rule for *praiṣa* and so forth (*praiṣādi-sūtra*) would be easily dispensable; furthermore, there would be no need for the mention of "kṛtya" and "tṛc" in the sense of fitness (*arha*). Thus ends the section on kṛtya suffixes.
Now begins the section on primary suffixes (kṛt-pratyayas), number 64.

SK 2895: *ṇvul-tṛcau* (A 3.1.133). These two suffixes (*ṇvul* and *tṛc*) occur after a verbal root. By the rule *kartari kṛt*, they occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). *Yuvor anākau*: [The substitutes] *an* and *āk* replace *yu* and *vu*. *kārakaḥ* / *kartā* ("one who does"). *voḍhum arhaḥ* → *voḍhā* ("one worthy to carry"). *kārikā* / *kartrī* ("female doer"). [In *kuṭitā*,] by the rule *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ...* there is the *ṅit*-designation. *koṭakaḥ* ("one who cuts"); because it is stated that [the suffix is] not *ṅit* when preceded by *añ* or *ṇi*, there is no *ṅit*-designation. *vija iṭ*: [the augment] *iṭ* is added after *vij*. *vijitā* ("one who has conquered"). *hanasto 'ciṇṇaloḥ*: [the substitution of] *ta* for *han* occurs except before *aciṇ* and *ṇal*. *ghātakaḥ* ("killer"). *āto yuk*: [the augment] *yuk* is added after a root ending in long *ā*. *dāyakaḥ* ("giver"). By the rule *nodāttopadeśasya...*, there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution]. *śamakaḥ* ("one who pacifies") / *damakaḥ* ("one who tames"). However, for roots that do not take *iṭ*, [there is no *yuk*]: *niyāmakaḥ* ("one who restrains").

And [the suffix *ṇvul* is applied] after the roots *jan* and *vadh*. From *jan*: *janakaḥ* (begetter). From *vadh* in the sense of "killing": *vadhakaḥ* (slayer). After the roots *radh* and *jabh*, [the suffix *ṇvul* is applied] before a vowel-initial affix: *randhakaḥ* (subduer), *jambhakaḥ* (crusher). Before an affix beginning with a vowel that does not have *iṭ*, [there is no substitution] for *radh*: *radhitā* (one who will subdue), *raddhā* (one who has subdued). After the roots *masj* and *naś*, there is the augment *num*: *maṅktā* (one who will dive), *naṃṣṭā* (one who will perish), *naśitā* (one who will perish). After the root *rabh*, except before the suffix *aś* and *liṭ*: *rambhakaḥ* (one who seizes). Also after the root *labh*: *lambhakaḥ* (one who obtains), *labdhā* (one who has obtained). After the roots *iṣ*, *sah*, etc., there is optionally *iṭ*: *eṣitā* or *eṣṭā* (one who desires), *sahitā* or *soḍhā* (one who endures). After the root *daridrā*, there is the elision of *āl*: *daridritā* (one who is poor).

In the case of the *ṇvul* suffix, [the form] is *daridrāyakaḥ*. Let there simply be the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*; the meaning is that they should apply not only where specifically prescribed, but elsewhere as well. And thus, by means of a *yogavibhāga*, the inclusion of the term *bahulam* serves the purpose of indicating that verbal nouns (*kṛt*) in general may deviate from their primary meanings. For example: *pādahārakaḥ* ("one who is carried by the feet"); here, *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). It should be stated that the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* after the root *kram-* applies when it occurs in the active voice (*kartari*) and is the domain of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Example: *prakrāntā* (feminine). Why "in the active voice"? Consider: *prakramitavyam* (neuter, gerundive). Why "in the middle voice"? [Consider: *prakrāntam* (neuter).

The term *viṣaya* (object) is used here in the sense of "that which is not other" (*ananyabhāva*). Therefore, there is no prohibition for the optional form prescribed by the rule *anupasargād vā*. Examples: *kramitā*. Being fit for that [action] is precisely what constitutes being its object; thus, according to some, the form *krantā* is also valid. In the rule *gameḥ iṭ*, the mention of the *parasmaipada* endings indicates the absence of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *na* (parasmaipada) affixes. Examples: *saṃjigamiṣitā*. Similarly, [the rule] *na vṛdbhyaś caturbhyaḥ* applies: *vivṛtsitā*. From a *yaṅ*-stem, the suffix *ṇvul* is added: because the elision (*allopasya*) is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivattvāt*), there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening. Example: *pāpacakaḥ*. However, from the *yaṅ*-lopa stem, it is *pāpācakaḥ*.

Pāṇini 3.1.134: *nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ*. After roots beginning with *nandi*, the suffix *lyu* (*ana*) is applied; after those beginning with *grahi*, the suffix *ṇini*; and after those beginning with *paci*, the suffix *ac*. Examples: - From *nandi*: "he causes joy" → *nandanaḥ*. - From *arda*: "he afflicts people" → *janārdanaḥ*; likewise, *madhusūdanaḥ* ("slayer of Madhu"). - From *bhīṣi*: "he terrifies intensely" → *vibhīṣaṇaḥ*. - From *lū*: *lavaṇaḥ*. In the *nandyādi* group, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is established by technical rule (*nipātana*). Examples: *grāhī*, *sthāyī*, *mantrī*, *viśayī*. The absence of *vṛddhi* strengthening is also due to technical rule: *viṣayī*. Here, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* also occurs: *paribhāvī*, *paribhavī*. In these cases, the optional absence of *vṛddhi* is established by technical rule.

The *pac-ādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). This is because the suffixes *ghañ* and *aṭhac* are not applied to the roots *kṛ* and *ghaṭ* in the two rules *śivaśamariṣṭasya kare karmaṇi ghañ* and *aṭhac*; furthermore, the rule for the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*) is prescribed when the suffix *ac* follows. For some [roots] in this list, the reading is intended for the purpose of attaching an *anubandha* (indicatory letter); for others, it is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*); and for others, it is for the purpose of subverting a sublater (*bādhakabādhanārtha*). Examples: from *pacati*, we have *pacaḥ*; likewise, *nadaṭ*, *coraṭ*, *devaṭ*, and so forth, which are marked with the *ṭi* indicatory letter. From these, we derive *nadī*, *corī*, and *devī*.

From the root *div*, the suffix *ka* is obtained by the rule *ig-upadhāt kaḥ*. [Examples: *jārabharā*, *śvapacā*. For these two, the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise be obtained in the sense of the object (*karman*). *Śvapāka* is also included because it is read in the *nyaṅku*-class. By the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ*. By the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke*, there is a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. [Examples: *cekriyaḥ*, *nenyaḥ*, *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*, *marīmṛjaḥ*. It should be stated that for the roots *car*, *cal*, *pat*, and *vad*, there is optionally reduplication (*dvitva*) and the addition of *āc* to the reduplicated stem (*abhyāsa*).

Due to the force of the long vowel in the *āgama*, there is neither the shortening of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) nor the retention of the initial consonant (*halādi-śeṣa*). Thus: *carācaraḥ*, *calācalaḥ*, *patāpataḥ*, *vadāvadaḥ*. In the case of the root *han*, there is also the substitution of *gh* for the reduplication. Because of the rule "after a reduplicated syllable, there is *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *h*)," the *gh* of the following syllable becomes *k*: *ghanāghanaḥ*. In the case of the root *pāṭ*, there is the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇiluk*), the substitution of *u* for the root vowel (*uk*), and lengthening of the reduplication: *pāṭūpaṭaḥ*. Optionally, one may apply the suffix *caraṅ*: *pāṭacaraḥ*. In the alternative (*pakṣe*), the forms are: *caraḥ*, *calaḥ*, *pataḥ*, *vadaḥ*, *hanaḥ*, *pāṭaḥ*. Regarding the word *rātri*, by the rule "before a *kṛt* suffix, the augment *mum* is optionally inserted," we have: *rātriṃcaraḥ* or *rātricaraḥ*.

SK 2897: *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* (A 3.1.135). The suffix *ka* shall be applied after these: roots with *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* as their penultimate vowel (*igupadha*), as well as *jñā*, *prī*, and *kṛ*. Examples: *kṣipaḥ*, *budhaḥ*, *kṛśaḥ*, *jñaḥ*; from *prī*, "he pleases," *priyaḥ*; from *kṛ*, "he scatters," *kiraḥ*. By the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* also apply: *kṣepakaḥ*, *kṣeptā*. SK 2898: *ātaś copasarge* (A 3.1.136). [The suffix *ka* is applied] after a root ending in long *ā* when a prefix (*upasarga*) precedes.

What [suffix] would it be? It is *śya*, which is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṇa*. Thus: *suglaḥ* (one who easily swallows), *prajñaḥ* (wise). SK 2899: *pā-ghrā-dhmā-dheḍ-dṛśaḥ śaḥ* (A 3.1.137). From the roots *pā* (to drink), *ghrā* (to smell), *dhmā* (to blow), *dheṭ* (to suckle), and *dṛś* (to see), the suffix *śa* is applied. *pibaḥ* (one who drinks); *jighraḥ* (one who smells); *dhamaḥ* (one who blows); *dhayaḥ* (one who sucks). Regarding *dhayā* (a girl who sucks): because the root *dheṭ* has the marker *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* would be expected—as in *stanandhayī*—just as with the suffix *khaś*. However, Haradatta maintains that *ṅīp* is not desired after *khaś* except in specific cases. *paśyaḥ* (one who sees). The suffix *ghra* is not used when forming a proper name (*saṃjñā*), because of the specific mention in the rule *vyāghrādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.56).
SK 2900: After a prefixless [verb root], and after the roots *limpa*, *vinda*, *dhāri*, *pāri*, *vedi*, *ujji*, *ceti*, *sāti*, and *sāhi*, [the suffix *ka* is applied]. (A 3.1.138)

The suffix *śa* may be applied [after these roots]: *limpaḥ*, *vindaḥ*, *dhārayaḥ*, *pārayaḥ*, *vedayaḥ*, *udejayaḥ*, *cetayaḥ*. The root *sāti* meaning "happiness" is a Vedic (*sautra*) root ending in the causative (*hetumaṇṇic*); hence *sātayaḥ*. By the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpanyāya*), when the suffix *kvip* is applied, we have *sāt* for the Supreme Self, and *sātvantaḥ* for the devotees. The root *ṣaha* in the sense of "endurance" belongs to the *curādigaṇa*; it may also end in the causative (*hetumaṇṇic*); hence *sāhayaḥ*. Why "without a prefix"? [Counter-example: *pralipaḥ*. It should be stated that [the suffix applies] optionally after *limp* with the prefix *ni*: *nilimpāḥ* (the gods). After the root *vid*, [the suffix applies] in the sense of a name (*saṃjñāyām*) following words such as *go*: *govindaḥ*, *aravindam*. SK 2901: After the roots *dā* ("to give") and *dhā* ("to place"), [the suffix *śa* is applied] optionally. (A 3.1.132)

[The suffix] *śa* occurs: *dadaḥ*, *dadhaḥ*. Optionally, the suffix *ṇa* will be mentioned later. [This applies] only when there is no prefix (*anupasargāt*): *pradaḥ*, *pradhaḥ*. By the rule *jvalitikasantebhyo ṇaḥ* (A 3.1.140), the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning with" (*ādyartha*). Thus, after roots beginning with *jvalati* and ending with *kas*, the suffix *ṇa* may optionally occur; in the alternative case, the suffix *ac* occurs: *jvālaḥ*, *jvalaḥ*, *jvalaḥ*; *cālaḥ*, *calaḥ*. [This applies] only when there is no prefix: *ujjvalaḥ*. There is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the root *tanoti*: here, the conditions "when there is no prefix" and "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) do not apply. From *avatanoti*, we derive *avatānaḥ*.

SK 2903: *śyai-ṅ*, *ava-sya-ti*, *sṛ*, *vṛt*, *iṇ*, *ava-sā*, *hṛ*, *lih*, *śliṣ*, and *śvas*—after these roots, the suffix *ṇa* shall always occur. Although the suffix *ṇa* is already established for *śyai-ṅ* and *ava-sya-ti* because they end in long vowels (*adanta*), their separate mention is to block [the application of] *ka* when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present. Examples: *avaśyāyaḥ* (dew), *pratiśyāyaḥ* (catarrh). [From *dā*: ] *dāyaḥ*; [from *dhā*: ] *dhāyaḥ*. [From *vyadh*: ] *vyādhaḥ*. The root *sru* means "to go"; with the prefixes *āṅ* and *sam*: *āsrāvaḥ* (flowing out), *saṃsrāvaḥ* (flowing together). [From *iṇ*: ] *atyāyaḥ* (passing beyond), *avasāyaḥ* (conclusion), *avahāraḥ* (withdrawal). [From *lih*: ] *lehaḥ* (licking); [from *śliṣ*: ] *śleṣaḥ* (clinging); [from *śvas*: ] *śvāsaḥ* (breathing). SK 2904:
After the roots *du* and *ni*, [the suffix *ṇa* occurs] when no prefix is present. (A 3.1.142)

The suffix *ṇa* would apply [to the root *du*]. From the sense "it burns," *dāvaḥ* [is derived]. Because of its association with *ni*, the suffix *ṇa* applies only to *du* when it possesses the *anubandha* (*dunoti*). But from *davati*, by [the rule for] *pacādyac*, we have *davaḥ*. From "he leads," *nāyaḥ*. But when there is a prefix—*pradavaḥ*, *praṇayaḥ*. By *vibhāṣā grahaḥ* (A 3.1.143), *ṇa* is optional; in the alternative case, *ac* [applies]. This is a restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, *grāhaḥ* refers to an aquatic animal, while *grahaḥ* refers to a planet. According to the *Kāśikā*, [the suffix applies] also after the root *bhū*: *bhavaḥ* means a god or transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); *bhāvāḥ* means categories of things. However, according to the view of the *Bhāṣya*, *bhāvaḥ* is derived with *ac* from the causative form of the root *bhū* in the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*).

SK 2906 *gehe kaḥ* (A 3.1.144): When "house" (*geha*) is the agent, the suffix *ka* occurs after the root *grah*. [Thus] *gṛha* means that which grasps grain and so forth. By virtue of being located therein (*tātsthyāt*), the word *gṛhāḥ* refers to the wife. SK 2907 *śilpini ṣvun* (A 3.1.145): The suffix *ṣvun* occurs when an artisan (*śilpin*) is the agent.

The suffix *ṣvun* occurs after the roots *nṛt*, *svan*, and *rañj* when expressing an agent who possesses skill (*kriyākauśala*) in that action; that is, in the sense of an artisan (*śilpin*). Examples: *nartakaḥ* (male dancer), *nartakī* (female dancer); *khanakaḥ* (digger), *khanakī* (female digger). Regarding the root *rañj*, it should be stated that there is an optional elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) before the suffixes *aka* and *ane*. Thus: *rajakaḥ* (washerman/dyer), *rajakī* (female dyer). However, according to the opinion of the *Bhāṣya*, the suffix *ṣvun* applies only after *nṛt* and *khan*. For the root *rañj*, on the other hand, the suffix *kvun* applies in the sense of an artisan or as a technical name (*saṃjñā*). With the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, we have *rajikā*. But in the sense of a woman married to a *rajaka* (a *puṃyoga*), the form is *rajakī*. SK 2908: *gas thakan* (Pāṇini 3.1.146).
The suffix *thakan* occurs after the root *gai* (to sing) when expressing an agent who is an artisan. Example: *gāthakaḥ* (bard/singer).
SK 2909: And the suffix *ṇyuṭ* [is applied after the root √gai]. [Thus: *gāyanaḥ* (a singer). Because it has the marker *ṭi*, [the feminine form is] *gāyanī*.
SK 2910: And [the suffix *ṇyuṭ* is applied after the root √han], when referring to rice (*vrīhi*) or time (*kāla*). [Thus: *ghāṇaḥ* (a variety of rice) and *ghāṇaḥ* (a period of time).

The suffix *ṇyuṭ* occurs after the roots *hā* and *hāṅ* when denoting a type of rice (*vrīhi*) or time (*kāla*), provided they function as the agent (*kartṛ*). "Because it abandons water (*udaka*), it is *hāyana* rice. "Because it abandons [all] states of being (*bhāva*), it is *hāyana*—the year. Or, it means "it moves" (*jihīte*) or "it attains" (*prāpnoti*). Pāṇini 3.1.149: *prusṛlvaḥ samabhihāre vun*.
By the inclusion of the term *samabhihāra* ("repetition" or "intensity"), proficiency in action (*sādhukāritva*) is indicated. Examples: *pravakaḥ*, *sarakaḥ*, *lavakaḥ*.

SK 2912: *āśiṣi ca* (A 3.1.150). The suffix *vun* occurs after a verbal root that denotes an object within the scope of a benediction (*āśis*), provided it expresses the agent. Examples: *jīvatāt* → *jīvakaḥ*; *nandatāt* → *nandakaḥ*. A benediction is a property of the speaker; this expression belongs to the one who wishes [it], such as a father or other relative. SK 2913: *karmaṇy aṇ* (A 3.2.1). The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a verbal root when an object is to be expressed.

When an object (*karman*) is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *aṇ* shall be added to the verbal root; this forms an *upapada-samāsa*. For example, "one who makes a jar" (*kumbhaṃ karoti*) is *kumbhakāraḥ*. In cases such as "one who sees the sun" (*ādityaṃ paśyati*), it does not occur because of a lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). The following Vārttika provides an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ* for the roots *śīli*, *kāmi*, *bhakṣi*, and *ācari*: [the suffix] *ṇa* is applied. Examples: *māṃsaśīlā* ("habituated to meat"), *māṃsakāmā* ("desirous of meat"), *māṃsabhakṣā* ("eating meat"), *kalyāṇācārā* ("of virtuous conduct"). [The suffix *ṇa* is also applied] after the roots *īkṣi* and *kṣami*: *sukhapratīkṣā* ("waiting for happiness") and *bahukṣāmā* ("patient with much"). If so, how are forms such as *gaṅgādharabhūdharādayaḥ* ("bearer of the Gaṅgā," "supporter of the earth") explained? They will be formed when the object is intended to be expressed as a residual factor (*śeṣatva*). SK 2914: *hvāvāmaś ca* (A 3.2.2).

The suffix *aṇ* shall apply [after a root ending in long *ā*]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the application of] *kā*. Examples: *svargahvāyaḥ*, *tantuvāyaḥ*, *dhānyamāyaḥ*. Pāṇini 3.2.3: *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ* (After a root ending in long *ā*, when no prefix is present, the suffix *ka* shall be used when an object is the attendant word [upapada]; *aṇ* does not apply). There is elision (*lopa*) of the final *ā*. Examples: *godah* ("cow-giver"), *pārṣṇitrah* ("heel-protector"). Why "when no prefix is present"? Consider *gosaṃdāyaḥ* ("one who binds cows"). Regarding the rule for the suffix *ka*: in all cases, after roots with a semivowel that undergoes vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), the suffix *ḍa* is used. Example: *brahmajyaḥ* ("one who overcomes Brahman"). Because of the inclusion of the word "in all cases" (*sarvatra*), the rule *ātaś copasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136) also applies: *āhvaḥ* ("invoker"), *prahvaḥ* ("bending forward").

SK 2916 *supi sthaḥ* (A 3.2.4). The rule *supi* is divided into a separate yoga. When a *sup*-ending word is an upapada, the suffix *ka* shall be added after a root ending in long *ā*. For example: *dvābhyāṃ pibati* (he drinks with two) becomes *dvipaḥ*; *samasthaḥ* (standing on level ground); *viṣamasthaḥ* (standing on uneven ground). Then follows *sthaḥ*: when *sthā* is preceded by a *sup*-ending word, the suffix *ka* shall be added. By virtue of the fact that this is a new rule (*ārambha*), it applies in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). For example: *ākhūnām utthānam* (the rising of mice) becomes *ākhūtthaḥ*. SK 2917 *praṣṭho ’gragāmini* (A 8.3.92).

*Pratiṣṭhate* means "he stands facing [forward]"; thus *praṣṭhaḥ* refers to a bull that goes at the front—that is, one who goes not behind. Why [is the prefix *pra-* mentioned]? [To exclude] *prasthaḥ*. **Sūtra A 8.3.97:** *ambāmbagobhūmisavyāpadvitrikusekuśaṅkvaṅgumañjipuñjiparamebarhirdivyagnibhyaḥ sthaḥ* The word *sthaḥ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the form ending in the suffix *kap*. The nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. After these [words], the *s* of *stha* becomes *ṣ*. Examples: *dviṣṭhaḥ*, *triṣṭhaḥ*. From this point forward, both [rules]—*karmaṇi* and *supi*—are understood to follow. Among those, in the case of intransitive verbs (*akarmakeṣu*), the rule *supi* is connected [to the following].

SK 2919: *tunda-śokayoh parimrjāpanudoh* (A 3.2.5). When *tunda* and *śoka* are the objects (*karman*) serving as co-occurring words (*upapada*), the suffix *ka* shall be applied after these two [roots]. It should be stated: "In the sense of laziness and the bringing of happiness. One who rubs his belly is *tundaparimṛjaḥ*, meaning a lazy person; one who removes sorrow is *śokāpanudaḥ*; one who brings happiness is *sukhasyāhartā*. In a sense other than laziness, it is simply *tundaparimārjaḥ*. And he who removes sorrow by teaching the worthlessness of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is *śokāpanodaḥ*. In the section concerning the suffix *ka*, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for roots such as *mūlavibhuja*: that which spreads its roots is *mūlavibhujaḥ*, namely a chariot.

This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Examples: *muhīdhraḥ*, *kudhraḥ*. [From the rule] *gilaḥ*: that which swallows is called *gila*. SK 2920: *pre dājñaḥ* (A 3.2.6). The suffix *ka* occurs after the roots *dā* (in its *dā*-form) and *jñā*, when preceded by the prefix *pra-* and having an object as a co-occurring word (*upapada*). This is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*. Example: *pathiprajñaḥ* ("one who knows the way"). Since it was stated that there must be no prefix (*anupasarga*), if there is any prefix other than *pra-*, the suffix *ka* does not apply. Example: *gosaṃpradāyaḥ* ("the handing down of the cows").
SK 2921: [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *saṃkhyā*] when it means "one who counts"; for example, *gosaṃkhyaḥ* ("one who counts cows").
SK 2922: [The suffix] *ṭak* is applied after the word *goṣṭha*; [for example, *gauṣṭhikaḥ*].

The suffix *ṭak* shall be applied after these two roots (*gai* and *pā*) when they are not preceded by a prefix, provided that an object is present as a co-occurring word (*upapada*). Examples: *sāmagaḥ* (one who sings Sāman hymns), *sāmagī* (a female singer of Sāman hymns). However, when a prefix is present, it is *sāmasaṃgāyaḥ*. It should be stated that [the suffix *ṭak* is applied] after the root *pā* ("to drink") when the objects are *surā* (liquor) or *śīdhu* (spirituous liquor): *surāpī*, *śīdhupī*. But here, *kṣīrapā brāhmaṇī* (a Brāhmaṇī woman who drinks milk); [in this case] *surāpā* means "she protects/guards the liquor" (*surāṃ pāti rakṣati*). A 3.2.9: After the root *hṛ* ("to take"), the suffix *ac* is applied when the action does not involve lifting (*anudyamana*).

The suffix *aṇ* is applied [after the root *hṛ*] when it means "one who carries" (*aṃśaharaḥ*). Why say "when not meaning to lift up"? [Because otherwise] *bhārahāraḥ* ("burden-carrier") would also be formed. There is an extension [of this rule] for the words *śakti*, *lāṅgala*, *aṅkuśa*, *tomara*, *yaṣṭi*, *ghaṭa*, *ghaṭī*, and *dhanus*: [the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *hṛ*] in these cases. *Śaktigrahaḥ*, *lāṅgalagrahaḥ*. And when the sense is "to be worn," [the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *hṛ*] with *sūtra*: *sūtragrahaḥ*. But where one merely takes up a thread (*sūtra*) and does not wear it, there only the suffix *aṇ* applies: *sūtragrāhaḥ*. SK 2924: *vayasi ca* (A 3.2.10). This is a rule concerning the sense of "lifting up. *Kavacaharaḥ kumāraḥ* ("a prince wearing armor").

SK 2925: *āṅi tācchīlye* (A 3.2.11). [The suffix *khañ* is applied after the root *hṛ* when preceded by *āṅ*, provided the sense is that of habitual practice. One who habitually gathers flowers is *puṣpāharaḥ*. Why "provided the sense is that of habitual practice"? [Consider: *bhārahāraḥ* ("one who carries a load"). SK 2926: *arhaḥ* (A 3.2.12). [The suffix *khañ* is applied after the root *hṛ* when preceded by *arha-*, meaning "deserving" or "worthy"].
The suffix *ac* may be used after the root *arh* when *karman* is the upapada; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. Example: *pūjārha-brāhmaṇī* ("a Brahmin woman worthy of honor").

Regarding *stambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ* (A 3.2.13), it should be stated that [the suffix *ac* applies] in the sense of "an elephant" and "a slanderer" respectively. *stamberamaḥ* ("elephant") means "one who delights in a clump of grass" (*stambe ramate*). In this *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending *ṅi*, either by the rule *kṛti* (A 6.3.64) or by the rule *halantāt* (A 6.3.9). *karṇejapaḥ* ("slanderer") means "one who whispers into the ear."

SK 2928: After the root *śam*, [the suffix *a* is applied] when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed (A 3.2.14). Examples: *śambhavaḥ*, *śaṃvadaḥ*. The repetition of the word "root" (*dhātu*) is for the purpose of ensuring the application [of the suffix] even in cases where there would otherwise be an exception; thus, it prevents the suffix *ṭa* from applying in the sense of cause (*hetu*) and so forth after the root *kṛ*. Example: *śaṃkarā* by name, a female wandering ascetic (*parivrājikā*) whose habit is to bring about welfare. SK 2929: After the root *śī* ("to lie down"), [the suffix *a* is applied] when the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is to be expressed (A 3.2.15).

*Śete* (he lies) [is used] with *sva* (one's own); thus, *svaśayaḥ* (one who lies on his own). An addition is made for *pārśva* (side) and others: *pārśvābhyāṃ śete* (he lies on his sides), hence *pārśvaśayaḥ* (one who lies on his side); *pṛṣṭhaśayaḥ* (one who lies on his back); *udareṇa śete* (he lies on his belly), hence *udaraśayaḥ* (one who lies on his belly). [The suffix is applied] when the agents are *uttāna* (supine) and others: *uttānaḥ śete* (he lies supine), hence *uttānaśayaḥ* (one who lies supine); *avamūrdhaśayaḥ* (one who lies head-downward). *Avamūrdhaḥ* means one whose head (*mūrdhan*) is bent downward (*av nataḥ*); the meaning is "he lies face-down. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffix *ḍa* is applied after *giri* (mountain): *girau śete* (he lies on the mountain), hence *giriśaḥ* (the Mountain-Dweller). How then is it that [it says], "That fair-haired woman attended upon Giriśa every day"? [In this case], the analysis is *giriḥ asyāsti* (he has a mountain), and the suffix *cha* is applied because it belongs to the *loman* group.

SK 2930: The suffix *ṭa* is applied after the root *car* when a word denoting a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is used as an upapada. For example: *kurucaraḥ* (one who moves among the Kurus), *kurucarī* (a woman who moves among the Kurus). SK 2931: The suffix *ṭa* is also applied after the root *car* when the words *bhikṣā*, *senā*, or *ādāya* are used as upapadas. For example: *bhikṣācaraḥ* (one who wanders for alms), *senācaraḥ* (one who moves with the army), *ādāyacaraḥ* (one who moves taking [something]).

One who goes for alms is a *bhikṣācara*. One who goes with an army is a *senācara*. The form *ādāya* ends in the suffix *lyap*; one who goes after having taken something is an *ādāyacara*. How is it that [the word] *sahacarīm* appears in the phrase "having looked at her standing companion"? Because the root *car* is listed among the *pacādi* group as *caraḍ*. Regarding the rule *puro'grato'greṣu sarteḥ* (A 3.2.18): one who moves in front is a *purassaraḥ*, an *agratassaraḥ*, or an *agresaraḥ*. The latter is derived from the sense "one who moves in front (*agre*), by means of the front (*agreṇa*), or toward the front (*agre*)"; here, in the sūtra, the form *agre* is also irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*) as ending in the vowel *e*. If so, how is it that [the word] *tadagrasaragarvitakṛṣṇasāram* ("that herd of black antelopes proud of their leader") is formed? Haradatta says it is due to the principle of diversity (*bāhulakāt*).

SK 2933: *pūrve kartari* (A 3.2.19). When the word *pūrva* is used as an *upapada* denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), the suffix *ṭa* shall be applied to the root *sṛ*. Thus, "one who goes first" is *pūrvasaraḥ*. Why "denoting the agent"? [Consider: "one who goes to the eastern region" is *pūrvasāraḥ*. SK 2934: *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu* (A 3.2.20). [The suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *kṛ* when expressing] cause, habitual disposition, or compliance.

When these meanings are to be expressed, the suffix *ṭa* is added after the root *kṛ*. By the rule *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa-kumbha-pātra-kuśā-karṇiṣu ca*, the *s* is substituted for the final vowel and following consonant. Examples: *yaśaskarī vidyā* (knowledge that brings glory), *śrāddhakaraḥ* (one who performs ancestral rites), *vacanakaraḥ* (one who carries out instructions).

Pāṇini 3.2.21: After the words *divā*, *vibhā*, *niśā*, *prabhā*, *bhāskara*, *anta*, *ananta*, *ādi*, *bahu*, *nāndī*, *kim*, *lipi*, *libi*, *bali*, *bhakti*, *kartṛ*, *citra*, *kṣetra*, *saṅkhyā*, *jaṅghā*, *bāhu*, *ahaḥ*, *yattad*, *dhanus*, and *arus*, [the suffix *ṭa* is added to the root *kṛ*].

After these [words], the suffix *ṭa* (which becomes *a*) shall be applied to the root *kṛ*, even when not preceded by a cause (*hetu*) and so forth. *divākaraḥ* (maker of the day), *vibhākaraḥ* (dispenser of light), *niśākaraḥ* (maker of night); [in *bhāskaraḥ*] the *s* is due to its inclusion in the *kaska*-group. *bhāskaraḥ* (sun-maker), *bahukaraḥ* (one who does much). The word *bahu* is mentioned separately from the category of numbers because it signifies abundance rather than numerical quantity. The words *lipi* and *libi* are synonyms. [Examples with] numbers: *ekakaraḥ* (doing one thing), *dvikaraḥ* (doing two things). [In *ahaskaraḥ*] the *s* is due to its inclusion in the *kaska*-group. There is the substitution of *ṣ* according to the rule "always in a compound, for what does not stand at the end of a following member. *dhanuṣkaraḥ* (bow-maker), *aruṣkaraḥ* (causing pain).

The Vārttika states: "Why is *ac* prescribed after the root *kṛ* when followed by *kiṃ*, *yat*, or *tat* in the sense of plurality? Thus: *kiṃkarāḥ*, *yatkarāḥ*, *tatkarāḥ*. Here, *ac* applies by virtue of its higher status, overriding the suffix *ṭa* which would otherwise apply in senses such as "cause" (*hetu*). When used in the sense of a female servant (*puṃyoga*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added: *kiṃkarī*. Regarding the rule *karmaṇi bhṛtau* (A 3.3.22):

when the word *karman* is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *kṛ*. Thus: *karmakaraḥ* means a hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*); another [type of] *karmakara* is one who performs work [not for wages].

SK 2937: The suffix *ṭa* is not applied after the root *kṛ* when preceded by the words *śabda*, *śloka*, *kalaha*, *gāthā*, *vaira*, *cāṭu*, *sūtra*, or *mantra*. This prohibits what would otherwise have been obtained by rule A 3.2.20 (*hetv-ādiṣu*); for example, *śabdakāra* and so forth. SK 2938: The suffix *in* is applied after the roots [preceded by] *stamba* and *śakṛt*. (A 3.2.24)

It should be stated that [the suffix *in* is applied] after the roots *vrīhi* and *vatsa*. *Stambakariḥ* means "rice" (*vrīhi*); *śakṛtkariḥ* means "calf" (*vatsa*). Why "after *vrīhi* and *vatsa*"? [Consider: *stambakāraḥ* ("one who makes a clump") and *śakṛtkāraḥ* ("one who makes dung"). (A 3.2.25) After the root *hṛ*, when *dṛti* or *nātha* are the attendant words (*upapada*), the suffix *in* is applied if the agent (*kartṛ*) is an animal. When *dṛti* or *nātha* are the attendant words, *in* is applied to the root *hṛñ* if the agent is an animal. *Dṛtihariḥ* means "one who carries a skin-bag" (*dṛtiṃ harati*); *nāthahariḥ* means "one who carries the nose-string" (*nāthaṃ nāsārajjuṃ harati*). Why "if the agent is an animal"? [Consider: *dṛtihāraḥ* ("a carrier of a skin-bag") and *nāthahāraḥ* ("a carrier of a nose-string").

SK 2940: *phalegrahir ātmambhariś ca* (A 3.2.26). One who grasps fruits is *phalegrahiḥ*. The final vowel *e* of the prefix (*upapada*) is substituted by *ai*, and the suffix *in* is applied to the root *grah*. One who nourishes oneself is *ātmambhariḥ*. The augment *mum* is added to *ātman*, and the suffix *in* is applied to the root *bhṛ*. By the word "and" (*ca*), *kukṣimbhariḥ* is also included. However, the followers of Candra read [the rule] as *ātmodarakukṣiṣu*. Murāri says: "The cakora birds, whose bellies are filled with moonlight (*jyotsnākarambham uparambharayaḥ*). SK 2941: *ejeḥ khaś* (A 3.2.28). [The suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *ej*.]

The suffix *khaś* occurs after the root *ej* when it is in the causative (*ṇic*) form. According to A 6.6.67, *mum* is the augment for *aruṣ*, *dviṣat*, and words ending in a vowel (*ajanta*), provided they are followed by a word ending in *khid*; however, this does not apply to indeclinables (*avyaya*). Because the suffix is marked with *śit*, the *śap* and other affixes are applied. Thus, "one who causes people to tremble" is *janamejayaḥ*. There is an extension of the rule for *khaś* after the roots *aja*, *dheṭ*, *tuda*, and *hā* when combined with the words *vāta*, *śunī*, *tila*, and *śardha* respectively. For example: *vātamajāḥ* refers to wild animals.

SK 2943 (*khity anavyayasya*, A 6.3.66): When a word ending in *khit* follows, the first member [of the compound] shall take a short vowel; then *mum* is added. Examples: *śunindhayaḥ* ("sucking a dog"), *tilantudaḥ* ("crushing sesame"). *Śardhaṃjahā māṣāḥ* ("beans that abandon the *śardha*"); the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "those which abandon *śardha*"—where *śardhaḥ* means the sound of flatulence (*apāna*). The root *jahāti* here has the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied. SK 2944 (*nāsikāstanayor dhmādheṭoḥ*, A 3.2.29): [The suffix *khaś* is applied after the roots *dhmā* and *dheṭ* when preceded by *nāsikā* and *stana*, respectively.]

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "It should be stated that [the suffix *kha* is applied] after the root *dheṭ* when combined with *stana*, and after the root *dhmā* when combined with *nāsikā*. Thus, one who drinks from the breast is called *stanandhayaḥ*. Because the root *dheṭ* has the marker *ṭi*, there is also the feminine form *stanandhayī*. Similarly, one who breathes through the nose is *nāsikandhamaḥ* or *nāsikandhayaḥ*. [Pāṇini 3.2.30] states: "Also after *nāḍī* and *muṣṭi*."

The suffix *khaś* is applied after the roots *dhmā* and *dheṭ* when *nāḍī* and *muṣṭi* are used as the objects (*karman*) respectively. This sequential correspondence is not intended. Examples: *nāḍindhamaḥ*, *nāḍindhayaḥ*; *muṣṭindhamaḥ*, *muṣṭindhayaḥ*. An addition should be made for *ghaṭī* and *khārī*: *ghaṭindhamaḥ*, *ghaṭindhayaḥ*, and so forth. *Khārī* is a specific measure; *kharī* means a female donkey.

By the rule *udi kūle rujivahoḥ* (A 3.2.31), the suffix *khaś* is applied after the roots *ruj* and *vah* preceded by the prefix *ut*, when *kūla* is used as the object. Example: that which breaks the bank is *kūlamudrujaḥ*; that which carries away the bank is *kūlamudvahaḥ*.

SK 2947: After *vah* and *abhra*, [the suffix] *liha* [is applied]. (*A 3.2.32*) *Vaha* means "shoulder"; that which licks the shoulder is a "shoulder-licking ox" (*vahaṃliho gauḥ*). Due to its inclusion in the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix. Because the *khaś* suffix has the marker *ṅit*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening. "Cloud-licking" refers to the wind (*abhraṃliho vāyuḥ*). SK 2948: After *pac*, [the suffix *khaś* is applied] when a measure (*parimāṇa*) is expressed. (*A 3.2.33*)
A cooking-pot that cooks a *prastha* [of grain] is a *prasthampacā sthālī*; a cauldron that cooks a *khārī* [of grain] is a *khārimpacaḥ kaṭāhaḥ*.
According to A 3.2.34, *mitanakhe ca*:
a Brahmin woman who cooks a moderate amount is a *mitampacā*; a gruel that burns the nails is a *nakhampacā*. In this context, the root *pac* signifies "to heat."

SK 2950: *vidhvaruṣos tudaḥ* (A 3.2.35). *vidhuntudaḥ* ("the moon-destroyer," i.e., Rāhu); when the suffix *mu* is applied, there is elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*). *aruntudaḥ* ("wounding the vital parts").
SK 2951: *asūryalalāṭayor dṛśitapoḥ* (A 3.2.36). [The suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *dṛś* following *asūrya*, and after *tap* following *lalāṭa*.]

*Asūryam* is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound where the members do not have a direct syntactic connection). Because the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the verb *dṛś* ("to see"), [the term] *asūryampaśyāḥ* refers to "those who do not see the sun," namely, the wives of kings. [The term] *lalāṭantapaḥ* refers to the sun. A 3.3.37 states: "In the case of *ugraṃpaśya*, *aramat*, *pāṇindhamāḥ*, and so forth."

These are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). With *ugram* as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), the suffix *khaś* is added to the root *dṛś-* when that word is used as an *upapada*. One who sees fiercely is *ugraṃpaśyaḥ*. Because it glows or shines by means of water (*irā*)—since water serves as its fuel—it is *iraṃmadaḥ*, meaning "the light of the clouds. Here, due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*), the suffix *śyan* is not applied. That path in which hands are blown upon is *pāṇiṃdhamaḥ*; the meaning is that it is shrouded in darkness and the like, for there, hands are blown upon to drive away snakes and other dangers. (SK 2953) *priyavaśe vadaḥ khac* (A 3.2.38).

The suffix *khac* is applied after the root *gam* when preceded by the words *priyaṃ* and *vaśaṃ*; this is stated for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *saṃjñā*. Examples: *mitaṅgamaḥ* ("an elephant"). It should be stated that *viha* is substituted for *vihāyas*; furthermore, it should be stated that *khac* optionally takes the marker *ḍit*. Examples: *vihaṃgamaḥ* ("a bird") and *vihaṅgaḥ* ("a bird"); *bhujaṃgamaḥ* ("a serpent") and *bhujaṅgaḥ* ("a serpent"). According to A 3.2.39, the suffix *khac* is applied after the root *tap* when preceded by *dviṣat* or *para*.

SK 2955: *khaci hrasvaḥ* (A 6.4.94). When followed by a suffix containing *khac*, there shall be shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) in the causative (*ṇau*). For example: one who torments an enemy (*dviṣantam*) or another is called *dviṣantapaḥ*; likewise, *parantapaḥ*. Because of the inclusion of both *ghaṭa* and *ghaṭī* [in the rule], the maxim regarding forms qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) is not universally valid. Therefore, it does not apply here: one who torments a female enemy (*dviṣatīm*) is called *dviṣatītāpaḥ*. SK 2956: *vāci yamo vrate* (A 3.2.40). [The suffix *khac* is applied after the root *yam* when preceded by *vāc*, provided it refers to a religious vow.]

When the word *vāk* is used as an upapada, the suffix *khac* is applied to the root *yam*, provided that a religious observance (*vrata*) is understood; furthermore, by A 6.3.69, *vācaṃyama-* and *purandara-* are established through the irregularity (*nipātana*) of the suffix *am* after *vāk* and *puraḥ*. Thus, *vācaṃyama-* refers to one who observes the vow of silence (*maunavratin*). Why "provided it is a vow"? [Consider: one restrains their speech due to inability or other reasons—this is a *vāgyāma* (restraint of speech), not a vow.

Pāṇini 3.2.41: *pūḥ-sarvayor dāri-sahoḥ*. [The suffix *kha* is applied after the roots *dṛ* and *sah* when preceded by *pur-* and *sarva-*. For example: *puraṃ dārayati* (he tears down the city) = *purandaraḥ*; *sarvaṃ sahati* (he endures everything) = *sarvasahaḥ*. The inclusion of the root *sah* is for the sake of non-designated (*asaṃjñā*) forms. According to the *Kāśikā*, there is also the rule *bhage ca dāreḥ*. They say this is obtained through *bāhulaka* (irregularity). For example: *bhagaṃ dārayati* (he tears open the vulva) = *bhagaṃdaraḥ*. Pāṇini 3.2.42: *sarva-kūla-abhra-karīṣeṣu kaṣaḥ*. [The suffix *kha* is applied after the root *kaṣ* when preceded by *sarva-*, *kūla-*, *abhra-*, and *karīṣa-*.]

*sarvaṅkaṣaḥ* means a wicked person; *kūlaṅkaṣā* means a river; *abhraṅkaṣaḥ* means the wind; *karīṣaṅkaṣā* means a whirlwind. (SK 2960) Regarding the rule *meghartibhayeṣu kṛñaḥ* (A 3.2.44): *meghaṅkaraḥ* ("cloud-maker"), *bhayaṅkaraḥ* ("fear-maker"). By the word *bhaya*, there is an extension of the rule to include that which ends with it (*tadantavidhi*). Thus: *abhayaṅkaraḥ* ("one who brings freedom from fear").

SK 2961: *kṣemapriyamadre ’ṇ ca* (A 3.2.44). After these [words], the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied to the root *kṛ*. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *khac* is also included. Thus: *kṣemaṅkaraḥ*, *kṣemakāraḥ*; *priyaṅkaraḥ*, *priyakāraḥ*; *madraṅkaraḥ*, *madrakāraḥ*. Although it could have been stated simply as "optionally" (*veti*), the explicit mention of *aṇ* is so that [the suffix] *ṭa* does not apply in the case of *hetu* and so forth. How then is the form *kṣemakarāḥ* (those who bring security) explained when it refers to those whose undertakings are small? It is explained by applying the suffix *ac* (as in *pac-ādyac*) when there is an intention to express the object (*karman*) as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*). SK 2962: *āśite bhuvaḥ karaṇabhāvayoḥ* (A 3.2.45). [The suffix *aṇ* is applied to the root *bhū* after the word *āśita* when the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) or an abstract state (*bhāva*) is intended.]

When the word *āśita* is used as an upapada, the suffix *khac* is added to the root *bhū*. Thus, that by which one becomes satiated is called *āśitambhava*, such as boiled rice (*odana*). Alternatively, the state of being satiated is *āśitambhava*. [Pāṇini 3.2.46] states:
"In the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *khac* is added after the roots *bhṛ*, *tṝ*, *vṛj*, *dhṛ*, *sah*, *tap*, and *dam*."

*Viśvambhara* means "one who bears the universe"; *viśvambharā* [is the feminine form]. *Rathaṃtara* is a *sāman*; here, the etymology is merely "one who crosses by means of a chariot" (*rathena tarati*), but there is no correspondence with the individual meanings of the parts. *Patimvarā* is a maiden; *śatruṃjaya* is an elephant; *yugaṃdhara* is a mountain. *Śatruṃsaha*, *śatruṃtapa*, and *ariṃdama*. It has been stated that the root *dam* (to subdue) signifies "pacification," and therefore it is transitive. However, according to another view, the root *dam* here includes an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*). According to A 3.2.47, *gamaś ca*: *sutaṃgama* ("one who goes to his son").
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the words *anta*, *atyanta*, *adhvan*, *dūra*, *pāra*, *sarva*, and *ananta* [in the sense of the seventh case]. (A 4.2.48)

The word *saṃjñāyām* (in the sense of a name) is no longer [applicable]. In these cases, the suffix *ḍa* shall be applied after the root *gam*. By virtue of the marker *ḍ*, there is elision of the final vowel even for non-bha-stems. Thus, one who goes to the end (*antam*) is called *antaga*, and so forth. There is an extension of the rule to include *sarvatra* and *panna*. One who goes everywhere is *sarvatraga*. One who goes to what has fallen (*pannam*, i.e., *patitam*) is *pannaga*. The form *pannam* is a neuter accusative singular of the past passive participle (*ktānta*) derived from the root *pad*, used here as an adverbial modifier of the action. There is also elision of the final syllable of *uras*. One who goes by means of the chest (*urasā*) is *uraga*. Regarding the words *su* and *dur*, when they denote the locus (*adhikaraṇe*): that which is gone to easily is *suga*; [that which is gone to with difficulty is] *durga*.

It should be stated that [the suffix] is seen elsewhere as well: *grāmagaḥ* ("one who goes to the village"). And it should be stated that when the suffix *ḍa* follows, *vihā* is the substitute for *vihāyas*: *vihagaḥ* ("a bird"). [Also:
*āśiṣi hanaḥ* (A 3.2.49).

One who kills an enemy is called *śatruha*. Why [is the suffix not used] in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*)? [Answer: *śatrughātaḥ* (the killing of an enemy).
