Regarding the rule *dārāv āhano ’ṇ antasya ca ṭaḥ saṃjñāyām*: when the word *dāru* is the subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after the root *han* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, and it should be stated that the letter *ṭ* is the substitute for the final part [of the root]. Thus, *dārvāghāṭaḥ* (a woodpecker). Regarding *cārau vā*: [the suffix *aṇ* with the substitution of *ṭ*] is optional when *cāru* is the subordinate term. Thus, *cārvāghāṭaḥ* (one who strikes what is beautiful). Regarding *karmaṇi sami ca*: when *karman* is the subordinate term, the aforementioned [suffix *aṇ* with the substitution of *ṭ*] is applied after the root *han* preceded by the prefix *sam*; this is the meaning. Thus, one who strikes a collection of letters (*varṇa*) is *varṇasaṅghāṭaḥ*; *padasaṅghāṭaḥ*. Alternatively, *varṇasaṅghātaḥ*; *padasaṅghātaḥ*. SK 2967: *ape kleśatamasoḥ* (A 3.2.50).

[The suffix *aṇ* with the substitution of *ṭ* is applied after the root *han* preceded by *apa*, when *kleśa* or *tamas* is the subordinate term. Thus, *kleśāpahaḥ* (one who removes affliction); *tamo’pahaḥ* (one who removes darkness).
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *han* preceded by *apa*.
According to A 3.2.51, the suffix *ṇini* is applied after the words *kumāra* and *śīrṣa*.
Thus, one who kills a child is a *kumāraghātī*; here, the substitution of *śīrṣa* for *śiras* is prescribed as a nipātana. One who kills the head is a *śīrṣaghātī*.
SK 2969: After the roots *jāyā* and *pati*, the suffix *ṭak* is applied [to form feminine nouns] when they denote a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

The suffix *ṭak* shall apply after the root *han* when it denotes an agent possessing that characteristic (*lakṣaṇavat*). Examples: *jāyāghna* "a man who kills his wife"; *patighnī* "a woman who kills her husband. SK 2970: And [the suffix *ṭak* is applied] when the agent is not a human being (*amanuṣyakartṛka*).

*Jāyāghna* means "having birthmarks"; *patighnī* means "a line on the hand" [indicating the death of a husband]; *pittaghnam* means "clarified butter that cures bile. Why say "not a human being"? [Consider: *ākhughātaḥ śūdraḥ* ("a Śūdra who kills rats"). But how is it that there are forms such as *balabhadraḥ*, *pralambaghnaḥ*, *śatrughnaḥ*, and *kṛtaghnaḥ*? They are established by belonging to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*. However, forms such as *coraghātaḥ*, *nagaraghātaḥ*, and *hastī* are formed by the suffix *aṇ* due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulakāt*). [This is supported by] Pāṇini 3.2.54: *śaktau hastikapāṭayoḥ*.

The suffix *ṭak* shall be applied after the root *han* when the sense of "capability" (*śakti*) is to be expressed. This rule is intended for cases where a human being is the agent. Examples: *hastighnaḥ* ("an elephant-killer") as a name; *kapāṭaghnaḥ* ("a door-breaker") as a thief. *Kavāṭa* is an alternative reading. Pāṇini A 3.2.55 states: *pāṇighatāḍaghau śilpini*. When *pāṇi* and *tāḍa* are used as subordinate words (*upapada*), the suffix *ṭak* is applied to *han*, and the elision of the *ṭi* portion (*ṭilopa*) and the substitution of *gh* for *h* are prescribed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Examples: *pāṇighaḥ* ("one who plays the hand-drum"); *tāḍaghaḥ* ("one who plays the *tāḍa* drum"). Why "when [denoting] an artisan" (*śilpini*)? Counter-examples: *pāṇighātaḥ* ("a blow with the hand"); *tāḍaghātaḥ* ("a blow with a *tāḍa*"). An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is made for *rājagha*: *rājaghaḥ* ("one who kills a king"), meaning one who strikes a king.

SK 2973: *āḍhya-subhaga-sthūla-palita-nagna-andha-priyeṣu cvyartheṣv acvau kṛñaḥ karaṇe khyun* (A 3.2.56). When these words—*āḍhya*, *subhaga*, *sthūla*, *palita*, *nagna*, *andha*, and *priya*—which do not have the sense of *cvi* and do not end in *cvi*, are used as objects (*upapada*), the suffix *khyun* is added to the root *kṛ*. For example: that by which they make one who is not wealthy (*anāḍhyam*) wealthy (*āḍhyam*) is called *āḍhyaṃkaraṇam*. Why "not having the sense of *cvi*" (*acvau*)? [Consider: *āḍhyīkurvanty anena* ("they make him wealthy by means of this"). According to the *Kāśikā*, because of the force of the prohibition, the suffix *lyuṭ* is also not applied here. However, according to the *Bhāṣya*, *lyuṭ* would indeed be applied. The phrase "not having the sense of *cvi*" (*acvau*) is for the sake of the subsequent rule. SK 2974: *kartari bhuvaḥ khiṣṇuc-khukañau* (A 3.2.57). When the agent (*kartṛ*) is to be expressed, the suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khukañ* are added to the root *bhū*.

The two suffixes [ṣṇu and ka] occur after the root *bhū* when it follows words such as *āḍhya* (rich) in the sense of the *cv*-suffix, provided that the *cv*-suffix itself is not present. For example: "one who becomes rich from being not rich" is *āḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ* or *āḍhyaṃbhāvukaḥ*. The suffix *kvin* occurs after the root *spṛś* (to touch) when it does not mean water (*anudake*). Example: *ghṛtaspṛk* (one who touches ghee). The requirement "when [the object] is an action" (*karmaṇi*) is no longer applicable here. Example: "one who touches with a mantra" is *mantraspṛk*. The rule for *ṛtvij*, *dadṛś*, *sraj*, *dag*, *uṣṇig*, *añcu*, *yuj*, and *kruñc* has already been explained. The suffix *kañ* also occurs after the root *dṛś* (to see) when preceded by pronouns such as *tyad* (that), provided it does not mean "perception" (*anālocane*). It should also be stated that this applies when preceded by *samāna* and *anya*. Examples: *sadṛk* (similar) and *sadṛśaḥ* (like); *anyādṛk* (different).
The suffix *kso* should also be stated [after these roots]: *tādṛkṣaḥ*, *sadṛkṣaḥ*, *anyādṛkṣaḥ*.

Pāṇini 3.2.61: After the roots *sad*, *sū*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *vid*, *bhid*, *chid*, *jin*, and *rāj*, the suffix *kvip* is applied when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present, even if it is not actually used.

The suffix *kvip* occurs after these [roots] when a verbal prefix (*upasarga*)—whether present or absent—is applied, provided a nominal stem (*sup*) is present as an upapada. Examples: *dyusat*, *upaniṣat*, *aṇḍasūḥ*, *prasūḥ*, *mitradviṭ*, *pradviṭ*, *mitradhruk*, *pradhruk*, *godhuk*, *pradhuk*, *aśvayuk*, *prayuk*, *vedavit*, *nivit*, and so forth. Regarding the root *nī* ("to lead"), it should be stated that the suffix *ṇi* is optionally applied after *agra* and *grāma*. Examples: *agraṇīḥ*, *grāmaṇī*.
(A 3.2.62) The suffix *ṇvi* occurs after the root *bhaj* when a nominal stem (*sup*) and a verbal prefix (*upasarga*) are present as upapadas. Examples: *aṃśabhāk*, *prabhāk*.

SK 2977: *ado 'nanne* (A 3.2.68). The suffix *viṭ* shall be applied after the root *ad* (to eat), provided it does not refer to food (*anna*). Examples: *āmāt* (one who eats raw meat), *sasyāt* (one who eats grain). Why say "provided it does not refer to food"? Consider *annādaḥ* (one who eats food). SK 2978: *kravye ca* (A 3.2.69). [The suffix *viṭ* is also applied] when the object is raw flesh (*kravya*).

The suffix *viṭ* is applied after the root *ad* (to eat). Although this was already established by the preceding rule, this specific statement is for the purpose of precluding the suffix *aṇ*. Thus, *kravyāt* means "one who eats raw meat. How then is it that [the forms] *kravyādaḥ*, *asrapaḥ*, and *āśaraḥ* occur? When the word *ākva-māṃsa* (raw meat) is used as an upapada, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; the substitution of *kravya-* for the upapada [of *āka*] occurs because the term belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. By A 3.2.70, *duhaḥ kab ghaś ca*: the suffix *kap* is applied after the root *duh* (to milk), and the letter *gh* is substituted for the final consonant. Thus, *kāmadughā* ("wish-fulfilling cow").

SK 2980: *anyebhyo ’pi dṛśyante* (A 3.2.75). The phrase *chandasīti* ("in the Vedic language") is no longer in force. The suffixes *manin*, *kvanip*, *vanip*, and *vic* may occur after verbal roots. SK 2981: *neḍvaśi kṛti* (A 7.2.8). [The augment *iṭ* is not applied] before a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *vaś*.
The augment *iṇ* shall not be applied after roots such as *vaś*. [Examples: *śṝ*: *suśarmā*; *prātarītvā*.

(Pāṇini 6.4.41) *viḍvanor anunāsikasyāt*: The substitute *ā* shall take the place of an *anunāsika* vowel before the suffixes *viṅ* and *van*. [Examples: from *jan*, *vijāvā*; from *oṇ*, *avāvā*; from *gaṇ*, *sugaṇ*. *vic*, *roṭ*, *reṭ*. *sugaṇ*.

SK 2983: *kvip* also occurs [as a suffix]. This is also observed; the rule *satsūdviṣa-* etc., is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of this very point. Examples: *ukhāsrat*, *parṇadhvat*, *vāhabhraṭ*. SK 2984: [The substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs before an ending (*antaḥ*).

The substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the root *an*, when standing at the end of a word, occurs after a cause situated in a prefix (*upasarga*), provided that [the cause] follows [the prefix]. *he prāṇ* (O, you who breathe). By the rule *śāsaḥ*—there is the substitution of *ī* [for the vowel of the root *śās*]. *mitraśīḥ* (one who instructs friends). The substitution of *ī* for the penultimate vowel of the root *āśās* should be stated before the suffix *kvip*. *āśīḥ* (blessing). [In the case of roots ending in *ṝ*,] there is the substitution of *ī* and *ū*. *gīḥ* (speech); *pūḥ* (city). [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.97: *is-man-traṅ-kviṣu ca* (and also before suffixes beginning with *iṣ*, *man*, *traṅ*, and *kvip*).

In these cases, there shall be shortening of the vowel *ch*. *tanucchad* (armor); [here] the lengthening occurs by the rule *anunāsikasya kvi...* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.15). *mo no dhātoḥ* (*Pāṇini* 8.2.64): *pratn* (ancient), *praśān* (tranquil). By the rule *cchvoḥ...* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.19), *ūṭh* is substituted: *akṣadyūḥ* (one who plays dice). By the rule *jvaratvara...* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.20), *ūṭh* is substituted: *jūḥ* (speed), *jūrau*, *jūraḥ*; *tūḥ* (crossing), *srūḥ* (flowing), *ūḥ* (protection). [In *janauḥ*, etc.,] there is *vṛddhi*: that which protects people is *janauḥ*, *janāvau*, *janāvaḥ*. *mūḥ* (root), *muvau*, *muvaḥ*; *sumūḥ*, *sumvau*, *sumvaḥ*. By the rule *rāl lopaḥ* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.21), [the *ūṭh* is elided]:
*mūrchā*, *mūḥ* (fainting), *murau*, *muraḥ*. *dhurvī*, *dhūḥ* (burden). [The rule] *gamaḥ kvau* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.40) [applies].

There should be elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). It should be stated that this applies to *gam* and other such roots: *aṅgagat*, *parītat*, *saṃyat*, *sunut*. It should also be stated that the suffix *ūṅ* is added to *gam* and others, and there is also elision: *agregūḥ*, *agrebrūḥ*. Regarding *sthaḥ ka ca* (A 3.2.77): because of the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *kvip* is also included. Examples are *śaṃsthaḥ* and *śaṃsthāḥ*. This rule is intended to supersede the application of the suffix *ac* prescribed by the rule *śami dhātoḥ* (A 3.2.15).

Pāṇini 3.2.78: *supy ajātau ṇinis tācchīlye*. When a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) that does not denote a genus (*ajāti*) follows, the suffix *ṇini* may be added to a verbal root to express habitual action (*tācchīlya*). Examples: *uṣṇabhojī* (one who habitually eats hot food), *śītabhojī* (one who habitually eats cold food). Why "not denoting a genus" (*ajātau*)? Consider: *brāhmaṇān āmantrayitā* (one who addresses Brahmins). Why "habitual action" (*tācchīlye*)? Consider: *uṣṇaṃ bhuṅkte kadācit* (he eats hot food only occasionally). In this regard, the author of the *Vṛtti* explained that the suffix *ṇini* is applied only after a case-suffix that is distinct from a prefix (*upasarga*), and he recorded the supplementary rule: "The addition [of *ṇini*] applies to the root *sṛ* when preceded by *ut*, *prati*, and *āṅ*. Haradatta, Mādhava, and others have followed this very view. However, because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*, it should be disregarded.

The suffix *ṇini* is well-established even after a prefix (*upasarga*): as in *sa babhūvopajīvinām anuyāyivargaḥ* ("He became a group of followers for those who lived off him"), *pataty adho dhāma visāraḥ* ("The spreading light falls downward"), and *na vañcanīyāḥ prabhavo ’nujīvibhiḥ* ("Masters should not be deceived by their dependents"). There is an extension [of the rule] for one who performs an action well (*sādhukārin*). Regarding *brahman*, there is the suffix *vada*. Two Vārttikas exist for the purpose of excluding the sense of habitual character (*atācchīlya*): *sādhukārī* ("one who acts well") and *brahmavādī* ("one who speaks of Brahman"). A 3.2.79: *kartary upamāne* ("when the agent is the object of comparison").

The suffix *ṇini* shall be applied. The meaning of the subordinate word (*upapada*) is the agent, which serves as the standard of comparison for the agent expressed by the meaning of the suffix. For example: "he cries like a camel" (*uṣṭra iva krośati*) results in *uṣṭrakrośī*; likewise, *dhvāṅkṣarāvī*. This rule is intended to express meanings other than habitual action (*atācchīlya*) and to denote a genus (*jāti*). Why specify "when [the subordinate word denotes] the agent"? Consider: "he makes the beans sound like cakes" (*apūpān iva bhaṣayati māṣān*). Why specify "when [there is] a standard of comparison" (*upamāne*)? Consider: "the camel cries" (*uṣṭraḥ krośati*). By the rule *vrate* (A 3.2.80), *ṇini* shall be applied. Example: "one who sleeps on the bare ground" (*sthaṇḍilaśāyī*).

SK 2991: *bahulam ābhīkṣṇye* (A 3.2.81). When frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇini* is applied after a nominal stem (*sup*) when it is used as an upapada. Example: *kṣīrapāyiṇa uśīnarāḥ* ("the Uśīnaras are habitual drinkers of milk").

SK 2992: *manaḥ* (A 3.2.82). [The suffix *ṇini* is applied after a verbal root ending in] *man*. [When frequency is to be expressed, provided the agent is not a human. Example: *dharmamānī* ("one who habitually thinks about dharma").
The suffix *ṇini* occurs after the root *man* when it follows a word in the locative case (*sup*). [Example: *darśanīyamānī*.

By the rule *ātmamāne khaś ca* (A 3.2.83), the suffix *khaś* occurs after the root *man*, which here functions with its own object (*svakarmaka*), when it follows a word in the locative case; the suffixes *aṇ* and *ṇini* also occur. [Examples: One who considers oneself learned is *paṇḍitammanyaḥ* or *paṇḍitamānī*. By the rule *khity anavyayasya*, [the final vowel of the preceding word is shortened]. [Example: *kālimmanyā*. Why "not an indeclinable" (*anavyayasya*)? [Counter-example: *divāmanyā*.

SK 2994: *ica ekāco 'mpratyayavac ca* (A 6.3.68). After a monosyllabic stem ending in *iC*, there shall be the suffix *am*; and that [suffix] shall behave like a primary suffix (*svādi*) when followed by a word ending in *khit*. [By A 7.1.24, *auto 'mśasoḥ*: after a stem ending in *ā*, the substitution of *o* occurs before the suffixes *am* and *śas*. *gāṃmanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself a cow"). [By A 7.1.25, *vāmśasoḥ*: after a stem ending in *ī*, the substitution of *u* occurs before the suffixes *am* and *śas*. *striyaṃmanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself a woman") or *strīṃmanyaḥ*. *nṛ*: *naraṃmanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself a man"), *bhuvaṃmanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself the earth"). *śriyam ātmānaṃ manyate śrimanyaḥ kulam* ("the family considers itself Śrī"). According to the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, the short vowel is substituted for the word *śrī*, and there is an absence of the augment *mum* and the suffix *am*.
SK 2995 *bhūte* (A 3.2.84): This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*), extending as far as [the rule] *vartamāne laṭ* (A 3.2.123). SK 2996 *karaṇe yajaḥ* (A 3.2.85).

When a word denoting an instrument (*karaṇa*) is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇini* shall be applied after the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) in the sense of a completed action, with the agent (*kartṛ*) as the referent. Examples: one who has sacrificed with Soma is a *somayājī*; one who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma is an *agniṣṭomayājī*. Regarding the rule *karmaṇi hanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.86): [the suffix *ṇini* is applied] after the root *han* (to kill) when a word denoting an object (*karman*) is the *upapada*.
This term *karmaṇi* governs the rules up to *sahe ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.96). Example: one who has killed his paternal uncle is a *pitṛvyaghātī*.

SK 2998: *brahmabhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip* (A 3.2.87). When these [words] are present as objects (*upapada*), the suffix *kvip* shall be applied to the root *han* in the sense of the past (*bhūte*). Examples: *brahmahā*, *bhrūṇahā*, *vṛtrahā*. Although this would be established by the rule *kvip ca* alone, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). According to the *Kāśikā*, there is a fourfold restriction here: [the suffix *kvip* applies] only to *brahman* and the others, only to the root *han*, only in the past sense, and only with the suffix *kvip*. According to the *Bhāṣya*, there is a twofold restriction: [the suffix *kvip* applies] only to *brahman* and the others, and only with the suffix *kvip*. SK 2999: *sukarmapāpamantrapuṇyeṣu kṛñaḥ* (A 3.2.89). [The suffix *kvip* is applied] to the root *kṛ* when *su*, *karman*, *pāpa*, *mantra*, or *puṇya* are present as objects.

The suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *kṛ* when used with the words *sukarma*, etc. According to the *Kāśikā*, there are three types of restrictive rules (*niyama*) here: 1. *Sukṛt*, *karmakṛt*, *pāpakṛt*, *mantrakṛt*, *puṇyakṛt*. Because of the restriction "only *kvip*," the suffix *aṇ* does not occur in the sense "he has performed a deed" (*karma kṛtavān*). 2. Because of the restriction "only after the root *kṛ*," the suffix *kvip* does not occur in the sense "one who has studied a mantra" (*mantram adhītavān*), as in *mantrādhyāyaḥ*. 3. Because of the restriction "only in the past tense" (*bhūte eva*), the suffix *kvip* does not occur when one intends to express "he performs or will perform a mantra. Since there is no restriction such as "only with *sva* and others," the suffix *kvip* occurs even with other governing words (*upapada*): *śāstrakṛt*, *bhāṣyakṛt*.
SK 3000: *suñaḥ* (A 3.2.90). [The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *suñ* when preceded by *soma*.

Thus, *somasut*. Regarding this, the *Kāśikā* states that there is a fourfold restriction (*niyama*) here; the same applies to the subsequent sūtra as well. SK 3001: *agnau ceḥ* (A 3.2.91). [The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *ci* when preceded by *agni*.]

*agnicit*. According to *Pāṇini* 3.2.92 (*karmaṇy agnyākhyāyām*), when a direct object (*karman*) is present as a governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *ci* (*cinoti*) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) itself, provided it refers to a specific place for the construction of a fire altar (*agni*). For example: "piled like a hawk" is *śyenacit*.

SK 3003 *karmaṇīni vikriyaḥ* (A 3.2.93): When *karman* is the governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *ini* shall occur after the root *krī* preceded by the prefix *vi*. The mention of "contemptible" (*kutsita*) must be supplied [to the rule]. Examples: *somavikrayī* (one who sells Soma), *ghṛtavikrayī* (one who sells ghee).
SK 3004 *dṛśeḥ kvanip* (A 3.2.94): The suffix *kvanip* occurs after the root *dṛś*.
In the sense of "having become" (*bhūta*) with respect to an object (*karmaṇi*), [the suffix *kvip* is applied]. One who has seen the further shore is *pāradṛś* or *pāradṛśvā*.
According to A 3.2.95, the suffix *kvanip* occurs after the root *kṛ* when combined with *rājan* or *yudh*.
The root *yudh* here has an implied causative meaning (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*). One who has caused the king to fight is *rājayudhvā*; one who has performed service for the king is *rājakṛtvā*.

SK 3006: *sahē ca* (A 3.2.96). The word *karmaṇi* ("in the sense of the object") is no longer in force. Examples: *sahayudhvā* ("one who has fought together"), *sahakṛtvā* ("one who has acted together"). SK 3007: *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ* (A 3.2.97). [The suffix] *ḍa* is applied after the root *jan-* when a locative case ending follows.

*sarasijam* [is derived from *saras-ija*]. *Mandurajaḥ* means "born in a stable" (*mandurāyāṃ jātaḥ*); the short vowel is applied by the rule *ḍyāpoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.63]. SK 3008: *pañcamyām ajātau* (A 3.2.98).

When a word ending in the fifth case occurs as an *upapada*, provided it is not a generic term (*jātiśabda*), the suffix *ḍa* is added to the root *jan*. Examples: *saṃskārajaḥ* ("produced by refinement"), *adṛṣṭajaḥ* ("produced by unseen merit/demerit").
SK 3009: And when there is a prefix, if it is a technical term (*saṃjñā*), [the suffix *kyap* is used];
*prajā* occurs in the sense of lineage (*santati*) or people (*jana*). SK 3010: With the prefix *anu*, [the suffix *kyap* is used] in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The suffix *ḍa* occurs after the root *jan* when preceded by a word in the accusative case (*anupūrva*). For example: *pumanujā*, meaning "born after following a man. SK 3011: *anyeṣv api dṛśyate* (A 3.2.101). The suffix *ḍa* is seen after the root *jan* even with other words as upapadas. Examples: *ajaḥ* ("unborn"), *dvijaḥ* ("twice-born"), *brāhmaṇajaḥ* ("born of a Brahmin"). The word *api* is intended to indicate a deviation from all restrictive conditions; therefore, it is sometimes seen after other roots and with other kārakas as well. For instance: *parisvā* ("one who has bathed around").
SK 3012: *ktaktavatu* is the term *niṣṭhā*.
These two [suffixes] receive the designation *niṣṭhā*.
SK 3013: *niṣṭhā* [is used after a root to denote the past].

The *niṣṭhā* suffixes (*kta* and *ktavatu*) occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*) expressing an actual state of being (*bhūtārtha*). In that regard, by the rule "of those two alone"—meaning in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)—the suffix *kta* is applied; and by the rule "the *kṛt* suffixes [occur] in the sense of the agent," the suffix *ktavatu* occurs in the sense of the agent. When *u* and *kā* are the indicatory letters (*it*), as in *snātam mayā* ("I have bathed") and *stutas tvayā Viṣṇuḥ* ("Viṣṇu was praised by you"), and *Viṣṇur viśvaṃ kṛtavān* ("Viṣṇu has created the universe").
Regarding the rule *niṣṭhāyām aṇyadarthe* (A 6.4.60):

when the *niṣṭhā* suffixes occur in a sense other than that of the causative (*ṇyad-artha*)—namely, other than the sense of the abstract action and the object—the vowel of the root *kṣi* becomes long.

SK 3015 *kṣiyo dīrghāt* (A 8.2.46): After the long [vowel] of the root *kṣi*, the *niṣṭhā* suffixal *t* shall be replaced by *n*. Examples: *kṣīṇavān*. However, in the sense of state (*bhāva*) or object (*karman*), it is *kṣitaḥ*; e.g., *kāmo mayā kṣitaḥ* ("desire was exhausted by me"). *śryukaḥ kiti*: [The suffixal *t* is replaced by *n* after roots ending in *ś*, *r*, or *u*, when followed by a *kit* suffix. Examples: *śritaḥ*, *śritavān*; *bhūtaḥ*, *bhūtavān*; *kṣutaḥ*. Regarding the root *ūrṇu*: it should be stated that it behaves like *ṇu*. By virtue of this, because it is a single-vowel (*ekāc*) root, the augment *iṭ* does not apply. Examples: *ūrṇutaḥ*, *nutavān*. *vṛtaḥ*. SK 3016 *rādābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ pūrvasya ca daḥ* (A 8.2.42): After the roots *rañj* and *dāp*, the *niṣṭhā* suffixal *t* is replaced by *n*, and the preceding *d* is also replaced by *n*. Examples: *raktaḥ*, *dattaḥ*.

The substitution of *n* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix does not occur after the letters *r* or *ḍ*. Furthermore, with respect to the *niṣṭhā*, the substitution of *n* does not occur for the preceding root-final *d* or the letter *r*. Root *śṝ*: By the rule *ṛta id dhātoḥ*, *ṛ* is replaced by *i*. By the rule *raparaḥ*, this *i* is followed by *r*. Then, by the rule on *ṇatva*, [the *n* of the suffix becomes *ṇ*]. Thus: *śīrṇaḥ*. Because the *vṛddhi* substitution is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) due to its being *bahiraṅga* (external), it does not apply here: *kṛtasyāpatyaṃ kārtiḥ* ("the descendant of Kṛta" = *Kārti*). *bhinnaḥ*; *chinnaḥ*. SK 3017: For a root beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), ending in long *ā*, and containing a semivowel (*yaṇvat*), the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is replaced by *n*. *drāṇaḥ*; *styānaḥ*; *glānaḥ*; *mlānaḥ*.

SK 3018: *lvādibhyaḥ* (A 8.2.44). From the twenty-one roots beginning with *lū*, the [suffix] *kta* is applied as previously stated. *lūnaḥ* ("cut"). *jyā* ("to grow old"): by *grahijyā-* (A 6.1.16), [the vowel is shortened]. *jīnaḥ*. *dugvor dīrghaś ca*: from the root *du* "to go," *dūnaḥ*. However, the root *ṭudu* "to afflict" is not included here because it possesses an *anubandha* (indicatory letter). Māgha uses the forms *mṛdutayā* and *dutayā*. *gūnaḥ* ("hidden"). *pūño vināśe*: from *pū* in the sense of destruction, *pūnā yavāḥ* ("the barley is spoiled"); the meaning is "destroyed. Any other [meaning] is *pūta*. *sinoter grāsakarmakartṛkasya*: from *siv* when the object is "food" (*grāsa*) and it functions as the agent. *sino grāsaḥ* ("the food is chewed"). Why say "food"? [Consider: *sitā pāśena sūkarī* ("the sow is bound by a snare").
What is the purpose of the phrase "the agent of the action" (*karmakṛt*)? [Examples: *sito grāso devadattena* ("the morsel was eaten by Devadatta").

Regarding the rule *oditaś ca* (A 8.2.45): from the root *bhujo*, we have *bhugnaḥ*; from *ṭuośvi*, *ucchūnaḥ*; from *ohāk*, *prahīṇaḥ*. It has been stated that the roots beginning with *svād* are *odit*. Thus: *sūnaḥ*, *sūnavān*; *dūnaḥ*, *dūnavān*. Because of the authority of its inclusion among the *odit* roots, the augment *iṭ* is not applied after *ḍīṅ*: *uḍḍīnaḥ*.

SK 3020: *dravamūrtisparśayoḥ śyaḥ* (A 6.1.24). When the meanings are liquidity (*drava*), solidity (*mūrti* = hardness), or touch (*sparśa*), there shall be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the root *śyaiṅ* before the suffix *niṣṭhā*.
SK 3021: *śyo 'sparśe* (A 8.2.47). [The substitution of *kṣa* for *śya* occurs] when the meaning is not touch.

The suffix *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) following the root *śyaiṅ* becomes *na* when the meaning is not "contact. By the rule *halaḥ*, there is lengthening: *śīnaṃ ghṛtam* ("the clarified butter has congealed"). Why say "not contact"? [Observe: *śītaṃ jalam* ("the water is cold"). Why say "in the sense of fluidity or form"? [Observe: *saṃśyāno vṛścikaḥ* ("a scorpion that has shriveled"); the meaning is "contracted because of the cold. (SK 3022) *prateś ca*: There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the root *śyaiṅ* preceded by *prati* when followed by *niṣṭhā*. [Result: *pratiśīnaḥ*.

SK 3023: *vibhāṣābhyavapūrvasya* (A 6.1.26). The semivowel of the root *śyai* preceded by *abhi* or *ava* may optionally undergo *saṃprasāraṇa*. Examples: *abhiśyānaṃ ghṛtam* ("the clarified butter has congealed") or *abhiśīnam*; *avaśyānaḥ* or *avaśīnaḥ vṛścikaḥ* ("a scorpion that has settled down"). This is a rule of restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*); therefore, it does not apply here: *samavaśyānaḥ*. SK 3024: *añco 'napādāne* (A 8.2.48). [The suffix *niṣṭhā* takes the substitute *na* after the root *añc* when there is no word denoting a point of departure (*apādāna*).]

The augment *iṭ* shall not occur after a root for which it is optionally prescribed (*yasya vibhāṣā*), even when the suffix *niṣṭhā* follows, provided that the action does not involve an ablative (*apādāna*). Since the root *knū* has an indicatory *ud*, the *iṭ* is optional by the rule *udito vā* regarding the suffix *ktvā*; therefore, *iṭ* does not occur here: *samaknaḥ*. Why "provided it is not an ablative"? Consider: *udaktam udakaṃ kūpāt* ("the water was drawn from the well"). Since the substitution of *n* for *t* is considered *asiddha* (not yet established), the rule *vraśca-* would have required the substitution of *ṣ* for *t*. It must be stated that the substitution for the *niṣṭhā* [suffix] is established (*siddha*) with respect to the rules concerning *ṣatva*, accent (*svara*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and the application of *iṭ*. Thus: *vṛkṇaḥ*, *vṛkṇavān*.

SK 3026 *pariskandaḥ* in the Eastern Bharata regions (A 8.3.75): When a retroflex *ṣ* would have been obtained by the preceding rule, its absence is prescribed as a nipātana. *pariskandaḥ*. Why say "in the Eastern [regions]"? [Because elsewhere] *pariṣkandaḥ* or *pariskandaḥ*; there is an option according to the rule *pareś ca*. Since the rule *stanbheḥ* would have caused the substitution of *ṣ*, [the following applies]:
SK 3027 *pratistabdha-nistabdhau ca* (A 8.3.114).
In this case, the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur.
According to Pāṇini 8.2.49, *divo 'vijigīṣāyām*:

the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix following *div* becomes *n* when not referring to the desire for victory (*avijigīṣā*). Thus, *dyūnaḥ*. However, when referring to the desire for victory (*vijigīṣā*), it is *dyūtam*.

SK 3029 *nirvāṇo ’vāte* (A 8.2.50). The word *avāte* is a separate rule. After the prefix *ni-* in the root *vāti*, the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix becomes *n*, provided that *vāta* is not the agent. Thus, *nirvāṇa* is used for fire and the sun; however, when *vāta* is the agent, it is *nirvāta*.
SK 3030 *śasuḥ kaḥ* (A 8.2.51).
The suffix *kta* alone [expresses the past]. *Śuṣkaḥ* ("dried"). By A 8.2.52, *pac* becomes *va*:
*pakvaḥ* ("cooked").

SK 3032: *kṣāyo maḥ* (A 8.2.53): [The substitution of] *m* occurs for the final phoneme of the root *kṣai*. Example: *kṣāmaḥ*. SK 3033: *styaḥ prapūrvasya* (A 6.1.23): [The substitution of *t* for the semivowel of the root *styai* occurs when it is preceded by *pra*.]
In the case of the root *styai*, there shall be *saṃprasāraṇa* before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes.

According to A 8.2.54, *prastyo 'nyatarasyām*, the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* may optionally become *m*. Thus we have *prastīmaḥ* or *prastītaḥ*. Why specify *pra-*? [Because] *styānaḥ* [is formed with the prefix *sam-*].

SK 3035: *anupasargāt phullakṣībakṛśollāghāḥ* (A 8.2.55). [The suffix] *ñi* is added to the root *phal*. *Phullaḥ*: the substitution of *l* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). This irregularity is also desired for the portion of the *ktavatu* suffix; thus we have *phullavān*. In the case of *kṣība* and the others, however, there is the elision of the *t* of the *kta* suffix itself. Because that [elision] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the absence of the augment *iṭ* which would otherwise apply is also prescribed as an irregularity. *Kṣībaḥ* means "intoxicated"; *kṛśaḥ* means "emaciated"; *ullāghaḥ* means "free from disease. Why "without a prefix" (*anupasargāt*)? [Because otherwise, by A 7.2.16, the augment *iṭ* would apply. SK 3036: *āditaś ca* (A 7.2.16). [The augment *iṭ* is applied after a root beginning with a vowel.]
When the suffix *niṣṭhā* follows, the augment *iṇ* shall not be applied.

(SK 3037) And by the rule *ti ca* (A 7.4.89), the augment *ut* shall be applied after the vowels *a* of the roots *car* and *phal*, when followed by a *kit* suffix beginning with *t*. Examples: *praphultaḥ*, *prakṣībitaḥ*, *prakṛśitaḥ*, *prollāghitaḥ*. How then is the expression "the mountain tree (*loghradrumaṃ*) in full bloom (*praphullam*)" to be explained? [Answer: Here, the root *phull* meaning "to blossom" takes the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class). The rule [A 7.4.89] is intended to exclude forms such as *phulta*. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the forms *utphulla* and *saṃphulla*.

SK 3038: *nudavidondatrāghrāhrībhyo ’nyatrasyām* (A 8.2.56). After these roots, the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is optionally replaced by *n*. Thus: *nunnaḥ* or *nuttaḥ*. Regarding *vid*, only the root belonging to the *raudhādika* group, meaning "to investigate," is understood here, because of its association with the following *und*. Thus: *vinnaḥ* or *vittaḥ*. However, from the root *vid* "to know," we have *viditaḥ*; from the root *vid* "to find," we have *vinnaḥ*. Regarding *undī*: SK 3039: *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām* (A 7.2.14). [The *iṭ* augment is added after roots ending in *śū* and those marked with *it* when followed by the *niṣṭhā* suffix.]

The augment *iṭ* is not applied to the *niṣṭhā* suffix after the root *śvi* or after roots marked with *īt*. Thus: *unnaḥ*, *uttaḥ*; *trāṇaḥ*, *trātaḥ*; *ghrāṇaḥ*, *ghrātaḥ*; *hrīṇaḥ*, *hrītaḥ*. By Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.57, *na dhyākhyāpṝmūrticchamadām*: the substitution of *n* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix does not occur after these roots. Thus: *dhyātaḥ*, *khyātaḥ*, *pūrtaḥ*. [In *pṛ*,] there is elision of *r* and *l*: *mūrtaḥ*, *mattaḥ*.

SK 3041 *vitto bhogapratyayayoḥ* (A 8.2.58): This is a nipātana (irregular form) of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *vid* (to find), used in the senses of "that which is enjoyed" (*bhogya*) and "that which is known" (*pratīta*). *Vittaṃ* means wealth; *vittaḥ* means a person [of known reputation]. Why these two? [To exclude: *vinnaḥ*. Because of the rule *vibhāṣā gamahana...* (A 7.2.68), there is an option (*veṭ*) for the suffix *kvasu*; therefore, here [in the case of *vid*], the augment *iṭ* does not apply. SK 3042 *bhittaṃ śakalam* (A 8.2.59): *Bhittam* means a fragment or piece.
The other [form] is *bhinnam*.

According to A 8.2.60, *ṛṇam* is derived from the root *ṛ* with the suffix *kta*; in the context of debt and lending, the substitution of *na* for the *t* of the suffix is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). The other [form] is *ṛtam*.
SK 3044: For the root *sphāy*, [the substitute] *sphī* occurs before the suffix *niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini A 6.1.22); [thus,] *sphītaḥ*.
SK 3045: [The augment *iṭ* is added] after the root *iṇ* before the suffix *niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini A 7.2.47).

The augment *iṭ* shall be applied after the root *kuṣ* when followed by the suffix *niṣṭhā*. This is a restatement of the rule because the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā" would otherwise apply. Example: *niṣkuṣitaḥ*.

By the rule *vasatikṣudhor iṭ* (A 7.2.52), the augment *iṭ* is always applied after these two roots (*vas* and *kṣudh*) when followed by the suffixes *ktvā* or *niṣṭhā*. Examples: *uṣitaḥ*, *kṣudhitaḥ*.

SK 3047 *añceḥ pūjāyām* (A 7.2.53): The augment *iṭ* shall be applied after the root *añc* when it has the sense of honoring (*pūjā*), in the case of the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*. [Examples: *añcitaḥ* ("honored"). SK 3048 *lubho 'vimohane* (A 7.2.54): [The augment *iṭ* is applied] after the root *lubh* when it does not mean "to delude" (*avimohana*). [Example: *kṣudhitaḥ* ("hungry").

After the root *lubh*, the augment *iṭ* must always be applied before the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*, except when the sense is "greed" (*gārdhya*). Examples: *lubhitaḥ* (in the sense of greed); but *lubdhaḥ* (when the sense is greed). SK 3049: After the root *kliś*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied before *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*. Since [the rule] *kliśa upatāpe* (Pāṇini 1.586) requires *iṭ* obligatorily, and since *kliśū* in the sense of "afflicting" (*vibādhana*) already allows for optionality before *ktvā*, this rule provides an option specifically for *niṣṭhā* where a prohibition would otherwise have applied. Examples: *kliśitaḥ* or *kliṣṭaḥ*.
SK 3050 pūṅaśca (A 7.2.51):
After the root *pūṅ*, the augment *iṭ* may optionally occur before the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*.
SK 3051 pūṅaḥ ktvā ca (A 1.2.22): [The suffix *ktvā*] following *pūṅ* is marked with the *kṛt* designation.

The suffixes *ktvā* and the *seṭ* *niṣṭhā* should not be *kiṭ* after the root *pū*. [Examples: *pavitah*, *pūtah*. The mention of *ktvā* is for the sake of the subsequent rule; for in the rule "after a root with *n* as its penultimate vowel" (*nopadhāt*), it is only *ktvā* that is connected [to the condition].

(A 1.2.11) *niṣṭhā śīṅ khidimidikṣvididhṛṣaḥ*: After these roots—*śīṅ*, *khid*, *mid*, *kṣvid*, and *dhṛṣ*—the *seṭ* *niṣṭhā* should not be *kiṭ*. [Examples: *śayitaḥ*, *śayitavān*. The specific mention of the *anubandha* (*ī*) is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa forms: [examples] *śeśyitaḥ*, *śeśyitavān*. It should be stated that the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs in the sense of the commencement of an action (*ādikarmaṇi*).

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.71: *ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca* (The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent in the case of an initial action; and by the word "ca," it is also used in the sense of the action or the object).
Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.17: *vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ* (In the case of the action or an initial action, the augment *iṭ* is optional).

In the sense of a state (*bhāva*) and in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarma*), the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied to the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Examples: *prasveditaś Caitraḥ* (Caitra has begun to sweat); *prasveditaṃ tena* (he has begun to sweat). Here, the root *ñiṣvidā* from the *bhvādi* class is understood, because of its association with roots beginning with *ñī*. However, for the root *svidyati* [from the *divādi* class], the form is only *sviditaḥ*. [Examples of other roots: *Ñimidā*: *prameditaḥ*, *prameditavān* (he has begun to become soft/dissolved). *Ñikṣvidā*: [From the *divādi* and *bhvādi* classes] *prakṣveditaḥ*, *prakṣveditavān* (he has begun to cry out/shout). *Pradharṣitaḥ*, *pradharṣitavān* (he has begun to assault/overpower); *pradharṣitaṃ tena* (he has been assaulted by him). Why "with the augment *iṭ*" (*seṭ*)? [Counter-examples without *iṭ*: *prasvinnaḥ*, *prasvinnaṃ tena*, etc. (he has sweated; he has been made to sweat by him).

SK 3055: *mṛṣa* [is used] in the sense of endurance (*titikṣā*) (A 1.2.20). Why would the *kta* suffix not occur after this root? [Examples: *marṣitaḥ*, *marṣitavān*. Why [is it specified] "in the sense of endurance"? [Counter-example: *apamṛṣitaṃ vākyam*; the meaning is "unclear. SK 3056: After a root having *u* as its penultimate vowel (*udupadha*), the *kta* suffix is optionally used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) or a beginning of an action (*ādikarman*) (A 1.2.21).

After a root having *u* as its penultimate vowel (*udupadha*), when used in the sense of a state (*bhāva*) or a beginning of action (*ādikarman*), may the suffix *niṣṭhā* with the augment *iṭ* optionally not take the suffix *kin*. Examples: *dyutitam* / *dyotitam*; *muditam* / *moditaṃ sādhunā* ("delighted by the good man"); *pradyutitaḥ* / *pradyotitaḥ*; *pradmuditaḥ* / *pramoditaḥ*; *sādhuḥ*. Why "having *u* as its penultimate vowel"? Consider *viditam*. Why "in the sense of a state" and so forth? Consider *rucitaṃ kārṣāpaṇam* ("the coin has pleased him"). Why "with the augment *iṭ*" (*seṭ*)? Consider *kruṣṭam*. This [application of *kin*] is desired only after roots that have the *śap* verbal class marker (*śabvikaraṇa*). It does not apply here: from the root *gudh*, we have *gudhitam*. [This is governed by] A 6.4.52: *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi*. (SK 3057)

There is elision (lopa) of the *ṇi* [of the causative suffix]. Examples: *bhāvitaḥ*, *bhāvitavān*. By the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*, the augment *iṭ* is not applied. There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Examples: *śūnaḥ*, *dīptaḥ*. From *guhū*: *guḍhaḥ*. From *vanu*: *vataḥ*. From *tanu*: *tataḥ*. Regarding the root *pat* with the desiderative suffix (*san*), although the absence of *iṭ* would normally apply because it is marked with *veṭ*, the augment *iṭ* occurs by virtue of a formal exception (*nipātana*) in the sūtra *dvitīyāśrita-* etc. Example: *patitaḥ*. Since the presence of *iṭ* is already established for this root by the rule *se'sici* because it is marked with *veṭ*, the fact that roots such as *kṛntati* are marked with *īdit* serves to indicate that the application of these markers is not universal (*anityatva*). Consequently, forms such as *dhāvitam ibharājadhiyā* are possible. From the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, the restriction *ekācaḥ* (from one-syllable roots) follows. Example: *daridritaḥ*.

The words *kṣubdha*, *svānta*, *dhvānta*, *lagna*, *mliṣṭa*, *viribdha*, *phāṇṭa*, and *bāḍha* are used in the senses of "churned," "mind," "darkness," "adhering," "indistinct," "unlabored," "clear," "unmanifest," "voice," and "excessive" respectively. (A 7.2.28)

The eight roots beginning with *kṣubh* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) as aniṭ roots when they denote the objects *mantha* and so forth in their collective sense. *Mantha* refers to parched grain mixed with a liquid substance; it denotes both the stirred drink and the churning stick. If it means "stirred," then *kṣubdha* is used for *mantha*. *Svānta* means the mind (*manaḥ*). *Dhvānta* means darkness (*tamaḥ*). *Lagna* means stuck or attached. The substitution of *ṇatva* (the change of *n* to *ṇ*) also occurs here due to irregular formation. *Mliṣṭa* means indistinct. *Viribdha* means a tone or sound. For the two roots *glecch* and *rebhṛ*, the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel is also irregularly prescribed.

*Phāṇṭa* is a specific kind of decoction that can be prepared without effort. Mādhava, however, states in his *Vedabhāṣya* that a substance which has reached a state prior to becoming butter (*navanīta*) is called *phāṇṭa*. *Bāḍham* means "exceedingly" or "intensely. In other contexts, it means "agitated. As for the form *kṣubdhaḥ* in the phrase *rājā kṣubdhaḥ*, this is due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the grammatical rule concerning the substitution of *ṣ* for *kṣ*. *Svanitam*, *svanitam*, *dhvanitam*, *lagitam*, *mlecchitam*, *virebhitam*, *phaṇitam*, and *vāhitam* [are derived from their respective roots].
The rule *dhṛṣi-śasī vaiyātye* (A 7.2.19) [prescribes the substitution of *ktvā* for *ktvā* after these roots when expressing impudence].

These two [roots] take the *iṭ* augment only in the state of completion (*niṣṭhā*) when they mean "lack of discipline" (*avinaya*); thus, *dhṛṣṭaḥ* and *viśastaḥ*. In other cases, they are *dharṣitaḥ* and *viśasitaḥ*. However, regarding the action itself (*bhāva*) or the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*), the root *dhṛṣ* does not exist when it means "lack of discipline. For this very reason, the Vṛtti states that this rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Haradatta says that the result of *dhṛṣ* being marked with the letter *ā* (*ādittva*) must be considered. Mādhava, however, states that there is an option (*vikalpa*) in the case of the action itself or the beginning of an action when it does not mean "lack of discipline": *dhṛṣṭam* / *dharṣitam*; *pradhṛṣṭaḥ* / *pradharṣitaḥ*. SK 3060: *dṛḍhaḥ sthūlabalayoḥ* (A 7.2.20). [The form *dṛḍha* is substituted for the root *dṛh* in the sense of "thick" (*sthūla*) and "strong" (*bala*).]

The suffix *kta* is applied after [the roots] *dṛh* and *dṛh*, meaning "to grow strong. There is the absence of *iṭ*; there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *t*; there is the elision of *ha*; and because they are marked with *it*, there is the elision of *na*. Thus, *dṛhitaḥ*. The other form is *dṛṃhitaḥ*. Regarding the rule *prabhau parivṛḍhaḥ* (A 7.2.21):
[the roots] *vṛh* and *vṛh* mean "to increase. The irregular formation (*nipātana*) is as before. Thus, *parivṛḍhaḥ*. The other form is *parivṛṃhitaḥ*.

SK 3062 *kṛcchragahanayoḥ kaṣaḥ* (A 7.2.22): The augment *iṭ* shall not occur after the root *kaṣ* when followed by the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix -ta/-na), provided these two meanings—*kṛcchra* (difficulty) and *gahana* (impenetrability)—are intended. *Kaṣṭam* means suffering and that which causes it. *Kaṣṭam* may mean difficulty, hardship, or distress. *Kaṣṭo mohaḥ*: "a painful delusion. *Kaṣṭaṃ śāstram*: "a difficult treatise," meaning one that is hard to fathom. In other cases, it is *kaṣitam*. SK 3063 *ghuṣir aviśabdane* (A 7.2.23): [The augment *iṭ* is not applied to the root *ghuṣ*] except in the sense of making a sound.

The root *ghuṣ* shall be *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment) when followed by a *niṣṭhā* suffix. Example: *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* ("the rope has been loosened"). Why "not in the sense of making a sound"? Example: *ghuṣitaṃ vākyam* ("the speech has been uttered"). In the sense of making a sound, the meaning is "having made one's intention manifest. SK 3064: *ardeḥ saṃnivibhyaḥ* (A 7.2.24). The *iṇ* augment shall not be applied to the *niṣṭhā* suffix following the root *ard* when preceded by *sam*, *ni*, or *vi*. Examples: *samarṇaḥ*, *nyarṇaḥ*, *vyarṇaḥ*. Any other [form of] *arditaḥ* [is different].
SK 3065 *abheś cāvidūrye* (A 7.2.25): [The suffix -ta is applied after the root *ṛ* following the prefix *abhi* when meaning "not far"].

*Abhyarṇam* means "not very distant" or "not very near"; it is something different from being excessively close. SK 3066 *ṇer adhyayane vṛttam* (A 7.2.26): [The suffix -ta is applied after a root ending in the causative marker *ṇi* when preceded by *adhi*, provided the sense is "studied"]. *Adhyavṛttam* [means "studied"].

After a causative (*ṇyanta*) form of the root *vṛt*, there is the absence of the augment *iṭ* and the elision (*luk*) of the causative suffix (*ṇi*) when the meaning is "studied. For example, *chandas chātreṇa vṛttam* means "the Veda was studied by the student," which is to say it was accomplished or mastered. In other cases, however, *vartitā rajjuḥ* means "the rope was twisted. Regarding *śṛtaṃ pāke* (A 6.1.27): after the roots *śrā* and *śrapaya*, the substitution of *śṛ* is prescribed when the suffix *kta* follows, provided the sense is cooking milk or sacrificial oblation (*havis*). Thus, *śṛtaṃ kṣīram* means "milk that has cooked by itself," i.e., it has become soft or ripened on its own. Anything other than milk or sacrificial oblation, however, is *kṣāṇam* or *śrapitam*.

SK 3068: *dānta*, *śānta*, *pūrṇa*, *dasta*, *spaṣṭa*, *channa*, and *jñapta*—these, ending in the *niṣṭhā* suffix, are optionally substituted [for their respective roots] when following a causative (*ṇic*) affix. In the alternative case: *damitaḥ*, *śamitaḥ*, *pūritaḥ*, *dāsitaḥ*, *spāśitaḥ*, *chāditaḥ*. SK 3069: [The substitution does not apply] after the roots *ruṇaddhi*, *matvar*, *saṃghuṣ*, and *āsvan*.

After these roots, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied before the suffix *niṣṭhā*. Examples: *ruṣitaḥ* / *ruṣṭaḥ*; *āntaḥ* / *amitaḥ*; *tūrṇaḥ* / *tvaritaḥ*. The benefit of this rule is slight regarding roots beginning with *ā*. Examples: *saṃguṣṭaḥ* / *saṃghuṣitaḥ*; *āsvāntaḥ* / *āsvanitaḥ*. SK 3070: *hṛṣer lomasu* (A 7.2.29). After the root *hṛṣ*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied before *niṣṭhā* when referring to body hair (*loman*). Example: *hṛṣṭaṃ* / *hṛṣitaṃ loma* ("the hair has stood on end"). It is also used in the senses of "astonishment" and "resistance. Example: *hṛṣṭo* / *hṛṣito maitraḥ* ("Maitra is astonished" or "Maitra is struck down"). In other cases, however: the root *hṛṣu* means "to be false"; because it is marked with *ud*, there is no *iṭ* before *niṣṭhā*. The root *hṛṣa* means "to be pleased"; here there is *iṭ*.
SK 3071: *apacitaś ca* (A 7.2.30).
This is either a derivative form or a nipāta (irregular formation) from the root *cāy*. [The forms are] *apacitaḥ* and *apacāyitaḥ*.
SK 3072: *pyāyaḥ pī* (A 6.1.28). [The substitution of *pī* for *pyā* occurs in the context of the Aorist.]

Or it may occur in the *niṣṭhā* [past passive participle] suffix. This is an option that is fixed (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*). Therefore, when referring to one's own body part (*svāṅga*), it is obligatory: *pīnaṃ sukham* ("a swollen cheek"). In other cases: *pyānaḥ*, *pīnaḥ svedaḥ* ("swollen sweat"). It does not occur after a prefix: *prapyānaḥ*. However, it must occur after the prefix *āṅ* when combined with *andhu* and *ūdhas*: *āpīnondhuḥ* ("a swollen well"), *āpīnamūdhaḥ* ("a swollen udder"). SK 3073: In the *niṣṭhā* suffix, the vowel of *hlād* becomes short: *prahlannaḥ* ("refreshed").

SK 3074 (Pāṇini 7.4.40): For the roots *dyati*, *syati*, *māti*, *sthāti*, and *atti*, the vowel *i* shall be the substitute for the final [vowel] before an affix beginning with *t* that has a *k*-marker (*kit*). This is an exception to the rules regarding the substitution of *ī* and the change to *ad*. Examples: *ditaḥ*, *sitaḥ*; *mā*, *māṅ*, *meṅ*: *mitaḥ*; *sthitaḥ*. SK 3075 (Pāṇini 7.4.41): For the roots *śo* and *cho*, [the vowel *i* is the substitute] optionally.

*śitaḥ*, *śātaḥ*, *chitaḥ*, *chātaḥ*. Due to the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the substitution [of *ś* for *s*] is obligatory for the root *śo* (*śyai*) in the domain of *vrata*. *Saṃśitaṃ vratam*: "the vow is firmly undertaken"; the meaning is that it has been perfectly accomplished. *Saṃśito brāhmaṇaḥ*: "the Brahmin is firm in his vow"; the meaning is that he possesses steadfastness regarding the subject of the vow. (SK 3076) For the root *dhā*, [the substitute *hi* occurs] before an affix beginning with *t* that is marked with *k*. *Abhihitam*, *nihitam*.

SK 3077 (A 7.4.46): For the root *dā* which bears the designation *ghu*, the substitute *dath* shall occur before an affix beginning with *t* that has a *k*-marker (*kit*). [By P. 8.4.54] there is the substitution of *c* for *t*. Thus: *dattaḥ*. Why "of *ghu*"? [Consider: *dātaḥ*. This substitute may end in *t* (*tānta*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of lengthening in forms such as *vidattam* by A 6.3.125 (*upasargasya dasti*), because that rule is prescribed only before an affix beginning with *t*. [The substitute may] end in *d* (*dānta*) or end in *dh* (*dhānta*). One should not suspect that if it ends in *d*, the rule A 8.2.42 would apply to change the final *t* to *n*, or if it ends in *dh*, the rule A 8.2.40 would apply to change the *th* to *dh*; for both would contradict the *sannipātaparibhāṣā* (the metarule regarding the destruction of the cause of a grammatical operation). SK 3078 (A 7.4.47): After a prefix ending in a vowel, *t* is substituted for the initial *th* of the root *sthā*.

After a prefix ending in a vowel, the root *dā* (in the sense of giving) is replaced by *ta* before a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *t* that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*. The substitution of *t* for *d* occurs [by rule P. 8.4.41]. Thus: *prattaḥ*, *acattaḥ*. Regarding the forms *avadattam*, *vidattam*, *pradattam*, *sudattam*, *anudattam*, and *nidattam*, they are desired when referring to the commencement of an action (*ādikarman*). Because of the word *ca* ("and"), the forms are also used according to their regular derivation. [This is governed by] A 6.3.124: *dasti*.

There shall be a long vowel for a preposition ending in *i* when followed by a word beginning with *t*, provided that *t* is the substitute for *da*. The substitution of *c* for *t* (by P. 8.4.54, *khari ca*) is established here by virtue of its being the basis [for the application of the rule]. Examples: *nīttam*, *sūttam*. [In *dhītam*, *gītam*, and *pītam*,] there is the substitution of *ī* by P. 6.4.66 (*ghumāsthā...*). [The roots] *dheṭ* (to suck), *gai* (to sing), and *pai* (to drink). [In *jātam*, *sātam*, and *khātam*,] there is the substitution of *ā* by P. 6.4.42 (*janasanakhanām...*); [the root] *khan* (to dig). Regarding the root *ad* (to eat): [the substitute] *jagdhi* occurs before the suffix *lyap* and before a suffix having a *k* as an indicatory letter (P. 2.4.36).

*lyap* is a form where the locative case ending has been elided (*luptasaptamīkam*). *Jagdhi* shall replace *ad-* when followed by *lyap*, as well as by a *kit* suffix beginning with *t*. The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). [By Pāṇini 6.1.16] *dh* is substituted. [By Pāṇini 8.4.65] *jhar* is dropped before *jhari*. Thus, *jagdhaḥ*. In the sense of the commencement of an action (*ādikarmaṇi*), the suffix *kta* is used in the active voice (*kartari*) as well. *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ saḥ* ("He has begun the mat"). *prakṛtaḥ kaṭas tena* ("The mat was begun by him"). In the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix, there is lengthening [of the vowel] when it does not have the sense of the passive (*aṇyadarthe*). [By Pāṇini 8.2.46] *ṇatva* (substitution of *ṇ*) occurs after *kṣi* when it ends in a long vowel. Thus, *prakṣīṇaḥ saḥ*. SK 3081: [The suffix *kta* is used in the active voice] in the sense of reviling (*vākrośa*) and dejection (*dainya*). (A 6.4.61)

In the formation of the *niṣṭhā* suffix, the vowel of the root *kṣi* may optionally become long when expressing either abuse or dejection. Thus: *kṣīṇāyur bhava* ("May you have a diminished lifespan! or *kṣitāyur bhava*; *kṣīṇo 'yaṃ tapasvī* ("This poor man is emaciated") or *kṣito 'yaṃ tapasvī*. By Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.89, *ninadībhyāṃ snāteḥ kauśale*, the *s* of the root *snā* becomes *ṣ* after the words *ni* and *nadī* when skill (*kauśala*) is to be understood.
Thus: *niṣṇātaḥ śāstreṣu* ("Skilled in the sciences"); *nadyāṃ snātīti nadīṣṇaḥ* ("One who bathes in the river is called *nadīṣṇaḥ*"). [The suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *supi*.

SK 3083: *pratiṣṇātam* (A 8.3.90). The substitution of *ṣ* occurs for the *s* of the root *snā* when preceded by *prati*. *Pratiṣṇātaṃ sūtram* means "a purified thread"; elsewhere, it is *pratisnātam*. SK 3084: *kapiṣṭhalaḥ* in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*) (A 8.3.91).

*Kapiṣṭhala* is the name [of a person], whose son is *Kāpiṣṭhali*. [Question: What about in the case of a *gotra*? [Answer: *Kapisthala* means "the place of monkeys" (*kapīnāṃ sthalam*). According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.96, *vikuśamiparibhyaḥ sthalam*, the *s* of *sthala* becomes *ṣ* after these [prefixes]: *viṣṭhala*, *kuṣṭhala*, *śamiṣṭhala*, and *pariṣṭhala*.

SK 3086: *gatyarthākarmakaśliṣaśīṅsthāsavasajanaruhajīryatibhyaś ca* (A 3.4.72). After these [roots]—those meaning "to go," those that are intransitive (*akarmaka*), and *śliṣ*, *śīṅ*, *sthā*, *ās*, *vas*, *jan*, *ruh*, and *jṛ*—the suffix *kta* shall occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) as well as in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). Examples: *gaṅgā gataḥ* ("He has gone to the Gaṅgā"). *gaṅgāṃ prāptaḥ* ("He has reached the Gaṅgā"). *sa glānaḥ* ("He is weary"). *lakṣmīm āśliṣṭo hariḥ* ("Hari has embraced Lakṣmī"). *śeṣam adhiśayitaḥ* ("He has reclined upon Śeṣa"). *vaikuṇṭham adhiṣṭhitaḥ* ("He has occupied Vaikuṇṭha"). *śivam upāsitaḥ* ("He has worshipped Śiva"). *haridinam upoṣitaḥ* ("He has fasted on the day of Hari"). *rāmam anujātaḥ* ("He was born after Rāma"). *gurudam ārūḍhaḥ* ("He has mounted Garuḍa"). *viśvam anujīrṇaḥ* ("He has grown old with the universe"). In the alternative [when the suffix denotes the object], there are examples such as *prāptā gaṅgā yena* ("by whom the Gaṅgā was reached").

The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as well as [in the sense of the agent], after verbal roots whose meanings involve remaining stationary (*dhrauvya*), motion (*gati*), or consumption (*pratyavasāna*). (A 3.4.76)

The suffix *kta* may be used after these [roots] in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is also used as prescribed [in other senses]. "Stability" (*dhrauvya*) means steadiness. "The Gopīs, desiring to see him, said: 'This is where Mukunda sat; this is where the Lord of Ramā went; this is where Ananta ate. Since the root *ās* (to sit) is intransitive, the suffix occurs in the sense of the agent and the state (*bhāva*): 'Mukunda sat' (*āsito mukundaḥ*) or 'he sat' (*tena āsitam*). After roots meaning 'motion,' it occurs in the sense of the agent and the object (*karman*): 'The Lord of Ramā went here' (*ramāpatir idaṃ yātaḥ*) or 'this was gone by him' (*tenedaṃ yātam*). After the root *bhuj*, it occurs in the sense of the object: 'this was eaten by Ananta' (*anantenedaṃ bhuktam*)."

"How were the Brahmins fed? [The answer is: "They have eaten," where the suffix *ac* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). This is taught under the heading "in the present tense" (*vartamāne*). According to A 3.2.187, *ñītaḥ ktaḥ*:
from the root *ñikṣiv* (to spit), *kṣviṇṇaḥ*; from *ñiindhī* (to kindle), *iddhaḥ*.

SK 3089: *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaś ca* (A 3.2.188). Here, *mati* means desire (*icchā*), because it is mentioned separately from *buddhi*. Thus, *rājñāṃ mataḥ* means "desired" or "wished for by kings"; the meaning is "being desired by them. *Buddhaḥ* means known; *pūjitaḥ* means honored; *arcitaḥ* means worshipped. The particle *ca* serves to include those not explicitly mentioned, such as *śīlitaḥ*, *rakṣitaḥ*, *kṣāntaḥ*, *ākṛṣṭaḥ*, *juṣṭaḥ*, and so forth. SK 3090: *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* (A 3.3.114). [The suffix *kta* is used after a verbal root to denote an action in the neuter gender.]

The suffix *kta* occurs after a verbal root to denote an action characterized by the neuter gender (*klībatva*) and in reference to time in general (*kālasāmānye*). Examples: *jalpitam*, *śayitam*, *hasitam*. By rule A 3.2.103, *ṅvanip* is applied after the roots *su* (to press) and *yaj* (to sacrifice) to denote the past. Examples: *sutvā* (having pressed), *sutvānau*; *yajvā* (one who has sacrificed), *yajvānau*.

SK 3092: After the root *jṛ* ("to grow old"), the suffix *atṛn* is applied [in the sense of the past participle]. Thus: *jaraṃ*, *jarantau*, *jarantaḥ*. By the rule of "optionality of non-identical forms" (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*), the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is also applied: *jīrṇaḥ*, *jīrṇavān*. SK 3093: In the Vedic language, the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is used [for the past].
SK 3094: *liṭaḥ kānaj vā* (A 3.2.106);

SK 3095: *kuvasuś ca* (A 3.2.107). Regarding these, the view of the three great grammarians (*trimuni*) is that since the *liṭ* suffix is prescribed in Vedic for the general past tense (*bhūtasāmānya*), the *kvasu* and *kānac* suffixes prescribed for it are also Vedic. Nevertheless, poets employ them extensively, as in: *taṃ tasthivāṃsaṃ nagaropakaṇṭhe* ("him who had stayed near the city") and *śreyāṃsi sarvāṇy adhijagmuṣas te* ("of him who has attained all blessings," etc.).

SK 3096 *vasvekājād ghasām* (A 7.1.67): The augment *iṭ* is applied after the suffix *vasu* following roots that have become monosyllabic (*ekāc*) through reduplication, as well as after roots ending in long *ā* and the root *ghas*, but not after others. Examples of monosyllabic roots: *ādivān*, *ārivān*. Examples of roots ending in *ā*: *dadivān*, *jakṣivān*. Why [the restriction] "these" (*eṣām*)? [Counter-example: *babhūvān*. SK 3097 *bhāṣāyāṃ sadavasaśruvaḥ* (A 3.2.108): In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), the suffix *kvasu* is applied after the roots *sad*, *vas*, and *śru*.

After the roots *sad* and others, when expressing a general past action (*bhūtasāmānya*) in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*), the suffix *liṭ* may optionally occur; and for that *liṭ*, the suffix *kvasu* is invariably used. [Examples: *niṣeduṣīm āsanabandhadhīraḥ* ("steadfast in the practice of sitting cross-legged"); *adhyūṣuṣas tām abhajan janaḥ* ("the people resorted to her, who had dwelt there"). [The suffix *kvasu* is also applied after the following: *śuśruvān* ("one who has heard"), *upeyivān* ("one who has approached"), *anāśvān* ("one who has not eaten"), and *anūcānaḥ* ("one who has studied [the Vedas] thoroughly"). (A 3.2.102)

These [forms] are derived through irregular derivation (*nipātana*). After the root *i* preceded by *upa*, even in the common language (*bhāṣā*), the *liṭ* suffix is optionally used for the mere expression of the past; for that [past tense], the *kvasu* suffix is invariably applied, along with the augment *iṭ*. Examples: *upeyivān*; *upeyuṣaḥ svām api mūrtim agryām* ("having attained even his own foremost form"); *upeyuṣī*. Here, the act of approaching (*upetya*) is not intended to be expressed. Examples: *īyivān*, *samīyivān*. After the root *aś* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the *kvasu* suffix is applied, and the augment *iṭ* is optionally absent. Bhāravi [uses it] in the phrase: *ghṛtajayadhṛter anāśuṣaḥ*. After the root *vac* preceded by *anu*, the *kānac* suffix is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). One who has performed the recitation of the Veda is called *anūcānaḥ*. A 7.2.68: *vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām*.

From these [roots], the suffix *vasu* becomes *iḍ* optionally: *jagmivān* / *jaganvān*, *jaghnivān* / *jaganvān*, *vividivān* / *vividvān*, *viviśivān* / *viviśvān*. Because of its association with *viśin*, there is the inclusion of the root *vid* ("to find"); however, for the root *vid* ("to know"), it is *viditvān*. By the rule *neḍ vaśi kṛti*, the prohibition of *iṭ* applies. And from the root *dṛś*: *dadṛśivān* / *dadṛśvān*. SK 3100: *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāv aprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe* (A 3.2.124). The meaning is: when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with something not ending in the nominative case. The *śap* augment and so forth apply: "See Caitra who is cooking" (*pacantaṃ caitraṃ paśya*).

SK 3101 *nāme muk* (A 7.2.82): When *āna* follows, the augment *mum* is added to the vowel *a* of the stem. Example: *pacamānaṃ caitraṃ paśya* ("See Caitra cooking"). While the term *laṭ* is already understood from the previous rule, its mention here again is for the purpose of providing an additional application; thus, in some cases, even when there is coreferentiality with a nominative (*prathamā-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), [the suffix is applied]. Example: *san brāhmaṇaḥ* ("He is a virtuous Brahmin"). It should be stated that [this applies] after *māṅ* in the sense of reproach (*ākrośa*). Example: *mā jīvan yaḥ parāvajñā-duḥkha-dagdho 'pi jīvati* ("May he not live—he who lives even while consumed by the pain of others' contempt"). Although *luṅ* would have been expected by the rule *māṅi luṅ*, the elision (*luk*) occurs here by the force of this specific statement. SK 3102 *saṃbodhane ca* (A 3.2.125).

*he pacan* / *he pacamāna*. Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.126 (*lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*): After a verbal root meaning "to characterize" (*lakṣaṇa*) or "to be the cause" (*hetu*) of an action (*kriyā*), the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are applied in place of *laṭ* (the present tense marker). Examples: *śayānā bhuñjate yavanāḥ* ("The Yavanas eat while lying down"); *arjayanvasati* ("He dwells while earning [money]"); *hariṃ paśyan mucyate* ("One is liberated by seeing Hari"). In this context, "cause" (*hetu*) refers to both the fruit (*phala*) and the instrument (*kāraṇa*). Sūtra 3.1.95 (*kṛtyacaḥ*): [The suffix *śānac* is applied after a root ending in a *kṛt* suffix or the letter *c*. Example: *prapīyamāṇaḥ somaḥ* ("The Soma being drunk").
SK 3104 *īdāsaḥ* (A 7.2.86): After the root *ās*, the substitute *ī* shall be applied to the initial sound of the following suffix *an*. [By the rule *ādeḥ parasya*: *āsīnaḥ*.
SK 3105 *videḥ śatur vasuḥ* (A 7.1.36): After the root *vid*, the suffix *śatṛ* is replaced by *vasu*.
For a following *śatṛ* that comes after the root *vid*, there may optionally be the substitution of *vasu*. Thus: *vidan*, *vidvān*, *viduṣī*.
(SK 3106) *tau sat*:
those two, *śatṛ* and *śānac*, are designated by the technical term *sat*.

SK 3107: *lṛṭaḥ sad vā* (A 3.3.14). This is an option of restricted application (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Therefore, it is obligatory in cases of non-co-referentiality with the first case, in the case of suffixes and subsequent members of compounds, in the vocative, and when indicating a characteristic or a cause. Examples: *kariṣyantam* / *kariṣyamāṇam paśya* ("Look at him who will do"); *kariṣyataḥ apatyam* ("the offspring of one who will do" = *kāriṣyataḥ*); *kariṣyadbhaktiḥ* ("devotion to one who will do"). In the vocative: *he kariṣyan*. Also: *arjayiṣyan vasati* ("He dwells [there] intending to acquire"). Even in co-referentiality with the first case, it occurs optionally in some instances: *kariṣyatīti kariṣyan* ("intending to do, because he will do"). SK 3108: *pūṅyajoḥ śānan* (A 3.2.128). [The suffix] *śānan* is applied after the roots *pū* and *yaj*.
In the present tense: *pavamānaḥ* (purifying), *yajamānaḥ* (sacrificing).

According to Pāṇini A 3.2.129, *tācchīlya-vayovacana-śaktiṣu cānaś*: when these [qualities] are to be expressed—namely, habitual action (*tācchīlya*), age (*vayovacana*), and ability (*śakti*)—the suffix *cānaś* is used for the agent. Examples: *bhogaṃ bhuñjānaḥ* (habitually enjoying pleasures), *kavacaṃ bibhrāṇaḥ* (of an age capable of wearing armor), *śatrūn nighnānaḥ* (capable of slaying enemies).

SK 3110: After the roots *iṅ* (to study) and *dhṛ* (to hold), the suffix *śatṛ* occurs when the agent is not experiencing difficulty (A 3.2.130). Examples: *adhīyan* (studying), *dhārayan* (holding). Why "not experiencing difficulty"? [Counter-examples: *kṛcchreṇādhīte* (he studies with difficulty), *dhārayati* (he holds with difficulty). SK 3111: After the root *dviṣ* (to hate), the suffix *śatṛ* occurs when the object is an enemy (A 3.2.131).

*dviṣan* means "enemy. According to A 3.2.132, *suño yajñasaṃyoge*, [the suffix *śatṛ* is applied after the root *su*] when connected with a sacrifice: *sarve sunvantaḥ* means "all those performing the sacrifice," that is, all the performers of a *sattra*.
SK 3113 *arhaḥ praśaṃsāyām* (A 3.2.133): [The suffix *ini* is applied after the root *arh*] in the sense of praise; thus, *arhan*.

SK 3114 *ākvestacchīlataddharmatatsādhukāriṣu* (A 3.2.134): [The suffix *ini* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ā* or *kvi*] in the senses of "having that as one's habit," "having that as one's duty," or "being skillful at doing that."
The suffixes to be mentioned hereafter, extending up to *kvip*, are to be understood as applying to agents characterized by habit (*tacchīla*), duty (*taddharma*), or proficiency (*tatsādhukārī*).
[Pāṇini 3.2.135] *tṛn*: *kartā kaṭān* ("one who habitually makes mats").

SK 3116: The suffix *iṣṇuc* is added after the verbs *alaṃ-kṛ*, *nir-ā-kṛ*, *pra-jan*, *ut-pat*, *ut-pad*, *ut-mad*, *ruc*, *apa-trap*, *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, *sah*, and *car*. Examples: *alaṃkariṣṇuḥ* (one who adorns sufficiently), *nirākariṣṇuḥ* (one who rejects), *prajaniṣṇuḥ* (one who procreates), *utpatiṣṇuḥ* (one who flies up), *utpaciṣṇuḥ* (one who cooks thoroughly), *unmadiṣṇuḥ* (one who goes mad), *rociṣṇuḥ* (one who shines), *apatrapiṣṇuḥ* (one who feels shame), *vartiṣṇuḥ* (one who turns), *vardhiṣṇuḥ* (one who grows), *sahiṣṇuḥ* (one who endures), *cariṣṇuḥ* (one who wanders). SK 3117: In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffix *iṣṇuc* is added after the verb *ṇī* (to lead). Example: *nayiṣṇavaḥ* (those who lead).
The suffix *ṇu* is added after the word *vīrudh* in the sense of "one who will cross over" (*pārayiṣṇu*).

By the rule *bhuvaś ca chandasīti eva* (A 3.2.138), [the suffix *ṇu* is added] after the root *bhū* in the Vedic language; thus, *bhaviṣṇuḥ*. How then is the expression *jagatprabhor aprabhaviṣṇu vaiṣṇavam* ("the Vaiṣṇava [nature] of the Lord of the world is not capable") to be explained? Poets are unrestrained. The particle *ca* in the rule has the purpose of including what has not been mentioned; thus, the *vṛtti* states *bhrājiṣṇuḥ*. Similarly, *kṣayiṣṇuḥ*. This is not seen in the Bhāṣya.

SK 3119: *glājisthaś ca gsnuḥ* (A 3.2.139). The phrase *chandasi* ("in the Veda") is no longer applicable here. This [suffix] is marked with *g*, not *k*; therefore, there is no substitution of *ī* for the vowel of *sthā*. Examples: *glāsnuḥ* ("weary"), *jiṣṇuḥ* ("victorious"), *sthāsnuḥ* ("stationary"). Because it is marked with *g*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening. By the word *ca* ("and"), the root *bhū* is also included. In the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*, because the letter *g* is elided (*praśleṣa*) [from the preceding rule], there is no insertion of the augment *iṭ*. Example: *bhūṣṇuḥ* ("prospering"). There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of this suffix to the root *daṃś* in the Veda: *daṅkṣṇavaḥ paśavaḥ* ("biting animals"). SK 3120: *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* (A 3.2.140). [The suffix *knu* is added after these roots.]
*trasnuḥ*, *gṛdhnuḥ*, *dhṛṣṇuḥ*, *kṣipnuḥ*;
[and] by rule A 3.2.141, the suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied after the eight roots beginning with *śam*.

The *Kāśikā* states that the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), while the *Bhāṣya* calls it an *anubandha*. By this, in forms such as *śaminitarā* and *śaminītara*, there is an optional shortening (*hrasva-vikalpa*) according to the rule *ugitaś ca*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the augment *num* in forms like *śamī* or *śaminau*, because the term *jhal* is drawn back [from the previous rule] so that the application of that [augment] is restricted to bases ending in *jhal* consonants. Furthermore, by the rule *nodāttopadeśasya*, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies. Thus: *śamī*, *tamī*, *damī*, *śramī*, *bhramī*, *kṣamī*, *klamī*, *pramādī*.

From the root *mad* preceded by the prefix *ut*, the suffix *ghinuṇ* is also applied by the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), in addition to *iṣṇuc* prescribed by the rule *alaṃkṛñ-ādi-sūtra*. Thus, one has *unmādī*. However, the principle that "the rule of optional forms does not apply to [suffixes] expressing habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*)" is merely a general tendency. Pāṇini A 3.2.142:

*saṃpṛcānurudhāṅyamāṅyasaparisṛsaṃsṛjaparidevisaṃjvaraparikṣipapariraṭaparivadaparidahaparimuhaduṣadviṣadruhaduhayujākrīḍavivicatyajarajabhajāticaraapacarāmuṣābhyāhanaś ca*. [The suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied after the following roots: *saṃ-pṛc*, *anu-rudh*, *aṅ-yam*, *āṅ-yas*, *pari-sṛ*, *saṃ-sṛj*, *pari-dev*, *saṃ-jvar*, *pari-kṣip*, *pari-raṭ*, *pari-vad*, *pari-dah*, *pari-muh*, *duṣ*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *ā-krīḍ*, *vi-vic*, *tyaj*, *raj*, *bhaj*, *ati-car*, *apa-car*, *ām-uṣ*, and *abhi-ā-han*.

The suffix *ghinuṇ* shall occur [after roots ending in long *ī*, *ū*, or *ṝ*, as well as after the roots *saṃ-pṛc*, *anu-rudh*, etc.]. Examples: *saṃparkī* (one who associates), *anurodhī* (one who complies), *āyāmī* (one who stretches), *āyāsī* (one who exerts oneself), *parisārī* (one who wanders around), *saṃsargī* (one who joins), *paridevī* (one who laments), *saṃjvārī* (one who suffers heat/distress), *parikṣepī* (one who throws around), *parirāṭī* (one who cries out), *parivādī* (one who reviles), *paridāhī* (one who burns/afflicts), *parimohī* (one who is deluded), *doṣī* (one who finds fault), *dveṣī* (one who hates), *drohī* (one who seeks to harm), *dohī* (one who milks), *yogī* (one who is joined/devoted), *ākrīḍī* (one who plays), *vivekī* (one who discriminates), *tyāgī* (one who abandons), *rāgī* (one who has passion), *bhāgī* (one who shares/participates), *aticārī* (one who transgresses), *apacārī* (one who behaves improperly), *āmoṣī* (one who steals), *abhyāghātī* (one who attacks).
[By the rule] *vau kaṣalasakatthasrambhaḥ* (A 3.2.143):
*vikāṣī* (one who shines forth), *vilāsī* (one who sports), *vikatthī* (one who boasts), *visrambhī* (one who trusts/confides).
And after the root *laṣ*, [the suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied] (A 3.2.144). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is also applied after *lau*.

Examples: *apalāṣī* ("one who desires away"), *vilāṣī* ("one who desires about"). SK 3125: After the roots *lap*, *sṛ*, *dru*, *math*, *vad*, and *vas*, preceded by *pra*, [the suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied] (A 3.2.145).

*pralāpī*, *prasārī*, *pradrāvī*, *pramāthī*, *pravādī*, *pravāsī*. SK 3126: *nindahiṃsakliśakhādavināśaparikṣipapariraṭaparivādivyābhāṣāsūyo vuñ* (A 3.2.146). The first case ending (*prathamā*) is used here in the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamyarthe*). The suffix *vuñ* is applied after these [roots]. Examples: *nindakaḥ*, *hiṃsakaḥ*, and so forth. Since the formation is already established by the suffix *ṇvul*, the explicit mention of *vuñ* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so on, suffixes such as *tṛc* and others do not apply by virtue of the rule regarding dissimilar forms (*vāsarūpanyāya*).

SK 3127: After the roots *div* and *krūś*, when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present, [the suffix *ṇvul* is applied]. Examples: *ādevakaḥ* ("one who reviles") and *ākrośakaḥ* ("one who abuses"). Why "when a prefix is present"? [Counter-examples: *devayitā* ("one who plays/shines") and *kroṣṭā* ("one who cries out"). SK 3128: After a root that signifies motion or sound and is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *yuc* is applied.

The suffix *yuc* shall be applied after a verbal root meaning "to move" (*calana*) or "to sound" (*śabda*). Examples: *calanaḥ*, *copanaḥ*, *kampanaḥ*, *śabdanaḥ*, *ravaṇaḥ*. Why say "after an intransitive root" (*akarmakāt*)? Consider: *paṭhitā vidyām* ("one who has studied the science"). SK 3129: *anudāttetaś ca halādeḥ* (A 3.2.149). The suffix *yuc* shall be applied after an intransitive root that begins with a consonant and has an anudātta vowel as its penultimate phoneme. Examples: *vartanaḥ*, *vardhanaḥ*. Why say "having an anudātta penultimate vowel" (*anudāttetaḥ*)? Consider: *bhavitā* ("one who will be"). Why say "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*)? Consider: *edhitā* ("one who will prosper"). Why say "after an intransitive root" (*akarmakāt*)? Consider: *vasitā vastram* ("one who has worn a garment").

SK 3130: *ju-caṅkramya-dandramya-sṛ-gṛdhi-jvala-śuca-laṣa-pata-padaḥ* (A 3.2.150). The root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root meaning "to go" and "to move swiftly. [The derivatives are: *javanaḥ*, *caṅkramaṇaḥ*, *dandramaṇaḥ*, *saraṇaḥ*. Since the formation was already established by the preceding rule (*ju-sṛ-...*), the inclusion of *pada* is so that the suffix *ukañ* prescribed by the rule *laṣa-pata-pada* (A 3.2.154) does not supersede it. Consequently, among those suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), there is no mutual application of the *vāsarūpa* rule (A 3.1.94). Therefore, the suffix *tṛn* is not applied after the root *kṛñ* with the prefix *alam*. SK 3131: *krudhamaṇḍārthebhyaś ca* (A 3.2.151). [The suffix *tṛn* is also applied after roots meaning "to be angry" (*krudh*) and "to adorn" (*maṇḍa*).]
*krodhanaḥ* (wrathful), *roṣaṇaḥ* (angry), *maṇḍanaḥ* (adorned), *bhuṣaṇaḥ* (decorated).
SK 3132 states: *na yaḥ* (A 3.2.152);
the suffix *yaC* shall not occur after a root ending in the letter *y*. Examples: *knūyitā* (one who causes to swell), *kṣmāyitā* (one who trembles).

SK 3133 (*sūdadīpadīkṣaś ca*, A 3.2.153): The suffix *yuc* shall not occur after these roots. Thus: *sūditā*, *dīpitā*, *dīkṣitā*. Since the rule *namikampi-* (A 3.2.167) already establishes the exclusion of *yuc* by means of the suffix *ra*, the explicit mention of *dīp* serves to indicate that the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*) does not apply to derivatives expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*); this is a general principle. By this, we have *kamrā* and *kamanā* for a young woman, and *kamprā* and *kampanā* for a branch. If *yuc* does not occur after *sūd*, how is the form *madhusūdanaḥ* explained? It belongs to the *nandy-ādi* group (A 3.1.134). SK 3134 (*laṣapatapadasthābhūvṛṣahanakamagamaśṝbhya ukañ*, A 3.2.154): The suffix *ukañ* occurs after the following roots: *laṣ*, *pat*, *pad*, *sthā*, *bhū*, *vṛṣ*, *han*, *kam*, *gam*, and *śṝ*.
*lāṣukaḥ*, *pātukaḥ*, and so forth. According to A 3.2.155 (*jalpabhikṣakuṭṭaluṇṭavṛṅaḥ ṣākan*), [the following are formed]:
*jalpākaḥ*, *bhikṣākaḥ*, *kuṭṭākaḥ*, *luṇṭākaḥ*.
SK 3136: After the root *pra-ju*, the suffix *ini* is applied (A 3.2.156). Examples:
*prajavī*, *prajavinau*, *prajavinaḥ*. SK 3137: The suffix *ini* is applied after the roots *ji*, *dṛkṣi*, *viśrī*, *ṇu*, *mā*, *vyath*, as well as after *apa-paribhū* and *pra-sū* (A 3.2.157).

*jayī*, *darī*, *kṣayī*, *viśrayī*, *atyayī*, *vamī*, *avyathī*, *abhyamī*, *paribhavī*, *prasavī*. By A 3.2.158 (*spṛhigṛhipatidayinidrātandrāśraddhābhya āluc*), the suffix *āluc* is added after the following roots: *spṛhi*, *gṛhi*, *pati*, *dayi*, *nidrā*, *tandrā*, and *śraddhā*. The first three of these belong to the *cur*-class (*curādi*) and end in the letter *a*. Examples: *spṛhayāluḥ*, *gṛhayāluḥ*, *patayāluḥ*, *dayāluḥ*, *nidrāluḥ*. The root *drā* preceded by *tan-* [is included]; the form *tad-* is irregularly prescribed as ending in *n* (*tando*). Example: *tandrāluḥ*. It should be stated that [the suffix *āluc*] is also added after the root *śīṅ*. Example: *śayāluḥ*.
SK 3139: After the roots *dā* (to give), *dhā* (to place), *sī* (to lie down), *śad* (to fall), and *sad* (to sit), the suffix *ru* is applied.
Examples: *dāruḥ*, *dhāruḥ*, *seruḥ*, *śadruḥ*, *sadruḥ*.
SK 3140: After the roots *sṛ* (to flow), *ghas* (to eat), and *ad* (to eat), the suffix *kmarac* is applied.
*sṛmaraḥ*, *ghasmaraḥ*, *admaraḥ*. According to Pāṇini A 3.2.161 (*vidibhidicchideḥ kurac*), [the suffix] *kurac* is applied:
*bhaṅguraḥ*, *bhāsuraḥ*, *meduraḥ*.
By A 3.2.163, *iṇ-naś-ji-sṛtibhyaḥ kvarap*, the suffix *kvarap* is applied after the roots *iṇ*, *naś*, *ji*, and *sṛ*.
Thus: *itvaraḥ*, *itvarī*, *naśvaraḥ*, *jitvaraḥ*, *sṛtvaraḥ*.
By A 3.2.164, *gatvaraś ca*, the form *gatvaraḥ* is also derived [from the root *gam*].

In the case of the root *gam*, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) is also prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*): *gatvarī*. According to Pāṇini 3.2.165, the suffix *ūka* is applied after the root *jāgṛ*: *jāgarūkaḥ*.

SK 3146: *yajajapadaśāṃ yaṅaḥ* (A 3.2.166). The suffix *ūka* shall be applied after these roots ending in *yaṅ*: *yaj*, *jap*, and *daś*. The mention of *daśām* is by way of indicating the future elision of the nasal (*n*). Examples: *yāyajūkaḥ*, *jañjapūkaḥ*, *dandaśūkaḥ*. SK 3147: *namikampismyajasakamahiṃsadīpo raḥ* (A 3.2.167). The suffix *ra* is applied after the following roots: *nam*, *kamp*, *smi*, *ajas*, *kam*, *hiṃs*, and *dīp*.

*namraḥ* (bowed); *kampraḥ* (trembling); *smeraḥ* (smiling). The root *jas*, preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*), denotes continuous action; thus *ajasram*, meaning "constantly. *kamraḥ* (desiring); *hiṃsraḥ* (injuring); *āśaṃsuḥ* (hopes); *dīpraḥ* (shining). According to Pāṇini A 3.2.168, *u* is added after the suffixes *san*, *āśaṃsa*, and *bhikṣu*: thus *cikīrṣuḥ* (desiring to do), *āśaṃsuḥ* (hoping), and *bhikṣuḥ* (a mendicant).

SK 3149 *vindur icchuḥ* (A 3.2.169): The augment *num* is applied after the root *vid*, and the change to *ch* is prescribed for the root *iṣ*. One who knows by habit is *vinduḥ*; one who desires is *icchuḥ*. SK 3150 *kyāc chandasi* (A 3.2.170): [The suffix *u* is applied] after a word ending in *kyac* in the Vedic language.
"He goes toward the gods, desiring their favor" (devāñ jigāti sumnayuḥ). *Ādṛgamahanajanah kikinau liṭ ca* (A 3.2.171):

After roots ending in long *ā*, long *ṛ*, and after the roots *gam* and others, the suffixes *kikin* occur in the Vedic language; these two suffixes function like the *liṭ* (perfect) suffixes. Examples: *papiḥ somam* ("one who has drunk Soma"), *dadir gāḥ* ("one who has given cows"), *babhrir vajram* ("one who has carried the thunderbolt"), *jagmir yuvā* ("a youth who has gone"), *jaghniḥ vṛtram amitriyam* ("one who has slain the hostile Vṛtra"), *jajñiḥ*. In the common language (*bhāṣā*), [the suffix *kikin* occurs] after the roots *dhā*, *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *gam*, *jan*, and *nam*: Examples: *dadhiḥ*, *cakriḥ*, *sasriḥ*, *jagmiḥ*, *jajñiḥ*, *nemiḥ*. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) should be made for the forms *sāsahi*, *vāvahi*, *cācali*, and *pāpati*.
The suffixes *k* and *kin* are prescribed after roots ending in *yaṅ*, following words such as *saha*, and the *nīṭh* augment (*nīg*) is not applied to the root *pat*.
By A 3.2.172, the suffix *nañjiṅ* is prescribed after the roots *svap* and *tṛṣ*:
*svapnak*, *tṛṣṇak*, *tṛṣṇajau*, *tṛṣṇajaḥ*. According to the *Kāśikā* and other works, it should be stated that this also applies to the root *dhṛṣ*: *dhṛṣṇak*.
SK 3153: After the roots *śṛ* and *vand*, the suffix *āru* is applied (A 3.2.173). Examples:
*śarāruḥ* ("one who tears apart"), *vandāruḥ* ("one who pays homage").
SK 3154: After the root *bhī*, the suffixes *kru* and *klukan* are applied (A 3.2.174).
*bhīruḥ* / *bhīlukaḥ*. The suffix *kruk* should also be mentioned: *bhīrukaḥ*. According to A 3.2.175 (*stheśabhāsapisakaso varac*), [the following are formed]:
