When a vocative in grammatical apposition follows, the preceding substantive (viśeṣya) is not treated as if it were non-existent [for the purposes of the preceding rule]. Examples: *agne tejasvin* ("O radiant Agni"), *agne trātaḥ* ("O protecting Agni"). Why specify "the general term" (*sāmānyavacana*)? To prevent this from applying in cases such as *aghnyeṣu mā bhūt* ("among the inviolable ones"). Example: *aghnye devi sarasvati* ("O inviolable goddess Sarasvatī"). When the general term is optionally [treated as non-existent] in relation to a specific term (*viśeṣavacana*), [the following applies]. SK 3655.

In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya has supplied the term *bahuvacanam* ("plural") and applied the term *sāmānyavacanam* ("general term") to the preceding rule. When a plural general term precedes a vocative singular qualifier, it may be treated as if non-existent (*avidyamānavat*). For example: *devīḥ ṣaḍ uru naḥ kṛṇota*. Here, *ṣaṭ* is a qualifier of *devīḥ*. [Another example: *devāḥ śaraṇyāḥ*. In this case, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) of the second word is optional. Pāṇini 2.1.2: *subāmantrite parāṅgavatsvare* ("A case-inflected word in a vocative construction is, for the purposes of accentuation, like a part of the following word").

A word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is treated like the member of a compound (*aṅgavat*) when another word follows it, provided that an accentual operation is to be performed. In the example *dravatpāṇī śubhaspatī* ("O you two with swift hands, lords of beauty"), the word *śubha* is derived from the root *śubh* with the suffix *kvip*. It is a genitive plural form (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). When it enters into the body of the following word (*paraśarīrānupraveśe*), it receives the acute accent on its first syllable according to the rule for vocatives (*ṣāṣṭhika āmantritādyudāttatvam*). One should not suspect the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) by the eighth rule (*aṣṭamika*), because the preceding vocative is considered non-existent (*avidyamānatvena*), and thus [the word *śubhaspatī*] begins a new metrical quarter (*pādāditvāt*). In the example *yat te divo duhitarmarta bhijanam*, the word *divaḥ* receives the elision of the accent (*aṣṭamiko nighātaḥ*) by the eighth rule. In the example *paraśunā vṛścan* ("cutting with an axe"), [the same rule applies].

The sixth [case] refers to the vocative case and the kāraka (grammatical participant). The meaning is that a list must be made of those which end in the sixth case, those which end in the vocative, and those which denote a kāraka. Therefore, it does not apply here in the following examples: *ayam agne jaritā* ("this one, O Agni, is the singer") and *etenāgne brahmaṇā* ("with this prayer, O Agni"). Alternatively, it is established by the continued application of the rule for "capability" (*samarthānuvṛtti*). It should be stated that [the rule applies] when it is like a preceding member of a compound: *ā te pitarmarutām* ("hither, O father of the Maruts") and *prati tvā duhitardivaḥ* ("toward you, O daughter of heaven"). It does not apply to indeclinables (*avyaya*): *uccair adhīyāna* ("studying loudly"). However, it is desired in the case of an avyayībhāva compound: *upāgny adhīyāna* ("studying near the fire").
Pāṇini 8.2.4: *udāttasvaritayor yaṇaḥ svarito ’nudāttasya*.

A circumflex (*svarita*) vowel shall take the place of an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel that follows a *yaṇ* substitute for an acute (*udātta*) or a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel. For example: *abhy abhi hi* (from *abhi + abhi*). This is because the *yaṇ* substitute here is circumflex. In *khalapvyāśā*, because this circumflex is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by virtue of belonging to the third pāda [of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*], the rule for the suppression of the remaining vowels (*śeṣanighāta*) does not apply. Pāṇini 8.2.5: *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*. When a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) takes the place of two vowels, one of which is acute, the resulting single substitute is acute.

An *ekādeśa* (single substitute) for [a vowel] together with an acute (*udātta*) [vowel] shall be acute. Examples: *vo ’śvāḥ*; *kvāvaraṃ marutaḥ*. Rule A 8.2.6: "Or, a circumflex (*svarita*) [is substituted] for [an acute vowel] at the beginning of a word that is unaccented (*anudātta*)."

When an unaccented vowel at the beginning of a word follows an accented vowel, the single substitute for both may optionally be *svarita*. In the alternative case, it is accented (*udātta*) by the preceding rule. As in: *vīdaṃ jyotir hṛdaye* ("this light in the heart") and *asva śloko divīyate* ("his fame is proclaimed in heaven"). Due to the principle of restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the *svarita* occurs when the short vowels *i* and *u* are involved; however, when they enter into a long vowel (*dīrgha*), it is accented (*udātta*). Furthermore, in the case of the *pūrvarūpa* substitution according to *eṅaḥ padāntāt...* (Pāṇini 6.1.109), it is indeed *svarita*: as in *te 'vadan* ("they said") and *so yam āgāt* ("he has come here"). And it is stated in the *Prātiśākhya*: "In the case of the coalescence of two *i*-sounds, and in the cases of *kṣaipra* and *abhinihata* [sandhis]. (SK 3660) *udāttād anudāttasya svaritaḥ* (A 8.4.66).

An unaccented vowel following an acute accent (*udātta*) shall become circumflex (*svarita*). *agnim īḷe*. Because this [circumflex substitution] is also treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the remaining low pitch (*nighāta*) does not apply. *tam īśānāsaḥ*. SK 3661: *nodāttasvaritodayamagārgyakāśyapagālavānām* (A 8.4.67). An unaccented vowel followed by an acute or a circumflex accent shall not become circumflex, according to the views of Gārgya, Kāśyapa, and Gālava. However, according to the view of Gārgya and others, it would indeed become circumflex. *pra ya āruḥ*; *vośvāḥ kvā bhīśavaḥ*.
Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.23: *ekaśruti dūrāt saṃbuddhau*.

In addressing someone from a distance, a sentence should be pronounced in a monotone (*ekaśruti*). This is an exception to the rule of three accents (*traisvarya*). Example: "Come, O young student! Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.34:
*yajñakarmaṇyajapanyūṅkhasāmasu*. In the performance of a sacrifice, [the monotone applies], except for the *japa*, the *nyūṅkha*, and the *sāman* chants.

In the performance of a sacrifice, a mantra should be pronounced in the *ekaśruti* (monotone) mode, with the exception of *japa* (muttering) and similar practices. For example: *agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakud*. Why "in the sacrifice"? Because at the time of private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), it must be in the *traisvarya* (three accents) mode. Why "with the exception of *japa*"? For instance: *mamāgne varco vihaveṣv astu*. What is called *japa* is a practice performed in a whisper, such as that of one submerged in water. What is called *nyūṅkha* consists of sixteen *o*-sounds. The name *sāman* applies to chanted melodies. (Pāṇini 1.2.35: Or the *vaṣaṭ* call may be pronounced louder;
in the sacrificial ritual, the word *vauṣaṭ* may either be pronounced louder or in the *ekaśruti* mode.

Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.36: *vibhāṣā chandasi*. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), there may optionally be monotony of pitch (*ekaśruti*). This is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*): in the *saṃhitā* texts, there is threefold accentuation (*traisvarya*); in the Brāhmaṇas, there is monotony for the followers of the Ṛgveda (*bahvṛca*). For others as well, the arrangement is according to their respective tradition.
Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.37: *na subrahmaṇyāyāṃ svaritasya tūdāttaḥ*. In the *subrahmaṇyā* litany, however, the circumflex (*svarita*) becomes acute (*udātta*).

In the *nigada* recitation known as *subrahmaṇyā* during the sacrificial rite, the monotonous accent (*ekaśruti*) that would otherwise apply by the rules "optionally in the Veda" (*vibhāṣā chandasi*) shall not occur; instead, the circumflex (*svarita*) and the acute (*udātta*) accents shall be used. For example: *subrahmaṇyo3m*. [The suffix *yat* is applied here in the sense of "one who is proficient in the *subrahmaṇī*. One should not argue that this rule prescribing the acute accent here is redundant, since the result would already be established by the rule "a single substitute for an acute and another vowel is acute" (*ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*). This is because the word "anudātta" (grave) continues to apply from that previous rule. The final syllable of the form *asau* is acute.

In that very same *nigada*, the final syllable of a word ending in the nominative case shall be acute (*udātta*). In *gārgyo yajate*, the initial acute (*ādyudātta*) which would have been obtained by virtue of the suffix being marked with *ñ* is superseded by this rule; for *amuṣya*, the final syllable is acute. For a word ending in the genitive case as well, it is as before: *dākṣeḥ pitā yajate*. [In a word] ending in *-syā*, the penultimate syllable is also acute. Because of the word "also" (*ca*), the final syllable is included; thus, there are two acute syllables: *gārgyasya pitā yajate*. Optionally, for a proper name (*nāmadheya*) ending in *-syā*, the penultimate syllable may optionally be acute: *devadattasya pitā yajate*. (Pāṇini 6.2.140) *deva-* and *brahman-* [in a *nigada*] are unaccented (*anudātta*). (A 1.3.38)
In these two cases, within the *subrahmaṇyā* formula, the circumflex (*svarita*) becomes unaccented (*anudātta*). [Example: *devā brahmāṇa ā gaccha*.

According to A 1.2.39, "In continuous speech (*saṃhitā*), for unaccented vowels following a circumflex," there shall be monotonous pitch (*ekaśruti*) for the unaccented vowels that follow a circumflex in continuous speech. [Example: *imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati*.
SK 3669 *udāttasvaritaparasya sannataraḥ* (A 1.2.40):

For that which has an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel following it, there shall be a lower-pitched (*sannatara*) accent for the unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel. Examples: *sarasvati śutudri*; *vyacakṣayatsvaḥ*. SK 3670 *tasya param āmreḍitam anudāttaṃ ca* (A 8.1.3): The subsequent [portion] of that [word] is called the reduplicated form (*āmreḍita*), and it is unaccented (*anudātta*).
The subsequent form of a reduplicated word shall be unaccented (*anudātta*). For example: *dive dive*. These are the common accentual rules.
Now, the accentual rules for verbal roots (*dhātu*):
The final syllable shall be udātta. *gopāyataṃ naḥ* / *asiḥ satyaḥ*. SK 3672:

*svapādīnāṃ hiṃseś cāniṭy ajādau lasārvadhātuke pare ādir udātto vā syāt* (A 6.1.188). For the verbs beginning with *svap*, as well as for *hiṃs*, when followed by a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a vowel that lacks an *iṭ* augment, the initial syllable may optionally be udātta. *Svapādi* is a sub-group within the *adādi* class. Examples: *svapanti*, *śvasanti*, *hiṃsanti*. In the alternative case, the accent is on the middle syllable due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). This [initial udātta] is desired only before *kṅit* suffixes. Not here: *svapāni*, *hinasāni*.
SK 3673 *abhyastānām ādiḥ* (A 6.1.189):

When followed by a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*yajādi*) that lacks the *iṭ* augment, the first syllable of reduplicated (*abhyasta*) roots is acute (*udātta*). Example: *ye dadati priyā vasu*. This [rule] supersedes the acute accent of the *cit* suffix because it is later in the sequence. Example: *dadhānā indre*. SK 3674 *anudātte ca* (A 6.1.190): [The same applies] when followed by a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix that is unaccented (*anudātta*).

When a *lasārvadhātuka* affix that lacks an acute accent (*anudātta*) follows, the first syllable of reduplicated (*abhyasta*) roots is acute. *dadhāsi ratnaṃ draviṇaṃ ca dāḍhuṣe* (you bestow treasure and wealth upon the giver).

Regarding the rule *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-hu-mada-jana-dhana-daridrā-jāgarāṃ pratyayāt pūrvaṃ piti* (A 6.1.192): when a *pit* *lasārvadhātuka* affix follows, the syllable preceding the affix in the case of the reduplicated roots beginning with *bhī* shall be acute. *yo 'gnihotraṃ juhoti* (he who offers the Agnihotra); *mamattu naḥ parijmā*; *mātā yadvīraṃ dadhanat*; *jāgarṣi tvam*.
SK 3676: A syllable preceding the suffix *liti* is acute (*udātta*). Example: *cikīrṣakaḥ*. SK 3677: In the case of the suffix *ṇamul*, the first syllable is optionally acute.

When the suffix *ṇamul* follows, the first syllable of reduplicated forms (*abhyasta*) is optionally acute (*udātta*). Thus, *lolūyam-lolūyam*; in the alternative case, the accent is that of the *liṭ*-suffix. By Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.195, *acaḥ kartṛyaki*: when the *yak* of the agent (*kartṛ*) follows, the first syllable of verbal roots ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) in their original form (*upadeśa*) is optionally acute. Thus, *lūyate kedāraḥ svayam eva*.
SK 3679: *caṅy anyatarasyām* (A 6.1.218).

When a root ending in *caṅ* follows, the penultimate syllable is optionally acute (*udātta*). In *mā hi cīkaratām*, the vowel of the root is acute; in the alternative case, the *caṅ* is acute. Thus end the rules regarding the accent of roots. Now, the accents of suffixes [begin]. 70.

SK 3680: *karṣāt tv ato ghañ-anta udāttaḥ* (A 6.1.159). For the root *karṣati* and for [roots] ending in long *ā*, the final syllable of the form ending in *ghañ* shall be acute (*udātta*). Because it is indicated with the suffix *śap*, *karṣaḥ* belongs to the *tud*-class and is therefore acute on the first syllable. Examples: *karṣaḥ*, *pākaḥ*. SK 3681: *uñchādīnāṃ ca* (A 6.1.160). And [the final syllable of] *uñcha* and so forth is also acute.

The final syllable shall be udātta. Among the *uñchādi* group, the word *yuga* is irregularly formed with the suffix *ghañ*, without *guṇa* substitution, in the sense of a specific time period and as a part of a chariot or similar object. As in: *vaiśvānaraḥ kuśikebhir yugeyuge* ("Vaiśvānara [is praised] by the Kuśikas age after age"). In other cases: *yogeyoge tavastaram* ("at every conjunction, the most powerful one"). The word *bhakṣa* ends in *ghañ*. As in: *gāvaḥ somasya prathamasya bhakṣaḥ* ("the cows are the first portion of the Soma"). The words *uttama* and *śaśvattama* also [have this accent]. As in: *uduttamaṃ varuṇa* ("O Varuṇa, [release us] from the highest") and *śaśvattamam īḷate* ("they praise the most constant one"). [This applies to] *caturaḥ* before the locative plural ending *śas* (Pāṇini A 6.1.167).

The word *catur* has an acute accent (*udātta*) on its final syllable when followed by the suffix *śas*. As in *caturaḥ kalpayantaḥ*. However, this does not apply here [in the case of *catasraḥ*] because of the rule *aci raḥ*, which substitutes *r* for the final vowel; since that substitution is treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) in a rule concerning what precedes it, the accentuation does not apply. Thus: *catasraḥ paśya*. [The form *catasraḥ* is derived from the root *cat-* with the suffix *uran*; due to the *nit*-marker, it has an acute accent on the first syllable. SK 3683: *jhaly upottamam* (Pāṇini 6.1.180).

In a word ending with a case-suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant following the words *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, or *catur*, the penultimate syllable shall be acute (*udātta*). Examples: *adhvaryubhiḥ pañcabhiḥ*; *navabhir vājair navatī ca*; *saptabhyo jāyamānaḥ*; *ā daśabhir vivasvataḥ*. Why "penultimate"? Consider: *ā ṣaḍbhir hūyamānaḥ*; *viśvair devais tribhiḥ*. Why "before a *jhal* [consonant]"? Consider: *navānāṃ navatīnām*. According to A 6.1.181, *vibhāṣā bhāṣāyām*, this rule is optional in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*) within the aforementioned scope.

SK 3685 *sarvasya supi* (A 6.1.191): When followed by a *sup* [suffix], the first syllable of the word *sarva-* shall be acute (*udātta*). Example: *sarve nandanti yaśasā* ("All rejoice in glory"). SK 3686 *ñnityādir nityam* (A 6.1.197): When followed by a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, the first syllable of the word is always acute.

The first syllable of *nidanta* and *ñidanta* shall be udātta. In the phrase *yasmin viśvāni pauṃsyā*, the word *pauṃsya* is derived from *puṃs-* with the suffix *ṣyañ* by virtue of its inclusion in the *brāhmaṇa*-group (*brāhmaṇādi*). In *sute 'dadhiṣva naścanaḥ*, [the word] *canaḥ* is derived from the root *cāy-* with the suffix *asun*; because of the letter *ca* in the rule *cāyer an ne hrasvaś ca*, there is also the augment *nuṭ* for *asun*. By the rule *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne* (A 6.1.199), the first syllable of *pathin* and *mathin* shall be udātta when followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]. As in *ayaṃ panthāḥ*. Why "when followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna*"? Consider *jyotiṣmataḥ patho rakṣa*. By the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent that replaces an udātta vowel), the word becomes antodātta (accented on the final syllable).
SK 3688: *antaś ca tavaiyugapat* (A 6.1.200). For a word ending in the suffix *tavai*, both the beginning and the end are simultaneously acute-accented (*ādyudātta*). Example: *harṣase dātavā u*.
SK 3689: *kṣayo nivāse* (A 6.1.202). [The word *kṣaya* is acute-accented on the final syllable when it means "dwelling."]
It shall have the acute accent on the first syllable. [In the rule] *sve kṣaye śucivrata* (SK 3690), [it is stated:

*jayaḥ karaṇam* (A 6.1.202). A word meaning "instrument" (*karaṇa*) that is the word *jaya* shall have the acute accent on its first syllable. For example: *jayo 'śvaḥ* ("a horse that conquers by means of this").

SK 3691: And in the case of *vṛṣan* and so forth, the first syllable is acute (*udātta*). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Examples: *vājebhir vājinīvatī*; *indraṃ vāṇīḥ*. SK 3692: When used as a name (*saṃjñā*), the word that serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) has its first syllable acute.

A word used as a comparison is acutely accented on its first syllable when it forms a name (*saṃjñā*). For example, *cañcā* ("a wooden doll"), which is like a *cañcu* (beak). Here, there is the elision (*lup*) of the suffix *kan*. This very rule indicates that in certain cases involving the prescription of accent, the technical designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply. Why "when it is a name"? Consider *agnir māṇavakaḥ* ("The boy is fire"). Why "comparison"? Consider *jaitraḥ* ("victorious"). (A 6.1.205) A word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix (*kta* or *ktavatu*) consisting of two syllables has an acute accent on its first syllable when it is a name, but this does not apply to the vowel *ā*. Examples: *dattaḥ*. Why "consisting of two syllables"? Consider *cintitaḥ*. Why "not *ā*" (*anāt*)? Consider *trātaḥ*. Because the term "name" (*saṃjñā*) is understood from the previous rule, it does not apply here: *kṛtam*, *hṛtam*.
SK 3694: *śuṣka* and *dhṛṣṭa* are udātta on the first syllable. This is for the purpose of excluding technical (*saṃjñā*) usage; thus, *atasam na śuṣkam* ("the fuel is not dry").
SK 3695: *āśitaḥ kartā* (A 6.1.207). [The word *āśita* is udātta on the first syllable when it denotes the agent.]
The word *āśita*, when denoting the agent, has its first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*). As in: *kṛṣann it phāla āśitam* ("the ploughshare, while plowing, has eaten").

Regarding the rule *rikte vibhāṣā* (A 6.1.208), in the word *rikta*, the initial syllable is optionally acute. However, when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), by the rule *niṣṭhā ca dvyajanāt* (A 6.1.205), there is obligatory acute accent on the first syllable by means of prior exclusion (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the words *juṣṭa* and *arpita* are optionally acute on the first syllable (A 6.1.209). In the Mantras, they are always [acute on the first syllable] (A 6.1.210).

This sūtra could be omitted; for [the forms] *juṣṭo damūnāḥ* and *ṣaḍara āhur arpitam*, etc., are already established by the preceding rule alone. Furthermore, because the reading in the Vedic text (*chandas*) is fixed, it is impossible to produce a contrary form. Moreover, in the case of *arpitāḥ ṣaṣṭir na calācalāsaḥ*, we observe that the final syllable is udātta.
According to A 6.1.211, when the suffix *ṅasi* follows *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the first syllable would be udātta: *nahiṣas tava* and *no mama*.
*tubhyaṃ hinvānaḥ* / *mahyaṃ vātaḥ pavatām*. SK 3701 *yato ’nāvaḥ* (A 6.1.213).

The first syllable of a word ending in *yat* that has two vowels (*dvyac*) is acute, except for words meaning "boat" (*nau*). In the examples *yuñjanty asya kāmyā*, the suffix *yat* is added to the root *kam* with the *ṇiṅ* affix; thus, it is *kāmya*. [Question: Why "except for boat"? [Answer: As in *navatiṃ nāvyānām* ("ninety boats").
According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.214, the first syllable of words ending in *ṇyat* derived from the roots *īḍ*, *vand*, *vṛ*, *śaṃs*, and *duh* is acute.

Examples: *īḍyo nūtanair uta* ("He is to be praised by the new ones"), *ājuhvāna īḍyo vandyaś ca* ("Being invoked, he is to be praised and worshipped"), *śreṣṭhaṃ no dhehi vāryam* ("Grant us the most excellent treasure"), and *uktham indrāya śaṃsyam* ("A hymn to be recited for Indra").
SK 3703 *vibhāṣā veṇvindhānayoḥ* (A 6.1.215): The first syllable is optionally acute (*udātta*). Example: *indhāno agnim*.
SK 3704 *tyāgarāgahāsakuhaśvaṭhakrathānām* (A 6.1.216).
The first [syllable] may be acute (*udātta*). The first three [terms] end in *ghañ*; the [following] three end in *pac-ādyac*. According to A 6.1.219, *matoḥ pūrvam āt saṃjñāyāṃ striyām*:
before the suffix *mat*, there is an acute *ā* when a feminine name is formed. Examples: *udumbarāvatī*, *śarāvatī*.

SK 3706 *anto ’vatyāḥ* (A 6.1.220): In the word *avati*, the final syllable is udātta. In *vetravatī*, [the final syllable] would have been anudātta because the suffix *ṅīp* is marked with *p*. SK 3707 *īvatyāḥ* (A 6.1.221).
The same applies as before even for words ending in *īvat*. Examples: *ahīvatī*, *munīvatī*.
Now, the Phiṭ-sūtras, Chapter 1, Section 1.

1. The final syllable of a *phiṭ* [word] is acute. A nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is called *phiṭ*. Its final syllable shall be acute. Example: *uccaiḥ*. 2. For words meaning *pāṭala*, *pālaṅka*, *amba*, and *sāgara*, the final syllable is acute. *Pāṭala*, *phaleruhā*, *surūpā*, and *pākala* are synonyms. Since the rule "the final syllable is acute when preceded by a light vowel" would have applied, this is an exception. *Apālaṅka*, *vyādhighāta*, *ārevata*, and *āragvadha* are synonyms. *Ambārtha* means "mother. Example: *mātā*. Since the rule "for words ending in *un* or *ṛvan*, the first syllable is acute" would have applied, this is an exception. *Sāgaraḥ*, *samudraḥ*.

3. For words meaning "house" (*geha*), [the suffix] is not feminine. *Geham*. This is stated because [the previous rule] *nabviṣayasya* would otherwise apply. Why say "not feminine"? [Consider] *śālā*; this word is udātta on the first syllable precisely because of the exclusion (paryudāsa) in this very rule, which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). 4. And for *guda*, [the suffix] is udātta on the final syllable, but not in the feminine. *Gudam*. Why say "not feminine"? [Consider] *āntrebhyas te gudābhyaḥ*. Here, by the rule *svāṅgaśiṭām adantānām*, the udātta on the first syllable applies as an internal operation (*antaraṅga*); from that, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. 5. For a word denoting the feminine that has *dhi* or *ya* preceding [the final vowel], [the suffix is udātta on the final syllable].

The final vowel *a* preceded by *dhakāra* or *yakāra* is acute (*udātta*). This applies when [the word] would otherwise fall under the rule *antardhā strīviṣayavarṇanāmnaḥ*. For example: *chāyā*, *māyā*, *jāyā*. When the rule *yāntasyāntyāt pūrvam* would apply, resulting in an initial acute, [this sūtra prevails]. Why is *strī* (feminine) specified? Consider *bāhyam*; because it ends in *yaj*, it is acute on the first syllable by that rule. Why is *viṣaya* (domain/subject) mentioned? Consider *ibhyā* and *kṣatriyā*. The word *ibhya* is acute on the first syllable by the rule *yato nāvaḥ*; however, the word *kṣatri* is acute on the middle syllable by the rule *yāntasyāntyāt pūrvam*.

[The suffix *kan* is applied after the group of words beginning with] *aśman* [to form names of things other than living beings]. [Nouns ending in *kan* have their first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*) under certain conditions: 1. *nakha* (nail); 2. *ukhā* (pot); 3. *sukha* (happiness); 4. *duḥkha* (suffering). Regarding *nakha*: although the rule *svāṅgaśiṭām* would normally require the first syllable to be acute, this is overridden. Regarding *ukhā*: since it is a specific type of vessel (*bhāṇḍaviśeṣa*) and is artificial (*kṛtrima*), the rule *khayyuvarṇaṃ kṛtrimākhyā ced* would normally require the vowel *u* to be acute; however, this is overridden. Regarding *sukha* and *duḥkha*: the rule *nabviṣayasya* would normally apply; however, this is overridden. Why say "after *aśman* etc."? Consider *śikhā* (crest) and *mukha* (face). For *mukha*, the rule *svāṅgaśiṭām* or *nabviṣayasya* would result in the first syllable being acute.

Regarding *śikhā*, however, because it is stated in the *Uṇādi* sūtras that the suffix *kha* is *nitt* (having an indicatory *n*) and the vowel is short (*hrasva*), it should be understood that the feminine suffix *ṭāp* applies even before [the addition of the suffix], according to the rule *svāṅga-śiṭām*. [The rule] *hiṣṭha-vatsara-tiśat-thāntānām*: For these, the final syllable shall be acute (*udātta*). *Biṃhiṣṭhaḥ* ("most abundant") is derived from *bahula* with the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*. Although the initial acute accent would normally apply due to the *nitt* quality [of the suffix], in examples such as *baṃhiṣṭhair aśvaiḥ suvṛtā rathena* ("with most abundant horses, on a well-rolling chariot") and *yad baṃhiṣṭhaṃ nātibibheḥ* ("that which is most abundant, you do not fear"), the initial acute accent occurs by way of metrical displacement (*vyatyaya*). *Parivatsaraḥ* ("a full year").

They say that here the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) preceding member is superseded. *Saptatiḥ*, *aśītiḥ*. This occurs where [the rule] *laghāvante* would otherwise apply. *Catvāriṃśat*. Here too, as before. Regarding *abhyūrṇvānā prabhṛthasyāyoḥ*: they say that here the *prakṛtisvara* of the indeclinable preceding member is superseded. This has already been explained by the rule *thāthādisūtra*. 8. In the sense of "skilled" (*sādhu*), the final syllable of *dakṣiṇa* is acute (*udātta*).

However, in the absence of the meaning "one who speaks well" (*sādhuvācin*), when there is a fixed application (*vyavasthā*) as a pronominal (*sarvanāman*), the first syllable is acute according to the rule *svāṅgaśiṭām*. But in other meanings, the heavy penultimate syllable is acute according to the rule *laghāv anta*. The lexicon states: "The word *dakṣiṇa* [is used] in the senses of 'straight,' 'generous,' and 'obedient to the will of another. [Rule 9: "In the designation of a limb of one's own body (*svāṅgākhyāyām*), the first syllable is optionally acute. Here, both the first and last syllables of *dakṣiṇa* are acute by turn: *dakṣiṇo bāhuḥ* ("the right arm"). Why is the word "designation" (*ākhyā*) mentioned? [Because] for one sitting facing west, the left hand becomes "right" (in that relative sense). [Rule 10: "And in the Vedic language (*chandasi*)."

This [rule] is for the sake of non-limbs (*asvāṅga*). [The word] *dakṣiṇaḥ* [is used]; in this context, both the first and last syllables are acute (*udātta*) by turn. 11. If it is a name of a deer (*mṛga*), [the word] *kṛṣṇa-* has its final syllable acute. Since [by rule P. 6.2.25] the acute would have been on the first syllable of the colors (*varṇa*) ending in *-taṇ*, the acute on the final syllable is prescribed here. Examples: *kṛṣṇānāṃ vrīhīṇām* ("of black rice grains"); *kṛṣṇo no vṛṣabhaḥ* ("our black bull"). But when it is a name of a deer: *kṛṣṇo rātryai* ("the black one for the night"). 12. Optionally so for a proper name (*nāmadheya*). It remains *kṛṣṇasya* as before; or alternatively: *ayaṃ vā kṛṣṇo aśvinā* ("this black one, O Aśvins"); *kṛṣṇārṣiḥ*. 13. For *śukla-* and *gaura-*, the initial syllable is acute.

Some say that [the word *aṅguṣṭha*] should always be udātta; however, it is more appropriate to understand that the particle *vā* (or) carries over from the previous rule. This is because we observe it as having the final syllable udātta in examples such as *saro gauró yáthā piba*. Rule 14: In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the words *aṅguṣṭha*, *udaka*, *baka*, and *vaśā* have the final syllable udātta. Since [by Pāṇini 6.2.173] the second syllable would have been expected to be udātta for *aṅguṣṭha*—as it belongs to the class of body parts (*svāṅga*) beginning with *akurvat*—this rule is commenced to ensure the final syllable is udātta. The inclusion of *vaśā* is for the purpose of restriction, meaning [the final udātta applies] only in the Vedic language. Therefore, they say that in common usage (*loka*), it has the initial syllable udātta. Rule 15: And the same applies to the word *pṛṣṭha*.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the final syllable shall be acute (*udātta*); optionally so in the common language (*bhāṣāyām*). For example: *pṛṣṭham*. (16) If it is a name for a type of grass, as in *arjunasya*, this is an exception to the rule that words ending in *-anarvan-* have an acute accent on the first syllable. (17) If it is a name for a master (*svāmin-*) as in *aryasya*, this is stated to exclude names of directions. By this very indication (*jñāpaka*), words synonymous with "direction" (*dik-paryāya*) are understood to have an acute accent on the first syllable, as in *indra āśābhyaḥ pari*. (19) Among the names of constellations (*nakṣatra*), those whose domain is water (*ab-viṣaya*) shall have an acute accent on the final syllable. This applies to *āśleṣā*, *anurādhā*, and others, which would otherwise fall under the rule that words with a light penultimate syllable have an acute accent on the final syllable.

20. Regarding *jyeṣṭhā*, *śraviṣṭhā*, and *dhaniṣṭhā*, since they would otherwise be acute on the first syllable due to having the suffix *-iṣṭhan*, this rule is stated [as an exception]. 21. If preceded by *ku*, provided it is the name of the constellation Kṛttikā, it does not have the acute on the final syllable. For example: *kṛttikā* (the constellation Kṛttikā). Some, however, explain that this applies to those [words] ending in *āp* which are preceded by *ku*, and thus they say that even in cases such as *āryikā* and *bahulikā*, there is no acute on the final syllable. 22. And for *ghṛta* and so forth, the acute is on the final syllable. Example: *ghṛtaṃ mimikṣe*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words). 23. *Jyeṣṭha* and *kaniṣṭha* have the acute on the final syllable when referring to age.

The final syllable shall be udātta (acute-accented). *Jyeṣṭha* [in the sense of] "elder" [is acute on the final]; *kaniṣṭha* [in the sense of] "younger" [is acute on the final]. Why [specify] "in respect to age"? [Because otherwise] *jyeṣṭhaḥ* [meaning] "best," and *kaniṣṭhaḥ* [meaning] "smallest," [would not be so accented]. In these latter cases, by virtue of the *niṭ* designation, they are indeed ādyudātta (acute on the first). 23. For *bilva* and *tiṣya*, the svarita (circumflex) is optional. For these two, the final syllable may optionally be svarita; in the alternative case, it is udātta. Thus ends the first quarter in the Phiṭ-sūtras. The second quarter begins.

24. Now, "before Śakaṭi" (atha ādiḥ prāk śakaṭeḥ): this is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). It applies up to the point where "of *śakaṭi* and *śakaṭa*" [is stated]. 25. For a feminine-stem word ending in a short vowel, the first syllable shall be acute (*udātta*). Examples: *baliḥ*, *tanuḥ*. 26. For a neuter (*napuṃsaka*) stem that does not end in *-i* and is not the domain of the suffix *naP*, the first syllable is acute. Example: *vane* (from *vana-*, with *naP*); but *sarpiḥ* (ending in *-i*). *Nap* refers to the neuter gender. 27. And for grasses and grains consisting of two syllables (*dvyacām*), the first syllable is acute. This means those with two vowels. Examples: *kuśāḥ*, *kāśāḥ*, *māṣāḥ*, *tilāḥ*. But for polysyllabic ones, as in *godhūmāḥ*, it is not so. 28. For the word *vraja-* when used as a numeral.

Five; four. (29) In the case of words ending in *ś* or *ṣ* that denote one’s own limbs (*svāṅga*), the first syllable is acute (*udātta*). [Examples: *śiṭ* (referring to a name), *sarvanāman* (pronoun); *karṇābhyāṃ chubukād adhi*; *oṣṭhāv iva madhu*; *viśvo vihāyāḥ*. (30) In the case of living beings (*prāṇin*), if preceded by *k*, the first syllable is acute. [Examples: *kākaḥ*; *vṛkaḥ*; *śukeṣu me*. Why "of living beings"? [Counter-example: *kṣīram*, *sarpiḥ*, *madhu*, *udakam*. (31) When followed by a *kh*-class consonant (*khay*), a word ending in *u* is acute if it denotes something artificial (*kṛtrima*). [Example: *kandukaḥ*. (32) Words ending in *un* or *arvan* [have their first syllable acute].

33. Among the words *una*, *varuṇam*, *vo*, *riśādasam*, *ṛ*, *svasāram*, *tvā*, *kṛṇavai*, *van*, *pīvānam*, and *meṣam*, the first syllable is acute (*udātta*). Examples: *etaḥ*, *hariṇaḥ*, *śitiḥ*, *pṛśniḥ*, *harit*. 34. For a word ending in a short vowel, except for those containing the vowel *ṛ* and those expressing a habitual action (*śīlya*), the first syllable is acute. Example: *miniḥ*. 35. For a word not used in gambling (*adevana*), the first syllable is acute. Example: *tasya nākṣaḥ*. However, in the case of gambling: [the rule does not apply].

Do not gamble with dice. (36) In the case of *ardha* when it does not signify an equal portion: *ardho grāmasya* ("half of the village"). But when it signifies an equal share: *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ* ("half of a long pepper"). (37) For words beginning with *pītadru*, the first syllable is acute. *Pītadruḥ* means "sarala" (a type of pine). (38) And for *grāma* and so forth: *grāmaḥ*, *somaḥ*, *yāmaḥ*. (39) For a word ending in *lup* that is the name of the object compared (*upameyanāmadheya*): *cañceva cañcā* ("like a beak, a beak"). There is a variant reading *sphigantasya*; *sphig* refers to the *lup* suffix. This is a designation of the Easterners (*prācām*).

40. In the case of these names used as objects of comparison—namely *vṛkṣa*, *parvata*, *vyāghra*, *siṃha*, and *mahiṣa*—the first syllable is not acute (*udātta*). Examples: *tāla iva tālaḥ* (a palm tree like a palm tree), *merur iva meruḥ* (Mount Meru like Mount Meru), *vyāghraḥ* (a tiger), *siṃhaḥ* (a lion), *mahiṣaḥ* (a buffalo). 41. If it is the name of a specific king and ends in *yaman* or *vā*, the acute falls on the penultimate syllable (*yamanvā vṛddhaḥ*). Example: *Āṅgaḥ*; counter-example: *Aṅgāḥ*. 42. When a word has many vowels (*bahvac*), the acute falls on the heavy (*guru*) syllable if there is a light (*laghu*) syllable at the end, or if there are two light syllables [at the end]. When a light syllable is at the end, or when two light syllables are present, the acute of a polysyllabic word falls on the heavy syllable.

*Kalyāṇaḥ* (auspicious) and *kolāhalaḥ* (clamor). 43. For these three—[names] of women, [words for] colors, and those preceded by *akṣu*—the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the first syllable when they denote females. *Mallikā* (jasmine); for color: *śyenī* (falconess), *hariṇī* (doe). Those preceded by the word *akṣu* are "preceded by *akṣu*" (*akṣupūrva*). Example: *tarkṣuḥ* (a hyena). 44. And among birds, the light (short) syllable that comes first is acute. The preceding light syllable shall be acute. Examples: *kukkuṭaḥ* (cock), *tittiraḥ* (partridge), *khañjarīṭaḥ* (wagtail). 45. Not so in the case of names of seasons or living beings. The acute accent obtained according to the rule does not apply here. Example: *vasantaḥ* (spring).

The first syllable is acute (udātta) in the following cases: 46. In words ending in *kṛ*, such as *kṛkalāsa* ("lizard"); in words ending in *dhān*, such as *vṛddhadhānāḥ* ("old grains"); in words ending in *kānt*, such as *śyāmākāḥ* ("millet"); and in words ending in *ṣānt*, such as *māṣāḥ* ("beans"). 47. In names of countries (*janapada*) not ending in *ṣ*, the first syllable is acute, as in *kekayaḥ*. 48. In words beginning with *haya* where the letter *l* is not conjunct, the acute accent falls on either the final syllable or the penultimate syllable; *haya* here refers to the technical term *hal* (consonants). Examples: *palalam* ("meat") and *śalalam* ("thorn"). Why "beginning with *haya*"? Counter-example: *ekalaḥ*. Why "not conjunct"? Counter-example: *mallaḥ*. Furthermore, for words ending in a vowel (*iganta*) consisting of two syllables, the first syllable is acute, as in *kṛṣiḥ*. Thus ends the second quarter of the Phiṭ-sūtras. The Third Quarter:

50. Now, the second [syllable] before the prefix *pra*. The section concerning the second syllable extends from this point up to the rule beginning with "of that which ends in *iṣ*, preceded by *ha*. 51. For words consisting of three syllables (*tryaca*), before the word *makara*. The section concerning three-syllable words extends from this point up to the rule beginning with "*makara-varūḍha*. 52. Among parts of the body (*svāṅga*) that do not begin with the *ka*-group, *r*, or *v*. With the exception of those beginning with the *ka*-group, *r*, or *v*, the second syllable of three-syllable words denoting parts of the body is acute (*udātta*). Example: *lalāṭam* (forehead). However, for words such as *kurva*, etc., it is not so: *kapolaḥ* (cheek), *rasanā* (tongue), *vadanaṃ* (mouth). 53. And for words beginning with *ma*: *mayalaḥ* (a type of fish), *makaraḥ* (crocodile).

54. Among vegetables (*śāka*), [the initial syllable of] *śādīnāṃ* (e.g., *śādvala*) and *śītanyā* (e.g., *śītanyāya*) is acute. In *śatapuṣpā*, [the initial syllable] is acute. 55. Among those ending in *-p-*, such as *gurvādīnām*, [the initial syllable of] *pādapaḥ* and *ātapaḥ* is acute. However, among those beginning with *laghu*, [the initial syllable of] *anūpam* is acute; but among those consisting of two syllables, [the initial syllable of] *nīpam* is acute. 56. Among those joined with suffixes that do not cause the *ṇic*-strengthening (*aṇyantānām*), [the initial syllable of] *yute*, *ayutam*, *ani*, *dhamaniḥ*, *aṇi*, and *vipaṇiḥ* is acute. 57. For *makara*, *varūḍha*, *pārevata*, *vitasa*, *tekṣu*, *ārji*, *drākṣā*, *kalomā*, *kāṣṭhā*, *peṣṭhā*, and *kāśī*, the first syllable is optionally acute. For these, either the first or the second syllable is acute: *makaraḥ*, *varūḍhaḥ*, and so forth.

48. *chandasi ca* (also in the Vedic language). This rule is commenced for the sake of words beginning with *ama*. According to the usage of the examples (*lakṣya*), it should be understood that both the first and the second syllables are acute (*udātta*). 59. *kardamādīnāṃ ca* (and of *kardama* and others). Either the first or the second syllable is acute. 60. *sugandhitejanasya te vā* (of *sugandhitejana*, [the first or] the second [syllable is acute], or the word *te*). When the word *te* follows, all three—the first, the second, and *te*—are acutely accented by turn. Example: *sugandhitejanāḥ*. 61. *najaḥ phalāntānām* (of words ending in *phala* preceded by the negative particle *na*). Either the first or the second syllable is acute. Example: *rājādanaphalam*. 62. *yāntasyāntyāt pūrvam* (of a word ending in *ya*, the syllable preceding the final one is acute). Example: *kulāyaḥ*.

63. In the words *sthānta*, *nāla*, and *ghunī*, the syllable preceding the final one is acute (*udātta*), as are the word *nā* and the syllable *ghu*. Example: *sanāthā sabhā*. 64. In the words *śiśumāra*, *udumbara*, *balīvarda*, *uṣṭra*, *āra*, *puru*, and *vasa*, the syllable preceding the final one is acute, or alternatively, the second syllable from the end is acute. 65. In the words *sāṃkāśya*, *kāmpilya*, *nāsikya*, *dārvādhāṭa*, and *ānaḍuhya*, the second syllable from the end is optionally acute. 66. In words ending in *īṣā* that begin with *haya* or similar terms, the first syllable is optionally acute. Examples: *halīṣā*, *lāṅgalīṣā*.

67. In the case of *udīra*, *dāśera*, *kapāla*, *palāla*, *śaivāla*, *śyāmāka*, *śārīra*, *śarāva*, *hṛdaya*, *hiraṇya*, *araṇya*, *apatya*, and *devara*, the first syllable shall be acute (*udātta*). 68. In the case of *mahiṣī* and *aṣāḍhā*, when they are used as names for a wife and a brick respectively, the first syllable is acute. Examples: *mahiṣī jāyā* ("the buffalo-cow is the wife") and *aṣāḍhā upadadhāti* ("he lays down the Aṣāḍhā bricks"). Thus ends the third quarter in the Phiṭ-sūtras.

The Fourth Pāda. 69. In the words *śakaṭi* and *śakaṭī*, each syllable is acutely accented (*udātta*) alternately. *Śakaṭiḥ*; *śakaṭī*. 70. In the name of a Brāhmaṇa called *goṣṭhaja*, each syllable is acutely accented alternately. *Goṣṭhajo brāhmaṇaḥ*. In other cases, *goṣṭhajaḥ* refers to an animal; it is oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived compound. 71. In the word *pārāvata*, with the exception of the penultimate syllable, the remainder is acutely accented in sequence. *Pārāvataḥ*.

72. In the words *dhūmra*, *jānu*, *muñja*, *keśa*, *kālavāla*, and *sthālīpāka*, the syllable preceding *dhū* is unaccented (*anudātta*). Among these four [groups], excluding the four beginning with *dhū*, the remaining ones are successively acute (*udātta*). 73. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the words *kapikeśa* and *harikeśa* [are treated as follows]: *kapikeśaḥ*; *harikeśaḥ*. 74. The two terms *nyaṅ* and *svar* are circumflex (*svarita*). This is clear. Examples: *nyaṅṅuttānaḥ*; *vyacakṣayatsvaḥ*. 75. In the words *nyarbuda* and *vyalkaśa*, the final syllable is circumflex (*svarita*), as are the finals of *yathā*, *anya*, *kanyā*, *rājan*, and *manuṣya*. It should be circumflex.

The field for sesame is *tilyam*, as in "from which [comes] the boat" (*nāvaḥ*). This being the case [according to the rule], [the following exceptions apply]: In the Veda (*chandasi*), the words *bilva*, *bhakṣya*, and *vīrya* have a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on the final syllable. For example: *na no bilvasya udatiṣṭhat*; *uta tvaḥ paśyan*; *nabhantām anyake same*. The word *simasmai* has an acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable. The mention of "Atharvaṇa" is illustrative (*prāyika*); or rather, it refers to that which is seen there [in the Atharvaveda]. Therefore, even in the Ṛgveda, as in *vāsas tanute simasmai*, this [accentuation] indeed occurs.

80. The particles (nipātas) beginning with *svāhā* have the acute accent on their first syllable (*ādyudātta*). 81. The prefixes (*upasargas*), with the exception of *abhi*, [have the acute accent on the first syllable]. 82. The final syllable of the group beginning with *eva* [is acute]. There is a variant reading, *evamādīnām*. Thus: *eva*, *evam*, *nūnam*, *saha te putra sūribhiḥ*. Regarding the word *saha*, the ancients maintain that in the section of the sixth book, third chapter, beginning with *sahasya saḥ*, the word *saha* has the acute accent on its first syllable; however, this should be considered. 83. In the group beginning with *vāc*, both syllables are acute. The mention of "both" (*ubhau*) is for the purpose of setting aside the rule that "a word has one [syllable] unaccented" (*anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam*).

84. The particles beginning with *ca* (the *cādayaḥ*) are unaccented (*anudātta*). This is clear. 85. In the case of *yathā* at the end of a *pāda*, [the first syllable is acute]. As in: *tannemim ṛbhavo yathā*. Why "at the end of a *pāda*"? Consider: *yathā no aditiḥ karat*. 86. In a reduplication where the second member begins with *pra* or similar particles (*prakārādi*), the final syllable of the subsequent member is acute. As in: *paṭupaṭuḥ*. 87. All remaining [syllables] are unaccented. "Remaining" means that which follows the first member of a reduplicated word. As in: *praprāyam*; *divedive*. Thus ends the fourth quarter of the *Phiṭ-sūtras* composed by Ācārya Śāntanava. Now follow the remaining rules for the section on accents (*svaraprakaraṇa*). (72)
SK 3708 *ādyudāttaś ca* (A 3.1.3): A suffix shall be acutely accented on its first syllable only. *agniḥ*; *kartavyam*.
SK 3709 *anudāttau suppitau* (A 3.1.4): The case endings (*sup*) and those suffixes marked with *p* (*pit*) are gravely accented.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. [In the case of] *yajñasya*, [the final vowel is not acute]. In *na* and *yo yucchati*, because the *śap* and *tiP* suffixes are unaccented (*anudātta*), the *svarita* and *pracaya* accents apply. SK 3710: *citaḥ* (A 6.1.163). That which is marked with the *cit* indicator shall have an acute accent (*udātta*) on its final syllable. The mention of *cit* along with the base (*prakṛti*) is for the sake of forms like *bahvacaḥ* and *akaḥ*. The meaning is that when a suffix marked with *cit* follows, it should be stated that the acute accent falls on the final syllable of the entire combination of base and suffix. For example: *nabhantām anyake same*; *yake sarasvatīm anu*; *takat sute*.

SK 3711 *taddhitasya* (A 6.1.164): The final syllable of a *taddhita* suffix that contains a *cit* marker is acute (*udātta*). Although this was already established by the preceding rule, this [present rule] is for the purpose of overriding the accent of the *ñit* suffixes. Example: *kauñjāyanāḥ*.
SK 3712 *kitaḥ* (A 6.1.165): [The final syllable of a *taddhita* suffix] containing a *kit* marker is acute.

The final syllable of a *taddhita* derivative is acute-accented. For example: *yadāgneyaḥ*. According to A 6.1.166, the final syllable of the nominative plural *jasi* after *tisṛ* is acute-accented: *tisro dyāvaḥ savituḥ*.

SK 3714: *sāvekācas tṛtīyādir vibhaktiḥ* (A 6.1.168). *Sau* refers to the locative plural (*saptamībahuvacanam*). In that context, a case ending beginning with the third case (*tṛtīyādi*) following a monosyllabic (*ekāc*) word is acute (*udātta*). Example: *vācā virūpaḥ*. Why [is it] *sau*? [So that] in forms such as *rājñā*, etc., it does not apply even though the word *rājan* is monosyllabic; [thus we have] *rājño nu te*. Why "monosyllabic" (*ekācaḥ*)? [So that it does not apply in] *vidhate rājani tve*. Why "beginning with the third case" (*tṛtīyādiḥ*)? [So that it does not apply in] *na dadarśa vācam*. SK 3715: *antodāttād uttarapadād anyatarasyām anityasamāse* (A 6.1.169). [An acute accent is optionally applied] to a case ending beginning with the third case, following a final syllable (*uttarapada*) that is acutely accented on the last vowel, provided it is not a permanent compound (*anityasamāsa*).

Except in the case of compounds prescribed by the *nitya* (obligatory) rules, when the final member (*uttarapada*) is oxytone and consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*), the case-ending beginning with the third case (*tṛtīyādi*) following it may optionally be acute. For example: *paramavācā*. Regarding A 6.1.170, *añceś chandasy asarvanāmasthānam*:

a case-ending following *añc-* is acute in the Vedic language. In *indro dadhīcaḥ*, the rule *cau* [A 6.2.142] would have resulted in the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member (*pūrvapada*). While the term "beginning with the third case" (*tṛtīyādi*) is understood from the previous context, the inclusion of the term *asarvanāmasthāna* ("not a sarvanāmasthāna ending") is for the purpose of including the *śas* ending. For example: *pratīco bahūn*.

Pāṇini 6.1.171: *ūḍidampadādyappumredyubhyaḥ*. After these [words], a case-ending that is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* is acute (*udātta*). Examples: *praṣṭhauhaḥ*, *praṣṭhauhā*. The mention of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) containing *ūṭ* must be made; otherwise, it would not apply here: *akṣadyuvā*, *akṣadyuve*. [Also after] *idam*: *ebhir nṛbhir nṛtamaḥ*. It does not apply in the case of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), because the word "from an acute-final [word]" (*antodāttāt*) is understood [in the rule]. Nor should it be argued that there is no acute-final status there either, for in the rule *idamo 'nvādeśe 'śanudāttaḥ tṛtīyādau*, the substitution of *aś* as unaccented (*anudātta*) is prescribed for the third case and onwards. Example: *pra te babhrū*.

*mābhyām gā anu*, *paddannomāshṛnniś*—these are the six beginning with *pad*. *padbhyāṃ bhūmiḥ* / *dadbhir na jihvā* / *aharaharjāyate māsimāsi* / *manaś cimne hṛda ā* / *ap* / *apāṃ phenena* / *pum* / *abhrāteva puṃsaḥ* / *rai* / *rāyā vayam* / *rāyo dhartā vivasvataḥ* / *div* / *upa tvāgne divedive*. According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.172, a case ending beginning with *śas* is acute-accented after the word *aṣṭan* when it ends in a long vowel: *aṣṭābhir daśabhiḥ*.
Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.173: *śaturanumo nadyajādī* (A 6.1.173).

After a word ending in the *śatṛ* suffix that is oxytone (*antodātta*), the following feminine suffix *nadī* and the *ajādi* case endings beginning with *śas* shall be acute (*udātta*). Example: *acchā ravaṃ prathamā jānatī* (RV 1.124.2); *kṛṇvate*. Why "after an oxytone [word]"? Consider *dadhatī*. Here, the first syllable is acute by the rule *abhyastānām ādiḥ* (6.1.189). Why "after one ending in *anu*" (*anumaḥ*)? Consider *tudantī*. Here, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is acute. Because it follows a root taught as having *a* as its penultimate (*adupadeśāt*), the *śatṛ* suffix receives the *nighāta* (non-acute) accent by the rule *lasārvadhātuka* (6.1.186). Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.174: *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* (A 6.1.174). [The same endings are acute] after a word containing a vowel (*yaṇ*) that is acute and preceded by a consonant (*hal*).

When a *yaṇ* substitute occurs in place of an acute-accented vowel and is preceded by a consonant, the following *nadī* suffixes and case-endings beginning with *śas* shall be acute. For example: *codayitrī sūnṛtānām*, *eṣā netrī*, and *ṛtaṃ devāya kṛṇvate savitre*.

According to A 6.1.175 (*noṅdhātvoḥ*), the case-endings beginning with *śas* following a *yaṇ* substitute for either the particle *uṅ* or a verbal root shall not be acute. For example: *brahmabandhvā* and *setpṛśniḥ subhve*.

SK 3722 *hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup* (A 6.1.176): After a word ending in a short vowel that has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*), and after the suffix *nuṭ*, the suffix *matup* is acute (*udātta*). Example for [a word] ending in a short vowel: *yo 'bdimān udanimān iyarti* ("He who possesses water and possesses moisture moves"). Example for *nuṭ*: *akṣaṇvantaḥ karṇavantaḥ sakhāyaḥ* ("Friends possessed of eyes and possessed of ears"). Why "after one having its final syllable accented"? Consider: *mā tvā vidadiṣumān* ("May he not find you, O possessor of arrows"). In rules concerning accentuation, the rule that "a consonant is as if non-existent" does not apply here. Examples: *marutvān indra* ("O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts") and *niyutvān vāyav ā gahi* ("O Vāyu, come hither with your team"). And also after the word *re*: *revān id revataḥ*. SK 3723 *nām anyatarasyām* (A 6.1.177).
In the suffix *matup*, when it follows a word ending in a short vowel that is oxytone (*antodātta*), the following *nām* is optionally acute (*udātta*). As in: *cetantī sumatīnām*.
According to A 6.1.178, *ṅyāś chandasi bahulam*, the *nām* following a word ending in a feminine suffix *ṅī* is optionally acute in the Veda.
As in: *devasenānām abhibhañjatīnām*. Because of the mention of "optionally" (*vā*), it is not so here: *jayantīnāṃ maruto yantu*.

Pāṇini 6.1.179: After *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, and *catur*, an initial consonant of a case-ending (*hal-ādi*) is acute. For example: *āṣaḍbhir hūyamānaḥ* ("being offered with six") and *tribhis tvaṃ deva* ("O God, by three").
Pāṇini 6.1.182: [The acute accent does not apply] after *go*, *aśva*, *ansu*, a word ending in *avarṇa* (a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ), *rāj*, *aṅku*, *ṛtvij*, or *kṛt*.

In these cases, what was stated previously does not apply: *gavāṃ śatā*, *gobhyo gātum*, *śunaś ciccheṣam*. [The rule] *sau prathamaikavacanē avarṇāntāt* [applies]: *tebhyo dyumnam*, *teṣāṃ pāhi śrudhī havam*. SK 3727: *divo jhal* (A 6.1.183).

A case-ending (*vibhakti*) beginning with a *jhal* consonant following *div-* is not acute-accented (*anudātta*). Examples: *dyubhir aktubhiḥ*. Why specify *jhal*? [Counter-example: *upa tvāgne divedive*.

SK 3728 *nṛ cānyatarasyām* (A 6.1.184): A case-ending following *nṛ*, beginning with a *jhal* consonant, is optionally acute (*udātta*). Example: *nṛbhir yemānaḥ*. SK 3729 *titsvaritam* (A 6.1.185): An affix marked with the indicator *ti* has the circumflex (*svarita*) accent.

This has been explained by the preceding commentary. Where [is it used]? In the case of *nūnam*: according to A 6.1.186, "The *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes following a verbal root that ends in a *tās* affix, or which is marked with an anudātta vowel, or which is taught with an *ṅit* marker, are anudātta, except for those ending in *ah* or *hi*."

After this [affix], a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix shall be *anudātta*. For example: *tāsi* [in the formation of] *kartā*, *kartārau*, *kartāraḥ*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accentuation of suffixes (*pratyayasvara*). [The rule applies to] that which has an *anudātta* indicatory letter (*it*): *ya āste*. [The rule applies to] that which has a *ṅit* indicatory letter: *abhicaṣṭe anṛtebhiḥ*. [The rule applies to] that which is taught with a short *a* as its penultimate vowel (*adupadeśāt*): *purubhujā canasyatam*. By this [rule], even the accent of a *cit* indicatory letter (*citsvara*) is superseded: *vardhamānaṃ sve dame*. Why [is it said] "after *tāsi* etc."? Consider: *abhi vṛdhe gṛṇītaḥ*. Because of the inclusion of the word "original teaching" (*upadeśa*), it does not apply here: *hato vṛtrāṇy āryā*. Why is the mention of *la* (the *l*-class suffixes) included?

"How many are cooking here? (*katīha pacamānāḥ*). What is the purpose of [specifying] *sārvadhātuka*? [Consider: "He slept" (*śiśye*). What is the purpose of [specifying] *an-ṅiṅoḥ*? [Consider: "He shrinks" (*hnute*). [Consider: "What he studies" (*yad adhīte*). It should be stated that [the augment] does not occur after the roots *vid*, *indh*, and *khid*: "The king kindles" (*indhe rājā*). And this is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *anudāttasya ca yatrānudātte* (Pāṇini 6.1.59).
*Ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām* (A 6.1.187): The initial syllable of a form ending in *sic* is optionally acute (*udātta*). [Examples: "You two went with Aśvin" (*yāsiṣṭaṃ vartir aśvinā*).
SK 3732: *thali ca seṭīḍanto vā* (A 6.1.196).

When a *thal* affix follows that is marked with *seṭ*, the final syllable (*anta*) or the initial syllable (*ādi*) may be acute (*udātta*). When these three [conditions] do not apply, then by the rule *liti* (A 6.1.193), the syllable preceding the affix would be acute. In *lulavitha*, all four syllables may alternatively be acute.
SK 3733: *upottamaṃ riti* (A 6.1.297).
In a word ending with the suffix *rit*, the penultimate syllable shall be acute (*udātta*). As in *yadāhavanīye*. Thus end the rules regarding the accent of suffixes (*pratyayasvara*).
Now, the rules regarding the accent of compounds (*samāsasvara*).

SK 3734: In a compound, the final syllable shall be acute-accented (*udātta*). Example: *yajñaśriyam*. SK 3735: In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Example: *yajñaśriyam*.

The first member of a compound, when joined with an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent, shall remain in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *satyaś citraśravastamaḥ*. Why specify "acute" and so forth? It is so that when the first member is entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*), there may be only the final acute of the compound, as in *samapādaḥ*. In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the first member remains in its original form] when it signifies equality, or when it is a word ending in the third, seventh, or second case, or is a comparative (*upamāna*), an indeclinable (*avyaya*), or a gerundive (*kṛtya*) [A 6.2.2].

These seven, when functioning as the prior member (*pūrvapada*) in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, retain their original form (*prakṛti*). 1. *tulyaśvetaḥ* ("as white as"): [This is a *tatpuruṣa*] by the rule "Words denoted by *kṛtya* suffixes and words meaning 'equal' (*tulya*), when not followed by a generic term (*ajātyā*). 2. *kirikāṇaḥ* ("blind in one eye from a wound"): [This is a *tatpuruṣa*] by the rule "One who is blind in one eye due to a *kiri* (wound). 3. *patayanmandayasakham*: [The word *sakha* is used] in the sense of "intoxicating" (*mandayati*) Indra, who is the companion (*sakhi*). This is a *saptamī-tatpuruṣa* (locative compound). 4. *śastrīśyāmā* ("dark-complexioned like a knife"). 5. [The rule applies] to indeclinables (*avyaya*), the negative particle (*nañ*), and particles (*nipāta*): *ayajñaḥ* ("this is no sacrifice"). What is the purpose of this specific enumeration? [To exclude cases such as: *snātvākālakaḥ* ("one who turns dark after bathing"), *muhūrtamukham* ("a face for a moment"), *bhojyoṣṇam* ("food that is hot"). [Note: Regarding the rule A 6.2.3, *varṇo varṇeṣv anete*, it means that a color-word (*varṇa*) retains its original form when followed by another color-word, provided it is not *eta*.]

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the final member denotes color and excludes the word *eta*, the preceding member denoting color remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *kṛṣṇasāraṅgaḥ* (a black-spotted deer), *lohitakalmāṣaḥ* (red-spotted). The word *kṛṣṇa* ends in the suffix *na*, and the word *lohita* ends in the suffix *it*. Why "color" (*varṇa*)? [Counter-example: *paramakṛṣṇaḥ* (an extremely black person). Why "in colors" (*varṇeṣu*)? [Counter-example: *kṛṣṇatilāḥ* (black sesame seeds). Why "excluding *eta*" (*anete*)? [Counter-example: *kṛṣṇaitaḥ* (a black-and-white animal). (A 6.2.4) *nādhalavaṇayoḥ pramāṇe*: [The same applies] before the words *nātha* and *lavaṇa* when they denote a measure.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound where these two words as final members denote a measure (*pramāṇa*), the preceding member shall remain in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *aritragādham udakam* ("water as deep as a boat's oar"); the meaning is "that which has that [oar] as its measure. *golavaṇam* ("salt for a cow"); the meaning is "as much as is given to a cow. The word *aritram*, ending in the suffix *-itra*, is oxytone (*madhyodātta*). "Measure" (*pramāṇa*) here means quantity or mere delimitation, and not specifically length. Why "in the sense of measure"? Consider *paramagādham* ("extremely deep").
[Sūtra 3739: *dāyādyaṃ dāyāde* (A 6.2.5). [The word *dāyādya* retains its original form when followed by *dāyāda*.]

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛti-svara*). *Dhanadāyādaḥ*. The word *dhana*, ending in the suffix *kyu*, is udātta on its first syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*). Why "inheritance" (*dāyādya*)? [Answer: *Paramadāyādaḥ*. SK 3740:

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when followed by *ciram* or *kṛcchram*, the first member which expresses an obstruction (*pratibandha*) retains its original accent. *Gamanaciram*. *Vyāharaṇakṛcchram*. Because of a deficiency in the causes [for action], the act of going becomes delayed for a long time and is joined with difficulty; thus it arises as an obstruction. Why "obstruction"? [Answer: *Mūtrakṛcchram* ("difficult urination").

SK 3741: *pade 'padeśe* (A 6.2.7). When the word *pada* following [a compound] signifies a pretext (*vyāja*), the preceding member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) in a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Examples: *mūtrapadena prasthitaḥ* ("set out with the pretext of urinating"), *uccārapadena*. The word *mūtra* ends in the suffix *ghañ*; the word *uccāra* also ends in *ghañ* and has its final syllable acute by the rule *thā-tha-ādi-svareṇa*. Why "when not a pretext"? Consider *viṣṇupadam*. SK 3742: *nivāte vātatrāṇe* (A 6.2.8). [The preceding member retains its original accent] when *nivāta* means a shelter from the wind.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the word *nivāta*, meaning "protection from wind," follows, the first member retains its original form (*prakṛti-svara*). Examples: *kuṭī-nivātam*, *kuḍya-nivātam*. The word *kuṭī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* (belonging to the *gaurādi* group); the word *kuḍya* ends in the suffix *ḍyañ*. Others say it ends in *yañ*. Why "when meaning protection from wind"? [Counter-example: *rājanivāte vasati* ("he lives in a king's shelter"). This word *nivāta* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) for "side" or "flank. SK 3743: In the case of *śārada*, when it does not denote a season, [the first member retains its original form]. (A 6.2.9)

*Ārtava* means "born in the season" (*ṛtau bhavam*). When the word *śārada*, which denotes something other than that [seasonal meaning], follows as the second member in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the first member shall have its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Example: *rajjuśāradam udakam* ("freshly drawn water"). The word *śārada* here has the sense of "new. Its analysis (*vigraha*) is not within its own constituent parts (*asvapadavigraha*). It means "just now drawn from a rope" (*rajjoḥ sadya uddhṛtam*). The word *rajju* is derived with the suffix *asuṇ* after the root *sṛj*, and is thus established as having an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). Why "not seasonal" (*anārtave*)? Consider: *uttamaśāradam* ("the best autumn"). (Pāṇini 6.2.10: *adhvaryukaṣāyayor jātau*).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound following these two [words] when they denote a genus (*jāti*), the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Examples: *kaṭhādhvaryuḥ*, *dauvārikakaṣāyam*. The word *kaṭha* ends in the suffix *ac* added after the root *kath* (belonging to the *pacādi* class). From that, by the rule *vaiśampāyanāntevāsibhyaś ca*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied; then, by the rule *kaṭhacarakāl luk*, there is elision of the *ṇini*. The word *dauvārika* ends in the suffix *ṭhak* meaning "appointed at the gate" (*dvāri niyuktaḥ*), and it is oxytone (*antodātta*). Why "when denoting a genus"? Consider *paramādhvaryuḥ*. (A 6.2.11) [The first member retains its original accent] in the words *sadṛśa* and *pratirūpa* when they signify similarity (*sādṛśya*).

Of these two, the former [is used] by its own nature (*prakṛtyā*). [The word *pitṛsadṛśaḥ*] means "resembling a father. Why [is it said] "in the sense of resemblance" (*sādṛśye*)? [Consider: *paramasadṛśaḥ*. In this case, the meaning of the compound is "being honored," not "resemblance. In a *dvigu* [compound], when the final member denotes a measure (*pramāṇa*), the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) in that *tatpuruṣa* compound. [Example: *prācyasaptasamaḥ*. [Analysis: "Seven years are its measure" (*sapta samāḥ pramāṇam asya*). [By the rule] *pramāṇe lo dvigor nityam*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *mātrac*. Thus: *prācyasaptasamaḥ*. Why "in a *dvigu*" (*dvigau*)? [Consider: *vrīhiprasthaḥ*. Why "when denoting a measure" (*pramāṇe*)? [Consider: *paramasaptasamam*.

SK 3747: In a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the word *vāṇija-* follows, the first member denoting "that which is to be gone to" (*gantavya*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Examples: *madravāṇijaḥ*, *govāṇijaḥ*. These are locative compounds (*saptamīsamāsa*). The word *madra* ends in the suffix *-rak*. Why say "that which is to be gone to"? [Counter-example: *paramavāṇijaḥ*. SK 3748: In a neuter compound, the first members *mātra*, *upajñā*, *upakrama*, and *chāyā* retain their original accent when followed by another word. (A 6.2.14)

In the case of *mātrā* and so forth, when they follow [another word] in a neuter Tatpuruṣa compound, the same applies. *Bhikṣāmātram* means "of the same measure as alms. The word *bhikṣā* ends in the suffix *ap*, according to the rule *guroś ca halaḥ*. *Pāṇinyupajñam*: the word *pāṇini* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*). *Nandopakramam*: the word *nanda* ends in the suffix *ac*, according to the rule *pacādyac*. *Iṣucchāyam*: the word *iṣu* has its first syllable accented acute because it contains the *niṭ* marker. Why "in the neuter"? [Consider: *kuḍyacchāyā*. (SK 3749) *Sukhapriyayor hite* (A 6.2.15).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound where these two [words] have "beneficial" (*hita*) as their subsequent member, it is likewise so: *gamanapriyam* ("pleasant for going"), *gamanasukham* ("comfortable for going"). In the word *gamana*, the accent is that of the *liṭ*-suffix. What is the purpose of [specifying] "beneficial"? [Consider: *paramasukham* ("supreme happiness"). And when "pleasure" (*prīti*) is understood: what was stated previously applies when pleasure is implied. *brāhmaṇasukhaṃ pāyasam* ("the milk-rice is pleasing to the Brahmin"); *chātrapriyo 'nadhyāyaḥ* ("the holiday is dear to the student"). The words *brāhmaṇa* and *chātra* are oxytone due to the accent of their respective suffixes. What is the purpose of [specifying] "pleasure"? [Consider: *rājasukham* ("the king's happiness").

SK 3751: *svaṃ svāmini* (A 6.2.17). When the word *svāmin* follows, a preceding member denoting "one's own" (*sva*) likewise [retains its original accent]. Example: *gosvāmī*. Why say "one's own"? [Counter-example: *paramasvāmī*. SK 3752: *patyāv aiśvarye* (A 6.2.18). [The same applies] when the word *pati* follows, provided it signifies lordship (*aiśvarya*).

*damūnā*, *gṛhapatiḥ*, *dame*. (Pāṇini 6.2.19) In a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the word *pati* follows and denotes lordship (*aiśvarya*), these [words] do not retain their original form (*prakṛti*). The lord of the earth: *bhūpatiḥ*. Lord of speech: *vākpatiḥ*. Lord of thought: *citpatiḥ*. Lord of the remarried woman: *didhiṣūpatiḥ*.

In the scope already mentioned, [the word] *bhuvanam* [is formed] according to Pāṇini 6.2.20; for example, *bhuvanapatiḥ*. The word *bhuvana* ends in the suffix *kyun*, according to the rule "after the roots *bhū*, *sū*, *dhū*, and *bhrasj*.
According to Pāṇini 6.2.21, [the suffix *kan* is applied] when there is a possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) regarding that which is suspected, afflicted, or near at hand.

The determination of existence (*astitvādhyavasāya*) is *saṃbhāvana* (possibility). There is the suspicion of going; there is the hindrance to going; there is the proximity of going. Or rather, it is possible that going is suspected, hindered, or [considered] very near. What is the purpose of the term *saṃbhāvane*? [Answer: *paramanedīyaḥ* (extremely near). Regarding the rule *pūrve bhūtapūrve* (A 6.2.22): *āḍhyo bhūtapūrvaḥ* becomes *āḍhyapūrvaḥ*. In the context of grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*), the word *pūrva* signifies "having been previously" (*bhūtapūrve*). Why is *bhūtapūrve* specified? [Counter-example: *paramapūrvaḥ* (simply "previous").

SK 3757: *savidha-sanīḍa-samaryāda-saveśa-sadeśeṣu sāmīpye* (A 6.2.23). In these [words], when used in the sense of proximity, the preceding member remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *madra-savidham*, *gāndhāra-sanīḍam*, *kāśmīra-samaryādam*, *madra-saveśam*, *madra-sadeśam*. Why "in the sense of proximity"? [Counter-example: *sa-maryādam kṣetram* ("a field with a boundary"), *caitra-samaryādam* ("having a boundary belonging to Caitra"). SK 3758: *vispaṣṭādīni guṇavacaneṣu* (A 6.2.24). [Words] beginning with *vispaṣṭa* remain in their original form when followed by words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*).

*vispaṣṭakaṭukam*. In *vispaṣṭa*, the word *vispaṣṭa* has the udātta accent on its first syllable because it belongs to the group beginning with *gati* and *anantara*. Why [is the word] *vispaṣṭa* mentioned? [To exclude examples like] *paramalavaṇam*. Why [is the word] *guṇa* mentioned? [To exclude examples like] *vispaṣṭabrāhmaṇaḥ*. [The words are: *vispaṣṭa*, *vicitra*, *vyakta*, *saṃpanna*, *paṇḍita*, *kuśala*, *capala*, *nipuṇa*. Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.25: *śrajyāvamakanpāpavatsu bhāve karmadhāraye*.

When the word *avama*—which possesses the substitutes *śra*, *jya*, *kan*, and so forth—and when the second member (*uttarapada*) contains the word *pāpa*, the first member (*pūrvapada*) expressing a state (*bhāva*) remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *gamana-śreṣṭham*, *gamana-jyāyaḥ*, *gamana-avamam*, *gamana-kaniṣṭham*, *gamana-pāpiṣṭham*. Why say "and so forth" (*śretyādi*)? [To exclude cases like] *gamana-śobhanam*. Why say "expressing a state" (*bhāve*)? [To exclude cases where the first member is not a state, such as] *gamyate 'nena iti gamanam* ("that by which one goes is going"). [In this case: *gamanaṃ śreyaḥ* = *gamana-śreyaḥ*. Why say "the substitute *ka*" (*keti*)? [To ensure the rule does not apply] in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). SK 3760: And *kumāra* [remains unchanged] in a *karmadhāraya* compound. Example: *kumāra-śramaṇā*. The word *kumāra* is udātta on the final syllable.
SK 3761: *ādiḥ pratyenasi* (A 6.2.27).

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, when *pratyenas* follows, the first syllable of *kumāra* is acute (*udātta*). One whose sin (*enas*) has departed is *pratyenas*; thus, *kumārapratyenāḥ*. SK 3762: *pūgeṣv anyatarasyām* (A 6.2.28). [In a *karmadhāraya* compound] when a group name (*pūga*) follows, the first syllable of *kumāra* is optionally acute. Thus, *kumārajīmūtaḥ* or *kumārajīmūtaḥ*.

The term *pūga* refers to groups; among these, it is said: "kumāracātakāḥ" and "kumārajīmūtāḥ. In the absence of the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*), the form remains simply "kumāraśca" [by A 2.1.59].

According to A 6.2.29, *igantakālakapālabhagālaśrāveṣu dvigau*, [the final member of a *dvigu* compound ending in a vowel or *ka* retains its original accent when followed by *kāla*, *kapāla*, *bhagāla*, or *śrāva*.]

In these cases, it is first by its own nature (*prakṛti*). "Five *aratnis* are its measure" is *pañcāratniḥ*. "Existent for ten months" is *daśamāsyaḥ*; "existed for five months" is *pañcamāsyaḥ*. Under the governing rule "that which is requested for that" (*tam adhīṣṭa-*), the suffix *yap* is applied after a *dvigu* compound: *pañcakapālaḥ*, *pañcabhagālaḥ*, *pañcaśarāvaḥ*. By the rule *nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ*, the word *pañcan* has the acute accent on its first syllable. What about in cases where the [final member] does not end in a short vowel (*iganta*)? *pañcāśvaḥ*. Why "in a *dvigu* compound"? Consider *paramāratniḥ*. SK 3764: *bahv anyatarasyām* (A 6.2.30). [The feminine suffix *īp* is optionally applied after a *dvigu* ending in *bahu-*. *bahukhaṭvā*, *bahukhaṭvī*. *bahuyavaḥ*, *bahuyavī*. *bahutaṇḍulā*, *bahutaṇḍulī*. *bahudhānyā*, *bahudhānyī*. *bahuyavā*, *bahuyavī*. *bahutaṇḍulā*, *bahutaṇḍulī*. *bahudhānyā*, *bahudhānyī*. [The suffix *īp* is optionally applied after a *dvigu* ending in *bahu-*. *bahukhaṭvā*, *bahukhaṭvī*. *bahuyavaḥ*, *bahuyavī*. *bahutaṇḍulā*, *bahutaṇḍulī*. *bahudhānyā*, *bahudhānyī*. *bahuyavā*, *bahuyavī*. *bahutaṇḍulā*, *bahutaṇḍulī*. *bahudhānyā*, *bahudhānyī*.
