[The suffix *īp* is optionally applied after a *dvigu* ending in *bahu-*. *bahukhaṭvā*, *bahukhaṭvī*. *bahuyavaḥ*, *bahuyavī*. *bahutaṇḍulā*, *bahutaṇḍulī*. *bahudhānyā*, *bahudhānyī*. *bahuyavā*, *bahuyavī*. *bahutaṇḍulā*, *bahutaṇḍulī*.

Or likewise, when the word *bahu* [is used]: *bahvaratniḥ*, *bahumāsyaḥ*, *bahukapālaḥ*. The word *bahu* is oxytone (*antodātta*). When it undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution, the rule *udāttasvaritayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.4) applies.

A 6.2.31 states: *diṣṭivitastyoś ca*; in a *dvigu* compound, when these two follow, the preceding member may optionally remain in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *pañcadiṣṭiḥ*, *pañcavitastiḥ*.

SK 3766: *saptamī siddha-śuṣka-pakva-bandheṣv akālāt* (A 6.2.32). A locative case-ending word denoting time other than "time" (*akāla*) retains its original accent when followed by *siddha*, *śuṣka*, *pakva*, or *bandha*. Examples: *sāṅkāśyasiddhaḥ* ("accomplished in Sāṅkāśya"). Here, *sāṅkāśya-* ends in the suffix *ṇya*. *ātapaśuṣkaḥ* ("dried in the sun"). *bhrāṣṭrapakvaḥ* ("cooked in a frying pan"). Here, *bhrāṣṭra-* ends in the suffix *ṣṭran*. *cakrabandhaḥ* ("bound by a wheel"). The word *cakra-* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Why "other than time" (*akālāt*)? Consider *pūrvāhṇasiddhaḥ* ("accomplished in the forenoon"). [In this case,] the accent of the locative case is superseded by the accent of the whole compound (*kṛtsvara*), and thus it is restated here as an exception. SK 3767: *pari-prati-upa-apā varjyamāna-ahorātrāvayaveṣu* (A 6.2.33). The words *pari*, *prati*, *upa*, and *apa* retain their original accent when they signify exclusion (*varjyamāna*) and are followed by parts of a day or night.

These [prefixes] are [accented with udātta] when the following word (*uttarapada*) denotes that which is excluded (*varjyamāna*) by nature, or when it denotes a part of a day or night. Examples: *paritrigartaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("It rained all around Trigarta"); *pratipūrvāhṇam* ("toward the forenoon"); *upapūrvāhṇam* ("up to the forenoon"); *upapūrvarātram* ("up to the first part of the night"); *apatrigartam* ("excluding Trigarta"). The prefixes [beginning with *prati*] are acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). Since this is already established for *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds, this rule is intended for the sake of *avyayībhāva* compounds. In these cases, the following word (*uttarapada*) is exclusively that which is excluded, because it is only those two [prefixes, *apa* and *pari*] that possess the sense of exclusion. Furthermore, parts of a day or night are also considered "excluded" in relation to those two. Why say "that which is excluded"? (Consider: *agniṃ prati* ("toward the fire"); *pratyagni*.

SK 3768: *rājanyabahuvacanadvandvendhakavṛṣṇiṣu* (A 6.2.34). In a *dvandva* compound denoting members of the *rājanya* (kṣatriya) class that ends in the plural and refers to the Andhaka or Vṛṣṇi clans, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛti-svara*). Examples: *śvāphalkacaitrakāḥ*; *śinivāsudevāḥ*. Here, *śini-* is acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of being a name; it is used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇayā*) to refer to his descendant. Why "denoting a *rājanya*"? Consider: *dvaipyabhaimāyanāḥ*. Those born on an island are *dvaipyāḥ*; the youthful descendant of Bhīma is *bhaimāyanaḥ*. These belong to the Andhaka and Vṛṣṇi clans, but they are not *rājanyas*.

The mention of *rājanya* here is for the purpose of including those Kṣatriyas who belong to consecrated lineages; these [others] are not like that. Why is the plural used? [To include] Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva. What is the purpose of the rule regarding *dvandva* compounds? [To exclude cases such as] "the princes of the Vṛṣṇis" (*vṛṣṇikumārāḥ*). What is the purpose of the restriction to the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis? [To exclude cases such as] "the Kurus and Pañcālas" (*kurupañcālāḥ*). SK 3769: *saṃkhyā*.

In a *dvandva* compound, a preceding member denoting a number remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *dvādaśa* ("twelve"), *trayodaśa* ("thirteen"). In the case of *tri*, the substitution of *traya-* is prescribed as having an acute accent on the first syllable.
SK 3770: *ācāryopasarjanaś cāntevāsī* (A 6.2.36).

In a *dvandva* compound consisting of pupils (*antevāsin*) who have as their subordinate member (*upasarjana*) a teacher (*ācārya*), the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Examples: *pāṇinīyarauḍhīyāḥ*. These two [words] are middle-acute (*madhyodātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix *cha*. The mention of "having a teacher as the subordinate member" is an adjective qualifying the *dvandva* itself; it is so that the entire *dvandva* may be understood as having the teacher as its subordinate member. Therefore, this does not apply here: *pāṇinīyadevadattau* (where Devadatta is not a pupil of Pāṇini). Why say "teacher"? [Counter-example: *chāndasavaiyākaraṇāḥ* (where both are students, not teacher-student pairs). Why say "pupil"? [Counter-example: *āpiśalapāṇinīye śāstre* (where both are names of treatises). SK 3771: *kārtakaujapādayaś ca* (A 6.2.37). The compounds beginning with *kārtakaujapa* also [retain the original accent of the first member].

In a *dvandva* compound, the first member retains its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *kārtakaujapau* (the descendants of Kṛta and Kujapa); these two end in the suffix *aṇ*, meaning "this belongs to Kṛta" and "this belongs to Kujapa. *sāvarṇimāṇḍūkeyau*. [The following list applies: *mahān-vrīhi-*, *aparāhṇa-*, *gṛṣṭi-*, *iṣvāsa-*, *jābāla-*, *bhārata-*, *hailihila-*, *raurava-*, and *pravṛddha-* (Pāṇini 6.2.38).

The word *maha-* is acutely accented on the final syllable when it occurs naturally as the first member in compounds with the ten items beginning with *vrīhi* (rice): *mahāvrīhiḥ*, *mahāparāhṇaḥ*, *mahāgṛṣṭiḥ*, *maheṣvāsaḥ*, *mahāhailihilaḥ*. This accentuation applies specifically to the compound prescribed by the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.61). It does not apply here: *mahato vrīhiḥ* → *mahadbrīhiḥ*. And [the word] *kṣullaka-* is [optionally acutely accented on the final syllable] in the compound *vaiśvadeva*: *cān mahān*. Thus, we have *kṣullakavaiśvadevam* and *mahāvaiśvadevam*. [Derivation: from the root √lā ("to take") with the prefix *kṣudh-*, we derive *kṣulla-* in the sense "one who takes away hunger. From that, with the suffix *ka* in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñātādi*), the word *kṣullaka-* has the acute accent on the final syllable.

SK 3774: *uṣṭraḥ* [is compounded] with *sādi* and *vāmin* (A 6.2.40). Examples: *uṣṭrasādī*, *uṣṭravāmī*. The word *uṣṭra* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) because it is derived from the root *uṣ* with the suffix *ṣṭran*. SK 3775: *go* [is compounded] with *sāda*, *sādi*, and *sārathi* (A 6.2.41).
gosādaḥ, gosādiḥ, gosārathiḥ. [SK 3776] kurugārhapata-riktaguru-asūta-jarati-aślīla-dṛḍharūpa-apāra-ivaḍava-taitila-kadrū-paṇya-kambala dāsībhārāṇāṃ ca (A 6.2.42).

In these seven compounds, as well as in *dāsībhāra* and others, the first member (*pūrvapada*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). For example: *kurūṇāṃ gārhapatam* becomes *kurugārhapatam*. Here, the word *kuru* ends in the suffix *-u*. It should be stated that this applies to *vṛji* as well: *vṛjigārhapatam*; the word *vṛji* is acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). In *rikto guruḥ*, it becomes *riktaguruḥ*; according to the rule "optionally in the case of *rikta*," the word *rikta* is acute-accented on the first syllable. In *asūtā jaratī*, it becomes *asūtajaratī*. In *aślīlā dṛḍharūpā*, it becomes *aślīladṛḍharūpā*; the word *aślīla* is acute-accented on the first syllable because it is a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*).

That which possesses *śrī* is called *ślīla*. The suffix *lac* is applied because it belongs to the *sidhmādi* group; the substitution of *l* for *r* occurs because it belongs to the *kapilakādi* group. *Pārevaḍavā* means "like a mare on the far shore. Due to a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*), this is a compound in the sense of "likeness" (*iva*), and there is no elision of the case-ending. The word *pāra* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable) because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group. *Taitilakadrūḥ* means "the female of the Taitila birds. [The term] *taitila* ends in the suffix *aṇ*, meaning "the descendant of Titili" or "his pupil. The word *paṇya* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) because it ends in the suffix *yat*. It should be stated that the form *paṇyakambalaḥ* is used when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

In other cases, such as when "paṇitavya" is combined with "kambala," the rule *samāsāntodāttatva* (the final syllable of the compound being udātta) applies; however, for a specifically prescribed compound ending in a *kṛtya* suffix, this particular accent is ordained by the rule *kṛtyāḥ*. For example: *dāsyā bhāraḥ* becomes *dāsībhāraḥ*, and *devahūtiḥ*. Whatever *tatpuruṣa* compound is intended to have the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of its first member, even if no specific statement has been made regarding it, all such cases are to be understood as included within the category of *dāsībhāra* and similar forms. As in: *sa rāye sa puraṃdhyām*.

*Pura* means "body" (*śarīra*), derived from the sense "that in which something is placed" (*dhīyate asyām*). The suffix *ki* is applied according to the rule *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca*. The elision of the case-ending (*aluk*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*). The word *pura* is acutely accented on the first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasya*.

According to the rule *caturthī tadarthe* (A 6.2.46), when the subsequent member expresses the purpose of that which is denoted by a word ending in the dative case, that dative-final word retains its original form (*prakṛti*). For example: *yūpāya dāru* becomes *yūpadāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post").
SK 3778 *arthe* (A 6.2.44): When followed by the word *artha*, a word ending in the dative case remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). Example: *devārtham*.
SK 3779 *kte ca* (A 6.2.45): [The same applies] when followed by a word ending in the suffix *kta*.
When followed by a word ending in *kta*, a word ending in the dative case retains its original form (*prakṛti*). *go-hitam*.

(SK 3780) In a *karmadhāraya* compound, when followed by a word ending in *kta*, a preceding word that does not end in *niṣṭhā* retains its original form. *śreṇi-kṛtāḥ*. The word *śreṇi* is udātta on the first syllable. *pūga-kṛtāḥ*. The word *pūga* is udātta on the final syllable. Why "in a *karmadhāraya*"? [Consider: *śreṇyā kṛtam* = *śreṇi-kṛtam*. Why "not ending in *niṣṭhā*"? [Consider: *kṛtākṛtam*.

SK 3781 *ahīne dvitīyā* (A 6.2.47): In a compound ending in a word with the suffix *kta* that expresses "not inferior" (*ahīna*), a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) retains its original accent (*prakṛti-svara*). Examples: *kaṣṭaśritaḥ* ("one who has resorted to hardship"), *grāmagataḥ* ("one who has gone to the village"). The word *kaṣṭa* is oxytone (*antodātta*); the word *grāma* has the accent of the *ni*-suffix (*nitsvara*). Why say "not inferior"? Consider *kāntārātītaḥ* ("one who has passed beyond the forest"). It should be stated that this applies when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*). Thus, it does not apply here in *sukhaprāptaḥ* ("one who has attained happiness"). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *thātha-*. SK 3782 *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* (A 6.2.48):

[In a compound ending in a word with the suffix *kta* expressing "not inferior,"] a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) [retains its original accent] when it denotes the object (*karman*) [of the action expressed by the *kta*-suffix]. *kaṣṭaśritaḥ*: one who has resorted to hardship. *grāmagataḥ*: one who has gone to the village. The word *kaṣṭa* is oxytone (*antodātta*). The word *grāma* has the accent of the *ni*-suffix (*nitsvara*). Why "not inferior"? [Consider: *kāntārātītaḥ*: one who has passed beyond the forest. It should be stated that [this applies] when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*). Thus, it does not apply here in *sukhaprāptaḥ*: one who has attained happiness. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *thātha-*. SK 3782 *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*: [In a compound ending in a word with the suffix *kta* expressing "not inferior,"] a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) [retains its original accent] when it denotes the object (*karman*) [of the action expressed by the *kta*-suffix].

When a word expressing an object (*karman*) ending in a *kṛt* suffix with the suffix *kta* follows, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *tvotāsaḥ* ("protected by you"), *rudrahataḥ* ("struck by Rudra"), *mahārājahataḥ* ("struck by a great king"). [In the rule,] "Rudra" refers to a word ending in *r*. Why "object"? [Consider: *rathena yātaḥ* ("gone by chariot") = *rathayātaḥ*. SK 3783: *gatir anantaraḥ* (A 6.2.49). When a word expressing an object ending in *kta* follows immediately, a preceding *gati* particle remains in its original form. This is an exception to the rule *thā-tha-...* (A 6.2.144). Example: *purohitam* ("placed before"). Why "immediately"? [Consider: *abhyuddhṛtaḥ* ("drawn out"). However, when the first member is a *kāraka*, the accent of the *sthāthādi* group (A 6.2.144) prevails because it is taught later. Example: *dūrād āgataḥ* ("come from afar").

SK 3784: *tādau ca niti kṛtyatau* (A 6.2.50). When a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *ta*, followed by a *n*-augment and excluding the word *tu*, follows, a preceding *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Examples: *agne rāyo nṛtam asya prabhūtau* ("O Agni, [grant] abundance of wealth to this man"); *saṅgatiṃ goḥ* ("the acquisition of a cow"). This is an exception to the accent rule for *kṛt* suffixes (*kṛtsvara*). Why "beginning with *ta*" (*tādau*)? Consider *prajalpākaḥ*. Why "followed by *n*" (*niti*)? Consider *prakartā*; here the suffix ends in *tṛc*. Why "ending in *tu*" (*atau*)? Consider *āgantuḥ*. SK 3785: *tavai cāntaś ca yugapat* (A 6.2.51). When the suffix *tavai* follows, both the *gati* and the end of the word retain their original accents simultaneously.

In a word ending in a *pratyaya* (suffix), the final syllable is acute (*udātta*), and an immediately preceding *gati* (preverb) remains in its original form (*prakṛti-svara*); both of these [rules] apply simultaneously. For example: *anvetavā u*. This is an exception to the *kṛt-svara* rule. (A 6.2.52) *aniganto ’ñcatau vapratyaye*:

A *gati* that does not end in *i* remains in its original form when followed by the root *añc-* provided it ends in the suffix *va*. Example: *ye parāñcas tān* ("those who are turned away"). Why say "not ending in *i*"? Consider: *pratyañco yantu* ("let them go forward"). Because this rule is subsequent to the *kṛt-svara*, it prevails. Example: *jahi vṛṣṇyāni kṛṇuhī parācaḥ* ("strike down the virile powers; make them turn away"). Why say "provided it ends in the suffix *va*"? Consider: *udañcanam* ("a water-drawing vessel").

SK 3787 *nyadhī ca* (A 6.2.53): When followed by a word ending in the suffix *v*, even if it ends in a vowel (*iganta*), the words *ni* and *adhi* remain in their original form (*prakṛti*) before the root *añc*. Examples: *nyaṅṅuttānaḥ* ("lying face down") and *adhyaṅ* ("lying upon"). In the former, the vowel *a* of the root *añc* becomes *svarita* according to the rule *udāttasvaritayor yaṇ*. SK 3788 *īṣad anyatarasyām* (A 6.2.54): [The word *īṣat* remains in its original form] optionally.

*īṣat-kaḍāraḥ* ("slightly tawny"). In this case, the word *īṣat* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). In examples such as *īṣad-bhedaḥ*, the accent is simply that of the *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛtsvara*). SK 3789: *hiraṇyaparimāṇaṃ dhane* (A 6.2.55). A preceding member denoting a measure of gold (*suvarṇa*) optionally retains its original accent when followed by *dhana*. For example, *dvi-suvarṇam* means "that whose measure is two *suvarṇas*"; when this is a *dhana* (wealth), it becomes *dvisuvarṇa-dhanam*. Even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the option prevails because this rule is subsequent [to other rules]. Why say "gold" (*hiraṇya*)? [Counter-example: *prastha-dhanam* ("wealth measured by a *prastha*"). Why say "measure" (*parimāṇa*)? [Counter-example: *kāñcana-dhanam* ("gold-wealth"). Why say "wealth" (*dhana*)? [Counter-example: *niṣka-mālā* ("a necklace of *niṣkas*").

Pāṇini 6.2.56: *prathama* [is used] in the sense of "having recently attained" (*aciropasaṃpattau*). Alternatively, the word *prathama* remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*) when expressing novelty (*abhinavatve*). Example: *prathamavaiyākaraṇaḥ*. The meaning is: "one who has just now begun to study grammar. The word *prathama* is derived from the root *prath-* with the suffix *am*, and is not a *jha*-ending stem. Why say "recently" (*acira*)? [Counter-example: *prathamo vaiyākaraṇaḥ* ("the first grammarian"). Pāṇini 6.2.57: *katara* and *katama* [remain in their original form] in a *karmadhāraya* compound.

Or [it may be] by nature. *Katarakaṭhaḥ*. The mention of *karmadhāraya* is for the sake of subsequent rules; here, however, it is established simply because it is explicitly stated [in the rule]. SK 3792: *āryo brāhmaṇakumārayoḥ* (A 6.2.58). *Āryakumāraḥ*, *āryabrāhmaṇaḥ*. Because *ārya-* ends in the suffix *ṇya*, it has a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on its final syllable. Why "noble" (*ārya*)? [Consider: *paramabrāhmaṇaḥ*. Why "brāhmaṇa and so forth"? [Consider: *āryakṣatriyaḥ*. Only when it is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

SK 3793: In a *karmadhāraya* compound, the word *rājan* optionally remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by *brāhmaṇa* or *kumāra*. Examples: *rājabrāhmaṇaḥ*, *rājakumāraḥ*. The separation of this rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. SK 3794: In a *karmadhāraya* compound, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) remains in its original form when followed by *pratyenasi*. (A 6.2.60)

A word ending in the genitive case, such as *rājan* ("king"), remains in its original form when followed by *pratyenas* or another [word] in a compound: *rājapratyenas*. Why "genitive"? [To show that it does not apply] elsewhere; for example, it does not apply in other cases. SK 3795:

When a word ending in the suffix *kta* follows [another word] in a compound expressing the sense of "permanence" (*nitya*), the preceding member optionally remains in its original form. Example: *nityaprahasitaḥ*. This is a compound with a word denoting time (*kāla*) in the accusative case. The word *nitya*, ending in the suffix *tyap*, is udātta on the first syllable. The word *hasita* is udātta on the final syllable by the rule regarding *tha-tha-ādi* compounds. Why "expressing the sense of permanence"? [To show that it does not apply] in cases like *muhūrtaprahasitaḥ*.

SK 3796: In the case of a craftsman (*śilpin*), the word *grāma* may optionally remain in its original form [with its accent]. *grāmanāpitaḥ* ("the village barber"). The word *grāma* has its first syllable acute-accented (*ādyudātta*). Why "village"? [Counter-example: *paramanāpitaḥ* ("an excellent barber"). Why "craftsman"? [Counter-example: *grāmarathyā* ("the village road"). SK 3797: And the word *rājan* [remains in its original form] when it denotes praise (*praśaṃsā*). [A 6.2.63]

When followed by a word denoting an artisan (*śilpin*), the word *rājan* may optionally remain in its original form (*prakṛti*) when used for the purpose of praise. Examples: *rājanāpitaḥ* ("a barber who is a king") and *rājakulālaḥ* ("a potter who is a king"). Why "when used for praise"? Counter-example: *rājanāpitaḥ* (used without praise). Why "when followed by a word denoting an artisan"? Counter-example: *rājahastī* ("a royal elephant"). SK 3798: *ādir udāttaḥ* (A 6.2.64). This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*).

Pāṇini 6.2.65: *saptamī-hāriṇau dharmye ’haraṇe*. A word ending in the locative case and a word expressing "one who takes" (*hārin*) are both *ādyudātta* (have the acute accent on the first syllable) when followed by a word meaning "righteous" (*dharmya*), provided that the act does not involve taking away property. One who accepts what is given is called a "taker" (*hārī*). "Righteous" (*dharmya*) refers to that which is to be given as prescribed by custom. Examples: *mukuṭe-kārṣāpaṇaḥ* ("a kārṣāpaṇa coin for the crown"), *hale-dvipadikā* ("two paces for the plough"). This is a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) according to the rule *saṃjñāyām*. The elision of the case-ending (*aluk*) occurs by the rule *kāranāmni ca*. Examples: *yājñikāśvaḥ* ("a horse for the sacrificer"), *vaiyākaraṇahastī* ("an elephant for the grammarian"). In some cases, this custom dictates that a kārṣāpaṇa or similar coin must be given for items like a crown, while a horse or similar animal must be given for those such as a sacrificer. Why specify "righteous" (*dharmye*)? [To exclude cases where the giving is not customary].

*stamberamaḥ* (an elephant); *karmakaravarddhitaḥ* (one raised by a laborer). Why "not in the sense of taking" (*aharaṇe*)? As in *vāḍavaharaṇam*. This belongs to a mare (*vaḍavā*), hence it is *vāḍava*; that which is given after the sowing of seed for the sake of nourishing its body is called *haraṇa*. Even though the accent *kṛtsvara* [the acute on the final syllable of a *kṛt*-derivative] exists, it is overridden by the *hārisvara* [the acute on the first syllable of a word ending in *hārin*]; this is made known by the prohibition in the rule *aharaṇe*. Therefore, in the form *vāḍavahāryam*, the *hārisvara* is established. SK 3800: *yukte ca* (A 6.2.66).

In a compound expressing "being engaged in" (*yukta*), the first member has the acute accent on its initial syllable. As in *goballavaḥ* (a cow-herder). One who is intent upon what must be done is "engaged" (*yukta*).
SK 3801: In the case of *adhyakṣa* meaning "overseer," [the compound is neuter]; e.g., *gavādhyakṣaḥ*.
SK 3802: And when *pāpa* means "craftsman," [the compound is neuter].

In the case of *pāpanāpitaḥ* and *pāpāṇakaḥ*, only those [compounds] explicitly mentioned by their specific forms (*pratipadokta*) are included; therefore, it does not apply to a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). According to A 6.2.69, when contempt is expressed, the suffix *kan* is applied after a word denoting a lineage (*gotra*), a pupil (*antevāsin*), a young Brahmin (*māṇava*), or a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*).

*bhāryāsauśrutaḥ*: This is a derisive expression regarding the son of Suśruta, because his wife is the most prominent [member of the family]. *antevāsī*: A resident pupil. *kumārīdākṣāḥ*: Those who desire to obtain a young girl and study the treatises taught by Dākṣi and others are thus derided. *odanapāṇinīyāḥ*: "Those for whom rice-gruel is their only portion. *māṇava* refers to a young student; *bhikṣāmāṇavaḥ* means a young student who thinks, "I shall obtain alms. *bhayabrāhmaṇaḥ*: One who becomes a Brāhmaṇa out of fear. Why say "in the case of *gotra*, etc."? [Counter-example: *dāsīśrotriyaḥ* ("one whose Vedic scholar-wife is a slave-girl"). Why say "in the case of derision"? [Counter-example: *paramabrāhmaṇaḥ* ("an excellent Brāhmaṇa"). SK 3804: *aṅgāni maireye* (A 6.2.70). [The word *aṅga* is compounded with the name of a liquor to denote that liquor.]

*Maireya* is a specific type of intoxicant. *Madhumaireya*: here, *madhu* is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of that which is a modification of honey. Why [is it called] a "constituent part"? [Consider] *paramamaireya*. Why [is it called] *maireya*? [Consider] *puṣpāsava* (flower-liquor). [A 6.2.71:
Words denoting *bhakta* (food) [are compounded with words ending in the genitive case] when they signify things for the sake of that [food].

*Bhakta* means food. *Bhikṣākaṃsaḥ*, *bhājīkaṃsaḥ*: *bhikṣā* and the others are specific types of food. Why [is it called] "words denoting *bhakta*"? [Consider] *samāśālayaḥ*. Here, *samaśanam* is *samāśa*; thus, only the action is expressed. Why "for the sake of that"? [Consider] *bhikṣāpriyaḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; in this case, the first member has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

SK 3806: *gobinḍāla-siṃha-saindhaveṣūpamāne* (A 6.2.72). Examples: *dhānyagavaḥ*, *gobinḍālaḥ*, *tṛṇasiṃhaḥ*, *saktusaindhavaḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "grain like a cow" (*dhānyaṃ gaur iva*). This belongs to the *vyāghrādi* group. Grain arranged in the shape of a cow is called by the term *dhānyagavaḥ*. Why "when there is a standard of comparison" (*upamāne*)? [Consider: *paramasiṃhaḥ* ("a supreme lion"). SK 3807: *ake jīvikārthe* (A 6.2.73). [This rule applies when the suffix *aka* is present and the compound denotes one's means of livelihood.]

*dantalekhakaḥ* (tooth-scratcher): one whose livelihood is by means of scraping teeth; this is a *samāsa* compound meaning "one who constantly plays [at it]. Why [is the suffix] *aka* used? [Answer: *ramaṇīyakartā* (maker of beautiful things). Why [is it restricted to] "for the sake of a livelihood"? [Answer: *ikṣubhakṣikāṃ me dhārayasi* (you owe me a debt for eating sugarcane). [This is governed by] A 6.2.74: *prācāṃ krīḍāyām* ("in the sense of play, according to the Eastern grammarians").

In a compound denoting a game of the Easterners (*prāc*), when followed by a suffix ending in *aka*, the first member [of the compound] shall have its initial syllable acute-accented (*ādyudātta*). Example: *uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā* ("the game of breaking off *uddālaka* flowers"). The suffix *ṇvul* is applied here because it forms a name (*saṃjñāyām*). Why "of the Easterners" (*prācām*)? Example: *jīvaputrapracāyikā* ("the gathering of living sons"); this is a game of the Northerners (*udīcām*). Why "in a game" (*krīḍāyām*)? Example: *tava puṣpapracāyikā* ("your flower-gathering"); here *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of a turn or succession (*paryāye*). [This is governed by] A 6.2.75: *aṇi niyukte*.

In a compound ending in *aṇ*, when followed by another word expressing an agent (*niyuktavācin*), the first member is acute on its initial syllable, provided that the suffix *aṇ* does not follow the root *kṛ*. Examples: *tantuvāyaḥ* ("weaver"). Why "in the sense of a craftsman" (*śilpin*)? Consider *kāṇḍalāvaḥ* ("one who cuts stalks"). Why "not after the root *kṛ*"? Consider *kumbhakāraḥ* ("potter").

Also, in the case of a proper name (*saṃjñā*), when followed by a word ending in *aṇ*, the first member is acute on the first syllable. Example: *tantuvāyo nāma kṛmiḥ* ("the insect called *tantuvāya*"). The restriction "not after *kṛ*" still applies: *rathakāro nāma brāhmaṇaḥ* ("the Brāhmaṇa named *rathakāra*").

SK 3812: In the word *pāla*, [the vowel of the first member] is short when preceded by *go*, *tantri*, or *yava*. Examples: *gopālaḥ* (cowherd), *tantipālaḥ* (weaver), *yavapālaḥ* (barley-guard). This rule applies even when the meaning is not restricted [to a specific relationship]. Why say *go*? [Counter-example: *vatsapālaḥ* (calf-herder). Why say *pāle*? A word expressing a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is acute on its first syllable when it stands as a prior member before a word ending in the suffix *ṇini*, provided that the word is used in its primary sense (*prakṛti*). Examples: *uṣṭrakrīḍī* ("one who plays like a camel"), *dhvāṅkṣaravī* ("one who cries out like a crow"). The mention of "standard of comparison" is for the purpose of distinguishing the scope of this rule from the preceding one. Why "in its primary sense"? Consider *vṛkavañcī* ("one who deceives like a wolf"). Why the mention of "primary form" (*prakṛti*)? This is so that the rule applies only where the word expresses its meaning through its own base-form independently of any prefix (*upasarga*). It should not apply here: *gardabhoccārī* ("one who excretes like a donkey").

SK 3816 *dīrghakāśatuṣabhrāṣṭravaṭaṃ je* (A 6.2.82): [the same applies when these words] precede the suffix *je*. Examples: *dīrghajīvī*, *kāśajīvī*, *tuṣajīvī*, *bhrāṣṭrajīvī*, *vaṭajīvī*.

SK 3818 (*grāme ’nivasantaḥ*, A 6.2.84): When the word *grāma* follows, the preceding member is acute-accented, provided that it does not denote those who dwell there. In *guhodakam*, once the accent has been applied, there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) here. According to the rule *svarito vānudātte padādau*, it may optionally be circumflex (*svarita*) if the following word begins with an unaccented vowel. Why say "not entire"? Consider *śītodakam*. Examples: *gargatrirātraḥ* ("the three-night sacrifice of the Gargas"). Why "in a *dvigu*"? [Counter-example: *ahorātraḥ* ("day-and-night"). Why "denoting a rite"? SK 3832: In the case of the word *sabhā*, when it is neuter, [the first member has its final syllable accented with the *udātta*].

In a compound where *sabhā* occurs as the final member and the compound is neuter, the first member has its final syllable udātta. Examples: *gopālasabham*, *strīsabham*. Why "in *sabhā*"? Example: *brāhmaṇasenam*. Why "neuter"? Example: *rājasabhā*. SK 3837: *dikśabdā grāmajanapadākhyānacānarāṭeṣu* (A 6.2.103). Words denoting directions (*dikśabda*) are oxytone when followed by these [words]: names of villages (*grāma*), names of districts (*janapada*), narratives (*ākhyāna*), and *cānarāṭa*. Examples: *pūrveṣukāmaśamī* (East-Eṣukāmaśamī); *aparakṛṣṇamṛttikā* (West-Kṛṣṇamṛttikā). In the case of a district: *pūrvapañcālāḥ* (Eastern Pañcālas). SK 3840: *bahuvrīhau viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām* (A 6.2.106). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *viśva*, when it constitutes the first member (*pūrvapada*) and forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*), shall have its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the initial accent (*ādyudātta*) that would otherwise apply by virtue of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*). Examples: *viśvakarmā*, *viśvadevaḥ*; "the Lord of all the gods" (*āviśvadevaṃ satpatim*). Why "in a *bahuvrīhi*"? Consider: *viśve ca te devāś ca* = *viśvadevāḥ* ("all the gods"). Why "when it is a proper name"? Consider: *viśvadevaḥ* ("one who has all the gods [as deities]"). The section on *bahuvrīhi* continues until before the rule for *avyayībhāva*. SK 3841: *udarāśveṣuṣu* (A 6.2.107). [The word *viśva* is also *antodātta* when it is the first member in a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *udara*, *aśva*, or *iṣu*. Examples: *viśvōdaraḥ*, *viśvāśvaḥ*, *viśvēṣuḥ*. The word *viśva* is used here as a synonym for "all" (*sarva*). It does not mean "entire" (*kṛtsna*), because in that case the accent would be governed by the following rule (*viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām*). Nor does it mean "every single one" (*pratyeka*), because in that case the accent would be governed by the preceding rule (*bahuvrīhau viśvam*). Thus, it refers to something that is "not a part" (*asarvāvayava*) yet is "numerically complete" (*sakalasaṃkhyāparicchinna*). For example, "one whose belly contains all [food]" or "one who possesses all horses. In the case of *iṣu*, it means "one who possesses all arrows," such as Arjuna. The term *saṃjñāyām* ("in the sense of a name") continues to apply. [Examples: *vṛkodaraḥ*, *haryaśvaḥ*, *maheṣuḥ*.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound expressing censure, when *udara*, *aśva*, and *iṣu* follow, the first member has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*). [Examples: *ghaṭodaraḥ*, *kaṭukāśvaḥ*, *calācaleṣuḥ*. In the case of *anudaraḥ*, the rule *nañsubhyām* (A 6.2.172) applies by way of supersession (*vipratiṣedha*).
SK 3843 *nadī bandhuni* (A 6.2.109):

When the word *bandhu* follows, a preceding member ending in a feminine suffix (*nadī*) has its final syllable acutely accented in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Example: *gārgībandhuḥ*. Why "feminine suffix" (*nadī*)? Example: *brahmabandhuḥ*; here the word *brahman* is acutely accented on the first syllable. Why "when *bandhu* follows" (*bandhuni*)? Example: *gārgīpriyaḥ*. SK 3844 *niṣṭhopasargapūrvam anyatarasyām* (A 6.2.110): [In a *bahuvrīhi*,] a word preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*) and ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix may optionally have its final syllable acutely accented.

A prior member ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix is optionally acute on the final syllable. Examples: *pradhautapādaḥ*. Why "ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix"? Consider *prasevalamukhaḥ*. Why "preceded by a prefix"? Consider *śuṣkamukhaḥ*. (SK 3845) *uttarapadādiḥ*: The governing rule for the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) extends until the end of the *ā* section [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī]. However, the governing rule for the "initial" (*ādi*) extends as far as the rule *prakṛtyā bhagālam* [A 6.2.117].
SK 3846 *karṇo varṇalakṣaṇāt* (A 6.2.112):

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *karṇa*, when following a word denoting color (*varṇa*) or a word denoting a mark (*lakṣaṇa*), has its first syllable acute-accented (*ādyudātta*). Examples: *śuklakarṇaḥ* ("white-eared"), *śaṅkukarṇaḥ* ("conch-eared"). Why "karṇa"? [Counter-example: *śvetapādaḥ* ("white-footed"). Why "denoting color or a mark"? [Counter-example: *śobhanakarṇaḥ* ("handsome-eared"). SK 3847 *saṃjñāupamānayoś ca* (A 6.2.113): [The word *karṇa*] also has its first syllable acute-accented when it follows a proper name (*saṃjñā*) or a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). [Examples: *kālakarṇiḥ* ("named Kālakaṛṇa"), *vyāghrakarṇaḥ* ("tiger-eared").]

The word *karṇa* has an initial udātta accent. Examples: *maṇikarṇaḥ* ("jewel-eared"); in the sense of comparison (*aupamye*), *gokarṇaḥ* ("ox-eared"). A 6.2.114 states that *kaṇṭha*, *pṛṣṭha*, *grīvā*, and *jaṅghā* [have an initial udātta] in a Bahuvrīhi compound when they denote a name (*saṃjñā*) or a comparison (*aupamya*). Examples: *śitikaṇṭhaḥ* ("blue-throated"), *kāṇḍapṛṣṭhaḥ* ("arrow-backed"), *sugrīvaḥ* ("handsome-necked"), *nāḍījaṅghaḥ* ("long-shanked"). In the sense of comparison: *kharakaṇṭhaḥ* ("donkey-throated"), *gopṛṣṭhaḥ* ("cow-backed"), *aśvagrīvaḥ* ("horse-necked"), *gojaṅghaḥ* ("ox-shanked").

SK 3849: *śṛṅgam avasthāyāṃ ca* (A 6.2.115). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *śṛṅga* has its first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*) when it denotes a state (*avasthā*), as well as when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*) or a comparison (*upamā*). Examples: *udgataśṛṅgaḥ* ("one with horns grown out"), *dvyaṅgulaśṛṅgaḥ* ("one with horns two fingers long"). Here, "state" refers to a particular stage of life of a cow or similar animal, such as the emergence of its horns. In the sense of a name: *ṛṣyaśṛṅgaḥ*. In the sense of a comparison: *meṣaśṛṅgaḥ* ("horn-like," i.e., having horns like those of a ram). Why specify "state"? [Counter-example: *sthūlaśṛṅgaḥ* ("thick-horned"). SK 3850: *naño jaramaramitramṛtāḥ* (A 6.2.116). [In a *bahuvrīhi*, the words *jara*, *mara*, *mitra*, and *mṛta* following the negative particle *nañ* have their first syllable acute.]

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, these words following the negative particle *nañ* are udātta on their first syllable: *na me jarā ajaram*, *amaram*, *amitramardaya*, *śravo deveṣv amṛtam*. Why "following *nañ*"? [Consider] *brāhmaṇamitram*. Why "in a *bahuvrīhi*"? [Consider] *aśatruḥ*. (SK 3851) *manas-* following *su-* [is udātta], except for *loman-* and *uṣas-*. (A 6.2.117)

After the particle *su*, a word ending in *-man* that is unaccented on its first syllable shall be acute-accented, provided it is not *loman* or *uṣas*. This is an exception to the rule *nañ-subhyām*. Examples: *sukarmāṇaḥ*, *suyujaḥ*; *sa no vakṣad animānaḥ suvahnā*; *śivā paśubhyaḥ sumanāḥ suvarcāḥ*; *supeśaskarati*. Why "after *su*"? Consider *kṛtakarmā*. Why "ending in *-man*"? Consider *surājā*. Why "not *loman* or *uṣas*"? Consider *sulomā*, *sūṣāḥ*. However, in the case of the suffix *kap*, because it applies later, the accent of *kap* takes precedence; thus we have *sukarmakaḥ*, *susrotaskaḥ*. Also, *kratu* and others [are acute-accented after *su*]. (A 6.2.118)

When followed by *su*, [the first member of a bahuvrīhi compound] shall be udātta on its initial syllable. As in: *sābhrājyāya sukratuḥ* (of good intellect), *supratīkaḥ* (of beautiful countenance), *suhavyaḥ* (of good offerings), *supratūrtim anehasam* (of swift and unerring course). Pāṇini A 6.2.119 states: "In the Veda, a two-syllabled word that is udātta on its initial syllable [becomes udātta on its initial syllable when following *su* in a bahuvrīhi]. That is to say, when a two-syllabled word is udātta on its initial syllable, it becomes udātta on its initial syllable when it follows *su* in a bahuvrīhi compound. Examples: *adhā svaśvāḥ* (then with good horses); *surathān ātithigve* (good chariots for Ātithigva). Here, *aśva* and *ratha* are udātta on their initial syllables due to the *nit*-accent (A 6.1.197). Why specify "udātta on the initial syllable"? Consider: *yā subāhuḥ* (she who has beautiful arms). Why specify "two-syllabled"? Consider: *sugurasatsu-hiraṇyaḥ* (with beautiful bellies and gold). Here, the word *hiraṇya* consists of three syllables.

SK 3854: In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the words *vīra* and *vīrya*, when following the particle *su*, are acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*). For example: *suvīreṇa rayiṇā* ("with wealth consisting of excellent heroes") and *suvīryasya gomataḥ* ("of one possessing excellent heroic power and cattle"). The word *vīrya* ends in the suffix *yat*. Since the rule "the word ending in *yat*, except for *nau*, is acute on the first syllable" (*yato ’nāvaḥ*) would already have provided the acute accent for *vīrya*, the explicit mention of *vīrya* here is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this specific rule does not apply there. For if it did apply there, the desired result would have been established by the preceding rule alone. SK 3855: In an *avyayībhāva* compound, the words *kūla*, *tīra*, *tūla*, *mūla*, *śālā*, *akṣa*, and *sama* [are acute on the first syllable].

*upakūlam*, *upatīram*, *upatūlam*, *upamūlam*, *upaśālam*, *upākṣam*, *suṣamam*, *niḥṣamam*—these belong to the class beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*. Why is there mention of *kūla* and the others? [To exclude cases like] *upakumbham*. Why is it specified as being in an *avyayībhāva* compound? [To exclude cases like] *paramakūlam*. In a *dvigu* compound, the words *kaṃsa*, *mantha*, *śūrpa*, *pāyya*, and *kāṇḍa* [take the suffix *ac*]. Examples: *dvikaṃsaḥ*, *dvimanthaḥ*, *dviśūrpaḥ*, *dvipāyyam*, *dvikāṇḍam*. Why is it specified as being in a *dvigu*? [To exclude cases like] *paramakaṃsaḥ*.

SK 3857: *tatpuruṣe śālāyāṃ napuṃsake* (A 6.2.123). In a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *śālā*, when it is neuter, the final member (*uttarapada*) has its first syllable acute-accented (*ādyudātta*). Example: *brāhmaṇaśālam*. Why "in a *tatpuruṣa*"? Example: *dṛḍhaśālaṃ brāhmaṇakulam* ("a firm house belonging to a Brahmin family"). Why "in the case of *śālā*"? Example: *brāhmaṇasenam* ("an army of Brahmins"). Why "when neuter"? Example: *brāhmaṇaśālā* ("the house of a Brahmin," feminine). SK 3858: *kanthā ca* (A 6.2.124). [The same rule applies] when the final member is *kanthā*. Example: *māhiṣmatīkantham*. Why "in a *tatpuruṣa*"? Example: *dṛḍhakanthā māhiṣmatī* ("the city of Māhiṣmatī has a firm rampart"). Why "when neuter"? Example: *māhiṣmatīkanthā* ("the rampart of Māhiṣmatī," feminine). SK 3859: *upamānaṃ śabdārthaprakṛtāv eva* (A 6.2.125). When the final member is *kanthā*, the first syllable of the preceding member (*upamāna*) is acute-accented only if it is the actual form of the object being compared. Example: *kharakaṇtham* ("a donkey-rampart"). Why "only if it is the actual form of the object being compared"? Example: *uṣṭrakanthā māhiṣmatī* ("Māhiṣmatī has a rampart like a camel's neck"). Why "when neuter"? Example: *uṣṭrakanthā māhiṣmatī* ("Māhiṣmatī has a camel-like rampart," feminine). SK 3860: *paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* (A 2.4.26). A *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa* take the gender and number of their final member (*para*). SK 3861: *pūrvavad aśvavaḍavau* (A 2.4.27). The *dvandva* *aśvavaḍavau* takes the gender and number of its first member (*pūrvavat*). SK 3862: *hemantaśiśirāv ahorātre ca cchandasi* (A 2.4.28). In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the *dvandva* *hemantaśiśirau* and *ahorātre* take the gender and number of their first member. SK 3863: *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi* (A 2.4.29). The words *rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha*, when forming the final members of a *dvandva* or *tatpuruṣa*, are masculine. SK 3864: *apathaṃ napuṃsakam* (A 2.4.30). The word *apatha* is neuter. SK 3865: *ardharca-ādayaḥ puṃsi ca* (A 2.4.31). The group beginning with *ardharca* may optionally be masculine. SK 3866: *paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* (A 2.4.26). [Reiteration of the previous rule. SK 3867: *upasajjanaṃ pūrvam* (A 2.2.30). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is placed first. SK 3868: *rājā ca* (A 2.2.31). The word *rājan* is also placed first in a *bahuvrīhi*. SK 3869: *dvy-ekayor dvivacanaikavacane* (A 1.4.22). The dual suffixes are used for two things, and the singular suffixes for one thing. SK 3870: *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (A 1.4.21). The plural suffixes are used for many things. SK 3871: *sy-ād-āviṣṭāstibhyo 'dbhyaḥ* (A 7.3.109). After the personal endings *si*, *ādi*, *āva*, *āma*, *it*, *as*, and *ti*, the augment *at* is inserted before the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes. SK 3872: *ārdhadhātukaṃ śeṣaḥ* (A 3.4.114). All suffixes other than those defined as *sārvadhātuka* are *ārdhadhātuka*. SK 3873: *ārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ* (A 7.2.35). The augment *iṭ* is added to an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (other than *y*). SK 3874: *uto vṛddhir luki hali* (A 7.3.89). After a verbal root ending in *u*, the substitution *vṛddhi* occurs before a *hal*-beginning *ārdhadhātuka* suffix that causes the elision (*luk*) of the *vikaraṇa* suffix *śnu*. SK 3875: *guṇo yaṅlukyoḥ* (A 7.3.92). In the *yaṅ* formation and the *yaṅluk* formation, the substitution *guṇa* occurs for the penultimate vowel of a verbal root ending in *u*. SK 3876: *nityaṃ kauṭilye gatau* (A 3.1.23). The suffix *yaṅ* is always applied after a verbal root meaning "motion" to express crookedness. SK 3877: *gāṅ liṭi* (A 2.4.49). In the *liṭ* tense, the substitute *gāṅ* is applied for the verbal root *iṇ*. SK 3878: *āta au ṇalaḥ* (A 7.1.34). For the *ṇal* suffix, the substitution *au* occurs for a verbal root ending in *ā*. SK 3879: *aster bhūḥ* (A 2.4.52). In the *liṭ* tense, the substitute *bhū* is applied for the verbal root *as*. SK 3880: *bruvo vaciḥ* (A 2.4.53). In the *liṭ* tense, the substitute *vac* is applied for the verbal root *brū*. SK 3881: *cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ* (A 2.4.54). In the *liṭ* tense, the substitute *khyāñ* is applied for the verbal root *cakṣiṅ*. SK 3882: *vacy-aś-osty-arthānāṃ bhāve* (A 3.3.110). The suffix *ghañ* is applied after verbal roots meaning "to speak" (*vac*), "to go" (*as*), and "to be" (*ty-artha*) to denote an action (*bhāva*). SK 3883: *saṃpṛca-anurudha-avasa-abhra-lya-kṣi-ahi-asū-asū-yā-jā-vā-padi-kṣi-nī

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in a neuter noun, the word *kanthā* as the final member (*uttarapada*) has its first syllable (*ādyudātta*) accented. Examples: *sauśamikantham*, *āhvarakantham*. Why "in the neuter"? Consider *dākṣikanthā* (which is feminine). Regarding the rule *ādiś cihaṇādīnām* (A 6.2.125): in a neuter *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *kanthā*, the first syllable of words such as *cihaṇa* is acute. Examples: *cihaṇakantham*, *mandurakantham*. Although the term "first syllable" (*ādi*) was already present [from the previous rule], its mention here again is for the purpose of ensuring that the first syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is also acute.

SK 3860: *cela-kheṭa-kaṭuka-kāṇḍa* [are compounds] in the sense of reproach (A 6.2.126). The words *cela* and so forth as final members [of these compounds] have their first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*). Examples: *putracela-* ("a worthless son"), *nāgarakheṭa-* ("a wretched town"), *dadhikaṭuka-* ("sour curds"), *prajākāṇḍa-* ("an incompetent offspring"). Because the reproach of sons and the like is expressed through their similarity to *cela* and the others, the compound is formed according to the *vyāghrādi* group. Why "in the sense of reproach"? Consider *paramacela-* ("an excellent garment"). SK 3861: *cīra* [as a final member] when it is a standard of comparison (A 6.2.127).
*Vastra-cīra* means "cloth like a bark-garment"; *kambala-cīra* [is another example]. What is the purpose of the comparison? *Parama-cīra*.

In the case of *palala-sūpa-śākaṃ miśre* (A 6.2.128), [we have] *ghṛta-palalam*, *ghṛta-sūpaḥ*, *ghṛta-śākam*. This is a compound formed by the rule *bhakṣyeṇa miśrīkaraṇam*. Why "when mixed" (*miśre*)? [Consider: *parama-palalam*.

SK 3863: In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the words *kūla*, *sūda*, *sthala*, and *karṣa* have their first syllable acute-accented when they form a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *dākṣikūlam*, *śāṇḍisūdam*, *dāṇḍāyanasthalam*, *dākṣikarṣaḥ*. These are names of villages. Why "when it is a proper name"? Example: *paramakūlam* (not a name). SK 3864: In a *tatpuruṣa* compound that is not a *karmadhāraya*, the word *rājya* has its first syllable acute-accented. (A 6.2.130)

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, excluding a *karmadhāraya*, the final member (*uttarapada*) beginning with *rājya-* has its first syllable acute-accented (*ādyudātta*). Example: *brāhmaṇarājyam*. Why "excluding" (*aka*)? Consider *paramarājyam*. In cases such as *celarājya*, the accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) prevails by way of prior exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Examples: *kucelam*, *kurājyam*. SK 3865: *vargyādayaś ca* (A 6.2.131). Examples: *arjunavargyaḥ*, *vāsudevapakṣyaḥ*. The restriction "excluding a *karmadhāraya*" still applies: *paramavargyaḥ*. The group beginning with *varga* is a sub-group within the *digādi* class.
SK 3866: *putraḥ pumbhyaḥ* (A 6.2.132).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the word *putra* following masculine words is udātta on its first syllable. Examples: *dāśakiputraḥ*, *māhiṣaputraḥ*. Why "son" (*putra*)? [Counter-example: *kaunaṭimātulaḥ* (where *mātula* follows). Why "masculine words" (*pumbhyaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *dākṣīputraḥ* (where *putra* follows a feminine word). SK 3867: *nācāryarājartviksaṃyuktajñātyākhyebhyaḥ* (A 6.2.133). [The rule does not apply] after words denoting a teacher (*ācārya*), a king (*rājan*), a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*), those connected by marriage (*saṃyukta*), or kinsmen (*jñāti*).

The word *putra* (son), when following these [words], does not have its first syllable acute-accented (*ādyudātta*). By the inclusion of the term "name" (*ākhyā*), synonyms and their derivatives are also included. Examples: *ācāryaputraḥ*, *upādhyāyaputraḥ*, *śākaṭāyanaputraḥ*, *rājaputraḥ*, *īśvaraputraḥ*, *nandaputraḥ*, *ṛtvikputraḥ*, *yājakaputraḥ*, *hotuḥ putraḥ*. [The term] *saṃyuktāḥ* refers to relatives by marriage; example: *śyālaputraḥ*. [The term] *jñātayaḥ* refers to kinsmen related through mother or father; example: *jñātiputraḥ*, *bhrātuṣputraḥ*. SK 3868: Words such as *cūrṇa* (powder) and others [do not have an acute accent on the first syllable] when following a genitive case ending that does not refer to a living being (*aprāṇiṣaṣṭhyāḥ*). (A 6.2.134)

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, these words following a non-living being in the genitive case are *ādyudātta*. Examples: *mudgacūrṇam* ("flour of beans"). Why "non-living being"? Consider *matsyacūrṇam* ("fish-flour"). SK 3869: And six items beginning with *kāṇḍa*, when following a genitive of a non-living being, are *ādyudātta*. Examples: *darbhakāṇḍam* ("a stalk of *darbha* grass"), *darbhacīram* ("a strip of *darbha* grass"), *tilapalalam* ("sesame paste"), *mudgasūpaḥ* ("bean soup"), *mūlakaśākam* ("radish vegetable"), *nadīkūlam* ("river bank"). Why "six"? Consider *rājasūdaḥ* ("king's cook"). Why "non-living being"? Consider *dattakāṇḍam* ("Datta’s section").

SK 3870: *kuṇḍaṃ vanam* (A 6.2.136). In a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the second member denotes a "forest" (*vana*), the word *kuṇḍa* has its first syllable acute-accented (*ādyudātta*). Example: *darbhakuṇḍam*. Here, the word *kuṇḍa* is used in the sense of similarity. Why say "forest"? [Counter-example: *mṛtkuṇḍam* (an earthen bowl). SK 3871: *prakṛtyā bhagālam* (A 6.2.137). [In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the word *bhagāla* retains its original form.]

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the final member (*uttarapada*) "bhagāla" retains its original accent (*prakṛti*). Examples: *kumbhībhagālam*, *kumbhīnadālam*, *kumbhīpālam*. These are *madhyodātta* (accented on the middle syllable). The term "by its original form" (*prakṛtyā*) is understood [from the preceding rule] up to the word "end" (*antaḥ*).
A 6.2.138: In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *śiti* always retains its original accent when it does not end in *bha*. (SK 3872)

After *śiti*, a following word consisting of more than one syllable is, by its original nature (*prakṛti*), [anudātta]. Examples: *śitipādaḥ* ("white-footed"), *śityaṃsaḥ* ("white-shouldered"). The word *pāda-* is udātta on the first syllable because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group; the word *aṃsa-* is [udātta on the first syllable] because its suffix is marked with *ṇi*. Why "after *śiti*"? Example: *darśanīyapādaḥ* ("beautiful-footed"). Why "more than one syllable" (*abahvac*)? Example: *śitibhasat* ("white-cheeked"). The word *śiti-* is udātta on the first syllable. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*). Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.139 states: "A *kṛt*-derived word following a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada* [is anudātta]."

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix shall have its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Examples: *prakārakaḥ*, *praharaṇam*, *śoṇā dhṛṣṇū nṛvāhasā*, *idhmapravraścanaḥ*. [The rule applies] from the time of the *upapada*. Example: *uccaiḥkāram*, *īṣatkaraḥ*. Why say "after a gati"? [Consider: *devasya kārakaḥ*; here the genitive case is characterized as a "residual" (*śeṣa*) genitive. The mention of *kṛt* is for the sake of clarity. In the case of *prapacatitarām*, when the compound is formed with a word ending in *tarap* etc., the suffix *ām* is added; some hold that in that instance, because it is "left behind" (*satiśiṣṭa*), the accent of *ām* prevails. Others, however, maintain that the mention of *kṛt* is for the purpose of including forms like *prapacati* (where the *kṛt* suffix has been elided).

SK 3874: *ubhe vanaspatyādiṣu yugapat* (A 6.2.140). In these [compounds], both the preceding and following members retain their original accent simultaneously. *vanaspatim vana ā* (the Lord of the Forest); *bṛhaspatim yaḥ* (who [is] Bṛhaspati). Here, the word *bṛhat* is prescribed as having its first syllable acute (*ādyudātta*). *harṣayā śacīpatim* (gladden the Lord of Śacī). The word *śacī* has its first syllable acute because it belongs to the *śārṅgarava* group; this is seen from the usage *śacībhir naḥ*. *tanūnapād ucyate* (Tanūnapāt is spoken of); *narāśaṃsam vājinam* (Narāśaṃsa, the vigorous one). The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by way of a formal prescription (*nipātana*). *śunaḥśepam*. SK 3875: *devatādvandve ca* (A 6.2.141). [In a compound consisting of the names of two deities, both members retain their original accent.]

Both [members of the compound] are by nature [accented] simultaneously. Examples include *indrāvaruṇau*, *indrābṛhaspatī*, and *kyam*. What is the deity? *plakṣanyagrodhau*. Why "in a *dvandva* [compound]"? [Consider] *agniṣṭomaḥ*. (A 6.2.142:
Not when the second member begins with an unaccented vowel, except in the case of *pṛthivī*, *rudra*, *pūṣan*, and *manthin*).

When the latter member of a compound is not *pṛthivī* or others [of that class], the previously mentioned rule does not apply when it is unaccented (*anudātta*). Examples: *indrāgnibhyāṃ kaṃ vṛṣaṇaḥ*. Why "not *pṛthivī* etc."? Example: *dyāvāpṛthivī janayan*. Here, *dyāvā* is prescribed as ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable), while *pṛthivī* is antodātta (accented on the last syllable). *Somārudrau*. The word *rudra* ends in *ra* due to the rule *roder ṇiluk ca*. *Indrāpūṣaṇau*. The word *pūṣan* is prescribed as antodātta by the rule *śvannukṣanpūṣan*. *Śukrāmanthinau*. *Manthin* is antodātta because it ends in the suffix *-in*.

The mention of the word *uttarapada* is for the purpose of qualifying the *uttarapada* [in the rule] "when preceded by an unaccented initial" (*anudāttādau*), so that it does not qualify the *dvandva* compound itself. The phrase "when preceded by an unaccented initial" is intended to distinguish the respective domains of the positive injunction and the prohibition.
(SK 3877) *antaḥ*:
This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).

Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.144: *thāthaghañktājabitrakāṇām*. For words ending in *tha*, *atha*, *ghañ*, *kta*, *ac*, *ap*, *itra*, and *ka*, when they follow a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada*, the final syllable is acute (*udātta*). Examples: *prabhṛthasyāyoḥ* ("the offering of Ayo"). Here, *bhr̥* takes the suffix *tha* [forming *bhṛtha*]. *āvasathaḥ* ("dwelling"). Here, *vas* takes the suffix *ghañ*. *prabhedaḥ* ("breaking open"). Here, *bhid* takes the suffix *ghañ*. *kta*: *dhartā vajrī puruṣṭutaḥ* ("the wielder of the thunderbolt, praised by many men"). The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "praised (*stuta*) by many (*puruṣu*) in many places (*bahupradeśeṣu*). *ac*: *prakṣayaḥ* ("destruction"). *ap*: *pralavaḥ* ("cutting off"). *itra*: *pralavitram* ("a tool for cutting off"). *ka*: *govr̥ṣaḥ* ("bull among cows"). The suffix *ka* is applied because the word belongs to the *mūlavibhujādi* group. The rule applies only when following a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada*. Thus, in *sustutaṃ bhavatā* ("it has been well-praised by you"), the accent does not apply because *su-* is not a *gati* here.

SK 3879 *sūpamānāt ktaḥ* (A 6.2.145): A word ending in the suffix *kta*, when following the word *su* or a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), has its final syllable acutely accented. Example: *ṛtasya yonau sukṛtasya śaśaplutaḥ*. SK 3880 *saṃjñāyām anācitādīnām* (A 6.2.146): In a proper name (*saṃjñā*), a word ending in *kta* has its final syllable acutely accented, except for those beginning with *ācita*.

A word ending in *kta* following a term denoting direction (*gati*), an agent (*kāraka*), or a secondary word (*upapada*) is udātta on its final syllable, with the exception of *ācita* and others. Examples: *upahūtaḥ śākalyaḥ* ("Śākalya has been invited"); *parijagdhaḥ kauṇḍinyaḥ* ("Kauṇḍinya has been swallowed"). Why "following [a word]"? Consider *ācitam* ("heaped up") and *āsthāpitam* ("established"). SK 3881: *pravṛddhādīnāṃ ca* (A 6.2.147). For these words beginning with *pravṛddha*, the subsequent member ending in *kta* is udātta on its final syllable. Examples: *pravṛddhaḥ* ("grown"), *prayutaḥ* ("separated"). This rule is commenced for the sake of non-technical terms (*asaṃjñā*). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).

SK 3882: After a *kāraka* [agentive word], the final syllable of the words *datta* and *śruta* is acute (*udātta*) when they form a name (*saṃjñā*) in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*). Examples: *devadattaḥ*, *viṣṇuśrutaḥ*. Why "after a *kāraka*"? Consider: *saṃbhūto rāmāyaṇaḥ* ("Rāmāyaṇa was produced"). Why "of *datta* and *śruta*"? Consider: *devapālitaḥ*. Because of this restriction, the rule *anaṅ sau* does not apply here even though it is a name; however, the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* does apply. Why "only" (*eva*)? So that there may be a restriction to the *kāraka*, but not a restriction to *datta* and *śruta*. Even after a non-*kāraka*, the final syllable of *datta* and *śruta* becomes acute: e.g., *saṃśrutaḥ*. Why "in the sense of a blessing"? Consider: [examples where it is not a blessing].

*Devakhātā* means "dug by the gods. In this context, the restriction is intended to apply only when [the agent] is equivalent to a blessing (*āśis*). Therefore, in the expression *anāhataḥ nadati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta sounds without being struck"), this is not the name of a particular conch shell. According to the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 6.2.48), there is only the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound.
Furthermore, [this applies] by the rule *itthambhūtena kṛtam* (A 6.2.149).

In the sense of "done in such a state," whatever compound occurs, the final member ending in *kta* shall have its final syllable udātta. Examples: *suptapralapitam* ("prattling while asleep"), *pramattagītam* ("singing while intoxicated"). In the word *kṛtam*, the root *kṛ* is used in the general sense of action and does not refer solely to the manifestation of what was previously non-existent; therefore, even things like "prattling" (*pralapita*) are considered "done" (*kṛta*). This is an exception to the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). [The following sūtra applies:
A word ending in *an* denoting an abstract quality (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*) [has its final syllable udātta]. (A 6.2.150)

A word ending in the suffix *ana*, which expresses an action (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*) and follows a *kāraka* [as its prior member], is udātta on its final syllable. Examples: *payaḥpānam* (the drinking of milk), *rājabhojanāḥ śālayaḥ* (rice for the king’s meal). Why "ending in *ana*"? Consider *hastādāyaḥ* (taking with the hand). Why "expressing an action or an object"? Consider *dantadhāvanam* (tooth-cleansing), where the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). Why "following a *kāraka*"? Consider *nidarśanam* (an illustration). SK 3885: Words ending in *man*, *ktin*, *vyākhyāna*, *śayana*, *āsana*, *sthāna*, *yājaka*, etc., and those ending in *krīta* [are udātta on their final syllable when following a *kāraka*]. (A 6.2.151)

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, these subsequent members following a *kāraka* [agentive] word are udātta on their final syllable. This is an exception to the accent rule for *kṛt*-suffixes (*kṛtsvara*). Examples: *rathavartma*, *pāṇinikṛtiḥ*, *chandovyākhyānanam*, *rājaśayanam*, *rājāsanam*, *aśvasthānam*, *brāhmaṇayājakaḥ*, *gokrītaḥ*. Why "following a *kāraka*"? Consider *prabhūtau saṅgatim*; here the accent is governed by the rule *tādau ca niti...*. (Pāṇini 6.2.152: *saptamyāḥ puṇyam*)

The word *adhyayanapuṇya* has its accent on the final syllable. This is obtained by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-*. Why [is it specified] "of the locative case"? [Consider: *vedapuṇyam* ("merit through the Veda"), where the compound is not formed with a word in the locative case. According to A 6.2.153, a word meaning "deficient" (*ūna*) and the word *kalaha* take the third case in a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

*māṣona* ("deficient by a māṣa"), *māṣavikala* ("lacking a māṣa"). This [rule] is an exception to the rule whereby the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) in the prior member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Regarding this, some maintain that the term *artha* is used here to denote the actual form [of the word]. Thus, *dhānyārtha* ("having grain as its purpose/value") is included. However, since the inclusion of words having that meaning is already established by the fact that the word *ūna* is used here to indicate the sense [of deficiency], the mention of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is for the sake of clarity. SK 3888: *miśraṃ cānupasargam asandhau* (A 6.2.154). [The word *miśra*, when not preceded by a prefix and not joined in sandhi, retains its original accent.]

*Saṃdhi* (union) is the state of having a single purpose through a formal agreement (*paṇabandhena*). Examples: *tilamiśrāḥ* ("mixed with sesame"), *sarpirmiśrāḥ* ("mixed with ghee"). Why [is it specified] "mixed" (*miśra*)? [Consider: *guḍadhānāḥ* ("barley grains with molasses"—here there is no formal agreement). Why "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*)? [Consider: *tilasaṃmiśrāḥ* ("well-mixed with sesame"). This very example serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that when "mixed" (*miśra*) is mentioned, it includes [the case where] a prefix is present. Why "not in the sense of *saṃdhi*"? [Consider: *brāhmaṇamiśro rājā* ("a king accompanied by Brahmins")—meaning he has attained a state of union (*aikārthya*) together with the Brahmins. SK 3889:

When there is a negation of a quality (*guṇapratiṣedhe*), the taddhita suffixes having the senses of "to be accomplished" (*sampādya*), "worthy" (*arha*), "beneficial" (*hita*), and "capable" (*alam*) [do not undergo elision of the negative particle *nañ*]. (A 6.2.155)

Words ending in *taddhita* suffixes having the sense of "produced from" (*saṃpādya*) and so forth, when following the negative particle *nañ* and expressing the negation of a quality, are udātta-accented on the final syllable. *karṇaveṣṭakābhyāṃ saṃpādi* (produced from ear-rings) → *kārṇaveṣṭakikam*; not produced from ear-rings → *akārṇaveṣṭakikam*. One who deserves cutting → *chaidikaḥ*; not deserving cutting → *acchaidikaḥ*. Not beneficial for calves → *avatsīyaḥ*. Not capable of causing distress → *asāntāpikaḥ*. Why "of *nañ*" (*nañaḥ*)? [Because if it were not specified, the rule would apply even when another word intervenes: one who deserves a donkey-chariot → *gārdabharathikaḥ*.

*dvigārdabharathikaḥ* ("one who possesses two donkey-carts"). What is the purpose of the restriction regarding the negation of a quality (*guṇapratiṣedha*)? *agārdabharathikaḥ* ("other than one who possesses a donkey-cart")—this is not a negation of a quality. For a "quality" (*guṇa*) is said to be that which constitutes the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning, such as "being accomplished" (*saṃpāditva*) and so forth. This rule applies where its negation is expressed, as in: "The face is not accomplished by means of ear-rings. Why [is the word] *saṃpet* [used]? *pāṇinīyaḥ* ("one who studies the work of Pāṇini")—this is not a negation of a quality. *apāṇinīyaḥ* ("not a follower of Pāṇini"). Why [specify] "secondary derivatives" (*taddhitāḥ*)? *voḍhā* ("one who is able to carry")—this is not a secondary derivative. *na voḍhā* ("not a carrier")—this is not a negation of a quality.
SK 3890 *yayatoś cātadarthe* (A 6.2.156):

When the suffixes *ya* and *yat* are present, which are *taddhita* suffixes, the final syllable of the subsequent member ending in those suffixes shall be acute-accented when it follows the negative particle *nañ* in a context where there is a negation of a quality (*guṇapratiṣedha*). Example: A collection of ropes is *pāśyā*. Not a collection of ropes is *apāśyā*. Why "not in the sense of that" (*atadarthe*)? Consider *apādyam* (that which is not to be drunk). Why "a *taddhita* suffix"? Consider *adeyam* (that which is not to be given). Why "negation of a quality" (*guṇapratiṣedhe*)? Consider *adantyam*, meaning "other than what is eaten by teeth. [Note: By the rule "when a suffix with a specific *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include one without that *anubandha*," this does not apply here: *avām* (not a boat) and *adevyam* (not fit for a god). SK 3891 *ackāvaśaktau* (A 6.2.157): [The final syllable of a word ending in] the suffix *aca* or the suffix *ka* is acute-accented when it denotes incapacity.

A word ending in *aj* or *kānta*, when following the negative particle *nañ*, is udātta on its final syllable provided that incapacity (*aśakti*) is understood. For example: *apacaḥ* ("one who cannot cook") or "incapable of cooking"; *avilikhaḥ* ("one who cannot scratch"). Why "when incapacity is understood"? [Consider: *apaco dīkṣitaḥ* ("the initiated one who has not cooked"). This applies only when there is a negation of a quality (*guṇapratiṣedha*). In other cases, this *apacaḥ* is different from the one [meaning "incapable"]. A 6.2.158: *ākrośe ca*. When an insult (*ākrośa*) is expressed, words ending in *ac* or *kānta* following *nañ* are udātta on their final syllables. For example: *apaco jālmaḥ* ("you incompetent fool!"). One is thus insulted by saying, "He is incapable of cooking. Also: *avikṣipaḥ*.

SK 3893 (A 6.2.159): In a compound with *nañ*, when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*) or an insult (*ākrośa*), the final syllable is udātta. Example: *adevadattaḥ* ("not Devadatta" / "you scoundrel Devadatta").
SK 3894 (A 6.2.160): Words ending in kṛtya suffixes, *uka*, *iṣṇu*, and *cāru* etc., [have their final syllable udātta].

The suffixes following *nañ* shall be udātta when they end in the word-final position. *akartavyaḥ* (not to be done); *uk*: *anāgāmukaḥ* (one who does not come). *iṣṇuc*: *analaṅkariṣṇuḥ* (one who does not adorn). In the mention of *iṣṇuc*, there is also the inclusion of *khiṣṇuc* because it is prescribed with an initial *i*-vowel. *anāḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ* (one who does not become wealthy). *cārvādiḥ*: *acāruḥ* (unpleasant); *asādhuḥ* (improper). *rājāhnoś chandasi* (in the Veda, [the udātta applies] to *rājan* and *ahan* after *nañ*): *arājā* (non-king); *anāhaḥ* (non-day). In the common language (*bhāṣā*), the accent of *nañ* itself remains. SK 3895: *vibhāṣā tṛnnannatīkṣṇaśuciṣu* (optionally so in the case of *tṛn*, *anna*, *atīkṣṇa*, and *aśuci*).
*tṛn*: *akartā* (non-doer). *anna*: *anannam* (non-food). *atīkṣṇam* (not sharp). *aśuci* (impure). In the alternative (*pakṣe*), the accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) applies.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, [the suffix *ṣaṣṭhī* is applied] after the words *idam*, *etad*, and *tad*, when they denote the first [in a series] or a ordinal number used in counting actions. (A 6.2.162)

In these cases, the final syllable of these two [words] is acute (udātta). *Idam-prathamaḥ* means "he for whom this is the first"; *etad-dvitīyaḥ*; *tat-pañcamaḥ*. Why [is it specified] "in a bahuvrīhi compound"? [Consider: *anena prathamaḥ = idaṃprathamaḥ* ("first by this"). The compound is formed by a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) based on the rule *tṛtīyā* [2.1.30]. Why [is it specified] "after *idam*, *etad*, and *tad*"? [Consider: *yat-prathamaḥ* ("first who"). Why [is it specified] "of the first and ordinal numbers"? [Consider: *tāni bahūny asya = tadbahuḥ* ("one for whom those are many"). Why [is it specified] "in the counting of actions"? [Consider: *ayaṃ prathamaḥ pradhānam yeṣām te = idaṃprathamāḥ* ("those for whom this is the first, i.e., the principal").

This is a calculation of substances (*dravyagaṇana*). What is the purpose of this calculation? "Those for whom this is the first" are *idam-prathamāḥ*; the meaning is "those for whom this is primary. Because the final member of the compound is subject to grammatical operation (*kāryitva*), when the suffix *kap* is added, the preceding part [the first member] has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Thus: *idaṃprathamakaḥ*. The governing rule *bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 6.2.1) is to be understood as applying prior to the rule *vanaṃ samāse* (Pāṇini 6.2.175). SK 3897: *saṃkhyāyāḥ stanaḥ* (A 6.2.163): In a *bahuvrīhi*, the word *stana* is accented on its final syllable when preceded by a numeral. Examples: *dvistanī* ("two-breasted"), *catuḥstanā* ("four-breasted"). Why "preceded by a numeral"? Consider *darśanīyastanā* ("having beautiful breasts"). Why "the word *stana*"? Consider *dviśirāḥ* ("two-headed").
SK 3898: *vibhāṣā chandasi* (A 6.2.164): [The substitution of *i* for *ī* is optional] in the Vedic language;
e.g., *dvistanāṃ karoti*. SK 3899:
*saṃjñāyāṃ mitrājinayoḥ* (A 6.2.165): [The substitution of *i* for *ī* is optional] when a name is formed with the words *mitra* or *ajina*; e.g., *mitriyaḥ* or *mitrīyaḥ*, *ajiniyaḥ* or *ajinīyaḥ*.

*devamitraḥ* (friend of the gods), *kṛṣṇājinam* (black antelope skin). Why [is the rule] stated "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*)? [Consider] *priyamitraḥ* (dear friend). There is a prohibition regarding the sage (*ṛṣi*) when [the word] *mitra* follows: *viśvāmitra* is a sage. A word following that which expresses an intervening agent (*vyavāyin*), provided it does not mean "another person" (*anaram*), has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). For example, *vastrāntaraḥ* (one for whom a cloth is the intervening medium); here, *antara* means an intervening agent. Why "of that which expresses an intervening agent"? [Consider] *ātmāntaraḥ*; the meaning is "having another nature."

SK 3901: *mukhaṃ svāṅgam* (A 6.2.167). [The word] *mukha* [is used as a bahuvrīhi compound] when it denotes a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*). Example: *gauramukhaḥ* ("one with a fair face"). Why "a limb of one's own body"? [Counter-example: *dīrghamukhā śālā* ("a hall with a long front entrance"). SK 3902: *nāvyayadikśabdagomahatsthūlamuṣṭipṛthuvatsebhyaḥ* (A 6.2.168). [The rule A 6.2.167 does not apply] after an indeclinable, a word denoting a cardinal direction, *go*, *mahat*, *sthūla*, *muṣṭi*, *pṛthu*, or *vatsa*.

*uccairmukhaḥ*, *prāṅmukhaḥ*, *gomukhaḥ*, *mahāmukhaḥ*, *sthūlamukhaḥ*, *muṣṭimukhaḥ*, *pṛthumukhaḥ*, *vatsamukhaḥ*. In these cases, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member applies. By this rule, even the optional alternative (*vikalpa*) characterized by the comparison [of the preceding members] *go*, *muṣṭi*, and *vatsa* is set aside. [Pāṇini 6.2.169: "After a word ending in *niṣṭhā* [a kṛt suffix], when preceded by a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), [the first member retains its original accent] optionally."

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word "mukha" (face), when it follows a term ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix or denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), is oxytone provided it refers to a part of the body (*svāṅga*). Examples: *prakṣālitamukhaḥ* ("one whose face has been washed"). In this case, by the rule *niṣṭhopasarga-pūrva-*, there is optionally an oxytone on the final syllable of the first member; furthermore, because the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), the accent of a *gati* particle may also occur. Example with a standard of comparison: *siṃhamukhaḥ* ("lion-faced"). Pāṇini A 6.2.170 states: "The past passive participle (*kta*) following words denoting genus (*jāti*), time, or *sukha*-type words, as well as [words] other than clothing (*anācchādana*), is oxytone except when it means 'done,' 'measured,' or 'accepted' (*akṛta-mita-pratipannāḥ*). *Note: The text provided contains a mix of Sanskrit commentary and the sūtra itself. The translation reflects the grammatical analysis.*

*sāraṅgajagdhaḥ* (devoured by a deer), *māsajātaḥ* (born after a month), *sukhajātaḥ* (born in happiness), *duḥkhajātaḥ* (born in suffering). Why [is the word] *jāti-kāla* mentioned? [To exclude examples such as] *putrajātaḥ* (a son born). Why [is the word] *anācchādana* (non-clothing) mentioned? [To exclude examples such as] *vastracchannaḥ* (covered with a garment). Why [is the word] *akṛta* (unmade) mentioned? [To exclude examples such as] *kuṇḍakṛtaḥ* (made into a bowl), *kuṇḍamitaḥ* (measured by a bowl), *kuṇḍapratipannaḥ* (placed in a bowl). From this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), it follows that a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix is placed at the end [of the compound].

By Pāṇini 6.2.171, *vā jāte*, the word *jāta* following words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), happiness (*sukha*), and so forth, may optionally have its final syllable acute-accented (*antodātta*). For example: *dantajātaḥ* ("one whose teeth have grown") and *māsajātaḥ* ("one born a month ago").

SK 3906 (A 6.2.172): In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when preceded by the negative particle *nañ* or the word *su*, the final member (*uttarapada*) is accented on its last syllable. Examples: *avrīhiḥ* (one who does not possess rice), *sumāṣaḥ* (one who possesses good beans). SK 3907 (A 6.2.173): When the suffix *kap* is added [to a *bahuvrīhi*], the preceding member is accented on its last syllable.

When the suffix *kap* follows, the first syllable of that compound which has as its final member a word standing after the negative particle *nañ* or the word *su* becomes acute; provided that *kap* follows. Examples: *abrahmabandhukaḥ*, *sukumārīkaḥ*.
[Additionally: When a short vowel stands at the end of the final member, the syllable preceding the final one becomes acute (A 6.2.174).

In a compound where the final member ends in a short vowel, the penultimate syllable is acute (udātta), except when the suffix *kap* follows; however, in a *bahuvrīhi* following *nañ* or *su*, the accent falls on the syllable preceding the final one. Examples: *avrīhikaḥ* ("one who does not have rice"), *sumāṣakaḥ* ("having good beans"). Although the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) was already understood from the previous rule, its repetition here serves to restrict the application due to a difference in the scope of operation: in the case of a final short vowel, the acute falls only on the syllable preceding the end, and not on the syllable preceding *kap*. Example: *ajñakaḥ* ("ignorant"); here, the acute falls only on the final syllable of the form ending in *kap*. SK 3909: In a *bahuvrīhi* expressing abundance, the word *bahu* is treated like *nañ* with respect to the final member. (A 6.2.175)

The accent of a word following *bahu*—provided that *bahu* expresses the plurality of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*)—shall be the same as that of a word following *nañ*. Examples: *bahuvrīhikaḥ*, *bahumitrakaḥ*. Why specify "of the subsequent member"? [Counter-example: *bahumānaḥ* ("one who has pride in many things"). SK 3910: *na guṇādayo 'vayavāḥ* (A 6.2.176).

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, words such as *guṇa* and others, when they follow *bahu* and denote parts (*avayava*), are not udātta at the end. Examples: *bahuguṇā rajjuḥ* ("a rope with many strands"), *bahvakṣaraṃ padam* ("a word with many syllables"), *bahvadhyāyaḥ* ("one with many chapters"). The class beginning with *guṇa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Why specify "parts"? [Counter-example: *bahuguṇo dvijaḥ* ("a twice-born man with many virtues"). Here, "virtues" (*guṇa*) refers to study, learning, good conduct, and so forth.
SK 3911: After a prefix (*upasarga*), a word denoting a limb of one’s own body (*svāṅga*) that is fixed (*dhruva*) and not *parśu* [is unaccented].

Examples: *prapṛṣṭhaḥ*, *pralalāṭaḥ*. "Fixed" means having a single, constant form. Why "after a prefix"? Example: *darśanīyapṛṣṭhaḥ*. Why "a limb of one's own body"? Example: *praśākho vṛkṣaḥ* ("a tree with spreading branches"). Why "fixed"? Example: *udbāhuḥ* ("with arms raised"). Why "not *parśu*"? Example: *viparśuḥ*. SK 3912: In a compound (*samāsa*), the word *vana* [is unaccented]. (A 6.2.178)

In a simple compound (*samāsa-mātra*), the word *vana* following a prefix (*upasarga*) has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). These [words] are *pravaṇa*. According to A 6.2.179, *antaḥ*, the word *vana* following this [prefix] has its final syllable accented. For example, *antarvaṇo deśaḥ* ("a region within the forest"). This rule is intended for cases where there is no prefix (*anupasarga*).
SK 3914 *antaś ca*:

The word *antaḥ*, when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*). Examples: *paryantaḥ*, *samantaḥ*. SK 3916 *na nivibhyām*: [The rule does not apply] after the prefixes *ni* and *vi*.

*nyantaḥ*, *vyantaḥ*: when the *yaṇ*-substitution has been applied, the circumflex (*svarita*) occurs according to the rule "of the *yaṇ* resulting from an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel" (*udāttasvaritayor yaṇaḥ*). *A 6.2.182* (*parer abhitobhāvi maṇḍalam*): A word beginning with *kūla* and so forth, as well as the word *maṇḍala*, have their final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*) when they follow *pari* and denote something that exists on both sides (*abhitaḥ*). Examples: *parikūlam*, *parimaṇḍalam*.
SK 3918: *nirudakādīni ca* (A 6.2.183): [The words] beginning with *nirudaka* are *pragṛhya*. Why [is it specified] "not a body part" (*asvāṅgam*)? [Consider: *prapadam*. SK 3919:
*abher mukham* (A 6.2.185): [The word *mukha* following the prefix *abhi-* is *pragṛhya*.]

*Abhimukham*. Since [the form] is already established by the rule *upasargāt svāṅgam* (Pāṇini 6.2.177), this [sūtra] is for the sake of forming a *bahuvrīhi*, for the sake of [denoting] non-permanent [parts], and for the sake of [denoting] non-limbs (*asvāṅga*). Examples: *abhimukhā śālā* ("a hall facing [towards something]");
*apāmukham* ("the side opposite the mouth"). The division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of subsequent rules.

SK 3921: *sphigapūtavīṇāñjodhvakrkṣisīranāmanāma ca* (A 6.2.187). These words ending in *apa-* are udātta on the final syllable. *apasphigam*, *apapūtam*, *apavīṇam*, *añjam*, *apāñjaḥ*, *adhvan*, *apādhvā*. This [form] occurs even in the absence of the rule *upasargād adhvanaḥ* (A 6.2.189); this very fact is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the suffix applies only after a compound-ending (*samāsānta*). *apakukṣiḥ*, *sīranāma*: *apasīram*, *apahalam*, *nāma*, *apanāma*. The inclusion of *sphiga*, *pūta*, and *kukṣi* is for the purpose of excluding *bahuvrīhi* compounds, for the purpose of excluding things that are not stable (*adhruva*), and for the purpose of excluding non-body-parts (*asvāṅga*).

SK 3922 *adher uparistham* (A 6.2.188): In the word *adhidantaḥ*, "a tooth grown upon another," the prefix *adhi-* [takes the acute accent] because it means "standing above" (*uparistham*). It refers to a tooth born above another tooth. Why say "standing above"? [Counter-example: *adhikaraṇam*.

SK 3923 *ator ap-pradhāna-kanīyasī* (A 6.2.189): [The acute accent falls on the prefix *ati-* when it occurs before a word ending in the suffix *-ap*, provided that the word is not the principal member of the compound, or when it is the word *kanīyas-*.]

The word *anu*, when it expresses "subordinate" (*paramapradhāna*) and ends with an udātta accent, [forms a compound with a word ending in the sixth case]. *Anujyeṣṭhaḥ* means "one who follows the eldest. This is a *prādi*-compound in which the meaning of the first member is predominant (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*). *Anukanīyān* means "one who follows the youngest"; this is a compound in which the meaning of the second member is predominant (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*). And the mention of the word *kanīyas* is for the sake of emphasizing the subordinate sense. Why [is the condition] "not preceded by *apa*" (*apra*) stated? [Consider: *anujyeṣṭhaḥ* in the sense of "the eldest has followed. (A 6.2.190:
*puruṣaś cānvādiṣu*) [The word *puruṣa* also forms a compound with words beginning with *anu* and others.]

The word *puruṣa* is oxytone when it follows the prefix *anu* in the sense of "designated" (*anvādiṣṭa*). *Anupuruṣaḥ* means "a man who has been designated. Why say "designated"? [Counter-example: *anupuruṣaḥ* meaning "a man who has followed. Regarding the rule *ater akṛtpade* (A 6.2.191): a word ending in a non-ṇamul kṛt-suffix following *ati*, as well as the word *pada*, is oxytone. Examples: *atyaṅkuśo nāgaḥ* ("the elephant that has passed beyond the goad"); *atipadā gāyatrī* ("the Gāyatrī that has exceeded the [standard] measure"). Why say "non-ṇamul kṛt-suffix"? [Counter-example: *atikāraḥ*. It should be stated: "after *ati*, [the final syllable is acute] when there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātu-lopa*). This should not apply here: *śobhano gārgyo 'tigārgyaḥ* ("a fine descendant of Garga"). But it should apply here: *atikrāntaḥ kārum atikārukaḥ* ("one who has surpassed a craftsman").

SK 3926: *ner anidhāne* (A 6.2.192). "Non-placement" (*anidhāna*) means the absence of manifestation; the meaning is that what is other than that is "placement," i.e., manifestation. [Examples: *nimūla*, *nyakṣa*. Why "in the sense of non-placement"? [Counter-example: *nihito daṇḍo nidaṇḍaḥ* ("the staff was placed down").
