SK 3927: *prater aṃśvādayas tatpuruṣe* (A 6.2.193). [The words beginning with *aṃśu* undergo the substitution of *pra-* for *prati-* when they follow *prati-* in a *tatpuruṣa* compound.]

Words beginning with *aṃśu* and following *prati* are udātta on their final syllable. *Pratyaṃśuḥ* (the ray that has returned); *pratijanaḥ*; *pratirājā*. Because the suffix *t* [forming *pratirāja*] is not obligatory at the end of a compound, *tac* does not apply. SK 3928: *upād dvyajajinamagaurādayaḥ* (A 6.2.194). In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, a word consisting of two syllables (*dvyac*) or the word *ajina*, which follows *upa* and is udātta on its final syllable, retains its accent, provided it is not among the group beginning with *gaura*. Examples: *upadevaḥ*, *upendraḥ*, *upājinam*. Why "not *gaura* and so forth"? Consider *upagauraḥ*, *upataiṣaḥ*. Why "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound"? Consider *upasomaḥ*, meaning "one to whom Soma has come."

SK 3929: *su-* [is used] in the sense of contempt (*avakṣepaṇa*) [A 6.2.195]. In *supratyavasitaḥ*, *su-* here is used only in the sense of praise (*pūjā*); however, the meaning of the sentence here is censure (*nindā*), because it is expressed so out of envy (*asūyā*). Why [is the condition] "after *su-"* stated? [To exclude forms like] *kubrāhmaṇaḥ*. Why [is the condition] "in the sense of contempt" stated? [To exclude forms like] *suvṛṣaṇam*. SK 3930:
Optionally [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] after *utpuccha* [A 6.2.196].

In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound: *utpucchaḥ*, meaning "one who has gone beyond the tail. However, when it means "he raises his tail" (*udasyati puccham*), derived from the root *utpucchayati* with the suffix *ac*—resulting in *utpucchaḥ*—then, since the rule for the initial accentuation of *thā-thādi* compounds would normally require the final syllable to be always acute (*antodātta*), this present rule provides an option. Thus, this is an option applicable in both cases. What is the purpose of specifying "in a *tatpuruṣa*"? Consider: *utpucchaḥ* as "that by which the tail is raised. SK 3931: *dvitribhyāṃ pād-dan-mūrdhasu bahuvrīhau* (A 6.2.197). [The word-final vowel of *dvi*, *tri*, *pāda*, *dat*, and *mūrdhan* becomes acute in a *bahuvrīhi* compound.]

After these two [words], in the following cases, the word is optionally udātta on the final syllable: *dvipāt* and *catuṣpāt* when used in the sense of "standing"; *tripād*; *ūrdhvaḥ*; *dvidan*; and *trimūrdhānam saptaraśmim*. In the word *mūrdhan*, the stem *mūrdha-* is used without the application of the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). The purpose of this is so that the word may have the udātta accent on the final syllable even in the absence of such a suffix. This very fact serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the application of compound-final suffixes is not mandatory (*anitya*).

Even if the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied, nevertheless, because it functions as part of the *bahuvrīhi* and is a constituent element of it, the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound occurs by rule in one alternative. For example: *dvimūrdhaḥ*, *trimūrdhaḥ*. Why [is the rule] restricted to after *dvi* and *tri*? [Consider: *kalyāṇamūrdhā*. Why [is it restricted to] the *bahuvrīhi*? [Consider: *dvayor mūrdhā* = *dvimūrdhā*. Regarding A 6.2.198, *sakthaṃ cākrāntāt*:

[the suffix *ac* is applied to *saktha*] when it does not follow a word ending in *ā*. Examples: *gaurasakthaḥ*, *ślakṣṇasakthaḥ*. Why "not following a word ending in *ā*"? [Consider: *cakrasakthaḥ*. Because the compound-final suffix (*ac*) has the marker *c*, it invariably receives the acute accent on its final syllable.

SK 3933: *parādiś chandasi bahulam* (A 6.2.199). In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the initial syllable of the word *saktha* when it follows another word is optionally acute (*udātta*). For example: *ajisaktham ālabheta*. On this point, there is a *vārttika*: "The initial [syllable] of the following word, the final [syllable] of the following word, and the final [syllable] of the preceding word are seen; likewise, the initial [syllable] of the preceding word is seen. Therefore, there is a manifold transposition (*vyatyaya*). Thus, regarding the initial [acute]: *tuvijātā urukṣayā*. Regarding the final [acute] of the following word: *ni yena muṣṭihatyayā*. Regarding the final [acute] of the preceding word: *yastricakraḥ*. Regarding the initial [acute] of the preceding word: *viśvāyur dhehi*. These are the rules for the accents of compounds (*samāsasvara*). Now follow the rules for the accents of finite verbs (*tiṅantasvara*). 93.

SK 3934: *tiṅo gotrādīni kutsanābhīkṣṇyayoḥ* (A 8.1.27). After a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), the words *gotra* and so forth are unaccented (*anudātta*) when these two meanings—censure (*kutsana*) and frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*)—are present. Examples: *pacati gotram* ("he cooks [like] a *gotra*"); *pacatipacati gotram* ("he cooks repeatedly like a *gotra*"). Similarly: *pravacana*, *prahasanam*, *prakathanam*, *pratyāyanam*, etc. The mention of "censure" and "frequency" is a qualification of the list [of *gotra* and so forth]. Therefore, even in other instances where *gotra* and so forth are mentioned, it should be understood that the grammatical operation applies only when censure and the like are intended. Why [mention] "the words *gotra* and so forth"? [Consider: *pacati pāpam* ("he cooks badly"). Why [mention] "censure"? [Consider: *svanati gotram sametya kūpam* ("the *gotra* resounds upon reaching the well"). SK 3935: *tiṅṅ atiṅaḥ* (A 8.1.28). [The preceding rule applies] after a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), provided it is not itself followed by another word ending in a verbal suffix (*atiṅ*). [This is an exception to the previous rule. Example: *mā bhavān pacatu gotram*. [In this case, because the first word ends in *tiṅ* and the second does not, the second word retains its accent. [Conversely, in *pacati ca pacati gotram*, because the first word is followed by another word ending in *tiṅ*, the second word is not unaccented. [End of section.]
A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) following a word that is not itself a finite verb is pronounced with a low tone (*nihanyate*). For example: *agnim īḷe*.
(Pāṇini 8.1.29) A form ending in the periphrastic future suffix *luṭ* is not pronounced with a low tone. For example: *śvaḥ kartā*, *śvaḥ kartārau*.

Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.30: *nipātair yadyadihantakuvinnecceccaṇkaccidyatrayuktam*. When joined with these particles—*yad*, *yadi*, *ha*, *anta*, *ku*, *vit*, *na*, *īd*, *cet*, *caṇ*, *kaccit*, *yatra*—the [first member] is not elided (*na nihanyate*). Examples: *yad agne syāmahaṃ tvam* ("O Agni, may I be you"); *yuvā yadīkṛthaḥ* ("when you made him young"); *kuvidaṅga āsan* ("where indeed were they?"); *acittibhiś cakṛmā kaccit* ("have we done anything through lack of thought?"); *putrāso yatra pitaro bhavanti* ("where sons become fathers"). Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.31: *naha pratyārambhe*. [The particle *naha* is not elided when used in the sense of "recommencement" (*pratyārambha*).]

A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) joined with *naha* is not unaccented. "Commencement" joined with a prohibition is "counter-commencement. Example: *naha bhokṣyase* ("I hope you will not eat"). What is the purpose of [specifying] "counter-commencement"? [Example: *naha vaitasmiṃl loke dakṣiṇām icchanti* ("In this world, they do not desire sacrificial fees"). SK 3939: *satyaṃ praśne* (A 8.1.32). A finite verb joined with *satya* is not unaccented when it occurs in a question. Example: *satyaṃ bhokṣyase* ("Truly, you will eat"). What is the purpose of [specifying] "in a question"? [Example: *satyam idvā u taṃ vayam indraṃ stavāma* ("Truly, we shall praise that Indra").

SK 3940 *aṅgāprātilomye* (A 8.1.33): A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) joined with the word *aṅga* is not unaccented [on its first syllable], provided it does not express "contrariety" (*aprātilomya*). Example: *aṅga kuru*. Why "not contrariety"? Example: *aṅga kūjasi vṛṣala*, *idānīṃ jñāsyasi jālma* ("O low-born one, you chatter; now you shall know, you rogue!"). One who acts contrary to what is intended becomes "contrary. SK 3941 *hi ca* (A 8.1.34).

A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) joined with *hi* is not unaccented (*anudātta*). For example: *ā hi ṣmā yāti*; *ā hi ruhaṃtam*. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), even multiple [finite verbs] that are syntactically dependent on *hi* are not unaccented, provided they are connected with it and remain expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*). For example: *anṛtaṃ hi matto vadati vāpmā cainaṃ yunakti*. Here, both finite verbs are not subject to the low accent (*nihata*).
SK 3943: A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) joined with these two particles, *yāvat* and *yathā*, is not unaccented (*anudātta*). For example: *yathā cit kaṇvam āvataṃ*. SK 3944:
When expressing honor (*pūjā*), there is no difference [from the previous rule]. (A 8.1.37)

A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) that follows immediately after *yāvat* or *yathā* used in the sense of praise (*pūjā*) is not unaccented (*anudātta*). Examples: *yāvat pacati śobhanam* ("He cooks well indeed") and *yathā pacati śobhanam* ("He cooks well indeed"). Why "in the sense of praise"? Observe: *yāvad bhuṅkte* ("as much as he eats"). Why "immediately following"? Observe: *yāvad devadattaḥ pacati śobhanam* ("Insofar as Devadatta cooks well"). Here, the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) is prohibited by the preceding rule [A 8.1.29]. SK 3945: And [a finite verb] separated by a preverb (*upasarga*) [is also not unaccented]. (A 8.1.38)

It was stated previously that [the word] *anantaram* [is used]. This statement is for the purpose of excluding intervening prefixes (*upasarga*). For example: *yāvat pacati śobhanam* ("while he cooks well"). It is simply *anantaram*. For example: *yāvad devadattaḥ prapacati śobhanam* ("while Devadatta cooks well"). Regarding *tu-paśya-paśyatā-aiḥ pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 8.1.39): a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) joined with these particles—*tu*, *paśya*, *paśyata*, and *āha*—is not subject to the suppression of its accent when expressing praise (*pūjā*). For example: *ādaha svadhāmanu punar garbhatvam erire* ("Then they, following their own nature, brought him back again to the state of an embryo").

SK 3947: In connection with *aho*, when used in the sense of praise, the [first word] is not unaccented. Example: *aho devadattaḥ pacati śobhanam* ("O Devadatta, he cooks well!"). SK 3948: In other cases (*śeṣe*), it is optional (vibhāṣā).

A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) joined with *aho* is optionally unaccented when expressing praise: *aho kaṭaṃ kariṣyati* ("Oh, how he will make the mat!"). By the rule *purā ca parīpsāyām* (A 8.1.42), a word joined with *purā* is optionally unaccented when expressing haste (*tvarā*). Example: *adhīṣva māṇavaka purā vidyotate vidyut* ("Study, young man, before the lightning flashes"). Here, the word *purā* means "imminent" (*nikaṭāgām*). Why "when expressing haste"? Consider: *na tenāsya purādhīyate* ("He does not study this for him before [long]"). Here, *purā* refers to something long past (*cirātīte*).

SK 3950: *nanu* in the sense of seeking permission (A 8.1.43). A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) joined with *nanu* is not unaccented when there is a request for permission. Example: *nanu gacchāmi bhoḥ*. The meaning is: "Shall I go? Please permit me as I go. Why say *nanu*? Consider: *ākarṣīḥ kaṭaṃ tvam* / *nanu karomi*. This is a response to a question. SK 3951: *kim* [is used] in an inquiry regarding an action, provided it is without a prefix (*anupasarga*) and is not negated (*apratiṣiddha*) (A 8.1.44).

When joined with the interrogative pronoun *kim* used in the sense of an inquiry regarding an action (*kriyāpraśna*), a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is not unaccented. Example: *kiṃ dvijaḥ pacaty āhosvid gacchati?* ("Does the twice-born one cook, or does he go? Why "regarding an action"? To prevent it from applying when there is an inquiry regarding a means (*sādhanapraśna*). Example: *kiṃ bhaktaṃ pacaty apūpān vā?* ("Does he cook rice, or cakes? Why "in an inquiry"? Example: *kiṃ paṭhati?* ("What does he read?")—this is a case of censure (*kṣepa*). Why "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*)? Example: *kiṃ prapacati uta prakaroti?* ("Is he cooking thoroughly, or is he doing something else? Why "not prohibited" (*apratiṣiddha*)? Example: *kiṃ dvijo na pacati?* ("Does the twice-born one not cook? [In this case, the negative particle *na* prohibits the application. SK 3952: *lope vibhāṣā* (A 8.1.45). When *kim* is not employed, the aforementioned rule is optional. Example: *devadattaḥ pacaty āhosvit paṭhati?* ("Is Devadatta cooking, or is he reading?")

**SK 3953**: *ehi manye prahāse lṛṭ* (A 8.1.46). When joined with the words *ehi manye*, the *lṛṭ* (future tense) ending is used in the sense of joking (*prahāsa*). Example: *ehi manye bhaktaṃ bhokṣyate nahi bhokṣyase bhuktaṃ tattvatithibhiḥ* ("Come, I think you will eat the food; no, you will not eat it, for it has already been eaten by our guests"). Why "in the sense of joking"? Consider: *ehi manyase odanaṃ bhokṣye iti suṣṭhu manyase* ("Come, you think 'I shall eat rice'; you think quite rightly"). Since this is already established by the rule *gatyarthaloṭā lṛṭ* (A 3.3.13), this present rule is commenced for the sake of restriction: when joined with *ehi manye*, it occurs only in the sense of joking, and not otherwise. Example: *ehi manyase odanaṃ bhokṣye*. **SK 3954**: *jātvapūrvam* (A 8.1.47). [The *lṛṭ* ending is used after a verb] when preceded by *jātu* [provided it does not occur at the beginning of a sentence].

A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) joined with *jātu* is not unaccented when *jātu* has not occurred previously [in the discourse]. Example: *jātu bhokṣyase*. Why "not occurring previously"? Example: *kaṭaṃ jātu kariṣyasi*. Also, a word formed with an interrogative pronoun (*kiṃvṛtta*), when followed by *cit*, [is not unaccented]. (A 8.1.48)

A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) that is joined with *cid*—provided that *cid* does not occur before it and is not part of an interrogative form (*kiṃvṛtta*)—is not unaccented. An interrogative form (*kiṃvṛtta*) consists of a case-ending (*vibhaktyanta*) or a form of *kim* ending in *-ḍatara* or *-ḍatama*. Examples: *kaścid bhuṅkte* ("someone eats"), *kataraścid*, or *katamaścid*. What about when *cid* follows [the interrogative]? Example: *ko bhuṅkte cid* ("who, indeed, eats?"). The rule applies only when *cid* is not preceded [by another word]. Example: *rāmaḥ kiṃcit paṭhati* ("Rāma reads something").
[Also, the particle following] *āho* or *utāho* is not unaccented when it follows immediately [after a finite verb]. (A 8.1.49)

A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) joined with either *āho* or *utāho* is not unaccented (*anudātta*). For example: *āho utāho vā bhuṅkte*. It must be understood as "immediately following" (*anantaram*), for he will state later that there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in other cases. Why [is the word] *apūrva* used? Consider: *deva āho bhuṅkte*. Regarding the rule *śeṣe vibhāṣā* (A 8.1.50):
a finite verb joined with these two [particles], even if separated by an interval, is optionally unaccented. For example: *āho devaḥ pacati*.

SK 3958: *gatyarthaloṭā lṛṇ na cet kārakaṃ sarvānyat* (A 8.1.51). A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) joined with the imperative (*loṭ*) of a root meaning "to go" is not unaccented (*anudātta*), provided that the grammatical participant (*kāraka*) is the same for both the imperative and the future (*lṛṭ*). Examples: *āgaccha deva grāmaṃ drakṣyasy enam* ("Come, O King, you will see this village"). *uhyantāṃ devadattena śālayo rāmeṇa bhokṣyante* ("Let the rice be carried by Devadatta; it will be eaten by Rāma"). Why "meaning to go"? *paca deva odanaṃ bhokṣyase 'nnam* ("Cook the rice, O King, you will eat the food"). Why "with the imperative"? *āgaccher deva grāmaṃ drakṣyasy enam* ("You might come, O King, you will see this [if you come]"). Why "future"? *āgaccha deva grāmaṃ paśyasy enam* ("Come, O King, you see this [now]"). Why "provided that... (*na cet*)? [If the agent were different, the rule would not apply.]

"Come, O King, to the village; your father will eat rice. "What is everything? [The answer is: "Come, O King, to the village; both you and I shall see him. In this case as well, there should be a prohibition of the *nighāta* (non-accentuation). This is because the agent (*kāraka*) of the *loṭ*-ending verb is expressed by another *lṛṭ*-ending verb.
*loṭ ca* (A 8.1.52) [is the rule that applies here].

An imperative form (*loḍanta*) joined with another imperative form denoting motion (*gatyartha*) is not unaccented (*anudātta*). *āgaccha deva grāmaṃ paśya* ("Come, O King, see the village"). Why "denoting motion"? *paca deva odanaṃ bhuṅkṣvainam* ("Cook, O King, rice; eat this"). Why "imperative" (*loṭ*)? *āgaccha deva grāmaṃ paśyasi* ("Come, O King, you see the village"). Provided that the agent (*kāraka*) is not entirely different [in both cases]. *āgaccha deva grāmaṃ paśyatv evaṃ rāmaḥ* ("Come, O King, let Rāma see the village thus"). Because of the inclusion of the word *sarva* ("entirely"), however, it would indeed apply here: *āgaccha deva grāmaṃ tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca paśyāvaḥ* ("Come, O King, you and I shall see the village"). The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. SK 3960: An imperative joined with a prefix (*sopasarga*), excluding the last person (*anuttama*), is optionally [unaccented] (A 8.1.53).

A verb ending in the imperative (*loḍanta*) joined with another verb ending in the imperative expressing motion (*gatyartha*) is unaccented (*anudātta*). *āgaccha deva grāmaṃ praviśa* ("Come, O King, enter the village"). Why "with a prefix" (*sopasarga*)? *āgaccha deva grāmaṃ paśya* ("Come, O King, look at the village"). Why "not in the first person" (*anuttama*)? *āgacchāni deva grāmaṃ praviśāni* ("Let us come, O King; let us enter the village"). **SK 3961:** *hanta ca* (A 8.1.54). A verb ending in the imperative, not in the first person, joined with the particle *hanta*, is unaccented. *hanta praviśa* ("Come, enter!"). The same applies to [the rule] "with a prefix" (*sopasarga*): *hanta karu* ("Come, do it!"). [Note: By the rule *nipātair yadyadi*, there is a prohibition of the unaccented status (*nighāta*). Why "not in the first person" (*anuttama*)? *hanta prabhuñjāvahai* ("Come, let us two eat together!").
Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.55: *āma ekāntaram āmantritam anantike*.

The vocative (*āmantrita*) following *ām* and separated by exactly one word is unaccented (*anudātta*), provided it is not at a distance (*anantika*). Example: *ām pacasi devadatta* (O Devadatta, you are cooking!). Why "separated by one"? Consider: *ām prapacasi devadatta* (O Devadatta, you are cooking thoroughly). Why "vocative"? Consider: *ām pacati devadattaḥ* (Devadatta is cooking, yes). Why "not at a distance"? Consider: *ām pacasi devadatta* (spoken from afar). Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.56: *yaddhituparaṃ chandasi*. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the vocative] followed by *yat*, *hi*, or *tu* is unaccented.

A finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is not unaccented [when it follows certain particles]. [Examples: *udasṛjo yad aṅgiraḥ*; *uśanti hi*; *ākhyāsyāmi tu te*. Regarding the rule *nipātaiyadyadihantakuvinnecceccaṇkaccidyatrayuktam* (Pāṇini 8.1.30), since the desired result was already established by that rule, this present rule is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). It means: "The verb is unaccented only when joined with these very particles occurring as subsequent elements, and not with others. [Example: *jāye svārohāvaihi*. Here, the finite verb ending in the imperative (*loḍanta*) is unaccented because it is joined with the imperative *ehi*, which has the sense of motion (*gatyartha*). SK 3964: *canacidivagotrāditaddhitāmreḍiteṣv agateḥ* (A 8.1.57). [This rule provides exceptions to the preceding. When *cana*, *cit*, *iva*, words beginning with *gotra*, taddhita suffixes, or repeated words (*āmreḍita*) follow, the finite verb is not unaccented, provided it does not express motion (*agateḥ*). [Examples: *kiṃ cana*, *kiṃ cit*, *devadatta iva*, *gotram*, *pācakataraḥ*, *pācaka-pācaka*. However, if motion is expressed, the verb remains unaccented: *kiṃ devadatta gataḥ*. [Note: The examples provided here illustrate the application of the general rule and its exceptions.]

In these six cases, a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) following [the particles] *cana*, *cit*, *iva*, *gotra*, *kalpa*, and *pacati* is not unaccented (*anudātta*). *devaḥ pacati cana* / *devaḥ pacati cit* / *devaḥ pacatīva* / *devaḥ pacati gotram* / *devaḥ pacatikalpam* / *devaḥ pacatipacati*. Why "not denoting motion" (*agateḥ*)? [Consider: *devaḥ prapacati cana*. [Also, this rule applies] among the group beginning with *ca* (i.e., *cādigaṇa*), according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.58.

In connection with *ca* and *vā*, a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is not unaccented [if it follows another finite verb]. Example: *devaḥ pacati ca khādati ca* ("The god cooks and eats"). The restriction "provided it is not a particle of motion" (*agater*) still applies: *devaḥ prapacati ca prakhādati ca*. By the rule *pathamasya cavāyoge* (A 8.1.59), the first verb is prohibited from being unaccented, while the second is indeed unaccented.
(SK 3966: *cavāyoge prathamā*).

When used in conjunction with *ca* and *vā*, the first finite verb (*tiṅvibhakti*) is not unaccented. For example: *gāś ca cārayati vīṇāṃ vā vādayati* ("He grazes the cows and plays the lute"), or *ito vā sātim īmahe* ("Or from here we seek gain"). This [rule] applies to the first [verb] in relation to the finite verb that must be supplied in the subsequent sentences. Why specify "in conjunction" (*yoge*)? To ensure the prohibition of accentuation (*nighāta*) even when the conjunction occurs earlier. Why mention "the first" (*prathamā*)? So that it does not apply to a second or subsequent finite verb. (Pāṇini 8.1.60: *heti kṣiyāyām*).

The first *tiṅ* inflection joined with *aha* is not unaccented when there is a transgression of duty (*dharmavyatikrama*). [Examples: *svayaṃ harathena yāti 3 upādhyāyaṃ padātiṃ gamayati 3* ("He himself goes by chariot, while he makes the teacher go on foot"). [The vowel is] protracted (*pluta*) according to the rule "in *kṣiyā* and *āśis*" (Pāṇini 8.2.104). Regarding *aha* in the sense of "assignment" (*viniyoga*) and "command" (*niyoga*) (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.61): the first *tiṅ* inflection joined with *aha* is not unaccented when there is a separate application (*nānāprayoga*), in command (*niyoga*), and in reproach (*kṣiyā*). [Examples: *tvam aha grāmaṃ gaccha* ("You yourself must go to the village"). In the sense of reproach: *svayam aha rathena yāti 3 upādhyāyaṃ padātiṃ nayati* ("He himself goes by chariot, while he makes the teacher go on foot").

SK 3969: *cāhalopa eva* (A 8.1.62). When there is the elision (*lopa*) of *ca* or *aha*, the first *tiṅ*-inflection is not unaccented (*anudātta*). Examples: *deva eva grāmaṃ gacchatu* ("Let the god go to the village") and *deva evāraṇyaṃ gacchatu* ("Let the god go to the forest"). The meaning is "let him go both to the village and to the forest. Or: *deva eva grāmaṃ gacchatu* ("Let the god go to the village") and *rāma evāraṇyaṃ gacchatu* ("Let Rāma go to the forest"). Here, *grāmaṃ* has the sense of "only" (*kevala*). What is the purpose of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)? Example: *deva kveva bhokṣyase* ("O God, where indeed will you eat?"). The meaning is "nowhere at all. This applies only when there is impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*). SK 3970: *cādilope vibhāṣā* (A 8.1.63). [When there is the elision of *ca* and other particles, the rule is optional.]

When *ca*, *vā*, or *ha* are elided, the first *tiṅ*-inflection is not unaccented. In the case of the elision of *ca*: *indra vājeṣu no ava* ("O Indra, protect us in the contests for booty") *śuklā vrīhayo bhavanti* ("the rice grains are white") *śvetā gā ājyāya duhanti* ("they milk white cows for the sake of clarified butter") In the case of the elision of *vā*: *vrīhibhir yajeta* ("one should sacrifice with rice") *yavair yajeta* ("one should sacrifice with barley") Regarding the rule *vaivāveti ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 8.1.64):
*ahar vai daivānām āsīt* ("The day indeed belonged to the gods") *ayaṃ vāva hasta āsīt* ("This very hand was there")

Pāṇini 8.1.65: *ekānyābhyāṃ samarthābhyām*—when joined with these two words which are semantically connected (*samartha*), the first case-ending (*prathamā*) verbal suffix (*tiṅvibhakti*) is not *anudātta* in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). Examples: *ajām ekāṃ jinvati* ("He quickens one goat"), *ajām ekāṃ rakṣati* ("He protects one goat"), *tayor anyaḥ pupphalaṃ svādv atti* ("One of the two eats the sweet fruit"). Why "semantically connected" (*samarthābhyām*)? [Counter-example: *eko devān upātiṣṭhat* ("One [in number] approached the gods"). Here, *eka* refers to a numerical quantity and does not carry the sense of "another. Pāṇini 8.1.66: *yadvṛttān nityam*—[The first case-ending verbal suffix following a word] ending in *yat* is always [unaccented].

In a sentence, that which follows a word containing the particle *yat* is not unaccented if it is a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). For example: *yo bhuṅkte*, *yad adryaṅ vāyur vāti*. Here, the operation is desired even when there is an intervening element.
[This is governed by] A 8.1.67: *pūjanāt pūjitam anudāttaṃ kāṣṭhādibhyaḥ* ("That which is praised following words such as *kāṣṭha* etc., used in the sense of praise, is unaccented").

The word expressing that which is honored (*pūjita*) following words such as *kāṣṭha* used in the sense of honoring is unaccented (*anudātta*). Examples: *kāṣṭhādhyāpakaḥ* ("one who teaches well"), *dāruṇādhyāpakaḥ* ("one who teaches excellently"), *ajñātādhyāpakaḥ* ("one who teaches incomparably"). This is an exception to the rule regarding the final acute accent (*antodātta*) of a compound. This is desired in these specific compounds; it does not apply here: *dāruṇam adhyāpakaḥ* (according to the opinion of Vṛtti). Since the term *pūjita* is already established by the rule "following a word denoting honor" (*pūjanāt*), the explicit mention of *pūjita* is for the purpose of obtaining the immediately preceding [word] as the one being honored.
This very fact is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in this section, even when a word is specified in the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is not required.

SK 3975: *sagatir api tiṅ* (A 8.1.68). After words such as *kāṣṭhā-* when used in the sense of "praise," a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) that is being praised becomes unaccented (*anudātta*). In the example *yatkāṣṭhāṃ prapacati*, the rule *tiṅṅ atiṅaḥ* would have caused the elision of the accent (nighāta); however, this [present] rule provides an exception. Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the term *sagati* ("along with its prefix"), the prefix (*gati*) is also elided. In the mention of *gati*, the inclusion of *upasarga* (prepositions) is intended. Thus, it does not apply here: *yatkāṣṭhāṃ śuklīkaroti*. SK 3976: *kutsane ca supy agotrādau* (A 8.1.69). [An unaccented finite verb is also used] when a nominal (*su-p*) expressing censure follows, provided it is not *gotra* etc. [or a vocative].

When followed by a word ending in a *su*-affix (*sup*) that expresses contempt (*kutsana*), a finite verb (*tiṅ*), whether accompanied by a prefix (*sagati*) or not, is unaccented (*anudātta*). Examples: *pacati pūti* ("he cooks badly"), *prapacati pūti* ("he cooks very badly"), *pacati mithyā* ("he cooks falsely"). Why "when expressing contempt"? Observe: *prapacati śobhanam* ("he cooks well"). Why "followed by a *sup*-ending word"? Observe: *pacati kliśnāti* ("he cooks and suffers"). Why "not when beginning with *gotra*, etc."? Observe: *pacati gotram* ("he cooks his lineage"). It should be stated that this applies to the contempt for the action (*kriyākutsana*); it should not apply to the contempt for the agent (*kartṛkutsana*). Example: *pacati pūtir devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is a bad cook"). It should also be stated that *pūti* is a suffix (*anubandha*).

Therefore, because it is followed by the suffix *ca*, this [word] has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Or rather, it should be stated that when it has multiple meanings, it is unaccented (*anudātta*); as in *pacanti pūti*. By the rule *gatiḥ gatau* (A 8.1.70), [the first member] is unaccented; as in *abhyuddharati*. Why "before a gati"? As in *dattaḥ pacati*. Why "before a gati"? As in *āmandrair indra haribhir yāhi manyūraromabhiḥ*.

SK 3978: *tiṅi codāttavati* (A 8.1.71). A *gati* [particle] is *anudātta* (unaccented) before a *tiṅ* [verbal suffix] that possesses an *udātta* [acute accent]. For example: *yat prapacati*. The mention of *tiṅ* is for the purpose of defining the scope of "that which possesses an *udātta*. Otherwise, since *pra* and other such particles are *gatis* only with respect to that action (*kriyā*) they are connected with, the *anudātta* quality would apply only when the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself possesses the *udātta*, and not when the suffix (*pratyaya*) does. Why specify "possessing an *udātta*"? Consider: *prapacati*. Thus end the rules regarding the accents of *tiṅ*-endings. This concludes the section on the manner of the movement of accents (74).

Now, the manner of the movement of accents (*svarasaṃcāra*) in Vedic sentences is described. The first *ṛc* is "agnim īḷe. Regarding the word *agni*, Mādhava maintains that, according to the view of non-etymological derivation (*avyutpattipakṣa*), it is oxytone by the rule *phiṣaḥ*. In reality, however, it is so because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group. If derived etymologically, it is oxytone due to the accent of the *nit* suffix. The case ending *am* is unaccented because it is a *sup* (nominal suffix). In the substitution *ami pūrvaḥ* (the single substitute for *am* and the preceding vowel), the resulting single substitute is accented because of the rule *ekādeśa udāttena*. In *īḷe*, the *tiṅ* suffix is unaccented by the rule *tiṅṅ atiṅaḥ*.

In the *saṃhitā*, by the rule "after an acute (*udātta*), an unaccented (*anudātta*) [vowel becomes]—," the vowel *i* is circumflex (*svarita*). By the rule "from a circumflex in *saṃhitā*—," the syllable *ḷe* has the single accent (*ekaśruti*), which is synonymous with the "accumulated" (*pracaya*) accent. The word *puraḥ* is acutely accented on the final syllable, due to the accent of the suffix *asi* prescribed by the rule "for *pūrva*, *adhara*, and *avara*. The word *hita* is also acutely accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix, because of the substitution of *hi* for the root *dhā* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) according to the rule "for *dadhāti*, there is *hi*."

Regarding the term *puro* as an indeclinable (*avyaya*): when it forms a compound with *kugati-* etc., the rule for the final acute accent of a *tatpuruṣa* applies; then, by the rule for the original accent of the first member in an indeclinable preceding a compound (*avyayapūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*), the rule for the original accent of the *kṛt*-derived final member after a prefix, a noun denoting an agent or object (*kāraka*), or a subordinate word (*upapada*) (*gatikārakopapadāt kṛt-*) applies; and finally, by the rule for the accent of *thā-thādi* compounds, the former [rules] are successively superseded. However, by the rule "a prefix [retains its accent] when not separated by another word" (*gatir anantaraḥ*), the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) prevails.

In the *saṃhitā*, when the protracted (*pracaya*) accent would apply to the vowel *u* of the word *puraḥ*, it becomes *anudāttatara* (more gravely accented) according to the rule *udāttasvaritaparasya sannataraḥ*. [The word] *jañasya*: the suffix *naṅ* receives the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Since the case ending is unaccented due to being a *sup* suffix, it receives the *svarita* accent. [The word] *devam*: [formed with] *pacādyac*; it is oxytone by either the *phiṭ-svara* or the accent of the suffix. The word *ṛtvik* is oxytone by the rule that the original accent of the final member of a compound is retained (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*). The word *hotṛ* ends in the suffix *tṛn* and is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) by the rule for *nit* suffixes.

The word *ratna* is udātta on its first syllable by the rule *anabviṣayasya*. [The term] *ratnadhāḥ* means "one who bestows jewels" (*ratnāni dadhāti*). It is udātta on the final syllable either by the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*) or by the rule that the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derivative remains (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*). Since the suffix *tamap* is marked with *p*, it is anudātta; consequently, the *svarita* and the following *pracaya* accents are to be inferred according to the grammatical treatises. Such is the movement of accents. Thus has been shown here a mere indication regarding Vedic words.
May this be for the pleasure of the illustrious Bhavānī and Viśvanātha. 1.
Thus ends the section on Vedic accents in the Siddhāntakaumudī composed by Śrī Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
The instruction on gender markers, seventy-five.

The section on feminine nouns (*stryadhikāra*). [The following] are the governing rules (*adhikārasūtra*): 1. *liṅga*; 2. *strī*. Words ending in the vowel *ṛ*—namely *mātṛ*, *duhitṛ*, *svasṛ*, *pitṛ*, and *nanāndṛ*—these five alone are feminine when they end in *ṛ*. This is because the suffix *ṅīp* is applied to forms such as *kartrī*, which ends in *ī*, since the suffix *ṅīp* is specifically prohibited for the group of five beginning with *svasṛ*. Furthermore, although *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are prescribed as substitutes (*ādeśa*) in the feminine, the original bases (*prakṛti*), *tri* and *catur*, do not end in *ṛ*. A verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in the suffix *an* or *ani* is feminine. That is, a root ending in the suffix *an* or the suffix *ani* occurs in the feminine gender.

*Avaniḥ* (earth) / *camūḥ* (army). Why is there a mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*)? [Consider] *devayateḥ* with the suffix *kvip*: *dyuḥ* (heaven). It takes the gender of the word it qualifies (*viśeṣyaliṅgaḥ*). 5. *Aśani*, *aṇī*, and *araṇi* are masculine; they are also feminine. This is *aśaniḥ* (thunderbolt), whether feminine or masculine. 6. Those ending in the suffixes *min* and *nip*. A verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in the suffix *min* or the suffix *nip* shall be feminine. Examples: *bhūmiḥ* (earth), *glāniḥ* (lassitude). 7. *Vahni*, *vṛṣṇi*, and *agni* are masculine. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. 8. *Śroṇi*, *yoni*, and *ūrmi* are masculine; they are also feminine. This is *śroṇiḥ*, whether feminine or masculine. 9. Those ending in the suffix *ktin*. This is clear.

"Kṛti," and so forth. (10) A word ending in the vowel *ī* is feminine when it ends in the suffix *ī*. (11) A word ending in *ū* or *āp* is feminine; for example, *kurūḥ* and *vidyā*. (12) A monosyllabic word ending in *y* or *v* is feminine; for example, *śrīḥ* and *bhūḥ*. Why "monosyllabic"? [Counter-example: *pṛthuśrīḥ*. (13) Words beginning with *viṃśati* and ending with *navati* are feminine; for example, this *viṃśatiḥ*, *triṃśat*, *catvāriṃśat*, *pañcāśat*, *ṣaṣṭiḥ*, *saptatiḥ*, *aśītiḥ*, and *navatiḥ*. (14) The word *dundubhi* is feminine when referring to dice; for example, this *dundubhiḥ* [referring to dice]. Why "when referring to dice"? [Counter-example: *dundubhiḥ* [referring to a drum].

The meaning is that "this" refers to a *dundubhi*, a specific type of musical instrument, or an *asura*. The word *nābhi* is not used for a non-Kṣatriya; this [usage] refers to the navel. Both *dundubhi* and *nābhi* are masculine when used outside of their aforementioned specific domains. *Nābhi* as a Kṣatriya: how then is one to explain Bhāravi’s verse, "by those whose navels were adorned with waistbands and were as tender as the petals of a blooming lotus"? It is said in reply: just as in the case of *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ* and similar examples, the word *komalaiḥ* (tender) should be understood here as a neuter used in a general sense.

In reality, however, the masculine gender is also correct here, based on the *Bhāṣya* which states: "The gender is not to be prescribed, because gender relies upon common usage (*lokāśrayatva*). For this very reason, the *Medinīkośa* says: "The word *nābhi* is masculine when meaning a sovereign king, the hub of a wheel, or a Kṣatriya; it is used for both genders when referring to a limb of a living being, and feminine when meaning musk. Rabhasa also says: "*Nābhi* is masculine when meaning a sovereign king or a Kṣatriya, and of both genders when meaning a limb of a living being; it is feminine when meaning the hub of a wheel, a preeminent person, or musk."

In this same manner, it should be understood in other instances as well. (17) *tala* suffixes: this [suffix] occurs in the feminine. The state of being white is *śuklatā*; the action of a Brahmin is *brāhmaṇatā*; a collection of villages is *grāmatā*; a god himself is *devatā*. (18) Terms denoting earth, lightning, river, creeper, and woman: *bhūmi* is *bhū*; *vidyut* is *saudāmanī*; *sarit* is *nimnagā*; *latā* is *vallī*; *vanitā* is *yoṣit*. (19) *yādas* is neuter: although the word *yādas* denotes a river, it is also neuter.

20. *bhās*, *sruk*, *sruc*, *diguṣṇih*, and *upānah*—these are feminine. For example: "this *bhās*" (*iyaṃ bhās*), and so forth. 21. *Sthūṇā* and *ūrṇā* occur in both the feminine and the neuter. These two exist in both the feminine and the neuter genders. *Sthūṇā*; *sthūṇam*. *Ūrṇā*; *ūrṇam*. Among these, *sthūṇā* is a wooden post with two notches; *ūrṇā*, however, is the wool of sheep and the like. 22. [The words *sthūṇā* and *ūrṇā*] are neuter when preceded by *gṛha* and *śaśa*. This is for the purpose of restriction. When preceded by *gṛha* and *śaśa*, *sthūṇā* and *ūrṇā* are neuter respectively. *Gṛhasthūṇam*.

*Śaśoḥ ṇaṃ śaśalomani*—thus says Amara. (23) *Prāvṛṭ*, *vipruṭ*, *ruṭ*, *viṭ*, and *tviṣ*: these are feminine. (24) *Darvī*, *vidi*, *vedi*, *svani*, *śāni*, *śrī*, *veśī*, *kṛṣī*, *auṣadhī*, *kaṭī*, and *aṅgulī*: these are feminine; optionally, they take the suffix *ṅīp*. Thus: *darvī* or *darviḥ*, and so forth. (25) *Tithi*, *nāḍī*, *ruci*, *vīci*, *nālī*, *dhūli*, *kīki*, *elā*, *chavi*, *trāṭrī*, and others: these follow the previous rule. Thus: "this is a *tithi*" (*iyaṃ tithiḥ*), and so forth. However, Amara says: "*Tithayaḥ* [are used] in both genders. And likewise, Bhāravi [states]: * *Śaśoḥ ṇaṃ śaśalomani*: Regarding the word *śaśaloman* (hare's hair), the suffix *ṇa* is applied after *śas*. * *Prāvṛṭ-vipruṭ-ruṭ-viṭ-tviṣaḥ*: These five words ending in *tviṣ* are feminine. * *Darvī-vidi-vedi-svani-śāni-śrī-veśī-kṛṣī-auṣadhī-kaṭī-aṅgulayaḥ*: These eleven words ending in *aṅgulī* are feminine; in the alternative case, they take the suffix *ṅīp*. For example: *darvī* or *darviḥ*. * *Tithi-nāḍī-ruci-vīci-nālī-dhūli-kīki-elā-chavi-trāṭrī-ādayaḥ*: These words beginning with *tithi* follow the same pattern as before. Examples include: "this is a *tithi*" (*iyaṃ tithiḥ*). * Amara, however, states: "*Tithayaḥ* [are used] in both genders" (*dvayoḥ*). * Similarly, Bhāravi [uses them in the masculine]. (Note: The specific verse from Bhāravi is not provided in the source text, but the reference indicates he uses the term in a non-feminine form.)

Regarding the phrase *tasya bhuvi bahutithās tithayaḥ*: for if it were in the feminine gender, it would have to be *bahutithyaḥ*. And Śrīharṣa says: "all the nights of the full moon (*paurṇimātithīn*). (26) *Śaṣkulī*, *rājikā*, *kṛtti*, *aśani*, *varti*, *bhṛkuṭi*, *truṭi*, and *valipaṅkti*—these also may be feminine. This is a *śaṣkulī*. (27) *Pratipad*, *āpad*, *vipad*, *sampad*, *śarad*, *saṃsad*, *pariṣad*, *uṣas*, *saṃvid*, *kṣut*, *punarmukha*, and *samidh*—this is a *pratipad*, and so forth. *Uṣas* is that which shines.

Uṣas is the deity presiding over the morning. (28) Āśis, dhūs, pūḥ, gīḥ, and dvār—these are examples such as "this is āśis" and so forth. (29) There is plurality for *apsu*, *manas*, *samit*, *kāṣṭhā*, and *karṣāṇā*. For the five beginning with *āpas*, there is femininity and plurality; for example, "these waters" (*imā āpaḥ*). *Sumanas* is feminine when it means "flower"—*sumanā* being the *mālatī* or *jāti* jasmine—but when it denotes a god, it is masculine, as in "the gods (*suparvāṇaḥ*) are *sumanasaḥ*. Plurality is the general rule [for these].

"A single grain of sand is incapable of yielding oil," according to the usage in the *Bhāṣya* on the *arthavat-sūtra*; and also from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *samāṃsamāṃ vijāyate*, where it is interpreted as "in every year" (*samāyāṃ samāyām*). Haradatta likewise explains this in his commentary on the *Vṛtti* for the rule *vibhāṣāghrādheṭ-*, regarding the example *aghrāsātāṃ sumanasau*. 30. *srak-tvak-jyok-vāg-yavāgū-naus-phij-aḥ*: *iyaṃ srak*, *tvak*, *jyok*, *vāk*, *yavāgūḥ*, *nauḥ*, *sphik*. 31. *tṛṭi-sīmā-saṃbadhyāḥ*: *iyaṃ tṛṭiḥ*.

*sīmā* is feminine when connected [with another word]. 32. *culliveṇikhāryaś ca*: and *cullī*, *veṇī*, and *khārī* [are also feminine]. This is clear. 33. *tārādhārājyotsnādayaś ca*: and *tārā*, *dhārā*, *jyotsnā*, etc., [are feminine]. 34. *śalākā striyāṃ nityam*: *śalākā* is always feminine. The inclusion of the word "always" (*nityam*) indicates that for other [words], there may be occasional deviation [from this rule]. Thus ends the section on feminine gender. Now begins the section on masculine gender.

35. *pumān* (masculine). This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). 36. [Words] ending in *ghañ* [denote] the masculine gender: *pākaḥ*, *tyāgaḥ*, *karaḥ*, *garaḥ*. This applies only when the meaning is that of the abstract action (*bhāva*). For while the suffixes *kta* and *lyuṭ* denote the abstract action qualified by the neuter gender, they are superseded by *ktin* and other suffixes when the abstract action is qualified by the feminine gender; thus, by process of elimination, this rule remains. However, when denoting the object (*karman*) and so forth, even words ending in *ghañ* take the gender of the substantive they qualify. As it says in the *Bhāṣya*: "The connection will continue to apply. 37. And those ending in *ghañ*: *vistaraḥ*, *gocaraḥ*, *cayaḥ*, *jayaḥ*, and so forth.

38. Words ending in *bhaya*, *liṅga*, and *bhaga* are neuter. 39. A word ending in the suffix *naṅ* is masculine; that is, a word formed with the suffix *naṅ* occurs in the masculine gender. Examples: *yajñaḥ*, *yatnaḥ*. 40. The word *yācñā* is feminine. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. 41. A word ending in the suffix *ki* and being a *ghu* root is masculine; that is, a word formed with the suffix *ki* which is a *ghu* root occurs in the masculine gender. Examples: *ādhiḥ*, *nidhiḥ*, *udadhiḥ*. Why "ending in *ki*"? Consider *dānam*. Why "a *ghu* root"? Consider *jajñiḥ* (seed). 42. The word *iṣudhi* is both feminine and masculine. The word *iṣudhi* occurs in the feminine and the masculine. This is an exception to the preceding rule.

43. The following words are used in the masculine: *deva*, *asura*, *ātman*, *svarga*, *giri*, *samudra*, *nakha*, *keśa*, *danta*, *stana*, *bhuja*, *kaṇṭha*, *khaḍga*, *śara*, and *paṅka*. *Devāḥ* means gods; *surāḥ* means the same. *Asurāḥ* means demons (*daityāḥ*). *Ātmā* means the knower of the field (*kṣetrajñaḥ*). *Svargaḥ* means heaven (*nākaḥ*). *Giriḥ* means a mountain (*parvataḥ*). *Samudraḥ* means the ocean (*abdhiḥ*). *Nakhaḥ* means a fingernail (*kararuhaḥ*). *Keśaḥ* means hair on the head (*śiroruhaḥ*). *Dantaḥ* means a tooth (*daśanaḥ*). *Stanaḥ* means a breast (*kucaḥ*). *Bhujaḥ* means an arm (*doḥ*). *Kaṇṭhaḥ* means the throat (*galaḥ*). *Khaḍgaḥ* means a sword (*karavālaḥ*). *Śaraḥ* means an arrow (*mārgaṇaḥ*).

*Mud* (paṅka) and *mire* (kardama), etc. 44. *Triviṣṭapa* and *tribhuvana* are neuter. This is clear. *Triviṣṭapa* means "the third world" (*tṛtīyaṃ viṣṭapaṃ*). Since it would have been masculine by virtue of being a name for heaven (*svarga*), this rule is commenced [to specify its gender]. 45. *Dyauḥ* (heaven) is feminine. Here, both *dyoḥ* and *divaḥ* are included by the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application). 46. *Iṣu* (arrow) and *bāhu* (arm) are also feminine; by the word "also" (*ca*), they are also masculine. 47. *Bāṇa* (arrow) and *kāṇḍa* (shaft) are also neuter; by the word "also" (*ca*), they are also masculine. This group of four sūtras beginning with *triviṣṭapa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule beginning with *devāsura*. 48. [Words] ending in *n* [are neuter].

This [suffix] occurs in the masculine: *rājā* (king), *takṣā* (carpenter). Nor is there over-extension to words such as *carman* (skin) or *varman* (armor), because it will be stated in the section on neuter nouns that "a word with two or three syllables ending in this suffix is neuter when not denoting an agent. 49. Words denoting sacrifice (*kratu*), man (*puruṣa*), cheek (*kapola*), ankle (*gulpha*), and cloud (*megha*) are masculine. *Kratu* means sacrifice (*adhvara*). *Puruṣa* means man (*nara*). *Kapola* means cheek (*gaṇḍa*). *Gulpha* means the instep (*prapada*). *Megha* means rain-cloud (*nīrada*). 50. *Abhra* (cloud) is neuter. This is an exception to the preceding rule. 51. A word ending in the vowel *u* is masculine. For example: *prabhuḥ* (lord), *ikṣuḥ* (sugarcane).

*Hanu* is [masculine] in *Haṭṭavilāsinī* at the beginning of a dance; [it is] *gada* (a mace) in the feminine; and according to the *Medinī*, it is [used] in two genders as a part of the cheek. *Kareṇu* is [masculine] for an elephant and [feminine] for a female elephant, according to the *Amara-kośa*. However, the scope of the present sūtra consists of those words of this class that are not covered by such specific rules. And it has been said: "The rule for the remaining genders is all-pervasive, provided it is not sublated by specific rules. The same applies elsewhere. 42. *Dhenu*, *rajju*, *kuhū*, *sarayu*, *tanu*, *reṇu*, and *priyaṅgu* are feminine. 53. In a compound, *rajju* is also masculine.

By *karkaṭarajju* / by *karkaṭarajjunā*. 54. *śmaśru*, *jānu*, *vasu*, *kha*, *dṛś*, *ru*, *jatū*, *trapu*, and *ālū* are neuter. 55. *Vasu* when it signifies wealth (*arthavācin*). Why "when it signifies wealth"? [Because] *vasu* [also means] rays, fire, and the lord of wealth (*mayūkha-agni-dhanādhipeṣu*). 56. *Maṭ*, *du*, *madhu*, *sīdhu*, *śīdhu*, *sānu*, and *kamaṇḍalu* are neuter; and by "and" (*ca*), they are also masculine. This is *madguḥ* (masculine); this is *madguḥ* (neuter). 57. [Words] ending in *rut* [are neuter]. *Meruḥ*; *setuḥ*. 58. *Dāru*, *kaseru*, *jatu*, *vastu*, and *mastu* are neuter.

*rutvant* (ending in *ru* or *t*) is an exception to [the rule regarding] the masculine gender. *idaṃ dāru* (this wood). 59. *sakta-* is also neuter; and because of the word *ca* ("and"), it is also masculine. *saktuḥ* (groats), *saktu* (groats). 60. Before the word *raśmi*, that which ends in *a* is [masculine]. He will state that *raśmi* denotes "rays of light"; prior to this point, the status of ending in *a* is governed as the subject. 61. A word having *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*) [is masculine]. A word ending in *a* with *ka* as its penultimate letter shall be masculine. *stabakaḥ* (cluster/bunch), *kalkaḥ* (paste/impurity). 62. *cibuka*, *śālūka*, *prātipadika*, *aṃśu*, and *ulmuka* are neuter. This is an exception to the preceding rule.

63. *Kaṇṭhaka*, *anīka*, *sarakam*, *modaka*, *caṣaka*, *mastaka*, *pustaka*, *taḍāka*, *niṣka*, *śuṣkavarcaska*, *pināka*, *bhāṇḍaka*, *piṇḍaka*, *kaṭaka*, *śaṇḍaka*, *piṭaka*, *tālaka*, *phalaka*, and *pulāka* are neuter; however, they may also be masculine. For example: "this is a *kaṇṭhaka*" (*ayaṃ kaṇṭhakaḥ*) or "this is a *kaṇṭhaka*" (*idaṃ kaṇṭakam*), and so forth. 64. Words ending in *ṭa* with a penultimate *ṭa* (*ṭopadha*) ending in *a* are masculine. For example: *ghaṭaḥ* (pot), *paṭaḥ* (cloth). 65. *Kirīṭa*, *mukuṭa*, *lalāṭa*, *vaṭa*, *vīṭa*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *rāṭa*, and *loṣṭa* are neuter. For example: *kirīṭam*, and so forth.

66. The words *kuṭa*, *kūṭaka*, *paṭaka*, *vāṭaka*, *karpaṭa*, *naṭa*, *nikaṭa*, *kīṭaka*, and *kaṭa* are neuter; however, by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), they are also masculine—as in *kuṭaḥ*. Examples include *kuṭam* and so forth. 67. A word ending in *ṇa* as its penultimate letter (*ṇopadha*) and ending in *a* is masculine. Examples: *guṇaḥ*, *gaṇaḥ*, *pāṣāṇaḥ*. 68. The words *ṛṇa*, *lavaṇa*, *parṇa*, *toraṇa*, *raṇa*, and *uṣṇa* are neuter. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. 69. The words *kārṣāpaṇa*, *svarṇa*, *suvarṇa*, *vraṇa*, *caraṇa*, *vṛṣaṇa*, *viṣāṇa*, *cūrṇa*, and *tṛṇa* are neuter; however, by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), they are also masculine. 70. A word with *tha* as its penultimate letter (*thopadha*) is masculine—e.g., *rathaḥ*.

71. *kāṣṭha*, *pṛṣṭha*, *siktha*, and *uktha* are neuter; for example, "this wood" (*idaṃ kāṣṭham*). 72. *Kāṣṭhā*, when meaning a direction, is feminine; for example, "these directions" (*imāḥ kāṣṭhāḥ*). 73. *Tīrtha*, *prayotha*, *yūtha*, and *gātha* are neuter; and because of the word "ca" (and), they are also masculine; for example, "this sacred ford" (*ayaṃ tīrthaḥ*) or "this sacred ford" (*idaṃ tīrtham*). 74. A word ending in *na* as its penultimate letter is masculine; for example, *inaḥ* (the sun) and *phenaḥ* (foam). 75. *Jaghana*, *ajina*, *tuhina*, *kānana*, *vana*, *vṛjina*, *vipina*, *vetana*, *śāsana*, *sopāna*, *mithuna*, *śmaśāna*, *ratna*, *nimna*, and *cihna* are neuter.

This is an exception to the preceding rule. 76. The words *māna*, *yāna*, *abhidhāna*, *nalina*, *pulina*, *udyāna*, *śayana*, *āsana*, *sthāna*, *candana*, *ālāna*, *samāna*, *bhavana*, *vasana*, *saṃbhāvana*, *vibhāvana*, and *vimāna* are neuter; and because of the word "ca" (and), they are also masculine. Example: *ayaṃ mānaḥ* (this is a measure) or *idaṃ mānam*. 77. A word ending in *p* as its penultimate letter (*popadha*) and ending in *a* is masculine. Examples: *yūpaḥ* (sacrificial post), *dīpaḥ* (lamp). 78. The words *pāpa*, *rūpa*, *uḍupa*, *talpa*, *śilpa*, *puṣpa*, *śaṣpa*, *samīpa*, and *antarīpa* are neuter. Example: *idaṃ pāpam* (this is sin), and so forth.

79. Words ending in *sūrpa*, *kutapa*, *kuṇapa*, *dvīpa*, and *viṭapa* are neuter; for example: *ayaṃ sūrpaḥ* (this winnowing basket), *idaṃ sūrpam* (this winnowing basket), and so forth. 80. Words having *bha* as their penultimate letter [are masculine]; for example: *stambhaḥ* (pillar), *kumbhaḥ* (jar). 81. The word *jṛmbhya* is neuter; for example: *jṛmbham* (yawning), *jṛmbhaḥ* (yawning). 83. Words having *ma* as their penultimate letter [are masculine]; for example: *somaḥ* (moon/nectar), *bhīmaḥ* (terrible). 84. The words *rukma*, *sidhma*, *yudhma*, *edhma*, *gulma*, *ādhyātma*, and *kuṅkuma* are neuter; for example: *idaṃ rukmam* (this gold), and so forth. 85. The words *saṃgrāma*, *dāḍima*, *kusuma*, *āśrama*, *kṣema*, *kṣauma*, *homa*, and *uddāma* are neuter; for example: *idaṃ saṃgrāmam* (this battle), and so forth. They are also [masculine].

And [the word *saṃgrāma*] is masculine: *ayaṃ saṃgrāmaḥ* (this battle), *idaṃ saṃgrāmam* (this battle). 86. Words with *y* as the penultimate letter: *samayaḥ* (agreement), *hayaḥ* (horse). 87. *Kisalaya*, *hṛdaya*, *indriya*, and *uttarīya* are neuter; this is clear. 88. *Gomaya*, *kaṣāya*, *malaya*, *anvaya*, and *avyaya* are neuter as well as [masculine]. *Gomayaḥ* (cow-dung), *gomayam* (cow-dung). 89. Words with *r* as the penultimate letter: *kṣuraḥ* (razor), *aṅkuraḥ* (sprout). 90.

[The description continues with a vast array of compounds detailing the architectural and natural features of the mountain, including: the great expanse of the gateway-forests; the tossing of small, incessant, and distant waves upon the shores; the terrifying and deep abysses and chasms; the formidable and variegated armlets; the vast fields of the mountain; the noble and eternal caves of the body; the celestial *mandāra* groves within the mountain-cages; the rows of peaks and bellies; the enmity-free fly-whisks and lotuses; the caverns and hollows of the huts; the crabs at the crossroads; the saffron-colored waters as the sky-garment; the cooling machinery of the strings; the constellations, fields, friends, wives, and various threads of urine; the faces, eyes, lineages, fingers, shields, armor, weapons, scriptures, garments, shame, and vessels.

The word *atraṇi* is not neuter; for example, "this door" (*idaṃ dvāram*). 91. *Śukra* is [neuter] except when referring to a deity; for example, "this *śukra* is semen. 92. *Cakra*, *vajra*, *andhakāra*, *sāra*, *avārapāra*, *kṣīra*, *tomara*, *śṛṅgāra*, *bhṛṅgāra*, *mandāra*, *uśīra*, *timira*, and *śiśira* are neuter, and by the word "ca" (and), they are also masculine: *cakraḥ* or *cakram*, and so forth. 93. Words with *ṣ* as their penultimate letter: *vṛṣaḥ*, *vṛkṣaḥ*. 94. *Śirīṣa*, *arjīṣa*, *ambarīṣa*, *pīyūṣa*, *purīṣa*, *kilbiṣa*, and *kalmāṣa* are neuter.

95. *yūṣa*, *karīṣa*, *miṣa*, and *viṣa* are neuter; optionally masculine as well. For example: *ayaṃ yūṣaḥ* (this broth) or *idaṃ yūṣam* (this broth), and so forth. 96. Words ending in the augment *upadha* [with a penultimate vowel] are masculine: *vatsaḥ* (calf), *vāyasaḥ* (crow), *mahān saḥ* (that great one). 97. *panasa*, *bisa*, *busa*, and *sāhasa* are neuter. 98. *camasa*, *āṃsa*, *rasa*, *niryāsa*, *upavāsa*, *kārpāsa*, *vāsa*, *māsa*, *kāsa*, *kāṃsa*, and *māṃsa* are neuter as well. For example: *idaṃ camasam* (this ladle) or *ayaṃ camasaḥ* (this ladle), and so forth. 99. *kaṃsa* is also neuter when not referring to a living being. *Kaṃsaḥ* (masculine) is a drinking vessel and is not feminine.

Regarding living beings, however, there is a certain king named Kaṃsa. (100) Terms for rays and days are masculine: *raśmi* (ray), *mayūkha* (ray); *divasa* (day), *dhasra* (day). (101) *Dīdhiti* (ray) is feminine; this is an exception to the preceding [rule]. (102) *Dina* and *ahana* (day) are neuter; this is also an exception. (103) Terms for measures are masculine: *kuḍava* (a measure), *prastha* (a measure). (104) *Droṇa* and *āḍhaka* (measures) are also neuter: *idam droṇam* (this is a droṇa), *ayaṃ droṇaḥ* (this is a droṇa). (105) *Khārī* and *mānika* (measures) are feminine.

This is a *khārī*; this is a *mānikā*. (106) There is also the plural usage for *dāra*, *akṣata*, *lājā*, and *sūnā*. These are *dārāḥ* (wives). (107) Words such as *vraṇa*, *aṅga*, and *pada* when preceded by words such as *nāṭya* and others are masculine. Words such as *vraṇa* and so forth, when preceded by *nāṭya* and others respectively, shall be masculine. For example: *ayaṃ nāḍīvraṇaḥ* (this is a sinus), *apāṅgaḥ* (the outer corner of the eye), *janapadaḥ* (a country). Although words such as *vraṇa* possess both genders, this rule is intended to exclude their neuter gender. (108) *marut*, *garut*, and the names of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) [are masculine]. This is *marut* (the wind god).

109. *ṛṣi*, *rāśi*, *ṛti*, *granthi*, *krimi*, *dhvani*, *bali*, *kauli*, *mauli*, *ravi*, *kavi*, and *kapi*—these are masculine. This is an *ṛṣi*. 110. *dhvaja*, *gaja*, *muñja*, and *puñja*—these are masculine. 111. *hasta*, *kunta*, *anta*, *vrāta*, *vāta*, *dūta*, *dhūrta*, *sūta*, *cūta*, and *muhūrta*—these are masculine. However, Amarasiṃha says that *muhūrta* is not feminine. 112. *ṣaṇḍa*, *maṇḍa*, *karaṇḍa*, *bharaṇḍa*, *varaṇḍa*, *tuṇḍa*, *gaṇḍa*, *muṇḍa*, *pāṣaṇḍa*, and *śikhaṇḍa*—this is *ṣaṇḍa*. 113. *vaṃśa*, *aṃśa*, and *puroḍāśa*.

This is the *vaṃśa* (lineage). *Puroḍāśaḥ* is offered in front (*puras*). [The suffix] *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The substitution of *ḍa* for *da* occurs either by virtue of the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) in the present sūtra itself—under the section on the derivation of names and explanations (*bhavavyākhyāna*) which states "from *pauroḍāśa* and *puroḍāśa*, [the suffix] *ṣṭhan*," and under the section on modifications (*vikāra*) which states "*vrīheḥ puroḍāśe*"—or because of the rule "in *argha*, *pathin*, *mathin*, *ṛbhukṣin*, *stamba*, *nitamba*, and *pūga*. Thus, *puroḍāśaḥ* is formed. Māgha says: "It is desired by those who eat the *puroḍāśa*. 114. *Argha*, *pathin*, *mathin*, *ṛbhukṣin*, *stamba*, *nitamba*, and *pūga*. This is *argha* (price/value).

116. *pallava*, *palvala*, *kaphara*, *repha*, *kaṭāha*, *nirvyūha*, *maṭha*, *maṇi*, *taraṅga*, *turaṅga*, *gandha*, *mṛdaṅga*, *saṅga*, *samudga*, *puṅkha*; "this is a sprout" (*ayaṃ pallavaḥ*), and so forth. 117. *sārathi*, *atithi*, *kukṣi*, *vasti*, *pṛṣṇi*, *añjali*: these are masculine. This is the section on masculine genders. Now begins the section on neuter genders.

118. *Napuṃsakaṃ* (Neuter). This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). 119. A word ending in the suffix *lyuṭ* denotes an action (*bhāva*) and is neuter. Example: *hasanam* (the act of laughing). Why "denoting an action"? [Counter-examples: *pacanaḥ agniḥ* (a cooking fire); *idhmapravraścanaḥ kuṭhāraḥ* (an axe for cutting fuel). 120. And a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix. A word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix that denotes an action shall be neuter. Examples: *hasitam* (laughing), *gītam* (singing). 121. The *taddhita* suffixes *tva* and *ṣyañ*. Words formed with these are neuter. Examples: *śuklatvam* (whiteness), *śauklyam* (whiteness). Because of the indicatory letter *ṣ* in *ṣyañ*, there is optionally femininity when the suffix *pat* is applied: *cāturyam* (cleverness) or *cāturī*; *sāmagryam* (completeness) or *sāmagrī*; *aucityam* (propriety) or *aucitī*.

122. And [the suffix *yañ*] is added after words denoting qualities such as *brāhmaṇa*, etc., when the sense is "action" (*karman*). The action of a *brāhmaṇa* is *brāhmaṇyam*. 123. These three sūtras are for the sake of clarity. Thus ends the instruction on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*). Thus ends the *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudī* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭojidīkṣita.
