Now I shall proclaim the science of phonetics (*śikṣā*) according to the doctrine of Pāṇini; one should know it according to the sequence of the treatise as it has been stated for both the world and the Veda. Even though the meaning of words is well-known, it remains uncomprehended by those lacking intelligence; therefore, I shall again clarify the rule for the pronunciation of speech. (2) Sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes (*varṇa*) are recognized in the opinion of Śambhu; they were proclaimed by the Self-Existent One (*Svayambhū*) himself for both the Prakrit and the Sanskrit languages. (3)

There are twenty-one vowels and twenty-five consonants (*sparśas*). The eight letters beginning with *ya* are recorded [as semivowels], and four are recorded as the *yamas*. The *anusvāra*, the *visarga*, and the two [nasalized sounds] dependent on *ka* and *pa* should be known as *duḥspṛṣṭa*, as well as the protracted (*pluta*) *ḷ*-vowel. The self (*ātman*), having come into contact with objects through the intellect (*buddhi*), joins the mind (*manas*) with the desire to speak. The mind strikes the bodily fire (*kāyāgni*), and that [fire] impels the vital air (*māruta*).

Moving within the chest, the vital air (māruta) produces a deep (mandra) tone; that is associated with the morning chant (prātaḥsavana) and rests upon the Gāyatrī meter. (7) In the throat, it produces a middle (madhyama) tone associated with the midday chant (mādhyandinasavana) and the Triṣṭubh meter; in the head, it produces a high (tāra) tone associated with the third pressing (tārtīyasavana) and the Jagatī meter. (8) That vital air, having been expelled and struck against the head, reaches the mouth and generates the phonemes (varṇa); their classification is traditionally held to be fivefold: (9) According to pitch (svara), duration (kāla), place of articulation (sthāna), effort (prayatna), and external emission (anupradāna).

Thus those who know the phonemes have spoken; understand that skillfully. (10.2) The three accents—acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*)—and [the distinctions] short, long, and protracted (*pluta*) are regulated by duration when vowels (*ac*) follow. (11) In the acute accent are *niṣāda* and *gāndhāra*; in the grave are *ṛṣabha* and *dhaivata*; for these six—*ṣaḍja*, *madhyama*, and *pañcama*—originate from the circumflex. (12) There are eight places of articulation for the phonemes: the chest, the throat, and likewise the head;

The root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate; closure (*saṃvāra*) and opening (*vivṛtti*), as well as *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *r*; the root of the tongue, and the *upadhmānīya*—this is the eightfold movement of the *ūṣman* (sibilants and *h*). If there is a connection with closure (*saṃvāra*) and the following word begins with *u* or another vowel, one should know that such a word ending in a vowel is [an *ūṣman*]; any other [word] is clearly not an *ūṣman*. The letter *h*, when joined with the fifth [consonants of the five classes] and combined with the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), [is also an *ūṣman*].

One should know that [the vowel *a*] is produced from the chest; they say that [the vowel *a*] which is not joined [with another consonant] is produced from the throat (kaṇṭhya). 16 *k*, *kh*, *g*, *gh*, *ṅ*; *c*, *ch*, *j*, *jh*, *ñ*; *ṭ*, *ṭh*, *ḍ*, *ḍh*, *ṇ*; *t*, *th*, *d*, *dh*, *n*; and *p*, *ph*, *b*, *bh*, *m* are produced respectively from the throat, the palate, the roof of the mouth, the teeth, and the lips. *Ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ṣ*; *ṭ*, *ṭh*, *r*, *ṣ*; and *ḷ*, *ḷ*, *l*, *s* are recorded as being produced from the root of the tongue, the teeth, and the teeth respectively. 17 *K* is said by the wise to be produced at the root of the tongue (*jihvāmūla*), and *v* is recorded as being produced from both the teeth and the lips (*dantyoṣṭhya*). *E* and *ai* are produced from the throat and the palate (*kaṇṭhatālavya*), while *o* and *au* are recorded as being produced from the throat and the lips (*kaṇṭhoṣṭhya*). 18 The half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) belonging to *e* and *ai* would be produced from the throat. For *o* and *au*, there is one mora; between those two, there is the distinction of being open (*vivṛta*) or closed (*saṃvṛta*). 19 *(Note: The provided text ends with verse 18, but the Sanskrit fragment includes the beginning of verse 19 regarding the morae of the diphthongs.)*

19. It should be known that the *saṃvṛta* (closed) [articulation] has one measure (*mātrā*), while the *vivṛta* (open) has two measures. All voiced sounds (*ghoṣavat*) are *saṃvṛta*, and all unvoiced sounds (*aghoṣa*) are traditionally held to be *vivṛta*. 20. The articulation (*karaṇa*) of the vowels (*svara*) and the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is traditionally held to be *vivṛta*. Even more open than those are the vowels *e* and *o* (*eṅ*), and likewise *ai* and *au* (*aic*). 21. The nose (*nāsikā*) is said to be the place of articulation (*sthāna*) for the *anusvāra* and the *yama*s. The *ayogavāha*s should be understood as sharing the places of articulation and the points of contact (*āśrayasthānabhāgin*) of their respective bases. 22. The resonance of the *alābu* gourd and the *vīṇā* lute follows the sounds of the dentals, the labials, and the vowels.

An *anusvāra* must always be applied after the sounds *h*, *r*, and *ḷ*, as well as before *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*. An *anusvāra* is also used before a hiatus (*vivṛti*) and at a pause (*virāma*) when two syllables follow. One should separate the two labials (*oṣṭhya*) where there are the vowels *u* and *ū*. Just as a tigress carries her cubs by her fangs without harming them—fearing both their falling and their being crushed—one should employ the phonemes in that same manner. Just as a woman from Saurāṣṭra pronounces "takram" [as *takkram*].

In this way, the *raṅga* sounds should be applied with pressure, as if upon one's own spokes. (26) When applying the color of the *raṅga*, one should not swallow the preceding syllable; one should apply a long vowel and subsequently perform the nasalization (*nāsikya*). (27) One *mātrā* is in the heart, half a *mātrā* is in the head, and likewise half a *mātrā* is in the nose; thus the *raṅga* has a duration of two *mātrās*. (28) Standing at the *utkara* from the heart, one should resonate it through the bronze vessel.

"Gentleness and the two measures" is illustrated by the example "jaghanvān. One should cause a tremor in the middle, yet both sides should remain equal; one should cause a tremor with movement, as illustrated by the example "like a charioteer. Thus should the phonemes (varṇas) be employed—neither indistinct nor suppressed. By the correct employment of phonemes, one is exalted in the world of Brahman. [31] 6. One who sings, one who recites too fast, one who shakes his head, and likewise one who merely copies the text—[these do not attain the goal].

One who does not understand the meaning, and one with a weak voice—these six are the lowest of reciters. (32) Sweetness, clarity of syllables, proper division of words, a melodious tone, steadiness, and mastery over tempo—these six are the qualities of a reciter. (33) Doubtful, timid, overly loud, indistinct, nasalized, crow-like, reaching the head, and likewise devoid of proper placement; (34) Muttered, bitten [by the teeth], hurried, rejected, too slow, faltering, and sung out [in melody]—[these are faults]. (35)

One should recite without pressing the words and syllables too hard, nor with a slurred or nasalized tone. (35) In the morning, one should recite with a steady voice resembling the roar of a tiger; at midday, with a voice reaching the throat, similar to the cry of a cakravāka bird. (36) One should know that the third session is high-pitched; that [recitation] should always be performed with the voice situated in the head, with a resonance equal to the cries of the peacock, the swan, and the cuckoo. (37) // 7 //

The vowels (*ac*) are unaspirated; the *gaṇa* (nasals) are slightly bent and unaspirated; the *śal* (fricatives) are traditionally held to be aspirated; and the remaining consonants (*hal*) are said to be fully contacted. Understand them now according to their external effort (*anupradāna*). The nasals (*ña-ma*), the cerebrals (*ṇara*), and the voiced stops (*h-jha-ṣa*) are known as nasalized (*nādinaḥ*). The semivowels (*yaṇ*) and the voiced unaspirated stops (*jaś*) have slight resonance (*īṣannāda*). But the aspirates beginning with *kha* and *pha* are breathy (*śvāsinaḥ*). One should know that the sibilants (*caraḥ*) have slight breath (*īṣacchvāsa*). This is declared to be the domain of speech (*gor dhāma*). By this [grammar] composed by Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī, the earth has been pervaded.

Chandas is the feet of the Veda, while Kalpa is said to be its hands; Jyotiṣām-ayana is its eye, and Nirukta is called its ear. Śikṣā is the nose of the Veda, and Vyākaraṇa is remembered as its mouth. Therefore, having studied it together with its auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), one is glorified in the world of Brahman. The acute accent (udātta) is declared to be on the forefinger, its head resting at the base of the index finger; the circumflex (svarita) is held between the middle and the ring finger, and the grave (anudātta) is indeed on the little finger.

43. One should know the *udātta* [accent] to be on the forefinger (*pradeśinī*), the *pracaya* on the middle finger, the *nihata* on the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*), and the *svarita* on the ring finger (*upakaniṣṭhikā*). 44. [The nine types of word-arrangements are: *antodātta*, *ādyudātta*, *udātta*, *anudātta*, *nīcasvarita*, *madhyodātta*, *svarita*, *dvyudātta*, and *tryudātta*. 45. *agniḥ*, *somaḥ*, *pra vo vīryam*, *haviṣām*, *svar bṛhaspatiḥ*, *indrābṛhaspatī*.

The word *agni* has its accent on the final syllable; *soma* has its accent on the first syllable; *pra* is accented acute (*udātta*); *va* is unaccented (*anudātta*); and *vīryam* has a low-svarita (*nīcasvarita*). (46) In oblations (*haviṣām*), there is an accent on the middle syllable; *svar* is a svarita produced at the root of the ear; and the *pracaya* (continuous) accent is said to pervade the entire mouth. (48) The blue jay utters [the vowel] for one measure (*mātrā*); the crow, however, for two measures; the peacock cries for three measures; and the mongoose for half a measure. (49) [Knowledge] obtained from a false teacher is burnt, discolored, and consumed.

There is no liberation for one through the recitation [of such a mantra], just as there is no freedom from the sin of a venomous snake. (50) The Veda (*brahman*), when clearly derived from a sacred source (*sutīrtha*), well-established, and properly transmitted within its own tradition (*svāmnāyya*), shines forth when employed by one with a beautiful voice and eloquent mouth. (51) A mantra deficient in accent (*svara*) or phoneme (*varṇa*), if incorrectly employed, does not convey its intended meaning. That verbal discharge destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [the demon Vṛtra] was destroyed due to a lapse in accent. (52) [Recitation] without syllables destroys longevity; that which is indistinct (*vikhara*) afflicts one with disease.

The unbroken [Veda] falls upon the head like a thunderbolt in the form of a weapon. (53) But he who studies it without his hands, devoid of accents and phonemes, being consumed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [verses], enters a low birth. (55) Śaṃkara gave the Śāṃkarī [grammar] to the wise son of Dakṣī; having extracted speech from all verbal forms, the Goddess [bestowed it]—such is the tradition. (56) Salutations to that Pāṇini, who, having received the collection of phonemes from Maheśvara, proclaimed the entire grammar.

57. Homage to that Pāṇini, by whom the speech of men has been cleansed with the pure waters of words, and by whom the darkness born of ignorance has been shattered. 58. Homage to that Pāṇini, by whom the eye of the world blinded by ignorance was opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge. 59. That twice-born man who, being self-restrained, should always recite here this [work] issued from the mouth of the Three-eyed One—

He becomes possessed of wealth, grain, cattle, sons, and fame, and he enjoys incomparable happiness in heaven—yes, in heaven! (60, 11). Now, as for the training: one's own [vocal effort] is high-pitched (*udātta*), the letter *ha* [is unvoiced], and among vowels, that which is unaspirated (*aspṛṣṭa*) is high-pitched; the blue jay (*cāṣa*) [is used for the *svarita* accent], and Śaṅkara [is the authority]. Thus, the eleventh [chapter]. Here ends the *Pāṇinīya-śikṣā*.

Now follows the instruction on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*). 1. Gender [is now taught]. 2. Feminine (*strī*). 3. Words ending in *ṛ*—namely *mātṛ*, *duhitṛ*, *svasṛ*, *potṛ*, *nanāndṛ*—are feminine. 4. A verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in the suffix *ū* is feminine. 5. *Aśani*, *bharaṇi*, and *araṇi* are feminine and also masculine. 6. Words ending in the suffix *min* are feminine. 7. *Vahni*, *vṛṣṇi*, and *agni* are masculine. 8. *Śroṇi*, *yoni*, and *ūrmi* are masculine and also feminine. 9. Words ending in the suffix *ktin* are feminine. 10. And those ending in *ī* are feminine. 11. And those ending in *ūṅ* and *āp* are feminine. 12. A monosyllabic word ending in *y* is feminine. 13. Numbers beginning with twenty (*viṃśati*) up to ninety-nine (*navati*) are feminine. 14. *Dundubhi* is feminine when referring to dice. 15. *Nābhi* is feminine when not referring to a Kṣatriya.

16. Both [the masculine and neuter forms] occur except when referring to a male person. 17. Words ending in the suffix *-tal* [are feminine]. 18. Words denoting earth, lightning, river, creeper, and woman [are feminine]. 19. The word *yādas* (sea-monster) is neuter. 20. The words *bhās*, *sruc*, *sraj*, *diś*, *dṛś*, *uṣṇih*, and *upānah* [are feminine]. 21. The words *sthūṇā* and *ūrṇā* are feminine, and also neuter. 22. The words *gṛha* and *śas* are neuter. 23. The words *prāvṛṣ*, *vipruṣ*, *ruṭ*, *tṛṣ*, *viṭ*, and *tviṣ* [are feminine]. 24. The words *darvī*, *vid*, *vedī*, *khani*, *śāṇī*, *aśri*, *veśī*, *kṛṣi*, *oṣadhi*, *kaṭi*, and *aṅguli* [are feminine]. 25. Likewise, the words *tithi*, *nāḍī*, *ruci*, *vīci*, *nālī*, *dhūli*, *kiṭi*, *kelī*, *chavi*, *rātri*, and so forth [are feminine].

26. *śaṣkulī*, *rājikā*, *kuṭī*, *aśani*, *varti*, *bhrukuṭi*, *truṭi*, and *valipaṅkti*; 27. *pratipad*, *āpad*, *vipat*, *saṃpat*, *śarad*, *saṃsad*, *pariṣad*, *uṣas*, *saṃvit*, *kṣut*, *punarmukha*, and *samidh*; 28. *āśis*, *dhur*, *pūr*, *gī*, and *dvār*; 29. *ap*, *manas*, *samāsikatā*, and *varṣā* may also be plural; 30. *srak*, *tvac*, *jyok*, *vāc*, *yavāgū*, *nau*, and *sphic*; 31. *tṛṣ*, *sīmā*, and *asaṃbādhā*; 32. *culli*, *veṇī*, and *svāya*; 33. *tārā*, *dhārā*, *jyotsnā*, and so forth; 34. *śalākā* is always feminine.

35. *pumān* (man) [is masculine]. 36. A word ending in the suffix *ghañ* [is masculine]. 37. And one ending in *gha*. 38. The words *bhaya* (fear), *liṅga* (mark/sign), and *bhaga* (fortune/organ) are neuter. 39. A word ending in the suffix *naṅ* [is neuter]. 40. *Yāñcā* (request/solicitation) is feminine. 41. A word ending in the suffix *ky* and designated as *ghu* [is masculine]. 42. *Iṣudhi* (quiver) is also feminine. 43. Words denoting: gods (*deva*), demons (*asura*), self (*ātman*), heaven (*svarga*), mountain (*giri*), ocean (*samudra*), nail (*nakha*), hair (*keśa*), tooth (*danta*), breast (*stana*), arm (*bhuja*), neck (*kaṇṭha*), one's own limb (*sv-aṅga*), arrow (*śara*), and mud (*paṅka*) [are masculine]. 44. *Triviṣṭapa* (heaven) and *tribhuvana* (the three worlds) are neuter. 57. *Śmaśru* (beard), *jānu* (knee), *svādu* (sweet), *aśru* (tear), *jatu* (lac), *trapu* (tin), and *tālu* (palate) are neuter. 55. *Vasu* is neuter when it signifies wealth.

56. *madgu*, *madhuśīdhu*, and *sānu* are neuter when followed by *kamaṇḍalu*. 57. Words ending in *rut* [are neuter]. 58. *dāru*, *kaseru*, *jatru*, *vastu*, and *mastu* are neuter. 59. *Saktu* is neuter as well [as masculine]. 60. From *prāc* up to *raśmi*, words ending in *a* [are neuter]. 61. Words having *ka* as their penultimate letter [are neuter]. 62. *Cibuka*, *śālūka*, *prātipadika*, *aṃśuka*, and *ulmuka* are neuter.

63. *kaṇṭaka*, *anīka*, *saraka*, *modaka*, *caṣaka*, *mastaka*, *pustaka*, *taḍāka*, *niṣka*, *śuṣkavarcaska*, *pināka*, *bhāṇḍaka*, *kaṭaka*, *śaṇḍaka*, *piṭaka*, *tālaka*, *phalaka*, *kalka*, and *pulāka* are neuter; and [words ending in] *ka*. 64. A word having *ṭa* as its penultimate letter is neuter. 65. *kirīṭa*, *mukuṭa*, *lalāṭa*, *vaṭa*, *vīṭa*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *raṭa*, and *loṣṭa* are neuter. 66. *kuṭa*, *kūṭa*, *kapaṭa*, *kavāṭa*, *karpaṭa*, *naṭa*, *nikaṭa*, *kiṭa*, *kaṭa*, and [words ending in] *ka* are neuter. 67. A word having *ṇa* as its penultimate letter is neuter. 68. *ṛṇa*, *lavaṇa*, *parṇa*, *toraṇa*, *araṇa*, and *uṣṇa* are neuter.

69. Words ending in *kārṣāpaṇa*, *svarṇa*, *suvarṇa*, *vraṇa*, *caraṇa*, *vṛṣaṇa*, *viṣāṇa*, *cūrṇa*, and *tṛṇa* are neuter; as is [the word] *napuṃsaka*. 70. A word having *tha* as its penultimate letter [is neuter]. 71. *Kāṣṭha*, *pṛṣṭha*, *siktha*, and *uktha* are neuter. 72. *Kāṣṭhā*, when meaning "direction," is feminine. 73. *Tīrtha*, *protha*, *yūtha*, and *gāthā* are also neuter. 74. A word having *na* as its penultimate letter [is neuter]. 75. *Jaghana*, *ajina*, *tuhina*, *kānana*, *vana*, *vṛjina*, *vipina*, *vetana*, *śāsana*, *sopāna*, *mithuna*, *śmaśāna*, *ratna*, *nimna*, and *cihna* are neuter.

76. The words *māna*, *yāna*, *abhidhāna*, *nalina*, *pulina*, *udyāna*, *śayana*, *āsana*, *sthāna*, *candana*, *ālāna*, *samāna*, *bhavana*, *vasana*, *saṃbhāvana*, *vibhāvana*, and *vimāna* are neuter. 77. The word *popadha* [ending in -p] is neuter. 78. The words *pāpa*, *rūpa*, *uḍupa*, *talpa*, *śilpa*, *puṣpa*, *śaṣpa*, *samīpa*, and *antarīpa* are neuter. 79. The words *śūrpa*, *kutapa*, *kuṇapa*, *dvipa*, and *viṭapa* are neuter as well. 80. The word *bhopadha* [ending in -bh] is neuter. 81. The word *talabha* is neuter; *jambha* is neuter as well. 83. The word *mopadha* [ending in -m] is neuter.

84. *rukma*, *sidhma*, *yugma*, *edhma*, *gulma*, *adhyātma*, and *kuṅkuma* are neuter. 85. *saṃgrāma*, *drāḍima*, *kusuma*, *āśrama*, *kṣema*, *kṣauma*, *homa*, and *uddāma* are neuter, and [also masculine]. 86. A word ending in *y* [is masculine]. 87. *kisalaya*, *hṛdaya*, *indriya*, and *uttarīya* are neuter. 88. *gomaya*, *kaṣāya*, *malaya*, *anvaya*, and *avyaya* are neuter, and [also masculine]. 89. A word ending in *r* [is masculine]. 90. [Continued...]

The door, the mouth, the expansion, the buttermilk, the circle, the casting, the small hole, the noise, the shore, the distance, the difficulty, the fissure, the abyss, the pit, the fear, the deep, the cruel, the variegated, the armlet, the field, the interior, the body, the cave, Mount Mandara, the cage, the old, the belly, the row, the enmity, the chowrie, the lotus, the thicket, the hollow, the cave, the hut, the crab, the crossroads, saffron, water, clothing, coolness, the thread, the machine, the constellation, the field, the friend, the wife, the umbrella, the string, the face, the eye, the lineage, the finger, the shield, the plough, the weapon, the treatise, the garment, shame, and the vessel.

The word *nakṣatra* (constellation) is neuter. (91) *Śukra* (semen) is [neuter] when it does not refer to a deity. (92) The words *cakra*, *vajra*, *andhakāra*, *sāra*, *vāra*, *pāra*, *kṣīra*, *tomara*, *śṛṅgāra*, *bhṛṅgāra*, *mandāra*, *uśīra*, *timira*, and *śiśira* are neuter, and [masculine as well]. (93) A word having *ṣ* as its penultimate letter [is neuter]. (94) The words *śirīṣa*, *rjīṣa*, *ambarīṣa*, *pīyūṣa*, *purīṣa*, *kilbiṣa*, and *kalmāṣa* are neuter. (95) The words *yūṣa*, *karīṣa*, *miṣa*, *viṣa*, and *varṣa* are neuter, and [masculine as well]. (96) A word having *s* as its penultimate letter [is neuter]. (97) The words *pāna*, *sabis*, *vasu*, and *sāhasa* are neuter.

98. *camasa*, *sarasa*, *niryāsa*, *upavāsa*, *kārpāsa*, *vāsa*, *māsa*, *kāsa*, *kāṃsa*, and *māṃsa* are neuter; [and] 99. *kaṃsa* is also [neuter] when not referring to a living being. 100. Words denoting rays of light and days [are neuter]. 101. *dīdhiti* is feminine. 102. *dina* and *ahana* are neuter. 103. Words denoting measures [of capacity] [are neuter]. 104. *droṇa* and *āḍhaka* are also neuter. 105. *svārī* and *mānikā* are feminine. 106. *dāra*, *akṣata*, *lāja*, and *asūna* are also plural [in their usage]. 107. Words for wounds (*vraṇa*), limbs (*aṅga*), and feet (*pada*) [are neuter] when preceded by *nāḍī*, *apa*, and *jana*.

108. Marut, garut, tara, and dṛtvij; 109. The sages Ṛśi, rāśi, dṛti, granthi, krimi, dhvani, balikauli, ravi, kavi, and kapimuni; 110. Dhvaja, gaja, muñja, and puñja; 111. Hasta, kunta, anta, vāta, vrāta, dūta, dhūrta, sūta, cūta, and muhūrta; 112. Ṣaṇḍa, maṇḍa, karaṇḍa, bhaṇḍa, varaṇḍa, tuṇḍa, gaṇḍa, muṇḍa, pāṣaṇḍa, and śikhaṇḍa; 113. Vaṃ, āṃ, śa, and puroḍāśa; 114. Hrada, kanda, kunda, budbuda, and śabda.

115. *ardhapathi*, *mathi*, *ubhukṣi*, *stamba*, *nitamba*, and *pūga*; 116. *pallava*, *palvala*, *kaphara*, *repha*, *kaṭāha*, *nirvyūha*, *maṭha*, *maṇi*, *taraṅga*, *turaṅga*, *gandhaskandha*, *mṛdaṅga*, *saṅga*, *samudra*, and *puṅkha*; 117. *sārathi*, *atithi*, *kukṣi*, *vasti*, *pāṇi*, and *añjali*.

118. [A compound ending in a neuter word is neuter]. 119. [Words] ending in *lyuṭ* (ana) denote the abstract state (*bhāva*); so too do those ending in the *niṣṭhā* suffixes (*kta* and *ktavatu*). 120. The secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) *tva* and *yañ* [denote the abstract state]. 122. [The suffix *yañ* is applied] after words denoting qualities such as "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*), etc., when the object (*karman*) is expressed. 123. The suffixes *yat*, *yaṭ*, *gha*, *ghañ*, *aṇ*, *vyañ*, *cha*, and *śa* [are applied] in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). 124. A *dvandva* compound is singular [when it denotes a collective]. 125. [The *dvandva* compounds] "winter and cool season" (*hemanta-śiśira*) and "day and night" (*aho-rātra*) are singular, except in the Vedic language (*abhāṣāyām*). 126. A *tatpuruṣa* compound that is not a negative (*nañ*) or a *karmadhāraya* is [neuter if its final member is feminine]. 127. [The word] *chāyā* is [neuter] when it does not mean "abundant. 128. [The word] *sabhā* is [neuter] when preceded by a word denoting a king or a non-human being. 129. [The words] *surā*, *senā*, *chāyā*, *śālā*, and *niśā* are [neuter] and also [feminine].

130. [Words ending in] *paravat* [are neuter]. 131. [The words] *apatha*, *puṇyāha*, and *napuṃsaka* [are neuter]. 132. A word beginning with a numeral followed by *rātri* [is neuter]. 133. A *dvigu* compound [ending in *rātri*] is also feminine. 134. Words ending in *is* and *us* [are neuter]. 135. The word *arcis* is also feminine. 136. The word *chadis* is exclusively feminine. 137. Words denoting mouth, eye, iron, forest, flesh, blood, bow, hole, water, plough, wealth, and food [are neuter]. 138. The words *sīra*, *artha*, and *odana* are masculine. 139. The words *vaktra*, *netra*, *araṇya*, and *gāṇḍīva* are also masculine. 140. The word *aṭavī* is feminine. 141. A word whose penultimate letter is elided [is neuter].

142. *tūla*, *upala*, *tāla*, *kusūla*, *tarala*, *kambala*, *devala*, and *vṛṣala* are masculine. 143. *śīla*, *mūla*, *maṅgala*, *sāla*, *kamala*, *tala*, *msala*, *kuṇḍala*, *palala*, *mṛṇāla*, *vāla*, *nigala*, *palāla*, *biḍāla*, *khila*, and *śūla* are masculine and [also neuter]. 144. Numerals beginning with *śata* (one hundred) are [neuter]. 145. *yātrā*, *mātrā*, *abhrastrā*, *daṃṣṭrā*, and *varatrā* are feminine only. 155. *bhṛtra*, *amitra*, *chātra*, *putra*, *mantra*, *vṛtra*, *meḍhra*, and *uṣṭra* are masculine. 156. *patra*, *pātra*, *pavitra*, *sūtra*, and *chatra* are masculine and [also neuter].

157. *balakusuma*, *śulba*, *pattana*, and *raṇa* are [masculine] designations. 158. *Padma*, *kamala*, and *utpala* are [neuter], and they are also masculine. 159. *Āhava* and *saṃgrāma* are masculine. 160. *Āji* is exclusively feminine. 161. A genus of fruits [is feminine]. 162. A genus of trees is exclusively feminine. 163. *Viyat*, *jagat*, *sakṛt*, *śakan*, *pṛṣat*, *śakṛt*, *yakṛt*, and *udaśvit*. 164. *Navanīta*, *avatāna*, *ṛta*, *amṛta*, *nimitta*, *vitta*, *citta*, *pitta*, *vrata*, *rajata*, *vṛtta*, and *palita*.

165. *Śrāddha*, *kuliśa*, *daiva*, *pīṭha*, *kuṇḍa*, *aṅka*, *aṅgada*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, *akṣi*, *asthi*, *āspada*, *ākāśa*, *kaṇva*, and *bīja* [are neuter]. 166. *Daiva* is also masculine. 167. *Dhānya*, *ājya*, *sasya*, *rūpya*, *paṇya*, *varṇya*, *dhiṣṇya*, *havya*, *kavya*, *kāvya*, *satya*, *apatya*, *mūlya*, *āśikya*, *kuḍya*, *madya*, *harmya*, *tūrya*, and *sainya* [are neuter]. 168. *Dvandva*, *barha*, *duḥkha*, *baḍiśa*, *āpiccha*, *bimba*, *kuṭumbaka*, *kavaca*, *kavara*, and *vṛndāraka* [are neuter]. 169. *Akṣa* is [neuter] when it means a sense organ.

170. [The dual ending] *au* is used for both feminine and masculine nouns. 171. [The following are masculine: *go*, *gaṇi*, *yaṣṭi*, *muṣṭi*, *pāṭali*, *vasti*, *śālmalī*, *triṭima*, *simarīci*. 172. [Also masculine: *mṛtyu*, *sīdhu*, *karkandhu*, *sindhu*, *kaṇḍu*, *reṇu*. 173. A quality-word (*guṇavacana*) ending in the vowel *u* is neuter. 174. [A word ending in a *taddhita* suffix] expressing the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) is neuter.

175. [The following are] both masculine and neuter: 176. *dhṛta*, *bhūta*, *mustaka*, *kṣvelita*, *airāvata*, *pusta*, *busta*, *lohita*; 177. *śṛṅga*, *ardha*, *nidāgha*, *udyama*, *śalya*, *dṛḍha*; 178. *vraja*, *kuñja*, *kutha*, *kūrca*, *prastha*, *darpa*, *arbha*, *ardharca*, *puccha*; 179. Words ending in *kabandha*, *oṣadhi*, and *āyudha* [are masculine]; 180. *daṇḍa*, *maṇḍa*, *khaṇḍa*, *śava*, *saindhava*, *pārśva*, *ākāśa*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *aṅkuśa*, *kuliśa*; 181. *gṛha*, *meha*, *deha*, *paṭṭa*, *paṭaha*, *aṣṭāpada*, *arbuda*, and *kakuda*.

182. The remainder [of the words] are of all genders (*avaśiṣṭaliṅga*). 183. The indeclinables (*avyaya*), as well as *kati*, *yuṣmad*, and *asmad*. 184. Numerals ending in *ṣ* or *n* are feminine (*asaṃkhyā*). 185. And those expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*) are likewise. 186. And the *kṛtya* suffixes [denote feminine action]. 187. The suffix *lyuṭ* denotes instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*). 188. The group beginning with *sarva* are pronouns (*sarvanāman*). Thus ends the *Liṅgānuśāsana* composed by the venerable sage Pāṇini.
